en: *Jaiminīya-Brāhmaṇam*.
Books 1 and 2, edited by Gerhard Ehlers, Berlin, 1996; based on the edition by Raghu Vīra and Lokesh Candra, incorporating the emendations by Bodewitz, and, in part, the Grantha manuscript VOHD Ī, 2.
No. 535, Book 3, edited by M. Kobayashi, Kyoto, 1996, based on the edition by Raghu Vīra and Lokesh Chandra.
{This version is provisional. A new edition is being prepared by G. Ehlers.} Mahābrāhmaṇa (Bar: 1–360; Ed.:
Regarding this, they say: "With what does one offer? Into what is it offered?"
One offers with the breath itself; in the breath the offering is made. Thus, when they churn the fires, they generate the vital breaths.
As long as they churn, one does not breathe at that time.
At that time, his vital breaths reside in the two kindling woods.
As he is being churned, ashes fall away;
verily, food is thereby produced for him.
"Food has been produced for me"—thus he should know that.
The smoke resounds after him;
his mind is born at that moment.
One should know this: "The mind has been born for me. Then the charcoal subsides;
it is the eye itself that is born for him.
"He should know this: 'My eye has been born.
This very coal swallows these ashes;
it creeps sideways just as a newborn infant would reach for the breast."
His ear is born at that moment;
he should know: "My ear has been born.
He shakes the grass above.
His very breath is born; one should know that "this breath of mine has been born. With the sound "bhā," it blazes up.
Speech alone is born as his wife. He should know this: "This speech has been born for me. He then brings forth these five vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Having divided them into three groups and made them the gods, he sits offering oblations into them.
Indeed, these very ones become his gods into whom he sits offering oblations. 1.1.1.1 (Ed.: 1,1)

Regarding this, when they ask, "With what does one offer? Into what is it offered?"—with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone one offers, and into the vital breath it is offered. Thus, one offers this very food into the vital breath.
This [person] is one who does not die of hunger, for he remains offering into those vital breaths while causing them to increase.
Now, this indeed is the property of a Brāhmaṇa: that which is the sacrificial oblation (havis). He places it within himself, in these immortal vital breaths (prāṇas).
Thus, being placed within his own self, it does not perish.

When the mind departs, when the breath, when the eye, when the ear, or when speech departs, it goes to these very fires. Then they cast this body of his into these very fires with the words: "From this you were born; let him be born from you, svāhā!

Thereupon he comes into being as one consisting of oblation, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of speech, consisting of the Ṛgveda, consisting of the Yajurveda, consisting of the Sāmaveda, consisting of the Brahman, consisting of gold, and immortal.
His vital breaths indeed become immortal;
he makes this body immortal. He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, attains immortality. 2. (Ed.: 1,2)
Prajāpati sat for a thousand years.
Having completed seven hundred years, he won this very victory which is his victory.

As he was ascending to the heavenly world, he said to the gods, "Do you complete these three hundred years. "So be it," they replied. Having completed those three hundred years, they won that very victory which Prajāpati had won.
All these [deities] were indeed of the same measure as Prajāpati, saying, "Ayā3m! Ayā3m!
They said, "Indeed, we have attained this through divine bodies, through immortal bodies;
men will not attain this."
"Come, let us prepare this sacrifice.
They prepared it for the duration of a year.
They said, "This is indeed great; let us prepare it completely."
They prepared that twelve-day rite.
They said, "Indeed, this is great; let us prepare it together.
They prepared that six-day *pṛṣṭhya* rite.
They said, "Let us indeed gather this great thing together.
Therefore, he is not defeated.
Indeed, this Agnihotra is invincible.
He who knows thus is certainly not defeated.
When he touches water in front, since water is truth and consecration (dīkṣā) is truth, that is his very consecration.
He offers with the eight-syllable formula: "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā!
The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables.
That indeed is the morning pressing (*prātassavana*).
With the mind, he offers the subsequent oblation with the *niṣkevalya* [śastra];
that indeed is the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*).
He eats from what has been wiped off.
That indeed is the third pressing;
for that third pressing is, as it were, licked up.
He touches water above;
that is his *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath).
When he offers these two evening oblations, it is as if he has sacrificed with all these sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) by means of these two very oblations.
Now, when he offers these two morning oblations, by means of these very two oblations, it becomes as if he has sacrificed with all these sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*).
This Agnihotra is indeed without end.
Now, one who desires cattle should offer the Agnihotra in the evening when the cattle have gathered together.
The Agnihotra is indeed the Brahman;
by means of the Brahman, he thus secures the cattle for himself.
In the morning, before they have been released;
for the Agnihotra is indeed Brahman;
by means of Brahman he thus encloses the cattle.
He thus encloses these cattle on both sides for the Brahman;
he secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Now, for one who desires heaven:
"Two oceans, unswerving, vast and wide, roll on like the footsteps upon a path.
Indeed, there are two oceans that do not move: day and night.
Those who offer their oblations at night enter the ocean that is the night;
then those who offer when the sun has risen enter the ocean that is the day.

Now, there is indeed a way of crossing over these two: it may be like a sudden leap, or by means of a bridge or a causeway—before darkness falls after sunset, and before sunrise after the break of dawn.
Moreover, these two, day and night, are indeed the dappled and the brindled;
for the day is the dappled one, and the night is the brindled one.
Those who offer oblations at night enter the dark night itself;
but those who offer oblations after sunrise enter the variegated day itself.
The escape from these two is this: before the onset of darkness when the sun has set, and before sunrise when it has clearly dawned.
Moreover, Savitṛ alone is their splendor.
Savitṛ indeed is Prajāpati;
Prajāpati is the Viśvedevas.
In Prajāpati himself, that [offering] of his becomes offered among all the gods. This Agnihotra is indeed dedicated to Prajāpati.
Now, when this [sun] shines forth in the morning, it is in this very splendor (*dyumna*) that Prajāpati brought forth creatures.
Savitṛ is indeed Prajāpati;
Prajāpati is the Viśve Devāḥ.
Thus, his offering is made in Prajāpati, that is, among the Viśve Devāḥ.
This Agnihotra is indeed sacred to all the gods (vaiśvadeva).
Moreover, it joins day and night together with such a face;
for the Agnihotra is food.
Thus he places food at the very mouth of day and night;
in this very same way, they join it again in the morning.
The Agnihotra, indeed, is food.
By thus covering the mouth of day and night with food itself, he is released from these two deaths that are day and night. That sun, indeed, when setting, shines forth in six ways.
"Vymrucat," so indeed did the men of old, the knowers of antiquity, say of him; "now, however, he has set (nyamrucat).
When he sets, he enters the Brāhmaṇa through faith, the cattle through milk, Agni through brilliance, the plants through sap, the waters through essence, and the trees through the *svadhā* offering.

When a Brāhmaṇa cleanses the Agnihotra vessels and when he sweeps around [the fire], he thereby gathers back into him that very faith with which he entered it. Then, when they milk the milk, he thereby gathers back into him that milk with which he entered the cattle. Then, when he pushes out the embers, he thereby gathers back into him that brilliance with which he entered the fire.
Now, when he illuminates it with a blade of grass, whatever sap has entered the plants, that very sap he thereby gathers into him.
Then, when he pours water upon it, whatever essence has entered the waters, that very essence he thereby gathers into him.
Then, when he places a kindling stick upon it, whatever self-power has entered the trees, that very self-power he thereby gathers into him.
Having thus prepared it, he offers it in the evening;
he dwells through that night which serves as the period for the embryo's formation.
In this very same way, having collected [the materials] again, he offers in the morning.
He brings him (Agni) into being;
as he is being born, he destroys all evil for him.
The gods were indeed born from Prajāpati;
he who knows thus is likewise born.
As great as was the world that Prajāpati conquered, so great does he conquer.
Then he reflects: "Verily, this one is collecting me limb by limb; come, let him go to old age with his limbs intact, with his body whole, and uninjured.
And so, indeed, he goes to old age with his limbs intact, with his body whole, and uninjured. Then he reflects: "Verily, this one knows me limb by limb; come, let me enter into him."

It enters into one who knows this. He who shines yonder is indeed that one hero; he is Indra, he is Prajāpati. Into him, for one who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, that [offering] becomes truly offered. 8 (Ed.: 1,8)
Whatever evil is done by day, Āditya causes that to be done; whatever [evil is done] by night, Agni does that.
The two of them said, "If we are indeed to become thus, we shall certainly not be able to sustain offspring. Come, let us both offer ourselves into one another as food.
When the sun sets, he offers himself into the fire;
whatever evil the sun commits during the day, the fire removes that from him during the night.
The fire rises after the rising sun;
thus he offers himself to the sun.
Whatever evil the fire commits during the night, the sun destroys that for him during the day.
Just as a snake might free itself from its skin, or just as one might pull a reed from its sheath, even so are they freed from all evil who, knowing this, offer the Agnihotra sacrifice.
By the very evening oblation, whatever evil he commits during the day, his fires drive that away during the night.

By the morning oblation itself, whatever evil he commits during the night, that the sun destroys for him by means of the day. Just as a snake might free itself from its slough, or as one might pull out a reed from its sheath, even so does he free himself from all evil.
Just as when gold is smelted, no trace of impurity whatsoever remains, even so, for one who knows this and offers the Agnihotra, no trace of impurity whatsoever remains. 10 (Ed.: 1,10)
Now, Nāgarī Jānaśruteya used to say: "When that sun sets, it enters Agni as its very womb.
When one offers these two evening oblations, one thereby stands upon the back of that very sun; it is just as if one were to stand with both feet firmly planted.
Now, when he offers these two morning oblations, he causes him [the sacrificer] to rise by means of them.
Just as an elephant might lift up one sitting upon its back and rise, even so this deity, having taken hold of the one who knows this and who offers the oblations, rises up.
She leads him to that world which is beyond this, where there is nothing further.
Whatever is beyond the sun, that is immortal; that he conquers. Now, what is on this side of the sun, namely day and night, those two churn it asunder, just as a whirlwind might churn it asunder.
Indeed, there are many worlds beyond the sun.
All these [worlds] become attained by him; they are conquered by him. For one who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, there is freedom of movement within all of them. 11 (Ed.:
The gods indeed contended with Death.
That which is Death is none other than Agni.
They said, "Come, let us strive to conquer him."
They said, "Let us offer an oblation of clarified butter; by that we shall seek to conquer him.
"So be it," they replied, and they offered an oblation of clarified butter.
He made it into food; it blazed up against him.
Therefore, whenever they offer an oblation of clarified butter, it blazes up against [the fire].
They said, "Let us offer an oblation of animal flesh; by that we shall seek to conquer him."
"So be it.
Having immolated the animal and taken portions of its fat, they offered the animal-oblation.
They turned that into food; it blazed up against them.
Therefore, wherever they offer the animal oblation, it indeed flares up again.
They said, "Let us offer an oblation of milk; by that we shall seek to conquer him.
"So be it," [they replied].
They offered an oblation of milk;
by that they conquered him.
Therefore, wherever they offer an oblation of milk, it becomes nothing but glowing coals.
They said, "We have indeed conquered him with food; come, let us seek to conquer him in a way that cannot be defeated.
(12) They said, "Let us offer an oblation of Soma; by means of that, let us seek to conquer him. (13)
"So be it. They sacrificed with Soma;
they offered the oblation of Soma.
By means of that, they led him forward.
Therefore, wherever they offer a Soma-oblation, there are indeed embers.
He who, knowing thus, offers both the clarified butter oblation and the animal oblation, approaches his dear abode by that act.
Now, in that he offers the oblation of milk, he conquers him by that very act.
And in that he offers the oblation of Soma, it is just as when one has conquered and then pursues the victory further.
He thus transcends these two deaths, namely day and night.
With the words, "For out-breath, thee," he places a fuel-stick on the fire; with the words, "In the in-breath I have placed immortality, svāhā! he makes an oblation.
Then he touches the *sruk* ladle: "The heart is the forward motion; the mind is the continuity; the eye is the bending; the ear is the inclining; speech is the arrival.
It has stood as an accepted, pleasing oblation for the gods. He has placed me in immortality."
"May the vital breaths enter me for the sake of further merit-making.
He indeed performs further meritorious deeds;
moreover, evil speech does not come to him in that world who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice. 14 (Ed.: 1,14)
Regarding this they say: "When a person who is living performs both what is good and what is evil, what is the distinction between those two—the ill-done and the well-done?
Indeed, whatever good a person does while living, that he attains [fully] in his vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Now, that which is the body is the evil deed.
When one who knows this departs from this world, his good deed ascends along with his vital breath (*prāṇa*), while his evil deed is left behind along with the body.
Regarding this, they say: "That is indeed difficult to understand, for when one is mortal, he must dwell together with his evil deed."
Or rather, he who turns away from this even while still living—that is well known. This, indeed, amounts to the Agnihotra itself. 15 (Ed.:
The vital breaths follow after the mind, and the self follows after speech.
When one offers the first oblation with speech and the subsequent one with the mind, one thereby separates evil deeds from good deeds.
Therefore they say: "These two oblations must not be mixed."
"For by means of these two, he turns away both evil deeds and good deeds.

When he offers the first oblation of the evening offerings with speech, he turns away from whatever evil he has done during the day by means of that [speech]. Then, when he offers the latter [oblation] with the mind, he turns away from whatever evil he has done during the night by means of that [mind].

Now, when at the morning oblations he offers the first oblation with speech, he turns away from whatever evil he has committed during the night by means of that [speech]. And when he offers the second [oblation] with the mind, he turns away from whatever evil he has committed during the day by means of that [mind]. Thus, he who, knowing this, performs the Agnihotra, goes on day after day turning away from evil-doing. (16)
There are indeed two wombs:
one is the womb of the gods, and the other is the womb of human beings.
There are indeed two worlds:
one is the world of the gods, and the other is the world of men.
That which is the human womb is indeed the world of men.
That is the generative organ of the woman;
from it offspring are born.
Therefore, one should desire a beautiful wife, thinking: "May my self be produced in a beautiful [offspring]."
Therefore, one should hold one's wife in contempt, thinking: "Lest another should be born from my womb, in my world.
Indeed, when he is about to be born, the vital breaths enter him first, and then the seed is emitted;
he then brings these vital breaths and spaces into manifestation.
Therefore, from that very same seed which exists, whatever kind [of being] one is, such a kind is born.
Now, this Āhavanīya fire is the womb of the gods, the world of the gods;
for this indeed is the womb of the gods, the world of the gods.

Therefore, if one were to offer in the *gārhapatya* fire, they would consider him to be doing what is not done. When he offers—that is, when he does what is right—he pours himself into this very womb of the gods.
Thus, his self comes into being in that sun up there.
He who knows this is indeed twofold in nature and twofold in origin; he who does not know this is indeed single in nature and single in origin. When one who knows this departs from this world... (17)
His breath departs first.
It then reports this extent to the gods: "This much good was done by him; this much evil."
Then he ascends upwards together with the smoke.
Of this very [sacrifice], the seasons are the gatekeepers.
One should announce [one's arrival] to them by means of this.

From the far-seeing one, the seasons have brought forth seed from the half-monthly libation, from the father’s source. As such, impel me into the male progenitor; let the seed of the male progenitor be poured into the mother. Being born again and again, he [is formed] by the twelfth and the thirteenth month.
"I have found that; I have found it back. O seasons, you who are immortal, lead me to him!
Thus he says. The seasons lead him to him, just as one who knows leads one who knows, and one who understands leads one who understands. So indeed do the seasons lead him.
They surpass him.
He comes upon that one who is glowing.
When he has arrived, he asks him: "Who are you?"
Whoever announces him by name or by lineage, he says to him: "This self of yours which was in me—that is yours.
When one has thus attained that self, the seasons, having fled together, drag it away while it is still grasped by its footprints. Day and night seize his world.
Therefore, he should address him with this: "Who am I? You are light.
As such, I have gone to you, the heavenly light.
For Prajāpati is indeed who.
Now, one who knows thus indeed possesses the heavenly world; for he goes to the heavenly world.
He says to him: "Whoever you are, that am I."
"Whoever I am, that you are; come!
He approaches this very essence of well-done deeds.
His sons inherit his property, and his ancestors [inherit] his meritorious actions.
He who knows this is twofold in nature and twofold in inheritance;
he who does not know this offers the Agnihotra as being single in nature and single in inheritance. 18 (Ed.:
The Agnihotra cow is indeed speech;
her calf is the mind.
For by means of the mind, one milks speech when it has been offered.
One milks the mother cow when she has been made over to her calf.
Now, this mind is indeed prior, and speech follows after it;
therefore, the mother follows after the calf as it goes on ahead.
The heart is the central pillar, the udder is the supporting beam, and the vital breath is the rope.
By means of the vital breath alone, speech and mind are bound together;
for with a rope one indeed binds both the calf and the mother.
Janaka of Videha then asked Yājñavalkya: "Do you know the Agnihotra, Yājñavalkya?
"I know it," he replied.
"In what way? [he asked].
"Regarding milk: if there were no milk, with what would one offer?
With rice and barley."
"If there were no rice and barley, with what would one offer?
"With whatever other grain there might be.
"If there were no other grain, with what would one offer?"
Regarding the phrase "with wild plants":
if there were no wild plants, with what would one offer the oblation?
With water.

"If there were no water, with what would one offer? He replied, "In that case, nothing at all would exist here; yet this [offering] is indeed offered as if it were real, in faith. He said to him, "Do you know the Agnihotra, Yājñavalkya? Homage be to you! O Venerable One, we shall give you a thousand [cows]."
Then he approached him with this song:
"What does the Agnihotrin who knows [this] do when he stays away from his home?"
"How is it that his poetry [is preserved], how is it that he is continuous with the fires? [He asked.
"If, having established the sacred fires, one then goes away on a journey, how does his [connection] remain as if he has not gone away?
He, Vājasaneya, replied:
"He who is the swiftest among beings, he, the wise one, finds it even while dwelling afar; such is his poetic power, such is his continuity through the fires.
"Mind," he said.
The mind, indeed, is the swiftest among things in the world.
"By the mind alone it remains unforsaken," so he said.
Then he approached him with a song.
"If he goes far away and then becomes negligent there,
in what [place] is that oblation of his offered which they offer for him at home? Vājasaneya said this:
"He who is awake among beings, he is the wise one; while traveling abroad, he knows that [Self].
In him is his oblation offered, even though it is offered in his house—[the thought] 'this is what they offer for him.
'It is the vital breath (prāṇa),' he said."
Breath indeed is the one that awakens among beings;
breath alone becomes his offering, whether it has been offered or not.
Therefore they say: "The *agnihotra* is breath."
For as long as one breathes with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for that long one performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice. 20 (Ed.:

The milk in the cow belongs to Rudra; when it has been let loose, it belongs to Vāyu; while being milked, to the Aśvins; when milked, to Agni and Soma; when placed on the fire, to Varuṇa; when bubbling, to the Viśve Devas; when rising, to Pūṣan; when overflowing, to Sarasvatī; when curdling, to Mitra; when removed from the heat, to Dhātṛ; when ladled out, to Bṛhaspati; when moved forward, to Savitṛ; when being carried, to Heaven and Earth; when set down, to Indra and Agni; the first oblation belongs to Agni; the second to Prajāpati; when offered, it belongs to Indra.
This Agnihotra is seventeenfold; indeed, the Vājapeya is seventeenfold.

He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, conquers both worlds: that which belongs to the one who has offered the Agnihotra and that which belongs to the one who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice.
"There are three pitfalls in the Agnihotra," Śāṇḍilya used to say;
"that which one offers when the fuel-wood is not yet aflame—that is a pitfall."
He who offends her becomes a pillar;
he who brings these two together becomes a pillar.
He offers into the blazing kindling wood while it is turned upward toward him.
He offers the subsequent oblation after having passed over [the previous one].
He who, knowing thus, performs the *agnihotra*, indeed thrives with seventeen-fold increases of prosperity for each of the seventeen thousand years.

Āruṇi Vājasaneya, Praku Vārṣṇa, Priya Jānaśruteya, Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, and Vaiyāghrapadya—these five were great Brahmans. They said, "This Janaka of Videha is instructed in the Agnihotra; he considers himself as if superior to us. Come, let us debate him on the Agnihotra.
So they went.
They said to the religious student (brahmacārin), "Teach us!
He spoke to them.

For those to whom he had spoken, he prepared separate seats, separate waters for washing, separate offerings of honey-mixture (madhuparka), separate dwellings, and fivefold honors for each of the five.
Then a fellow of theirs came to them, having shaved off his hair and beard, clipped his nails, anointed himself with ghee, and carrying a staff and sandals.
He said to them, "O Brahmins, how is it that you do not greet me?
They replied, "You have spoken over us."
Then the first among them questioned them: "O Brahmins, how is it that you, venerable sirs, perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice?
"We have indeed been out-talked," they said. "Since you, Gautama, being the first, have questioned us who are many, answer us in turn.
He said, "O Emperor, I offer the *agnihotra* as glory (*yaśas*) itself; therefore I am glory, and glory indeed shall remain with my offspring in the end.

Gautama said to him, "What is glory? Pointing to the fire, he said, "This is glory"; pointing to the sun, he said, "That is glory. "I offer this [fire] as glory into that [sun] as glory in the evening; I offer that [sun] as glory into this [fire] as glory in the morning. These two will lead me to where all desires are; these two will conquer rebirth for me."
"May I gratify the gods with this well-offered sacrifice," he praised.
Then he asked another: "Venerable sir, how do you perform the Agnihotra?
He replied, "O Emperor, I perform the Agnihotra as Truth alone. Therefore, I am Truth; therefore, for me who speaks as Truth, there is radiance."

Yājñavalkya said to him: "What is the truth? Pointing to the fire, he said, "This is the truth. Pointing to the sun, he said, "That is the truth. He [the king] said: "I am that which is the truth over there; in this truth here, I offer my evening oblation; in that truth over there, I offer my morning oblation. May these two lead me to where all desires are fulfilled; may these two deliver me from renewed death.
He praised them, saying, "May I satisfy the gods with a well-offered sacrifice."
Then he asked another: "How, venerable sir, do you perform the *agnihotra*?

Prakru Vārṣṇa replied: "O Emperor, I perform the *agnihotra* with the thought, 'The greatest and best of my possessions. Therefore, I am the possessor of the greatest and best of possessions; indeed, the greatest and best of my possessions will remain with my offspring to the very end."
He said to him: "Agniveśya, what is the most abundant and the best among riches?"

Pointing to Agni, he said: "This is the most abundant and the best of riches. Pointing to Āditya, he said: "That is the most abundant and the best of riches. [He continued: "I, being that which is the most abundant and the best of riches, offer my evening oblation in this which is the most abundant and the best of riches; I offer my morning oblation in that which is the most abundant and the best of riches. These two alone will lead me to where all desires are fulfilled; these two will conquer rebirth for me."
"May I gratify the gods with this well-offered oblation," he praised thus.
Then he asked another: "Venerable sir, how do you perform the Agnihotra sacrifice?
He replied: "O Emperor, I perform the Agnihotra sacrifice as *tejas* (splendor) alone; therefore I am *tejas*, and indeed *tejas* shall remain at the end within my offspring."

He said to him, "Kāṇḍvīya, what is that light? Pointing to the fire, he said, "This is light. Pointing to the sun, he said, "That is light. [Kāṇḍvīya replied: "I am that light; I offer this light into that light in the evening, and I offer that light into this light in the morning. These two will surely lead me to where all desires are fulfilled; these two will conquer death for me again.
"May I satisfy the gods with a well-offered sacrifice," he thus praised.
Then he asked him another question: "How, O Blessed One, do you perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice?

He replied: "O Emperor, as Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi Vaiyāghrapadya, I perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice with the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*. For that which is the *arka* is the food of the gods; the horse is the *medha*, the sacrificial essence."

He said to him, "O Vaiyāghrapadya, who is the *arka*? Who is the horse? What is the sacrifice (*medha*)? What is the sacrificial (*medhya*)? Pointing to the fire, he said, "This is the *arka*. Pointing to the sun, he said, "That is the horse; that is the sacrifice; that is the sacrificial. "Therefore," he continued, "I offer this horse—the sacrifice, the sacrificial—into that *arka* in the evening; and I offer this *arka* into that horse—the sacrifice, the sacrificial—in the morning. These two alone shall lead me to where all desires are fulfilled; these two shall overcome my repeated death for me."
Having praised him, saying, "Well-offered!", he said: "Truly, to whoever shall tell me the performance and the goal of the Agnihotra, to him I shall grant a boon.
They replied: "Indeed, we have not recited the performance and the goal of the Agnihotra; do you tell us the performance and the goal of the Agnihotra, and we shall each grant you five boons."

Pointing to Agni, he said, "This is the *iti*"; pointing to the sun, he said, "That is the *gati*. "Therefore," he said, "I offer this *iti* in the evening into that *gati*, and I offer this *iti* in the morning into that *gati*. May these two lead me to where all desires are; may these two enable me to conquer death again.
Having praised him, saying, "Well-offered!", they said, "Choose boons, whatever we may grant you.
He replied, "This itself is my boon: I shall give you five thousand [cows] each, along with a hundred horses."
These indeed are the meditations upon the Agnihotra; these are the desires.
He who knows this thus, and he for whom one knowing this thus performs the Agnihotra, attains these very desires. 25 (Ed.:
One who is establishing the sacred fires should draw them out only in the morning.
He offers twice in the evening and twice in the morning;
thus, four oblations are accomplished.
Cattle are indeed four-footed, both those that are domestic and those that are wild. It is for them that he thus provides a share and a portion.
This Agni, indeed, is death; his name is "Licking" (Rihat).
Having pacified that very [Agni] with those oblations, he conquers the earth among the worlds and Agni among the gods.

He who, knowing thus, performs the *agnihotra*, ascends to union (*sāyujya*) and co-residence (*salokatā*) with the god Agni. Having mounted the smoke as his chariot, he proceeds toward co-residence with Vāyu.
He offers for two days;
thus eight oblations are completed.
Indeed, animals—both those that are domestic and those that are wild—are eight-hoofed.
He thus distributes this [oblation] among them individually.
Vāyu is indeed death; his name is Ajira (the Swift).
Having appeased him with those oblations, he conquers the intermediate space of the worlds and the god Vāyu among the gods.

He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, attains union with the god Vāyu and residence in the same world as him. 26 Having mounted a chariot made of wind, he then proceeds toward residence in the same world as Āditya. 27–28 (Ed.: 1,27–28) 1.1 (Ed.: 1,29)
He offers for three days.
Twelve oblations are completed;
twelve months are a year.
The year, indeed, is all this.

Whatever he eats here, whatever he drinks, and whatever he gives away to anyone whatsoever—all that becomes for him as if not eaten; for as long as he lives, he remains one who observes the vow of fasting.
This sun, when it sets, is truly death; such is its name.
Having pacified that very [fire] with those oblations, he conquers the world of heaven among the worlds and the god Āditya among the gods.
He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, ascends to union with and the same world as the god Āditya.
Having mounted the chariot that is the rays themselves, he proceeds toward the same world as the moon.
He offers for four days. Sixteen oblations are thus completed.
The Brahman indeed consists of sixteen parts.
The gods consist of sixteen parts.
This whole [universe] consists of sixteen parts. Whatever foul or evil deed one performs here, by that alone it is [exhausted] from a single part.
Just as gold, when processed while being heated, attains the state of pure gold, even so, having cast off impurity and evil upon his enemies and rivals, he proceeds toward the heavenly world.
This, indeed, is the hare-marked one (the moon), which is that which is within the moon;
for it rules over all this.
This indeed is Yama, who is within the moon;
for he restrains all this.
This indeed is Death, namely Yama, whose name is "the eater."
Having pacified that very [fire] with those oblations, he conquers the vigor of the worlds and [attains] Yama, the god of the gods.
He who, knowing thus, performs the Agnihotra, ascends to union with and residence in the same world as the god Yama.
Then, having ascended his own golden ship, he proceeds toward the same world as Prajāpati.
He offers for five days;
thus twenty oblations are completed.
Prajāpati consists of twenty-one parts.
This Prajāpati is indeed death; his name is "the Abundant One" (prabhūman).
Having pacified him with those oblations, one conquers the worlds of the sky and the god Prajāpati among the gods.
He who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, ascends to union with and residence in the same world as the god Prajāpati (1,29).
Now, that which is indeed called *nabhas* is truly *abhīr* (fearless).
For having reached it, one does not fear anything whatsoever. (1,30)
Therefore, that is the *nabhas*.
He offers for six days;
thus, twenty-four oblations are completed.
The Gāyatrī indeed consists of twenty-four syllables;
there are twenty-four Vasu deities;
they are dependent upon the Gāyatrī.
From them—the Gāyatrī from the Vasu gods—she milks out desires and cherished objects with each single syllable.
Thus, for one who offers oblations, she milks them.
Indeed, he wins the Gāyatrī among the meters and the Vasus among the gods.
He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, attains union with and residence in the same world as the Vasu gods.
(28) He offers for seven days. (29–30)
They amount to twenty-eight oblations.
The *uṣṇih* consists of twenty-eight syllables;
there are twenty-eight gods of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
They are dependent upon the *uṣṇih* meter.
From them—the *uṣṇih*, the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, and the gods—it milks out all desires and cherished objects, syllable by syllable. Thus it milks out for him who offers oblations.
Verily, he conquers the *uṣṇih* among the meters and the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases among the gods.
He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, ascends to union with and residence in the same world as the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, the gods of the gods.
He offers for eight days.
They amount to thirty-two oblations.
The anuṣṭubh indeed consists of thirty-two syllables,
and there are thirty-two Viśvedevas.
They are dependent upon the *anuṣṭubh*.
From them—the *anuṣṭubh*—for the sake of the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*), she milks out desires and specific wishes, syllable by syllable.
Thus, for him who offers oblations, she milks it out.
He who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, wins the Anuṣṭubh among the meters and attains union with and residence in the same world as Viśvān Devāḥ, the All-Gods, among the gods.
He offers for nine days.
They amount to thirty-six oblations.
The *bṛhatī* indeed consists of thirty-six syllables.
There are thirty-six Sādhyas, the gods. They are dependent upon the Bṛhatī.
From those Sādhyas, the gods, the Bṛhatī milks out their desires and longings syllable by syllable.
In this way, for one who offers the Agnihotra, it yields milk.
He indeed conquers the *bṛhatī* among the meters and the Sādhyas among the gods.
He attains union with and residence in the same world as the Sādhyas among the gods, he who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra.
He offers for ten days.
They amount to forty oblations.
The *paṅkti* meter indeed consists of forty syllables.
The forty Maruts are the gods; they are dependent upon the *paṅkti* [meter]. From them—the *paṅkti* for the Marut gods—it milks out all desires and longings, one by one syllable.
Thus, for one who offers it in this manner, [the fire] yields milk.

He indeed wins the *paṅkti* among the meters; he ascends to union with and co-residence in the same world as the Maruts, the gods of the gods, he who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra. 30 (Ed.: 1,34)
He offers for eleven days;
thus, they amount to forty-four oblations.
The *triṣṭubh* indeed consists of forty-four syllables;
there are forty-four Rudras, the gods;
they are dependent upon the *triṣṭubh*.
From them—the Triṣṭubh meter and the Rudra deities—he milks out all desires and cherished objects by means of each individual syllable.
Thus, for him who offers oblations, she milks;
indeed, he wins the Triṣṭubh among meters and the Rudras among the gods.
He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, ascends to union with and residence in the same world as the Rudra deities. 31 (Ed.:
1,36) |p1 He offers for twelve days.
They amount to forty-eight oblations.
The Jagatī indeed consists of forty-eight syllables;
there are forty-eight Āditya gods.
They are dependent upon the *jagatī*.
From them—the *jagatī* and the Āditya gods—it milks out desires and cherished objects one syllable at a time;
thus it milks them out for him who offers oblations.
He indeed conquers the Jagatī among the meters and the Ādityas among the gods. He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, attains union with and residence in the same world as the Ādityas, the gods.
In this state, indeed, the Brahman does not shine forth—being without a protector, without a refuge, and without a superior.
Then, for twelve days, that Brahman performed the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Having offered it for twelve days, he brought forth renown, glory, progeny, and immortality.
Having offered that Agnihotra for twelve days as an oblation to Brahman and having transferred it to Prajāpati, it ascended to the heavenly world.
Prajāpati indeed performed that Agnihotra for twelve days;
having offered it for those twelve days, he extracted from it wisdom, intelligence, reflection, and austerity.
Prajāpati, having performed that Agnihotra for twelve days and having withdrawn it from the gods and the seers, ascended to the heavenly world itself.
Then the gods and the seers performed that Agnihotra for twelve days;
having sacrificed for twelve days and having withdrawn it from the men of old, they too ascended to the heavenly world itself.
Now, indeed, that Agnihotra the Brahman offered for twelve days; Prajāpati [offered it] for twelve days; the gods and the seers [offered it] for twelve days.
Having offered it for twelve days each, they obtained their desires and all their wishes. What need is there to mention him who should offer it as long as he lives? 33 (Ed.: 1,37)
Now, one should indeed offer that Agnihotra for three days with milk alone;
for that is the form of the Agniṣṭoma.
For one who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, his sacrifice becomes as that of the Agniṣṭoma.
One should indeed offer that Agnihotra with curds for three days;
that is the form of the Vājapeya.
For one who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, it becomes as if he has sacrificed with the Vājapeya.
One should indeed offer that Agnihotra for three days with clarified butter;
that is the form of the Aśvamedha.
For one who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, it becomes as if he has sacrificed with the Aśvamedha.
One should indeed offer that Agnihotra with water for three days;
that is the form of the Puruṣamedha.
He who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, has indeed performed the Puruṣamedha sacrifice.

The sacrificer himself, wearing unwashed garments, should offer the Agnihotra while the fires are kept perpetually burning and he does not go abroad. On the thirteenth night, having sacrificed with Soma or with an animal victim, he may discontinue [the perpetual fire].
Just as one would acquire wealth by making a sacrifice with a final conclusion (*sāvasāna*), so is that [act].
Indeed, those ancient men performed that *agnihotra* for exactly twelve days.

Therefore, among them, the milch-cow yields milk, the ox draws [the cart], the horse—appointed for the installation (*ādhāna*)—draws, the mule stands nearby, and the elephant, with its girth-band tightened, draws. 34 (Ed.: 1,38)
Agnihotra-vidhi |c35 (Ed.: 1,39) |p1:
"Bring forward the Agnihotra cow," he says.

When [the milk] has been poured in, [he recites]: "Heaven and Earth have been approached; the Rudras receive the milk of the Vasus; you are the makers of beings; the danger from enemies has been driven out. With these words, he removes the embers.

Then he places [the vessel] over the fire, saying: "Thou art placed for Vaiśvānara; may Agni not burn away thy brilliance; for the sake of truth, thee! Then he illuminates it, saying: "May light be united with light."
Then he pours water back [into the fire] with the formula: "With that essence of yours which has entered into the waters, may you become united.
By this, he brings together again whatever of his the quarters had swallowed there; [he does so] thinking, "The *rakṣas* is excluded, the enemies are excluded. He carries fire around it three times.

Then he takes down [the potsherds] with the formula: "Support the sky! Support the mid-region! Support the earth! Support my offspring and cattle as I offer! "You are the makers of beings; the danger from enemies has been repelled," with these words he pushes back the embers. Then, taking both the *sruva* ladle and the *sruk* spoon, he heats them over the fire with the formula: "The *rakṣas* is burnt up; the enemies are burnt up."
Then he cleanses the *sruk* spoon: "In harmony with the gods who come in the evening," at evening;
"in harmony with the gods who come in the morning," in the morning;
"thee, golden-hued, made of gold, with a golden shaft, with immortal leaves, the stream of sacrifices."
He indeed becomes the stream of sacrifices. Then he says, "I shall lead [the fire] forward. He should say, "Om! May I [lead] myself toward the heavenly world. 35 (Ed.: 1,39)
That first ladle he draws up is indeed the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
He for whomsoever, knowing thus, draws up the first ladle, has effectively sacrificed by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Now, that second *sruva* ladle which he raises is indeed the form of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices.
He for whom, knowing this, the second *sruva* is raised, has indeed sacrificed with the *Cāturmāsya* offerings.
Then, that third *sruva* ladle which he raises is the form of the *iṣṭi* and *paśubandha* sacrifices.
The sacrifice has indeed been performed with the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices by him who, knowing this, draws the third ladleful.
Now, as for the fourth ladleful which he draws, that is the form of the Tryambaka offerings, the Vājapeya, and the Aśvamedha.
The sacrifice has indeed been performed with the Tryambaka offerings, the Vājapeya, and the Aśvamedha by him who, knowing this, draws the fourth ladleful.
Then, having taken a fuel-stick (*samidh*), he goes forward toward the east.

[He thinks: "The man is the fuel; him I kindle with food. By the splendor of food, lead me to the heavenly world, to that which is the beloved abode of the gods and the seers (*ṛṣi*); there, lead this Agnihotra of mine. He sets it down silently.
Then he places the fuel-stick upon the fire, saying: "I place thee, the golden ladder, the means of ascent to the heavenly world—svāhā!"
Then he offers. With the first offering he attains the gods;
then with the second offering he attains the seers. 36 (Ed.: 1,40)
Then he wipes it.
By that which he wipes first, he gratifies the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases say to him: "May your faith not depart; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world.
Then, when he wipes a second time, he thereby gratifies the cups and the ancestors.
The cups and the ancestors say to him: "May your faith not depart; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world."

Now, as for why he eats twice with his finger: when he eats the first time, by that the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*) are satisfied. Those two, the out-breath and the in-breath, say to him: "May your faith not depart; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world.
Then, when he eats the second time, by that the up-breath (*udāna*) and the in-breath (*apāna*) are satisfied.
The out-breath (udāna) and the in-breath (apāna) said to him: "May faith not depart from you; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world.
Then, in that he eats with the offering-ladle (sruk), thereby he gratifies the common breath (samāna), the circulating breath (vyāna), and the embryos.
The common breath, the circulating breath, and the embryos said to him: "May faith not depart from you; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world."
Now, when he eats from the ladle, by that he gratifies the divine folk.
Those divine folk say to him: "May your faith not depart; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world.
Then, when he pours out the rinsing water of the ladle, by that he gratifies the birds.
The birds said to him: "May your faith not depart; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world.
Then, when he cleanses those offering-spoons and pours out the water toward the north, he thereby gratifies the seers (ṛṣis).
The seers said to him: "May your faith not depart; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world."
Now, when he pours out the rinsing water from the pot, he thereby gratifies the serpent-folk.
Those serpent-folk say to him: "May your faith not depart; be satisfied with all desires and attain the heavenly world.
Then, having walked around either from behind or from the front, he sits down to the south of the fires; thus becoming Prajāpati himself, he sits thinking, "Who am I? Who belongs to me? (37)
Bhṛgu Vāruṇi was indeed a learned man. He thought himself superior even to his father, superior to the gods, and superior to other learned Brāhmaṇas.
Varuṇa reflected: "My son indeed does not understand anything; come now, I shall instruct him.
He seized his vital breaths, and he (the son) became exhausted.
Exhausted, he departed for the world beyond.
He arrived in that world;
a man, having torn another man apart, then devoured him.
He said, "Alas! This has come to be; what indeed is this?
They said to him, "Ask Varuṇa, your father; he will explain this to you. He went for a second time.
A man indeed devoured a man who was crying out.
He said, "Alas! What has happened here? What is this?
They said to him, "Ask Varuṇa, your father; he will explain this to you."
A third time he came.
A man indeed swallowed another man who remained silent and did not speak.
He said, "Alas, this has come to pass! What indeed is this?"
They said to him, "Ask your father Varuṇa; he will explain this to you.
He went for the fourth time.
Two women were guarding a great treasure.
He said, "Alas, this has come into being! What indeed is this?
They said to him, "Ask your father Varuṇa; he will explain this to you.
So he went to the fifth [generation].
A stream of blood and a stream of clarified butter flowed side by side.
A naked man, bearing a club, guarded that which was the stream of blood.
Then, as for the stream of clarified butter, golden men with golden chalices offered all objects of desire from it.
He said, "Alas, this has come to be! What indeed is this?
They said to him, "Ask Varuṇa your father; he will explain this to you.
He went to him for the sixth time.
There were five rivers, lotus-pools with white lotuses, flowing with honeyed water.
In them there was dancing and singing, the sound of lutes, throngs of Apsarases, a fragrant scent, and a great noise.
He said: "Ah, this has come into being! What indeed is this?"
They said to him, "Ask your father Varuṇa; he will explain this to you.
He then turned back from that very place.
He went to Varuṇa. Varuṇa said to him, "Have you come, my son? "I have come," he replied.
"Did you not see it, father? "I did not see it, father. "What, father?"
"A man indeed cuts down a man, and then he eats him," [the other] said.
"Om," he replied.

"Those who, while performing the Agnihotra in this world, cut down trees and place them [on the fire] without knowing this—those very trees, having assumed the form of men in yonder world, eat them in return."
"What is the expiation for that?
"That very fuel-stick which he places upon the fire is its expiation; by it he is released from that.
"What is the second?"
"A man indeed eats a man who is crying out in pain," he said.
"Yes," he replied.
"Those who, in this world, cook animals for those performing the *agnihotra* who do not know this—those very animals, having assumed human form, eat them in the other world."
"What is the expiation for that?
"The very first oblation which one offers with speech—that is its expiation; by it one is released from that.
"What is the third?"
"A man indeed eats a man who remains silent and does not speak," [he said].
"Yes," he replied.

"Those who, in this world, offer the *agnihotra* without knowing this, and cook rice and barley while remaining silent and not speaking—those very rice and barley grains, having taken on the form of a man, eat them back in that other world."
"What is the expiation for that?
"In that he offers the subsequent oblation with the mind—that is its expiation; by that he is released from it.
"And what is the fourth?"
"Two women guarded great wealth," he said. "Yes," he replied.
"They were faith and lack of faith."

Or, those in this world who, not knowing thus, offer the *agnihotra* without faith—whatever they offer goes to lack of faith (*aśraddhā*), and whatever they offer with faith goes to faith (*śraddhā*).
"What is the expiation for that?
"When he eats twice from it with his finger, that is its expiation; by that, he is released from it. (39)
"What is the fifth? [They replied:
"A stream of blood and a stream of ghee flowing side by side."
That which had become a stream of blood was guarded by a naked black man armed with a club;
but as for the stream of clarified butter, golden men poured out all desires from golden chalices.
"Om," he said.
Furthermore, those who cause the blood of a Brāhmaṇa who performs the Agnihotra in this world but does not know this [teaching] to flow—that is each of those streams of blood.
Now, as for that black, naked man with a club who protected her—it was Anger; that indeed was his food.
"What is the atonement for him? [he asked].
In that he eats [the remnant] with the offering-ladle (*sruk*), that is his expiation; by means of it, he is released from that.
Now, when he cleanses this ladle and pours out the water toward the north, that is a stream of ghee (*ghṛtakulyā*). Of that stream, golden men, with golden bowls, pour forth all desires.
"What is the sixth?
"The five rivers—lotus ponds filled with white lotuses—that flow with honeyed water.
In them there was dancing, singing, the sound of lutes, throngs of *apsarases*, a fragrant scent, and a great roar."
"Om," he said.
"These worlds have become mine alone. [The other asked:
"By what means are they to be conquered?"
"By this very [mixture] consisting of five portions, having been raised five times," he said. "Indeed, there is truly no room for the conquest of the worlds other than through the Agnihotra.
Today itself shall be the fast-day (upavasatha) for my establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya)."
They did for him accordingly.

He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra—him the trees do not devour in yonder world after having assumed human form; neither do cattle, nor rice and barley; neither does his merit from sacrifice and charitable works go to ruin, nor does his faith and lack of faith perish; he secures for himself a stream of blood and a stream of clarified butter.
This indeed is Agni Vaiśvānara, who shines yonder. Night is his fuel; day is his light; the rays are his smoke; the stars are his sparks; and the moon is his embers.
Into this very Agni Vaiśvānara, day after day, the gods offer the immortal waters.
When that oblation has been offered, King Soma comes into being.
The fire Vaiśvānara is indeed the thunder;
its fuel is the sky, its light is the lightning, its smoke is the clouds, its sparks are the hailstones, and its embers are the thunderbolt.
Into this very Vaiśvānara fire, day after day, the gods offer King Soma.
From that oblation, when it has been offered, rain comes into being.
Earth itself is the Vaiśvānara fire.
The intermediate space is its fuel; fire is its flame; wind is its smoke; rays are its sparks; and the quarters are its embers.
Into this very Vaiśvānara fire, the gods offer rain day after day.
From that oblation, when offered, food comes into being.
The person (*puruṣa*) indeed is the Vaiśvānara fire.

His speech is the kindling wood, his sight is the light, his breath is the smoke, his mind is the sparks, and his hearing is the embers. Into this very Vaiśvānara fire, the gods offer food day after day.
From that oblation, when it has been offered, semen comes into being.
Woman indeed is the Agni Vaiśvānara;
her lap is the fuel, her womb the flame, desire the smoke, sexual pleasure the sparks, and touch the embers.
Into this very Vaiśvānara fire, the gods offer semen day after day. From that oblation, once it has been offered, a person comes into being.
Thus, in this fifth creation, the person is born from the gods.
In the fifth emission, the divine waters speak with the voice of a man: "Just as he departs for that world...
Of him, Agni himself is Vaiśvānara.
In that fire, the plants and the trees are the kindling; light itself is the light; smoke itself is the smoke; sparks themselves are the sparks; and embers themselves are the embers.
Into this very Vaiśvānara fire, day after day, the gods offer the person.
From that oblation once offered, the person comes into being in yonder world.
That world of his becomes subject to rising again.
Of this very god, day and night, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the year are the guardians—he who shines yonder.
Day and night move about.
One of the harter-deities, whose hand holds a club, approaches him with a rein and asks, "Who are you, O man?
Would he, being ignorant, proceed to perform the Pravargya?
Indeed, [the deity] strikes at him.
When he has been overcome, his good deeds perish in three parts.
He takes up one third;
one third passes away into the quarters.
With the third [verse], he descends to this world. He rejoices in whatever world of his has been won through giving.
But from that point on, death indeed reaches him at the end.
For him who knows thus, there is no more death by defeat.
When he becomes afflicted with illness, he should say, at a place where the ground is level and well-prepared: "Churn the fires for me here!
For he is capable of becoming free from disease.
But if that were not so, then when he has departed from this world, they should take hold of him.
They should carry the two fires placed in separate vessels; they should take a firebrand from the *anvāhāryapacana* fire.
They should take the sacrificial implements, clarified butter, water, wood for the funeral pyre, a cow to be slaughtered in his honor (*anustaraṇī*), a razor, and nail-clippers.
They go to where there is level, good ground that is clear;
there they distribute his sacred fires.
Then, having dug a pit in this direction, they shave off his hair and beard.
Having shaved off his hair and beard, they clip his nails.
Having clipped his nails, they remove his intestines.
Having removed the intestines, they make it free of excrement.
Having made it free of excrement, they fill the excrement into the pit with earth. In this way, they conceal his evil.
Having washed the intestines and placed them back [in their positions], they bring him [the fire] forward.

Having set it down between the fires, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya, purified it, and taken four portions, he goes to the Āhavanīya; when it is provided with fuel-sticks and [the sacrificer] has taken hold of him, he offers:

“This one indeed is from you; you are this one. This is your womb; you are the womb of this one. O Jātavedas, father who creates the world for the son, lead him indeed to the world of those who have performed good deeds. From this one you were born; let this one be born from you, svāhā!”

From that, he comes into being as one consisting of oblations, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of speech, consisting of the *Ṛgveda*, consisting of the *Yajurveda*, consisting of the *Sāmaveda*, consisting of the *Brahman*, consisting of gold, and immortal.

Upon it they place him. He should place the two *sruva* ladles in his nostrils; the *juhū* in his right hand, the *upabhṛt* in his left; the *dhruvā* on his chest; the *agnihotra-havaṇī* in his mouth; the *camasa* cup on his head; the *iḍopahavana* vessel in his ears; the two *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessels in his ears; the *pātrī* for collecting remnants in his belly; the *dṛṣad* and *upala* grinding stones in his testicles; the *śamyā* peg in his penis; the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) on his lap; the wooden sword (*sphya*) along his spine; the two pestles and the two winnowing baskets on his sides;
and the mortar in his feet. They place the remaining sacrificial implements upon him.
They cast the earthen vessels into the water; they indeed give away the iron ones.
Then they fill it up with clarified butter;
they pour clarified butter into the sacrificial vessels. 44 (Ed.: 1,48)
Then they bring this cow to be immolated as a companion.
Having sprinkled it and led it around three times counter-clockwise, he should strike it with the blunt side [of the axe].
Some lead [the victim] around clockwise;
however, one should not do so.
Having extracted its omentum, they wrap it around the head.
The kidneys are in the hands, the heart in the chest, and the arms in the forearms.
They distribute the other limbs according to their respective parts.
Then they cover him with a skin, saying: "May you prosper with your own body."
Having spread [the grass], they set it on fire. He should act in such a way that the Āhavanīya fire reaches him first;
thus the world of the gods comes to meet him.
Then, as with the Anvāhāryapacana fire, the world of the ancestors comes back to him. Then, as with the Gārhapatya fire, he becomes firmly established in this world through offspring and cattle.
When it is kindled, its smoke alone shakes off his body.
Because he shakes (dhunoti), he is therefore called Dhuna. Indeed, this one is named Dhuna;
they call him "smoke" (dhūma) cryptically, for it is by means of a cryptic designation.

For the gods, it is as if they prefer what is out of sight. From smoke, he indeed goes to the night; from the night, to the day; from the day, to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, to the month.
There, in that month, his body and his breath come together.

One of the Haris, who has a club in his hand, approaches him with a rein and asks, "Who are you, O man? (45). To him he should reply: (46). He should say: "I am a Brahmin. "From what lineage? "From the lineage of the Brahmins. "What is your name? "My name is ‘The Truth’. (47). If he says, "I do not know," he should strike him with the club. If he knows, he should answer. If he does not answer, he should strike him with the club. If he answers, he should release him. (48). Then he should say, "I am a Brahmin. "From what lineage? "From the lineage of the Brahmins. "From the far-seeing one, the seasons have brought the seed, half-monthly, from the pressed juice that honors the fathers.
When they offer yonder King Soma who is "far-seeing," that is what is meant by this.
"Send me forth among men as a doer."
For they impel him toward this agent who is male;
"He was poured into the mother by the male agent," for they pour him into the mother.
Being born again and again, he [the year] consists of twelve months plus a thirteenth;
that which shines yonder is this thirteenth.

"I have found him, I have truly found him! O mortals, bring that immortal one here—by means of the father who is the thirteenth with the twelve, by that mother, by that faith, by that food, and by that truth! Day is my father, night is my mother; I am the Truth! O mortals, bring that immortal one here! Thus he says.
The seasons bring him to be taken away.
Just as one who knows brings one who knows, and one who understands brings one who understands, so do the seasons bring him. They indeed lead him away.
He who knows this is no mere human;
indeed, he who knows this is one of the gods.
His fathers and grandfathers, swift as thought, come back to him, saying: "What have you brought for us from there?"
He should reply to them: "Whatever merit I have performed, that is yours.
His sons inherit his estate; his ancestors inherit his good deeds, and those who hate him inherit his evil deeds.
Having thus divided this [self] into three parts, he attains the same world as that one who shines yonder. 46 (Ed.: 1,50)
Those who offer the Agnihotra indeed enter upon a long sacrificial session (*sattra*);
this sacrificial session indeed lasts until old age.
For one is indeed released from this [bond] either by old age or by death.

Regarding this they say: "If, while this performer of a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattrin*) is offering the *agnihotra*, his fires should become separated while he is on a journey, or if they should become mixed up, what rite is there to be performed? What is the expiation?
A wheel is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
The thunderbolt indeed passes through his fires when either a yoked animal passes between them or they move together.
He should indeed perform an expiation, even by means of an *iṣṭi* sacrifice;
however, one should not know it thus.
Verily, he who establishes the sacred fires extends these worlds.

Of him, this very world becomes the *gārhapatya* fire, the intermediate space becomes the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and yonder world becomes the *āhavanīya* fire. Indeed, among these worlds, birds move at will, both in proper order and out of order.
He should know: "Even if [wild animals] pass between my fires within the village, there is no affliction for me, nor is there any harm whatsoever.
However, there are three domestic animals that are disliked: the wild boar, the sheep, and the dog.
If any one of these should pass between [the fires], what is the ritual act to be performed there? What is the expiation? (47)
Now, some indeed proceed from the Gārhapatya fire up to the Āhavanīya fire while scattering a handful of loose soil, reciting this verse: "Viṣṇu strode through this [world].
But one should not do so.
If someone were to say there, "He has indeed seized the mouth of the sacrificer; soon he will seize the mouths of his enemies and will block the eldest son," it would surely happen exactly so.
One should act in this very way:
taking either a water-pot or a water-jar, one should go from the Gārhapatya fire to the Āhavanīya fire, pouring out water while reciting this very verse: "Over this Viṣṇu strode."
The *ṛc* is indeed the purifier of the gods; these waters are the purifier of the gods. Therefore, whatever in this sacrifice remains unpacified or impure, water is the pacifier of all that.
With water they thus appease it.

Regarding this, they say: "If, while this performer of a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattrin*) is offering the *agnihotra*, the *agnihotra* milk being milked should spill, what is the ritual action to be performed there? What is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*)?"
Whatever remains there in the pot, with that he should offer.
If, however, the pot should be turned upside down or should break, what rite is to be performed there, and what is the expiation?
Having touched it with the expiation for spilling—saying, "It has not been spilled; it has been placed"—he should then offer with whatever else he may find.
When it indeed spills, then it is poured out. Milk is indeed seed, and this earth is the womb. Thus, he establishes that seed in the womb.
The seed that is spilled from him is immediately procreated by one who knows thus. Indeed, from yonder the rain-cloud pours down; hereupon the plants and trees are born.
From man the seed is spilled; from cattle [it is spilled].
From that, all this was produced. He should know: "The gods have come to me; my progeny has increased; I shall become better. And so indeed it shall be.
Moreover, wherever that [semen] has spilled, there he should pour out either a vessel of water or a water-pitcher with these *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Svaḥ!"
These indeed are the *vyāhṛtis*, the expiations for all [faults].
Thus, by means of this entire [set], he performs the expiation. 49 (Ed.:
Then, having collected these potsherds, he should scatter them where the ashes of the Āhavanīya fire have been removed.
This indeed is the ritual act in this case.
Now, however, they say: "If [the oblation] should spill from that which has been carried forward toward the east, what is the ritual act there? What is the expiation?"
Whatever may remain in the *sruva* ladle there, with that he should offer.
If, however, the *sruva* should be turned downward or should break, what rite is to be performed there, and what is the expiation?
The touching [of the vessel] has been explained for that case.
Now, some indeed go back from that very point and pour [the milk] up again.
One should not do it in that way.
For if someone were to say there, "Since he has turned back that which he intended to perform with this Agnihotra, therefore this of his will not be conducive to heaven," it would surely be so.
One should act exactly in this manner.
Wherever [the oblation] might spill, there he should sit down.
Then they should bring a cooking pot for it, and having cleansed both the dipping-spoon and the offering-spoon;
This means: "I shall indeed lead this [victim] up for him. Then, having led it up as it has been led, and having taken a fuel-stick, he should go forward toward the east.
Just as one would rise up and cook enemies, even so, having struck away non-prosperity and evil, he reaches the oblation.
Now, some indeed do not accept this, saying:
"The Agnihotra of one whose offering they perform with the remains of the Agnihotra is as if unoffered, for that [remnant] is exhausted. One should not know it thus.
When this [milk] becomes free from weariness (*ayātayāma*), they then perform the curdling of its oblation.

Regarding this, they say: "If, while a long-term sacrificer is offering the *agnihotra*, the milk being milked for the *agnihotra* should become impure (*amedhya*), what is the ritual action to be performed there? What is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*)?"
Regarding this, some indeed think that it must certainly be offered, saying, "The gods do not feel revulsion toward anything.
One should not know it thus.
A man, indeed, might feel revulsion; the gods, however, feel no revulsion.
One should act in this very manner:
having drawn out some hot ashes from the *gārhapatya* fire, one should pour it into that [ash] silently;
thus it is neither offered nor unoffered.
One should moisten it with water;
by means of water alone one obtains it.
Now, if one should find something else, one should offer that.
Now, moreover, they say: "If the milk should become impure, what rite is there to be performed? What is the expiation?
One should push back those very embers upon which one was about to place it over the fire, and into those very embers one should pour it silently.
That [milk] is neither offered as a sacrifice nor not offered.
One should cause it to flow out with water;
by means of water alone one obtains it.
Now, if one should find anything else, one should offer that.
Now, moreover, they say: "If that which has been placed on the fire should become impure, what rite is to be performed there? What is the expiation?
One should push back those very embers upon which it was placed and pour it silently back onto them.
That is neither offered nor unoffered.
In that he pours it out among them, by that it is offered; and in that he follows it along with them, by that it is not offered. He should pour water after it;
verily, by means of water, he attains it.
Now, if he should find something else, he should offer with that.
Furthermore, they say: 51 (Ed.:
If that which has been carried forward should happen to fall upon something impure, what rite should be performed there, and what is the expiation?
Regarding this, some indeed think that it must certainly be offered, saying, "This is as if dead; an omission of the offering is not appropriate for it.
Then others, having sprinkled it with water, pour it away.
But one should not do it in that way.
For if someone were to say there, "This Agnihotra has indeed been poured away; this sacrificer will be poured away," it would surely happen exactly so.
One should do it in this manner alone.

Having placed a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire itself and having drawn out some hot ashes from the Āhavanīya, he should pour it silently into those ashes. That is neither an oblation nor a non-oblation. He should follow it by pouring water over it.
Verily, he obtains it by means of water.
Now, if he should find anything else, with that he should offer.
Furthermore, they say: "If it should rain, what rite is there to be performed? What is the expiation?"
He should know: "May my semen not go upward; may my procreation increase; may I become better. And so it shall indeed be.
Now, moreover, they say: "If, when the first oblation has been offered, the embers should follow after, where should he offer the second?
He should place a piece of wood that is nearby there and offer upon it.
For fire is indeed in wood.
If it should not remain in that [wood], one should offer gold into it;
for gold is indeed the seed of Agni.
He who is the father is indeed the son;
therefore, one should offer oblations into gold.
Furthermore, they say: 52. (Ed.: 1,56)
If the sacrificer should die when the oblation has been placed on the fire, what rite should be performed there and what is the expiation?
One should cause it to overflow by adding fuel around it.
This indeed is the ritual procedure here;
moreover, this very [rite] is the expiation for all *haviryajña* sacrifices.
Furthermore, they say: "If the sacrificer should die when the fire has been carried forward (*uddruta*), what is the ritual procedure there? What is the expiation?"
If that which was previously prescribed as the fourfold-drawn portion should have been assigned, one should pour it out right there.
This indeed is the ritual action in this case.
Furthermore, they say: "If the sacrificer should die after the first oblation has been offered, what is the ritual action there? What is the expiation?"
Regarding this, some indeed think that it must certainly be offered, saying, "The Agnihotra of one for whom the first offering has been made becomes a complete offering.
One should not know it thus;
for one does not offer the Agnihotra for one who is deceased.
Whatever portion of four ladlings has already been assigned, one should pour that very amount into it.
This indeed is the ritual action here. 53 (Ed.:

Regarding this, they say: "If, while one who is performing a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) is offering the Agnihotra, the Agnihotra-cow should sit down while being milked, what rite is to be performed there, and what is the expiation?
Some indeed cause her to stand up with a Yajus formula:
"She sits down having gazed upon the lack of livelihood and the evil of the sacrificer for whom the Agnihotra-cow sits down while being milked."
They cause her to rise with the words, "The goddess Aditi has risen.
This goddess Aditi is indeed this [earth];
thus they cause her to rise for him.
"Life he has placed in the lord of the sacrifice"—thus they bestow life upon him. "Making a portion for Indra"—thus they bestow power (*indriya*) upon him.
"For Mitra and Varuṇa"—Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing; thus they bestow out-breathing and in-breathing upon him.
When that very oblation has been offered, they give her to a Brāhmaṇa whom they do not intend to visit for a year, saying, "We shall cause misfortune to settle upon him, so that he may suffer want.
Regarding this, Vājasaneya said: "The cow indeed turns away from those who lack faith."
For they pierce it by means of non-activity;
one should act in this very manner.
Having seized the staff, one should crush her with it and raise her up.

Just as, for example, when one drives [animals], a mule might stumble even when yoked, or a bull might sit down; yet, by means of that same animal when driven with a staff or prodded with a goad, one reaches whatever path one desires—exactly so, by means of this [offering] when driven with a staff or prodded with a goad, one reaches whatever heavenly world one desires.
One should perform it upon oneself alone;
thus one places prosperity within oneself. 55 (Ed.: 1,59)

Regarding this, they say: "If the calf of the *agnihotrī* cow belonging to one who performs the *agnihotra* for a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*) should be lost, what rite is to be performed there? What is the expiation? Concerning this, Āruṇi said: "The sky, indeed, is the *agnihotrī*; the sun is her calf; and this very earth is the *agnihotra* vessel."
The calf of one who knows thus does not perish as an *agnihotra*-calf; for where could it possibly perish?
Nor indeed does the *agnihotra* milk of one who knows thus spill while being milked.
For on this very [earth] he finds firm support.
Indeed, for one who knows this, the Agnihotra cow does not sit down while being milked.
When it rains heavily, they say of her, "Ah, she has sat down and rained! because she has indeed sat down.
Now, moreover, they say: "If this [cow] should yield blood, what rite is to be performed there, and what is the expiation?
She who yields blood yields either the lack of sustenance or the evil of the sacrificer. Having said, "She has stepped out," he should tell [the attendants] to cover the *anvāhāryapacana* fire.
Having placed that [mixture] on the fire and made a stirring-stick, he should cook it.
He should pour that very same [liquid] silently;
for Prajāpati is indeed undefined.
The Agnihotra belongs to Prajāpati.
Moreover, [it is performed] with these sacred utterances (vyāhṛti): "bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ.
These sacred utterances indeed constitute the universal expiation for all faults.
By all of this, he performs an expiation;
moreover, they say: 56 (Ed.:
"If the fires should go out, what rite is to be performed there, and what is the expiation?
Regarding this, some indeed churn [the fire] from a firebrand itself, saying, "From whatever part of a man he perishes, from that very part one seeks his expiation.
But one should not know it thus.
For one should indeed proceed from there taking only a firebrand, or else a chip from the firebrand;
one should act in this very manner.
One should break off [a piece] from the firebrand itself and churn it out upon the two kindling woods.
Verily, he attains that desire which is [fulfilled] when the fire-stick is churned from the fire-brand, and also that which is [fulfilled] when it is churned from the two kindling woods.
Now, they say: "If the Āhavanīya fire, once taken out, should go out, what rite is to be performed there, and what is the expiation?
This [Āhavanīya] remains as if not gone out as long as the Gārhapatya has not gone out.
Even if it should go out many times, one should lift it up again and again.
This indeed is the ritual action in this case.
Furthermore, they say: "If the Gārhapatya fire should go out after the Āhavanīya has been lifted up, what is the ritual action there? What is the expiation?"
Now, some indeed draw it out from that very spot toward the east.
One should not do it in that way.
For if someone were to say there, "He has surely cut off the breaths of this sacrificer from the front; this sacrificer will die," it would indeed happen so.
Now, some indeed bring it from that very place back towards the west, saying:
"The Gārhapatya is indeed the out-breath (prāṇa), and the Āhavanīya is the in-breath (apāna);
these two, the out-breath and the in-breath, being in harmony, consume the food."
The Gārhapatya fire is indeed the house;
houses are a firm foundation.
If someone were to say of him at that point, "This sacrificer has indeed fallen away from this foundation; he will die," it would surely happen exactly so.
Now, some indeed churn it on the Gārhapatya fire itself and place it thereon.
One should not do it in that way.
For if someone were to say of him, "He has produced fire within fire; his hateful rival will soon be born," it would surely happen exactly so.
Now, some indeed follow it [the fire] and churn [the fire-drill].
One should not do so.
For if someone were to say of him, "They have consumed even what remained; not even a single heir of his shall be left," it would surely come to pass exactly so.

One should act in this very manner. One should cause [the fires] to ascend into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) with the verse: "This is thy seasonal womb, from which being born thou didst shine; knowing it, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth, and then increase our songs.
Or [one may do so] with [the verse]: "Having gone forth, he should dwell while offering oblations."
At the end of the ninth [night], his *ubhayatohotra* sacrifice becomes offered throughout the night; he does not incur any reproach whatsoever.
On the following morning, having removed the ashes and smeared [the ground] with a lump of dung, he should re-establish the fires according to their respective places.
This indeed is the ritual procedure here.
Now they say: "If the sun should set while the Āhavanīya fire has not yet been carried forward, what rite should be performed there, and what is the expiation?
For indeed, from such a person all the gods depart when the sun sets while his Āhavanīya fire has not been carried forward.
Having tied a piece of gold with a blade of *darbha* grass, he should carry it behind him.
This is made as a form of that which shines yonder;
for this is indeed the form of the day.
Thus the form of that day is established.
Having kindled the fuel, they should carry it forward to the east.
Having added fuel to it and taken four portions of clarified butter, he should offer it with the formula: "Svāhā to all the gods!"
Just as one might address a person staying in a guest-house who is walking along in anger with a bull-cow or with some other beloved object, even so does he address all the gods.
They all become entirely free from anger toward him.
Now, moreover, they say: "If the sun should rise while the Āhavanīya fire has not yet been carried forward, what rite is to be performed there, and what is the expiation?
For indeed, from him whose Āhavanīya fire rises while it has not been carried forward, all the gods depart.
He should carry silver tied with a blade of *darbha* grass forward.
That is made into the form of the moon.
This is indeed the form of the night;
thus it is made into the form of the night.
Having kindled that firewood, they should carry it towards the south.
