Having piled it up and taken four portions of clarified butter, he should offer it with the formula, "To the Viśve Devas, svāhā!
Knowing that where it is blazing, there indeed is the Gārhapatya fire here, he should thus draw it forth.
That very one is the kinsman.
Now, some say: "It is indeed those who, seeing the heavenly world, offer oblations to the sun.
He who has attained prosperity, or he who desires to depart quickly from this world, should be one who offers the oblation after sunrise. 59
Now, moreover, they say: "If the fires should become mixed, what rite is to be performed there, and what is the expiation?
If another fire should come burning from the rear, he should know: "The seed has come to me from behind; my progeny shall increase, and I shall become more excellent."
It would indeed be so;
however, if one were to scratch his heart, he should perform an *iṣṭi* sacrifice for Agni Vivici.
These same fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, the two *vārtraghna* *ājyabhāga* offerings, and the two *virāj* *saṃyājyā* verses [are used].
Now, these are the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*:
"O Agni, your flames, impelled by the wind, spread in all directions; pure, O pure one, they move with great power.
The divine Navagvas, exceedingly destructive, boldly strike down the forests, shattering them."
Now follows the *yājyā*:

"O Agni, the human tribes praise you—the knower of the *hotṛ*-office, the discerning one, the best bestower of jewels; though dwelling in secret, O blessed one, visible to all, possessing great mental power, worthy of excellent sacrifice, and resplendent with clarified butter."

Moreover, one who wishes to separate himself from evil should sacrifice with this [offering]. Verily, he quickly separates himself from evil. But if this [fire] should come burning toward him from there, he should offer a sacrifice to Agni Saṃvarga.
These same fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, the two *vārtraghna* *ājyabhāga* offerings, and the two *virāj* *saṃyājyā* verses;
now follow these two *yājyā-puronuvākyā* verses.
"Do not abandon us in this great contest, like a bearer of burdens;
win the assembly and win the wealth! This is the *yājyā*.
"Cross over from the further distance to the nearer one where I am; come to me! And furthermore, with this [verse], he should sacrifice if he desires to separate himself from his rival.
Verily, he quickly gathers [the merit] for him.
Now, moreover, they say: "If one should carry fire into the fire, what rite is there, and what is the expiation?
One should perform an *iṣṭi* sacrifice for Agni Agnimat.
These same fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are the *vārtraghna* verses; the two *saṃyājyā* verses are the *virāj*s.
Now, these are the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*:
"By Agni, Agni is kindled, the sage, the master of the house, the youth..."
"Carrying the oblations, with the sacrificial ladle as his mouth," [is the introductory formula].
Now follows the *yājyā*:
"For you, O Agni, by means of fire, are a sage through a sage, being one who exists."
"Friend, you are kindled by your friend"—thus [it is said].
Moreover, one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with this [verse];
he indeed becomes radiant and possessed of spiritual luster.
Now, moreover, they say: "If the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires should become mixed together, what rite should be performed there, and what is the expiation?
One should offer an *iṣṭi* sacrifice to Agni Vīti.
These same fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, the two *vārtraghna* *ājyabhāgas*, and the two *virāj* *saṃyājyas* [are used].
Now, these are the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*: "O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation;
sit down as the Hotṛ upon the sacrificial grass."
Now follows the *yājyā*:
"He who, possessing oblations, seeks to win over Agni for the feast of the gods—to him, O Purifier, be gracious; to him, O Purifier, be gracious. (61) [Ed.: 1,65]
Procreation is light;
Agni is the light among the deities;
the Virāj is the light among the meters.
The Virāj indeed comes to rest in Agni as speech;
it attains the state of the Virāj.
Therefore, this [Agni] is called "Light" (jyotis).
Two *stomas* carry the morning pressing; it is just as the eye and the breath.
Two *stomas* carry the midday pressing; it is just as the ear and the two arms. Two *stomas* carry the third pressing; it is just as the middle [body] and the foundation.

By means of the *dhinkāra* as light, the gods bestowed light upon the *trivṛt* for the sake of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). By means of the *trivṛt* and spiritual luster, they bestowed light upon the *pañcadaśa* for the sake of vigor and heroism.
By means of the *pañcadaśa*, vigor, and heroism, they bestowed light upon the *saptadaśa* for the sake of progeny, cattle, and procreation.
With the seventeenfold [stoma], they bestowed light upon the twenty-onefold for the sake of support, through offspring, cattle, and progeny.
Indeed, this stoma goes bestowing light upon the stoma;
therefore it is called the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Now, because he leads the *stotra* toward the *stoma* and the *savana*, it is therefore called the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
Furthermore, because the sacrifice, when fully praised, attains the *virāj*, and the *virāj* is light (*jyotis*), it is for this reason alone that it is called the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. 1-62 (Ed.:
This sacrifice is indeed not one-sided; it is commensurate with a man.
Whatever desire one brings it forth with, that desire is fulfilled for him. For he goes by means of a two-wheeled vehicle (asthūri) to wherever he wishes to go.
When Prajāpati created offspring, he created them by means of the Agniṣṭoma;
indeed, he created them by means of the tenth chant of the Agniṣṭoma and by means of the tenth month of the year.
Then, he enclosed them with the twelfth chant of the Agniṣṭoma and with the twelfth month of the year.
Therefore, animals carry their embryos for ten months;
they are born in the eleventh month.
No one ever exceeds the twelfth month, for it is encompassed by that [eleventh].
Of those that had been taken up, a mule leaped over them.
Pursuing it, he took its seed;
he wiped it upon a donkey, then upon a mare, then upon domestic animals, and then upon plants.
Therefore the donkey has double seed; therefore the mare has double seed;
therefore animals produce two at a time;
therefore plants, though not anointed, hum.
Therefore, a mule should not be given on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), for it has floated beyond, it has stepped over, it has taken away the seed, and it is indeed childless.
It should be given at the *ṣoḍaśin* chant;
for the *ṣoḍaśin* is redundant among the chants, and the mule is redundant among animals.
They place that which is indeed redundant as redundant for the sake of the conformity of the sacrifice.

He who, knowing thus, chants the *udgītha* with the *agniṣṭoma*, produces offspring that have not yet been born and takes hold of those already born. This *agniṣṭoma* is indeed the sacrifice of the eldest, the sacrifice of Prajāpati.
He who knows thus attains preeminence and excellence. 2-63 (Ed.:
1,68) |p1 Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning.

Prajāpati, indeed, is the deity Mind. He desired: "May I become many; may I procreate; may I attain abundance. From his head, from his mouth, he emitted the Trivṛt Stoma, the Gāyatrī metre, the Rathantara Sāman, the deity Agni, the Brāhmaṇa among men, and the goat among animals.
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa has the Gāyatrī for his metre and Agni for his deity; therefore he is the mouth of creatures, for he was created from the mouth. He desired, "May I indeed be propagated."
From his two arms, from the chest, he created the fifteenfold *stoma*, the *triṣṭubh* metre, the *bṛhat* sāman, Indra as the deity, the *rājanya* as the human being, and the horse as the animal.

Therefore, the *rājanya* has the *triṣṭubh* as his metre and Indra as his deity. And therefore, he performs heroic deeds with his two arms, for he created him from the chest by means of heroic power through his two arms.
He desired, "May I indeed be propagated.
From the very middle of his belly, he emitted the seventeenfold *stoma*, the *jagatī* metre, the *vāmadevya* *sāman*, the Viśvedevas as the deity, the Vaiśya as the human, and the cow as the animal.
Therefore, the Vaiśya has the Jagatī for his metre and the Viśvedevas for his deity.
And therefore he is prolific, for he created him from the belly, which is the organ of procreation. He desired, "May I indeed be propagated."

From the very foundation of his feet, he created the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), the *anuṣṭubh* metre, and the *yajñāyajñīya* chant; [but] no deity whatsoever, nor a Śūdra man, nor a sheep as an animal.
Therefore, the Śūdra has the *anuṣṭubh* as his metre and the master of the house as his deity.
For this reason, he desires to live by the mere washing of feet, for he created him from the foundation of the feet.
By means of this very creation, Prajāpati created offspring.
He who knows this thus attains abundance in offspring and cattle.
Therefore, they praise this sacrifice most highly, namely the Agniṣṭoma, for it is indeed the sacrifice of Prajāpati. 4-65 (Ed.: 1,69)
Audumbarī |c66 (Ed.:
1,70) |p1 Prajāpati distributed strength among the creatures.
That became an udumbara tree;
Prajāpati is the Udgātṛ priest,
and the udumbara belongs to Prajāpati.
They choose other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), but not the Udgātṛ.
When the Udgātṛ takes hold of the Udumbara post with the first ritual act, he chooses himself for the office of the priest by means of that very deity.

He takes hold of it [with the formula]: "I set thee in the seat of life, in the shadow of the well, in the heart of the ocean; homage to the ocean, homage to the eye of the ocean; mayest thou not abandon me from the womb."

When he says, "I set thee in the seat of life," the sacrifice is indeed life; thus its seat is prepared. "In the shadow of the shelter," the sacrifice is indeed the shelter; thus this Sadas is made its shadow.
"The heart of the ocean," for the heart is in the middle of the self; therefore the Audumbarī post is measured in the middle of the Sadas.

"Adoration to the ocean, adoration to the eye of the ocean! Speech, indeed, is the ocean; the mind is the eye of the ocean. It is to these two deities that he pays homage when about to perform the office of the *ṛtvij*. "Do not abandon me from the *yonirvān*! The *sāman*, indeed, is the *yonirvān*. It is to the *sāman* that he pays homage when about to perform the office of the *ṛtvij*.
The *sāman* does not desert him.
He who, knowing thus, pays homage to the *sāman*, does not meet with misfortune through the *sāman* and is not deprived of the *sāman*.
He who speaks ill of him meets with misfortune. 5–66 (Ed.:
The Sadas is indeed the belly of Prajāpati.
The Udumbara tree is vigor. In that the Udumbara post is erected in the middle of the Sadas, he thereby places food and vigor in the very midst of creatures.

Therefore, food eaten from the middle satisfies. Therefore, wherever this [oblation] is made exhausted of its power (*yātayāmnī*), there the offspring become hungry; yet they indeed become prosperous.
"Should I touch water or not? they deliberate.
For everything here is possessed of a self;
he who desires food for himself, it is him that one hates most intensely.
If he were to touch [the water], he would blow away his food;
if he were not to touch it, he would exclude himself from food.
Having touched it, he sings the *udgītha* with that which has been touched by himself; thus he does not blow away his food, nor does he exclude himself from food.
The *sāman* is the food of the gods; the *udumbara* tree is strength.
When the *udgātṛ* leans against the *audumbarī* post, he thereby bestows strength upon the *sāman*, which is the food of the gods.
Therefore, wherever they perform the priestly office with the *sāman*, that is what the gods eat most abundantly.
Prajāpati is the *udgātṛ*.
The udumbara is vigor.
This very Prajāpati, resting in vigor, distributes vigor and food for his offspring.
Sitting facing north, he sings the udgītha.
Thus he causes the northern quarter to partake of nourishment. Sitting facing west, he chants the *prastāva*; thus he causes the western quarter to partake of nourishment.
Sitting to the south, he performs the *pratihāra*.
Thus, he causes the southern direction itself to partake in nourishment (*ūrj*).
The other officiating priests perform their priestly duties facing eastward.
Thus they cause the eastern quarter to partake of nourishment.

Therefore, among the quarters, this one is the most powerful, the most fit for subsistence, and is cherished by the greatest number. Therefore, when people fall into want of livelihood, they go toward the east.
For this [northern] direction is the most powerful and the most conducive to livelihood among the directions; it is beloved by the majority.
Now, since the *udgātṛ*s have the north as their deity, why do they perform the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) after turning back toward the other directions? One should say:
"For the attainment of the directions, for the propitiation of the directions."

"Therefore, food exists in all directions. He makes an offering over the post made of Udumbara wood with the mantra: "Support the sky, fill the mid-region, make firm the earth with thy base; let Dyutāna Māruta set thee up by the steadfast law of Mitra and Varuṇa; satisfy Heaven and Earth with clarified butter; make the plants full of good fruit, Svāhā! By this, he anoints these very worlds with essence. 7-68 (Ed.: 1,72)
The Cleansing of the Vessel |c69 (Ed.: 1,73) |p1 Prajāpati created living beings.
He desired to emit fire from his mouth.
That fire, loathing it, sprang upward from the mouth and was emitted after having licked the brain.
The gods and the seers approached him and said, "This brain has been torn out; let it not be lost. Let us put this back into some part of the body."
They said to Bṛhaspati, "Take the Soma in this [vessel].
Bṛhaspati replied, "This [Soma] is, as it were, harsh, unpurified, impure, and uncooked.
They said, "We shall make this [Soma] for you purified, pure, and cooked."
"Bring it to me," he said. "So be it," [the other replied].
He gave it to him.
He accepted it with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I accept thee.

Verily, he thus accepted it with the limbs of the gods. Having accepted it, he purified it with the formulas: "May the Vasus purify thee with the Gāyatrī metre, bestowing good progeny and the increase of wealth; may the Rudras purify thee with the Triṣṭubh metre, bestowing good progeny and the increase of wealth; may the Ādityas purify thee with the Jagatī metre, bestowing good progeny and the increase of wealth."
Thus, he purifies him by means of both the meters and the deities.
Having purified him, he places it behind the axle, saying: "Thou art Bārhaspatya; thou art made of wood; thou art the head of Prajāpati; thou art the vessel of Āyu.
When he says, "Thou art Bārhaspatya," it is because Bṛhaspati indeed first received him.

When he says, "Belonging to the trees," it is because they dedicate it to the trees. When he says, "The head of Prajāpati," for this was indeed the head of Prajāpati. When he says, "The vessel surpassing life-span," for this vessel indeed surpasses all other vessels.
Furthermore, that very vessel which is yoked first and unyoked last surpasses all other vessels.
He who knows this attains the vessel of the superior.
Having placed it behind the axle, he sings the Gāyatra on the Viśvarūpā verses. 8-69 (Ed.: 1,73)
Homage to the ancestors who dwelt of old; homage to those who sit together. I yoke my speech, a hundred-footed [song], I sing it with a thousand paths.
"The Gāyatra, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, all forms brought together—the gods have made them their abodes. [He recites:
"The homage to the fathers who sat before"—for it is the fathers who sit here first.
He thus pays homage to them.

With the words, "Homage to those seated together," he pays homage to those very Brahmins with whom he sits down when about to perform the priestly office. With the words, "I yoke the hundred-footed speech," he yokes speech itself as the hundred-footed one.
With the words, "I sing of her who has a thousand paths," he sings of her while she is indeed already yoked, having become one who possesses a thousand paths.

With the words, "The Gāyatra, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagat"—these are indeed the three pressings; thus he takes them into himself. With the words, "All forms brought together"—the sacrifice is indeed all forms; thus by this he brings the sacrifice together.
"The gods made dwellings," he says; by this, he makes the sacrifice possessed of the gods.
Kusurvinda Haudālaki sang forth the *soma* verses.

Then those sons of Kaśyapa, known as the Asitamṛgas, said: "Who is this cruel one among us who sings the *udgītha* at the end? Come, let us revile him. Desiring to revile him, they approached the place of sacrifice (*āstāva*).

He said: "Homage to the Brahmins! Before today’s morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), I have already completed the sacrifice with the *gāyatra* chant upon the *viśvarūpa* verses. Just as one might drive away a weak, exhausted ascetic by means of cattle, so indeed shall we drive away this body of the sacrifice."

They rose up and went forth, saying: "Homage be to this Brāhmaṇa! May he indeed know this! For one who knows thus, his sacrifice becomes established through the Gāyatra [Sāman] upon the Viśvarūpā verses before the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*). 10-71 (Ed.:
Regarding this, they say: "O Adhvaryu, what praised *stotra* did the Hotṛ recite in response with the *prātaranuvāka*?
He says, "We performed that which was our duty; ask the Hotṛ. [The Adhvaryu asks:
"O Hotṛ, what praised *stotra* did you recite in response with the *prātaranuvāka*?"
"We have performed that which is our duty," said the Udgātṛ; "Ask the Udgātṛ! [They asked:
"Udgātṛ, did the Hotṛ recite in response with the Prātaranuvāka the stotra that was chanted?
He should reply: "We have performed that which is our duty; we have sung what was to be sung here."
If they should say to him, "Did you sing the darknesses, or the lights?", he should reply, "I sang the lights, not the darknesses.
That which is the *ṛc* is light; that which is the *sāman* is light.
That light is these deities. "I have sung these very lights; let me pierce you with darkness and evil," he says. Thus, he pierces them with both darkness and evil. 11-72 (Ed.: 1,76)
Kalaśaprohaṇa |c73 (Ed.:
1,77) |p1 They approach from behind, facing eastward.
They thus secure speech itself at the beginning. If they were to sit down facing eastward in front, they would place speech behind them;
speech would then be liable to desert them.
Speech indeed departed from the gods;
it entered the trees.
This same [speech] is that which is in the dice.
When they push the *droṇakalaśa* down below the axle, they thereby secure divine speech.
The *udgātṛ*s push the *droṇakalaśa* down below the axle for the sake of the *udgītha*;
thus, from this very world, they exclude their hateful rival.
He removes the bright [substance] from above.
Thus he separates his hateful rival from that very world.
He who knows this separates his hateful rival from both these worlds.
One should not touch the axle;
for if one were to touch the axle, one would smear prosperity upon the rival.
One pushes [the cart] between the two wheels.

Therefore, that which is between the two wheels of the cart is most fit for subsistence; therefore, one who is yoked [to the cart] enjoys [the food] between the two poles. 12-73 (Ed.: 1,77) |c74 (Ed.:
The Vasus indeed pushed this [chariot] forward first.
They grew weary;
they called upon the Rudras.
The Rudras pushed it forward. They grew weary.
They called upon the Ādityas.
The Ādityas pushed him up.
He pushes him up with: "May the Vasus push you up with the Gāyatrī metre; may the Rudras push you up with the Triṣṭubh metre; may the Ādityas push you up with the Jagatī metre.
Thus, he pushes him up following the elevation of the deities.
"By the impulse of god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I push thee forward"—with these words he should indeed push it forward.
Thus he pushes it forward by means of the limbs of the gods.
Bṛhaspati, indeed, pushed this one forward first.
He was deprived of his form and splendor.
He reflected, "What is the expiation for this?
and he perceived it in the *droṇakalaśa* itself.

He touched it, saying: "Thou art the protector of the body; protect my body! Thou art the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me! Thou art the bestower of life; bestow life upon me! Thou art the bestower of vigor; bestow vigor upon me!
Whatever of his own self had been lost there, he restored that by means of this [formula].

The Udgātṛ touches it with this very same formula: "Thou art the protector of the body; protect my body! Thou art the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me! Thou art the bestower of life; bestow life upon me! Thou art the bestower of vigor; bestow vigor upon me!"
Whatever of his own self is measured out here, that he causes to swell by means of this very [vessel].
Indeed, this world is twofold: the Brahman and the Kṣatra.
Both of these are the *droṇakalaśa*.
He who knows thus secures both the spiritual power (*brahman*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*). 13–74 (Ed.:

Having placed the pressing-stones directly before him, he touches them, saying: "The falcons, the swift ones, the embryos of Truth, the grandsons of the moving waters, the peaks of the mountains—bring us that hero upon whom we many depend for our livelihood, one who makes [us] free from imprecation, who cannot be imprecated, and who is the maker of imprecation against another.
Verily, a hero is born to him—one who makes [others] free from imprecation, who cannot be imprecated, and who is the maker of imprecation against another.
He places the *droṇakalaśa* vessel over [the Soma], saying: "Here, I place myself upon spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)."

If there should be a Rājanya who has been excluded from this [kingdom], one should turn the pressing-stones away from him, silently cover the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, and while pouring it out, he should push it down toward the south, saying: "Here I cast out so-and-so from the people; here I cast down his kingdom. He should thus overturn the *droṇakalaśa* vessel face-downward.

Having turned the pressing-stones toward him, he should, while pronouncing the name of that Rājanya who belongs to him, cover the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, saying: "Here I cover so-and-so over the people.
The other is driven away, while the other enters.
If, having understood this, he should not respect him, he should desire: "May he be confined right here within me.

Having turned the pressing-stones away from him and silently placed [the stone] upon the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, he should place the *upāṃśusavana* stone on top of it with the formula: "Here do I place the people (*viś*) upon so-and-so.
When they have been completely crushed, the people rise up against him.

If, having discovered him, he should attack him, [the sacrificer] should place the pressing-stones face upwards and set the *droṇakalaśa* vessel over them, saying: "In this [vessel] I place that [attacker] within my people.
He thus gains mastery over his own people, his own people come to him, and he becomes one who has secured his position without interval.
The *droṇakalaśa* is indeed the kingdom; the pressing-stones are the subjects.
If the *droṇakalaśa* were loose, the kingdom would be loose.
Following that are the subjects;
following the subjects is the sacrificer; following the sacrificer are the offspring.
He makes it firm with the formula: "May the two goddesses, the Dhiṣaṇās, set thee down; sit thou in the firm seat; sit for strength.
These two, indeed, are the goddesses Dhiṣaṇās; this is the firm seat.
With these very worlds he thus makes him firm: "For sap, for strength, sit thou!
Rain, indeed, is sap; that which increases above the rain is strength.
By this very means, he wins that.
Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the sun with darkness;
the gods and the seers then treated him medically.
They said to Atri, "O Seer, you must drive this away.
"So be it," he replied.
Then Atri drove it away.
They said, "He who found light for us when we were pierced by darkness—let light be his share. Therefore, this gold is carried here;
formerly, indeed, it was carried as a hundred-māna weight.
Now, whatever they give at this time—this gold, indeed, is the light in all the worlds. He who, knowing this, gives gold here, places the light in all the worlds. 15-76 (Ed.: 1,80)
Pavitravitāna |c77 (Ed.:
1,81) |p1 That which he first shook off became a black ewe.
That which he struck away a second time became the Dhūmrāvir sheep;
that which he struck away a third time became the Phalgunī sheep.
If one should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," one should throw a black [wool] into his filter; he indeed becomes worse off.
Now, if he should desire of someone, "May he be neither here nor there," he should place smoke upon that person's filter; thus he becomes neither here nor there.

Now, if he should desire of someone, "May he become better, may he attain radiance," he should make his filter bright; thus he indeed becomes better and attains radiance, for even there the sun is present.

Having brought it down between those two [strainers], he cleanses it with the formulas: "May the Vasus cleanse you with the Gāyatrī metre; may the Rudras cleanse you with the Triṣṭubh metre; may the Ādityas cleanse you with the Jagatī metre.

He spreads it out with its fringes pointing northward over the strainer with the verse, "The strainer of Brahmaṇaspati is spread for you," for the sake of attainment. "For the one desiring heaven, [he uses]: 'The strainer of heat is spread upon the station of heaven.'"
"He has shone forth, the dappled one, seeking the first light of the dawn"—this [verse] is for one desiring offspring.
One should perform the sacrifice with all [the verses], for the attainment of all these desires.
He brings forward the King (Soma).

He addresses it with the mantra: "Flow pure, O Sudhāman, toward the dear abodes of the gods; you have flowed for the gods three times, for the Ādityas three times, and for the Aṅgirases three times. With that fourth sacred power (*brahman*) with which you flowed for Bṛhaspati, flow pure for me!
It becomes well-being for the Udgātṛ, well-being for the sacrificer, and well-being for the offspring.
When the Adhvaryu, drawing the Āgrayaṇa cup, utters the sound *hiṃ*,
that very act becomes the *hiṃ*-utterance.
Then the Udgātṛ sings the Gāyatra on a single verse: "Upward your pressed juice has been born" (*uccā te jātam andhas*).
By the word "upward" (*ud*), he carries the oblation from here to the gods. With the words "Seated in heaven, he bestows [it] upon the earth," he causes rain to descend from yonder.
He makes these two worlds dwell together. These two worlds overflow with desire for him who knows thus. 16-77 (Ed.: 1,81)
Bahiṣpavamāna-Stotra (Bar: 78–100; Ed.: 1,82–104) Sarpaṇa |c78 (Ed.: 1,82)
It is as if they perform a cruel act toward the sacrifice when, having struck King Soma with the pressing-stones in the two oblation-houses, they proceed to the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant.
"What is the expiation for that? they ask.
"They should touch water," [they reply].
Water, indeed, is the pacification of everything. By means of water, they thus pacify him. Speech, indeed, was weary at the outset of this path when they proceed to the *bahiṣpavamāna*.

Prajāpati said to her: "I shall grant you a portion; then you may glide away. When about to glide for the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, he should offer an oblation with the formula: "May I be dear to Speech, dear to the Lord of Speech; O divine Speech, place me in that which is the honeyed part of your speech, svāhā to Sarasvatī!
If he were to offer it with "To Sarasvatī, svāhā!", he would enclose Sarasvatī, who is Speech, within the *svāhā*-utterance.
Now, when he offers with "Svāhā to Sarasvatī," he places speech above the utterance of *svāhā*. With that [speech] held in check, he extends the sacrifice;
for by means of speech the sacrifice is extended upwards.
"You are Vekurā by name, sent for a divine task; be auspicious and well-yoked for us; may there be true blessing for the sacrificer, svāhā!"—thus he should offer. Speech indeed is Vekurā;
speech is the Brahman.
Having offered that oblation into the speech of the Brahman himself, he creeps forward; he does not meet with misfortune.
(16) It is as if they go to the forest who creep for the *bahiṣpavamāna*. (17–78) (Ed.: 1,82) (79) (Ed.: 1,83) (1)
The Lord, or a Rakṣas, or some other destructive power might strike them down.

Then he offers the second oblation: "May the god Sūrya protect me from the Rakṣases of heaven; may Vāta [protect me] from those of the intermediate space; may Agni [protect me] from those of the earth, svāhā!
Having thus entrusted himself to those who are the lords of these worlds, he creeps forward and does not meet with misfortune.
When Prajāpati created the sacrifice, he created it in the Havirdhāna shed itself.
Once created, it ran away toward the north.
Having reached it there, they praised it with this [hymn].
When, having gone northward, they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*, they chant after having reached the sacrifice itself.
Verily, he who knows the divine steed becomes a steed;
the sacrifice, indeed, is the divine steed.
Now, whoever mounts a human steed that is unappeased and unwiped, he indeed either harms him or utterly destroys him.
What then [would happen] if one were to mount a divine steed that is unappeased and unwiped? |||18-79 (Ed.:

The Adhvaryu creeps forward while carrying the prastara-bunch. He consecrates it with the formula: "This divine, vigorous one I cleanse. Having thus cleansed and pacified it, he ascends; he does not come to ruin.
He who sings the *udgītha* for Soma settles upon the field of the gods.
Now, he who settles upon [a field] without having announced it to the human lord of the field, him indeed that [lord] either harms or drives away.
But what [harm could come] to one who would settle upon [a field] without having announced it to the divine lord of the field?
"Sing the udgītha! Sing the udgītha for Soma! he says.
Soma is indeed the lord of the field (*kṣetrapati*) among the gods.
Having thus announced it to Soma, the lord of the field of the gods, he sings the udgītha; he does not meet with misfortune.

"For my splendor, for my holy luster, for my food, for my abundance, for my prosperity, for my procreation—for the abundance of offspring, for the prosperity of offspring, for the procreation of offspring, for the sovereignty of King Soma, and for my status as a village headman.
Grāva Maitreya used to say: "What shall I sing for one, and what for another?
He would always say this with that [formula]: "Sing out, O Soma! Sing out, O Soma! This for so-and-so; this for so-and-so!"
Verily, all his desires were fulfilled for him.
These fires on the hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), when they are carried forth, are indeed the snares of the gods that are spread out.
Whoever approaches them without knowing this fastens the snares of the gods upon himself.
This, indeed, is the door of the sacrifice: that which lies between the Āgnīdhra shed and the Cātvāla pit. One should descend by it; one should give by it.
The altar is indeed named Dhā. As he descends toward it, he should say: "Thou art Dhā; bestow prosperity upon me; may we, long-lived and resplendent, ascend from thee.
He does not bind himself with the snares of the gods, nor does he meet with misfortune. 19-80 (Ed.: 1,84)

Verily, by thus maintaining the continuity of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), they proceed to the heavenly world when, having drawn the cups between the two *havirdhāna* sheds, they proceed for the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant.
They proceed in an unbroken succession.
The heavenly world is, as it were, continuous;
[they proceed] for the sake of the continuity and non-interruption of the heavenly world itself.
They glide along like clouds.
The heavenly world is, as it were, turned away from here.
Just as that [sun] rising there becomes, as it were, veiled by clouds because it is turned away, even so is this [case].
It is for the attainment of the heavenly world and to prevent injury.

The Adhvaryu creeps first; he is the breath of the sacrifice. Therefore, if they were to be cut off, they would be cut off from the breath, and they would be liable to die. The Prastotṛ creeps second; he is the mouth of the Sāman.
Therefore, if they were to be excluded, they would incur primary affliction.
The Udgātṛ moves forward third; he is Prajāpati, belonging to all the deities. Therefore, if they were to be excluded, they would suffer total ruin.

The *pratihartṛ* creeps along as the fourth, [chanting] the fourth part of the *sāman*. Therefore, if they should cut off [any part], they should restore it by means of their own fourth part. The sacrificer creeps along as the fifth.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
cattle are fivefold.
Therefore, if they were to be cut off, they would be cut off from the sacrifice and from cattle.
Brahmā, as the sixth, glides along.
There are indeed six meters.
By means of the meters, they thus strike away the *rakṣas*, the evil.
Indeed, all this is the *brahman*.
Since the *brahmán* priest stands behind, having struck away the *rakṣas*, the evil, by means of the *brahman* itself, they proceed to the heavenly world.
They creep along carrying the *prastara* (grass-bundle).
The *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer; the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) is the offspring.
In that they carry the *barhis* grass-bundle over and over the *prastara*, they thereby place the sacrificer above his offspring.
Therefore, the sacrificer stands ever above the other offspring. If he were to throw it down, the sacrificer would belong to the heavenly world and would be cut off from this world.
If he were to throw it beyond [the altar], he would find firm support in this world, but he would be cut off from the heavenly world.
Regarding this they say: "The wife is indeed half of the self of the sacrificer;
in that she remains outside the altar-ground, he is not thereby cut off from this world."
"He should indeed eat from this [vessel]," [it is said].
"Or rather, there is no wife present;
even if there were one, he should eat from one [vessel] and pass by the other."
In that he pours out [the oblation], by that he [attains] the heavenly world;
in that he throws [it] beyond, by that he is not cut off from this world. 21-82 (Ed.:
Verily, at that time, when this Cātvāla pit was here, the Āditya was present;
Agni was there. He (the Āditya) scorched all this world.

The gods were afraid of its burning. They said, "This one will surely burn up everything here; let us carry it away from here. They took it up from this world with three verses, from the intermediate space with three verses, and they caused it to go to heaven with three verses.
Thereupon he turned away. They saw this very highest syllable, *āvat*, and with it they made him face toward them.
Thereupon, this [sun] shines hitherward.
By means of this very syllable, they placed Agni in this world.
If he should desire of a sacrificer, "May he be one who belongs to the heavenly world," he should sing for him while making him look toward the *cātvāla* pit.
From there, they take it up with three verses; with three verses they cause it to go from the intermediate space, and with three verses they cause it to go to heaven.
The sacrificer becomes one who possesses the world of heaven, yet he is liable to die prematurely.
For they chant with the verses directed forward.
When they are about to chant with all [the verses], he should first recite the last one, then the next-to-last, then the next-to-last;
thus all of them become directed backward.
Regarding this, they say: "This [sacrifice] has descended back to the sacrificial session; indeed, one sacrifices out of a desire for heaven.
Because the very last syllable there is an *āvat*, it is not cut off from this world.
He sings the last [verse] as having the *rathantara* as its characteristic.
This earth, indeed, is the *rathantara*;
thus he establishes himself upon this very earth.
Prajāpati created offspring. Once created, they surrounded him on all sides, seeking food. For them, he created edible food by means of the *hiṃkāra*.
He warded off that which was created by the syllable *oṃ*.
This Udgātṛ is Prajāpati;
food-seekers surround him on all sides from every direction.
For by means of the *hiṃ* syllable alone he creates food from them;
he then restrains that which has been created by means of the *oṃ* syllable.
If, having uttered *hiṃ*, he were not to utter *oṃ*, the food would simply pass away from him.
If he should utter the *sāman* first, he would seize the power of the *kṣatra*.
For the *sāman* is indeed the *kṣatra*.
If he should utter the *ṛc* first, he would seize the power of the *viś*.
The *ṛc* is indeed the peasantry (*viś*).
He first utters the *yajus*;
for the *yajus* is the sacred power (*brahman*).
Thus he indeed produces spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
[He says: "Bhūr bhuvas svar! I shall make honey; I shall produce honey; honey shall come to be; blessing upon blessing; food and strength.
For what is expressed by "bhūr bhuvas svar" is indeed the Brahman, this very sacrificial formula (*yajus*).
When he says, "I shall make honey," offspring indeed are honey; it is them that he thereby makes. When he says, "I shall produce honey," he thereby produces them.
When he says, "It will become honey," he thereby leads them to prosperity.
"Bhadram-bhadram" (Prosperity—prosperity).
Whatever wealth a man possesses is prosperity; the home is prosperity; offspring are prosperity; cattle are prosperity.
By this [formula], he secures all that.
"Food and vigor," [he says]. Rain, indeed, is food; that which increases after the rain is vigor.
By this very means, he wins that.
One should chant the *udgītha* after having fashioned Prajāpati.
Verily, he who sings the udgītha after having fashioned Prajāpati succeeds for himself.
"The quarters, the intermediate quarters, the fore-quarters, the by-quarters, the up-quarters, the quarters"—
Prajāpati is indeed the quarters.
Having thus fashioned Prajāpati, he sings the udgītha.
He for whom one knows this prospers.
Kapivana Bhauvāyana used to say: "What do those who go to the sacrifice gain, who either slither away or run off without having partaken of the *devasoma*?"
When they have sat down for the *bahiṣpavamāna*, he should say to a Brāhmaṇa whom he considers as if pure, "Come, take my hand.

Having invited him with that, he should then address him with the mantra: "O gods, whatever Soma-drinking there is here at this sacrifice on the sacrificial grass and at the altar, of that we partake. Whether he runs forward or not, his divine Soma has indeed been consumed.
The wild animals have this as their abode:
because they chant the *bahis-pavamāna* in the forest, therefore the wild animals frequent the forest. They chant in forward-moving [verses].
Therefore, wild animals, from the forest itself, drive toward the forest.
They chant with uniform meters;
therefore, wild animals are uniform in form.
The highest syllable is the one that protects.
Therefore, even when one person after another is found to be unshakable in the village,
they nevertheless carry away what has been killed in the forest back into the village.
Having praised, they run forward;
thereby they cause the sacrificer himself to go to the heavenly world.
They raise up their arms.
Thus they establish the sacrificer himself in the heavenly world. Those who cause one who is mortal to attain immortality indeed commit an act of falsehood;
they are deprived of their form and their splendor.
If another person should rise while he is rising, one should rise after him, holding onto him as he rises.
One is not deprived of beauty or luster, nor does one meet with misfortune;
one may know what is to come.

If these subjects should be like those fleeing in haste, the security of their livelihood (*yogakṣema*) will be in a state of flight; one should know that in such a case, this Udgātṛ has sung the chant poorly. But if they should be as if at peace, the security of their livelihood will be peaceful.
In that same way, one should know: "This Udgātṛ has sung forth.
For this is indeed the wise one.
One who desires a village, one who desires prosperity, and one who desires offspring should take *upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ* as the opening verse (*pratipad*).
For they sing along with this [earth] here;
indeed, everything here sings along with her.
He who knows thus is procreated with offspring and cattle upon this very earth.
The men are indeed the subjects of the gods; Soma Indu is the ruling power.
By this [verse], he wins both the common people (*viś*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
With the words "He seeks to sacrifice to the god," he sacrifices to all the deities without interruption.
One who desires offspring should take as the introductory verse (the *pratipad*) the words "Hither, unto the newborn, the swift one."
Verily, offspring are near to oneself; verily, one is procreated with offspring and cattle through oneself.
One who desires offspring should make this very [verse] the introductory verse (*pratipad*).
For by saying "apturam," having attained [it], he becomes better and more prosperous in himself.
"With cattle, the breakage is adorned"—
the sacrifice, indeed, is the breakage with cattle.
The cattle are the adorned;
by this [offering], he wins both the sacrifice and the cattle.
"The gods have approached the drop," [he says].
King Soma is indeed the sacrificer; the *stomas* are the gods. It is the *stomas* alone that cause him to go to the heavenly world. 25-86 (Ed.: 1,90)
The *kāmya-pratipad* (verse for specific desires):
"Flow on as the foremost of speech"— one who desires preeminence should use this as the introductory verse (*pratipad*).
Prajāpati created offspring. Once they were created, they did not turn toward him. He desired, "May I attain preeminence among these offspring."
He saw this introductory verse;
he praised with it.
Thereupon, he indeed attained preeminence among those creatures.
He who knows this attains preeminence among his own people.
This indeed is the successful *stotriya* verse for which the beginning is "pavasva.
By means of that very successful *stotriya*, his hymn becomes successful.
He who knows the divine couple is procreated through that couple.
"Pavasva" and "vāca" constitute the divine couple;
he who knows this is procreated through that couple.
This is the opening verse for all three *sāmans*: "Flow on" (*pavasva*) is for the *vāmadevya*; "Speech" (*vācaḥ*) is for the *rathantara*; and "The foremost" (*agriya*) is for the *bṛhat*.
By means of these openings of all these *sāmans*, the chant becomes perfected.
[The verse is: "O Soma, with thy wondrous aids... (*soma citrābhir ūtibhiḥ*).
Soma is indeed the wonder (*citra*) of the gods.
By means of Soma, the wonder of the gods, he becomes manifold and procreates.
"Over all poetic insights" (*abhi viśvāni kāvyā*).
By this [verse], one secures all poetic wisdom.
One who desires a firm foundation in the community should use "Flow on, O Indu, as a bull, pressed! as the opening verse.
"Make us glorious among the people"— for indeed, she becomes glorious among the people. "The pressed [Soma] is a bull"—
for he becomes like a bull, like a procreator, and like a sovereign lord over that people in which he prospers.
He becomes like a bull, indeed like a procreator, and like a sovereign ruler over that people in which he prospers, provided he knows this.
For everyone in a people desires to prosper and acts as an enemy. [The verse says: "Slay all those who hate us."
By this [verse], he repels all enemies.
He should make "Flow with that stream" the introductory verse for one who is about to engage in battle;
[and the following verse]: "With which the cattle have come here, the womenfolk, to our homes."
He who engages in battle desires to carry off the cattle of the enemy; he carries off the cattle of the enemy. He should employ this very introductory verse as a means of winning and a messenger.
He who goes forth for the sake of gain desires to take away cattle belonging to others. He takes away cattle belonging to others, and cattle belonging to others bow down to him, who knows thus.
For one who is ill, he should make "O Agni, you purify our lives" the opening verse.
The fire indeed departs from his body, and the breath departs to the wind.
By means of the purifying fire itself, he joins together his body with the breath. Those for whom one who has been consecrated dies should employ this very introductory verse.
Those for whom one who has been consecrated dies are considered as if impure and unholy.
By means of this very *pavamāna* fire, he makes them purified and fit for sacrifice.
One should employ this same introductory verse.
One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Agni is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
By means of Agni alone, one becomes possessed of the *brahman* and splendor among the gods. One who practices sorcery should make this very verse his opening formula (*pratipad*).
For Agni is indeed the *brahmán* among the gods.
By means of Agni alone, the Brahman of the gods, strike down him whom he hates.
One who desires food should make this very verse the introductory formula (*pratipad*).
For with the words "Bring hither to us strength and nourishment," he thereby secures both nourishment and strength.
One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should perform this very same ritual procedure.
For whoever practices malevolent magic, whoever seeks to harm, and whoever desires evil—that is indeed misfortune (*ducchunā*).
With the words, "Drive misfortune far away," he drives his hateful enemy, the source of evil, far away and downward.
One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should take *davidyutatyā rucā* as the opening verse (*pratipad*). Indeed, the Gāyatrī is radiant;
the Gāyatrī is spiritual luster.
The *triṣṭubh* is vigor and heroism;
the *jagatī* is procreation.
He who knows this becomes endowed with sacred splendor, vigor, and heroism, and he is propagated through offspring and cattle.
"Paristobhantyā kṛpā somāś śukrā gavāśiraḥ.
The bright Soma-draughts are indeed the sacrifice;
the milk-mixture is cattle.
By this [rite], he wins both the sacrifice and cattle.

One whose father or grandfather was more distinguished, yet who considers himself as it were inferior, should take "Asya pratnām anu dyutām" as the opening verse (*pratipad*). Whatever prosperity belonged to his father or grandfather, that very prosperity he attains.
"They have milked the bright [soma], the shameless.
The sacrifice, indeed, is the bright;
cattle are the shameless.
By this, he wins both the sacrifice and cattle.
"The milk, the seer who won a thousand," [he says].
He becomes possessed of milk, and a hero is born to him as a winner of a thousand. 28-89 (Ed.: 1,93)
One should use "ete asṛgram indavaḥ" as the introductory verse (*pratipad*) for many sacrificers performing the sacrifice together;
with "eta eta," he thus addresses them for the sake of seniority and preeminence.
By means of this very metrical form, he makes them equal sharers;
thus the blessing of the sacrifice reaches them equally.
When Prajāpati created offspring, he created them by means of this very introductory formula.

With "These" he created the gods; with "They have flowed forth," the humans; with "Drops," the ancestors; with "Across the filter," the cups; with "Swift ones," the hymns; with "All," the recitations; and with "For good fortune," he endowed those who were born with good fortune. He who, knowing this, chants the *pratipad* with this [verse], creates offspring as Prajāpati himself;
moreover, he thereby endows them with good fortune.
One should use "They have been let loose, the prize-winners" as the introductory verse for three sacrificers;
by means of this metrical form, he makes them equal sharers,
and thus the blessing of the sacrifice reaches them equally.
"The Soma-draughts seek cattle and horses"— by this he obtains for them indeed cattle and horses. "The bright ones, swift for the sake of heroes"—
the sacrifice, indeed, is the bright one.
Offspring and a hero.
By this [offering], he secures for them both sacrifice and offspring.
For two co-sacrificers, he should use "For you two indeed are the lords of heaven" as the opening verse.
By means of this metrical form, he makes these two equal sharers;
thus the blessing of the sacrifice reaches them equally. 29-90 (Ed.:
"O Indra and Soma, lords of cattle, you who are masters, cause our prayers to swell!
For indeed, Indra and Soma desired, "May we attain sovereignty and overlordship over all creatures.
They saw this introductory verse (*pratipad*).
With that [sāman], the two of them praised. Thereupon, they indeed attained sovereignty and overlordship over all creatures.
He who praises with this introductory verse (pratipad) attains sovereignty and overlordship over his own people.
One whose kinship is with a Rājanya should use "O Indu, for Indra accompanied by the Maruts" as the introductory verse;
for the Rājanya belongs to Indra,
and the subjects belong to the Maruts.
Thus they make the people (viś) follow the path of the ruling power (kṣatra). Therefore, the people follow the path of the ruling power.
"He who conquers is not conquered," so it is said.
He indeed conquers and is not conquered;
he strikes the enemy by attacking him;
having attacked the enemy, he indeed slays him who was to be slain by another.
No enemy rises up against him.
"Flow on, thou winner of thousands," he says;
for he who conquers everything indeed triumphs.
The All-conqueror conquers everything; he who praises with this introductory verse (*pratipad*) is victorious. 30-91 (Ed.:
"Driving away the adversaries, he purifies himself"—this one should make the introductory verse for one who is being accused.
Indeed, adversaries who are displeasing attend him whom they accuse; [with this verse] he strikes away the evil adversaries.
"O Soma, [go] away from the stingy ones," he says.
For those whom they accuse follow him as if they were stingy ones. "Going to Indra's appointed place," he says.
He whom they curse becomes a non-god, one devoid of sensory power.
By means of this [offering], they make him possessed of sensory power and endowed with the gods.
One who is ill, especially one who has been long ill, should perform the *pratipad* (introductory verse) dedicated to Agni and Varuṇa.
He who is afflicted by illness, or has been long ill, is indeed seized by Agni and Varuṇa.
By means of Agni, they release him from what belongs to Agni; by means of Varuṇa, from what belongs to Varuṇa.
One who desires to lead [the ritual] forward should make that verse the opening (pratipad) in which a shorter one follows a longer one, or a longer one follows a shorter one.
"Either the longer seeks to reach the shorter, or the shorter seeks to reach the longer.
He who knows thus attains the longer by means of the shorter.
One who desires, "May I alone be preeminent among my own people and attain splendor," should take as his introductory verse: "This god is immortal."
"He is this one, he is this one"—thus indeed does he address them for the sake of seniority and preeminence.
He alone becomes the foremost among his own people and attains luster. Yet, there is the danger that another such hero may not be born among his offspring.
"This one alone, and no other than this," so indeed does speech address him. But that is not really so;
for he has said, "The immortal god."

He who, being a hero, does not have a heroic and powerful son born to him is indeed both godless and mortal. But he who, being a hero, has a heroic and powerful son born to him—he is indeed a god and he is immortal.
A heroic and powerful son is born to that hero; he is joined with progeny and is not cut off from it. 31-92 (Ed.: 1,96)
Dhūrgāna |c93 (Ed.:
1,97) |p1 The gods and the asuras contended with one another.
Those gods released the razor-edged thunderbolt, which was Puruṣa himself.
They hurled it at the Asuras;
having driven away the Asuras, it turned back toward the gods.
Therefore the gods were afraid.
Having approached him, they shattered him into three parts.
Having been shattered into three parts, he stood up once more.
Taking hold of him, they gazed around.
They saw the deities and the meters entered into that person.
They said, "Indeed, the deities and the meters have entered this person."
"Or rather, he might follow us into this world with merit, with the results of sacrifices and charitable works, with austerity, and with good deeds.
"Then let us act in such a way that he does not follow us," they said.
"Let us lay evil upon him."
Therefore, they attributed this evil to him:
sleep, lassitude, anger, hunger, the desire for dice, and the desire for women.
These evils indeed cling to a person in this world. [They thought:

"Whoever, having crossed over this [evil], should desire to do what is good in this world—may you, O Agni, make him desirous of wealth in this world. Thus they established Agni in this world, Vāyu in the intermediate space, and Āditya in heaven.
Ugradeva Rājani said: "I do not bear malice toward a human being; for I have heard of three of the gods who were most excellent, yet I bore malice toward them. He was one who bore malice.

For those deities are indeed hostile toward him who acts with hostility toward them; however, those deities are not hostile toward him who knows thus. Moreover, they desire to harm him who desires to harm one who knows thus.
Those gods said, "Let us indeed overcome the Asuras by means of those very deities, the meters, which have entered into man.
They deprived them of their breath by means of the *gāyatrī*, their sight by means of the *triṣṭubh*, their hearing by means of the *jagatī*, and their speech by means of the *anuṣṭubh*.

From this very world they excluded them by means of the *gāyatrī*; from the intermediate space, by means of the *triṣṭubh*; from yonder world, by means of the *jagatī*; and from the cattle, by means of the *anuṣṭubh*.
They excluded them from everything.
Thereupon, the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
He prospers in his own person, and his hateful rival is defeated, for one who knows thus.
Because the gods overthrew the Asuras, that is the "overthrowing" (*dhūstva*) nature of the *dhū*s. He overthrows his hateful rival, for one who knows thus.
When Prajāpati created offspring, he created them by means of the *dhurs* alone. He poured forth semen with the *retasyā*;
he set in motion the breath with the *gāyatrī*, the eye with the *triṣṭubh*, the ear with the *jagatī*, and speech with the *anuṣṭubh*.
He establishes himself by means of the *paṅkti* [verse].
Having become Prajāpati himself, he creates offspring—he who, knowing thus, chants the *dhur*s as the Udgātṛ priest. 34-95 (Ed.:
He sings on the *retasyā* [verse].
He thereby pours forth semen.
He sings as if continuously.
Semen is, as it were, continuous.
He sings as if in secret;
for semen is, as it were, in secret.
He should not touch a *ṛc* verse.
If he were to touch a *ṛc*, he would cut off the seed.
He sings [the *sāman*] with three suppressions (*tryudāsa*).
By the first *udāsa* he grasps the out-breath (*prāṇa*), by the second the in-breath (*apāna*), and by the third the diffused breath (*vyāna*).
He sings with three *udāsas*:
by the first *udāsa* he grasps his own self, by the second his wife, and by the third his offspring.
He sings the *tryudāsā*.
By the first *udāsa*, he ascends this very world; by the second, the intermediate space; by the third, yonder world.
He who, knowing thus, sings the *tryudāsā*, truly conquers for himself the worlds of his rival.
He who would wish to cut off the world of his rival should sing only the *dvyudāsa* [stotra].
His hateful rival perishes quickly, and he himself attains prosperity. However, he is liable to die prematurely.

For he departs from his vital breaths; [this is] for the sake of rising up. He should desire to act in such a way that he may reach a full lifespan, and by another means, he should seek to cut off the world of his rival.
One should sing only with the *tryudāsa* [intonation] and must not utter the *hiṃ* syllable;
for if one were to utter the *hiṃ* syllable, one would sever the seed with the thunderbolt of the *hiṃ* syllable.
Regarding this, they say: "By means of the *hiṃ* syllable, Prajāpati created food for his offspring. If he were not to utter the *hiṃ*, the offspring would be hungry.
Therefore, one should indeed utter the *hiṃ*: *abhāyi dāyivaṃ o yā hiṃ kṣate bhūḥ*."
In that he does not release the *hiṃkāra*, he thereby does not cut off the seed, nor does he pass between [himself and] the *hiṃkāra*.
Regarding this, they also say: "The seed is indeed softer than that, while the *hiṃkāra* is as it were harsher;
one might even cut it with a blade of grass."
At the very moment of the *hiṃ*-utterance, one should mentally contemplate the *hiṃ*-utterance;
thus, one does not interrupt the seed, nor does one pass over the *hiṃ*-utterance.
He makes "bhūḥ" the finale (*nidhana*).
When Prajāpati first uttered speech, he uttered only "bhūḥ.
He created this [earth].
When he makes "bhūḥ" the finale (nidhana), he thereby establishes seed upon this very earth.
Moreover, he thereby causes it to attain prosperity.
He sings the *gāyatrī*.
The Gāyatrī is indeed breath.
He interlocks two of its syllables;
he thereby interlocks the out-breath and the in-breath.
Therefore, the out-breath and the in-breath, being interwoven, move along with living beings both hitherward and thitherward, never becoming exhausted.
He makes "sat" the finale;
for breath indeed is "sat."
In the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself, he thus finds firm support.
He sings the *triṣṭubh* [verse].
The *triṣṭubh*, indeed, is sight.
He illumines two syllables of it; he thereby bestows the two eyes. Therefore, the two eyes are as if yoked together.
He makes "Light" the finale.
Light is indeed sight;
thus he establishes himself in sight.
He sings the Jagatī.
The Jagatī is indeed the ear;
he causes its four syllables to shine forth.
He thereby bestows the sense of hearing itself.
There are two ears and two *pariśravaṇas*.
Therefore, although being in one place, he hears all the directions.
Even if he turns away and hears someone speaking behind him,
he makes "iḍā" the finale;
for cattle indeed are the iḍā.
Thus he finds firm support in cattle.
He sings an *anuṣṭubh* verse;
the *anuṣṭubh*, indeed, is speech.
He sings while pushing it toward himself, so that speech does not depart.
For if he were to sing while pushing it away, he would scorch speech, and speech would be likely to depart from him.
Since he sings while pushing it toward himself, he thereby establishes speech within his own self.
He sings both the expressed and the unexpressed pada of that [verse].
By means of the expressed, one indeed enjoys speech; the unexpressed is what sustains it. He who knows thus enjoys speech and lives by means of it.

If he were to sing only the defined (*nirukta*) [syllables], people would indeed speak, but they would not remain silent. On the other hand, if he were to sing the undefined (*anirukta*), people would remain silent and would not speak.
Because he sings both the defined and the undefined in the verses, therefore people both speak and remain silent.
He makes "Speech" the finale.
Speech, indeed, is the Brahman. Thus he establishes himself in the Brahman that is speech.
He sings the *paṅkti* [verse].
The seasons, indeed, are the *paṅkti*.
Of it, he causes six syllables to shine forth.
There are six seasons. Thus, he finds firm support in the seasons. 37-98 (Ed.:
Regarding this they say: "Verily, they create a conflict for the meters when, while it is the *gāyatrī* at the morning pressing, all the meters are sung; thus the offspring become quarrelsome.
He who should desire, "May the offspring prosper in peace," should not separate the *dhurs*.
For he would make the sacrifice headless for the sacrificer and would accept sacrificial gifts through falsehood.
The sacrificer gives the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) with the thought, "May [the priest] not make me a Brahmin.
He should therefore act in such a way that he does not render the sacrifice headless for the sacrificer, nor should he accept the sacrificial fees through falsehood;
he should indeed sing [the vyāhṛtis].
But he who desires to overcome you with this [chant] and is unable to overcome it, meets with misfortune.

If he is unable to overcome the *retasyā*, he himself becomes seedless, and seedless embryos are born. If he is unable to overcome the *gāyatrī*, he himself becomes prone to death, and dead embryos are born.

If he is unable to sing out the *triṣṭubh*, he becomes blind himself, and blind children are born. If he is unable to sing out the *jagatī*, he becomes deaf himself, and deaf children are born. If he is unable to sing out the *anuṣṭubh*, he becomes tongueless himself, and tongueless children are born.
If one is unable to sing the *paṅkti* [verse] separately, the seasons become confused.
He who should not desire to sing them separately should sing them with their form hidden from view.
However, the *retasyā* is sung in both ways. 38-99 (Ed.: 1,103)
When the *gāyatrī* has been introduced, while singing the *gāyatra* chant itself, he should mentally go to the earth;
he should breathe out and breathe in.
He makes "sat" the finale.
Thus he sings it with its form in a hidden manner.
When the *prastāva* has been chanted on a *triṣṭubh*, he should go mentally to the intermediate space while singing the *gāyatra* itself.
One should desire to see with the eyes;
he makes "Light" the *nidhana*.
Thus, he sings it by means of its form in a hidden manner.
When the *jagatī* has been introduced, while singing the *gāyatra* chant itself, he should mentally go toward the quarters and the cattle;
he should listen with his ears alone.
He makes "iḍā" the *nidhana*.
He thus sings her with that form which is beyond the reach of sight.
When the *prastāva* has been chanted on an *anuṣṭubh*, while singing the *gāyatra* melody itself, he should go mentally to heaven;
singing it with his voice, he makes "Speech" (*vāk*) the *nidhana*.
Thus he sings it by means of its hidden form.
When the *paṅkti* has been introduced, while singing the *gāyatra* itself, he should mentally traverse the seasons;
thus he sings it by means of its hidden form.
He sings this final triplet quickly;
for this triplet is indeed generative. He who knows thus is quickly procreated with offspring and cattle.
When Prajāpati created offspring, he created them by means of this very triplet:
"O Sage, your flowing streams have been released, O powerful one," with these words he created them in successive streams;
and with "they have been released through the sheep's wool," he created them.
He was afraid that they, once created, would spill away.
He saw this last [verse], containing the word "ocean" (*samudra*).
With it—[beginning with] "O drops, toward the ocean"—he enclosed them on all sides with the ocean.
These [sacrificial portions] of his are not cast away; his wealth is not cast away by one who knows thus. They have gone to the womb of the Cosmic Order (ṛta). They go.
The house is indeed the womb of *ṛta*. From this very syllable (*akṣara*), through its creative power (*kratu*), born creatures go forth and return again. 39-100 (Ed.:
The gods and the Asuras contended for these worlds, for this world-habitation.
Those gods desired: "May we conquer these worlds; may we conquer the Asuras, our rivals and enemies."
They saw these *ājya* chants;
they praised with them,
and by means of them, they won these worlds.
By means of the offering to Agni, they won this very world; by that to Mitra and Varuṇa, the intermediate space; by that to Indra, yonder world; and by that to Indra and Agni, the quarters.
Because they won these worlds, that is the reason for the *ājya* (clarified butter) nature of the *ājya* hymns.
He who knows thus wins these worlds; he wins his rival, the hateful enemy.
Those gods said, "Let us divide these [worlds].
They could not reach an agreement regarding their division.
They said, "Let us run a race toward them, making the mountain the goal."

Because they said, "Let us run a race for them," that constitutes their second reason for being called *ājya*. And because they made the mountain their goal (*kāṣṭhā*), therefore that mountain is named Kāṣṭha.
They were created foot by foot.
Of them, Agni won the first, then Mitra and Varuṇa, then Indra.
Then there was one that remained unwon.
Indra knew: "Agni will indeed conquer this.
He said: "O Agni, whichever of us two shall conquer this, let that be common to us both. "So be it," [replied Agni].
Agni won that;
it became common to both of them: one had a stotra of one and a half [verses], the other had one of one and a half;
the sacrifice belongs to Indra and Agni.
He who thus knows these *ujjitīs* of the gods, wherever he desires, "May I win here," there he wins.

Regarding this they say: "Since all the *ājya* chants have the same finale (*nidhana*), by what means are they kept from being redundant? One should say: "By having different deities; therefore they are not redundant."
Moreover, if he should say, "Because they are of various forms," it is for that very reason.
These, indeed, are the domestic animals.
Because they chant the Ājya-stotras within the Sadas, therefore domestic animals have their dwellings within the village.
In the *parācī* verses, however, [they chant] with a return [to the beginning].
Therefore, domestic animals set out in the morning facing away [from home], and they return in the evening.
They chant in verses of various forms.
Therefore, domestic animals are of various forms;
they chant over verses addressed to various deities.
Therefore, domestic animals return to their respective homes in the evening, each according to its own kind.
The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle, yet for a long time they did not prevail.
This entire world belonged to those Asuras.
Then, among the gods, there was only one syllable, namely Speech (vāc).
Agni said, "I have indeed perceived this, how I shall conquer this.
They said, "In that case, speak it!"
He said, "Having brought all this together by means of the syllable (akṣara), let us attach burden to burden.
Because he said, "Having brought all this together by means of the syllable, let us attach burden to burden," that is the *ājyadhū* (the burden of the *ājya*); such is your nature.
They, having brought all this together by means of the syllable, attached burden to burden.
They conquered them.
He who knows thus conquers his rival, the hateful enemy. If he should sing out the other *dhur*s, he should likewise sing out the *ājya-dhur*s.

If one who knows this should say, when two villages are at war, "I place you together with the syllable (*akṣara*)," he indeed conquers that village as the superior village. Moreover, in whichever village such a knower resides, he likewise conquers that village.
Those gods said, "Let us divide these [worlds] among ourselves."
When they were divided, they did not obtain equal portions.
They said, "Let us run a race for them, making the mountain the goal.
Because they said, "Let us run a race for them," that is their second reason for being called *ājya*.
And because they made the mountain their goal (*kāṣṭhā*), therefore that mountain is named Kāṣṭha.
All of them were created at one and the same time.
Among them, Agni alone won.
As he was departing, his axle broke while he had not yet reached his destination.
His chariot wheel fell and rolled around the end of its casing, leaving a black mark.
They looked at him and said, "This one will surely become an eater of food and the most excellent; indeed, evil shall revolve around him.
He who, knowing this, turns [the bowl] away, becomes an eater of food and the most excellent among his own people;
moreover, they cause that very evil of his to revolve away.
Having won, that Agni ran away.
Indra said to him, "Let there be a share for both of us.
He replied, "No."
"Whatever one among those who have taken wives acquires, that indeed belongs to all of them together; let it be ours together," he said. "No," he replied.
"Then look upon me with favor," [the other said].
He looked down at him.

He said, "Do not look down at me for the sake of conciliation; let there be union between us. [The other replied,] "Whatever indeed I shall look down upon, with that very thing there shall be union for me."
"No," he said, "you looked upon me with favor; it was indeed together that we both came into being.
"Then let us two ask [the gods]," they said.
The two of them asked Prajāpati.
Prajāpati said, "Indeed, you looked upon him for the sake of conciliation; he belonged to both of you together. They replied, "So be it."
That became common to the two of them: one had a stotra of one and a half [verses], and the other had a stotra of one and a half.
The sacrifice belongs to Indra and Agni.
Mitra and Varuṇa, the out-breath and the in-breath, departed from the cattle, thinking to themselves, "The cattle will not breathe along with us, nor along with our two [breaths]."
Those cattle lay there breathless, bloated with air.
Then they reported this to Mitra and Varuṇa: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, the out-breath and the in-breath have departed from the cattle; thus they lie here breathless, bloated with air.
The two of them, having approached, said: "Let the cattle breathe through us two."
"By us two, by means of the two *anuvākyās*," they said.
For them, they prepared this *ājya* offering for Mitra and Varuṇa;
from that, indeed, cattle breathed through them.

He who thus knows this victory of Agni, wherever he desires, "May I win here," there he wins. And he who knows this prosperity of Indra, wherever he desires, "May I be prosperous," there he becomes prosperous.
And he who knows this arrangement of Mitra and Varuṇa, wherever he desires, "May it be arranged for me here," there it is arranged for him. 44-105 (Ed.: 1,109)
Indeed, all these *ājya* chants belong to Indra and Agni;
they chant over verses addressed to Agni, and thereby [the rite] belongs to Agni.
The *gāyatrī* is the metre; therefore it belongs to Agni. The fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*) is the chant; therefore it belongs to Indra.
Thus, they chant this very [laud] dedicated to Indra and Agni in the verses addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa; therefore it belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa.
The metre is the gāyatrī; therefore it belongs to Agni. The stoma is the pañcadaśa; therefore it belongs to Indra.
Thus, although this [sāman] belongs to both Indra and Agni, they chant it upon verses addressed to Indra; therefore it belongs to Indra.
The *gāyatrī* is the metre; therefore it belongs to Agni. The *pañcadaśa* is the *stoma*; therefore it belongs to Indra.
Thus, this [sāman] belongs to both Indra and Agni; they chant it upon verses addressed to Indra and Agni, and therefore it belongs to Indra and Agni.
The metre is the gāyatrī; therefore it belongs to Agni. The stoma is the pañcadaśa; therefore it belongs to Indra.
Thus, this indeed belongs to both Indra and Agni.
Indra and Agni are the deities of the sacrifice.
Thus, at the morning pressing, they establish the sacrifice in its own deity. 45-106 (Ed.:
1,110) The Rule for Singing the Gāyatra (Bar: 107-111; Ed.: 1,111-115).
Prajāpati created offspring;
he created them without breath.
Into them he placed vital breath by means of this very *sāman*. The *gāyatra* is indeed vital breath;
he who knows thus reaches a full lifespan.
Seeking to find his vital breath (*prāṇa*), those *rakṣas* followed after him. He protected himself by singing this very *sāman*.
Because he protected himself while singing (*gāyan*), that is the reason for the *gāyatra* nature of the *gāyatra*.
He who knows this is rescued from all evil. That [chant] should be sung as if rising upward;
for the heavenly world is indeed situated above.
It is for the attainment of the heavenly world itself.
It should be sung with three turns;
for these worlds are indeed three.
For the attainment of these worlds, it should be sung with three introductory exclamations;
for there are indeed three vital breaths: prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna.
For the continuity of these [breaths].
For him who knows thus, the out-breath (prāṇa), the in-breath (apāna), and the diffused breath (vyāna) are extended. It should be sung with three turns.
There are indeed these three worlds. For the continuity of these worlds—these worlds extend for him who knows thus. 46-107 (Ed.: 1,111)
"But they say that one must not approach that which has the ancestors as its deity.
For that which causes exhaustion is indeed what has the ancestors as its deity for him.
If he should become exhausted midway, he should breathe out at the middle of the *ṛc*.
The *ṛc* is indeed breath;
the *gāyatra* is breath.
This is in the midst of the breath; he brings the breath into equilibrium.
If he should go astray from the *ṛc*, he should sing the *prāṇa-apāna-vyāna* [hymn].
"Prāṇa" consists of two syllables.
"Apāna"—three times.
"Vyāna"—three times.
That makes eight.
The *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables. Therefore, he does not depart from the *gāyatrī*. One must not go into the forest without having reached the *sāman*.
Whosoever indeed enters the forest interior of the *sāman* either suffers total loss or perishes.
This is the forest interior of the *sāman*: when the *prastāva* is taken up without being chanted (*anabhisvarita*).
One should chant the *udgītha* after having completed it with the *svara*.
This indeed is the own-nature of the *sāman*, namely the tone (*svara*). By means of its own nature, he thus causes it to prosper. This indeed is the food of the *sāman*, namely the tone.
Verily, by means of food he thus causes it to prosper.
That which is tone is indeed the abode of the Sāman; verily, by means of its abode, he thus causes it to prosper.
This, indeed, is the dear abode of the *sāman*, namely the tone (*svara*). By means of its own dear abode, he thus causes it to prosper. 47-108 (Ed.:
The oblation of the sacrifice did not reach the gods.
Prajāpati considered: "How indeed might the oblation of the sacrifice reach the gods?
He extracted these two syllables from the Gāyatrī.
That very [syllable] became the two-syllabled *vaṣaṭ*-call.
From that, the oblation of the sacrifice went to the gods.
Indeed, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is food.
Food belongs to him who knows thus.
Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra;
these two syllables were its two wheels.
This [cup] is indeed a thunderbolt. He who should touch these [cups] would be touching a thunderbolt.
Verily, he who approaches one thing that has been milked with another thing that has been milked does not swell.
Now, he who approaches the milk from that which has been milked becomes nourished.
Indeed, he who approaches these two syllables approaches the milk from that which has been milked. Therefore, one should not approach these two syllables.

For one for whom every *gāyatrī* is sung, everything is obtained in his house. For one by whom it is sung deficiently, he is liable to become harsh. Having held back one or another syllable, he should proceed with the twenty-fourth [verse] of the speech.
Neither is his *gāyatrī* sung deficient, nor does it fail to touch [the goal].
He who knows the *aṃśu* as the single syllable becomes an eater of food and the most excellent among his own people.
Moreover, he himself sings the *udgītha* for that assembly.
Speech, indeed, is the *aṃśu* [stalk], consisting of a single syllable;
that is the *gāyatra*.
Of the Gāyatrī when it has been introduced, that which is the syllable following the first is the sacrificial stake (sthāṇu).
Whoever begins by chanting that [syllable] seizes the stake. And whoever carries it away makes the Gāyatrī defective.
If the *gāyatrī* has a flaw, the sacrifice flows away following it; following the sacrifice, the sacrificer; and following the sacrificer, his offspring.
Sadhryaśva Taigmāyudhi used to say: "Who indeed today will press upon the two 'rasadihas' on my chest?
These two, indeed, are the two 'rasadihas,' namely the two final syllables of the *gāyatrī*.
When he begins the *udgītha* for you, [the breath] flows away from the essence in the heart; it sinks down into the chest. He who removes these two makes a breach in the *gāyatrī*.
Following the breached *gāyatrī*, the sacrifice flows away; following the sacrifice, the sacrificer; and following the sacrificer, his offspring. 49-110 (Ed.: 1,114)
Having extracted all those syllables, he should place speech [within them];
for speech is indeed Brahman.

Just as one might cross over thorny brambles after covering them with a hide, even so, having crushed the sacrificial post (yajñasthāṇu) with speech and the sacred word (brahman), he passes safely beyond it and does not meet with misfortune.
The Pratihartṛ priest indeed cuts himself off from the Sāman if he does not perform the *pratihāra* for the Gāyatra.
He should perform the *hiṃkāra* mentally while the [Sāman] is being introduced (*prastūyamāna*).
He should say, "O Speech, turn away!

In this way, he is not cut off from the *sāman* and does not meet with misfortune. Indeed, for one who knows the syllable that possesses the *aṃśu*, the *aṃśumatī* verses, when joined together, carry him forward.
Speech, indeed, is the syllable.
Of it, breath is the ray.
He who knows this, the *aṃśumatī* [rays] carry him along when they are joined together. 50-111 (Ed.: 1,115)
The Midday Pressing (Mādhyaṃdinasavana) (Bar: 112–151; Ed.: 1,116–155).
The Mādhyaṃdinapavamāna Stotra (Bar: 112–123; Ed.: 1,116–127). 112 (Ed.: 1,116).
The *pratipad* verses contain the word "Marutvat.
They draw the cup for Indra accompanied by the Maruts (*marutvant*), for it was Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, who slew Vṛtra; [this is] for the sake of the slaying of Vṛtra.
"High is thy birth, O Soma-juice" (*uccā te jātam andhasaḥ*)—thus they become verses containing the word "andhas" (Soma-juice).
The day, indeed, is blind; the commencement is from the day itself.
The sacrifice, indeed, is blind.
It is indeed the commencement of the sacrifice.
"There are three draughts (*andhas*) in the sacrifice," so the ancient Brahmins used to reflect, namely: *uccā te jātam andhasā*, *vasor mandānam andhasaḥ*, and *purojitī vo andhasaḥ*.
There are three enjoyments in the animal sacrifices: in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.
By this very means, he wins them.
These two worlds, being together, went apart; nothing whatsoever remained common to them.
Those gods and men were hungry.
For the gods live by what is given from here, and men by what is given from yonder.
Prajāpati saw these *ṛc* verses: "High is thy birth, O juice... and so forth.
With the words "He has risen," he carried the oblation from here to the gods;
with the words "Seated in heaven, he has given to the earth," he caused rain to fall from yonder.
He thus made these two worlds dwell together.
These two caused his desire to overflow;
these two worlds cause the desire of one who knows this to overflow.
Regarding those [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa already explained. 1-112 (Ed.: 1,116)
