Then follows the āmahīyava [sāman]. Prajāpati created offspring.
He created them without food.
Craving food, they began to devour one another.
Prajāpati reflected: "How can these creatures of mine not eat one another?"
He saw this Sāman.
With it he bestowed food upon them; indeed, he bestowed rain by means of the [Sāman] without a finale (*apranidhana*). He rained for them, but he did not withhold it.
He saw this *nidhana*;
he approached it;
from that, he drew them upward.
Indeed, by the power of this *sāman*, Parjanya both rains and holds back the rain.
He who should desire rain should chant with this very [sāman] that lacks a final *nidhana*;
Parjanya will indeed become a rain-giver for him.
If it should rain excessively, he should resort to this very *nidhana*. Parjanya pours rain for him and he draws [the water] up for him, who knows thus.

Because the offspring, being well-satisfied, honored him, that is the reason for the *āmahīyava*’s name *āmahīyavatva*. His wives, being well-satisfied, honor him as one who is well-satisfied, provided he knows this.
They, finding food, did not turn away from him.
They were as if at a shared feast.
For food is indeed prosperity. He grieved.
He did not diminish.
He reflected: "How indeed might I create these creatures so that, once created, they would not disregard me?
He saw this *sāman*.
Therefore, he did not praise. [2-113] (Ed.:
1,118) He approached the *nidhana* with the thought, "I shall praise. [1]
He gratified them;
they came under his control.
He who knows thus gratifies his hateful rivals and brings his own people under his control.

Because she saw them while they were being honored (*āmahīyamānā*), that is the reason for the *āmahīyava*’s name *āmahīyavatva*. Furthermore, because he honored them after bringing them under his control (*vaśe kṛtvā*), that too is the reason for the *āmahīyava*’s name *āmahīyavatva*.
He who knows thus brings his own people under his control and exalts himself.
Therefore, if those who are his own subjects should be as if unsubdued, he should recite this very [text] while sitting in their midst;
thus he brings them under his control.
Now, the people of Uttarakuru say that the Kurus and Pañcālas consume Soma for which no *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
The *hotṛ* utters the *vaṣaṭ* call for each individual deity, while the *udgātṛ* does so for all of them together;
for the *udgātṛ* belongs to all the deities.
One should utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with the *nidhana* of the *āmahīyava* chant.
They consume only that Soma over which the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
Regarding this, Mārja Śailana used to say: "One indeed gratifies one's rivals by means of the *nidhana*.
One should utter the *vaṣaṭ* before the *nidhana*, saying: "Vauṣaṭ! O Earth, give!"
He consumes only that Soma which has been consecrated with the *vaṣaṭ* call. 3-114 (Ed.:
1,119) |p1 He who knows the udder of the sacrifice milks the sacrifice.
The Pavamāna is indeed the sacrifice.
Of it, the Gāyatrī is the udder.
One should make the Gāyatrī consist of four verses.
Verily, he thereby provides the udder for the sacrifice and milks the sacrifice.
He who knows the support of the sacrifice establishes the sacrifice; he stands firm by himself.
The Pavamāna is indeed the sacrifice.
The Gāyatrī is its very foundation.
One should make the Gāyatrī consist of four verses;
thereby, one establishes the foundation of the sacrifice itself.
He establishes the sacrifice; he stands firm by his own self.

With the verses, "High is thy birth through the soma-juice," "Following its ancient splendor," and "With these [verses] the noble one goes to all [the worlds]," he should perform the *gāyatra* chant. In those [verses], he should perform the *āmahīyava*.
In that he places a *dhāyyā* as the fourth [verse], by that it becomes a four-verse hymn.
By means of the *pratitiṣṭhīs*, he establishes the sacrifice; he himself stands firm. 4-115 (Ed.:
Three meters indeed carry the sacrifice: the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī.
To them, this Anuṣṭubh is attached from the end.
By means of it, the gods desired to go to the heavenly world.
They did not pervade [the world] with it.
They placed four-footed animals upon it—the cow, the horse, the goat, and the sheep.
With it, they pervaded [the world].
They said, "Having gone to the heavenly world, this [meter] has indeed become the Bṛhatī, for by it we have pervaded this [world].
That is precisely the reason for the Bṛhatī's name as Bṛhatī. Before that, there was no meter named Bṛhatī.
This Bṛhatī is indeed cattle.
He intones the Prastāva with that [syllable] with which they approach the Nidhana;
thus he takes up the beginning once again.
Therefore, from whatever [source] animals are born, from that they arise;
they are born again from that very same source.
One should not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with the *bṛhatī* metre, lest there be a failure to release the animals.
If one were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* with the *bṛhatī*, one would strike away the cattle with the *vajra*-like *vaṣaṭ*-call.
The gods, having slain the Asuras, considered themselves as if unpurified and impure.
They desired, "May we be purified, fit for sacrifice, and cooked; may we go to the heavenly world.
They saw these *ṛc* verses and purified themselves with them.
"Being purified, O Soma, with your stream, you flow, clothing yourself in the waters," he says.
The waters are indeed the filter; by means of the waters, they purified him.
"O bearer of jewels, you sit upon the womb of Ṛta"—
Ṛta is indeed the intermediate space;
by this [verse], they passed beyond the intermediate space.
"The well, the golden god"—
the well, the god, is yonder world;
it was by means of this [verse] that they approached yonder world for worship.
Thereupon, indeed, they became purified, fit for sacrifice, and cooked; they went to the heavenly world.
One who praises with these *ṛc*s becomes purified, fit for sacrifice, and cooked; he goes to the heavenly world. 6-117 (Ed.:
Among them is the Raurava. Agni, indeed, was Ruru; he saw this Sāman.
Because Agni, being Ruru, saw this Sāman, that is the reason for the name Raurava of the Raurava.
Ruru, being old and desiring cattle, performed austerities. He saw this Sāman;
with it, he praised.
He approached this *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
from it, he indeed obtained cattle.
This is a Sāman pertaining to cattle;
he who knows thus secures cattle for himself and becomes rich in cattle.
Furthermore, because the aged Ruru saw it, it is therefore called the Raurava.
Then follows the Yaudhājaya.
Indra, while living through battle, saw this *sāman*. Because Indra, while living through battle, saw this *sāman*, that is the reason for the name Yaudhājaya.
He who knows this conquers his hostile rival as if with a weapon.
Yudhājīva Vaiśvāmitra, desiring a firm foundation, performed austerities;
he beheld this Sāman.
He praised with it.
Thereupon, he indeed became firmly established.
This, then, is the *pratiṣṭhā* (establishment) *sāman*.
He who knows thus finds firm support.
Furthermore, because Yudhājīva Vaiśvāmitra saw [this], it is therefore called the Yaudhājaya. 7-118 (Ed.:
By means of the *yaudhājaya* [sāman], the gods, having overwhelmed the Asuras, seized the property of those who were crying out with the *raurava* [sāman].
By means of the *yaudhājaya* alone, one who knows thus, having overwhelmed his hateful rival, seizes the property of that rival as he cries out with the *raurava*.
By means of the *raurava*, the gods ascended upward to the heavenly world.
The Asuras followed after them, crying out "O vā!
The gods perceived this;
they saw this *stobha*.
With that, they struck them down, crying out, "O hā! Vā! It!
The divine spring, the vein, cried out, "O hā! O hā! Vā! It! and they made it touch the earth.
The *sāman* was as if reaching the end; the world of heaven was indeed above.
The Udgātṛ should draw out [the chant] above the *pratihāra* for the attainment of the heavenly world.
With the sound "ṇyāyā au ho vā ho iḍā," having connected it by means of the tone itself, he attains the heavenly world.
Indeed, there are just so many *sāmans*, just so much is the construction of the *sāman*, and just so much is the kinship of the *sāman*. It is the *svāra* [sāman].
The *svāra* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Now follows the *nidhanavat* [chant].
The *nidhana* is indeed the self (*ātman*). Now follows the *aiḍa*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
He thus joins together his own vital breath, himself, and those cattle.
For one who knows this, the chant is performed with the complete fulfillment of the *sāman* and with the entire kinship of the *sāman*. 8-119 (Ed.: 1,123)
There are indeed only two kinds of *sāman*: that which possesses *stobha* and that which is without *stobha*.
Of these two, that which possesses *stobha* is the *kṣatra*.
Now, that which is without *stobhas* is the Brahman;
he who knows thus secures both the Brahman and the Kṣatra.
Furthermore, the Yaudhājaya with three *nidhanas* is for the fulfillment of the *savana*s.
By means of the *pavamāna*, food is indeed bestowed upon the gods.
That [sāman] has its *nidhana* in the middle; this is for the sake of distinguishing it as food.
For if all food were bestowed upon the gods, that food would not remain here for humans and cattle to subsist upon.
In that it has the *nidhana* in the middle, it is for the sake of the excellence of food.

Indeed, the Asuras desired to cause a destruction of the sacrifice of the gods; at whatever time they do not chant or recite during the time of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), the gods became aware of that.
They saw this Sāman. They praised with it.
By means of the first *nidhana*, they encompassed the morning pressing; by the second, the midday pressing; and by the third, the third pressing.
He raised up those very same vajras;
the Asuras did not dare to attack those very vajras that had been raised.
Then indeed the gods prevailed, and the Asuras were defeated.
He prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is defeated, he who knows thus. Moreover, that *pavamāna* chant is indeed unprepared in which the *triṇidhana* does not occur.
Therefore, that it contains the *triṇidhana* is for the sake of the successful preparation of the pressings (*savana*).
The gods and the asuras were engaged in conflict, yet for a long time they did not achieve victory.
Bṛhaspati was the domestic priest of the gods, and Uśanas Kāvya was the domestic priest of the asuras.
That which was performed as the Brahman on the lower side was performed on the upper side. That same Brahman did not distinguish itself.
The Gandharva Triśīrṣan understood their victory.
He became envious. Within the waters, he had a city on ships drifting about. Indra perceived this: "Triśīrṣan indeed knows the secret of victory."
He approached his wife for the sake of this very victory.
He said to her, "Ask your husband: 'Among these gods and asuras who have been at war for so long, which of them will be victorious?
And so, while they were conversing, he arrived.
He indeed clung to that very navel-ring, having become either a leech or a grass-leech.
She asked her husband: "These gods and asuras have been at war for a long time; which of them will be victorious? 10-121 (Ed.:
"Speak loudly," he said. "The earth indeed has ears.
Even now, people say this: "Speak loudly; the earth indeed has ears.
"No," he said. "Speak [just as you are]."
He said: "These two Brahmins know this [sacrifice] equally: Bṛhaspati among the gods and Uśanas Kāvya among the Asuras.
Whatever those two perform, that comes out exactly the same. Whatever oblations one offers, those the other [offers]."
Having come together, they dispersed again each according to their own way.
"Whichever of the two shall join whichever of them, those shall be victorious," [said the gods].
Then Indra, having understood that, became a parrot and flew up.
Seeing him flying away, he said: "Those for whom this one with green wings flies shall be victorious.
He went to Uśanas Kāvya among the Asuras. He said to him: "O Seer, whom do you strengthen—this people? You indeed belong to us, or we to you; turn back toward us!"
"Tell me," he said, "with what do you invite me?
"With those wish-fulfilling cows belonging to Virocana, the son of Prahlāda," [the other] replied.
And with those very cows, they both ran away.
The Asuras pursued those two;
they followed after them.
He said, "O seer, these Asuras have indeed come after us."
"Indeed, let us do so," he said, "so that these [demons] shall not follow after us.
They both agreed to this. 11–122 (Ed.:

"Armed with good weapons, the divine *indu* flows clear, slaying the malevolent and guarding the strongholds; he is the father of the gods, their progenitor, most skillful, the pillar of heaven, and the support of the earth.
Thus [he said]. He raised himself up to the pillar of heaven. The Asuras did not surpass him.
The two of them came to the gods with these wish-fulfilling cows.

When they had arrived, they magnified them [with the verse]: "The seer, the inspired one, the leader of the people, the skillful and wise Uśanas by his poetic insight—he indeed discovered that which was hidden among these, the secret and mysterious name of the cows.
These are the verses pertaining to cattle.

Verily, he secures cattle; he becomes possessed of many cattle, having praised with these verses. Among them is the Auśana hymn. Uśanas Kāvya, indeed, desired an immortal world among the Gandharvas from among the gods.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
Thereupon, he attained immortality among the gods and the world of the Gandharvas.
This is the Sāman known as *lokavid*.
By praising with this, one attains immortality among the gods and the world of the Gandharvas.
Because Uśanas Kāvya perceived it, it is called the *auśana*.
That [hymn] is performed with the *svāra* chant. Indeed, it is by means of the *svāra* that food is finally bestowed upon the gods.
At the end of the *pavamāna*, there is the *ṛksama*.
They do not let the *ṛc* exceed the *sāman*, nor the *sāman* the *ṛc*.
Therefore, the reason they do not chant in this way or that way during the *pavamāna* [laud] is for the sake of its equality and for the sake of making it uniform.
The *gāyatra* [chant] at the beginning has the *anusvāra* following each word (*padānusvāra*), and at the end of the *pavamāna*, the *anusvāra* follows each word.
Therefore, living beings have breath on both sides—both upward and downward.
The *gāyatrī* consists of two *sāman*s;
that which is this downward breath is indeed it.
Therefore, by means of this breath, one performs two things: one produces ash and one produces wind.
The Bṛhatī consists of two syllables;
that which is this forward-moving breath is indeed it.
Therefore, by means of this breath, he performs two functions: he emits seed and he urinates.
The *triṣṭubh* verse has a single *sāman*;
it is the navel itself.
In that [chanting], there is one *sāman*.
Therefore, with this [breath], he performs only one thing: namely, that he breathes out after those who have breathed out their breaths. 12-123 (Ed.:
When Prajāpati created the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans], he first beheld the Bṛhat as the mind;
he uttered the Rathantara as speech.

Because he uttered the *rathantara* after speech, therefore the *rathantara* attained its first union. Then, because he saw the *bṛhat* before the mind, therefore they are called "the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*.
Mind is indeed prior, and then speech.
The mind is indeed the *bṛhat*, speech is the *rathantara*.
The *rathantara* is indeed the *ṛc*, the *bṛhat* is the *sāman*.
The *rathantara* is indeed the spiritual power (*brahman*), the *bṛhat* is the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
This, indeed, is the Rathantara; that is the Bṛhat. That which is as if moving is the Rathantara; that which is established is the Bārhata.
Those animals which have teeth on one side are connected with the *rathantara*;
those which have teeth on both sides are connected with the *bṛhat*.
Indeed, that lightning which strikes crosswise is connected with the *rathantara*.
That [verse] which is upward-facing belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman.

Having gathered together the greatness of the Rathantara, one should chant the udgītha with the Rathantara, saying: "With that greatness of yours which is in Agni, that greatness of yours which is in the waters, that greatness of yours which is in the chariot, that greatness of yours which is in the thunder, and that greatness of yours which is in the wind—with that, become united; O Rathantara, be full of wealth for us!
Thus it becomes full of wealth for the udgātṛ, full of wealth for the sacrificer, and full of wealth for the offspring.
The gods and the Asuras contended.
Those gods created the razor-edged thunderbolt, which was indeed the Puruṣa.
The Asuras overcame him. Having driven away the Asuras, he turned toward the gods;
therefore, the gods were afraid.
Having approached it, they push forward the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans].
This very thunderbolt, with its razor-sharp edge, pushed forward by the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*, is indeed a man.
Whomever one hates, one should place him within the mouth of that [thunderbolt] formed by the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*.
If the Soma sacrifice is connected with the *rathantara*, when the *rathantara* has been chanted, he should say: "Homage to Mother Earth; O *rathantara*, do not harm me!

If the Soma sacrifice is connected with the *bṛhat*, when the *bṛhat* has been chanted, he should say: "I take refuge in Father Heaven; O *bṛhat*, do not harm me! Then he should recite the following consecration:

"Seize the vital breaths of so-and-so with [your] vital breaths! With a sharper axe, seize his life-force and vital breaths! Struck by wrath, strike him down with the staff of fury! Draw the bow and pierce him with the arrow!"
Verily, he places him at the very mouth of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans].
He whom he hates, his vital breath shall abandon before the end of a year.
Verily, he who knows the chariot of the gods becomes a master of the chariot.
The sacrifice is indeed the chariot of the gods.

Its forepart is the *bahiṣpavamāna*; the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] are the two horses; the *ājya* [stotras] are the yoking-thongs; the two *pavamāna* [stotras] are the reins; and the two wings are the [other stotras].
The two side-poles are the Auśanaka and Kāveya; the two shafts are the Naudhasa and Kāleya; the seat is the Vāmadevya; the lap is the Yajñāyajñīya; and he who sits upon it is this very Person.
This indeed is the chariot of the gods. He becomes a charioteer who knows thus.
If the *soma* sacrifice should be based on the *rathaṃtara*, one should not omit the *bṛhat*. If the *soma* sacrifice should be based on the *bṛhat*, one should not omit the *rathaṃtara*.
For the *bṛhat* is indeed milk.
[He sings] the *rathantara*.
When the *prastāva* of the *rathantara* has been chanted, having uttered "ho," he should take up the beginning [of the next section].
Thus, he yokes the *bṛhat* at the very beginning of the *rathantara*.
When the *bṛhat* has been chanted as the *prastāva*, having uttered "ā," he should take up the beginning (*ādi*).
Thus, he yokes the *rathantara* at the head of the *bṛhat*.
He makes the chariot of the gods free from a single horse, establishes the sacrifice, and stands firm by himself.
This *rathantara* is indeed the chariot of the gods.
When the *rathantara* has begun its prelude (*prastāva*), one should touch the earth with both hands, so that there may be no injury to the chariot of the gods.
He chants one syllable as a *stobha*;
therefore, the chariot moves along, coming to rest from spoke to spoke. He chants two syllables as a *stobha*.
The chariot has two sides;
by means of these two sides, he thus establishes the chariot of the gods.
He utters three syllables as a chant.
The sacrificer indeed has two feet;
the self is the third.
Thus, the sacrificer himself becomes firmly established.
Now, there are these three worlds; he thereby attains them.
He utters four syllables as a *stobha*.
There are four quarters;
there are four-footed animals.
Thus he finds firm support in the quarters and in the animals.
He utters five syllables as *stobhas*. The sacrifice is fivefold; cattle are fivefold.
And thus it becomes firmly established in the sacrifice and in the sacrificial animals.
He utters six syllables as a *stobha*.
There are indeed six seasons.
Thus he finds firm support in the seasons;
moreover, there are six meters,
and it is those very meters that he thereby attains.
He chants seven syllables as stobhas.
The Śakvarī verses consist of seven feet; cattle are associated with the Śakvarī.
Thus, he finds firm support in cattle through the *śakvarī* [verse].
Moreover, there are seven meters, each increasing by four syllables;
there are seven vital breaths in the head.
He obtains those very same [syllables];
he utters eight syllables as stobhas;
for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables.
Luster is spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), and the *gāyatrī* is luster; thus he finds firm footing in luster and spiritual splendor.
Moreover, [he finds it] in four-hoofed animals.
He utters nine *stobha* syllables.
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person.
Verily, he thus snatches away the vital breaths of his hateful rival and bestows the vital breaths upon himself;
moreover, he obtains the chant of the Trivṛt Stoma. He utters ten syllables as stobhas.
The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the Virāj is food.
Thus, he establishes himself in the Virāj, that is, in food.
Now, there are ten vital breaths;
he thereby obtains those very ones.
He utters eleven syllables as a *stobha*.
The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables;
the *triṣṭubh* is power and vigor.
Thus, he establishes himself in power and vigor.
He chants twelve syllables as stobhas.
The jagatī indeed consists of twelve syllables;
the jagatī is cattle.
Verily, he thus finds firm support in cattle and in the Jagatī metre;
moreover, there are twelve months, and it is those very months that he thereby attains.
He chants the stobha with thirteen syllables.
That which is the thirteenth month, the intercalary month, that he thereby attains.
He chants the stobha with fourteen syllables.
The year, indeed, consists of fourteen [parts].
He thus establishes himself in the year itself.
He utters fifteen syllables as a *stobha*.
There are fifteen nights in a half-month.
Thus, by [chanting] in half-months, he attains the year.
He chants sixteen syllables as *stobhas*.
Man indeed consists of sixteen parts (*kalā*). By means of those very parts, they carry away the hateful, evil enemy downward;
he attains prosperity for himself.
Moreover, he obtains the chant of the *ṣoḍaśin* stoma itself.
He utters seventeen syllables as *stobhas*.
Prajāpati, indeed, is seventeenfold.
Thus he finds firm support in Prajāpati. 17-128 (Ed.:
1,133) |p1 He should chant this other [verse] as a *stobha*.
One should sing only the *ṛc* verse.
In that he sings only the *ṛc*, he does not depart from the form of the *rathantara*;
for the *ṛc* is the *rathantara*, and the *sāman* is the *bṛhat*.
If, however, he should chant the *stobha*, he should chant it with exactly eight syllables.
Two of these are directed toward the calf;
he should look toward the one that beholds the sun (*svardṛś*), so that his sight may not be torn away.

If he were to respond with *yad īśānam indra*, the Lord (*īśāna*) would become envious of the cattle of the sacrificer. But because he responds with *yac chānam indra*, the Lord does not become envious of the sacrificer's cattle; the subjects remain peaceful and prosper.
At the response, at the point of the response, the Udgātṛ should say *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *rathantara* is their abode.
Thus, he establishes these cattle in their very abode.
He should say, "Of those that stand not."

If he were to say, "of that which stands," his prosperity would be liable to remain stationary. But when he says, "of that which does not stand," his prosperity does not remain stationary; many depart from him by means of his own movement.
He should transpose the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans].
If one were not to separate the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, they would crush the offspring and the cattle, just as two great trees, having come together, crush each other's branches.
"Ho vā hā" is the Bṛhat; "o vā hā" is the Rathantara.
Thus, he separates the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.
He who knows thus turns away from evil. 18-129 (Ed.:
1,134) |p1 One who desires to become such as he is should approach [the teacher] in this manner.
In this way, he who knows thus becomes possessed of rivals; he himself prospers, while his hateful rival is defeated.
When the Bṛhat and Rathantara were created, all creatures and cattle trembled with fear because of them.

The two of them scrutinized themselves, thinking, "What indeed is this cruel thing within ourselves, out of fear of which creatures and cattle tremble? They perceived it to be in the *nidhana* [the finale].
Having placed it in the forest, they returned to the village.
That very place became a salt-waste created by itself.
Therefore they say: "One should not dwell upon a salt-waste created by oneself; for he who dwells upon a salt-waste created by himself is liable to become more wretched.
Indeed, this [place] was consumed by the *nidhana*s of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [sāmans].
Indeed, these two, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, are [sāmans] that have no *nidhana* when sung in the village (*grāma*).
One may certainly chant with these two, even though they lack a *nidhana*, while in the village.
He begins the *prastāva* with an eight-syllable [phrase].
He begins the two subsequent [sections] with two-syllable [phrases], for the sake of advancing and to prevent failure.
He begins the *prastāva* with an eight-syllable [phrase].
He begins the *prastāva* with two syllables on the subsequent [verse].
Thus, he places the two-footed man upon the eight-hoofed animals.
Therefore, the two-footed man stands upon the eight-hoofed animals.
He begins the *prastāva* with an eight-syllable [phrase].
He begins the two subsequent [sections] with two-syllable [phrases]. Thus, they amount to twelve.
Twelve months are a year;
the year is Prajāpati, the sacrifice.
By this, he attains the year, Prajāpati, and the sacrifice.
He performs the Rathantara on the syllables.
Therefore, a chariot moves along, coming to rest at every step.
By means of the Rathantara, the gods, having hemmed in the Asuras, crushed them with the Bṛhat as if with a net.
Having enveloped his hateful rival with the *rathantara* [chant] alone, he overturns him like a net with the *bṛhat* [chant], he who knows thus.
With the *rathantara*, indeed, the gods went upward to the heavenly world.
Those Asuras and Rakṣases obstructed them from these worlds by means of ninety-nine [obstructions].
They were indeed called *rathāḥ*.
Those gods, having praised with the *rathaṃtara* alone and having mounted the *rathaṃtara*, went to the heavenly world.
They said, "We have indeed crossed over these *rathas*."
That indeed is the *rathantara*-ness of the *rathantara*.
He who knows thus overcomes his hateful rival. 20-131 (Ed.:
The chariot is indeed hunger, and the *rathaṃtara* is food. With food they strike down hunger;
having struck down each instance of hunger with food, they ascend to the heavenly world.
By means of the Bṛhat, the gods indeed desired to go to the heavenly world; with it they did not succeed.
They then added the Uṣṇih and Kakubh meters to it.
They pervaded [the world] with it.
Having gone to the heavenly world, they said: "Truly great (bṛhat) has this become, by which we have pervaded the heavenly world. That indeed is the greatness (bṛhattva) of the Bṛhat[-sāman].
One who desires heaven should ascend twelve *bṛhatī* ascents.
One who desires rain should agitate the ocean.
For as many syllables as there are in the *bṛhatī*, the *uṣṇih*, and the *kakubh*, so far from here is the heavenly world.
He who knows thus attains the heavenly world. 21-132 (Ed.: 1,136) |c133 (Ed.: 1,137) |p1 That [is] the Great.
The mind is the *bṛhat*.
The *prastāva* consists of twelve syllables; for such is the *sāman*.
Twelve months are a year;
the year is the *sāman*. There are three ascents of the *bṛhatī*, which are these very worlds.
These, moreover, become nine; they are the vital breaths themselves.
The mind is the tenth.
There are twelve bodies of the Bṛhatī; they are the months themselves.
The months are the rays;
the rays are the Maruts;
by them that sun is supported.
He who knows this thus, wherever he desires, "May I be established here," there he is established.
Verily, he who knows the *bārhatam* foot of the *bṛhatī* becomes wide-spread with offspring and cattle;
for the *bārhatam* foot of the *bṛhatī* consists of twelve syllables.
That should be sung as if drawing it together. He who knows the *trivṛt* [stoma] as contained within the *bṛhatī*, along with the gods and the *proḍha*, attains the measure of sovereignty.
Indeed, the *trivṛt* along with the gods is the ascent of the *bṛhatī*.
For one who knows this, although he is a Brahmin, there is the manifestation of a Kṣatriya.
Indra, having struck Vṛtra with his thunderbolt, thinking "I have not destroyed him," went to the furthest distance.
Prajāpati desired him, thinking, "May he come from that place."
He called out to him, "Tam o ho! He became [the king].
One should therefore make a Rājanya by means of the very words "O ho" for the sake of securing [his power].
He indeed goes downward; [this is] the Vāmadevya. 22-133 (Ed.: 1,137);
The gods, when they were about to go forth to battle against the Asuras, said: "Let us lay aside whatever excellent wealth we have and fight; let us run toward whatever being we may encounter today.
Cattle, indeed, were their excellent wealth.
Having laid that aside, they went forth to battle.
Those gods conquered the Asuras. Having been victorious, they were returning, and they came upon a single being. They did not recognize it, [thinking], "This is my desirable portion; this is mine."
They said, "Let us divide this. They could not reach an agreement on its division.
They said, "Let us ask Prajāpati himself."
They asked Prajāpati.
Prajāpati said: "This is indeed the desirable wealth of all of you; they will praise with this together for all of you, and it will reach all of you. Do not divide it among yourselves.
In that they praise in *gāyatrī* verses, by that it belongs to Agni.
For Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature.
In that [the midday pressing] has the *pṛṣṭha* chant, it belongs to Indra;
in that they praise with verses containing the word "kava," it belongs to Prajāpati.
In that it is undefined, it belongs to the Viśvedevas;
in that they chant for Mitra and Varuṇa, it belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa;
and this Vāmadevya is indeed cattle.
He should chant the *udgītha* without moving, so that cattle may not be lost.
If he were to chant while moving, he would cause the cattle to be lost.
Regarding this they say: "He should chant while covered, without moving, lest a bystander should utter a cry against him."
That which is the form of the beneficiary should chant the *udgītha* while remaining covered and motionless. 23-134 (Ed.:
In former times, they used to place the axle upon the heads of the people, thinking:
"Whoever shall not let it fall while singing the *udgītha*, he shall sing the *udgītha* for us. But that was merely a form of mockery.
One should certainly sing it as *kāmam*.
He sings its three syllables concealed;
for these worlds are indeed three.
Prajāpati is the Vāmadevya;
Prajāpati is the leader of the worlds.
He who is the leader of the worlds shall lead us to the worlds.
In the *vāmadevya* chant, one should also utter the *ṛṣabha* syllable:
"sau hau ho vā. This indeed is the *ṛṣabha*.
The Vāmadevya is the womb;
the bull is the procreative organ.
Thus, he joins the procreative organ to the womb in the very place of procreation, for the sake of generation.
That [hymn] should be sung as if it were hidden from view;
one should not touch the verse,
for the Vāmadevya is indeed the vital breath.
If he should touch a verse, it would be just as if a bird flying through the air were to strike a tree; that is exactly like that.
He should not move between the two footprints.
If he were to move between the two footprints, it would be just as if a pitfall were to fall upon him; that is exactly like that.
Because one begins by inhaling while taking up the subsequent word;
just as one steps forward by means of stepping, having stepped forward, one exhales—such is that. 24-135 (Ed.:
This *sāman* is, as it were, interrupted at the *pratihāra*.
One might, disregarding the *pratihāra*, transition [to the next part] with the words "kayā śacāyi vā rto hāyī.
But that is a difficult form; moreover, one might thereby become exhausted prematurely.
While the *pratihāra* is being chanted, the Udgātṛ should say, "Speech.
Speech, indeed, is Brahman.
By means of speech, he thus joins this [chant] with Brahman.
The Waters were indeed the wives of the gods. They desired a mate.
They approached Mitra and Varuṇa.
They conceived a fetus.
From that, the Revatī verses were released as cattle.
One who desires cattle should perform [the rite] with the Revatī verses.
He indeed becomes possessed of cattle;
yet he is liable to become childless, for he goes from the *kavatī* verses to those belonging to Prajāpati.
Now, Bharadvāja, desiring cattle, saw this *pṛśni-stotra*: "With what [splendor] will the Wondrous One come to us?", "The wealthy ones at our common feast," and "Come hither to us, the friends.

In that he inserts one *revatī* verse in the middle, by that he does not depart from cattle. And in that there are two *kavatī* verses belonging to Prajāpati on both sides, by that he does not depart from progeny.
That [chant] is the *svāra*. The *svāra* is indeed breath;
thus, he places breath within the cattle.
For the Lord, by means of the tone, would surely carry away the cattle of the sacrificer if he were to omit the tone.
Moreover, if he were to perform the *nidhana*, he would strike down the vital breath.
One should perform the *au ho hā yi* at the end of the first half-verse, and the *au ho hiṃ mā tā yā hiṃ me* at the second half of the final verse.
This is just as if one were to drive cattle into a pen by striking them with a wooden wedge; such is that [procedure].
Regarding this, they say: "The *svāra* should indeed be performed in its own source."

If someone should suspect one who has performed this [rite] in this manner, saying, "He has driven away the cattle of the sacrificer by means of the *svara*," he should say to him: "The *rathantara* has a *nidhana* at the beginning, and the *naudhasa* has a *nidhana* at the end; by these two, my offspring and cattle have been enclosed on both sides. Thus, I have placed the vital breath in the midst of the cattle.
Whoever suspects one who has performed it in this manner will meet with misfortune.
The *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables.
The Vasus are eight;
the morning pressing is in the *gāyatrī* metre;
in every syllable the deity is inherent.
The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables.
There are eleven Rudras.
The midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*.
In every syllable, a deity is inherent.
The *jagatī* meter consists of twelve syllables;
there are twelve Ādityas.
The third pressing belongs to the Jagatī.
In every syllable, the deity is inherent.
Now, do they lead the sacrificer into the sacrifice at each individual sacrifice?

He should say: "When Prajāpati created the Vāmadevya, he extracted three syllables from it; that became the three-syllabled Puruṣa. At the chant of the Vāmadevya, one should say 'Puruṣa'; thus they lead the sacrificer to the sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "One should not say 'Puruṣa'; one should meditate on him only indirectly and restrain [the mind] by the mind alone. But concerning this they also say: "One should neither meditate on him indirectly nor restrain [the mind] by the mind alone; for whatever one knows, by that very knowledge it is attained. 26-137 (Ed.: 1,141)
When the gods were about to go forth to battle against the Asuras, they said, "Let us set aside that which is our desirable wealth and fight; let us run toward whatever being we may encounter today.
That desirable wealth of theirs was indeed their vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Having set aside that weapon and approached him, it stood before him as he was being created, becoming one: the *ṛc*s, the *sāman*s, and the *yajus* verses; the cow, the horse, the goat, the sheep, rice, barley, the Brahmin, the Rājanya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra—whatever exists here, all that.
He then announced this to them: "This indeed is that desirable wealth of yours; it stands being created, having become one."
Those gods conquered the Asuras. Having emerged victorious, they returned and encountered a single being. They did not recognize it, thinking, "This desirable thing is mine; this is mine."
They said, "Let us divide this.
They could not reach an agreement on its division. He then said to them all, "They shall praise me for all of you; I shall favor all of you. Do not divide me."
In that they chant on *gāyatrī* verses, it belongs to Agni;
for Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature.
In that there is the *pṛṣṭha* chant at the midday pressing, it belongs to Indra.
In that they praise with the *kavatī* verses, by that it belongs to Prajāpati;
in that it is undefined (*anirukta*), by that it belongs to the Viśvedevas;
in that they praise for the Maitrāvaruṇa, by that it belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa.
He said to them, "Create me! They said, "So be it," and they intoned over him.
They said to him, "Create! Thus [ends] Pṛṣṭhadharma 27-138 (Ed.:
He created the Rathantara;
the sound of chariots was created after it.
They said, "We have succeeded with this hymn."
Therefore, during the chanting of the Rathantara, they make the sound of a chariot; one should understand this as: "We have succeeded through this chant. They said, "Just let it go forth!"
It created the Bṛhat.
After it, the roar of Parjanya was created.
They said, "We have succeeded with this hymn."
Therefore, they cause the drums to resound during the Bṛhat-stotra;
Parjanya becomes a rain-giver.
One should know this: "We have succeeded through this stotra."
They said, "Create [it] indeed!
He created the Vairūpa;
after it, the village-crier was created.
They said, "We have succeeded through this hymn.
Therefore, at the chanting of the Vairūpa hymn, they raise a shout of the village;
one should know that it is because they thought, "We have succeeded through this hymn."
They said, "Create it indeed!
He created the Vairāja;
after it, the roar of Agni was created.
They said, "We have succeeded with this hymn.
Therefore, they churn the fire during the Vairāja-stotra;
one should know that it is because [they thought], "We have succeeded with this hymn."
They said, "Create it indeed. He created that Śākvara [sāman]. After it was created, the sound of the waters was created in accordance with it.
They said, "We have succeeded with this hymn.
Therefore, they chant while placing water down near the Śākvara hymn;
one should know that it is because of this thought: "We have succeeded with this hymn."
They said, "Create it indeed.
He created the Raivata [Sāman].
After that, the lowing of cattle was created.
They said, "We have succeeded by means of this hymn.
Therefore, at the chanting of the Raivata hymn, they make the sound of cattle; they cause the calves to low together with their mothers.
One should know that it is because they thought, "We have succeeded by means of this hymn."
They said to him, "Create [them] indeed.
He did not create them.
It rose up from there like a back and like a hump.
The gods, having gathered it together, rose upwards.
They said, "This much indeed was this; this truly is the desirable wealth of us gods."
When they said, "This much indeed was this; this very thing is the desirable wealth of the gods," that is the reason for the *vāmadevya* being called *vāmadevya*.
Now, this *vāmadevya* is the father and mother of the *sāmans*.
For whatever a son oversteps, it is the father who pacifies it; the father is the restrainer.

In that it is performed in the middle, it serves for peace and for warding off [evil]. Now, among those Sāmans that have been sung, the Vāmadevya is their westernmost; and among those that have not been sung, it is their easternmost.
For the pacification and the warding off of both of these,
that *svadhū* should be sung neither too loudly nor too softly.
If one were to sing it loudly, he would go by way of the defeat of his superior rival.
If one were to sing in a low tone, he would go by way of subduing an inferior rival.
This earth indeed is his yoke-pole, and this intermediate space is [the axle].
Verily, it is this very thing that injures him who injures one who knows thus.
Regarding this, they say: "It does not touch this world by more than a span, nor does it touch that world by more than a span.
Furthermore, they say: "By as much as the afterbirth (*ulba*) of a cow that has recently calved, by just so much it does not touch this world, nor by so much does it touch that world.
Furthermore, they say: "By as much as the afterbirth (*ulba*) of dung, by just so much it does not touch this world, nor by so much does it touch that world."
Thus, one should sing while thinking in this very way.
Regarding this, they say: "Just as two wheels are supported by an axle, so too are these two worlds supported by this [Sāman].
It touches this world, as it were, and that world, as it were."
One should not sing along the path of another;
for he who sings along the path of another is liable to become a dependent.
One should sing only one's own path.
He who knows the honey of the gods becomes worthy of honey.
The Vāmadevya [sāman] is indeed the honey of the gods; he who knows thus becomes worthy of honey. 29–140 (Ed.: 1,144)
The Brahma-sāman:
These two worlds, having been together, became separated.
Nothing at all fell to their share.
Those gods and humans were hungry;
for the gods live on what is given from here, and humans on what is given from yonder.
The Bṛhat and the Rathantara said, "Let us exchange those two dear bodies of ours which we possess.
Now, the Śyaita was formerly the dear body of the Rathantara, and the Naudhasa that of the Bṛhat;
with these two they exchanged themselves.
Yonder [sun] made salt the bride-price for her from here; this [earth] made smoke the bride-price for her from there.
Yonder [sun] made rain the bride-price for her from here; this [earth] made the place of sacrifice the bride-price for her from there.
He who knows thus knows these two as having their own respective vehicles.
Menā and A-menā indeed would have quarreled over him;
therefore they say, "One must not cause Menā and A-menā to quarrel. For he ascends to the union of the Bṛhat and Rathantara.
That Lord was defeated.
They both said to their own bodies, "Come now, let us carry away [the victory] by means of our two *nidhana*s. 30-141 (Ed.:
In the beginning, indeed, the Śyaita had *padanidhana* as its finale and the Naudhasa had *vasunidhana* as its finale.
They contended with one another; from that time onward, people here dwell in each other's houses.
Indeed, from that point on, they either go according to their respective homes or according to their kinsmen.
They chant with the *rathantara*;
for this world is indeed the *rathantara*.
Then with the Vāmadevya;
this intermediate space is indeed the Vāmadevya.
Then with the Naudhasa.
The Naudhasa is indeed this [earth].
One thus conquers the worlds above, which are not separated from this one.
They praise with the Bṛhat.
That indeed is the Bṛhat.
Then, with the Vāmadevya [Sāman]:
this intermediate space (antarikṣa) is indeed the Vāmadevya.
Then [he sings] with the Śyaita. This Śyaita is indeed this [earth].
He conquers the worlds that are contiguous to that [world] on this side.
He who knows this conquers both worlds: those that are above and those that are below. 31-142 (Ed.:
1,147) |p1 Now follows the Naudhasa.
Nodhas, the son of Kakṣīvat, was for a long time wandering without a firm footing. He desired, "May I find a firm footing. He flew down toward the gods as they were distributing the *brahman*.
He said, "I am a seer, a composer of hymns; for a long time I have wandered without a firm footing. Give this to me, whereby I may find a firm footing."
To him they gave of the essence of the Brahman; that became the Naudhasa. With it he sang praise.
Thereupon he indeed became firmly established.
This is the *pratiṣṭhā* (establishment) *sāman*.
He who knows thus becomes firmly established.
The Naudhasa is indeed the essence of the Brahman.
For one who, knowing this, chants with the Naudhasa, his chant becomes praised by means of the Brahman and its essence.
That [chant] has a *nidhana* consisting of two syllables for the sake of stability.
The sacrificer is indeed two-footed, for the sake of stability.
Because Nodhas Kākṣīvata saw [this], it is therefore called the Naudhasa. 32-143 (Ed.:
1,147) The Rule for the Optional Brahman-sāmans.
One who desires cattle should perform the Śyaita [Sāman].
Prajāpati created cattle.
Once they were created, they departed from him. He desired, "May the cattle not depart from me; may they turn back toward me.
He saw this *sāman*.
He praised with that [verse].
He approached the *nidhana* (concluding chant) with the words "vasu. Now, *vasu* indeed means cattle.
Then indeed the cattle turned back toward him;
then they became non-departing from him. He said, "Have you not made these cattle white?"
That indeed is the "Śyaita-ness" of the Śyaita [Sāman].
This is a Sāman favorable to cattle.
Cattle, having become white, wait upon him; cattle turn toward him; cattle do not depart from him who knows thus.
That [nidhana] consists of two syllables for the sake of stability;
for the sacrificer is two-footed, [and it serves] for his firm establishment. 33-144 (Ed.:
One whose mind has departed from Gautama’s mind-rite should perform it.
Indeed, the mind departed from Gautama. He desired, "May my mind not depart; may my mind enter me again."
He saw these two *sāmans* and praised with them.
Thereupon, mind entered him again; mind did not depart from him.

The mind enters him again, and the mind does not depart from him who knows thus. "Drink! is the [refrain] of the Rathantara-sāman; "Drink, O! is that of the Bṛhat-sāman. Because Gotama saw this, they are called the two *manāryas* of Gautama. 34-145 (Ed.: 1,149)
One desiring procreation should perform [the sacrifice] on the two Janitra bricks of Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha, having been defeated and his sons slain, desired: "May I be propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle."
He saw these two *sāmans* and praised with them.
Thereupon, he indeed multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle.
These two are the *prajanana* (procreative) *sāmans*.
He who knows thus is procreated abundantly with offspring and cattle. That is the "birthplace" (*janitra*) of the *rathantara* *sāman*.
"Born from the parents" (*jānitrā*) is [the name] of the *Bṛhat-sāman*;
because Vasiṣṭha saw them, they are called "Vasiṣṭha’s parents" (*vasiṣṭhasya janitre*). 35-146 (Ed.:

One desiring long life should perform the *paurumīḍha* sacrifice with the *dakṣiṇā* consisting of a cow. Taranta and Purumīḍha were the two sons of Vaitadaśvi, who was the daughter of Mahya Ārcanānas. As they were traveling along, a woman approached them and said: "This son of mine is suffering; please provide a remedy for her."
The two of them, as if angry, said, "How could he speak to us in such a manner? "He should rather scatter [the grains] upon the chariot-poles," they said.
Then this woman, having placed her faith in the divine seers, thinking that those two were the makers of the mantras, scattered [the grains] upon the chariot-poles.

As they were returning, he went up to them and said, "The boy about whom you two said, 'Sow [the seeds] upon the husks,' here he lies, sown upon the husks. They both felt as if they had done something wicked.
They desired: "Let us go out from here; may we find a way and a refuge; may this boy live."
He saw this Purumīḍha-sāman. With it he praised:
"Praise Agni with songs for protection, him whose radiance is fierce; praise Agni, O Purumīḍha, for wealth, O men, the one who is renowned."
"What is the name of the boy?
"His name is Sudīti. Agni touched him with the words, "For Sudīti, a shelter! (RV 8.68.12).
He became exhausted and turned away.
He set him right with this *nidhana*, [singing] "of skill" (*dakṣāya*). The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed skill.
He thereby placed the vital breaths (prāṇa) within him. This is the Sāman called Gātuvin and Nāthavin;
for he found both a path (gātu) and a refuge (nātha).
He who knows thus finds a path and a protector.
Because Purumīḍha saw this, it is called the *paurumīḍha* *dakṣiṇidhana*. 36-147 (Ed.:
One who is practicing sorcery, or one who has rivals, should perform the seven-day sacrifice of Jamadagni.
Jamadagni was indeed the domestic priest of the Māhenas;
he surpassed them in wealth.
They indeed sought to harm him.
He reflected: "How might I kill seven of these domestic animals each day?
He saw this *sāman*.
He praised with that [verse].
Then indeed he struck at their domestic animals seven by seven on each day.
In the same way, they strike at these [animals] now.
That, moreover, is the slayer of rivals. He who knows thus strikes down his hateful rival.
And because Jamadagni perceived it, it is therefore called "the seven-day rite of Jamadagni."
Regarding this, there is this traditional verse:
"They grew beyond measure; they did not touch heaven as if from below. Having harmed Bhṛgu, the sons of Mahin perish in an irreparable way.
Indeed, he who harms one who knows thus perishes in an irreparable way. 37-148 (Ed.: 1,152)
The gods and the Asuras contended at the sacrifice.
Those gods struck down the Asuras from the *bahiṣpavamāna*.
Those Asuras took up the clarified butter for Agni;
those gods [took up] that for Mitra and Varuṇa;
those Asuras [took up] that for Indra.
Those gods [performed] the Aindrāgna;
those Asuras [performed] the Mādhyandina Pavamāna; those gods [performed] the Rathantara.
Those Asuras [chose] the Vāmadevya;
those Devas [chose] the Naudhasa;
those Asuras [chose] the Kāleya.
The Kāleyas pursued them.
By means of the Kāleya [chant], they drove them away from the Kāleyas. Because they drove them away (akālayan), that is the reason for the name "Kāleya."
He who knows thus drives away his hateful rival.
They settled down facing the various directions;
with the *kāleya* [hymn], they drove them around in succession.
That which they did not drive around in succession is precisely the reason for the *kāleya*’s name as *kāleya*.
He who knows thus drives his hateful rival away in succession. The sacrifice is indeed speed; the *stoma* is the finder of wealth.
By means of the sacrifice and by means of the *stoma*, they indeed drove them away. He who knows this drives away his hateful rival by means of the sacrifice and the *stoma*. 38-149 (Ed.:
The Asuras advanced with the *ṛc*, while the gods advanced with the *sāman*.
Those gods, having seized the Asuras by means of the *ṛc* itself, crushed them with the *sāman*.
One should likewise crush [the enemy] for the piercing of the hateful rival.
"O Indra, come hither with aid; sing aloud, O wise ones, while the soma is pressed"—this is for the one whose *sāman* is the *Rathantara*.
"O wise ones, [sing] the *Bṛhat*"—this is for the one whose *sāman* is the *Bṛhat*.
Indeed, both of these follow this very [principle].
Therefore, one should sing both melodic forms, that which belongs to the *rathantara* and that which belongs to the *bṛhat*. Indeed, their *brahmasāman*s are distinct;
nevertheless, it follows both of them.
Therefore, one should sing both forms.
That [verse] consists of the *iḍā*;
for the *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
With cattle indeed they drove them away.
Therefore, when two rivals—one possessing cattle and one without cattle—vie with each other, he who possesses cattle overcomes the other of the two.
This very *sāman* indeed followed after these creatures.
They perform this continuous *iḍā* offering for him at the end, so that the offspring are not displaced from their proper place.
Therefore, the offspring are not displaced from their proper place.
The gods, the ancestors, and humans were on one side; the *asuras*, the *rakṣases*, and the *piśācas* were on the other.
They contended for these worlds.
Now, the Gandharvas called Kalayas moved about within [them], paying no heed to either side.
Those gods, fathers, and humans overcame the Asuras, Rakṣases, and Piśācas.

They divided these worlds: the gods took possession of the world of the gods, the ancestors of the world of the ancestors, and human beings of the world of humans. The Gandharvas, the Kalas, approached them and said, "Grant us a share in these worlds. They replied, "You have acted with disregard; you did not show respect for others, nor for others."
Then they said, "Indeed, we have been mindful of you; do share [the world] with us.
They replied, "No. Our worlds have been well-distributed; we shall not be able to share them with you."
They said, "Let that which we ourselves see here be ours.
To them he gave these Kalindas, saying, "Exert yourselves in these. Because he gave the Kalindas to the Kalis, that is the reason for the Kalindas' name.
Kali, or someone else, saw this *sāman*. He praised with it.
By means of it, he saw this intermediate region, a world difficult to traverse.
He conquered it.
This is the *lokavid* Sāman;
one who praises with it finds the world.
Indeed, he does not surpass the world of the Gandharvas;
rather, he conquers as far as the very limit of the world of the Gandharvas.
And because Kali or someone else saw this, it is therefore called the Kāleya.
The gods, having extracted the third pressing from the first two pressings, went to the heavenly world. These worlds were thereby separated, and the sacrifice was separated.
Those gods desired, “May we reunite these worlds; may we reunite the sacrifice.”
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it. With it, they established these worlds; they established the sacrifice.
In that they established these worlds, that indeed is his [share] leading to heaven;
by it he conquers the world of the Gandharvas.
The sacrifice is indeed a tree, and the *stoma* is the finder of wealth (*vidadvasu*).

By means of the sacrifice and by means of the *stoma*, they indeed restored these worlds; they established the sacrifice. For one who knows thus, his sacrifice becomes firmly joined through both the sacrifice and the *stoma*, as do these worlds.
King Soma, indeed, [possesses] the *kāleya* [chant].
His sacrifice becomes possessed of Indra and possessed of the gods.
Just as here on earth a cow with her calf tied runs away when she is made to low (*hiṃkṛta*), even so indeed does Indra come to the Soma at the very moment they chant this *kāleya* hymn.
Therefore, one should never depart from this *sāman*, thinking: "May my sacrifice be possessed of Indra and possessed of the gods."
By this, he makes the sacrifice possessed of Indra and possessed of the gods. In that regard, the *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman;
for the *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
Thereby he finds firm support among the cattle. 40-151 (Ed.:
1,155) Third Pressing (Bar: 152-174; Ed.: 1,156-178) ® Ṛbhu-pavamāna Stotra (Bar: 152-163; Ed.: 1,156-167)
In the beginning, there were indeed two pressings;
by means of these two pressings, the gods conquered in the beginning.

Having conquered them, Indra approached them as they were seated according to their respective positions and said: "There are three meters; there are three vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna; there are these three worlds; and it is said, 'Three times among the gods. Come, let us perform these three pressings (savanāni). They replied: "We shall not be able to do so; indeed, we are exhausted by this previous performance. Indra said: "Well then, I myself shall fashion the third pressing out of my own self."
He fashioned the third pressing out of himself alone.
Now, that which is the third pressing is indeed Indra among the deities;
the praise of the deities belongs to him who, knowing this, chants with the third pressing.
The third pressing is, as it were, squeezed out;
Suparṇa, having brought the *jagatī* [verse], sucked it;
therefore, this [third pressing] is, as it were, pressed out.

With "svādiṣṭhayā" (most sweet), they indeed make it palatable; with "madiṣṭhayā" (most intoxicating), they place that exhilaration and essence within it. They pour in the milk-mixture (*āśira*), they proceed with the animal sacrifice, and by this means they cause it to swell.
"O slayer of demons, beholder of all people, [come] toward the womb fashioned by Ayu"—this is the transition to the two preceding pressings.
Regarding those [verses], the *gāyatra* has its *brāhmaṇa* already explained. 1-152 (Ed.: 1,156);
Now, the *saṃhita* [stoma] has two syllables in its *nidhana*; it is for the sake of stability.
Indeed, the sacrificer is two-footed; it is for the sake of his firm standing.
The gods and the Asuras were contending.
They said, "Let us deposit this wealth of both sides together;
whichever of us wins, let this wealth of both sides belong to them.
Thus, they deposited that wealth which belonged to both of them.
Those gods desired, "May we win this combined wealth, both kinds.
They saw this *sāman*; they praised with it.
By that, they won both kinds of wealth combined;
because they won both kinds of wealth combined, that is the reason for the name "combined" (*saṃhita*). He who knows thus wins both kinds of wealth combined against his hateful rival.
Regarding this, Āruṇi said: "That horse was indeed the *saṃhita*;
in it their wealth was concentrated. It was that very [horse] which the Asuras deprived themselves of."

"Verily, they thereby deprived Prajāpati [of his power]," it is said. Then indeed the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows this prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is defeated. 2-153 (Ed.: 1,157)
Now, this third pressing is, as it were, cut off from the midday pressing.
The gods, having observed this, understood: "This third pressing is indeed cut off from the midday pressing."
They saw this Sāman;
with it they restored that [world]. Because they restored it, that indeed is the "joinedness" (saṃhitatva) of the Saṃhitā.

This third pressing of his becomes continuous and uninterrupted for one who knows thus. Now follow the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* [verses]. Indeed, it was by means of the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* that Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra.
Standing on two *gāyatrī* verses, they two did not lift him up.
He placed four-footed animals upon them: the cow, the horse, the goat, and the sheep.
They two then lifted him up.
Standing in the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters, he extended his arms toward the *sabha* and *pauṣkala* meters and struck them.
He slew him.
Whoever knows thus slays his hateful rival. 3-154 (Ed.: 1,158)
He stumbled forward with one foot and backward with the other.
That which he stumbled forward upon became the *kakubh*.
Therefore, in the first half of the *kakubh*, there are the most numerous syllables.
Then, that which fell backward became the *uṣṇih*;
therefore, in the latter half of the *uṣṇih*, there are the most numerous syllables.
These two meters are the cow and the ox.
Therefore, animals consume most of their food with both the fore-part and the hind-part;
they carry with the fore-part, they yield milk with the hind-part, and they procreate.
He who knows thus obtains both: the milk of the cow and the milk of the ox. 4-155 (Ed.:
1,160) |p1 In these [waters] he establishes the assembly, for the sake of the assembly of the sacrifice itself.
Whatever in the sacrifice is ill-chanted, ill-recited, or defective, this [chant] serves for its restoration. "It is a gathering, it is not a dispersal"—with these words they indeed praise;
for this [chant] is truly named "The Gathering."

By means of the *sabhā* (assembly), the gods indeed took away from the Asuras their brilliance, strength, sensory power, vigor, cattle, and food; by means of the *sabhā*, they made the *sabhā* their own.
That is the essence of the *sabhā*.
He who knows this makes the brilliance, strength, sensory power, vigor, cattle, and food of his hateful rival his own by means of the *sabhā*; by means of the *sabhā*, he makes the *sabhā* his own.
Prajāpati created cattle. Once they were created, they departed from him. He desired, "May the cattle not depart from me; may they turn back toward me."
He saw this *sāman*.
He praised with it.
Thereupon, indeed, the cattle turned toward him; from that time on, they did not depart from him.
He said: "I have indeed become *sabha* (possessed of a hall) through cattle. That is the reason for the *sabha*'s name, *sabhatva*.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of a hall (*sabha*) through cattle.
Now, that [chant] is the *kākubha* *svāra*.
The *svara* is indeed breath (*prāṇa*), and the *kakubh* is the meter of the person (*puruṣa*). Breath is preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*), and the person is preeminence.
By means of preeminence itself they join together that preeminence; by means of preeminence they become established in preeminence.
Moreover, they thereby cause the sacrificer himself to prosper through the vital breath.
He who knows thus prospers for himself.
He did not distinguish those [beings] as having distinct forms.
He beheld this Pauṣkala Sāman;
with it, he differentiated their forms.
They became of various forms: white, ruddy, and black.
Indeed, previously they were of a single form, namely, only ruddy.
He who knows this secures cattle of many forms and various forms; he becomes possessed of much cattle.
Now follows the Pauṣkala.
Puṣkala Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, performed austerities;
he beheld this Sāman.
He praised with it.
Thereupon, he indeed obtained cattle.
This, therefore, is a *sāman* pertaining to cattle.
He who knows thus secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Because Puṣkala Āṅgirasa saw this [sāman], it is therefore called the Pauṣkala;
and it has four syllables as its *nidhana*.
Cattle indeed have four feet;
the *uṣṇih* is cattle.
[It serves] for the acquisition of those very former cattle. 5-156 (Ed.: 1,160)
In whatever manner they might approach the meters as before, they should make the *anuṣṭubh* the final one;
for the *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech.
They would indeed exclude that [verse] from the sacrifice;
therefore, they thus cause it to participate in the middle of the sacrifice. These [verses] are:
"purojitī vo andhasaḥ... and so forth.

For indeed, these go in front, conquering evil and striking away evil from the front. Through them, they settle into what has been conquered and won. [The verse: "For the pressed juice that intoxicates, O friends, strike down the dog, the long-tongued one."
Now, there was once a female Asura named Dīrghajihvī.
She used to lick every drop of Soma.
The northern ocean was her mouth.
Whosoever was pressed in the southern ocean, whether in the east or in the west, he would lick that very [Soma] up.
Indra, desiring to seize it, was unable to grasp it.
He said: "Let no one sacrifice; for this Dīrghajihvī licks up every Soma."
Now, Sumitra Kautsa was handsome.
He said to him, "Sumitra, you are indeed handsome; women are truly fond of a handsome man. You should try to make this Dīrghajihvī speak."

He went up to her and said, "O Dīrghajihvī, love me. She said, "Your penis is one, but my testicles are on every limb; that will not work. He went back again and said, "Your penis is one, but my testicles are on every limb; she told me that this will not work."
"I will make you whole, limb by limb," he said.
She went away covering those [wounds] of hers.
He said to her, "O Dīrghajihvī, desire me!"
She said, "One [penis] is yours; my testicles are on every limb. That does not work. He said, "Indeed, my penises are on every limb. "Then let me see them," she said. (7-158)
He showed them to her;
they, however, offered them to her as a choice.
He said, "Come.
"What is your name? "My name is Sumitra."
"Your name is indeed auspicious," he said.
Then the two of them came together;
and whenever he made love to her, he would embrace her right there.
She said, "O Sumitra, did you not say [that very thing]?
He replied, "I am indeed Sumitra toward Sumitra, but I am Durmitra toward Durmitra.
He then saw these *saumitra* sāmans.
He praised with them.
He invoked Indra with them.
Indra, raising this thunderbolt consisting of the *ānuṣṭubh* metre, rushed forward.
"O friends, with your victorious power, strike down the dog Dīrghajihvī for the sake of this exhilarating pressed juice!"—thus he spoke against her.
These are verses that slay the enemy and slay the Rākṣasas. By praising with these verses, one slays the hateful enemy and strikes away the Rākṣasa and evil.

"He who flows forth with a purifying stream when pressed, Indu, like a horse that accomplishes its task—the men [should] with all-encompassing thought [approach] that Soma which is difficult to pour out; may the pressing-stones be for the sacrifice. This is the transition to the two preceding pressings.
Regarding those [verses], there is the Śyāvāśva hymn.
Indeed, the descendants of Arcanānas, having abandoned Śyāvāśva as he was departing after having kindled the fire, went to the heavenly world.
He desired: "May I fly up to the heavenly world; may I unite with the Pratiṣṭhātṛs.
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it.

“With your victorious power, come to the soma-juice; come, O you who are to be exhilarated, for the pressing; seize the dog, O Anā!”—with these words, “Come! Ho! Come! indeed, the Maruts summoned him to the heavenly world.
Thereupon he indeed came together with the Pratiṣattris;
this very Śyāvāśva was together with the Maruts.
This is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows thus attains the heavenly world.
Because Śyāvāśva Ārcanānasa saw [this], it is therefore called the Śyāvāśva [Sāman].
Indeed, Indra went away from the third pressing, feeling loathing.
For it was, as it were, forgotten.
With this *sāman*, "ho i yā," all the gods summoned him back.
Thereupon, Indra returned to the third pressing.
Then it did not depart from him;
thus this *sāman* is accompanied by Indra.
His sacrifice becomes accompanied by Indra and accompanied by the gods; Indra turns toward his sacrifice, and Indra does not depart from his sacrifice, for one who knows thus.
That [hymn] is performed with the *svāra* (melodic) chant.
The *svāra* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Those who either fail to complete a sacrificial rite or do not fail to complete it are, as it were, deprived of their vital breaths.
For who indeed knows whether they will actually throw them down or not? In that it is the *svāra* [chant], they thus prosper through their vital breaths. 9-160 (Ed.:
Then follows the Āndhīgava.
It has the *nidhana* in the middle for the sake of stability.
Those who undertake the Ārbhava Pavamāna are, as it were, floating upon the ocean without a support.

In that it has its *nidhana* in the middle, it is for the sake of stability. Just as one who, having swum out into the ocean and found an island, rests after swimming back toward the shore, so indeed do those who sing this *nidhana* rest at will while they are singing.
This [chant] belongs to the *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
cattle are all food.
He who sets out upon a path without provisions does not reach its end.
Then, he who departs from that support (avasas) is indeed overtaken by it. Indeed, this atmosphere is an ocean without a foothold;
there is no going for one in this manner without a support, nor in this manner.
Thus, having made the cattle themselves their entire food and sustenance, they proceed.
The Śākyas, desiring food, consecrated themselves;
that Śākya Andhīgu perceived this Sāman.
He praised with that [verse].
They approach this ten-syllable *virāj* in the middle;
the *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
Food is the Virāj.
From that, indeed, they obtained the Virāj as food.
This is the Sāman for the attainment of the Virāj as food.
He who knows thus wins the Virāj and the food to be eaten; he becomes an eater of food and the best among his own people.
Because Andhīgu Śāktya saw this [sāman], it is therefore called the Āndhīgava. 10-161 (Ed.:
Then these [verses] come into being: "He flows toward the dear things, delighting.
Prajāpati created offspring;
he created them without breath.

With these very verses he bestowed the vital breaths upon them: "He purifies himself for the dear ones, bringing delight. The dear ones are indeed offspring; thus, with the breath, he purified himself toward them.
"The great one has grown over the names," he says. The names are indeed the offspring. "The great one, far-seeing, has mounted the chariot of the great Sūrya, which moves in all directions."
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed all-pervading (*viṣvaṅ*); it moves in every direction. These are the verses (*ṛc*) pertaining to long life.
Having praised with these verses, he attains a full lifespan.
Among them is the Kāva [hymn]. Kavi Bhārgava indeed desired an immortal world among the Gandharvas within the realm of the gods.
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he attained immortality among the gods and the world of the Gandharvas.
This is the Sāman known as the "Knower of the World.
By praising with this, one attains immortality among the gods and the world of the Gandharvas;
and because the sage Bhārgava perceived it, it is called the Kāva.
That [hymn] is performed with the *svāra* chant. Indeed, it is through the *svāra* that food is ultimately bestowed upon the gods.
At the end of the *pavamāna* [laud], there is the *ṛksama*.
They do not let the ṛc exceed the sāman, nor the ṛc the sāman.
Now, the reason they do not chant [the same verse] here and there during the Pavamāna is for the sake of its equality and for the sake of making it uniform.
The Gāyatra at the beginning has the anusvāra on the word, and the Gāyatra at the end of the Pavamāna has the anusvāra on the word.
Therefore, living beings have their vital breaths on both sides, both upward and downward.
Indeed, whatever boat a father and son embark upon does not suffer damage;
for this sacrifice is a divine boat.

These two, father and son, indeed generated this. There is a hymn by Uśanas at the beginning and one by Kava at the end; this is for the safety of the sacrifice. Therefore, when fishermen board a boat, it is father and son who board first.
These five meters occur in the Ārbhava Pavamāna, along with seven *sāmans*.
Thus they amount to twelve. Twelve months constitute a year.
These five *sāman*s indeed belong to the Mādhyandina Pavamāna; they are the seasons themselves.
The months are established in the Ārbhava Pavamāna, and the seasons in the Mādhyandina. This sacrifice, which is the year itself, is thus expanded.
The Saumyacaru.
Indeed, this year is Prajāpati.
For six months, he stands with one foot raised and the other lowered.
When he raises his foot while it is hot, then this [world] above becomes hot, and at that time, what is below becomes cold.
Therefore, in summer, heat is perceived above and coldness below.
Therefore, in the summer, they draw out cold water from wells.
Now, when it draws forth coldness, then this [atmosphere] becomes cold above and hot below;
therefore, in the winter, coldness is found above and heat is found below.
Therefore, indeed, in winter they draw out warm water from the wells.
In this very way, this Prajāpati, the year, sustains all creatures.
Now, they bring this *saumya* oblation of cooked rice.

Whatever deficiency or excess occurs in the sacrifice of the Udgātṛ while he is performing it, that indeed goes to the world of Yama. Therefore, they say even of one who has died, "We saw this in the assembly hall of Yama.
This [deficiency] is brought back again when they bring this pap of Soma (saumya caru).

He should gaze at it [the mirror], saying: "My mind that has gone to Yama, or whatever of mine has departed, we restore that again into us by means of King Soma. May the eye be placed in my mind, and my mind in my eye. Do not cut me off from the long-lived *ṛc*; may I not be separated from the portion of the *sāman*.
Furthermore, he should also gaze at his own reflection so as not to lose himself;
moreover, he should apply clarified butter to his eyes for the nourishment of his sight.
That consciousness, too, is non-existent.
He who does not perceive the self would be one whose life-breaths have departed.
Therefore, even from what is true, having brought more clarified butter, he should look all around at the self for the attainment of a full lifespan. 12-163 (Ed.: 1,167)
While the Aṅgirases were performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), gravel appeared in their eyes. They desired, "May we not be blind; may we see clearly."
They placed this dark *caru* of Soma upon their eyes.

They placed it with this mantra: "With that by which Nṛcakṣas won the race, with which he [won] the falcon, the bird, the well-winged one; that which they call the infinite eye in Aditi—may Soma, the Nṛcakṣas, bestow that upon me.
Thereupon, indeed, they became no longer blind; they saw.
He who knows this indeed becomes free from blindness; he sees clearly.
Regarding this, they say: "Should one eat it, or should one not eat it? He who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) yet lacks renown and is devoted to the Truth (*ṛta*)—he indeed may eat it.

Indeed, one who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) is here sufficient for glory. If one who is learned in the Vedas becomes devoid of glory in this world, his glory indeed goes to that world over there.
Therefore, it is brought back again by the fact that he eats this dark *caru* of Soma.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "This [soma] must certainly not be consumed. Who could thereby acquire glory when he would have to stay for many more nights?
Therefore, one should certainly not consume it. [End of Section 13-164 (Ed.:
This is indeed the fourth part of the *sāman*;
they thus establish the sacrifice within the *sāman* itself.
This is indeed the body of the *sāmans*. Thus, they make the *sāmans* possessed of a body.
For whoever should depart from this *sāman*, he would either become afflicted with skin disease, or evil report would be uttered concerning him.
This Gāyatrī, having become a bird, flew up to heaven at sunrise.
For this truth, the quarters took her fee in the form of the Anuṣṭubh.
Offspring come as a fee for him who knows thus; the fee is taken from the quarters for him who knows thus.
He chants the *prastāva* with the words, "vayo yajñā vo agnayaḥ. He performs the *pratihāra* with the words, "upoyigirā ca dakṣase popriṃ vayam amṛtaṃ jātevāṃho i vidosam.
There are two syllables in "yajñā," two in "gire," and two in "poprim. Thus, they amount to six.
The silent recitation (*tūṣṇīṃśaṃsa*) consists of six syllables. It is precisely at this point that the silent recitation is released in the *āgnimāruta* litany;
for it is the end.
Agni Vaiśvānara arose for the sake of creatures;
he scorched this entire universe.
The gods were afraid of his burning.
They said, "This one will surely burn up everything here.
"Come, let us transfer his splendor (*haras*) away."
They divided his portions.
Regarding that which they first divided, they disputed over it, saying, "What will this become?
They said, "It shall belong to us in every sacrifice."
That became the *yajñāyajñīya*.
That is the reason for the *yajñāyajñīya* being called *yajñāyajñīya*.
Because they drove away the second [verse], that became the *nārmedha*.
That which they pushed aside third became the Dāśaspatya;
that which they pushed aside fourth became the Viśoviśīya;
that which they pushed aside fifth became the Vāravantīya.
The sacrifice is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara.
Therefore, in that these Agniṣṭoma-sāmans occur, they thereby establish Agni Vaiśvānara in his own form. 15–166 (Ed.:
1,170) The Rule for the Optional Agniṣṭoma-sāmans.
One who desires a protector should perform the Nārmedha sacrifice.
Now, Nṛmedha and Suvrata were brothers.
The two of them performed the *tāuhanika* chants.
Nṛmedha sang the *ujjaga* for Suvrata;
however, that [hymn] had not yet been chanted with the *yajñāyajñīya* chant.
Then they rushed toward him, saying, "O Sacrificer, his two sons, Antakadhṛt Sauvratika and Nakira Śakapūta, have killed the son of this Udgātṛ.

Grasping his arms, he said, "O Brāhmaṇas, this is your sacrifice; with it, you may perform the sacrifice for whomever you desire. As for me, I shall surely cause him to perish by means of this [sacrifice].
He then wrapped him around an Udumbara post and set him ablaze with stalks of hemp.
He desired: "May I go forth from here; may I find a path and a refuge; may this fire not burn me.
He saw this *sāman* and praised with it.
Then indeed he found a way and a refuge;
fire did not burn him,
though it did burn even that peg with which he had been bound.
This is the *sāman* that finds the way and finds support. Indeed, he found that way and that support. He who knows thus finds the way and finds support.
Because Nṛmedha saw it, it is therefore called the Nārmedha.
One who desires preeminence should perform the Dāśaspatya sacrifice.
The gods and the asuras contended.
Those gods ran to Indra, saying, "With you as our sovereign, let us conquer this.
That Indra desired, "May we conquer the asuras."
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Then indeed the gods conquered the Asuras.
When he had conquered and was seated as the lord of ten, they brought forth the portions for him, saying, "To the lord of ten, to the lord of ten!
That is indeed the reason for the *dāśaspatya* (belonging to the lord of ten) being called *dāśaspatya*. "Bring forth the portion," [he says]; he becomes one entitled to a portion who knows thus.
One who desires food should perform the *viśoviśīya*. Agni, indeed, once desired: "May I be an eater of food, the best, and the overlord among every people (*viśoviśa*).
He saw this *sāman*.
He praised with that [verse].
Thereupon, he indeed became an eater of food, the most excellent lord over every people (viś).
Therefore, every people addressed him.

Because they carried him about from clan to clan (*viśoviśas*), that is the reason for the name of the Viśoviśīya sacrifice. He indeed becomes an eater of food, the best, and the overlord among the very clans; he who knows thus becomes an eater of food, the best, and the overlord among the very clans.
One who desires cattle should perform the Vāravantīya.
Prajāpati created cattle;
once created, they departed from him.

He restrained them by means of the Vāravantīya [chant] itself. Because he restrained them (*avārayata*), that is the reason for the name of the Vāravantīya. Thus, when the Vāravantīya serves as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman, it is for the sake of the presence of cattle and so that cattle do not depart. 17-168 (Ed.: 1,172)
He who knows the udder of the sacrifice milks the sacrifice when it has been offered.
The Yajñāyajñīya is indeed the udder of the sacrifice.
These are its teats: the Gāyatra, the Rathantara, the Bṛhat, and the Vāmadevya.
One should chant the Prastāva as if it were the Gāyatra; one should utter the Stobhas as if they were those of the Rathantara.
One should ascend as if upon the shoots of the *bṛhat* [sāman].
The *dhiṃkāra* is the *vāmadevya*;
