the *yajñāyajñīya* is itself [the goal].
Verily, by this the sacrificer milks the sacrifice; having sacrificed, he indeed becomes better.
"Sacrifice after sacrifice for you, O Agnis," it is said.
This indeed is the sacrifice, the very essence of sacrifice, namely the *yajñāyajñīya*.
It is called the *yajñāyajñīya* because it carries (*vahati*) sacrifice after sacrifice (*yajñam-yajñam*).
In ancient times, they used this alone to perform all the hymns of praise.

Regarding this they say: "Those who sacrifice ascend upwards to the heavenly world; they are liable to fall away. Therefore, when they chant the *yajñāyajñīya* at the end, since the *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed this earth, they thereby find firm support upon this very earth.
They chant while placing water nearby; for this *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara, and [they do so] for his pacification and to prevent him from burning.
The wife causes it to flow forth from her thighs;
thereby she pacifies Agni Vaiśvānara himself.
He causes her to move forward after having made her thigh bare;
for it is by making her thigh bare that the wife produces vigor. They cause her to count [the drops] for the sake of the depositing of seed.
Regarding this, they say: "When the *sāman* has been sung apart, the wife indeed takes away the offspring of the *udgātṛ*.
Therefore, he should look at her [the wife] with the verse: "O you who are lovely by name, in our sight; may we perceive all lovely things."
Offspring is indeed the desirable; thus he places offspring within himself.
"Of you, the vigorous one, rich in vigor, we deposit all seeds," with these words the other woman gazes back at him.
Regarding this, they say: "One should chant the *udgītha* while covered; for the *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara, and [this is done] for his appeasement and to prevent burning.
However, there is a danger that one might become subject to the ancestors as a deity if one were to chant the *udgītha* while covered.
Furthermore, they say: "One should chant the *udgītha* while covering only as much as the ear."
Regarding this, they say: "One hears with the ears and sees with the eyes.
Therefore, one should leave oneself uncovered when the Udgātṛ sings;
for at the third pressing, they pour the *āśir* (milk) into the Soma."
Offspring indeed are cattle, and the blessing is oneself.
Therefore, one should exclude oneself from everything if one were to sing the *udgītha* while covered. One should sing the *udgītha* uncovered. 19-170 (Ed.: 1,174)
The *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed the bird (*vayas*).
If he should desire of a sacrificer, "May he be one who attains the heavenly world," he should chant for him the verse, "O Agnis, the birds are your sacrifices."
Becoming a bird, he indeed carries him to the heavenly world.
But that [act] is, as it were, detrimental to longevity;
for that which is a bird is like something crushed, as it were, and without a firm foundation.
Therefore, one should not chant in this way:
"O *girā*, *girā*! O *cā*, *dākṣāsā*! For if one were to say "*girā*, *girā*," Agni Vaiśvānara would swallow the sacrificer.
Now, when he says, “O, *irā*! *Irā*! And the two *dākṣāsas*!”—*irā* is indeed food; thus he places food itself into the mouth of Agni Vaiśvānara.
However, he would be liable to become coarse if he were to say, “O, *irā*! *Irā*! And the two *dākṣāsas*! He should rather say, “O, *irā*! *Ihā*! And the two *dākṣāsas*! (20–171 [Ed.: 1,175])
Thus, indeed, he does not become harsh.
For this very reason, the Brahmins of old used to deliberate thus: "Who, indeed, will today enter the open mouth of the *śiṃśumārī*?"
This Yajñāyajñīya indeed stands facing upward with its mouth wide open in the single-pathed way;
having thus covered its food from the mouth, one passes safely beyond it with the verses:
"We [choose] the favor," and "The immortal, once born."
If he were to say "prapra vayam," the sacrificer would be liable to die prematurely;
but when he says "poprīḥ," this very [sacrifice] becomes for him a source of nourishment. "Hiṃ māyi dāyivam."

If he were to say "dāsam," the sacrificer would become a slave. Now, as for why he says "dāyivam": they say that the sacrifice, once fully praised, must be made to go to heaven; thus they cause the sacrifice, once fully praised, to go to heaven.
"I shall now praise my dear friend."
If one were to say, "I have not praised a dear friend," one would not praise a dear friend;
but when one says, "I have indeed praised a dear friend," one praises a dear friend. 21-172 (Ed.:
"Let us now praise the sons of Māyitrā, the offspring of vigor, for he is possessed of life"—

if one were to say "he does not possess life," the sacrificer would not be possessed of life. But because he says "possessed of life," the Udgātṛ thereby bestows life upon both himself and the sacrificer.
"Hiṃ! O Māyin! May we attain long life through the giving of oblations!
(VS 3.17). If one were to say "dāśema," they would be liable to bite him; but since he says "āśema," he indeed attains it.
"May we obtain him as the invoker; may he be our helper in the contests for booty; may he indeed prosper me.
For at this point the sacrifice has become, as it were, aged.
And: "And [he is] the protector of many."
If he were to say, "of the bodies," the sacrificer would be like a mere body. But when he says, "of many," he thereby makes him the protector of many.
Regarding this, they say: the *ṛc* verses of the *yajñāyajñīya* are deficient by one syllable;
that is a flaw in the sacrifice.
If the *udgātṛ* does not cover that [deficiency] while singing, he creates a flaw in the *yajñāyajñīya*.

The *yajñāyajñīya* flows away following the breach in the sacrifice; the sacrifice flows away following the sacrifice; the sacrificer flows away following the sacrifice; and the offspring flow away following the sacrificer.
One should place speech (*vāk*) within that [breach].
For speech is indeed the sacred power (*brahman*).
And indeed, speech is the savior of many. Some, however, establish it as "the cow" (gauḥ),
for the cow is indeed all food.
It is for the sake of securing all food whatsoever.
Regarding this, they say: "One need not pay heed to that;
for by the very fact that the *vāc* (speech) is the *nidhana*, one is thereby restored."

Regarding this, they say: "Just as the meters are released in their original order and according to seniority, so do creatures follow the arrangement and release of the meters until the end of the cosmic cycle.
He begins the *prastāva* with the six syllables, "yajñā vo agnayaḥ.
He takes up the *ādi* with the six syllables, "girā ca dakṣase."
These amount to twelve.
The *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables. They pile up the *jagatī* first.
By means of that *jagatī*, they are liberated.
"Pra vayam amṛtaṃ jātavedasam"—thus eleven syllables are obtained.
The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables.
They are released by means of a *triṣṭubh* verse. With the eight syllables of the verse, "I shall now praise my dear friend," they reach the *nidhana*.
The *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables.

Then they are released by means of the *gāyatrī*. Just as before, according to seniority, the meters proceed as they are being released; following the arrangement and release of the meters, living beings are likewise arranged. No one who has not yet died passes away before another. 23-174 (Ed.: 1,178) Ukthya (Bar: 175-187; Ed.: 1,179-191)
The gods and the Asuras contended at the sacrifice.
Those gods struck the Asuras out from the sacrifices.
Those Asuras, having extracted the essence and the vigor of the three pressings, entered into blind darkness.
Indeed, whatever is beyond the Agniṣṭoma is blind darkness;
whatever is beyond the year is blind darkness.
The sacrifice is indeed as great as the Agniṣṭoma;
it is also as great as the year.
There are twelve Stotras in the Agniṣṭoma.
Twelve months are a year;
there are twelve stotras and twelve śastras;
there are twelve fortnights of the waxing moon and twelve fortnights of the waning moon.
Then, that which was beyond that was blind darkness. They entered it.
Those gods followed after the Asuras.
The Asuras rose up against them with these very *ukthas*.
Because they rose up against them with *ukthas*, that is the *uktha*-ness of the *ukthas*.
Thereupon, they struck them down from there.
They entered indeed blind darkness, that is, the night. Indra said: "Who shall we two follow and enter here? (24-175; Ed.:
"I shall [do so]," said Varuṇa. "I will maintain the light for you both," said Agni.
They both followed after him.
They both recited one third [of the hymn].
By means of that, they caused the morning pressing (prātassavana) to swell.
Therefore, they chant the stotra on verses addressed to Agni, and the anuśaṃsa is recited for Indra and Varuṇa.
Therefore, they chant on *gāyatrī* verses;
for the morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatra*. He said: "Who and I shall we both follow after this?"
"And I," said Bṛhaspati.
They both descended after him;
they two alone recited one-third [of the Veda].
By that they caused the midday pressing to swell.
Therefore, they chant on verses addressed to Indra, and the hymn dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati is recited as an after-recitation.
For this reason, they chant on *kakubh* verses.
For the midday pressing belongs to the Kakubh metre.
He said, "Who and I shall we follow this [path]?
Viṣṇu replied, "I and you."
The two of them followed after him;
they both uttered one third [of the day] together,
and by that they caused the third pressing to swell.
Therefore, they chant praises in verses addressed to Indra; therefore, the [hymn] dedicated to Indra and Viṣṇu is recited after them.
And for that reason, they chant praises in *anuṣṭubh* verses, for the third pressing belongs to the *anuṣṭubh*.
He excluded them from everything.
Thereupon, the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
He who knows thus prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is defeated. 25-176 (Ed.: 1,180)
Now, these three two-deity offerings exist: the one for Indra and Varuṇa, the one for Indra and Bṛhaspati, and the one for Indra and Viṣṇu.
These indeed are the six wish-fulfilling cows that they cited from that [context]: the cow, the horse, the goat, the sheep, rice, and barley.
Six wish-fulfilling cows stand ready for him who knows this.
Indeed, the sacrifice is as great as the Agniṣṭoma.
Regarding this, they say: "If the sacrifice is only as great as the Agniṣṭoma, then when that [Agniṣṭoma] has come to an end, why do they introduce the Ukthas?"
He should say: "The *ṛc*s of the *yajñāyajñīya* are deficient by one syllable;
that is a flaw in the sacrifice;
they lead [the sacrifice] toward that."
They lead [the waters] forward with verses containing the word *pra*, while [the verses] contain the word *ehi*.
For this universe both goes forth (*pra*) and comes hither (*eti*);
thus they establish the sacrifice in him in a state of union.
They lead forward [the fires] with verses addressed to Agni, from those [verses] addressed to Agni.
That is just as if one were to place fires together within a fire. Or, he who would divide a single fire into many ways—those [fires] would indeed be many.
If one were to combine these many hundreds into a single [heap], it would be as if one were to place fires together within a fire; such is that. 26-177 (Ed.:
On those [verses], the Sākamaśva [is chanted].
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerity. They saw this *sāman*.
They praised with that.
Then, having become a horse, it carried them to the heavenly world.
Having reached the heavenly world, they said, "We have gone to the heavenly world together with the horse."
That indeed is the "Sākamaśva" nature of the Sākamaśva [chant]. This is a *sāman* that leads to heaven;
he who knows thus attains the heavenly world.
One who has rivals should perform the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya* [sāman].
Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra;
he was unable to strike him.
As soon as he saw him after departing, he struck him down.
He who knows this strikes down his hateful rival.
And because he saw him after departing (*pretya*), it is therefore called the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya*.
One whose [possessions] have not been conquered by anyone else as much as yours should perform the Satrāsāhīya sacrifice.
Indra conquered the Asuras;
he did not, however, conquer their *tvān* (possessions).
He desired, "May I indeed overcome all the Asuras.
He saw this Sāman;
with it he praised.
With it, he completely overpowered all the Asuras.
Because he completely overpowered all the Asuras with it, that is the reason for the name *satrāsāhīya*. He who knows this completely overpowers his hateful rival.
One who desires the office of domestic priest should perform the *daivodāsa* [sāman].
The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni, and the Rājanya belongs to Indra; this *sāman* is thus dedicated to both Agni and Indra.
Agni is indeed the *brahman*, Indra is the *kṣatra*.

By means of the *brahman* he thus supports the *kṣatra*, and by means of the *kṣatra* the *brahman*. In this way, the kingdom does not depart from him; he attains the office of the domestic priest (*purodhā*), and they place him at the front. 27-178 (Ed.: 1,182)
The Procedure for the Optional Ukthya Sacrifice |c179 (Ed.:
1,183) |p1 One seized by demons should perform the Hārivarṇa as the Brahman-sāman.
When the descendant of Aṅgiras was going to the heavenly world, the *rakṣases* followed him from these worlds.
They desired, "May we slay the *rakṣases*.
He, the descendant of Aṅgiras, perceived this *Sāman* called *Harivarṇa*.
He praised with that [hymn].
With it, he struck away the *rakṣases* from these worlds:
with "O thou of golden splendor," from this world; with "Thou shinest forth," from the intermediate space; and with "Day by day," from yonder world.
Then indeed, having driven away the *rakṣases* from all these worlds, they ascended to the heavenly world.
He who knows thus, having driven away the *rakṣases* from all these worlds, ascends to the heavenly world.
And because Harivarṇa Āṅgirasa saw it, it is therefore called the *hārivarṇa*. 28-179 (Ed.: 1,183)
One who desires a protector should perform the Traita rite;
for by means of the Āptyas, he found satisfaction when he encountered thirst in the forest.
They found a well in the desert.
That [well] did not wish to be descended into by one, nor by two;
Trita descended into it.
When the two of them drank from it, they were not satiated; then, having covered that very place with a chariot wheel, they departed with the cows.
He (Soma) desired, "May I go forth from here; may I find a way and a refuge.
He saw this *sāman*.
He praised with that [sāman].
He reached the *nidhana* with the words "sa sam indubhiḥ.
Parjanya caused him to float upward by means of rain.
For he caused that wheel of the chariot to float up by which it had been covered.
This is the *gātuvin* (path-finding) and *nāthavit* (refuge-finding) *sāman*. Indeed, he thereby found the path and the refuge.
He who knows thus finds a path and a protector.
He followed by means of his footprint.
Seeing him approaching, one became a bear and another a monkey, and they both leapt into the forest.
That, moreover, is the slayer of rivals. Indeed, he brought upon himself the state of having rivals when he turned them into a bear and a monkey.
Furthermore, Parjanya becomes truly rain-giving for him.
And that is indeed beneficial for cattle.
He has indeed made those cattle exclusive;
he secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle—he who knows thus.
Because Trita Āptya saw it, it is therefore called the *traita*.
One desiring food should perform the *traikakubha* sacrifice.
Indra delivered the *Yatis* to the *Sālāvṛkas*.
While they were being devoured, three boys remained: Rāyovāja, Pṛthuraśmi, and Bṛhadgiri.
They praised Indra.
He said to them, "O princes, with what desire do you praise me?
They replied, "Sustain us indeed, O Maghavan.
He sat down upon their shoulders.
These three peaks of his hung down;
these worlds, having been together, became divided into three;
after those [peaks], food was divided into three.
These three peaks of the three worlds hung down after the food.
He thought: "If I were to win the food of these three worlds by means of their three peaks, I should bring down these three peaks. He saw this *sāman*.
He praised with that [verse].
By means of it, he won for himself the three peaks of these three worlds as food.
By means of it, he brought down these three peaks.
In that he won for himself the three peaks of these three worlds as food, that is the reason for the *traikakubha*’s name *traikakubha*.
This is the *sāman* for the winning of food; he wins food and becomes the best eater among his own people, who knows thus. 30-181 (Ed.: 1,185)
This Sāman has three elements;
the verses are addressed to Indra.
The *sāman* belongs to Indra;
"Indra" is its *nidhana*.
There are three powers in man: the self, offspring, and cattle.
By this very means, he encompasses them within his own self.
He said to them, "What is the desire of one of you? What is the desire of another? What is the desire of yet another?
Rāyovāja replied, "I am desirous of cattle."
He gave him the *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
Then Pṛthuraśmi said, "I am desirous of the *kṣatra*."
To him he granted sovereign power (*kṣatra*). He was Pṛthu Vainya. Then Bṛhadgiri said, "I am desirous of food."
Therefore, he bestowed the syllable *atha*.
The syllable *atha* is indeed food.
One desiring offspring should perform the Saubhara.
One should conclude with the *nidhana* "hus.
One desiring food should perform the *Saubhara*;
one should conclude it with the *nidhana* "ūrj."
One desiring rain should perform the Saubhara. He should conclude with the *nidhana* "hiṣ.
One desiring to win over [others] should perform the Saubhara.
One should conclude with the *nidhana* "ud.
One desiring heaven should perform the *Saubhara*;
one should conclude it with the *nidhana* "o."

They asked the Bhāradvājāyaṇas, who were performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), "With what [sāman] did you chant, desiring offspring? "With the Saubhara," they replied. "With what, desiring food? they asked.
"By means of the Saubhara.
"For those desiring rain, by what [means]?
"By means of the Saubhara."
"By what means do they desire to grasp [the breath]?
"By the Saubhara chant.
"By what means do they desire heaven?"
"By means of the Saubhara.
Indeed, this *sāman* is just like that;
for these very desires are contained within it.
He wins these very desires.
Whatever desire one has when one chants with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him. 31-182 (Ed.:

One should perform the Saubhara as the Brahman-sāman if he should desire: "May there be born among my offspring one who is well-favored, handsome, having the form of a Kṣatriya, having the form of a man.
For the splendor of a man is his offspring;
the Saubhara is the splendor of the Bṛhat.
The *kṣatra* is the *bṛhat*.
This is the progeny of the *kṣatriya*.
Indeed, in the progeny of one who knows this, there is born a man who is well-appearing, handsome, having the form of a *kṣatriya*, and the form of a human being.
Prajāpati created offspring. Once they were created, they perished; they became these crawling creatures.
That other [he gave] to the serpents. He created a second [set]; they remained away from him.
They became fish.
He created a third [set of beings];
they remained beyond his reach.
They became birds.
He created fourths.
He reflected: "How indeed can these creatures of mine, once created, not perish?"
He saw this Sāman;
with it he touched them, saying, "Sustenance (ūrj).
They, being anointed by that sustenance, grew strong.
He said, "I have indeed well-supported these creatures. That is the reason for the name *saubhara*. He who knows thus supports his offspring well. 32-183 (Ed.: 1,187)
At the *atirātra* sacrifice, they chant for the *acchāvāka* priest with the *nārmedha* hymn;
they continue the night through with the *iḍā*.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who perform the *acchāvāka*sāman on *uṣṇih* verses indeed fall away from the *anuṣṭubh*s.
Now, among these [verses], one is an *arvāguṣṇih*, one is a *madhyauṣṇih*, and one is a *pura-uṣṇih*;
thus, the meter is not fixed.
Speech speaks what is not firmly grasped;
speech is the *anuṣṭubh*.
Therefore, they do not go beyond the *anuṣṭubh*.
That which is the last of these is the manifest *anuṣṭubh*.
Therefore, they do not depart from the *anuṣṭubh*.
Just as here on earth honey-makers collect the essences of flowers, even so did those deities collect the essences of the meters.
The praise of the meters becomes endowed with their essence for one who knows thus. Indeed, this Sāman is the form of day and night:
the verses belong to Indra, and the Sāman belongs to Agni.
The day belongs to Indra, the night to Agni.

Indeed, whoever should go beyond this *sāman* at the *atirātra*, he would be torn apart from the very form of day and night. If someone were to say of him then, "He has torn him apart from the form of day and night," it would surely be so.
Therefore, one should not proceed from this *sāman* during the *atirātra* sacrifice;
for the night is indeed much shorter than the day.
The *ehīḍam* [verse] serves to prevent [the sacrifice] from being torn asunder. That which remained over from both the *ṛc* and the *sāman* became the *udvaṃśīya*.
He who knows thus finds firm support through both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
One should perform that for one who is not cruel, but not for one who is cruel.
For a cruel person lives on limited [resources], whereas one who is not cruel lives on what is in excess;
[the rite is performed] for the sake of securing that which is in excess.
Now, indeed, by means of this *sāman*, the gods, having raised it up like a bamboo pole, overpowered the Asuras.
Because they overpowered the Asuras by raising it up like a bamboo pole, that is the reason for the name of the *udvaṃśīya*.
He who knows thus conquers what is unconquered and does not suffer defeat of what has been conquered.
This *sāman* is the form of all the *pṛṣṭha* chants. "They sing thee, the singers" is that of the *gāyatra*;
"They praise the song, the praisers" is that of the *rathantara*.
"Brahmāṇas tvā hoyi śatakrato" is for the Bṛhat [sāman];
"udvaṃśam iva yāyimirāyī" is for the Vairūpa;
"ud vaṃśāmī" is the *punarnitunna* for the Vairāja.
The syllables *vā*, *yā*, *vu*, *vā*, or *up* belong to the Mahānāmnīs; *mā* and *irā* belong to the Revatīs;
and *hā* and *yī* belong to the Vāmadevya.
In all this— the form of the *pṛṣṭha* chants, the essence, the brilliance, and the unconquered meter— he establishes himself at the very end of the sacrifice.
Indeed, wherever the *Ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is performed, it is complete in every respect when the *Udvaṃśīya* chant is employed.
He repeats the final foot once more;
by that, it is made into the *ṣoḍaśī* in that form.
Indeed, the *vajra* is the *ṣoḍaśī* for the sake of the enemy.
Verily, he hurls the thunderbolt at his hateful rival for his destruction.
Darkness indeed lay between the gods and the Asuras.
The gods perceived this *ardheḍa*.
Therefore, they went apart from it.
One should meditate upon him whom he hates with his mind.
By approaching this half-eaten portion, he indeed goes apart from him.
He chants the *svarita* accent on the syllable *adhyardha*.
Therefore, streams of milk flow over from the udder.
Aṣāḍha Sāvayasa won [the world] by means of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Now Atidhanva Śaunaka was present there. He performed the *udvaṃśīya* as the *acchāvāka*sāman at the *atirātra* sacrifice.
He said to him: "Do not do so! The *iḍā*-chant has been omitted; the tone is lost beyond [the proper place], and it lacks the form of the *paricarya*."
He said, "Having approached that entire *iḍā* and having made it continuous by means of the tone alone, we shall depart for the night. "No," the other said.
"For by means of this *sāman*, Indra pursued the Asuras."
Having recognized their strength and voice, they rushed toward him; they overpowered him, and he,
being thus overcome, struck this *ardheḍa* down.
"This [verse] beginning with *trāṇāya vai* is indeed for protection. One should perform the *nārmedha* [sāman].
That [verse] is addressed to *iḍā*.
Cattle, indeed, are *iḍā*;
by means of cattle, they truly struck them down from that night.
Therefore, the Nārmedha alone should be performed.
One desiring prosperity should perform the Āṣṭādaṃṣṭra;
for Vairūpa was indeed Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra, and he saw these two Sāmans for the sake of cattle, as it were, from among other seers.
He was afraid, thinking, "The two *sāmans* will become without *stotriya* verses for me.
He said, "May he prosper who shall satisfy my two *sāmans* with soma! These two *sāmans* are indeed dear to the *ṛṣis*.
Those who praise with these two indeed prosper. Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra Vairūpa, desiring cattle, performed austerities;
he saw these two *sāmans*.
He praised with those two.
He approached this *iḍā*;
the *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
Thereupon, he indeed acquired cattle.
These two are Sāmans pertaining to cattle.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Furthermore, because Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra Vairūpa saw [them], they are therefore called "Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra. That Aiḍa becomes the Acchāvāka-sāman;
for the iḍā is indeed cattle.
In this way, he establishes himself among the cattle. 36-187 (Ed.:
When Prajāpati distributed his bodies among the gods, he reserved for himself that which was associated with the *hari* (bay horses),
and he gave it to Indra. By means of it, Indra attained preeminence.
Now, when they chant on verses containing the word "hari," that indeed constitutes preeminence. These *harivatī* verses, though indirectly, result in *anuṣṭubh*s;
when they are thus chanted together, they consist of thirty-four syllables.
Regarding this, they say: "The world is established by means of those two which are the thirty-fourth syllables of the *sāman*.
If they were to chant on verses of thirty-five syllables, they would attain the higher form, the *bārhata*;
if they were to chant on verses of thirty-three syllables, they would attain the lower form, the *ānuṣṭubha*.
If there were a seventeenfold hymn-form (*saptadaśa-stoma*), they would attain the highest form.
If there were a fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*), they would attain the lowest form.
When they praise with the sixteenfold hymn-form (*ṣoḍaśin*) consisting of thirty-four syllables, they thereby cause him to prosper in his own abode.
By means of that which is thus successful, one becomes prosperous among one's own people. There are sixteen *stotras* and sixteen *śastras*;
that makes thirty-two.
The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables.
The sixteenfold [stotra] is of the *ānuṣṭubha* nature; thus it is perfected as an *anuṣṭubh*.
Indeed, some were the meters of the gods, while others were the meters of the asuras.
Among the gods, that which consisted of one syllable was the lowest, and that of seven syllables was the highest.
Among the Asuras, that which consisted of nine syllables was the lowest, and that of fifteen syllables was the highest.

Those gods desired: "May we overcome the Asuras by means of the less. By means of a single syllable, they overcame the fifteen-syllabled [verse]; by means of two syllables, the fourteen-syllabled; by means of three syllables, the thirteen-syllabled; by means of four syllables, the twelve-syllabled; by means of five syllables, the eleven-syllabled; by means of six syllables, the ten-syllabled; by means of seven syllables, the nine-syllabled; and by means of eight syllables, the eight-syllabled.
Since those sixteen became sixteen each, that is the reason for the name of the *ṣoḍaśin* (the sixteenfold).
Then the Gāyatrī itself became seventeenfold.
Therefore they say, "Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
Indeed, Indra desired to slay Vṛtra.
He ran to Prajāpati, crying, "The wealth! Vṛtra!
To him, Prajāpati gave this sixteenfold thunderbolt (*ṣoḍaśin*); taking whatever vigor he possessed, [Prajāpati] gave it to him in the form of *śakvarī* verses.
Yet, he was unable to slay him.
He ran toward him again, thinking, "Wealth indeed is Vṛtra.
To him, he gave the Śakvarī verses.
Then indeed Indra slew Vṛtra.
He who knows thus slays his hateful rival.
He reflected: "If I shall give this to him by day, their world of rivals will look down upon it during the night."
"If I were to give this to him at night, their world of enemies would look down upon them during the day," he thought.
He saw this [means] and gave it to him for exactly as long as the sun remains suspended;
by means of that, he separated the Asuras from both day and night.
He who knows thus passes his hateful rival between both day and night.
Just as one would [pass] by placing a firebrand aside, so is the *ṣoḍaśin* among the chants for the attainment of the heavenly world.
He who knows thus attains the heavenly world. 3-190 (Ed.: 1,194)
Regarding this, they say: "The *stoma* should indeed be made threefold (*trivṛt*)," for the thunderbolt (*vajra*) is indeed threefold.
The sixteenth [stotra] is the vajra.
Now, they say: "It should indeed be made fifteenfold," for the vajra is fifteenfold.
The *vajra* is the *ṣoḍaśin*.
Furthermore, they say that the *ṣoḍaśin* itself should be performed;
for the *vajra* is indeed fifteenfold.
Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, is sixteenfold. [Thinking], "With the thunderbolt accompanied by Indra, may I slay Vṛtra, evil," he indeed slays the hateful,
evil rival with the thunderbolt accompanied by Indra— he who knows thus.
Now, moreover, they say: "The *saptadaśa* alone should be performed.
For the *pañcadaśa* is indeed the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and Indra is the wielder of the thunderbolt; he is the sixteenth.
Prajāpati himself is the seventeenfold [stoma].
He is the executor, he is the protector, he is the one who gives the command: "Strike! Slay!
Do not retreat!"—[thinking] "With the thunderbolt accompanied by Indra and Prajāpati, may I slay Vṛtra, evil."
With the twenty-onefold thunderbolt, together with Prajāpati, he who knows this slays his hateful enemy and evil.
Now they say: "It should indeed be made twenty-onefold.
For it was from all seven *hotrā*s that Indra fashioned the thunderbolt; three [stotriyas] for each *hotrā*.
That [sāman] became the twenty-first sixteenfold chant.
By means of it, Indra slew Vṛtra.
He who knows this slays his hateful rival.
Regarding this, Yāmana Bhrātṛlāyana said: "This sixteenth [syllable] is for the sake of the perfection of the Virāj;
the sixteenth is indeed of the nature of the Virāj; it is established in the Virāj upon the Virāj."
Wherever one might perceive this Virāj being fully accomplished, there indeed it should be praised with this [hymn]. 4-191 (Ed.:
Indeed, the gods and the Asuras were arrayed against each other over day and night.
Those gods conquered the day.
Then the Asuras rushed toward the night. Those gods said, "We have indeed become masters of this world; how can we completely conquer the night? Let us join forces."
They applied themselves;
they strove in the latter half of the day.
Then the Asuras, having emerged from the night, strove in the former half.
This, indeed, is the latter half of the day, namely the evening;
and this, indeed, is the former half of the night, namely the evening.
Some strove for their own boundary, while others strove for their own.
The meters indeed were their own property;
they were arrayed against one another within the meters. 5-192 (Ed.:

The gods had the one-syllable [meter] as their lowest and the seven-syllable as their highest. The Asuras had the nine-syllable as their lowest and the fifteen-syllable as their highest. The seven-syllable and the nine-syllable were situated close together; the others were directed hitherward, and the others were directed thitherward.
Prajāpati, who is of the nature of the Anuṣṭubh, stood between them, having stepped across.
They remained there looking at one another and gazing intently, each seeking the other's weak point.
Those gods then ran to Prajāpati, saying, "Let us conquer the Asuras!"
To them he gave this sixteenfold thunderbolt, saying: "With this, having wrested their meters from them by means of your own meters, bring me back to my place.
They wrested the fifteen-syllable meter from him with the one-syllable meter, and the fourteen-syllable meter with the two-syllable meter;
thus it became the *anuṣṭubh*.
They bestowed her upon Prajāpati:
with a word of three syllables, they bestowed the word of thirteen syllables; with a word of four syllables, the word of twelve syllables.
Thus she became the Anuṣṭubh.
They presented her to Prajāpati.
By means of a five-syllable [meter], they formed an eleven-syllable [meter]; by means of a six-syllable [meter], a ten-syllable [meter].
Thus she became the Anuṣṭubh.
They united her with Prajāpati:
by means of a seven-syllable [meter] they obtained a nine-syllable one, and by means of eight [syllables], eight [syllables].
Thus she became the Anuṣṭubh.
They presented her to Prajāpati.
Having thus united the meters with their own meters, they drove away their wives.
While those wives were being driven away, Prajāpati, having become a reddish-brown horse, sniffed at them from behind.

These [syllables] are found one by one in the *udanta*s. By means of them, indeed, the gods prevailed and the asuras were defeated. He who knows this prevails in himself; his hateful rival is defeated. 6-193 (Ed.: 1,197)
The gods were indeed fewer, while the Asuras were more numerous. By means of this [rite], they [the gods] appropriated that which was more abundant from those who were fewer.
Therefore, a smaller village contends against a larger village; therefore, even those who are fewer conquer many enemies. He who knows thus appropriates the greater from the lesser.
This, indeed, is the manifest *paṅkti*: that which consists of five syllables and five feet.
They chant the *ṣoḍaśin* on *paṅkti* verses; for the *paṅkti* is the metre of man.
Since man is fivefold (*pāṅkta*), they thus fashion speech from man himself as something obtained;
therefore, man speaks all forms of speech,
for at this point all speech is indeed obtained.

Now, when they chant on *anuṣṭubh* verses, it is just as if one were to pour great oceans into a small jar that has been well-sealed; such is that. They transpose the smaller meters onto the larger meters.
These smaller meters indeed have their deities already won.
Therefore, they insert [verses] into the longer metres. Indeed, among the metres, that which consists of one foot of three syllables is the most powerful.
When they intermingle the metres with those [syllables], it is for the sake of attaining power.
He chants the *nidhana* over [the night]. The gods indeed overcame the night by means of the day;
he who knows thus conquers the world of his rival.
For this night is indeed like a vessel for one's rival.
They purchase the Soma with an earring.
Just as one who has mounted from ear to ear, so indeed is the *ṣoḍaśin* among the Stotras.
Those who say, "We do not purchase the *ṣoḍaśin*," nevertheless purchase the *ṣoḍaśin*.
In that the Soma-purchasing cow has ears reaching above her [shoulders], by that very fact their *ṣoḍaśin* is purchased; by that it is secured.
They purchase the Soma from the *adhikarṇi* [seller].
At each pressing they leave over some Soma.
They chant the praises on verses containing the word "people" (*janat*).
All forms are praised.
In that they purchase Soma with gold, the sacrificer thereby procreates him.
In that they leave over Soma from each pressing, the Adhvaryu thereby procreates him.
In that they praise with verses containing the word "people" (jan), the Udgātṛ thereby procreates him. In that all forms (rūpa) are recited after [the chant], the Hotṛ thereby procreates him.
These, indeed, are the means of procreation for the Ṣoḍaśin.
He who knows thus is propagated with offspring and cattle.
Indra, indeed, surpassed the *hara* [in power].
He said to the gods, "How may my *hara* not be exceeded?
The Viśve Devas said to him, "We shall praise you with a mantra containing the word *hari*; thus your *hara* will not be exceeded.
The Viśve Devas praised him with a mantra containing the word *hari*.
Then indeed, the *hara* did not exceed Indra. Therefore, when they chant on verses containing the word *hara*, they thereby endow Indra with *hara*.
Indeed, Indra is the deity nearest to the sacrificer.
When they chant on verses containing the word *dhara*, they thereby endow the sacrificer himself with sustenance and splendor.
He who knows this prospers. 9-196 (Ed.:
The Ṣoḍaśin is indeed like a side-horse among the Stotras.
When a side-horse draws without being yoked, it either breaks off or rubs away.
Therefore, the Samastoma occurs with the final Stotra.
Just as one would yoke a side-horse to a side-yoke, even so does he yoke the *ṣoḍaśin* after the preceding chants, so that it may not be lost.
Indeed, this *ṣoṣaśin* is like an axle for the chants;
by means of the final chant, it becomes a complete *stoma*, so that it may not be displaced.
Indeed, this Ṣoḍaśin is like a repetition among the Stotras.
By means of the final Stotra, it becomes a Samastoma for the sake of avoiding such repetition.
The Ukthas are indeed cattle.
The *ṣoḍaśin* is a thunderbolt.

In that they chant the *ṣoḍaśin* at the end of the *ukthas*, they enclose the cattle with the thunderbolt itself, so that they may not be lost. The wealth of one who knows thus is never lost. 10-197 (Ed.: 1,201)
Regarding this, they say: "The *ṣoḍaśī* [stotra] should not be performed with the *ukthya*.
For the *ukthas* are indeed cattle.
The *ṣoḍaśin* is a thunderbolt.
One should turn the thunderbolt against the cattle;
it should be performed as an *atirātra* sacrifice.
Water is indeed the pacification of everything. By means of water, they thus pacify him.

If the Soma were to be subject to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), one should fashion a golden thunderbolt with sharp points; then, whoever performs that rite, for each of them one should hurl it forth.
He hurls that very thunderbolt at him for his destruction.

When the Soma sacrifice has concluded, having turned the wooden trough (droṇakalaśa) upside down, and having made figures of men out of groats or out of green grass, he should cut their necks while pronouncing their names, saying: "Here I cut the neck of so-and-so; here [I cut] the neck of so-and-so; here [I cut] the neck of so-and-so. As many as are the names he pronounces, so many of them he cuts at the neck.
He gives it to the Brahman priest.
The Brahman priest is indeed the *brahman*;
the *vajra* is the *brahman*.
Verily, he thus establishes the thunderbolt in the Brahman.
Indra and Bṛhat both came into being together.
That Indra was surpassed by one great body.
He was afraid of it, thinking, "By this very [body] he will overcome me.
He said to the gods, "Let this sacrificial rite be the *ṣoḍaśin*."
"So be it. He became the *ṣoḍaśin*;
that was the birth of the *ṣoḍaśin*.
He who knows this surpasses his hateful rival in glory, having praised with the *bṛhat* *ṣoḍaśin* on *gāyatrī* verses in the two-footed form.
"With your bay horses, come to our pressed [juice]"—these indeed are the *gāyatrī* verses in the two-footed form.
Indra, for his part, desired to slay Vṛtra.
He ran to Prajāpati, crying, “The riches! Vṛtra! To him, Prajāpati gave this *apaharas* verse in the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
with it, he struck him down.
Because he bellowed without having struck [the enemy], that became the Nānada;
that is the reason for the Nānada’s name as Nānada.
Therefore they say: "The Nānada should be made the *ṣoḍaśin* chant, for with it he did not strike."
He ran back to him again, saying, "Wealth indeed is Vṛtra.
He fashioned the power of the seven *hotṛ* priests and gave it to him;
three for each *hotṛ* office.
He became the twenty-first *ṣoḍaśī*.
By means of it, Indra slew Vṛtra.
He who knows thus slays his hateful rival.
The *ṣoḍaśī* is indeed the twenty-first foundation (*āyatana*).

There are seven officiating priests (*hotrā*) who utter the *vaṣaṭ* call at the morning pressing, seven at the midday pressing, and seven at the third pressing. Moreover, it is that very *hara* (splendor/power) which he fashioned for him and bestowed.
Gaurīviti Śāktya indeed perceived this surplus of Brahman;
that became the Gaurīvita.
The Gaurīvita is indeed an excess of the *brahman*, and the *ṣoḍaśī* is an excess of the *stotras*.
When they chant the *ṣoḍaśī* with the Gaurīvita, they place that excess upon the excess for the sake of the regularity (*salomatā*) of the sacrifice.
Aupoditi Gaupālaya used to say: "Viśāla covered Libujā; he placed the Nānada in the *anuṣṭubh*; they chanted the *ṣoḍaśī* with the Gaurīvita; he did not fall away from prosperity."
He who knows this does not fall away from prosperity.
Moreover, it is prepared for his offspring like provisions for the morrow.
One who desires cattle should perform the *ṣoḍaśin* chant upon the *śakvarī* verses.
The *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed the thunderbolt;
the *śakvarī* verses are cattle.
By means of the thunderbolt itself, he wins cattle; he becomes possessed of cattle.
One who desires, "May I be a wielder of the thunderbolt," should perform the *ṣoḍaśin* chant upon the *śakvarī* verses.
For the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed the thunderbolt,
and the *śakvarīs* are the thunderbolt.
By means of the thunderbolt itself, he overcomes the thunderbolt; he becomes possessed of the thunderbolt.
One who desires food should perform the *ṣoḍaśi* chant on the *virāj* verses;
for the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed a thunderbolt.
Food is the Virāj.
By means of the thunderbolt, he secures food; he eats food and becomes an eater of food.
These [verses] consist of thirty-three syllables.
Then, those which are twenty-one are the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*).

And those which are twelve are procreation (*prajananam*). He who knows thus stands firmly upon the foundation and is procreated; he does not perish while remaining within [the foundation]. 13-200 (Ed.: 1,204)
"Bring forth [the song] for the great one, who increases the great"—these indeed are the *virāj* verses.
One should perform the *ṣoḍaśin* chant in *anuṣṭubh* verses if he should desire: "May no other speech speak over me."
The *ṣoḍaśī* is indeed the thunderbolt;
the *anuṣṭubh* is speech.
By means of the thunderbolt itself, he secures speech; no other speech speaks over him.
"Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra"—these indeed are the *anuṣṭubh* verses.
Now, these are three-syllabled, single-footed verses, such as "the *bhurij* and *śakvarī* meters of Viṣṇu.
By means of these, indeed, Indra slew Vṛtra; by means of these, he attained prosperity and food.
He who knows thus slays his hateful rival and attains splendor.
They chant the *ṣoḍaśin* after having bestowed gold;
thereby they make the *ṣoḍaśin* itself luminous.
He stands near the horse for the sake of attaining equality. By doing so, he stands scattering away their world of rivals.

He gazes at the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with the verse: "He from whom no other is born superior, who has come into being as all the worlds—Prajāpati, rejoicing in his offspring, he accompanies the three lights; he is the *ṣoḍaśin*. Thus he gazes at the *ṣoḍaśin* draught.
Indra the sovereign and Varuṇa the king—those two first partook of this portion for you; I partake after them of their portion: may Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma.
Of the gods, that which consisted of one syllable was the lowest, and that of seven syllables was the highest.
Of the Asuras, that which consisted of nine syllables was the lowest, and that of fifteen syllables was the highest.
Those gods desired: "May we, by means of the smaller, appropriate more from the Asuras.

By means of a single syllable, they appropriated fifteen syllables; by means of two syllables, fourteen syllables; by means of three syllables, thirteen syllables; by means of four syllables, twelve syllables; by means of five syllables, eleven syllables; by means of six syllables, ten syllables; by means of seven syllables, nine syllables; and by means of eight [syllables], eight [syllables].
In this very way, he who knows thus appropriates the greater from his hateful rival by means of the smaller. 14-201 (Ed.: 1,205)
1,206) |p1 The Asuras, driven away from the day, entered the night.
Those gods fashioned this thunderbolt with the Anuṣṭubh for its head;
with it they pursued them.
This [thunderbolt] is indeed speech.
They descended with speech as their light.
This [speech] is indeed the Virāj;
they descended with the Virāj as their light.

The Atirātra is indeed not like the Suyajña. In that there is a *pānta* [cup], by that very means the sacrifice is performed for the connection of the day and the night, for the sake of continuity and non-interruption.
Those metres which carry the day also carry the night: this is the Gāyatrī, this is the Virāj, this is the Kakubh, this is the Anuṣṭubh.
They chant on *bṛhatī* verses.
By that, they do not depart from the *bṛhatīs*.
Since those [verses] have feet consisting of twelve syllables, by that, they do not depart from the *jagatīs*.
He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call with a *triṣṭubh* verse.
By that means, they do not depart from the *triṣṭubh*. While they were fleeing away by means of the *sandhi*, he caused them to reach a state beyond being separated by means of the *āśvina* cup.
Verily, he who knows this causes his hateful rival to go to ruin, which is indeed impossible to overcome.
This night is indeed the measure of the Agniṣṭoma;
for there are twelve stotras of the Agniṣṭoma, and twelve [hours] of the night.
This night is indeed the correspondence of the Ukthya sacrifice:
there are three Ukthas, and the *saṃdhi* (connecting litany) has three deities. This night is indeed the correspondence of both the Agniṣṭoma and the year.
There are twelve stotras of the Agniṣṭoma; twelve months are a year.
By means of the night, however, a thirteenth month is obtained.
This night, indeed, is the summit of the sun.
He who knows this goes to the world of the sun.
This Atirātra sacrifice is indeed the all-encompassing sacrifice.
Indeed, there is no day without night, nor is there night without day.
Not one of these worlds exists alone.
Day and night, indeed, produce all this—the worlds, the past, and the future.
Regarding this, they say: "A sacrificer should not perform the *atirātra* for the first time.
For he would be exceeding his own [capacity] as well as two sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*).
The *agniṣṭoma*, indeed, is the *brahman*.
The Brahman is indeed the own property of the Brāhmaṇa.
For he holds the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, and the Ṣoḍaśin in contempt.

Regarding this, they say: "One wins only as much as the Agniṣṭoma by means of the Agniṣṭoma, only as much as the Ukthya by means of the Ukthya, and only as much as the Ṣoḍaśin by means of the Ṣoḍaśin."
"By means of the night, one wins everything.

Indeed, for one who, knowing this, connects four sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) by means of a single sacrificial rite, four heroic sons are born to him, and he finds firm standing in all cattle. 2-203 (Ed.:
The Asuras, driven out from the day, entered the night.
The gods perceived these Sāmans, these Paryāyas;
with them they pursued and overtook them.
They killed them by turns. Because they killed them by turns, that is the "turning" (paryāya) nature of the paryāyas.
He who knows thus kills his hateful rival by turns.
Those who were covered by the first night, they struck with the first *paryāya*.

In that the first feet of the first *paryāya* are repeated at the beginning, they thereby strike those very ones who were covered by the first night. Those who were covered by the middle night, they struck with the middle *paryāya*.
When the middle feet of the middle turn (*paryāya*) are repeated at the beginning, they strike down by means of that very [turn] those who were covered during the middle watch of the night.
Those who had been covered during the latter part of the night, they struck down with the final turn.
When the final feet of the final turn are repeated at the beginning, they strike down by means of that very [turn] those who were covered during the latter part of the night.
Moreover, they struck them again; it was just as if, having struck once, one were to strike again. He who knows thus strikes his hateful rival again and again. 3-204 (Ed.: 1,208)
The night is indeed named Śarvarī.
Those gods said, "Truly, Śarvarī has come upon us."
That, indeed, is the reason for the *apiśarvara* nature of the *apiśarvara* [sacrifices].
Truly, prosperity (*api*) comes to him during the night (*śarvaryām*) who knows this.
Indeed, this world was formerly among the Asuras.
Having conquered that, the gods said, "By what means might we join day and night together from above?
They saw this *rāthaṃtara* junction;
with it, they joined day and night together from above.
That which they joined together is the *saṃdhi* (union); that is the nature of the *saṃdhi*.
Indeed, the *uktha* of the *saṃdhi* belongs to the Aśvins; they chant the *saṃdhi* during the latter part of the night.

The Āśvina [śastra] is recited from the rising of the sun. This is for the continuity of day and night, and for the commencement of day and night. Having conquered day and night, the gods made the thunderbolt itself their enclosure (paridhi) for the protection of cattle and to prevent the Asuras from entering.
In that these *uṣṇih* verses are performed at the end, and since the *uṣṇih* is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), they thus enclose the cattle with the thunderbolt itself so that they may not be lost.
He whose wealth is not lost is he who knows this. 4-205 (Ed.:
This world, indeed, was originally among the Asuras.
Having conquered it, the gods said, "Let us divide this.
They could not reach an agreement regarding its division.
They said, "Let us run a race for this [earth].
They ran the race.
Agni's chariot was first, then that of Uṣas, then that of the Aśvins.
The two Aśvins made the horse swift in its swiftness.
As they were running, Agni stood up against them. They said, "Let us pass you by."
"No," he said, "let me have a share.
"A third for you," they replied, "but you must tell it to us as well. "So be it," he said, and he related it to them.
As they were running away, Uṣas rose up before them. They said to her, "Let us pass you.
She replied, "No; let me have a share."
"Recite the third [verse] for us," they both said, "and let it be explained to us.
"So be it," he replied, and he recited it for them.
They both won.
He who thus knows this victory of the Aśvins, wherever he desires, "May I win here," there he wins.
And he who knows this participation of Agni and Uṣas, wherever he desires, "May I be a participant here," there he becomes a participant.
Therefore, they chant on verses dedicated to various deities, yet it is designated specifically as the *āśvina*.

Those gods conquered the day.
Then the Asuras entered both the *ṛc* and the night.
Those gods said, "We have indeed become masters of this world."
"How may we completely conquer the night? How may we follow it with treasures? they asked Agni, saying, "By your meters."
With "By your hymn," he approaches Indra;
with "By your perfection," Prajāpati;
with "By your abode," the Viśve Devas.
Because they said to Agni, "By your metre," therefore they praise in *gāyatrī* verses.

Because they said to Indra, "By your *stoma*," therefore the fifteenfold *stoma* belongs to the night. Because they said to Prajāpati, "By your perfection," therefore it is perfected in the *anuṣṭubh*.
Because they said to all the gods, "By means of your own abode," therefore the *jagatī* verses are recited after them.
They fled from them by means of the *sandhi*, but [the gods] caused them to reach the *āśvina* [śastra], which is inseparable (*asaṃheya*).
Indeed, he who knows this causes his hateful rival to reach that which is inseparable. 6-207 (Ed.: 1,211)
Having indeed driven out the Asuras from the days and nights, the gods struck them down with the threefold thunderbolt.
These worlds, indeed, are the threefold.
With these very worlds they pinned them down.
Therefore they say: "The Asuras will not prevail so long as these worlds continue to exist," for they have been pinned down by these worlds.
This night, indeed, is the correspondence between the Agniṣṭoma and the year.
The year consists of twenty-four half-months, and there are twenty-four *ukthāmadāni* (hymn-joyful verses) in the night. There are three pressings (*savana*) and three rounds (*paryāya*).
In this way, they make the night possess three pressings;
moreover, they thus fashion it as if it were a day.
Having conquered both day and night, the gods led that sun westward by means of the pressings alone.
They [the gods] again established him facing eastward by means of various methods.
They supported him from the front with the Āśvina Śastra;
therefore they say, "The Āśvina [Śastra] should not be recited once the sun has risen."

It indeed moves him about. He who knows this thus: that yonder sun is led by his *savana*s and becomes turned westward; it is brought back again by the *paryāya*s and is supported facing eastward by the *āśvina* [cup] in front.
Both day and night of his are seized and secured for his enjoyment; for his sake, the sun moves its rays. 7-208 (Ed.: 1,212)
Now,
this *sandhi* belongs to the *rathaṃtara*.
Prajāpati gave his own daughter, Uṣas, to Bṛhaspati.
He assigned this thousand [cows] as the bridal procession for her, dedicated to the Aśvins.
He said to the gods, "This one is mine; this other is yours.
Therefore, when a man who is not cruel finds a wife, he assigns the bridal procession separately.
Those gods said, "Let us divide this. They could not reach an agreement on its division.
They said, "Let us run a race for it."
They went forth for the race.
Agni’s chariot was first, then that of Uṣas, then that of the Aśvins.
Those two Aśvins made their horse swift in the contest with a mare.
The gods said to them, "This is your choice; now let it be ours as well. Therefore, they chant on verses dedicated to various deities, yet it is called the *āśvina* [śastra].
They chant for Agni first, then for Uṣas, and then for the two Aśvins.
For thus are these their *ujjiti*s (modes of winning):
one *sāman*, two *chandas* meters.
He thereby places the two-footed [human] upon the four-footed cattle.
Therefore, he stands over the four-footed animals from among the two-footed.
He should recite the concluding verse before the sun has risen for one whom he desires should become worse;
he indeed becomes worse.
When it has dawned, he should hand [the fire] over to one whom he desires [with the thought]: "May he be neither near nor far.
He becomes neither near nor far;
indeed, Parjanya becomes very rainy for him.

When [the sun] has risen, he should conclude [the recitation] for one whom he desires: "May he become more excellent; may he attain splendor. He indeed becomes more excellent and attains splendor. 8-209 (Ed.:
The verses beginning with *pāntam ā vo andhasaḥ* are those containing the word *andhas*; for *andhas* is the day,
and *pāntam* is the night.
It is for the continuity of day and night, for the commencement of day and night. Among these [sāmans], there is the Vaitahavya with the *okonidhana*.
By means of the Vaitahavya with the *okonidhana*, the gods drove the Asuras away from their respective dwellings (*oka*).
He who knows thus repels his hateful rival from every single dwelling-place.
Indeed, the vital breaths are the dwelling-places;
it is the vital breaths of his hateful rival that he thereby appropriates, and it is the vital breaths that he bestows upon himself.

Regarding this they say: "Those who perform the *atirātra* sacrifice fall away from this world. In that regard, as for the fact that there is a finale (*nidhana*) consisting of the word *oka*, this world is indeed the dwelling-place (*oka*) of man; thus, they find firm support in this very world.
Vītahavya Āśrayasa, having been long exiled, while wandering, desired: "May I go back to my own dwelling-place."
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it;
he concluded with the *nidhana* "okā."
Then indeed he went down to his own abode.
This is that *kāmasani* Sāman; it was this very desire that he desired.
That desire of his was fulfilled. Whatever desire one praises with this *sāman* while desiring it, that desire is fulfilled for him.
Moreover, it is indeed prosperity and sovereignty.
He indeed attained sovereignty.
He who knows thus attains prosperity and attains sovereignty.
Because Vītahavya Āśrayasa saw it, it is therefore called the *vaitahavya* with the *okas* as its finale. 9-210 (Ed.: 1,214)
"Sing forth the exhilarating [song] for Indra"— thus they become verses containing the word *mada*.
Indeed, *mada* is essence (*rasa*).
This night is, as it were, like one that has been pressed;
they do not press [the Soma].
Because they leave over the *ṛjīṣa* from that third pressing, with that they perform the ritual on this [night].
In that these [verses] contain the word "mad" (intoxicating), they thereby place essence into her; by this they cause her to swell.
Among them is a verse addressed to Śakti.
By means of the Śakti [verse], the Śāktas indeed won cattle.
That is the Śāktya-nature of the Śāktya [Sāman].
This is a Sāman favorable to cattle;
he who knows thus secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
The Śākyas, desiring food, performed austerity. They saw this Sāman;
they praised with it.
Thereupon, they indeed obtained food.
Of this very [sāman], there is [a form] just as there is of the Gaurīvita;
for the Gaurīvita is indeed food.
Food, indeed, is what belongs to the morrow.
And this entire world has surpassed food;
for this night is that which has surpassed it.
That which is redundant is indeed redundant; they thus bestow food upon the night.
That [chant] is the *svāra*; the *svāra* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Food, indeed, is breath. This *sāman* is the attainment of food that has come toward one;
he who knows this secures food for himself and becomes the best of his own people, an eater of food.
Because they saw [it] through the power of Śakti, it is therefore called the Śāktya.
"vayam u tvā tadidarthā" is the [hymn] of Kaṇva.
Kaṇva Nārṣada, wandering for a long time without a firm foundation, desired, "May I find a firm foundation.
He saw this Sāman;
with it, he praised.
He took *rantāya* as the *nidhana*.
Indeed, he who does not find firm support becomes, as it were, unsteady; and the night, indeed, is flickering.
This is indeed delight (rati).
From that, he indeed became firmly established.
This, therefore, is the *pratiṣṭhā* chant.
He who knows thus finds firm support.
Because Kaṇva Nārṣada saw [this], it is therefore called the Kāṇva [Sāman].
"Pressed for Indra, for his delight"—thus they contain the word *madvan* (delight).
The *mada* is indeed the essence (*rasa*).
This night is as if studied, as if pressed;
they do not press [the soma].
Since they leave over the *ṛjīṣa* from the third pressing, with that they perform this rite.
In that these [verses] contain the word "intoxicating" (*madvatī*), they thereby place essence into it; verily, by this they cause it to swell.
Among them [he established] Śrautakakṣa.
Śrutakakṣa, the son of Kakṣīvat, desiring cattle, performed austerity;
he beheld this Sāman.
He praised with that [verse].
He approached this *iḍā* (the sacrificial food).
The *iḍā*, indeed, is cattle.
Thereupon, he indeed obtained cattle.
This is that Sāman which belongs to cattle;
one who knows thus obtains cattle and becomes possessed of many cattle.
That, moreover, is the *punarnitunna* metre.
Wherever the gods found the essence of the metres, they made it *punarnitunna* there; they struck it again and again.
This night is indeed like a meditation (*dhīti*).
In that there is again a *nitunna* metre, they thereby place essence into this [chant]; this is a continuation of essence.
Because Śrutakakṣa saw it for Kākṣīvata, it is therefore called the *Śrautakakṣa*. That is the *Aiḍa* chant for the *acchāvāka*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
thus he establishes himself firmly in cattle. 12-213 (Ed.:
"This Soma here is for thee, O Indra.
This is indeed a repetition regarding the oblation;
for they say to Indra, "Now this other sacrifice is for thee."
For this Rātri is performed as a second oblation. On these [verses] he recites the Aurdhvasadmana [stotra]. By means of the Aurdhvasadmana, the gods indeed sat upright in these worlds.
Because they sat upright (*ūrdhvā*) in these worlds, that is the reason for the *aurdhvasadmana* [chant] being called *aurdhvasadmana*. This is a *sāman* leading to heaven;
he who knows thus sits upright in the heavenly world by means of it.

By means of the *aurdhvasadmana* [sāman], the gods indeed appropriated the cattle of the Asuras with the words "with well-fashioned hymns" (*suvṛktibhiḥ*); with "the intoxication of men" (*nṛmādanaṃ*), they hurled the thunderbolt; and with "in battles" (*bhareṣv ā*), they ascended to the heavenly world.

In the same way, by means of the *aurdhvasadmana*, he appropriates the cattle of his hateful rival with the words "with well-fashioned hymns"; with "the intoxication of men," he hurls the thunderbolt; and with "in battles," he ascends to the heavenly world.
Regarding these, they say: "They should be approached separately."
"Indeed, these worlds are as if diverse; [the verses are recited thus] for the support of these worlds.
"With well-fashioned hymns" is this world; "the exhilaration of men" is the intermediate space; "in the battles" is yonder world.
Therefore, they should be approached separately, for the support of these worlds. 13-214 (Ed.: 1,218)
Regarding this, Jānaśruteya said: "The *nidhana* is indeed the vigor of the *sāman*.
They would cause it to be agitated and they would separate it if they were not to approach it."
"One should approach them together because of the vigorous power (*savīryatva*) of the *sāman*.
These [syllables] consist of four syllables;
we thereby establish ourselves in all four directions that exist in this world.
"May we be established in all those four directions that are in the intermediate space;
may we be established in all those four [directions] that are in yonder world. For indeed, by means of the *Aurdhvasadmana* [stotra], the night possesses a back-bone (*pṛṣṭhinī*).
This indeed is the Rathantara;
the Vāmadevya is the intermediate space; yonder world is the Bṛhat.
Indeed, those which are the best of these worlds are the *pṛṣṭhas*.
He who knows thus becomes one of them.
Prajāpati, indeed, is the *ūrdhvasadman*.
He who knows thus attains the state of Prajāpati. 14-215 (Ed.:
1,220) |p1 [The verse] "Come to us, O Indra, with food" is for the flute-player.
Veṇu Vaiśvāmitra desired, "May I be foremost, preeminent, and possessed of spiritual luster.
He saw this Sāman;
with it, he praised.

From that, indeed, he became foremost, preeminent, and possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*). He who knows this becomes foremost, preeminent, and possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge.
And because Vena Vaiśvāmitra saw [this], it is therefore called "the bamboo flute" (*vaiṇava*).
Now, they also call this the Āpāla [sāman].
For Apālā, the daughter of Atri, was afflicted with a skin eruption and a foul odor;
she desired, "May I cast off this evil complexion."
She beheld this *sāman* and praised with it. As she was descending toward the bathing place (*tīrtha*), she found a shoot of *soma*.
He devoured it.
Its teeth became like pressing-stones (*grāvan*). Indra ran toward it, thinking, "The pressing-stones are indeed speaking!"
She spoke aloud:
"The maiden, drawing down the water, has placed the *soma* into the strainer; bringing it to its resting place, she said, 'I shall press you for Indra, I shall press you for Śakra.
Having realized, "Indeed, her teeth speak like pressing-stones," Indra turned away.
He said to him:
"O you little hero who go from house to house looking about, drink this pressed soma, accompanied by parched grain, by flour-mash, by cakes, and by hymns!
But he paid no heed at all.
He said to him:
"We cannot even discern you, nor do we perceive you at all.
[Thinking], "He has praised me with the entire hymn before its time," he turned away.
"Flow around for Indra, O Indu, slowly, very slowly"— with these words, he drew the Soma from her mouth.
Indeed, for one who, knowing this, kisses the mouth of a woman, it becomes as if he has partaken of the drinking of Soma.
He said to her, "O Apālā, what is your desire?
She replied:
"These three elevated surfaces, O Indra, cause them to sprout anew: that head of my father, this fertile field, and this [wound] here upon my belly; make them all hairy."
"Your father was indeed bald," he said.
He made him bald;
his field did not yield grain.
He was born; indeed,
the hairs on her lap were not yet grown,
but they grew there.
He pulled it out from the hole of the chariot;
it became a lizard.
He pulled it out from the hole of the cart.
It became a lizard.
He pushed it over the yoke-hole;
it became a *saṃśliṣṭikā*.
Regarding this, the following verse is recited:
"O Śatakratu, through the hole of the chariot, the hole of the cart, and the hole of the yoke, O Indra, you thrice purified Apālā and made her sun-skinned.
That which was the most beautiful of all forms became her form.
This is the *kāmasani* Sāman. She indeed desired that desire; that desire of hers was fulfilled.
Whatever desire one has while praising with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him.
Furthermore, because Apālā, the daughter of Atri, saw [this], it is therefore called the "Āpāla" [sāman]. 16-217 (Ed.:
"Towards you, O bull, the pressed [juice]..."—this is the *ārṣabha* [sāman]. Indra, indeed, desired: "May I become the bull of all creatures; may I attain the state of a bull.
He beheld this sāman.
He praised with that [verse].
Thereupon, indeed, that bull became the lord of all creatures and attained the state of being a bull.
That is precisely what constitutes the "bull-nature" (ārṣabhya) of the bull.
He who knows this becomes a bull among his own people and attains the state of a bull.
Regarding this, they also say it is "Daivodāsa.
Divodāsa Vādhryaśva indeed desired: "May I obtain both the spiritual power (brahman) and the ruling power (kṣatra); being a king, may I become a seer (ṛṣi)."
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he acquired both the Brahman and the Kṣatra; being a king, he became a seer.
He attains both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*; being a king, he becomes a seer (*ṛṣi*)—he who knows thus.
Because Divodāsa Vādhryaśva saw [this], it is therefore called the "Daivodāsa" [sāman]. 17-218 (Ed.:
"O Vasu, this pressed juice," [is] the *gāra* hymn.
Indeed, the Asuras vomited up *garas* for the gods;
those [gods], not knowing [them], vomited them up, thinking they were merely food.
They thought themselves to be poisoned.
They desired, "May we strike down these swallowed poisons.
They saw this *sāman*.
They praised with that. With it, they struck away these swallowed embryos.
Those very things became these embryos.
In that they struck down the swallowed poisons (gara), that is the very reason for the name *gāra*.
Whoever might think himself a swallower of poison—having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that should not be eaten—he should praise with this [sāman].
Verily, he strikes away that swallowed poison.
Whatever evil has been committed by him, that he destroys.
That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman.
Cattle, indeed, are the *iḍā*.
Thus he finds firm support in the very cattle. "For this [heaven] follows by its might"— this is the *ghṛtaścut* finale.
Wherever the gods suffered a deficiency in their sacrifice, they replenished it with that which drips with ghee and that which drips with honey.
Therefore, they say: "May the stalk of Soma swell!
for this night is indeed like a deficiency in the sacrifice.
In that the *nidhana* is "ghṛtaścut," they thereby cause her to swell. Now, Ghṛtaścut and Madhuścut, two Aṅgirases, were left behind when the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world.
They desired, "May we fly after them to the heavenly world."
The two of them performed austerity.
They saw these two *sāmans*;
with them, they praised.
Having praised those two with the verses "O dripping with ghee" and "O dripping with honey," they flew up toward the heavenly world.
Ghee is indeed the end of milks; the heavenly world is the end of worlds.
Honey is indeed the end of juices; the heavenly world is the end of worlds.
By means of those two final *sāmans*, they indeed attained the final heavenly world.
He who knows this attains the final heavenly world by means of those two final *sāmans*.
Cattle, indeed, are dripping with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
The cattle drip honey.
Verily, by means of these two [verses], they two then won the cattle;
and having sacrificed with those cattle, they two went to the heavenly world.
These two *sāmans* are conducive to cattle and lead to heaven.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and goes to the heavenly world. 19–220 (Ed.:
These two *sāmans* are indeed the body of the sacrifice.
By means of these two, Indra milked the sacrifice and all desires. He who knows this indeed milks the sacrifice and all desires.
Of these two, one has the *yajus* as its finale (*nidhana*) and the other has the *sāman* as its finale. That which has the *ghṛtaścut* as its finale is the *yajus*-finale;
and that which has the *madhuścut* as its finale is the *sāman*-finale.
Whatever prosperity belongs to the Yajus and the Sāman, he who knows this attains that prosperity and obtains those desires.
Regarding this they say: "Since they proceed by day with clarified butter (ājya), by what means does their night become possessed of clarified butter?
One should reply: "By the *nidhana* [ending] 'ghṛtaścun'."
By this, indeed, the night becomes possessed of *ājya*.
And because the two Aṅgirases, Ghṛtaścut and Madhuścut, saw it, therefore it is called by that name. 20–221 (Ed.: 1,225);
Now follows the *maidhātitha* [sāman].

The Kāṇvāyanas, having risen from a sacrificial session (*sattra*), were returning while yoking their draft animals. They were called *udgathāḥ*. Thinking, "What is this high place? they approached a desert where many *urvāru* gourds were growing, lying there.
They desired: "May we release these very cattle that have become [lost]."

Medhātithi Kāṇva saw this Sāman. With it, they sat down [to perform the sacrifice], [chanting]: "Come here, sit down; sing forth to Indra, O friends who bring hymns of praise—the most abundant of the many, the lord of desirable things—Indra when the Soma is pressed. May he indeed be with us for our journey, for wealth, and for inspired wisdom."
Cattle indeed are wealth.
From that, they released those cattle that had come into being;
indeed, they released them by means of the *hiṃkāra*.
These very ones here are the cattle called "the speckled ones behind the sheep.
This is the *utsṛṣṭi* (emission) *sāman* of cattle;
he who knows this secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Because Medhātithi Kāṇva saw this [sāman], it is therefore called the *maidhātitha*.
Now follows the *saumedha*.
The gods, having slain the Asuras, considered themselves as if unpurified and impure.
They desired, "May we become purified and fit for sacrifice.
They saw this Sāman.
They praised with it.
Thereupon, they indeed became purified and fit for sacrifice. They said, "We have indeed become well-purified."
That indeed is the reason for Saumediha’s name, "Saumediha.
He who knows this becomes pure and fit for sacrifice.
Regarding this, they also call him "Paurvatitha."
The *pūrvatithi* was inferior to Śyāvāśva Ārcanānasa. He desired, "May I obtain cattle; may I attain abundance of cattle.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
"May he indeed come with thousandfold aids if he hears us"— with this [verse],
he won a thousand cattle and attained abundance of cattle.
This is a *sāman* that procures cattle.
He who knows thus encloses cattle for himself and attains abundance of cattle.
Because Pūrvatithi Ārcanānasa saw [this], it is therefore called "Paurvatitha.
There are *uṣṇih* verses beginning with "O Indra, when the Soma juices have been pressed."
The *uṣṇih* is indeed a divine city (*devapurā*).
In that they are performed at the end, they thus surround the divine city at the very end for the protection of the cattle and so that the Asuras may not enter. 22-223 (Ed.:
Among them, the Kautsa [hymn]:
Kutsa and Luśa both invoked Indra;
he came to the invocation of Kutsa.
He bound him to his testicles with a hundred she-goats.
Luśa spoke to him:

"For I have heard of you, O Indra, as one who acts according to his own will, the driver-away of the enemy, the bull who impels the weak; release yourself from Kutsa, come here! How can one like you remain bound by the testicles?"
Having torn them all apart, she rushed toward Luśa.
Kutsa called out after him with the words, "O Indra, when the Soma juices are pressed!
and he turned back toward him.
Luśa called out to that Indra, "Ho! Ho!
He stood between them.
He said to them, "Bring me a portion."
"I shall drink from one of you by myself, and from the other by means of its greatness.
"So be it. They both brought forth their respective portions.
One [of the two] won the self, the other the greatness;
Kutsa won the self, Luśa the greatness.
One drank from the self, the other from the greatness.
He drank by means of his own self from Kutsa’s [cup], and by means of his greatness from Luśa’s.
Both of these—his very self and his greatness—are indeed yours alone. This *sāman* is thus possessed of Indra.
The sacrifice of one who knows thus becomes possessed of Indra and the gods; Indra turns toward his sacrifice, and Indra does not depart from his sacrifice.
Because Kutsa saw this, it is called the *Kautsa*;
that is the *Aiḍa* chant for the *Acchāvāka*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
thus he establishes himself among cattle. 23-224 (Ed.:
Regarding this, they say: "The *rathantara* should be on the first triplet of verses, the *vāmadevya* on the second, and the *bṛhat* on the third, for the purpose of ascending these worlds;
for these worlds are indeed these *sāmans*."

This very world is the Rathantara; the intermediate space is the Vāmadevya; yonder world is the Bṛhat. Therefore, it should be performed in this very manner, for the purpose of ascending these worlds.
Indeed, these Sāmans are the out-breath (prāṇa), the diffused breath (vyāna), and the up-breath (udāna).
The *rathantara* is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the *vāmadevya* is the inter-breath (*vyāna*), and the *bṛhat* is the up-breath (*udāna*).
Therefore, it should be performed in this very manner, for the sake of the continuity and non-interruption of the out-breath, inter-breath, and up-breath.
Now, he who should desire, "May my offspring be more excellent," should perform the *rathantara* on the first triplet of verses and the *vāmadevya* on the two following ones.
The Vāmadevya is indeed Prajāpati.
Thus, they finally approach Prajāpati himself with his own sound for the sake of procreation.
One who desires prosperity or one who desires heaven should praise with the Bṛhat.
Prosperity is indeed the heavenly world.
He who knows this attains prosperity and goes to the heavenly world;
moreover, he does not abandon the world of his enemies.
For the night is indeed a vessel for one's rivals.
One who desires a firm foundation should chant with the *rathantara* [sāman];
for the *rathantara* is indeed a firm foundation.
He stands facing [the east]. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should chant with the *saṃdhi* on *gāyatrī* verses;
for the *gāyatrī* is indeed the Brahman.
He indeed becomes endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*).
One who desires manhood [should use] *kakubh* verses;
for the *kakubh* is indeed manhood.
He indeed becomes possessed of men;
one who desires cattle [should use] the *uṣṇih* verses,
for cattle are indeed the *uṣṇih*.
He indeed becomes possessed of cattle.
One who desires food should [use] the *virāj* verses; for the *virāj* is indeed food.
He indeed becomes an eater of food.
One desiring a firm foundation should [recite] in *anuṣṭubh* meters;
for the *anuṣṭubh* is indeed a firm foundation.
He stands facing [the fire].
Regarding the *paṅkti* verses: he who desires sacrifice, or who should desire, "May sacrifice come back to me," [should use them]; for sacrifice is indeed the *paṅkti*.
The sacrifice approaches him once again.
One who desires vigor and one who desires heroism [should recite] in *triṣṭubh* meters;
for the *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor and heroism.
He indeed becomes possessed of vigor and strength.
One desiring cattle should [chant] in *jagatī* verses;
for cattle are indeed the *jagatī*.
He indeed becomes possessed of cattle.
Regarding this, they say: "For him who chants in this manner, the chant is performed in only one metre and for only one desire;
however, for him who chants in the *bṛhatī* verses, the chant is performed in all metres and for all desires."
"For all these meters indeed resolve into the *bṛhatī*.
"The *gāyatrī* and the *jagatī*—those two are *bṛhatīs*.
The *uṣṇih* and the *triṣṭubh*—those two are *bṛhatīs*."
The *anuṣṭubh* and the *paṅkti*—these two are *bṛhatīs*.
Indeed, the *bṛhatī* is itself the *bṛhatī*.
Therefore, one should chant the stotra in *bṛhatīs* alone, for the attainment of all these meters and all desires.

Regarding this, they say: "Since the *trivṛt* is the lightest among the *stomas*, the *rathantara* the lightest among the *sāmans*, and the *āśvina* the heaviest among the *śastras*, why then is the *trivṛt* among the *stomas*, the *rathantara* among the *sāmans*, and the *āśvina* [śastra] capable of countering [the heaviness]?
He should reply: "The *trivṛts* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)."
All this is established in the vital breaths;
the vital breaths sustain all this;
the vital breaths support all this individually.
These worlds, indeed, are threefold.
Everything here is established upon these worlds;
these worlds support everything here.
These worlds are each established in this [Vāk].
Speech, indeed, is the Rathantara;
in speech all this is established.
Speech upholds all this;
speech supports all this individually.
This [earth] is indeed the *rathantara*.
Upon her all this is established;
she holds up all this;
she supports all this individually.
Therefore, the *trivṛt* among the *stomas*, the *rathantara* among the *sāmans*, is fit to counter-attack the *āśvina* recitation. Thus [ends] the *hiṃkāra*. 2-226 (Ed.:
Regarding this they say: "Since other sacrificial rites possess the *pavamāna* [laud], by what means does their night become possessed of the *pavamāna*?
One should reply: "By the *rāthaṃtara* *saṃdhi*.
For by this indeed the night becomes possessed of the *pavamāna*.
With that single *hiṃ* uttered, they chant the *stotra* directed toward the future.
For they indeed utter the *hiṃ* once at the end of the *trivṛt*, thinking, "May the beginning be the same as the conclusion.
However, the former *trivṛt* is the emission of seed, while the latter is procreation.

The self, indeed, is offspring and cattle; these are the *ṛc*-verses. The *rathaṃtara* is procreation. Just as if seed were cast but not produced, such is that if they should chant with the *hiṃ* uttered only once.
In that they utter the *hiṃ* call for every triplet of verses, it is for the sake of procreation.
