He who knows thus becomes manifold and is propagated. Moreover, if they were to chant with only a single *hiṃ* call, only one of their turns would possess a foundation, while two would be without a foundation.
In that they utter the *hiṃ* call for each triplet of verses (*tṛca*), by that very act their entire night becomes possessed of a foundation and possessed of the *pavamāna* chant.
As is the day, so is the night; as is the night, so is the day.
[The divisions are: the forenoon, midday, and afternoon; the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, and the last watch of the night.
In that they utter the *hiṃ* call for each triplet of verses, it is for the sake of the separation of day and night.

Regarding this, they say: "Since all sacrificial rites conclude according to the twenty-one-fold [stoma], and the *ukthas* indeed exceed the twenty-one-fold, how then does the night conclude according to their twenty-one-fold?"
He should say: "In that these become twenty-one Trivṛts and nine Ekaviṃśas.
Then Bhāllabeya used to say: "Who indeed today will sacrifice with a sacrificial rite that has light on both sides?
That sacrificial rite which is the Atirātra is indeed one that has light on both sides.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is threefold (*trivṛt*) at the beginning, and the *rathantara* *saṃdhi* is threefold at the end.
Agni is indeed the former threefold, and Āditya is the latter.
By means of Agni, this world is luminous; by means of Āditya, that [world].
The sacrificial rite of this [sacrificer] becomes possessed of light on both sides; he who knows thus becomes radiant in this world and in that world.
These two, indeed, are the Brahman and the Kṣatra.
The Trivṛt is the Brahman, and the Pañcadaśa is the Kṣatra.
These two, having joined together the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*, carry the night.
Having thus joined together the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*, they finally drive away evil.
Therefore, these two *stomas* are performed at the end for the very purpose of driving away evil.
He who knows thus drives away evil.

When those two become the Gāyatrī, since the Gāyatrī is indeed splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he thereby establishes himself in splendor and spiritual luster. Moreover, he thereby establishes the sacrificer in his life-span for the sake of attaining a full life.
The Gāyatrī is indeed the vital breath. He who knows this attains a full lifespan. 4-228 (Ed.:
"One should sacrifice with a sacrifice that is perfect through the Virāj," they say.
The Virāj is indeed food;
and King Soma is truly the food of the gods.
Having made that very [soma] into food, he offers King Soma to the gods.
Indeed, this [soma] is not food for the gods unless it has been pressed;
having pressed it and thus made it into food, he offers it to the gods.
Whatever one does here for the gods, the gods do that for him.
They, being successful, cause him to prosper with offspring, cattle, and food.
"One should not sacrifice beyond the Virāj," they say.
Whoever performs a sacrifice that exceeds the Virāj, he remains as a sacrificer in yonder world;
he stays there parched, rough, desiring to accomplish and obtain the Virāj but failing to attain it.
For how can he obtain that which he departs from here without having attained?
As they were sitting there like commoners, Asita Daivala said, "Who are these that sit here?
They replied, "We are those who have passed beyond Virāj.
He spoke to them.

He falls from his chariot. The wheel is in front of the hole in the path; the wheel turns back upon him who sacrifices with what is incomplete. "The immature one gives to the gods with a sacrifice that does not reach its goal; that very thing of his does not reach the world [of the gods]."
"Being cooked, yet not understanding, you have acted contrary to the will of the gods," he said to them; "you who have sacrificed beyond the Virāj.
Regarding this, they say: "From where did you take away the sacrifice? Where did you establish it? He should reply:
"From wherever I took it away, there I established it."
The sacrifice is indeed extended from the person; it is established in the person.
Now, King Āllakeya Māhāvṛṣa, whose mind was set on the heart, consecrated his son.
For him, Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi was the chosen Udgātṛ priest.
Then messengers from the Mahāvṛṣas ran toward him, saying, "Come! This is an assembly.
Running forward, he said, "O Udgātṛ, I shall entrust this son of yours to you.
He then returned once more to his home.
He said, "O Udgātṛ, where did you establish the sacrifice? Where the sacrificer? And where his cattle?
He did not answer him.
He said, "Initiate my son again."
"Indeed, we do not know where they have placed my son," he said.
They initiated him again,
and he himself sang the *ujjagau* chant for him.

If he had replied, "I have established the sacrifice in the sacrificer, the sacrificer in the Vāmadevya, and his cattle in the Rathantara," then this would indeed be the ultimate reach of speech, namely, "ten. 6-230 (Ed.:
1,235) |p1 This is indeed the ultimate reach of speech, namely, "ten."
"Speech has indeed stepped forth this far.
May I attain all that which is the furthest stride of speech.
Now, as for what follows—twenty, a hundred, a thousand—these are its very limbs and joints.
That is indeed the abundance of speech.
Moreover, in this very way one attains the entire Virāj;
for this ten-syllabled Virāj is truly the perfection of the person.
There are ten vital breaths in a person.
This, indeed, is the praise of these one hundred and ninety *stotriya* verses;
for when this Agniṣṭoma sacrifice has been completed, there are exactly one hundred and ninety *stotriya* verses.
That which is one hundred and eighty is the *kṛta*.

Indeed, that which is ten times [that] would be the *kṛta*. Regarding this, the Kurus say: "This [stoma] consisting of one hundred and ninety *stotriya*s is the *dvāpara*, for it is the lowest of the three ages (*yuga*s)."
The Kṛta indeed conquers the Tretā; the Tretā [conquers] the Dvāpara. Two *stotriya* verses are introduced;
thus it results in the Kṛta-stoma.
By means of what has been performed, he conquers that which he desires to conquer; by means of what has been performed, he breaks through.
Moreover, these two Pavamāna [stotras] are the wings.
He makes those two equal;
moreover, the Viśvajyotis becomes the sacrificial rite,
and it is also doubly praised.
Those two are the Virāj breasts;
that sacrificer has two feet for the sake of firm standing. 7-231 (Ed.:
Regarding this, Kahoḍa Kauṣītakeya used to say: "Alas, their Virāj has long breasts—those for whom the two 'breasts' are in the *stotriya* [verse].
He further said: "Surely they milk this Virāj from their neighbor.
Indeed, the gods venerated this very perfection in syllables.
The seers venerated her.
We too, in succession from one to another, venerate her alone. Of these one hundred and ninety *stotriya* verses, there are five thousand, four hundred and seventy-two syllables.
Those two which are the seventy-second syllables are indeed the two breasts of the Virāj.
"He is the two-footed sacrificer, for the sake of stability," they say. Regarding this, they ask: "If the Dvāpara-stoma is used, then by what means is the Kṛta-stoma [attained]?"
"One should say, 'By means of syllables';
or else, 'By means of hymns';
or else, 'By means of hymns and recitations.'"
Moreover, if one should say, "tenfold-made," by that very fact it is the *kṛta-stoma*.
Indeed, this very one attains the tenfold-made.
In the beginning, this world was indeed the great waters, a vast ocean.
That was the sovereignty of the waters, the kingdom of the waters, and the food of the waters.
Agni desired it, thinking: "May this sovereignty be mine, may this kingdom be mine, may this food be mine."
He perceived this perfection of the Agniṣṭoma.
With it, he drew out these waters—both those flowing upwards and those flowing downwards.
Singing this very *dinandina* stoma, he made this food entirely his own.
With nine sets of twenty-one [bricks], he pushed those upward.
He pushed them beyond the sky. These, having been pushed up, stand raining according to the seasons.
With twenty-one threefold [verses], he stood upon these downward-flowing [waters].
He pushed them beyond the earth.
These very waters, having been thus pushed aside, some people subsist upon by inhaling their fragrance.
Some [waters] stand still, others flow;
having thus separated and driven away these waters, he eats food in this world.

Neither small, nor middling, nor great food was left over for him. In just this way, having arrayed and driven away his hateful rival, he eats food in this world; neither small, nor middling, nor great food is left over for him who knows thus.
All the gods gathered around him as he had conquered that food.
They indeed could not find it.
For that twenty-first [verse] of the *yajñāyajñīya* lay there, having been placed within those nine *bahiṣpavamāna* verses; having become infinite and encompassing this food, it lay there.
Moreover, just as embers might be scattered in a vessel, even so was he infinite, visible within these worlds.
Not finding them, he said to them, "Praise me! 10–234 (Ed.:
1,239) |p1 The Vasus praised him with the Gāyatrī metre, with the Gāyatra Sāman, and with the morning pressing.
He invited them at that very pressing. The Rudras praised him with the Triṣṭubh metre, with the Traiṣṭubha Sāman, and with the midday pressing;
he invited them at that very pressing.

The Ādityas praised him with the Jagatī metre, with the Jāgata Sāman, and with the third pressing. They invited him back at that very same pressing. The Viśve Devas, Vāk, Manas, and Prajāpati praised him with the Anuṣṭubh metre, with the Yajñāyajñīya Sāman, and with the third pressing.
He invited them to that very *stotra*. Thus these gods prepared themselves for this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*).
Now, as for those who did not prepare themselves for it—
"Those who were constantly overcome by the hunger of the gods—
those who followed after him are these very ones who remain today."
And they shall indeed remain overnight.
This is the Vaiśvadeva-stoma;
for in ancient times, this stoma belonged to all the gods.
Therefore, because they praised Agni with it, that is its character as an *agniṣṭoma*.
They praised Agni with this [sāman];
indeed, they praise him with it, and they praise him with it for their own security and for safety.
Those who know this praise with it among the people; they become their own.
This very [sacrifice] amounts to nine twenty-one-fold stomas:
twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first.
One *stotriyā* verse remains over.
Indeed, it is the sacrificer who thus remains over, for whoever knows this.
Just as light would shine upon a mountain, even so does he shine among that community in which he exists, provided he knows this.
And that very [sacrifice] becomes twenty-one threefold [stomas].
Agni, indeed, is the threefold;
therefore, whatever is threefold, all that becomes Agni.
Whatever great prosperities there are, and whatever small ones, they all indeed come to one who knows thus. All desires come to him who knows thus.
This [breath] is established in yonder sun by means of twenty-one threefold [stomas], and yonder [sun] is established in this [breath] by means of nine twenty-one-fold [stomas].
These two are thus established in one another;
he who knows this becomes firmly established. 12-236 (Ed.:
That [sun] does not set, nor does this [person] follow after it;
rather, that [sun] sets into this very [person].
That is its "setting-ness" (astatva).
For that [sun] indeed sets toward this [earth];
this [fire] follows after that [sun].
That is the reason for its name, *amutva*.
For this one indeed follows after that one.
He who knows thus does not lose his hand, nor does he fail to follow it. These two deities are co-dwellers.
By means of these two, he attains companionship with them.
Moreover, these two deities remain in these worlds, driving away all evil from him.
For as long as this fire blazes in this world, for so long does the sun [blaze] in yonder world.
Indeed, for one who knows this, the world is not subject to exhaustion.
Just as here on earth a seeker of a dwelling-place strives to obtain a dwelling, so do the waters strive to obtain this world—both those which are yonder and those which are these.
That they do not mingle is solely due to the power of this Stoma.
This very *stoma* provides these [worlds] for him.

He who might indeed be the protector of one kingdom, or of two, or of three—he would surely consider himself a possessor of the worlds (*lokī*) by that means. But he alone among them would truly be a possessor of the worlds who is the protector of this world.
He who knows this becomes one of the protectors of this world;
by that he possesses the world.
Indeed, as long as there shall be Brahmins who know this, neither those waters yonder nor these here shall both together wipe away this world.

Now, of this very *agniṣṭoma*, the morning pressing (*prātassavana*) is accomplished as the *gāyatrī* metre, the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina savana*) as the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) as the *jagatī* metre.
Thus, this morning pressing is self-perfected.
The Gāyatrī alone is everything.
Now, there are four meters for the midday pressing: the Gāyatrī, the Bṛhatī, the Kakubh, and the Triṣṭubh.
Of this very Kakubh, which consists of twenty-eight syllables, he places twenty syllables upon the Gāyatrī.
That becomes a *triṣṭubh*.
Then, those eight which remain over, he places them upon the *bṛhatī*;
that becomes a *triṣṭubh*.
The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the *triṣṭubh*.
Now, there are six meters for the third pressing: the *gāyatrī*, the *uṣṇih*, the *kakubh*, the *anuṣṭubh*, the *jagatī*, and the *bṛhatī*.
Of this very *gāyatrī* consisting of twenty-four syllables, he places twenty syllables upon the *kakubh*.
That becomes a *jagatī*.
Then, those four which remain over, he places as *uṣṇih*s;
that becomes a thirty-two-syllabled *anuṣṭubh*.
The Anuṣṭubh is indeed the Anuṣṭubh.
He divides it into two parts;
he places sixteen syllables of it upon the Anuṣṭubh.
It becomes a *jagatī*. The *jagatī* itself is at the end. Then, those sixteen which remain over, he places them upon the *bṛhatī* of the *yajñāyajñīya*.
It becomes a *jagatī* consisting of fifty-two syllables.
Four syllables exceed the *jagatī*;
these are indeed the four-footed cattle.
The milking of the Virāj is indeed the udders;
it is also the foundation. Just as a four-footed animal would stand firmly, so [does he].
That indeed follows right here;
nothing is left over.
When there is a deficiency in the Vāmadevya [sāman], one lays down three [bricks]. (14-238)
The Yajñāyajñīya [Sāman] is one [syllable].
The morning pressing is indeed Gāyatra, the midday pressing is Triṣṭubh, and the third pressing is Jāgata.
For one who knows this, although he is a Brahmin, there is the radiance of a Kṣatriya and the wealth and prosperity of a Vaiśya.

Indeed, for him, the Gāyatrī is established syllable by syllable as the morning pressing, the Triṣṭubh as the midday pressing, and the Jagatī as the third pressing. There are sixty-nine Stotriya verses of the morning pressing; the midday pressing consists of sixty Triṣṭubhs; and the third pressing consists of twenty-four Jagatīs and one Kakubh.
The *kakubh* is indeed man. That sacrificer is thus supported upon this [metre] as it comes together;
therefore, he follows after it right here.
Nothing is left over. Having taken four syllables from one *kakubh* of twenty-eight syllables, he places three in the deficient *vāmadevya* and one in the *yajñāyajñīya*.
Then, that *gāyatrī* which remains, he places it here among the sixty-nine *stotriyas* of the morning pressing.
And that, indeed, is infinite.
He who knows thus conquers infinite prosperity. 15-239 (Ed.:
In this very way, two pressings result in the Bṛhatī metre.
The third pressing is exactly as it was before.
There are sixty-nine *stotriya* verses in the morning pressing.
These amount to forty-six *bṛhatī*s.
For those three *gāyatrī*s are two *bṛhatī*s;
thus they amount to forty-six *bṛhatī*s.
This very morning pressing, as it proceeds, attains the Bṛhatī metre.
Because the morning pressing, as it proceeds, attains the Bṛhatī, therefore a Brāhmaṇa, at the very moment of birth, is born as one who possesses a world.
Indeed, he makes that [world] greater by his conduct, or he makes it smaller.
Then, at this point, both the Udgātṛ and the Hotṛ complete the midday pressing. The Udgātṛ yokes four meters;
the Hotṛ recites them after him and brings forward three others: the Anuṣṭubh, the Paṅkti, and the Jagatī.
The gāyatrī and the jagatī—these two are bṛhatīs.
The uṣṇih and the triṣṭubh—these two are bṛhatīs.
The anuṣṭubh and the paṅkti—these two are bṛhatīs.
The *bṛhatī* is indeed the *bṛhatī*.

Because these two together accomplish the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), therefore a place for a *rājanya* should be prepared through his sacrificial merit (*iṣṭāpūrta*), faith, and devotion to the Brahmins. But because the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is exactly as it was before, therefore the *vaiśya* is more worldly than both the *brāhmaṇa* and the *rājanya*.
For the world is not as it is for the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya. Indeed,
the sacrificer is born into a well-established world.
Verily, by the first *stotriya* of the first *ṛc*-triad he conquers the earth; by the second, Agni; by the third, the atmosphere.
Verily, by the first *stotriya* of the second *ṛc*-triad he conquers Vāyu; by the second, the breath; by the third, the sky.
Verily, by the first *stotriya* of the third *ṛc*-triad he conquers Āditya; by the second, the lunar mansions; by the third, [the stars].
These Bahiṣpavamāna stotras consist of nine verses; there are nine worlds of the gods.
By means of these, he attains them.
These are three Virājs: the divine, the sacrificial, and the human.
Sucitta Śailana once challenged Janaka of Videha on these very points. He said, "Let faith enter me; let the officiating priests summon me.
Then, the Kurus and Pañcālas brought the officiating priests to him.
When they had arrived, Śailana became afraid, thinking, "These are like coming Brahmins with their inquiries; perhaps he will not spare me here.
He said, "O Emperor, I have a statement to make.
"There are these three Virājs: the insatiable, those that signify all desires, and those that signify food."

"Whosoever places you within those [vessels], choose him indeed as your Udgātṛ. He who knows these desires within them is truly the one who carries those desires to fulfillment; he who knows thus is also the one who carries one beyond repeated death. 1-241 (Ed.: 1,245)
Then he indeed set out to run;
as he was about to depart for it, he said:
He used to ask about the perfection of these *virāj* verses.
They, however, did not teach them.
But whoever among them did teach them—whichever single verse he taught—he would sit [and wait for him].
"I beheld a true Brahmin indeed, a Brahmin who was deliberating upon these [verses]: 'Run toward Śailana! That was his sacrificial distribution, just as Śailana desired it.
These are the three *virāj* verses: the divine, the sacrificial, and the human."
This divine Virāj is these worlds;
it is deficient.
It is deficient for the sake of providing space for the sacrificer.
He places the sacrificer within that [space].
Of this very [space], the moon is the cover.
For the moon is the food of the gods manifest before their eyes.
Now, these *bahiṣpavamāna* verses are the sacrificial *virāj*;
they are deficient.
They are deficient for the sake of providing a foothold for the sacrificer.
He places the sacrificer inside it.
For this very [vessel], the *hiṃkāra* is the lid;
for it is with the *hiṃkāra* that food is ultimately bestowed upon the gods.
This human Virāj consists of these vital breaths (prāṇas) within a person;
it is deficient.
That, indeed, is the sacrificer manifest.
Food is indeed the cover of this very [Virāj].
These three Virājs have the navel as their center.
One attains those desires which are contained within them.
But rather, it occurs here among them:
he is indeed released from repeated death;
he eats food in this world through many persons.
For that food which is in these [cows] is not for a single person alone.
Whatever indeed exists here in this world that possesses a self, all that stands with death having seized it from every side. And that which is death is the year itself.
The seasons are indeed its mouths. Therefore, whatever dies, it dies only in the seasons.
He who knows this does not die out of season.
Verily, he who knows thus is procreated with offspring and cattle during the seasons.
These are the nine *bahiṣpavamāna* verses.
These are six *bṛhatī*s.
And there are six mouths of Death, namely the seasons.
Now, indeed, it is only the *bṛhatī* that is capable of counteracting these mouths of Death, and no other metre.
He covers the opening of the season with a *bṛhatī* verse; [he does so] for the sake of the season, for the sake of the season.
Just as one might look back after passing over uneven ground by means of level ground, even so, having passed beyond this death, he looks back. They set forth against him this threefold thunderbolt.
Day after day, this very [Agni] follows along these worlds.
Regarding this, Nāgarī Jānaśruteya used to say: "The conflict between the gods and the Asuras will certainly not cease until this threefold thunderbolt follows along these worlds day after day.
For this Agni blazes upward; this Vāyu blows across; and yonder Āditya burns downward.
These, indeed, gaze at one another without blinking, thinking:
"How can there be a conflict between the gods and the asuras while these are thus?
This very threefold thunderbolt of his, revolving day after day around these worlds, wards off all evil for one who knows this. 3-243 (Ed.: 1,247)

Regarding this they say: "He indeed should sacrifice today, or he should cause another to sacrifice, who, while causing one to sacrifice with the *catuṣṭoma*, causes one to sacrifice with the *sarvastoma*.
There are nine of these *bahiṣpavamāna* chants.
Of these, there are twenty-seven verses.
By this, they do not interrupt the *triṇava* stoma. These *bahiṣpavamāna* chants consist of exactly nine [verses].
The *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables. That makes thirty-three.
By means of this, they do not interrupt the *trayastriṃśa* hymn-form.
Verily, by causing one to sacrifice with the Catuṣṭoma, he causes him to sacrifice with the Sarvastoma.
He who knows the lowest and the highest of the Stomas reaches the highest state.
The Trivṛt is indeed the lowest of the Stomas; the Trivṛt is the highest.
Regarding this, Prakru Vārṣṇa said: "I beheld the Trivṛt Stoma becoming the Trayastriṃśa;
therefore, I attained supremacy.
He who knows thus attains supremacy.

Now, Āruṇi used to say: "What could he practice against in sorcery, or what would one practicing sorcery against him care about, who knows this threefold, three-pointed thunderbolt—flawless, not failing, which follows these worlds day after day?
"He is indeed himself struck down by sorcery whom one who knows thus hates, or whom one who knows thus hates.
And this very threefold, three-pointed thunderbolt—flawless, not failing, following these worlds day after day—turns back upon him.
"For him, there is not even the slightest hope for prosperity; rather, it becomes his ruin.
Regarding this, Upajīva Khāḍāyana used to say: "I alone know this threefold thunderbolt directly."
"Therefore, both he whom I hate and he who hates me shall become worse day by day.
Fire is indeed the thunderbolt of this world, Vāyu of the intermediate space, and Āditya of the sky. This same [thunderbolt] exists within the self (adhyātma).
That which is Agni is speech itself;
that which is Vāyu is breath itself;
that which is Āditya is sight itself.
"Therefore, when I address one who hates me, when I breathe toward him, or when I look at him, I hurl a thunderbolt at him.
For him, there remains not even the slightest hope of prosperity.
Indeed, these very deities afflict him who afflicts one who knows this."

Now Śvetaketu Āruṇeya used to say: "Just as the appearance of a white horse with black ears might be when it has been brought here, even so do I know the appearance of this *stoma*; it is so beautiful to behold, so lovely in form.
Therefore, those who wish to see me in the forenoon wish to see me in the afternoon as well.
"It is not as if I am truly beautiful to behold; indeed, I never avoid anyone who possesses sight."
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "What is the white horse? What is the one?
Just as is the form of this Agni, just as his brilliance, just as that of Vāyu, and just as that of yonder Āditya—such indeed is the form of this Stoma, such is its brilliance.
It is this very thing that stands encompassing all creatures, desiring to be seen.
Therefore, at the *bahiṣpavamāna*, both those who understand it and those who do not—all being powerless—stand surrounding it, desiring to see it.
Moreover, these [verses] are indeed the glory of other deities as well;
for this *bahiṣpavamāna* is the gathered power, vigor, essence, and splendor of them.
He who thus knows this—the power, the vigor, the essence, and the splendor accumulated in these deities—becomes indeed possessed of power, possessed of vigor, renowned, and radiant.

Regarding this, they say: "When a man is about to unite with a woman, he seeks a secret place of concealment; yet other animals mate openly with one another. What is done in the sacrifice so that it is not likewise?"

He should say: "Because the *trivṛt* stoma, having stepped forward as it were from the *bahiṣpavamāna* and hidden itself beyond the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, causes the *gāyatrī* to fall; and because other officiating priests sit at the very end of the *dhiṣṇyas*, therefore it is so.
For man is connected with the *trivṛt* stoma, while other animals are connected with the *dhiṣṇyas*.
Regarding this, they also say: "When that *trivṛt* stoma causes the *gāyatrī* to fall, what does she produce from that?"
One should say, "The sacrifice ends with the *iḍā*, having seven naves.

That *gāyatrī* conceives the embryo; she gives birth to the *puronuvākyā*; the *puronuvākyā* [gives birth to] the *yājyā*; the *yājyā* [gives birth to] the *vaṣaṭkāra*; the *vaṣaṭkāra* [gives birth to] the oblations; the oblations [give birth to] the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); the sacrificial fees [lead to] the heavenly world.
Just as wealth would swiftly flow along a current, even so these deities carry him forth to the heavenly world.

The *trivṛt* stoma delivers him to the *gāyatrī*; the *gāyatrī* to the *puronuvākyā*; the *puronuvākyā* to the *yājyā*; the *yājyā* to the *vaṣaṭkāra*; the *vaṣaṭkāra* to the oblations; the oblations to the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*); and the sacrificial fees cause him to go to the heavenly world.
This sacrifice, ending with the *iḍā*, has seven naves.

For him, the *trivṛt* chant is indeed the navel; the *gāyatrī* meter is the navel; the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) is the navel; the offering verse (*yājyā*) is the navel; the *vaṣaṭ*-call is the navel; the oblations are the navel; and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are the navel.
This sacrifice inclines toward him who knows thus.
There are fifteen *ājya* stotras.
There are fifteen nights in the waxing half-month;
thus, by that very means, he attains it.
There are ten fingers on the hands; there are four [parts] to the forearms and upper arms;
that which is above the navel is the fifteenth.
He connects that very [stotra] here.
The midday [pavamāna-stotra] consists of fifteen [verses].
There are fifteen nights in a half-month.
By that very means, he obtains that.
There are ten toes;
there are four kneecaps.
That which is below the navel is the fifteenfold [stoma];
that very thing he joins here.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are seventeenfold.
There are twelve months; there are five seasons;
thus he obtains that very thing by means of it.
There are ten fingers on the hands;
there are seven vital breaths in the head;
that makes seventeen.
He connects that very thing here:
the Ārbhava [Śastra] consists of seventeen [verses];
there are twelve months.
There are five seasons;
by that very means he attains them in their proper order.
There are ten toes and fingers.
There are four [breaths] in the thighs and the anus;
three downward breaths;
that makes seventeen.
He connects that very thing here:
the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the twenty-first;
there are twelve months.
There are five seasons;
these worlds are three;
yonder sun is the twenty-onefold.
By that very means, one attains that.
There are ten fingers on the hand and ten on the foot.
The self is the twenty-first. He joins this very [element] here. 7-247 (Ed.:

Knowing this, having integrated his self into all this—day by day, half-month by half-month, month by month, season by season, and year by year—he crosses over that death which exists in the heavenly world.
One who knows this does not die again.
His bones consist of the *Ṛgveda*, and his flesh consists of the *Sāmaveda*.
This very one, having shaken off evil and shaken off the body, transcends this death and shakes off the body.
Now, these are the two Virājs, the divine and the human;
upon these two, this Āditya shines, mounted above.
The four quarters, the four intermediate directions, and these two worlds—
this is the divine *virāj*.
Now, the human [virāj]:
There are four eaters and six that are eaten. The Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra—these are the eaters.
The cow, the horse, the goat, the sheep, rice, and barley—these are the eaten.
Upon these two, this Āditya shines as one who has ascended.
Therefore, there is neither heat nor cold for him; he does not hunger, he does not thirst, and there is no obstacle whatsoever for him.
Indeed, he neither hungers nor thirsts, and no obstacle whatsoever arises for him who knows thus. (8-248 [Ed.: 1,252])
When the Udgātṛ sings the Bahiṣpavamāna, he indeed pours out the sacrificer as seed.
By means of the Retasyā, he impels the mind; by the Gāyatrī, the vital breath; by the Triṣṭubh, the eye; by the Jagatī, the ear; and by the Anuṣṭubh, speech.
He lays down the Paṅkti verses upon himself.
Now, that which is this final triplet is indeed birth;
by means of it, he brings forth [the sacrificer].

Because this is sung as if with sound and resonance, therefore embryos are born as if with sound and resonance. Regarding this, however, they say: it should be sung without sound. For when she is being delivered, she makes a harsh noise, and only then does she make a sound.
Moreover, as it were slowly and as it were silently, the great creation is brought forth.
Furthermore, that which is the *gāyatra* is indeed the truth. One should not covet its perfection by practicing the *rathantara*-like verses.
Therefore, it should be sung as unvoiced (*aghoṣa*) alone.
Now, the *ājya* chant dedicated to Agni has a single deity;
that is indeed the *preti*.
Then there is the offering to Indra and Agni, dedicated to two deities;
that indeed is stability.
This very [offering] is both departure and stability.
He who knows thus finds firm support.
By means of the *trivṛt* and the *pañcadaśa*, the person is established in this world. That which he takes away is the *trivṛt*.
That by which one stands firm is the fifteenfold [stoma].
Indeed, both of these are threefold, and both are fifteenfold.
The threefold *stoma* is indeed splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), while the fifteenfold is force and vigor.
Having established himself through vigor and heroism alone, he who knows thus takes away splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge. 9-249 (Ed.:
1,254) |p1 Now follows the Gāyatrī of the Mādhyandina Pavamāna.
This downward breath is indeed that very [Sāman]. On it there are two Sāmans.
Therefore, by means of this breath, one performs two things: he produces ash and he produces wind.
They have different introductory chants (*prastāva*) and different concluding chants (*nidhana*), with the *hiṃ* call in between.
Therefore, one does not roar after the other, nor does the other roar after this one;
for by this [chanting], it is thus expanded (*vihṛta*).
Now, as for the Bṛhatī:
that which is this forward-moving breath is indeed it;
upon it are two Sāmans.
Therefore, by means of this breath, one performs two things: one emits semen and one urinates.
They have different preludes and different finales, with the *hiṃ* sound in between.
Therefore, one does not trumpet after the other, nor does the other trumpet after him.
For by this it is spread out.
Now, as for the *triṣṭubh*:
that is indeed the navel.
In that [day] there is one *sāman*.
Therefore, with this single breath he performs that which he performs for the out-breaths as they go upward.
Now, the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]:
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed sensory power (*indriya*) and vigor (*vīrya*).
Therefore, whatever parts of a cow, a horse, or a man are the backbone (*anūka*), those are the strongest; for the *pṛṣṭha* chants are that very sensory power and vigor.
These [verses] occur in the *bṛhatī* meters.
Therefore, these [bones], like *bṛhatī*s, the *kīkasā*s, and like *bṛhatī*s, the *pariśava*s, converge upon the back. 10-250 (Ed.:
Now follows the Gāyatrī of the Ārbhava Pavamāna.
That which is this breath is indeed it. Upon that [Gāyatrī], there are two Sāmans.
Therefore, one performs two functions by means of the breath: one breathes out and one breathes in.
There are different preludes and different conclusions, with the *hiṃkāra* in between.
Therefore, one does not roar after the other, nor does the other roar after him.
For by this it is expanded.
Now follow the uṣṇih and kakubh [verses]:
"Your two eyes."
The metre is the same; there are two *sāmans*. Therefore, the two eyes see the same thing.
The *ṛc*s consist of three feet;
therefore, the eye is threefold: white, black, and the pupil.
The *ṛc*s consist of the "higher-and-lower" (*parovarīyasī*) type.
Therefore, a person sees what is higher and lower.
For there are two different preludes (*prastāva*) and two different conclusions (*nidhana*), with the *hiṃkāra* in between.
Therefore, the two eyes have distinct powers.
Now follows the Anuṣṭubh.
It is speech itself. In it there are two Sāmans.
Therefore, with speech one performs two things: by means of it one both eats food and speaks.
There are different preludes and different conclusions, with the *hiṃkāra* in between.
Therefore, one does not speak everything with speech as truth, nor does one speak everything as falsehood.
For by this it is expanded.
Now, as for the Jagatī:
that is indeed the ear.
On that [gāyatrī] there is one *sāman*.
Therefore, with this single ear, he performs only that which he hears.
It occurs on a four-footed *ṛc*.
Therefore, being in one place, he hears from all directions;
even when turning away, he hears those speaking behind him. Now follows the Yajñāyajñīya.
That is indeed the head.
For the head is supported upon the other limbs;
likewise, the *yajñāyajñīya* is supported upon the other chants (*stotra*).
He who knows thus becomes one who is pre-eminent among his own people. For the head is indeed above the other limbs;
likewise, the *yajñāyajñīya* is above the other chants.
He who knows thus becomes superior to others among his own people.
This very sacrifice is visibly free from evil;
indeed, there is neither one who speaks ill of it nor any doer of evil toward it.

If someone should utter a curse against him during the *bahiṣpavamāna* [laud], he should say to him: "I have spoiled the seed that was poured out; you have ruined the sacrifice. Your offspring shall be seedless.

If someone should utter a curse against him during the *ājya* [laud] dedicated to a single deity, he should say to him: "I have spoiled the advance of the sacrifice; you have ruined the sacrifice. You have advanced toward death; you shall die.

If someone should utter a curse against him during the *ājya* [laud] dedicated to two deities, he should say to him: "I have spoiled the foundation of the sacrifice; you have ruined the sacrifice. You shall be without a foundation."

If someone should recite over him during the Gāyatrī verse of the Mādhyandina Pavamāna, he should say to him: "I have struck down the downward breath of the sacrifice; a sacrificial disease will strike you down.
Furthermore, he should say: "A discharge will strike you down.

If someone should recite over him during the Bṛhatī verse, he should say to him: "I have struck down the penis of the sacrifice; a sacrificial disease that causes retention of urine will strike you down."
Then he might say, "You shall become seedless.

If one should utter a curse against him during the *triṣṭubh* verses, he should say to him: "I have struck at the navel of the sacrifice; the ruin of the sacrifice shall turn back upon you and slay you. If one should utter a curse against him during the *pṛṣṭha* verses, he should say to him: "I have struck at the power and vigor of the sacrifice; the thunderbolt of the sacrifice shall slay you."
Then he might say: "The killing of one who is unaware shall kill you.

If someone should recite over him while the *gāyatrī* of the *ārbhava-pavamāna* is being chanted: "You have struck at the breath of the sacrifice; you have harmed the sacrifice; the breath shall leave you," he should say this to him.
Then he might say: "You will die prematurely.

If someone should curse him with the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters, he should say to him: "I have struck out the two eyes of the sacrifice; you, who have ascended the sacrifice, will become blind. If someone should curse him with the *anuṣṭubh* meter, he should say to him: "I have struck out the speech of the sacrifice; your speech, O sacrificer, will depart from you."
Furthermore, he should say: "You will die of hunger.
If someone should curse him during the *jagatī* [chant], he should say to him: "I have struck at the ear of the sacrifice; you, the destroyer of the sacrifice, will become deaf.

If someone should curse him during the *yajñāyajñīya*, he should say to him: "I have struck at the head of the sacrifice; you, the destroyer of the sacrifice, your head shall fall off. 12-252 (Ed.: 1,255)
These indeed are the counter-utterances;
one who knows thus does not meet with sacrificial misfortune.
Whoever speaks ill of him meets with ruin. If anyone should speak ill of him, he should say to that person: "I know this sacrifice complete in its limbs, with its body, and in its entirety;
whatever deficiency you perceive therein, I shall close it up by means of that very [knowledge] of yours."
He who reviles one who knows this incurs misfortune.

This very Prajāpati is the Agniṣṭoma; having placed that twenty-first [verse] of the Yajñāyajñīya upon these nine Bahiṣpavamāna verses, he lies there milking these two sets of ten-syllable Virāj verses: five fifteen-syllable [Virājs] and five seventeen-syllable [Virājs].
These indeed are the five thirty-two-syllable Virājs.
Verily, he who knows thus milks the Virāj for all his desires.
The sacrifice of one who knows thus does not leak away, even if he speaks untruth.
Indeed, the sacrifice of one who speaks untruth leaks away; moreover, it becomes putrid.
The sacrifice of one who knows thus does not leak nor does it become putrid.
Therefore, the Kurus and Pañcālas do not milk those who hate them.
For that [sacrifice] belongs to Prajāpati.
Therefore, others indeed yield milk when their udders are full;
for they do not know that [milk].
Therefore, others indeed yield milk when their udders are full, yet they are as if more hungry.
This very Prajāpati, as the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, having become circular and having become infinite, lies there.
Following his example, other deities here also are circular: the sun is circular, the moon is circular, the sky is circular, the intermediate space is circular, and this earth is circular.
Moreover, whatever divine thing there is here in man, that is circular.
He who knows this conquers great, infinite, and circular prosperity, following after its very limb without ever losing it.
This sacrifice is indeed directed upwards, following along with the person.

His two feet are the *bahiṣpavamāna*. These four [parts of] the thighs and knees are the *ājya* [stotras]. That which is below the navel is the midday (*mādhyaṃdina*) [savana] consisting of three meters (*trichandas*).
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the *pṛṣṭhas*.
This is the *ārbhava*,
and this is the *agniṣṭomasāman*.
A Brahmin asked Nāgariṇa Dālbhya, "In what way is the sacrifice dependent on the person?
He replied, "It is dependent on the person in an upward direction.
Thus indeed he spoke.
He who thus knows this sacrifice being extended upwards within himself goes upward indeed, rising with offspring and cattle.
And he who knows it as turned backward becomes one who turns back toward prosperity.
For him, this very [portion] is the *bahiṣpavamāna*.
These are the *ājya* [stotras]. This is the midday [pressing].
The *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are indeed the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].
This is the Ārbhava [laud].
The Yajñāyajñīya is indeed the foundation;
thus one becomes established in prosperity.
He who thus knows these two sacrifices being performed within himself— to him both sacrifices bow down. Regarding this,
there is this verse:
"That which is its front is its rear, and that which is its rear is its front; like the gliding of a snake or a *śākala* [crab], I do not know which part is in front.
Śākala Gaupāyana went about measuring out a sacrifice.
He did not know this: "Which part of the sacrifice is the front? Which is the rear? Which is the smaller? Which is the larger?"
Regarding this they say: "From what is the most deficient part of the sacrifice?
"From that which is the most excellent.
"And from what is the most excellent?"
"Because it is the smallest. Indeed, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is the smallest part of the sacrifice; therefore, he spoke of this as "feet."
Man is indeed smallest at his feet;
yet he is greatest there,
for it is by means of his feet that he moves forward.
"Whence is the most excellent?
"From that which is the smallest.
"The *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed the smallest with respect to the sacrifice."
This head spoke:
"The person is indeed smallest at the head,
yet he is also the greatest."
"For by means of the two *akṣi* [verses] one goes seeing.
Regarding this they say: "If the sacrifice were performed upright, only the gods would live, not humans;
if it were performed inclined, only humans would live, not the gods."
The sacrifice is indeed performed upwards, downwards, and also crosswise. Therefore, if they should ask, "In which direction is the sacrifice? [one should answer accordingly].
"One should say, 'Above';
or else, 'Toward us';
or else, 'Across.'"
"One should say, 'All the quarters,' for indeed, all the quarters belong to one who knows thus; from that, the sacrifice prospers.
The Kurus and Pañcālas once engaged in a theological debate."
They approached a dog lying curled up.
They said, "Let our victory rest upon this very thing!
Then the Pañcālas asked the Kurus, "What is this [sign] of the sacrifice?"
They did not answer him.

Then Vāsiṣṭha Caikitāneya said: "Just as that one there lies having laid down that twenty-first [brick] of the *yajñāyajñīya* upon these nine *bahiṣpavamāna* bricks, even so does this [sacrificer] lie here, having joined together both ends.
Indeed, through this mode of lying, he attains the form of this sacrificial rite."
Therefore, although this [sacrifice] is *anukthya*, they say "vibhūti.
By means of it, they indeed conquered. 15-255 (Ed.:
Verily, the sacrificer is born twice: one birth is from a couple, the other from the sacrifice.
Now, that which is born from a couple is born for this world;
but that which is born from the sacrifice is born for yonder world—it is born for the world of the Gandharvas, it is born for the world of the gods, it is born for the heavenly world.
The sacrifice is indeed the sacrificer;
the sacrifice is King Soma.
Therefore, when they press King Soma with the pressing-stones in the oblation-holders, they thereby make the sacrificer himself into seed.
The Udgātṛ is Prajāpati;
he is Tvaṣṭṛ;
he is the shedder of seed.
He is the transformer of forms.
When he sings the *retasyā* at the *bahiṣpavamāna*, he thereby pours forth the sacrificer himself as seed.
If he were to sing a verse without a *sāman*, only bone would be produced, not flesh.
If one were to sing the Sāman without its corresponding Ṛc, only flesh would be produced, not bone.
He sings the Ṛc smeared with the Sāman;
therefore, a person is born smeared with hair, skin, and flesh.
One should not utter the *hiṃ* sound during that [chant].
For if one were to utter the *hiṃ* sound, he would cut off the seed with the *hiṃ* sound as a thunderbolt.
Indeed, whoever might even pierce it with a mere hair, he alone would cut it off.
One should sing while studying it;
for if one were to sing without having studied it, embryos would be born without seed. Indeed, embryos are born without seed in the path of one who sings badly. 16-256 (Ed.: 1,259)
He sings the Gāyatrī;
the Gāyatrī is indeed breath.
He interlocks two syllables of that [verse].
He thereby interlocks the out-breath and the in-breath.
Therefore, the out-breath and in-breath move through living beings in an interlocked manner, both forward and backward, without becoming exhausted.
One should sing while studying it.
If one were to sing without having studied it, dead fetuses would be born.
Indeed, dead fetuses are born along the path of one who sings badly.
He sings a *triṣṭubh* verse. The *triṣṭubh* is indeed sight; he causes two of its syllables to shine forth.
He thereby bestows the two eyes;
therefore the two eyes are as if yoked together.
One should sing while studying that [verse].
If one were to sing while not studying [the Veda], blind embryos would be born;
indeed, blind embryos are born from the path of one who sings badly.
He sings the Jagatī.
The Jagatī is indeed the ear.
He illumines four syllables of it;
he thereby bestows the ear itself.
There are two ears and two auditory passages.
Therefore, being present in one place, he hears all the directions;
even when turned away, he hears those speaking behind him.
One should sing while studying it.
If one were to sing without having studied it, deaf fetuses would be born.
Indeed, deaf fetuses are born in the womb as a consequence of the path of one who sings badly.
He sings the *anuṣṭubh*.
The *anuṵṭubh* is indeed speech;
he sings it while pushing it toward himself, so that speech may not depart.
If he were to sing while pushing the speech away, his speech would be liable to depart from him. Since he sings while pushing it toward himself, he thereby establishes speech within his own self.
He sings both the expressed and the unexpressed syllables of that [speech].
By means of the explicit (nirukta), they indeed enjoy speech; its unexplicit (anirukta) aspect is what sustains it. He who knows this enjoys speech and lives by means of it.
If he were to sing only the explicit, people would indeed speak, but they would not remain silent.
Now, if he were to sing what is unexpressed (*anirukta*), people would remain silent and would not speak.
Because he sings both the expressed (*nirukta*) and the unexpressed (*anirukta*) in the verses, therefore people both speak and remain silent. 17-257 (Ed.:
One should sing that [verse] with great force and resonance, with a striking sound. Indeed, this metre, the *anuṣṭubh*, is like something that strikes down.
By means of the *anuṣṭubh*—that is, by speech as the metre—the gods struck down the Asuras, rendering them voiceless.
In that he sings it with force, with resonance, and with a striking stroke—the enemy is indeed evil—thereby they strike down this enemy, this evil, headlong; he attains prosperity for himself.
He should sing it while reciting [the text]. If he were to sing it without reciting, embryos would be born without tongues.
Indeed, in the tracks of one who sings badly, embryos are born tongueless.
He sings the *paṅkti*; the *paṅkti* is indeed the seasons.
He sings that [sāman] as the Gāyatra, extended;
therefore embryos are stretched out when being born.
One should sing it while studying it.
If one were to sing without having studied [the hymn], the embryos would perish prematurely;
indeed, embryos often fall prematurely upon the path of one who sings badly.
Now, this final triplet is truly birth itself.
By that very means, he procreates.
The *retasyā* is indeed the mind (*manas*), the *gāyatrī* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *triṣṭubh* is the eye, the *jagatī* is the ear, and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech.
He who, knowing that the *retasyā* is the mind, chants the *udgītha*, is born from him as one of great mind and possessed of mental power.
Then, he who, knowing that the breath is the Gāyatrī, sings the Udgītha, attains a full lifespan. Furthermore, he who is born from him attains a full lifespan.
Then, he who, knowing that the eye is the Triṣṭubh, sings the Udgītha, is born from him with an unashamed face as one who sees; he becomes beautiful to behold.

Then, he who, knowing that the *jagatī* is the ear, sings the *udgītha*, from him is born one who is eager to hear, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), and one worthy of being heard. Then, he who, knowing that the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, sings the *udgītha*, from him is born a reciter (*śaṃstṛ*) and a singer (*udgātṛ*) who is master of speech.
O assembly-member! For it was thus that the Kurus and Pañcālas understood.
Therefore, among the Kurus and Pañcālas, a hero is born together with all heroes.
Now, formerly when they did not know this regarding the *udanta* (concluding verses), therefore in those *udanta* [sacrifices] a hero was not born together with all his heroes.

But since now those who know thus associate with the *udanta*-verses and those who know thus perform the sacrifice for them, from that time onwards, in the *udanta* sacrifices, a hero is born together with all his heroes.
The Kurus and Pañcālas indeed engaged in a theological debate (*brahmodya*).
The Pañcālas asked the Kurus: "What did we do at that sacrifice by which a hero was born among us together with all our heroes?
They did not answer them.
Because of that, they defeated them.

If they had replied, "Because we are knowers of this, and because those who know this officiate for us, therefore a hero is born among us together with all our heroes," then indeed, a hero is born together with all his heroes for him who knows this.
Regarding this, they say: "Should the *dhurs* be sung or not sung?"
"They are to be sung," they say. 19-259 (Ed.:
1,263) |p1 Kurus.
The morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī*, the midday pressing to the *triṣṭubh*, and the third pressing to the *jagatī*.
The *anuṣṭubh* is dependent upon these very [metres].

When he sings the *gāyatrī* at the morning pressing, which itself is of the *gāyatrī* nature—the *gāyatrī* being indeed the *brahman* and the morning pressing being the *brahman*—he thereby places the *brahman* in its own proper abode.

Now, as for the fact that he sings the *triṣṭubh*: the *triṣṭubh* is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*). These are the arts belonging to the ruling power: the elephant, the golden neck-ornament, the mule-chariot, the horse-chariot, the gold plate, and the bronze vessel. Having brought these together, he thus anoints them in the sacred word (*brahman*).

Then, as for the fact that he sings the *jagatī*: the *jagatī* is indeed the common people (*viś*). These are the arts belonging to the common people: cattle and horses, elephants and gold, goats and sheep, rice and barley, sesame and beans, clarified butter, milk, wealth, and prosperity. Having brought these together, he thus anoints them in the sacred word. The *anuṣṭubh* is dependent upon that very [sacred word].

Now, as for the fact that he sings the *anuṣṭubh*: the Śūdra is indeed *ānuṣṭubha*; having thus brought [the power] from the Śūdra, he anoints it upon the *brahman*. Just as one would strike a quiver with thorns, even so, having brought all these arts together, he anoints them upon the *brahman*.
"Therefore, they should be sung apart.
For indeed, from the time these [verses] were sung apart, the Brāhmaṇas have prospered here;
but when they did not sing them apart, the Brāhmaṇas were rich in food.
There was once a time when we were left with only one ox, or rather, only one cart remained; having yoked it, Satyayajña Pauluṣi was driving away.
Now, since these [verses] are sung apart here, from that time on these arts have been acquired among the Brāhmaṇas.
He sings the Gāyatrī first, and the Gāyatrī afterwards.
The Gāyatrī is indeed Brahman.
By means of Brahman, he thus encompasses these artistic forms on both sides.
These artistic forms, encompassed on both sides by Brahman, attend upon him who knows this.
"The *dhurs* should not be chanted," say the Pañcālas.
"For these *dhurs* are themselves already chanted;
by chanting them at each pressing, he ascends [to them]."
Now, when evil report follows after them, saying, "They have sung discordantly," it is said of two who fight or two who are at enmity, "The two have sung discordantly.
Furthermore, it is said of those who stand divided within a kingdom.
The morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī*, the midday pressing to the *triṣṭubh*, and the third pressing to the *jagatī*.
The *anuṣṭubh* is dependent upon them all.

When he sings the *gāyatrī* at the morning pressing—which is itself *gāyatra*—the *gāyatrī* is indeed the *brahman*; thus he causes the *brahman* itself to participate in its own domain for the sake of the *brāhmaṇa*.
He desires to take away from him what he wishes not to give;
moreover, it belongs to him alone,
for he indeed causes him to participate in his own property.

Now, as to why he sings a *triṣṭubh*: the *triṣṭubh* is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*); thus he causes the ruling power itself to participate in the Brāhmaṇa’s own domain. Consequently, it seeks to seize that which he is unwilling to give, and furthermore, it belongs to him alone.
For he indeed shares him out among his own people. Now, when he sings the *jagatī*, the *jagatī* is indeed the common people (*viś*); thus he shares the Vaiśya among the Brāhmaṇa’s own people.
He [the Brāhmaṇa] desires to take it from one who is unwilling to give it.
Or rather, it belongs to this very [Sāman] itself;
for he bestows it upon him in his own [domain].
The Anuṣṭubh is dependent upon that very thing.
Now, as to why he sings the *anuṣṭubh*: the Śūdra is indeed connected with the *anuṣṭubh*; thus he causes the Śūdra to participate in the property of the Brāhmaṇa.
He desires to take it away from him, and he seeks to seize it;
moreover, it belongs to him alone.
For he indeed bestows his own [portion] upon him.
If one desires to obtain it by means of the *yāvṛn-nātha-upavaṃka*,
therefore it should not be sung apart [from that].
For indeed, since these [Sāmans] were sung apart here, therefore the Brāhmaṇas here have been defeated. But when they did not sing them apart, the Brāhmaṇas were invincible.
The morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī*, the midday pressing to the *triṣṭubh*, and the third pressing to the *jagatī*.
The *anuṣṭubh* is dependent upon them all.
When he sings the morning pressing—which is indeed *gāyatra*—as being entirely *gāyatra*, he extracts for himself that exclusive share belonging to the *brahman*.

Thus, this exclusive share of the Brahmin is extracted for him. Now, in that the midday pressing—which is of the *triṣṭubh* nature—is entered upon by means of the *gāyatrī*, he thereby causes the Brahmin to participate in his own [share] as a Kṣatriya.
Thus, through faith, ritual action, and service, he desires to give to him.
When faith finds a kṣatriya, he then desires a brāhmaṇa;
he gives [the sacrifice] to him.
Now, that which is of the Jagatī metre—the third pressing—he introduces with the Gāyatrī; thus he causes the brāhmaṇa to share in his own portion among the vaiśya.
He desires to give to him with faith, through ritual action, and through proper conduct.
When faith indeed finds a Vaiśya or a Brāhmaṇa, he then desires [to give] to that very person;
he gives to him.
The *anuṣṭubh* meter is likewise dependent upon that.
Now, when he sings the *anuṣṭubh*, it is because the Śūdra is indeed of the nature of the *anuṣṭubh*; thus he causes the Brāhmaṇa to participate in his own property for the sake of the Śūdra.
He desires to give to him through faith, through ritual action, and through service.
When faith finds a Śūdra, he then desires a Brāhmaṇa;
he gives to him,
making his own [gift] exclusive.
Having drunk, he becomes one who does not drink among the nobility (*kṣatra*);
he goes to that which stands at the end, and he is not overcome by that which stands at the end.
A hundred attendants stand around him.

"But indeed, it is better that one who knows thus should not sing apart the *dhurs*. "If he were to sing them apart, he would do so knowing this; but if he does not sing them apart, he does not do so knowing this."
"That is distress, for he knows only one of the two," so said Śāṭyāyani.
He sings the *retasyā* [verse].
He pours out that seed.
That poured-out seed he causes to grow by means of the Gāyatrī, with a more extensive metre;
he causes it to grow by means of the Triṣṭubh, with a still more extensive metre.
He increases it with the Jagatī metre;
he increases it with each successively larger metre. Therefore, for one who is prospering, his strength becomes greater and greater.
He reaches the conclusion with the Anuṣṭubh, which is the smallest metre.
Therefore, it grows more and more in the later stages of life. It reaches its completion in the fifth [month];
therefore, in the fifth month, fetuses undergo transformation.
One reaches the conclusion with speech in the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
therefore, people listen to the speech of one who is aged.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* is indeed the head of the sacrifice.
That indeed is that; for even in the *retasya* [breath], the entire self is present. 24-264.

When he sings the *gāyatrī* at the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the *gāyatrī* is indeed breath; the *gāyatrī* is the head itself. Since the breath has its abode in the head, he thereby places the breath in its own proper abode.
He sings the *triṣṭubh*;
the *triṣṭubh* is indeed sight.
Having brought that very [light] from there, he fastens it to the head. Because he fastens it, the eye is as if fastened.
Though it has no other abode, he fastens it as having the midday as its abode.
Because he binds her while she is still elsewhere, having no fixed abode, therefore the eye departs even from one who is still alive.
He sings the Jagatī;
the Jagatī is indeed the ear.
Having brought that very [vessel] there, he fastens it upon the head. Because he fastens it, the ear is, as it were, fastened.
He fastens it while it is without a fixed abode, having the third pressing as its abode.
In that he binds her while she is still elsewhere, therefore the sense of hearing departs even from one who is alive.
He sings the *anuṣṭubh*;
for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech.
Having brought that very [speech] there, he yokes it to the head. Because he yokes it, speech is, as it were, yoked.
He yokes it while it is without a specific abode—either having the third pressing as its abode, or having all pressings as its abode.
In that he binds her while she still has another abode, therefore speech departs even from one who is still alive;
other vital breaths depart, but not the [chief] vital breath.
Regarding this they ask: "What is performed in the sacrifice because of which the other vital breaths depart from one who is still living, but the *prāṇa* does not?
He should reply: "Because he sings the *gāyatrī* in its own abode, therefore as long as he lives, the *prāṇa* does not depart.
Now, indeed, there are both the discernments and the recognitions of the poles (*dhur*).
The *retasyā* is indeed the mind; the *gāyatrī* is the breath;
the *triṣṭubh* is the eye.
The ear is the jagatī;
speech is the anuṣṭubh;
by means of the mind, one discerns both the well-disposed and the ill-disposed.
By means of the breath, one discerns what is fragrant and what is foul-smelling.
By means of the eye, one discerns what is beautiful to behold and what is not beautiful to behold.
By means of the ear, one discerns what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing.
Through speech one discerns what is sweet and what is not sweet.
These are the things to be known here. Indeed, he who knows this becomes distinguished and superior.
And those indeed are the designations:
the *retasyā* is the mind (*manas*), and the *gāyatrī* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The eye is the *triṣṭubh*;
the ear is the *jagatī*;
speech is the *anuṣṭubh*.
When this [rite] has been commenced, he should meditate with his mind upon the mind of whomever he may desire [to win].
When the *gāyatrī* has been introduced, he should meditate on the breath of whomever he desires by means of his own breath.
When the *triṣṭubh* has been introduced, he should meditate on the eye of whomever he desires by means of his own eye.
When the *jagatī* has been introduced, he should meditate on the ear of whomever he desires by means of his own ear.
When the *anuṣṭubh* has been chanted as the *prastāva*, he should meditate upon the speech of whomever he desires by means of his own speech.
These indeed are the designations (*saṃjñā*).
Verily, he who knows this recognizes him with whomsoever he desires to be in accord, thinking, "I am in accord with him."
Then he joins together these yokes of the gods and the yokes of men.
The mind, indeed, is the yoke of men;
the waters are the yoke of the gods.
When the *retasyā* has been chanted as the *prastāva*, he should mentally join the waters.
Thereby, he causes the mind of the sacrificer to fall away from within.
For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the yoke of man.
Vāyu is the divine attendant.
When the *gāyatrī* has been introduced, one should join Vāyu with the breath;
therein, one should cause the breath of the sacrificer to flow forth.
The eye is indeed the yoke of men;
the sun is the yoke of the gods.
When the *prastāva* has been chanted on a *triṣṭubh* verse, one should join the eye with the sun.
In that interval, he should cause the sacrificer’s sight to descend;
for the human yoke is the ear, while the divine yoke is the quarters.
When the *jagatī* has been introduced, he should join the quarters with his ear. He should cause the sacrificer’s hearing to descend into that space between them.
Speech, indeed, is the yoke-pole of men.
The earth is the burden of the gods.
When the *anuṣṭubh* has been chanted as the *prastāva*, one should join the earth with speech.
Thereby, one should cause the speech of the sacrificer to fall away within [the earth].
This indeed joins together the yoke of the gods and the yoke of men. Having joined together the yoke of the gods and the yoke of men, one crosses over that death which exists in the heavenly world.
One who knows this does not die again.
He unites his self with the deities.
Now, these great Brahmins were assembled: Āruṇi Jīvala, Kārīrādi Aṣāḍha, Sāvayasa Indradyumna, and Bhāllabeya.

Jīvala Kārīrādi and Indradyumna Bhāllabeya—these two came as guests to their teacher Āruṇi. They stayed as guests in the house of Aṣāḍha. Aṣāḍha said to him, "O Āruṇi, since we both practiced studentship together and learned together, by what means have you now surpassed us in recitation?"

"Since you are so dear to fame, so dear to sight, and so dear to gain—by what means have you attained this? He replied, "I meditate upon those very yokes. "What do you meditate upon in the yokes? he asked.
"Beloved," he said.
"What becomes of him who meditates upon their beloved?
"He indeed becomes beloved of fame, beloved of the eye, and beloved of gain."
"In this very way you are," they said.
Then they said to Jīvala Kārīrādi: "Since you alone are the best of that half [of the kingdom] upon which even kings wait upon you from below, by what means have you attained this?
He replied, "I meditate upon them as the yokes (dhūḥ) themselves."
"What do you venerate as that which stands upon the pole?
"I venerate prosperity (śrī)," he replied.
"What becomes of him who venerates the prosperity of these [rays]?"
"In whichever region he resides, he becomes the most eminent; even kings sit below him in attendance.
"It is exactly so," they said.
Then they said to Aṣāḍha Sāvayasa: "Since you are indeed the village headman of the Śārkarākṣas, by what means did you attain this?"
He said, "I meditate upon them as the yokes.
"What do you meditate upon in the yokes?
"As 'the born'."
"What does he become who worships their birth?
"Wherever he is born, there he becomes a village leader," they said,
"and you are exactly like that."
Then they said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, "Since your fame travels over and above others here, you are indeed a man of eloquent speech; by what means have you attained this?
He replied, "I meditate upon that very thing as being in the yokes.
"What is it that you meditate upon as being in the yokes? they asked.
Regarding "glory":
What becomes of him who meditates on glory as these [breaths]?
His fame rises higher and higher above others, and he indeed possesses eloquence.
"Even so are you," they said. They said, "If this has indeed come to pass,
let us explain this to him."
They said to Āruṇi, "You indeed are our teacher;
you speak first."
He said, "I meditate upon the Gāyatrī itself as the beloved.
The Gāyatrī is indeed breath;
breath is indeed the beloved.
"Indeed, there is nothing dearer than life.

He who thus meditates on this Gāyatrī as the dear one—just as life is dear to oneself, so he becomes dear to fame, so he becomes dear to sight, and so he becomes dear to gain. Then Jīvala Kārīrādi said, "I meditate on the Triṣṭubh itself as prosperity."

The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*), and the ruling power is indeed prosperity (*śrī*). He who thus worships this *triṣṭubh* as prosperity becomes the most excellent in whichever region he may be; even kings wait upon him from below.
Then Aṣāḍha Sāvayasa said: "I meditate upon the *jagatī* as abundance and procreation.
For the *jagatī* is indeed abundance and procreation among the meters.
He who thus meditates upon this *jagatī* as abundance and procreation attains abundance through offspring and cattle; wherever he is born, there he becomes a village leader.
Then Indradyumna Bhāllaveya said: "I meditate upon the *anuṣṭubh* itself as glory.
Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*;
and speech, indeed, is glory.

Speech moves above and beyond others, and fame moves above and beyond others. He who thus worships this *anuṣṭubh* as glory—for him, speech becomes this very *anuṣṭubh*, and his fame moves about above and beyond others, spreading through all discourse. Thus he becomes one who speaks with distinction. 29-269 (Ed.:
Indeed, they each proceeded by means of only one [of these].
Now, he who knows all these as being thus unified—verily, all these become unified for him; he becomes the foremost among his own people in a single way.

Regarding this, Vāsiṣṭha Caikitāneya said: "It is as if, having understood the yokes, these Brahmins, though deliberating upon them, have not reached that very yoke upon which all these [other] yokes depend."
He spoke that indeed regarding the *retasyā*. What they call "the single yoke" (*ekā dhūḥ*), that is indeed the *retasyā*, the yoke among yokes.
That is food.
The ornament of the yokes;
fragrant scent for the Gāyatrī; beautiful to behold for the Triṣṭubh.
It is to be heard for the sake of the Jagatī.
Whatever merit one speaks with speech, that belongs to the Anuṣṭubh.
Verily, he bestows food upon these [metres] who brings them into harmony by means of these [verses].
They, being eaten, make him the best eater of food among his own people. He who knows thus becomes the best eater of food among his own people. 30-270 (Ed.:

There are indeed these three oceans: Pavamāna Agni, Vāyu, and yonder Āditya. One should chant the *udgītha* while they are covered. For whenever Prajāpati bestows rain and food upon his creatures, these are then covered.
The Udgātṛ is Prajāpati. When he sings the Udgītha with the Pavamāna chants covered [by verses], he indeed covers the sacrificer with food; he covers himself; he covers his offspring.
"In that place where I sing the Udgītha, Parjanya becomes one who rains abundantly," so said Kūṭa Śailana.
Wherever Parjanya rains abundantly, there indeed the ox, the mule, the elephant, the gold necklace, and the man are auspicious.
Whatever form arises there, that indeed is auspicious; this is what the one who knows thus has said. He who separates the gods from men separates himself from evil.
The *pavamāna* [stotras] are indeed the gods; the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* and *uktha-stotras* are the creatures.
One should chant the *udgītha* with those *pavamāna* [stotras] which are concealed, indirect, and undefined.
For the gods are as if covered and as if unexpressed when they are out of sight; the *pṛṣṭha* chants and the *uktha*s are the subjects.
One should chant the *udgītha* with them uncovered and clearly expressed.
For humans are as if covered [in their true nature], yet they are manifest as it were.
This indeed separates the gods from humans; he who knows thus is separated from evil. 31-271 (Ed.:
He who sings the *udgītha* with the *pavamāna* verses indeed enters the assembly of the gods.

Just as one approaches a superior person, so should he sing the *udgītha*: practicing diligently, as it were, bowing respectfully, as it were, capable through his perfected skills, yet appearing as if being struck down.
It should be such that he makes known the one approaching him, and gives whatever he asks for. Such is it.

Now, if one who is unable [to perform the rite] with these [previously mentioned methods] should chant the *udgītha* without being hindered by those that have not succeeded, it would be just as if he were to measure out what he has not yet reached, or as if he were to ask for something and not give it; such indeed is that.
Furthermore, in this very case, both the success and the failure of the sacrifice are discerned.
For this *pavamāna* [laud] is indeed a means of overcoming.
He who enters the *atihāyyā* without being clothed is indeed smeared with mud and becomes exhausted;
but he who enters it clothed is neither smeared with mud nor does he become exhausted.
In this very manner, the *pavamāna* [laud]s are to be performed.
Regarding this they say: "Since other stotras have their *pratipads* consisting of *stotriya* verses, why then do the *pavamāna* stotras have *pratipads* that are not *stotriya*?
He should reply: "The *pavamānas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the *pāvamānya* verses are also the vital breaths."
"If they were to follow the *pavamāna* stotras with *pāvamānī* verses alone, they would wipe away their vital breaths as they depart.

Since they follow them with an *anuṣṭubh* verse—and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and the downward breath (*apāna*) is fixed in speech—they thereby sustain the downward breath by means of speech. 32-272 (Ed.:

Regarding this, they say: "This chant is, as it were, unappeased when they do not follow it with a *pratipad* corresponding to the *stotriya*. "How then does their *stotriya-pratipad* become led forward?
He should reply: "Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*."

Indeed, all the meters are to be expressed. In that there is [a hymn] for Agni, one for Indra, and one for Pavamāna, by this their *stotriya* and *pratipad* verses become led forward. These *pavamāna* chants are indeed called "Victories" (*jayas*).
By means of the *pavamāna* [stotras], the gods indeed drove the Asuras away as they were conquering.

In that the *pavamānas* proceed forward, it is just as one would go forward when conquering; such is that. Since they commence them with an *anuṣṭubh*, and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech (*vāk*), and speech is indeed the prompter, it is by means of speech that he says: "Go forward! Conquer! Step forward! Do not retreat!"
Just as one might say with words, "Go forward, conquer; do not retreat," such is that.
The *pavamāna* verses are indeed the gods; they are the hymns of praise belonging to the gods.
The gods are dependent upon them;
the subjects are the *pṛṣṭha* chants and the *uktha*s; these are the hymns of praise for the subjects.
The creatures are dependent upon them.
Therefore, because they chant with the *pavamāna* [laudations] directed only forward, the gods are turned away (*parāñcaḥ*).
The sun moves away; the moon moves away; the stars move away; and Agni moves away as he burns.

Now, because they praise with the *pṛṣṭha* chants, both moving away (*parācīnaiḥ*) and moving toward (*cārvācīnaiḥ*), therefore offspring move both away and toward [the source]. They set out in the morning facing away, and they return in the evening. Thus, the seed is emitted facing away, and it is born facing toward [the source]. 33-273 (Ed.: 1,276)
Pṛthu Vainya questioned the divine Vrātyas:
"The supreme abode of the sacrifice is fashioned in secret from the great intermediate space; why do the *pavamāna* [stages] proceed away, and why do the *ukthya* [stages] roar back toward us again?"

The gods follow one track of the sacrifice, while humans subsist on the other; therefore the *pavamāna* [laud] verses proceed forward, and therefore the *ukthya* [laud] verses call out back again. He who knows which gods are assigned among men and which men are assigned among the gods—he indeed becomes one who is assigned among the gods and one who is assigned among men.
He goes to that world where the gods dwell.
The deities do not depart from him.
The *pavamāna* [stotras] are indeed the gods; the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are the subjects; the *uktha* [śastras] are the cattle.
The Sāmans are indeed the gods; the meters are the progeny.
Now, since the Pavamāna-sāmans go forward in a straight line, this Ṛc then winds around them from behind; by that means, the gods are shared among men.
Now, because the *sāman* winds around the *ṛc* as it is being wound around in the *abhyāvartin* verses, by that means human beings have obtained a share among the gods.
He who knows this thus obtains a share among the gods and obtains a share among human beings;
he goes to that world where the gods are.
The deities do not depart from him.
He who indeed distinguishes between the form of a god and the form of a human turns away from evil.
The *pavamāna* chants are indeed the gods; the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* and *uktha-śastras* are the progeny.
Therefore, because they chant the *pavamāna* verses with *pāvamānī* verses alone, the gods are all of one form and entirely white.

Now, because they chant with the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* using various forms and various deities, therefore offspring are of various forms: white, ruddy, and black. Indeed, he who knows this distinguishes between the form of the gods and the form of men; he turns away from evil.
He who knows the portion of the gods carries away that portion; he becomes one whose portion is to be taken.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* is indeed the portion set aside for the gods. With it they chant, having uttered the sound *hiṃ* once and moving away; therefore the portion set aside is directed away.
This very one is the most excellent among the gods.
Its extraction [is as follows]:
"They take up the extraction of Prajāpati himself; he who knows thus becomes worthy of extraction."

Having extracted this essence of the sacrifice, he offers it to Prajāpati before anyone else; therefore, when they are about to chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*, they move forward as if bowing low, as if agitated.
Such indeed is the proper conduct toward one who is superior.
Therefore, one should not utter an exclamation during his chant.
For who indeed is worthy of censuring the serving of one who is superior?

Verily, he who censures the serving of one who is superior causes him to fall into that very affliction with which he desires to strike him. Now, when the Adhvaryu thereafter utters the directions, he bestows the essence of the sacrifice upon Prajāpati and causes it to swell.
Therefore, by means of this swelling and flavorful [chant], it becomes praised. He who indeed knows both the glory of the gods and the glory of men attains glory among the gods and glory among men.
The *pavamāna* verses indeed bring glory among the gods.
They are truly those vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
They announce him to the gods.
The *abhyāvarta* [verse] is for human glory.
These indeed are his out-breaths;
they announce him among men.
This, indeed, is both the glory of the gods and the glory of men.
He who thus knows this glory of the gods and the glory of men attains glory among the gods and glory among men.
Verily, he who knows both the measured and the unmeasured, for him both the measured and the unmeasured become abundant.
The *pavamāna* verses are indeed the gods; the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* are the creatures; the *sāman* is indeed the gods.
The progeny are the weapons.
Now, this very thing— indeed, all these deities are what constitute the hymns of praise.
In that the stotras are measured, therefore the gods are measured:
eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, and twelve Ādityas.
But because the śastras are unmeasured, therefore offspring are unmeasured.
"We do not know how many Brāhmaṇas there are, how many Rājanyas, how many Vaiśyas, or how many Śūdras.
This indeed is both the measured and the unmeasured. He who knows thus possesses much, both measured and unmeasured.

"Those who are turned hitherward, them they call turned away; those who are turned away, them they call turned hitherward. O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have fashioned, they carry [the sacrifice] like yoked horses through the mid-region.
The *pavamāna* verses are indeed turned away;
their cups are turned hitherward.
These indeed are those vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Therefore, one is able to breathe in and breathe out. They turn back toward this side.
Their cups are turned away. They are indeed the out-breaths. Therefore, having breathed out, one is able to breathe in. 36-276 (Ed.: 1,279)
He who knows the preeminence of the pressings attains preeminence; he does not fall away from preeminence. The *gāyatrī* is indeed the preeminence of the morning pressing.
In that regard, whatever other metre is employed there, it is nevertheless designated as *gāyatra*. The *triṣṭubh* is the preeminence of the midday pressing;
in that regard, whatever other metre is employed there, it is nevertheless designated as *traiṣṭubha*.

The *jagatī* is the preeminence of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). Therefore, when any other metre is employed there, it is nevertheless designated as being of the *jāgata* nature. This indeed is the preeminence among the pressings.
He who thus knows this preeminence of the pressings attains preeminence; he does not descend from preeminence.
Verily, he who knows the houses of the gods becomes a householder and acquires houses.
The meters, indeed, are the houses of the gods.
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables;
there are eight Vasus.
By means of the Gāyatrī itself, the Vasus become householders.
The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables;
there are eleven Rudras.
By means of the *triṣṭubh*, the Rudras become householders.
The *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables;
there are twelve Ādityas.
By means of the *jagatī*, the Ādityas are grasped.
