By means of the *anuṣṭubh* [meter] belong the Viśve Devās; by means of the pressings (*savana*) belong Indra and Agni.
He who thus knows these dwellings of the gods becomes a householder and acquires a home.
He who knows the satisfactions of the gods is satisfied himself; his offspring is satisfied.

Regarding this, Āheya Soma-pa used to say: "He indeed should sacrifice today, or he should cause another to sacrifice, who would know how all the deities are being fully satisfied at each pressing within the meters—syllable by syllable—without being crowded together, just as one might satisfy cows without crowding them at a great watering place on sandy ground."
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables;
there are eight Vasus;
the morning pressing belongs to the Vasus and is in the Gāyatrī metre.
In that regard, at your morning pressing, they find complete satisfaction, not crowding one another, syllable by syllable within the meters.
The *triṣṭubh* has eleven syllables;
there are eleven Rudras.
The midday pressing of the Rudras is in the Triṣṭubh metre.
At that midday pressing, they satisfy themselves, not crowding one another, syllable by syllable within the metres.
The Jagatī consists of twelve syllables.
There are twelve Ādityas.
The third pressing of the Ādityas is in the Jāgata metre.
Therefore, at the third pressing, they satisfy themselves by following each syllable of the metres without any crowding.

He who thus knows these satisfactions of the gods is satisfied himself; his offspring is satisfied. When one who knows this sacrifices, or one who knows this officiates at a sacrifice, the gods have no power over him to prevent them from coming.
And if they are about to consume [the food], whether they do so or not, they depart right there.
If one is pure, they consume it;
if one is impure, they merely look at it.
And that is indeed worthy of being staked, for one should stake even upon seeing it.
Verily, he who knows the vessel of the gods becomes a worthy recipient among his own people.
Now, the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the vessel of the gods.
He becomes a vessel for his own people who knows thus.
Just as people indeed desire to drink from a clean and pure vessel, even so do the gods desire to drink from a Brāhmaṇa who is clean and pure.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should indeed strive to be clean and pure. 39-279 (Ed.: 1,282)
Prajāpati created the gods; death, evil, was created after them.

Those gods approached Prajāpati and said, "For what purpose have you created us, if you were intending to let death and evil descend upon us? He said to them, "Gather the meters; enter them according to their proper place."
"Then you shall be turned away from death and evil," he said.
The Vasus gathered the Gāyatrī;
they entered it.
He covered them.
The Rudras gathered the *triṣṭubh* meter;
they entered it.
He clothed them.
The Ādityas gathered together the jagatī;
they entered it.
He clothed them.
The All-gods gathered together the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
they entered into it.
He covered them.
The Maruts gathered together the *paṅkti* [meter];
they entered into it.
He clothed them.
The Sādhyas and Āptyas fashioned the Aticchandas;
they entered into it.
He clothed them.
Indra and Agni entered the pressings themselves.
Then indeed, Death, the Evil One, could no longer perceive them.
For how could Death, the Evil One, prevail over one whom he does not perceive?
Death, the Evil One, does not find him who knows thus.
The meters indeed shielded them from death, from evil. Because the meters shielded them from death, from evil, that is the "meter-ness" (chanda-stva) of the meters.
The meters indeed shield him from death, from evil, who knows thus.
Whichever *chandas* (metre) one who knows this employs for the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), that very metre he then attains.
For if anyone censures him while he is performing [the rite] with a particular *chandas*, he is cut off from that [metre].
There is no affliction whatsoever for him who knows this.
Whoever speaks ill of him meets with misfortune.

Then Horjo Jānāyana asked Kapivana Bhauvāyana: "Since the morning pressing is in the *gāyatrī* metre, the midday pressing is in the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the third pressing is in the *jagatī* metre, then what is this *anuṣṭubh*—which is never exhausted—that descends upon the openings of the pressings and carries the sacrifice through to its end?"
He said: "Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*. By means of speech the sacrifice is performed.

Just as there, when a fine ox is bound with a rope, they run back again and again toward its adversary, or toward a heavy load to be carried, even so do they harness this speech, the *anuṣṭubh*, at the openings of the pressings for the purpose of returning."
For these openings of the pressings (savanamukhāni) are, as it were, adverse.
This very Speech (vāk), being untiring, carries the sacrifice through to its end.
Whoever knows this *anuṣṭubh* everywhere, for him there is merit everywhere.
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables;
the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables;
the Jagatī has twelve syllables.
"Speech" is the *nidhana* of the *yajñāyajñīya*;
that consists of thirty-two [syllables].
The *anuṣṭubh* has thirty-two syllables.
Or rather, it is for this [earth] at the morning pressing, at the midday pressing, and also at the third pressing;
or for this in the priesthood, in the nobility, and in the common people;
or for this in this world, in the intermediate space, and in yonder world.
Whoever thus knows this *anuṣṭubh* as being everywhere, for him everything indeed becomes meritorious. Now,
Keśin Dārbhya, having placed Keśin Sātyakāmin at the head of his priestly retinue, besieged Āśvatthin Āhīnasa.
The elder was Ahīna, and Keśin was the younger.
He said to him, "O Keśin, knowing what did you bring this prince to me?
He replied, "I taught him that we should worship the *anuṣṭubh* as all the meters, the *bṛhatī* as cattle, the sacrifice, and the heavenly world."
He perceived that it was indeed hunger.
He felt compassion for him.
He said to him, "Do not feel compassion."
"If you desire a *rājanya*, here is this *rājanya* for you.
"Indeed, we shall seek another *rājanya*," they said.
He replied, "This is not [done] out of a desire for a *rājanya*, O Keśin."
"Indeed, it was by recollecting his very studentship (*brahmacarya*) that he found this [knowledge]. He indeed practiced studentship.
We have heard this even from those who were nearly old: 'This boy has declared as much as he knows.'"
"In this very way, having recollected it, he found the shoulder," [it is said].
When he spoke of the *anuṣṭubh* as containing all the meters,
[he meant that] the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables.
The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables;
the *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables.
"Vāc" is the *nidhana* of the *yajñāyajñīya*.
That [verse] consists of thirty-two [syllables].
The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables.
He said that this *anuṣṭubh* comprises all the meters (*chandas*).
"The Bṛhatī [is] cattle. That which is the Anuṣṭubh is indeed the Bṛhatī;
for when four-footed cattle were established, this became the Bṛhatī.
"Regarding the word 'sacrifice' (yajña): for indeed, the sacrifice approaches him who possesses cattle. Regarding the phrase 'the heavenly world' (svargaṃ lokaṃ)":
For the *bṛhatī* is indeed the heavenly world.

Now, Saṃgamana Kṣaimi questioned Satyayajña Pauluṣi—who had been sent by his teacher Āruṇi—saying: "O Satyayajña Pauluṣi, since the *gāyatrī* is praised, the *triṣṭubh* is praised, and the *jagatī* is not praised, how do all of them together support the midday pressing?
He did not answer him.

Therefore, he defeated him. Had he replied: "Because both the Brāhmaṇa and the Vaiśya wait upon the Kṣatriya from below; and because these two have become his food; and because this is indeed the twelve-syllabled word," [he would not have been defeated]. 43-283 (Ed.: 1,285) |c284 (Ed.: 1,286)
When the meters divided these worlds, the Gāyatrī took this world for herself, the Triṣṭubh the intermediate space, and the Jagatī that [upper] world.
The Gāyatrī is indeed the Brahman;
the Triṣṭubh is the Kṣatra.
The *jagatī* is the peasantry.
This *triṣṭubh*, in this intermediate space, did not find a foothold; it did not take root. It pierced this *gāyatrī* from the front.
He brooded over her.
He was afraid of her, thinking, "She will take away my abode.
He said to her, "Homage be to you! With what desire do you pierce me?"
"Give me a gift," she said.
To her he gave two feet of eight syllables each; the *jagatī* verse followed after her.
He pierced it;
he brooded over it.
It was afraid of him, thinking, "He will take away my abode."
He said to her, "Homage be to you; with what desire do you pierce me? She replied, "Grant me a gift.
To her he gave a foot of twelve syllables.
He returned once more to this very Gāyatrī.
He said to her, "What is it that you desire now, since I have given it to you? She replied, "Give me your entire self."
"Then what will become of me? [He replied: "We shall have food in common; moreover, I will place you in front. "So be it," [he said].
They placed her in front.
He offered his entire self to her.
Because Gāyatrī offered her entire self, therefore a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Kṣatriya with his whole self.

Moreover, because the Jagatī did not surrender its entire self, therefore the Viś (the common people) moves as if departing from the Kṣatra (the ruling power). Whatever [portion] Gāyatrī and Jagatī both surrendered together, that became this Bṛhatī.
Therefore, the Bṛhatī has three feet of eight syllables each and one foot of twelve syllables.
This same Gāyatrī is yoked first with the verse, "High is thy birth, O Soma, from the plant" (*uccā te jātam andhasa*). This [verse] concludes the *purohita* [section].
He who knows thus obtains either the office of a domestic priest (*purodhā*) or at least the status of a domestic priest. 44-284 (Ed.: 1,286)
Then the Bṛhatī;
then the Triṣṭubh.
Thus, this food is grasped on both sides by both the priesthood (*brahman*) and the nobility (*kṣatra*).
And indeed, for one who knows thus, the food is approached as being grasped on both sides by both the priesthood and the nobility.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not bear malice toward a Kṣatriya, nor should a Kṣatriya bear malice toward a Brāhmaṇa.
For their food is common;
therefore, when a Brāhmaṇa goes to a great man, he seeks the Kṣatriya as the second protector of that food;
and when a Kṣatriya [goes] to a Brāhmaṇa, it is likewise.
He who knows thus finds a Kṣatriya as his husband.
In the beginning, indeed, the meters consisted of four syllables and did not carry the sacrifice. Now, the Soma was in Indra’s third heaven.
The fires, the Gandharvas, guarded him; they are indeed these very *dhiṣṇya* hearths.
They are also the venomous serpents.
He sat upon two golden cushions.
They used to fly back and forth in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Then these *chandas* said, "Let us fetch Soma; let us perform the sacrifice.
Thereupon, the *jagatī* flew up first, considering itself the most powerful, the strongest, the most abundant, and the most heroic.
When she had departed, the guardians of the Soma found three syllables. She returned with one syllable, bringing both consecration (*dīkṣā*) and cattle.
Therefore, whoever possesses cattle, consecration seeks him out.
Then the *triṣṭubh* flew up. As she was departing, the guardians of Soma found one syllable of hers.
She returned with three syllables, bringing with her both austerity (*tapas*) and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Therefore, sacrificial gifts are led forth in the world of the Triṣṭubh.
Therefore, they consider him alone to be performing ascetic toil who gives.
Then the Gāyatrī flew up.
The Anuṣṭubh, having gone after her as a mother, looked back upon her.
Therefore, a mother should look back at her son when he is departing; she should say, "Come back alive, bringing [wealth] with you."
With her two hands she gathered together two pressings, namely these syllables of theirs; with her mouth, one pressing.
She came with the entire sacrifice.
Regarding this they say: "The third pressing is indeed like something chewed, for she brought it with her mouth."

Having brought the Soma, she said: "I have indeed brought this Soma; come, let us perform this sacrifice. They both replied: "We two have indeed been excluded from our own [share]; we are not capable of that. Then Gāyatrī, employing herself in the morning pressing, said: "I alone shall carry this [sacrifice]."
He carried that away;
he established it.
Therefore, the morning pressing is called the Gāyatra.
She employed this as the midday pressing.
For it, the task was accomplished with a triplet of verses.
Then, the *triṣṭubh* became afraid.
She said, "May I also go? He replied, "Go. She said, "I shall tell you, provided that you speak."
He approached it with three syllables.
Having become a *triṣṭubh* consisting of eleven syllables, it carried the midday pressing;
he thereby established it.
When she said to the Triṣṭubh, "I will speak for you, but you must speak," therefore the midday pressing is called *traiṣṭubha*.
She then employed this third pressing for herself; for that [third pressing], a triplet of verses was prepared.
Then the Jagatī, being diminished, reflected.
She said, "May I also go? He said, "Go."
"I shall speak for you, but you must speak. She approached her with a single syllable.
Having become a *jagatī* of twelve syllables, she carried the third *savana*.
He established that.
She said to the Jagatī: "I shall speak for you, but you must speak. Therefore, the third pressing is called Jāgata. 46-286 (Ed.:
The Gāyatrī indeed carries the morning pressing; the Gāyatrī carries the midday pressing; the Gāyatrī carries the third pressing.

He who knows this thus—that the Gāyatrī carries the morning pressing, the Gāyatrī carries the midday pressing, and the Gāyatrī carries the third pressing—his glory and fame do not depart until old age.
Regarding this, Āruṇi said: "I know the Gāyatrī as she carries all the pressings."
"Therefore, my fame and renown shall not fade until old age.
Indeed, for one who knows this, his fame and renown do not fade until old age.
Then these meters said: "She is truly the best among us, she is the most powerful, she who brought the Soma and extended the sacrifice."
"Let us merge into this very one," [they said]. They merged into that through the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters by means of the two pressings (*savana*).
Then, because there are two eight-syllable feet in the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters, they merged into those by means of them.
Then, by means of the three eight-syllable feet of the *bṛhatī*, she attained it.
Then, by means of the four eight-syllable feet of the *anuṣṭubh*, she attained it. Then, by means of the five eight-syllable feet of the *paṅkti*, she attained it. 47-287 (Ed.: 1,289)
Originally, she had ten syllables in excess;
however, out of a desire for a sacrificial session (*apyayana*), she made her feet consist of eight syllables each.
Whether it be in the *aticchandas*, whether in the *virāj*, or in whatever meter an eight-syllable foot is found, by that very [foot] all the meters enter into the *gāyatrī*.
He who knows this thus—that all the meters enter into the *gāyatrī*—his own kinsmen recognize him for preeminence.
Regarding this they say: "The stomas pass beyond the *trivṛt*, but the meters do not pass beyond the *gāyatrī*."
One should not say, "The *stomas* do not surpass the *trivṛt*," nor "the meters do not surpass the *gāyatrī*.
For the *stomas* have a triple beginning, a triple middle, and a triple conclusion;
and thus the *gāyatrī* does not surpass all the meters.
Then Upāvi Āruṇi asked Āruṇi Āruṇeya: "Āruṇa, son of Āruṇi, for whom does the Anuṣṭubh lift up the sacrifice?
He did not answer him. He said: "I have won the prize; whom shall I speak against? Gautama has indeed not understood what was being told to me: 'Place me upon yourself.'"

If he were to reply, "The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed Prajāpati; Prajāpati is indeed *ka*; he raises it for the sake of *ka* (Prajāpati)," that is what he would have replied. But that is certainly not so. Since the *bṛhatī* comprises all the meters, and the *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world—he would have replied, "He raises it for the sake of *ka* (bliss), for the heavenly world. 48-288 (Ed.: 1,290)
"Should one sacrifice with the *rathantara* sāman or with the *bṛhat* sāman? they deliberate. "With the *rathantara* sāman," said Sāvayasa.
This is the Rathantara.
This we know.
Who would go from what is known to what is unknown?
Just as one sees only utter darkness at the far end of a deep, dug-out well, even so, indeed, is that world perpetually beyond the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*).
Who knows whether it exists there or not? Yet, indeed, that world is perpetually right here in this very world.
For it is from what is offered here that yonder world lives.
For those oblations which go from here, by them yonder world subsists.
Therefore, even if one were to sacrifice ten times, one should sacrifice with the *rathantara* sāman alone.
"One should sacrifice with the Bṛhat-sāman," so said Āruṇi and Sātyayajña.
"It is great;
it is that which has been undertaken, from which evil has been struck away, and which brings prosperity day by day."
They do not spit upon it, they do not step over it, and they do not sit upon it.
"Much," he says, "is this world censuring;
much is it scrutinizing."
In this world, both the doer of merit and the doer of evil live; but in that [other] world,
the doer of evil does not live, for it is a realm where evil has been struck down and which brings greater welfare day by day.
Indeed, this world is perpetually supported by that world;
for it is from the giving from beyond that this world lives. For whatever rain is bestowed from beyond, upon that this world depends for its life.

"Even he who should sacrifice ten times should sacrifice with the *bṛhat-sāman* alone," so it is said. "One should sacrifice with both *sāmans*," Śāṭyāyani used to say, "for the attainment of both these desires. "So be it," [he replied]; thus one attains both those desires.
Thus, this Sāman, being complete and properly joined, carries his sacrifice.
Of it, the *gāyatra* is indeed the *hiṃkāra*.
The *rathantara* is the *prastāva*;
the *vāmadevya* is the *udgītha*;
the *bṛhat* is the *pratihāra*.
The *yajñāyajñīya* is the *nidhana*. Indeed, each one of these [chants] has mastery over the heavenly world.
He who knows thus attains the heavenly world.
Now, this indeed is the *arkya*;
this is the *mahāvrata*.
Of it, the *gāyatra* is the head.
The Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] are the two wings;
the Vāmadevya is the body;
the Yajñāyajñīya is the tail.
He who knows thus obtains as much as he obtains through the Arkya-stotra and the Mahāvrata-sāman;
moreover, this is indeed a preparation for long life, for the Gāyatra is life itself.
The *rathantara* is the life of all; the *vāmadevya* is the life of the whole;
the *bṛhat* is the life of everything.
The *yajñāyajñīya* is exceeding life. Those who praise with this [sāman] become long-lived.
Moreover, these very five lights of his are kindled and shine in these worlds: Agni on earth, Vāyu in the intermediate space, Āditya in heaven, the Moon among the stars, and lightning in the waters.
Agni alone is [the deity] of the Rathantara;
Vāyu of the Vāmadevya; Āditya of the Bṛhat.
The moon belongs to the *gāyatra*;
lightning belongs to the *yajñāyajñīya*;
for water is indeed the *yajñāyajñīya*.
These are his five kindled lights that shine in these worlds; he who knows this [attains them]. 50-290 (Ed.:
1,293) |p1 He who knows both the end and the endlessness of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] indeed encompasses the end for the sake of prosperity and conquers the endless heavenly world.
This indeed is the Rathantara;
of it, the ocean is the limit.
"Ado" is the Bṛhat.
There is no end to that [ocean].
Thus indeed it was seen even beyond the ocean.
He who thus knows these two, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, as both having an end and being endless—verily he encompasses endless prosperity and conquers the endless world of heaven.
He who indeed knows the *stomyā* and the *stotriyā* of the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* becomes worthy of praise (*stomya*).

His own people praise him with these [verses], thinking, "This one is the best for us. "Towards you, O Hero, we cry out, like unmilked cows; towards the Lord of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, the Lord, O Indra, of that which stands still"—this is the *stomyā*.
"None other than you, neither celestial nor terrestrial, has been born nor will be born"—these are the *stotriya* verses.
"Seeking horses, O Maghavan Indra, seeking cattle, we, the prize-winners, invoke you"—by this verse, as it were, power is requested and valor is proclaimed.
He who thus knows these *stomyas* and *stotriyas* of the Bṛhat and Rathantara becomes himself worthy of praise.
One should praise with this [verse]: "He is our own, he is the best.
Moreover, by this very knowledge, all the *ṛcas* become known.
The Bṛhat and the Rathantara were indeed created;
after them, cattle were created. Those that were of the Rathantara nature were created following the Rathantara.
Those [sāmans] which are based on the Bṛhatī [meter] are the *bārhatas*;
Samada found them.
Standing there, he split them apart.
They said, "If we shall indeed become thus, we will certainly not be able to support offspring at that time; come,
let us exchange our forms."
They exchanged their forms.
That speech which was *rāthaṃtara* entered the *bārhata* cattle; that which was *bārhata* entered the *rāthaṃtara* [cattle].
The cow indeed belongs to the *rathantara* [sāman]; bent down as if crouching, she utters the speech belonging to the *bṛhat*, "bhā!"—thus [she speaks] only in a forward direction.
The sheep indeed utters the speech belonging to the *rathantara* with a bleating sound.
The goat is indeed the *bṛhatī* [meter], having ascended upwards;
she utters the speech belonging to the *rathantara*.
With the syllable *makat*,
those two did not succeed in producing a man.
They both said, "Let us both enter this [seed]."
"So be it. Both entered him.
Therefore, a man speaks both kinds of speech: that which belongs to the *rathaṃtara* and that which belongs to the *bṛhat*.

Those animals which belong to the *rathaṃtara* approach him, beholding his speech as belonging to the *rathaṃtara*. Those which belong to the *bṛhat* approach him, beholding his speech as belonging to the *bṛhat*.
Man, indeed, is the union of the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*.
He who knows this—that man is the cry of the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*—to him both kinds of cattle cry out together: those belonging to the *rathaṃtara* and those belonging to the *bṛhat*.
He who knows that man who is the cry of the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*—for one who knows thus, there is indeed this cry of the two.

Once, as Āruṇi was traveling along, men from the north sent messengers after him, asking: "O Āruṇi, son of Āruṇi, by how much do the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* chants procreate offspring? By how much do they attain divine glory?
But he did not answer them.
He said, "I know this which you wish to obtain from me as Brahman; however, I shall not speak it to you.
Then his pupils reflected, "He has answered thus because he is lacking in intelligence;
surely there was something he did not understand."
"Come, let us question him.
They said to him, "If you were to answer, how would you answer?
He replied, "In that he chants the *prastāva* of the first verse with an eight-syllable [phrase], he thereby causes eight-hoofed animals to be propagated."

"In that there are two syllables in the two subsequent [verses], it is by means of those two feet that they have attained glory among the gods through the *nidhana* itself," he said, "if one is to respond. "If one is to respond," he said, "he who knows the invocations to the gods for the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*, his call the gods come to hear."
The invocation of the gods for the *rathantara* is indeed directed upwards, while that of the *bṛhat* is directed downwards.

Therefore, because he begins the *prastāva* of the *rathantara* with its verse as if rising upwards before the *pariṣṭubh*, this world is directed upwards, this fire blazes upwards, the plants are directed upwards, the trees are directed upwards—indeed, everything is directed upwards.

Now, because he begins the *prastāva* with "ho" from the *bṛhat* by means of the *stobha* syllable *pariṣṭubhya*, therefore this world here is turned toward us; that sun shines toward us; the moon is turned toward us; the constellations are turned toward us; the rain comes toward us; indeed, everything is turned toward us.
He who thus knows these invocations of the gods for the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*, the gods go to his call.
The Bṛhat and Rathantara were created;
after that, cattle were created. Those that were of the Rathantara nature were created following the Rathantara.

Those which are connected with the Bṛhat-sāman are the *bṛhat*. Those cattle which are connected with the Rathantara-sāman are those to be eaten; whereas those which are connected with the Bṛhat-sāman are the eaters.
In that he begins the *prastāva* of the *rathantara* after completing the *ṛc* with the *pariṣṭobha*, therefore cattle belonging to the *rathantara* have bone as their foundation and are edible.

And because he begins the *prastāva* of the *bṛhat* after completing it with the *stobha*, therefore cattle belonging to the *bṛhat* have flesh as their foundation and are eaters. For one who knows thus, even though he is himself a consumer, there is much to be eaten; and from him is born a heroic eater.
The Bṛhat and Rathantara indeed place embryos among offspring in the middle;
therefore, they cause procreation at the very end by means of the Yajñāyajñīya.
In that he chants the *prastāva* of the first verse with an eight-syllable [phrase], they thereby place eight-hoofed cattle as embryos.
In that there are two syllables in the two final verses, it is by means of those [syllables]. Since this Yajñāyajñīya is thus performed at the end, it is indeed birth;
he causes procreation by means of it.
Therefore, one should grant a boon at the Yajñāyajñīya chant; just as they grant a boon when a son is born, so too [is this],
for that is indeed the birth of the sacrificer.
Now, those waters which the wife pours out are indeed the same waters that flow from the garment as it is being torn apart.
Furthermore, water is food;
thus, this very food is provided for those who have been born.
Now, that has *vāc* as its *nidhana*;
therefore, a boy, as soon as he is born, utters speech.
The Bṛhat and Rathantara were indeed created.
They were created with a common *nidhana*, or with internal *nidhanas*, or with external *nidhanas*.
They said, "Let us compete in a race regarding these two *nidhanas*."
"So be it.
They entered the race,
and the Bṛhat won it.
The Rathantara then thought itself to be inferior.
It said, "At the end of the pairing, grant me a connection in proper sequence.
"So be it," [he replied].
That became his mate. For him, he bestowed this first union, this forenoon.
Indeed, the forenoon is the union of the *rathantara*, and the afternoon is that of the *bṛhat*.
"’s" is the *nidhana* of the *rathantara*, and "has" is that of the *bṛhat*. These two are indeed the *aharnidhanas*, the *satyanidhanas*; for truth is the *nidhana* of these two.
Therefore, the sacrificer should perform the sacrifice with a chant that contains both [melodies].
Indeed, both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara are thereby secured;
truly, both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara become secured for him.
Regarding this, they say: "Are the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] with internal nidhanas, or with external nidhanas?
One should reply: "Both—with internal nidhanas and with external nidhanas.
For this Rathantara is indeed both.
That is the Bṛhat.
Of those two, this very intermediate space is the Nidhana. Therefore, it has an internal Nidhana.
Now, as they consider the atmosphere to be beyond the sky, so the waters are beyond the earth; thus [the *bahirnidhana*] is applied.

Regarding this, they say: "Is the *vāmadevya* within the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*, or are the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* within the *vāmadevya*? One should reply: "It is both: the *vāmadevya* is within the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*, and the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* are within the *vāmadevya*."
This earth is indeed the Rathantara;
yonder sky is the Bṛhat; this very intermediate space is the Vāmadevya.
Therefore, the Vāmadevya [sāman] belongs to the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans].
Now, just as they consider the intermediate space to be beyond the sky, so the waters are beyond the earth; thus, the Bṛhat and Rathantara are in the Vāmadevya. 56-296 (Ed.:
From whatever womb Prajāpati created living beings, that very place quivered.
It stood there glowing and shining;
he knew: "There is indeed something within."
He said to the gods, "There is indeed this [space] within; release [it] from here!
Agni released the *svāra* tones by means of the *gāyatrī*, and Indra [released] those with the *nidhana* by means of the *triṣṭubh*.
The All-Gods [are connected] with the Jagatī and the Īḍā-verses; Prajāpati [is connected] with the Anuṣṭubh and the Ṛksamans.
Now, that which is Gāyatra and has the *svāra* intonation belongs to Agni by its deity.
That which is in the *triṣṭubh* metre and has a *nidhana* is dedicated to Indra by deity;

that which is in the *jagatī* metre and is connected with the *iḍā* is dedicated to the Viśvedevas by deity; that which is in the *anuṣṭubh* metre and is an *ṛksamā* is dedicated to Prajāpati by deity.
Regarding this, they used to say: "Even though Saumapa was an expert in the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans], he did not arrange the sacrifice correctly;
for both of those [sāmans] have their nidhanas either inside or outside, whereas it is only the Svar-sāman that truly arranges the sacrifice."
In that it concludes within the *ṛc*, that is the *rāthaṃtara*;
and in that it over-sings beyond the *ṛc*, that is the *bārhata*.
Regarding this they ask: "How many *sāmans* are there? One should say: "Four.
For indeed, there are four *sāmans*: the *svāra*, the *nidhanavat*, the *aiḍa*, and the *ṛksamam*.
The four quarters;
the four-footed cattle;
the four meters that carry the sacrifice: the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and the Anuṣṭubh.
Now, these indeed are three: the *svāra*, that which has a *nidhana*, and the *aiḍa*. That which is the *ṛksama* is indeed the *svāra*.
The sacrifice consists of three pressings.
There are three vital breaths: prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna.
These are these three worlds.
And indeed, they are two only: the *svāra* and that which possesses the *nidhana*.
For the *hīḍā* is indeed the *nidhana*. These two worlds are as if entered;
they are the two vital breaths, *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
The person has two feet.
Now, that [Sāman] indeed consists of only one *svāra* tone; for whatever is the *nidhana*, the *yeḍā*, or the *ṛksama*, it is all transcended by the *svāra* itself.

This very *sāman* is indeed one, namely the *svāra*. That which blows here is it. And those [rays] which fly higher and higher, and those which creep below—they all subsist upon this very *svāra* breath.
He who knows this thus reaches a full lifespan.

He who, knowing this, prepares the *jāmi* (the sacrificial connection), for him that which is prepared becomes indeed non-*jāmi*. Therefore, one should arrange it so as to be non-*jāmi* again and again.
For that which is *jāmi* is indeed non-pairing and non-procreative.
It is as if two males were to lie together, or two females.
Would two males lying together procreate? Or would those two females [procreate], if they were not to find a partner for union?
Moreover, that which is non-incestuous is a pair; that is procreation.
The *svara* is indeed the self;
the *nidhana* is offspring.
The sacrificial food (iḍā) is cattle.
The wife is the Ṛgveda and the Sāmaveda.
Indeed, the self and the wife are equal.
Thus, on both sides of himself, he has enclosed offspring and cattle so that they do not escape.
He whose wealth is not lost is he who knows thus. 2-298 (Ed.:
One should not combine these *nidhanas*.
One should not perform them together with the *svara*.
The *svara* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
One should unite that breath with breath; the sacrificer would then be liable to die prematurely.
If one were to perform [the two] together at the *nidhana*, the *nidhana* is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*); he would thereby unite a thunderbolt with a thunderbolt.
A great battle would take place upon that very day.
The staff would strike down the *udgātṛ*, and the arrow the sacrificer.
If one were to perform [the *iḍā*] together with the *aiḍa* verses—the *iḍā* being cattle—one would thereby cause cattle to collide with cattle.
Mahādeva would cause the cattle of that half to perish; the Udgātṛ would suffer total loss,
and the sacrificer would be led to ruin.
If one were to perform the *ṛk* and *sāman* together, his wife would be liable to die prematurely, or death itself would strike the sacrificer.
For this indeed is the final death, namely, the *ahan-naṃṣṭra*.
The tiger is a thief;
therefore, one should not perform these *nidhanas* [of the Sāman], thinking, "Lest I become like him.
Indeed, these four Sāmans have four lineages of ṛṣis.
Regarding this, they say: "Who indeed has mastery over non-intoxication? Or rather, one does indeed become intoxicated.
If he should perform [the *svāra* chant] together with the *svāra*, the *svāra* is breath; thus he has made breath more abundant for himself. In that case, he should meditate: "I shall live long."

If he should perform [the *nidhana*] together with [the preceding part], he should reflect thereon thus: "That is indeed offspring; it is in offspring that I have established offspring; through this, I shall become possessed of offspring.
Furthermore, the *nidhana* is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
[He should think: "I have hurled this thunderbolt at my hateful rival."
If he should perform [the *iḍā*] together with the *aiḍa*, the *iḍā* is indeed cattle; thus he has produced more cattle among cattle. He should reflect thereon: "May I become rich in cattle.

If he should perform [the *nidhana*] together with the *ṛksama*, the *ṛksama* is indeed procreation; thus he has produced more procreation within procreation. He should reflect thereon: "I shall pour [seed] into wife after wife; I shall become many; I shall procreate. For in this way, that [result] does not pass him by.
If someone should investigate him who has acted in this manner, he should say to him: "I know this rightly, not wrongly.
Whatever wrong you know yourself to have committed in this matter, that shall belong to you alone;
yet, if indeed you previously performed the office of the *ṛtvij* priest with the *sāman*, you have thereby merely done what is kin-appropriate."
He who reviles one who knows thus meets with ruin.

Now, from these three forms, one should lead [the chant] from the midday pressing: [from the verses] containing the word *andhas*, those addressed to the Maruts, and those containing the word *pratna*.
Food, indeed, is the blind;
the Maruts are vigor;
the ancient world is heaven.
If it should go with the *andhasvat* [verse], it would depart from food;
if it should go with the *marutvat* [verse], it would depart from virility;
if it should go with the *pratnavat* [verse], it would depart from the heavenly world.
If he should not find room for all of these, he should lead [the sacrifice] with the Marutvatīya alone;
for the Marutvatīya is indeed vigor,
and by vigor, indeed, the ritual act is performed.
Through vigor one attains everything;
therefore, one should lead [the chant] from the Marutvatīya alone. Then, by means of the tone, he ascends to this Gāyatrī.
The breath is the tone.
By means of the breath, he thus ascends to the breath.
Indeed, the breath does not harm the breath.
When he ascends to the *gāyatrī* by means of the *svāra* [melodic tone], he thereby places the vital breath (*prāṇa*) first in the sacrifice.
Therefore, this vital breath is placed first. Moreover, that which is the *svāra* has Agni as its deity.
The Gāyatrī is this metre belonging to Agni.
By means of Agni itself, he thus ascends unto Agni.
Agni is indeed the deity among the gods who makes the way.

By whatever [means] Agni goes, he goes indeed making a path for himself. When he ascends to the *gāyatrī* with the tone (*svara*), he first yokes Agni, the path-maker, at the beginning of the sacrifice.
Thus, by means of Agni alone, he follows the path that has been made.

Just as one traveling on a path reaches his destination safely and unharmed, even so he who, knowing this, ascends to the Gāyatrī by means of the *svara* reaches the conclusion in safety and without harm. 5-301 (Ed.:
1,304) |p1 He ascends by means of the second *nidhana*.
The *nidhana* is indeed the *indranidhana*. Indra is the foremost of the deities.
Wherever the leader reaches the head of the village, there is no harm there.
He who, knowing this, ascends by means of the second *nidhana*, reaches the completion safely and unharmed.
Moreover, Indra and Agni are indeed the swiftest of the deities. It is just as if one were to choose the swiftest and most capable [horses] and employ them; such is that.
Then he ascends this Bṛhatī by means of the *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is cattle;
the Bṛhatī is cattle.
With cattle he thus unites the cattle.
For cattle, when united with cattle, shine all the more.
If he were to ascend [the chant] with the *nidhana*, the *nidhana* is indeed a thunderbolt; he would thus hurl a thunderbolt at the cattle.
If he should not find room for the *iḍā*, he should ascend by means of the tone (*svara*). The tone is breath;
the *bṛhatī* is cattle.
Verily, he thereby places the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the cattle. Now, this second [chant] has three *nidhanas*;
for these worlds are indeed three.
These *vajras* are the *nidhanas*.
By means of these *vajras*, he strikes away all evil from these worlds.
Moreover, these very *vajras* of his remain in these worlds, driving away all evil.
Now, there are three defects of the sacrifice.
He covers two of them;
one remains in its own place.
Then he ascends this *triṣṭubh* by means of tone.
Tone is breath.
This Pavamāna is measured by the person (*puruṣa*).
There is the *svāra* [sāman] at the beginning and the *svāra* at the end.
These two are the out-breath and in-breath of the person, distributed on either side.
From those two, he moves apart in all directions;
then comes the Rathantara.
That indeed is the emission of the seed.
Or else, the Vāmadevya is the *svāra*. The *svara* is indeed breath; thus, when this semen has been emitted, he restores the breath to it.
Now follows the *naudhasa* finale;
it is indeed birth itself; by means of it, he brings forth.
Now follows the Kāleya Aiḍa.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
cattle are food.
Whatever food is provided for those who have been born, that very thing is this.
Now, regarding the Gāyatrī verses of the Ārbhava-pavamāna, their Brāhmaṇa has already been stated;
then he ascends to this Kakubh verse by means of the tone.
The breath is the tone;
the *kakub* is indeed the expansion;
thus, he bestows breath through that very expansion.
If he were to ascend with the *nidhana*, the *nidhana* is indeed a thunderbolt; it would be just as if one were to strike a person who has been injured with a staff—such would that be.
But when he ascends with the *svara*, he thereby bestows vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon this [earth];
he heals her by means of this very act.
Then he ascends this *uṣṇih* verse with the *nidhana*.
The *nidhana* is indeed the thunderbolt (*vajra*),
and the *uṣṇih* is cattle.
At this time, at the third pressing, the animals are as if worn out.
Therefore, they say of an old animal, "One should make use of it. Moreover, having attacked with the thunderbolt and subdued it with the goad, they enjoy its transformation.
Now, when they call the Bṛhatī [verse] "the Nidhana," it is because at this time cattle are like youths, as if not yet matured.
Therefore, they say of a young animal, "It is one that moves while still alive. 7-303 (Ed.:
Then he ascends this Anuṣṭubh by means of the tone.
The tone is breath;
the Anuṣṭubh is speech.
This indeed is the divine couple: speech and breath.
He thus establishes that very divine couple.
If he were to conclude with the *nidhana*, the *nidhana* is indeed a thunderbolt; he would thereby strike away the divine couple with a thunderbolt.
If he should not find space for the *svarasāman*, he should ascend with the *vāṅnidhana*.
Speech is the *anuṣṭubh*;
speech is the *nidhana*.
Speech does not indeed injure speech.
Now, this second [form] has its *nidhana* in the middle;
for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech.
Now, in that there is a *nidhana* in the middle of the *anuṣṭubh* verse, that is indeed the emission of semen.
That [middle] becomes the *hiṃkāra*;
for the *hiṃkāra* is the navel.
Indeed, embryos held by the navel do not fall out from downward openings;
for embryos are indeed held by the navel.
This [verse] of his has ten syllables and has the *nidhana* placed in the middle.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* is food.
Indeed, it is upon this very food that embryos subsist while not yet eating.
Then he ascends this *jagatī* by means of the tone (*svara*).
The tone is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This *pavamāna* is commensurate with the person.
The *svāra* [chant] occurs at the beginning, and the *svāra* occurs at the end.
These two are the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*) of a person, held apart from one another; by means of them, he utters the *svarita* tone in all directions.
Now, as for the *yajñāyajñīya*:
it is indeed the emission of seed.
Now, as for the *sākamaśva*, it is the *svāra* chant.
The tone (*svara*) is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, when this seed has been emitted, he restores the vital breath to it.
Now follows the *saubhara* finale.
That is indeed birth;
by it, he causes [the sacrifice] to be born. Now follows the Nārmedha, which belongs to the *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
cattle are food.
Whatever food is provided for those who have been born, that very thing this [is].
Thus is the first section; thus the second; thus the third.
There are indeed three finales: *iḍā*, *svara*, and the finale itself as the finale.
Now, as for that which is the *ṛksama* and the *svāra*, they indeed consider it to be such; for the kinship and non-kinship of the *ṛksama* and the *svāra* are identical.
This world, indeed, is the *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is cattle;
this world is cattle;
this very intermediate space is the *svara*.
The breath is the *svara*;
the breath is the intermediate space;
yonder world indeed is the *nidhana*.
The *gati* is the foundation.
Now, he who would arrange those [verses] in the proper sequence without violating the rule of non-repetition (*ajāmi*) should first perform the *aiḍa*, then the *svāra*, and then the *nidhanavat*.
For in this way these worlds are arranged according to their proper order.
The self (ātman) is indeed the *nidhana*;
the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the *svara*;
cattle are the *iḍā*.

In that the *svāra* is performed between the *aiḍa* and the *nidhanavat*, thus indeed all these [elements] of his become continuous with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For this vital breath in the middle divides off the creatures, the cattle, and the worlds.
Now, indeed, as to how Bṛhat and Rathantara divided the *sāmans*.
Some of them were *rāthaṃtara* chants and others were *bārhata* chants;
then those in which they performed the *samapādana* became both *rāthaṃtara-bārhata* and *bārhata-rāthaṃtara*.
Now, that which has the *ṛc* as its *prastāva* and the *nidhana* within it is the *rāthaṃtara*. Then, that which has the *stobha* before [the *ṛc*] and the *nidhana* outside it is the *bārhata*.
Then, that which has the *ṛc* as its *prastāva* and the *nidhana* outside it is the *rāthaṃtarabārhata*.
Now, that which has a stobha at the beginning and an internal nidhana is the Bārhatarāthaṃtara.
Regarding this they ask: "How many sāmans are there?
One should say: "Four."
There are indeed four Sāmans: the Rāthaṃtara, the Bārhatam, the Rāthaṃtarabārhatam, and the Bārhatarāthaṃtaram.

Now, he who would arrange these so as to be non-repetitive (*ajāmi*) in their proper sequence should first perform the Rāthaṃtara, then the Bārhatam, then the Rāthaṃtarabārhatam, and then the Bārhatarāthaṃtaram.
Thus, he interweaves the six forms of these four Sāmans.
Indeed, everything is made consistent through the *nidhana*. Truly, he who would make the forms consistent makes it well-prepared.
One should begin the Gāyatrī with the *nidhana*.
The *nidhana* is vigor;
the Gāyatrī is vigor.
By means of vigor, he brings that vigor to fulfillment.
One should take hold of the Bṛhatī with the Aiḍa [Sāman];
cattle are the iḍā.
The *bṛhatī* is cattle;
thus he brings cattle into harmony with cattle.
The *svāra* [sāman] is the final one.
The breath is the tone.
The breath is the final [syllable].
He who knows thus reaches a full span of life.
The Rathantara or the Bṛhat is performed as the Pṛṣṭha-stotra with the *nidhana* [finale].
The *nidhana* is vigor;
the Pṛṣṭha is vigor.
By means of vigor, he brings that vigor to fulfillment.
The *svāra* is the *maitrāvaruṇa-sāman*; the breath is the *svāra*.
The Prāṇa is the Maitrāvaruṇasāman;
the Brahmasāman has a two-syllable *nidhana*; duality is the foundation.
The *brahmasāman* is the foundation;
the *aiḍa* is the *acchāvākasāman*; cattle are the *iḍā*.

The *paśu* verses are the *acchāvāka*sāman. One should begin the *gāyatrī* of the *ārbhava* [laud] with the *rathantara*sāman having an internal *nidhana*, and with the *bṛhat*sāman having an external *nidhana*. One should begin the *kakubh* with the [specific] tone.
The breath is the tone;
the *vivṛha* is indeed the *kakub*;
thus he bestows breath through the *vivṛha*.
One should begin the *uṣṇih* with the *aiḍa* [sāman] which possesses a *nidhana*.
The *nidhana* is vigor;
the *uṣṇih* is vigor.
The *iḍā* is cattle;
the *uṣṇih* is cattle.
One should approach it with whatever [meter] one desires.
One should begin the *anuṣṭubh* with the tone (*svara*).
The tone is breath;
the *anuṣṭubh* is speech.
By means of the breath itself, he thus continues the speech;
by means of the breath, he undertakes the speech.
The *svāra* tone is the final one.
The breath is the tone.
The breath is the final [syllable].
He who knows thus reaches a full lifespan. 11-307 (Ed.: 1,309)
The *yajñāyajñīya* has speech as its finale (*vāṅnidhana*) and is performed at the end.
Thus, this entire sacrifice, once completed, is deposited within speech itself.
The sacrificial merit of his offerings and charitable works does not perish for one who knows thus;
for there is no destruction of speech.
One should not omit the *marutvat* [stotra] at midday.
Therefore, he is possessed of form; therefore, he is endowed with vigor.
One should perform the Rathantara-sāman on Gāyatrī verses, and the Bṛhat-sāman on Triṣṭubh verses.
He makes the final [verse] of the Bṛhat-sāman a Bṛhatī verse containing three *nidhanas*.
Whatever in the sacrifice here becomes defective, that very thing he pacifies by means of this [verse].
He should not omit the Ārbhava [laud], for it contains the word *madvat* and the word *andhasvat*;
for by means of it, [the sacrifice] possesses form, and by means of it, it is powerful.
One should perform the Rathantara-sāman on Gāyatrī verses, and the Bṛhat-sāman on Anuṣṭubh verses.
He makes the Aiḍa-stotra with a nidhana in the middle on Anuṣṭubh verses as the last [part].
Whatever flaw there may be in the sacrifice, that he pacifies by means of this.

In that the *marutvat* and the *triṇidhana* do not separate from the midday pressing, and in that the *aiḍa*, whether it be *madvat*, *andhasvat*, or having its *nidhana* in the middle, does not separate from the Ārbhava pressing—thus indeed all these remain unseparated for him. Now, one should certainly not perform the *gāyatra* on a single verse (*ekarca*).

One should perform the *aiḍa* with its *nidhana* in the middle on an *anuṣṭubh* only when there is no desire [for specific results]. One may perform these two on a single verse in the *trivṛt* stoma only when there is no desire at all.
One should perform those very same *sāmans* of the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters either on two triplets (*tṛca*) or on two single verses (*ekarca*).
However, there is no such thing as a "triplet-and-single-verse" (*tṛcaikarca*).
Nor is there a final [verse] for a single verse, whether from the perspective of the *ṛc* or the *sāman*; that position does not belong to the *arbhave* nor to the *gāyatrī* *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
There are indeed three bellies of the sacrifice: the *gāyatrī*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *anuṣṭubh*; for it is into these that they pour [the offerings].
From there they extract it.
Now, just as a man who is well-fed in the middle might still hunger, so is that;
but just as the other limbs remain fixed, so do the other stotras remain fixed.

There are indeed four *sāmans* that do not have a fixed place among single-verse (*ekarca*) hymns: the *bṛhat*, the *rathantara*, the *vāmadevya*, and the *yajñāyajñīya*. Wherever these might be performed, one should apply them only to three-verse (*tr̥ca*) hymns, not to single-verse hymns.
Furthermore, one should certainly not be a practitioner who applies them to single-verse hymns.
That which is a single verse (*ekarca*) is, as it were, devoid of vigor.
This world, indeed, is a single verse;
this [world] is, as it were, cut off from these two worlds.
The *tṛca* is, as it were, more continuous in its vigor.
For these worlds are three;
indeed, these worlds are the *tṛca*.
Indeed, three are more powerful than one.
For it is from this that one who possesses more considers one who possesses less to be inferior.
Whatever pasture is greater and whatever prosperity is greater, that he wins by means of the *ṛc*-triad.
Now, that which is the smaller pasture-ground, the lesser prosperity—that he wins by means of a single verse (*ekarca*).
For a single verse is indeed greater than a triplet (*tṛca*).
"Ekarca" consists of three syllables.
"Regarding the *ṛca*: there are two [types].
For he who knows these *ṛk*-verses and *akṣara*-verses [as] *ṛca*-triplets, thinking, "Both types of *ṛca*-triplets have been made for me," indeed both types of *ṛca*-triplets are made for him.
Moreover, because the *ṛk* and the *sāman* are the *hiṃkāra*, by that means the *ṛca*-triplets are made for him."

Moreover, because there is the *prastāva*, the *pratihāra*, and the *nidhana*, he does not depart from the *ṛc*s for that reason. Prajāpati indeed stands at the morning pressing generating offspring, which is this *bahiṣpavamāna*.
That very deity, having become present, sits down upon this sacrificial seat.
Whatever world belongs to that deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus. [Then follows] the clarified butter for Agni.
That indeed is the Abhijit Stoma;
it is Agni himself,
for he conquered all this.
Having become that very deity, she sits down upon this *āstāva*.
Whatever world belongs to this deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.
Then follows the *ājya* chant for the Maitrāvaruṇa.
That indeed is the Viśvajit stoma.
Day and night are those two. Mitra, indeed, is the day.
Night is Varuṇa.
Thus, whatever worlds there are on this side of the sun, both day and night indeed attain them all;
yet they do not attain the world of those who know thus.
Having become that very deity, she sits down upon this sacrificial seat (āstāva).
Whatever is the world of this deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.
Then follows the Ājya-stotra for Indra.
That indeed is the Sarvajit (all-conquering) Stoma;
it is Indra himself,
for he conquered all this.
That very deity, having become that, sits down upon this sacrificial enclosure (āstāva).
Whatever is the world of that deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.
Then follows the Aindrāgna ājya-stotra.
That indeed is the Udbhid-stoma;
those two are Indra and Agni,
for they both split open (udabhinttām) this entire world through their race-course.
Having become that very deity, she sits down upon this sacrificial seat.
Whatever is the world of that deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus. 14-310 (Ed.:
Now follows the midday *pavamāna*.
That indeed is the *stoma* that wins wealth;
it is Vāyu himself.
For he, having become this breath, won all wealth.
Therefore, whatever is won by one who possesses breath, he becomes the owner of all that, provided he knows thus.
Having become that very deity, he sits down upon this place for chanting.
Whatever world belongs to this deity, that indeed is the world of one who knows thus.
Whether the *rathantara* or the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant,
it is indeed prosperity (*śrī*) that is the *stoma*.
For Śrī is the *pṛṣṭha* [chant].
Having become that very deity, she sits down in this place of chanting (*āstāva*).
Whatever is the world of this deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.
Then the Vāmadevya;
that indeed is the Śānti-stoma;
those are the waters.

When Agni Vaiśvānara burned this earth, they indeed extinguished him with water alone. Both of these are indeed Vaiśvānaras: the summer heat and the winter cold. Therefore, when the rainy season intervenes between them, it is for the sake of peace.
That very deity, having become that [form], sits down upon this place of chanting.
Whatever is the world of that deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.
Now, the Naudhasa or the Śyaita is the Brahman-sāman.
That indeed is the *stoma* consisting of all the meters;
that is the *brahman*;
for the *brahman* consists of all the meters.
That very deity, having become present, sits down upon this sacrificial seat (āstāva).
Whatever world belongs to that deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.
Now, [concerning] the Kāleya...
That *stoma* is indeed that essence;
it is food itself.
Whoever knows this becomes the world of that essence of food.
That very deity, having become that [form], settles upon this place of sitting (*āstāva*).
Whatever world belongs to that deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.
Now follows the *Arbhavapavamāna*.
That indeed is the Asita-stoma;
those are the quarters.
Verily, evil did not overcome the quarters as they were stepping forth.
Evil does not bind him who knows this.
Having become that very deity, he settles upon this place of assembly.
Whatever is the world of that deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.
Then the Yajñāyajñīya.
That is indeed the Nāka-stoma;
it is indeed the Āditya.
For this indeed does not rise for anyone else. Having become that very deity, it settles upon this sacrificial ground (āstāva).
Whatever is the world of that deity, that indeed becomes the world of one who knows thus.

This, indeed, is the power (*indriya*) of the *stomas*. These [three] are indeed the most powerful among the *stomas*. He who knows this becomes powerful; he becomes one who is not to be surpassed in all this. 15-311 (Ed.: 1,313)
In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this world.
He desired: "May I indeed be all this."
"May I overcome all this," he thought.
Having become Agni himself, he overcame the hostile armies;
having become the earth, he became the past and the future.
Having become water, he pervaded everything; having become mind, he perceived everything;
having become speech, he manifested everything.
Having become the eye, he saw everything;
having become the ear, he heard everything;
having become the wind, he became the vital breath of living beings.
Having become the intermediate space, he supported the sky;
having become the sky, he pervaded everything;
having become the Virāj, he became the sun.
Having become desire, he became Ananta;
having become Ananta, he became Death;
having become the year, he did not sound.
He who knows thus does not suffer loss.
Having become the moon, he encompassed the half-months;
having become Parjanya, he became the progenitor of creatures.
Having become the sacrifice, he sustains the gods.
These creatures of his, once created, did not come to an agreement;
having become Name, he entered them.

These [beings] are recognized by name, such as "this one" or "that one," or "the son of so-and-so. This very Agniṣṭoma is he who shines yonder; he is Indra, he is Prajāpati; one should worship him thinking, "He alone is all this. 16-312 (Ed.:
He sings the *retasyā* [verse]. The *retasyā* is indeed semen; it is for the continuity of semen and to prevent its interruption.
He sings [the verses] without the *hiṃ* sound.
The *hiṃ* sound is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
For if he were to utter the *hiṃ* sound, he would cut off the semen with that thunderbolt-like *hiṃ* sound.
If it were a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), he should chant [the *sāman*] without the *hiṃ*-utterance on that day;
for that day is indeed one.
If it is a two-day sacrifice (*dvyaha*), he should chant without the *hiṃ*-utterance on both days.
For one of those two is the departure (prāyaṇa), and the other is the rising (udayana).
If it is a three-day rite, they deliberate upon it: "Should he utter the *hiṃ* call, or should he not utter the *hiṃ* call?"
Regarding this, some say: "One may indeed chant the *retasyā* verses without the *ahiṃkāra* every day throughout the year;
for what has been infused is developed over the course of a year—it is for the sake of the development of the seed."
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "In that the seed is indeed poured out on the first day, that becomes the embryo.
But as for what is poured out thereafter, it is poured out as something already existing.
Therefore, on the first day alone, having sung the *retasyā* chant without the *hiṃ* call, one should sing it with the *hiṃ* call on the subsequent days.
Moreover, the *hiṃkāra* is indeed food;
for by means of food the embryo grows. It is for the sake of growth.
One should sing that [sāman] at the rising.
For what is the departure, that is the rising; thus it would be. 17-313 (Ed.:
Now, these *gaḍū* verses were learned by Ārkṣākāyaṇa Śālāvatya from Āruṇi;
these are the *dhur* verses of Āruṇi.
Regarding this, they ask: "What is the metre of the *retasyā*?"
One should say, "The Bṛhatī.
"How is it the Bṛhatī?
"One should say, 'For the mind is the Retasyā.'"
There is nothing whatsoever greater than the mind; moreover, all vital breaths are merged into the mind,
and all meters are merged into the Bṛhatī.
"Therefore, [the verse] 'The Bṛhatī is in the semen' (RV 8.6.31). They ask: 'By what has it increased? One should say: 'It has been increased by that,' namely, by the *retasyā*."
For all this has grown from semen;
by it the mind has grown,
by it the moon has grown— this is the deity.
This very Retasyā is indeed the moon.
It is the counterpart of semen, King Soma, the food of the gods, the gathered essence of all this;
upon it all the gods subsist.
Therefore they say: "Soma alone is the king, the Brahman;
for all the gods subsist upon him.
This very *retasyā* is indeed the Brahman.
The *brahman* has indeed praised for him who, knowing thus, chants with the *retasyā*. 18-314 (Ed.:
1,316) |c315 (Ed.: 1,317) |p1 He chants the *gāyatrī*.
The Gāyatrī is indeed breath. Of it, he interlocks two syllables:
"o3rvāṇo aśiśrāde3yurvaṃ devāya dā"—thus he interlocks them.
That is breath;
that is wind; he sings the *triṣṭubh*.
The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the eye. Of that [meter], he causes two syllables to shine forth; he causes these two to shine forth as "ṣo" and "dhā."
This is the eye;
that is yonder sun;
he sings the *jagatī*.
The ear is indeed the Jagatī.
Of it, he illuminates four syllables.
He illuminates two feet containing the word "śukra" (bright), namely: "soma-āś śukrāḥ."
This is the ear;
these are the quarters;
he sings the *anuṣṭubh*.
The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech.
Pushing it toward himself, he sings it:
"O3 vājaṃ vājy akrāmā3," singing the word with its phonemes articulated.
He utters "nūṣa. That is speech; that is Prajāpati.
He sings the *paṅkti* [verse].
The seasons, indeed, are the *paṅkti*.
He causes its six syllables to shine forth.
"Flow on, O Sūrya!"— with these words containing "Sūrya," he illumines the two feet.
These are the six seasons.
These six *dhurs* are deities.
By means of these, the gods overthrew the Asuras. Because they overthrew them (*adhūrvan*), they became the *dhurs*.
He who knows this has praised him with all these deities.
Furthermore, he who reviles one who knows this is cut off from all these deities.
Regarding this, some chant this *pāṅkti* verse apart, saying, "Embryos are not born unformed," [chanting]: "O gathering one, giver, O wise one, flow clear like the sun."
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "Because they sing this [Sāman] apart, therefore embryos here become confused.
Since embryos are born when they are extended, therefore this [Sāman] should be sung as the Gāyatra alone, in an extended manner."

Regarding this, they say: "Only he should sing the *dhurs* apart today who knows how to sing them together. On this point, some indeed say: "While singing apart during the *bahiṣpavamāna*, we sing them together when we perform [the verses] with the *o vā* as the *nidhana*, for by that very means they become sung together for us."
Therefore, they pay attention to the *ājya* [stotras], but not to the two *pavamāna* [stotras].
Now, some say: "We shall sing together while singing apart only in the *ājya* stotras," specifically in the *jagatī* verse of the Hotṛ’s *ājya*.
For the Hotṛ priest is connected with the Jagatī metre.
This [verse] occurs:
"O Agni, come hither for the feast" (RV 6.16.10).
The *gāyatrī* is for the Maitrāvaruṇa; for the Maitrāvaruṇa is connected with the *gāyatrī*.
This [verse] is: "Come to us, O Mitra and Varuṇa."
The *triṣṭubh* [verse] belongs to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin;
for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is indeed connected with the *triṣṭubh*. This verse is: "Come hither, for we have pressed [the Soma] for thee."
The *anuṣṭubh* belongs to the *acchāvāka*; for the *acchāvāka* is connected with the *anuṣṭubh*. This [verse] of his is: "O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed [soma]."
Now, in this very case, they are sung according to their proper form.
But for one who, having sung them at the morning pressing, sings them at the midday pressing and at the third pressing, his [verses] are indeed sung according to their respective positions.
For he causes these [verses] to fall from their position when, while they belong to the midday pressing and the third pressing, he sings them at the morning pressing alone.

Now, he who sings these [verses] at the morning pressing, and at the midday pressing, and at the third pressing—he alone establishes them in their proper abodes. Thus, they become sung with their proper abodes for him;
it is right here that they are sung together.
Thus said Āddhiya Sātyayajñi:
"Prosperity comes to him within his own community who, knowing this, does not sing the *dhurs* separately."
"Therefore, if one should sing apart the other *dhurs*, one should indeed sing apart both the *ājya-dhurs* and the *pavamāna-dhurs*.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "Those who sing apart the *dhurs* are pulling them asunder.
If he sings a *triṣṭubh*, he places that essence of the *triṣṭubh* which belongs to the midday pressing into the morning pressing."

If he sings one with the characteristics of the *rathantara*, whatever essence there is in the *rathantara* *pṛṣṭhas*, that he places in the morning pressing. If he sings a *jagatī*, whatever essence there is in the *jagatī* at the third pressing, that he places in the morning pressing.
If he sings an *anuṣṭubh*—for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech—he places that in the morning pressing.
This speech, being an *anuṣṭubh*, is bound at the morning pressing; it is not sufficient for anyone.
Even if one were to pour out clarified butter belonging only to Agni, those two pressings would be exhausted in their power (*yātayāman*) while [the other] remains empty.
Furthermore, if one intends to proceed in two ways within a single sacrificial rite, these juices become separated and exhausted in their power.
But that [way] is indeed discordant. There is no excellence in performing this [melody].
Therefore, one should sing it only as "o vā o vā."
Now, there are indeed two yokes: mind and speech.
For speech is produced from the mind;
thus, speech has the mind as its leader.
That mind carries speech forward;
speech, in turn, carries the mind forward.
That tone which arises from both the mind and speech—this is it.
He is Indra.
Indra is all the gods.
He who, knowing thus, sings the *udgītha*, leads [the sacrificer] to the world of the gods;
whereas others lead him either to the world of the Gandharvas or to the world of the ancestors.
Moreover, by means of these two [specific] yokes, all yokes are attained for him.
Prajāpati created the sacrifice.
He gave it to the gods.
With the Gāyatra [meter] he gave the morning pressing.
The midday pressing and the third pressing [are performed] with the *sāman*s.
The midday pressing had the *āmahīyava* as its opening hymn;
the third pressing had the *saṃhita* as its opening hymn.
They sacrificed with it. Of them, that which was the Gāyatra head came into being.
Those gods approached Prajāpati and said, "Indeed, there was only one Sāman, namely the Gāyatra."
"That which was our Gāyatra head has indeed come together. Therefore, fashion this sacrifice for us in such a way that we may all become complete in their limbs, possessed of bodies, and immortal.
He then extracted six Gāyatrī verses from that very morning pressing.
He brought down three [stotras] for the midday pressing;
he brought down three for the third pressing.
They said to him: "Since you have taken these away from here, what will happen here?"

He said, "I shall plant the meters here; by means of the meters these [verses] will be proclaimed. Because he said, "I shall plant the meters here; by means of the meters these will be proclaimed," therefore, although they are *gāyatrīs*, they are proclaimed by means of the meters.
Moreover, they sacrificed with a song of praise (*upagīta*).
They all indeed became immortal, complete with their limbs and their bodies. Whoever knows this becomes immortal, complete with his limbs and his body.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani used to say: "Therefore, he who knows this becomes superior. 23-319 (Ed.: 1,321)
Now,
this Āmahīyava [sāman], dedicated to Prajāpati, is performed at the beginning of the pressing;
it is self-praised, being that which belongs to Prajāpati.
Even though that [syllable] is already praised, this further praise is offered for the fact that he takes up [the recitation] with "Om":
that syllable is indeed yonder sun;
it is the uncrushable syllable of the threefold Veda.
When he takes up [the chant] with "Om," he thereby places that very Sun within his mouth.
Just as one might mix parched grain with honey, even so does he infuse essence into the Sāman by means of this syllable;
thus he causes it to swell.
Therefore, by means of this swelling and flavorful [part], it becomes praised.
Regarding this, the Kurus say: "The *sāman* sinks while being chanted during the *pratihāra*.
He says: "That which he takes up after the *pratihāra*, that he causes to rise."
This very Sāman is indeed sung as the *sāman*.

That which one sings as a *sāman* while [thinking] "I am singing this *sāman* as a *sāman*" is indeed well-sung. One should know that by means of this, one will attain preeminence among one's own people.
"Being purified, O Soma, flow in a stream," with these words he chants the *prastāva*.
"Clothed in waters, you flow"—these are eight syllables.
"Bringing treasures, to the womb of the Truth, being true"—these are eight [syllables].
Those are sixteen.
"sya sīdasi" consists of four [verses].
Then, those which are sixteen are that very animal consisting of sixteen parts.
Now, those four [verses] are the udders of this sacrificial animal.
Just as one might milk a suckling animal that has been presented, even so does he milk whatever desire he desires by means of this song. "That is beneficial for cattle," said Sucitta Śailana.
"He who, knowing thus, sings the Raurava [sāman], becomes possessed of cattle. (24–320;
1,323) |p1 One desiring offspring should rise up toward the *sāman* while it is being introduced.
When the *prastāva* has been performed, one who desires sovereign power [should do so].
While the *pratīhāra* is being chanted, one who desires cattle should sing out toward it.
Upon reaching the final note (*svara*) at the *nidhana*, he should meditate upon spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*).
For the *svar* is indeed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Regarding this, Jānaśruteya used to say, "There are four objects of desire for the *sāman*";
but Vaitahavya used to say, "There are only three objects of desire for the *sāman*."
Whatever one performs by means of speech, that is offspring;
for speech is born from the mind.
Therefore, when one performs something by means of speech, one should know this: "This is my offspring; through this, I shall become possessed of offspring."
Now, when he sings the *ṛc*, those are the cattle; for the *ṛc* is indeed cattle.
When he thinks, "I am singing the *ṛc*; these are my cattle; by this I shall become possessed of cattle," let him know it thus.

Now, when he reaches the *svara* as the *nidhana*, that is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). For the *svara* is indeed spiritual luster. When he reaches the *svara* as the *nidhana*, he should know this: "This is my spiritual luster; through this, I shall become possessed of spiritual luster."
"In this very [syllable], all these desires are obtained for one who knows thus.
That which is "Om" is this true syllable (akṣara).
Indeed, these *nidhana*s of the Yaudhājaya sāman are truly like thunderbolts (*vajra*).

Those gods, chanting with this truth "Om" and with these *nidhanas* of the *Yaudhājaya*, struck down the Asuras, their evil enemies. In the very same way, one who knows this, chanting with this truth "Om" and with these *nidhanas* of the *Yaudhājaya*, strikes down his hateful enemy, his evil rival.
That [sāman] consists of three *nidhanas*.
These three worlds are indeed these *vajras*, which are the *nidhanas*.
By means of these *vajras*, one drives away all evil from these worlds.
Moreover, these very *vajras* of his, having struck away all evil from these worlds, he ascends to the heavenly world with the syllable "Om. Now, this [hymn] of Uśanas is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Now, when the gods and the asuras were arrayed for battle, it said to them: "Three times a day I am *ṣṭubh*.
Because it said, "Three times a day I am *ṣṭubh*," it is therefore called *triṣṭubh*.
By means of this [metre], having praised three times, those gods struck down the asuras, their evil kinsmen.
In this very way, one who knows thus, having praised with this [hymn] three times, strikes down his hateful, evil rival.
Of him, it sprouts up three times.
For yonder sun is of the *triṣṭubh* nature: white, black, and man.
This eye is of the *triṣṭubh* nature: white and black, and the person (*puruṣa*).
Having brought it into correspondence with the most excellent deity, he sings the *udgītha*.
He who, knowing thus, sings the *auśana*, attains preeminence among his own people. 26–322 (Ed.: 1,324)
Now, regarding the *nirbādha* and *upastambha* bricks:
while the *hiṃ* is being uttered for the Sāman, one should mentally push away in that direction anyone whom one hates.
From that very point he perishes.
While being responded to, he should mentally paralyze him whom he hates in this very direction;
from that very point he also perishes.
Now, there are three [worlds] of the *sāman* that lead to heaven and three that lead to hell. That which precedes the *prastāva* leads to hell;
having caused one's hateful rival to fall into it, the *ādi* is the heavenly world, and therein one should establish oneself.
When the *pratihāra* has been performed before the *upadrava*, that [singer] goes to hell.
Having caused his hateful rival to fall, he should place himself in the *upadrava*, for the heavenly world is the *upadrava*.
When the *nidhana* has been performed before the *upadrava*, he goes to hell.
Having caused his hateful rival to fall, the *nidhana* is the heavenly world; therein one should place oneself.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "That part of the *sāman* which follows the *prastāva* is free from evil;
it is this very heavenly world."
Who would allow an enemy or rival to share in that?
While it has merely been commenced, before it has even begun, he alone is the one who suffers in hell.
Having caused that enemy or rival to fall, he should establish himself in the entirety of the *sāman*.
And also the sacrificer.
Having struck away evil, he goes to the heavenly world. This is that which, having performed, one considers oneself superior. 27-323 (Ed.: 1,325)
Or, whoever performs the office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) by means of the *ṛc* and *sāman*, which possess a foundation, becomes possessed of a foundation.
The *prastāva* is indeed the foundation of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
That which he sings as the *chandas* after the *prastāva* is the abode of the *sāman* in the *ṛc*. The *pratihāra* itself is the abode of the *ṛc* in the *sāman*.
That which he sings as the *chandas* after the *pratihāra* is the abode of the *sāman* in the *ṛc*.
The *nidhana* is indeed the abode in the *arcas* chant; that which he sings as the *atisvara* is the abode of the *sāman* in the *ṛc*.
He who thus performs the priestly office with these two—the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, both possessing an abode—becomes one who possesses an abode himself.
Now, this is indeed a dyad: the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
Of these two, that which is the truth among living beings wins that world which is to be won by truth.
Speech, indeed, is the truth of the *ṛcs*.
The mind is the *sāman*.
These two, indeed, are the truth of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
Truth prevails among offspring; one conquers that world which is to be conquered by truth.
One should sing the *sāman* with truth regarding the *ṛc*; one should recite the *ṛc* with truth regarding the *sāman*.
Indeed, both the *ṛc* and the *sāman* have mastery over the heavenly world.
Verily, these two cause him to go to the heavenly world.
He who sings these [verses] in this manner has mastery over the heavenly world;
therefore, they should be sung in this very way.
When about to chant the *rathantara* [sāman], he touches the earth, saying: "Homage to Mother Earth; O *rathantara*, do not harm me!

Then he gathers the greatness [of the *rathantara*] with the formula: "Whatever greatness of yours is in the fire, whatever greatness of yours is in the waters, whatever greatness of yours is in the chariot, whatever greatness of yours is in the thunder, and whatever greatness of yours is in the wind—with that, become united; O *rathantara*, be rich in wealth for us!"
Then he recites the Vāmadevya chant as a preliminary peace-utterance: "Thou art Prajāpati, O Vāmadevya; thou art the refuge of the Brahman; protect me! (ŚB 10.5.2.13).
Then he recites these immortal utterances: "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Who shall sing this udgītha? He indeed shall sing this udgītha!
(ŚB 10.5.2.14). Prajāpati, indeed, is "ka" (who).
He chooses that very person first for the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*).
Whatever he sings as the Udgātṛ, by means of speech alone his purpose is accomplished;
he becomes free from debt in his own person.
Then he breathes upon it.
Breath indeed is peace;
Agni indeed is the Bṛhat and Rathantara.
He pacifies them with the *prāṇa* [breath].

Now, those who chant the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* when they are not yet pacified—those young men learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) die prematurely; [therefore] one should personally chant the *Vāmadevya* afterwards.
Just as one might carry away a heated cauldron by grasping it with two handles, even so he carries this [sacrifice] away, having grasped it with the Bṛhat and Rathantara and the Vāmadevya.
These two do not cause him to fail;
he who, knowing thus, sings the Bṛhat and Rathantara, reaches a full span of life.
This [earth] is indeed the *rathantara*. Its calf is that which shines yonder.
When he utters the stobha "bhā-bhā," he sings while having placed that very sun in his mouth.
Just as one might milk a cow that has been let loose with her calf, even so does he milk the *Rathantara* by means of this song for whatever desire he may desire.
The *Rathantara* is indeed prosperity (*śrī*). These are its musical interjections (*stobhas*), namely those which are upon this earth.

This very prosperity is not to be obtained anywhere other than in the syllables (*akṣara*). When he chants the *stobha* in the syllables, he obtains this very prosperity and becomes established in it.
This prosperity, which resides in the syllables, is indeed established in one place.
Therefore, one should pause upon the syllables.
This *rathantara* [sāman] is rootless when it occurs elsewhere than on the syllables.
For from this very abode do those fall who chant the *stobha* syllables elsewhere than in the *akṣaras*. But he who chants the *stobha* in the *akṣaras* establishes himself in his own abode.
Therefore, one should chant the *stobha* only in the *akṣaras*.
"Those who sing of the deities among the Kurus and Pañcālas do not fall from their foundation," so said Śāṭyāyani.
Mind is indeed the prior, and speech is the subsequent; mind is indeed the *bṛhat*, and speech is the *rathantara*.

When the Bṛhat and the Rathantara went to the contest, the Bṛhat won it; the Rathantara thought itself defeated. Therefore, when he sings the Rathantara quickly, he thereby makes the mind and speech equal.
He gazes upon this *rathantara* [sāman], thinking: "May he who has made me equal with this quickly cast off evil.
He who, knowing thus, sings the *rathantara* quickly, indeed quickly casts off evil. 31–327 (Ed.:
One should sing that [verse] quickly, without shaking it with the *pūrṇamukha* [breathing technique]. This *Rathantara* is prosperity;
one thus bestows prosperity upon oneself.
Moreover, this Rathantara is Agni;
therefore, one should seek to be released from it quickly.
For where Agni stands near, he burns; and there, indeed, plants grow only at a great distance.
Wherever he goes fanning [the fire], there the plants quickly spring up.
"May I quickly be propagated with offspring and cattle"—thus, at every *pratihāra*, the Udgātṛ should say, "The *iḍā* has come.
For the *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
The *rathaṃtara* is the foundation (*āyatana*). Thus, he establishes these animals in their very foundation.
Now, some chant this with a single form, "bhā bhā," as a stobha.
"That yonder sun is *bhā*," so they say.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "That which is of a single form is without a mate and is procreative;
for that yonder [sun] is indeed *bhaga*."
This is a division:
this is a man, or this is a woman.
When that [heaven] rains, then this [earth] brings forth.
Indeed, when a man pours his seed into a woman, then she brings forth. Therefore, one should chant the *stobha* "abhubhābhibhabhebhabha" as a productive union.
As long as he should chant the *stobha*, so long shall his two hands remain upon the earth, so that the chariot of the gods may not stumble.
He chants the *stobha* with sixteen syllables.
