Man indeed consists of sixteen parts (*kalā*). Part by part he thus pours the sacrificer into this womb of the gods;
he is born from this womb of the gods for the sake of the gods.
Of the two [groups] consisting of fourteen and fourteen [syllables],
those which are ten are the *virāj*;
the *virāj* is food.
Now, those which are four are the four-footed animals;
thus he wins four-footed animals.
He utters sixteen syllables as musical interjections (stobhas).
Then, those which are fifteen are that thunderbolt; the fifteenth is the thunderbolt.
Now, that which is the sixteenth syllable is Indra.
Indra is the hurler of the thunderbolt; he is the sixteenth.
He made that Indra the sacrificer. Therefore, with the fifteenfold vajra, the Udgātṛ strikes down the hateful, evil rival of the sacrificer.
[This is done] fourteen times each on the two subsequent [stomas].
That thunderbolt is indeed one that has no support.
Therefore, the Udgātṛ carves out the rival in the very domain of the sacrificer’s rival; he brings about the destruction of the rival in the rival’s own domain.
No rival whatsoever remains for him who knows thus.
He chants sixteen syllables as *stobha*. In the two subsequent [sections] of fourteen [syllables each],
those amount to forty-four syllables.
The *triṣṭubh* consists of forty-four syllables.
Indra is connected with the *triṣṭubh*.
That very Indra has been placed in the middle of the meters, with many meters before him and many after him. 33-329 (Ed.: 1,331)
The meters are indeed all the *stomas*, all cattle, all the gods, all the worlds, and all desires. Thus,
he obtains all the *stomas*, all cattle, all the gods, all the worlds, and all desires.
The Rathantara is this Agni.
Agni, indeed, is death.
Therefore, whoever chants the *stobha* elsewhere than in the syllables (*akṣara*) is that very Udgātṛ who casts the sacrificer into the mouth of death.
Now, he who chants the *stobha* syllables—since the *stobha* is indeed food—he closes the mouth of death with each *stobha* and thus overcomes this death. Moreover, this *Rathantara* is the ocean;
therefore, he who chants the *stobha* elsewhere than on the syllables enters this very ocean.
Now, he who finds support in the syllables (*akṣara*)—just as one might cross from island to island by means of a boat or a raft—crosses over this ocean in just that way.
He utters, "Beholder of heaven" (*svardṛśam*).
For when one goes to heaven, then he becomes immortal.
He announced him to all the gods and all beings, saying: "This Brāhmaṇa has gone to the light; he has become immortal.
All the gods and all beings recognized him.
Now follows this Vāmadevya [Sāman]. It should be sung without taking breath up to the *pratihāra*. For the Vāmadevya is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
"Lest we cut off our vital breaths," he said. "One should not sing along the path of another;
for he who sings along the path of another is liable to become a dependent."
One should sing only the *svadhū* [verse].
Regarding this, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya used to say: "This Vāmadevya [Sāman] is as if withered, as if stripped bare;
for from it the Sāmans were created."
As if it were an old cart, or a mule that carries its load by breaking down at every step— for it indeed carries each back individually—
on that [cart] one should either sing the *pṛṣṭha* hymns or chant these *vyāhṛtis*: "The cow, the horse, the goat, the sheep, rice, and barley."
The *rathantara* is the cow;
the *bṛhat* is the horse; the *vairūpa* is the goat.
The sheep are the Vairāja;
rice grains are the Śakvarī; barley is the Revatī.
Those [beings] which are created from this essence, he places them within it;
he causes them to swell.
By means of that swelling, flavorful essence, the chant becomes successful.
If he should desire rain, having first uttered, "The waters, the wind; the waters, the wind," he should chant the Vāmadevya hymn.
Thus indeed it rains for him. Moreover, the Vāmadevya is indeed cattle.
He becomes possessed of cattle who, knowing thus, chants the Vāmadevya.
That indeed is well-chanted for the Brahman-sāman when one chants it after having brought it into correspondence with the worlds of Brahman.
It sprouts seven times for the Brahman-sāman.

In the seventh world is Brahman. He recited four times: "Vāsor māndāno vā" (The exhilarating one of the dwelling, or). He recited three times: "Āndhāsā bhī vātsān no vā" (From the pressed juices, or from the offspring of Vatsa, or).
These amount to seven. 35-331 (Ed.:
1,334) |p1 There is a world named Upodaka, in which this fire [resides].
In whom Vāyu is the abode of Truth;
in whom the Sun is unconquered;
in whom Varuṇa is the wise observer.
In which [world] there is Pradyu, where death [prevails];
in which there is Rocana, where hunger [prevails];
Viṣṭapa is the seventh, the world of Brahman, in which this Brahman [resides].
With the seventh shoot, he should place himself in the Viṣṭapa, the world of Brahman;
and likewise the sacrificer. Moreover, it causes him to go there.
In that he touches it as it were, he thereby endows it with its own dear abode.

When Sucitta Śailana used to chant, "O you who are like a cow seeking her calf," he caused [the sacrificer] to ascend to the world of Brahman; he endows him with his own dear abode. Thus, when it is complete, he indeed endows it with its own dear abode.
And that leads him to this world; by means of it, he reaches a full lifespan. 36-332 (Ed.:

Now, as for this *kāleya* [chant]: one should sing it as if spreading it out, as if causing it to be resolved, as if not confining it. Regarding this *kāleya*, the Brāhmaṇas of the Kurus used to deliberate thus in former times: "Would it be like a load of barley, or a load of beans, or a load of māṣa-beans? Such was their deliberation concerning this *kāleya*.
That [part] should be sung as if drawing it out.
Regarding this, some perform the *iḍā* for the *rathantara-sāman* as an upward extension, saying, "There is no *iḍā* for the performers.
But Śāṭyāyani said: "This *iḍā* is indeed thrown out; it is as if fallen away."
When approaching the *iḍā* at the very end, for one using the *bṛhat-sāman*, he should hold up the *dhaura* for the second *stotriya* verse.
Thus they do not depart from the form of the *bṛhat*.
Now, some indeed approach the *iḍā* of both the *rathantara-sāman* and the *bṛhat-sāman* as something raised upward, thinking, "The *iḍā* is unexhausted; it leads to heaven."
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "The *rathantara* is indeed Agni; the *vāmadevya* is Vāyu; the *naudhasa* is Indra."
The Viśve Devās [sing] the Kāleya.
Now, this very world is the heavenly world, and the Viśve Devās themselves are the gods.
Thus, they establish themselves in that heavenly world among the Viśve Devās.
If someone were to say of those who have performed it in that manner, "It will be thus" or "It will be so," then it would indeed be so.
Therefore, this *iḍā* should be drawn out to the very end for the sake of full life and so that this world may not be overturned. 37-333 (Ed.:
Now, this *brahman* is performed as the *saṃhita* at the beginning of the pressing (*savanamukha*). That which is the *brahman* is inherently praised;
yet, even though it is already praised, this further praise is performed when one takes up [the syllable] "Om" here.
That is this syllable, the Sun.
This is the unimpaired syllable of the threefold Veda.
When he takes up [the breath] with "Om," he thereby places that very Sun in his mouth.
Just as one might mix parched grains with honey, even so does he place essence into the *sāman* by means of this syllable;
he thereby causes it to swell.
Through that swelling and flavorful [essence], his chant becomes full of essence.
"The *sāman* sinks when it is being responded to," so say the Kurus.
"But when one takes up [the chant] above the *pratihāra*, that makes it rise.
Indeed, this *sāman* is sung over the *sāman*.
That indeed is well-sung:
when one sings a *sāman* upon a *sāman*, he should know this very thing thus: "I am singing this *sāman* upon a *sāman*," thinking, "By means of this, I shall attain preeminence among my own people.
Now, these two, the *uṣṇih* and the *kakubh*, should be sung without taking breath up to the *pratihāra*.
This metre is, as it were, shattered;
for the *uṣṇih* and the *kakubh* are the metres of man.
Now, while Śamastomī Bālāki was having his pupil Sāyaka Jānaśruteya chant the *udgītha* at his own sacrifice, he remarked:
"In such a manner indeed did this Jānaśruteya sing the *sāman*, that now his blood will surely flow forth.
Then, the followers of Ajina, while fighting, entered the sacrificial hall (*sadas*).
His staff fell down and caused blood to flow.
He said, "Now, how should one sing?
To him he said this: "One should not pronounce [the word] 'asṛk' (blood)."
One should chant only "dho.
One should not chant the entire third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) in a covered manner.
For if someone were to say of one who chants in this covered way, "This Udgātṛ has surely burnt himself and the sacrificer," then so indeed would it be.
One should illuminate it while saying "dṛṃhya" (be firm); for they praise [the act] with the words "dṛṃhīmān" (may he be firm).
Now, this is the Śyāvāśva [fire].
"Come hither, indeed, come hither!"—thus they sing these [verses].
This is speech;
speech is the *anuṣṭubh*.
"This should be said: 'May we be established through speech,'" [he thought].
Now, while Brahmadatta Caikitāneya was singing in that manner, Gaḍu Ārṣākāyaṇa addressed him from behind, saying:
"In this very way Dālbhya has sung for Śyāvāśva, so that his own evil shall mount upon him."
Then the other, having understood it, said: "In that very way indeed did Vāmadeva sing the Vāmadevya; he will move about as one who is harsh and without cattle.
Then Brahmadatta Prāsenajita [asked] Brahmadatta Caikitāneya...
(as in the edition).
The king of Kosala stood before him.
His son spoke as one from the east;
he said, "This man is indeed a pramaya."
"It is indeed fitting that I shall go again," he said.
He set out,
and then they brought him the Jaimava, his kinsman, from the Vailūnas.
He came to their assembly.
He stood up after the grass.
Formerly, he used to spring up.
Having given him much, he oppressed him.
Those two met together, and he said: "If it has come to this..."
"Come, let us both speak about this," [he said].
He replied: "The Gaḍūnas abandoned Śyāvāśva Ārcanānasa while he was carrying the sacrificial firewood; having left him behind, his rivals went to the heavenly world.
They called out to him with the words, 'O Śyāvāśva, come! O Śyāvāśva, come! Thus they summoned him.
"This one who is born [as a brother] is as if inferior.
When he sings "ai ho vā ehy ā," he thereby causes him to mount upon his own evil.
To him he said this: "He should sing only 'ai ho i yā.'"
"O ho" indeed is the name of Indra.
He who shines yonder is this very Indra;
and he is indeed that one after whom all the gods follow.
"Indeed, all his own people become followers of him who, knowing thus, sings the Śyāvāśva [sāman]," so it is said.
Now,
this Āndhīgava has its *nidhana* in the middle for the sake of stability.
Whatever in this sacrifice has been ill-chanted, ill-recited, or defective, that he thereby repairs. Now, this *kāva* [verse] sprouts five times;
for the *paṅkti* meter consists of five feet.
Cattle are fivefold;
the jagatī is cattle.
He thus extends these cattle among cattle.
"That is conducive to cattle," said Sucitta Śailana.
"He who, knowing thus, sings the Kāva [Sāman], becomes possessed of cattle; his lineage is not cut off from the family.
He explains that by "lineage" (tantrī), he means this very song.
Or rather, it is the pervasion of the heavenly world;
this Gāyatrī is indeed the earth, and the Triṣṭubh is the intermediate space.
That is the Jagatī.
By means of that third sprout, one ascends to the heavenly world.
"That is beneficial for cattle and leads to heaven," so he used to say.
He obtains both these desires.
Whoever knows the udder of the sacrifice milks the sacrifice when it has been offered.
The *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed the udder of the sacrifice. Its teats are the *gāyatra*, the *rathantara*, the *bṛhat*, and the *vāmadevya*.
One should chant the *prastāva* as if it were the *gāyatra*.
One should chant the *stobhas* as if they were the [verses] of the Rathantara;
one should ascend the *rohās* as if they were those of the Bṛhat;
the *dhiṃkāra* is the Vāmadevya.
The *yajñāyajñīya* [sāman] is performed by himself alone.
Indeed, it is this that the sacrificer milks from the sacrifice; having sacrificed, he indeed becomes more excellent.
It sprouts ten times for that [first one].
Six times for the two preceding ones.
Four times for the last one.
These become ten sprouts.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* is food.
That which burns yonder is indeed the Virāj.
In that very world of heaven they finally find firm support.
Now, one should sing the *ukthas* as if they were intermingled with the *chandas*.
For the hymns belong to the day;
then one should sing the night openly,
for the night is indeed hidden.
Regarding this, they say: "O Udgātṛ, have you sung the day in the night? Have you sung the night in the day?
He should reply: "Both," saying, "I have indeed sung the night in the day, and the day in the night.
For the day is manifest.
In that which he sings covered, he establishes a productive pair.
The night is indeed covered;
when he sings it openly, it is as if one were to place light in darkness—such is that.
Therefore, one should sing of the day with the form of the night, and of the night with the form of the day.
That indeed is well-sung.
Moreover, he sings while establishing day and night themselves within one another.
In that he sings of the day while it is manifest, he sings of it as concealed; therefore, this sun does not burn up everything here.
And in that he sings of the night while it is concealed, he sings of it as manifest; therefore, whatever exists here at night is perceived.
If one were to sing that [Sāman] while it is indeed concealed, there would be blinding darkness.
Now, the *rājānaḥ* are the *agniṣṭomasāmans*;
the sons of kings are the [sāmans] belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
The *viś* (the common people) are the meters.
Therefore, these three *sāmans* should be performed during the year.
Indeed, when the ruling power (*kṣatra*) is like the common people—that is, like a prince—it is prosperous.
Just as a kṣatriya might be accompanied by the common people like a prince, so is that [the Soma sacrifice].
Now, since these Sāmans are performed during the year, the singing of the Agniṣṭoma Sāmans follows from this.

Just as a king’s regalia consist of a tiger-skin rug, an antelope skin, a gem, gold, an elephant, a gold necklace, a mule-chariot, a horse-chariot, a golden plate, and a bronze vessel—such is this [Agniṣṭoma] the regalia of these Sāmans.

Therefore, one should sing only after having performed the chanting of the *agniṣṭomasāman*s; the others [the *stotras*] should be sung as they have been chanted, the others as they have been chanted. 43-339 (Ed.:
If two *soma* sacrifices should be performed simultaneously, one should commence the *prātaranuvāka* at the end of the night.
He who acts first wins the speech, he who acts first wins the deities, and he who acts first wins the meters; for the meters indeed comprise all the deities.
All the deities indeed desert them.
He should draw the *vasatīvarī* waters first;
for these *vasatīvarī* waters are indeed all the deities.
All the deities indeed abandon them. One should offer oblations when the fire is well-kindled; for Agni is all the deities.
Indeed, seeing all those deities, they sacrifice for the sake of overcoming the *chandas*.
One should offer in the *āgnīdhra* fire:
"To Saṃveśa, to Upaveśa, to the *gāyatrī* metre, to Overpowering, svāhā!"—thus one should sacrifice at the morning pressing.

At the midday pressing, he should offer with the formula: "To Saṃveśa, to Upaveśa, to the Triṣṭubh metre, to Overpowering—Svāhā! At the third pressing, he should offer with the formula: "To Saṃveśa, to Upaveśa, to the Jagatī metre, to Overpowering—Svāhā!
For by means of the metres, the gods indeed overcame the Asuras.
Those who press [the Soma] together act as if they were rivals; [the sacrificers] overcome them by means of the meters.
One should offer with the verses of Prajāpati.
Prajāpati is indeed all the deities.
All the deities indeed exclude them.
If they should desire, "May the Adhvaryu of these [priests] die," they should say to the Adhvaryu at the morning pressing, "Offer with the verses of Prajāpati.

If they should desire, "May the Hotṛ of these [priests] die," they should say to the Hotṛ at the midday pressing, "Offer with the verses of Prajāpati. If they should desire, "May the Udgātṛ of these [priests] die," they should say to the Udgātṛ at the third pressing, "Offer with the verses of Prajāpati."
The officiating priests have their respective stations in this way:
the *adhvaryu* is joined first;
his station is the morning pressing (*prātassavana*).
Then the Hotṛ:
his domain is the midday pressing. Then the Udgātṛ.
The third pressing is its abode;
they satisfy them according to their respective abodes.
If they should desire, "May the sacrificer among these die," they should say to the sacrificer, "Sacrifice with the verses of Prajāpati."
If they should desire, "May everyone indeed die," then everyone should offer at all the pressings.
Both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara are used;
for these two, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, are indeed Indra’s two bay horses.
The sacrifice is the chariot of the gods.
By means of Indra’s two bay horses and by means of the sacrifice, which is the chariot of the gods, he wins the race.
This, indeed, is the Rathantara.
"Then the *bṛhat* [sāman].
From this one and from that one—from the pair of today and tomorrow—they thus separate them.
"Forward for you, O strengths, reaching toward heaven"—this is the *ājya* chant for Agni.
A downward slope is the form of the deities; it is a form for overcoming. Thus, they indeed overcome them.

The *ābhīka*, the *abhinidhana*, the *abhīvarta*, and the *ābhīśava*—these are the *sāmans*; they are the form for overcoming. They indeed overcome those [enemies]. The *vihavīya*, the *sajanīya*, and Agastya’s *kayāśubhīya*—these are the *śastras*.
Then, by means of the *vihavīya* [verse], they invoke Indra alone among the deities; they thus win him over completely with the *sajanīya* [verse]. Indeed, the *rakṣases* followed after Agastya.
He desired, "May I slay the Rākṣasas.
He saw this *kayāśubhīya* litany;
with it, he struck down the Rākṣasas.
Verily, the *rakṣases* attend those who press the Soma together. Therefore, since there is the *kayāśubhīya* recitation, it is for the very purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*.
If the others should perform the *agniṣṭoma*, then they themselves should perform the *ukthya*.

one should then strive to master it."

If one among those who have been consecrated should die, they should cremate him, bind his bones in a cloth, and having purchased the Soma, they should consecrate and cause him to sacrifice together with whoever was his nearest relative.
For these men consecrate themselves by undertaking the same sacrifice, the same meritorious act;
it is through that very act that they bring about his release from debt.
They may perform this other rite:
having pressed the *soma* but without having drawn the other cups, they should place the sacrificial fees upon the corners of the altar and chant the Stotra on the *mārjālīya* fire-altar;
they chant with the verses of Arbuda.
The serpent is indeed *arbuda*.
With these [verses], he struck off the dead skin.
Indeed, those who perform [rites] for the deceased are as if dying themselves.
By means of these [verses], they strike away the very skin of the deceased.
They chant on three verses;
for the world of the fathers is three steps from here.
They cause him to go to the world of the fathers.
They chant while facing away;
they thus cause him to go away to yonder world.
The *yāma* chant is used;
they cause him to go to the world of the twins (*yamaloka*).
The *sāman* is neither preceded by a *prastāva* nor followed by a *pratihāra*.

Again they traverse the path.
The entire hymn of praise is unmeasured,
for that world is indeed unmeasured.
By this very means, they approach this world.
Regarding this, they say: "The *pavamāna* chants should consist of the *trivṛt* stoma;
the subsequent stotras should consist of the *saptadaśa* stoma."

The *trivṛt* [stomas] are indeed the vital breaths. Those who perform [the rites] for one who has died are deprived of their vital breaths. Therefore, in that the *pavamāna* [laudations] are *trivṛt*, they are thereby made complete through the vital breaths.
The subsequent stotras consist of seventeen verses.
Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold;
Prajāpati is the leader to the world of heaven.
"He who is the leader to the heavenly world, may he lead me to the heavenly world.

the subsequent stotras should be threefold (*trivṛt*).
Indeed, they seek the one who calls out as their mouth.
Just as with the first [verse], so too should he call out "hitherward" (arvāṅ); such is that. The subsequent [verses] are threefold.
The *trivṛt* [stomas] are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Thus, they go forth having actually ascended into the vital breaths.
Regarding this, they say: "Verily, those who perform [the funeral rites] for one who is dead fail with respect to the out-breath and the in-breath. 5-344 (Ed.: 1,346)
They draw the cups beginning with that for Mitra and Varuṇa.
Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breath and in-breath.
By means of the out-breath and the in-breath, they indeed prosper thereby.
Regarding this, they say: "One should not perform the *astha* sacrifices before a year has passed.
If they were to cause the *astha* sacrifices to be performed before a year has passed, they would incur harsh and blood-stained speech."
The *asthāni* offerings should indeed be performed at the end of the year.
[One does so] thinking, "Lest we encounter harsh and blood-stained speech.
Now, however, they say that one should carry away the *asthāni* to the very place where the others descend for the *avabhṛtha* bath.
For indeed, their application and liberation are equal;
one is liberated in accordance with that very liberation of theirs. 6-345 (Ed.:
If they should rise from the sacrificial session prematurely, they should perform a Viśvajit Atirātra sacrifice with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras and with the gift of all one's possessions (sarvavedasa).
The Pṛṣṭhas are indeed the seasons; the seasons are the year.
In this very way, the year is attained for them.
Then, they employ [the sacrifice] beyond [its limit] by means of those sacrificial gifts which they give.
Furthermore, they say: "They should sacrifice by means of that very Vaiśvānara Atirātra which is the introductory (prāyaṇīya) one."
Day and night, as they revolve, attain the year.
By that very means, the year is attained for them.
Now, those sacrificial gifts which they give, by means of them they extend beyond [the year].
If the sun should set while one round (*paryāya*) remains unstudied, they should chant for the Hotṛ with fifteen verses, and for the others with five verses each.

If the sun should set while two rounds remain unstudied, they should chant first for the Hotṛ and the Maitrāvaruṇa, and later for the Brahman and the Acchāvāka. If the sun should set while all the rounds remain unstudied, they should chant for the Hotṛ with six verses, and for the others with three verses each.
They should perform this for all [the gods] except for these [three].
Having approached the eleven [verses] consisting of single *ṛc*s, they should recite the twelfth as an *aindra* triplet; the whole [should be] a triplet.
Thus indeed did Mauñja Sāhaśravasa act.
Kapiṣvana Bhauvāyana said to him: "Alas, Mahāśāla Śrāvase, you have gone forth with the cows of Agavāyana!
Your offspring will become insane."
"But she will indeed be endowed with spiritual luster," he said.

"If you had addressed me," he continued, "you would have approached these twelve single-verse hymns; you would have chanted the *rāthaṃtara* *saṃdhi* on this triplet beginning with 'Agni, O Vivasvat, at dawn,' which is dedicated to Indra.
By using the word 'Agni,' you would not have departed from the form belonging to Agni."
With "To the Dawn," he offers the oblations for the dawn;
with "In harmony with the Aśvins," those for the Aśvins.
His offspring will not become insane.
"But she would indeed have been radiant with spiritual luster," he said.
Moreover, he said to him, "Even when they are merely bathing, let them not call out to you. He replied, "That was not recited [by me]."
Then some of them hid even though the sun had already risen.
On the following night, they gathered together and praised [the earth], saying, "This indeed is that which has surpassed us before.
They were successful.
They chant on *gāyatrī* verses;
for from the *gāyatra* pressing, the soma overflows.
They chant on verses addressed to the Maruts.
For the soma libation exceeds when it is accompanied by the Maruts; they chant upon verses containing the word "sucking" (dhayadvatīṣu),
so that the cows themselves suckle this [soma] for the Maruts.
The stotra lasts as long as the stotra of the *ājya* [śastra]. Whatever exceeds that, they arrange for that very thing.
If the Soma should be left over from the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), they should chant before the *ārbhava-pavamāna* with the verse: "O Sūrya, you are great indeed."
They chant on *bṛhatī* verses;
for from the *bārhata* pressing, the soma is left over.
They chant on verses addressed to Sūrya.
For the Soma-pressing belongs to Sūrya, and the Soma overflows.
As long as is the chant of the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, so long is the chant [of this]. Precisely that which overflows, they arrange accordingly.
If the Soma should remain over after the third pressing, they should perform the Ukthya.
If the Ukthya should remain over, they should draw the Ṣoḍaśin cup.
If the Ṣoḍaśin should remain over, they should perform the Atirātra.
The night does not indeed exceed him in his own desire.
One who desires cattle should cause cattle to exceed [the norm];
one who is a Vaiśya possessing cattle should cause cattle to exceed [the norm].
They chant the Bṛhat-sāman in Triṣṭubh verses.
The Triṣṭubh is indeed the kṣatra (the ruling power),
and the kṣatriya is indeed the giver of cattle.
"May he who is the giver of cattle bestow cattle upon us. 9-348 (Ed.:
1,351) |p1 They perceive [the result] as something excessive.
Then, if it should be said, "There is no *anuvaṣaṭkāra*," one should offer those [portions] as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*), pour them out again, and offer them at the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
But if there should still be a surplus, it should be set down together with the jar.

If it should rain while the King [Soma] is being pressed, he should say: "The drop has gone down to the drop; of you, O drop, who are endowed with power (*indriya*), full of sweetness, far-seeing, and invited—I, being invited, partake. May Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma. Regarding this, they say: "Indeed, this entire immortal food, which is water, comes to this world.
Thinking, "Truly, this entire immortal food has come to this world," one should partake [of the Soma].
That itself is the expiation in that case.
If they should overturn the cup, he should sit covering it with the upper garment;
for thus the King becomes united with the *ṛc*.
The Adhvaryu, having scattered that [grain] back and taken it up again, should go [to the Sadas].

If, however, it is for the purpose of purification (mārjya), he should take it from the Sadas and hand it over toward whichever Dhiṣṇya altar is nearest to it. Having purified it, they should prepare the other cups in the same manner as that one.
That itself is the expiation in that case.

If the pitcher should break at the morning pressing, they should perform the *bṛhatī* verses addressed to Viṣṇu at the midday pressing, [reciting]: "Viṣṇu brought all those... 10-349 (Ed.: 1,351); 1-350 (Ed.: 1,352). If the pitcher should break at the morning pressing, they should perform the *bṛhatī* verses addressed to Viṣṇu at the midday pressing.

If the pitcher should break at the midday pressing, they should perform the *anuṣṭubh* verses addressed to Viṣṇu, beginning with "Pavasva vājasātaye," during the *ārbhava-pavamāna* chant. If the pitcher should break at the third pressing, having performed the *ukthya*, they should perform the *brahmasāman* upon these verses beginning with "yat somam indra viṣṇave.
Indeed, that from which the pitcher breaks is a flaw in the sacrifice.
They acquire it by means of the Viṣṇu-sacrifice itself; for that [sacrifice] of his is accompanied by the gods. The Sāman has the *vaṣaṭ*-call as its *nidhana*.
Both of these are indeed fires: this earth and the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
It is into this kindled [fire] that the offering is made by means of the *sāman*.
The *Śrāyantīya* is the *brahmasāman*.
In this way, they indeed mix it thoroughly.
They chant the Yajñāyajñīya on Anuṣṭubh verses.
The Yajñāyajñīya is indeed speech.
Speech is the *anuṣṭubh*.
By means of speech, they thus bring this [rite] to fulfillment.
The *vāravantīya* is the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
The Vāravantīya is indeed power and vigor;
by means of power and vigor they thus cause this [sacrifice] to prosper.
One should also seek to repair what has been torn.
Now, if he should desire [the Soma] to be present,
he should say, "Bring another jar.
Having spread out a filter with its fringes pointing northward, he should place a splinter [of wood] upon it and then bring in the King [Soma].
Then he should pour [the drops] from the Āgrayaṇa cup; then he should pour out the Ekadhana waters—
one or two, as much as he deems sufficient.
That itself is the expiation in that case. 11-350 (Ed.:
1,353) |p1 If the *dhruva* ladle should spill, one should scrape it clean, turn it face down, and fill it up with whatever is pure.
If the Āgrayaṇa cup should be drawn first, one should fill it up from the others.
For the Āgrayaṇa cup is the self,
and the others are the vital breaths.
The self arises from the vital breaths, or the vital breaths arise from the self.
This [self] lies encompassing all the pressings for the very sake of the integrity of the sacrifice. If the speckled butter should spill, one should pour it back out and take it up again.
If a dog should lick [the oblation] or if it should become unfit for sacrifice, one should pour it out onto the *uttaravedi*, purify [the vessel], and take another [portion] with the *sruk*.
If they should lift up a *camasa* that has been set down as a *nārāśaṃsa*, he says: "It is not offered for consumption, nor is it consumed for offering.
One should pour that [remnant] between the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the ashes.
"Of the shaken and the unshaken, of the offered and the unoffered, of the drunk and the undrunk Soma—O Indra and Agni, drink the pressed [juice], Svāhā! With this *yajus* some pour it out.
"Silently indeed," Śāṭyāyani used to say.
Having rinsed the cup, he should seek to obtain [the remainder] of whichever draught the Adhvaryu would proceed with.
Verily, they destroy the breath of him whose cup they destroy. The cup is indeed the breath;
thus, by means of the breath itself, they restore him.
If they should lift [the cups] up, he should say, "Lift them up again together! and then they should lift them up following that very one.
If they should chant the *udgītha*, they might even cut them off from those very [singers].
If they should consume [the soma] around, he should seek their invitation (*upahava*).
If the sun should set while he is moving outside the sacrificial altar, or if they should cause him to be heard [by the call], he should seek an invitation (*upahava*) from the *gṛhapati*.
Prajāpati indeed is the *gṛhapati*;
it is through Prajāpati that he thus invites him.
If the pressing-stone should break, they should chant the *brahmasāman* of the radiant Maruts.
Or, if there should be another stone, they should press with that.
If they cannot find such a one, they should fashion one from *audumbara* wood or *pālāśa* wood and press with that.
That itself is the expiation in that case. 12-351 (Ed.:
1,354) |p1 If they should carry off the un-purchased King Soma, they may wish to purchase it back.
They might even run toward a mountain;
the consecrated one (dīkṣita) should remain seated for that long.
If they should carry off the purchased [Soma], they should press it having obtained any [Soma] whatsoever.

By the very same means by which he was purchased in the previous purchase, by that very same means this one becomes purchased for him. However, something must be given to the Soma-seller; [he says], "Lest our pressing be ruined.
If they should not find him, they should press *babhru* fibers from the *phālguna* plants.
Indra struck Vṛtra with his thunderbolt.
The Soma that flowed out from him became those brown-husked *phālguna* grains;
and that which flowed from the extraction of the omentum became those red-husked grains.
Therefore, only tawny cotton-seeds are to be pressed, for they are more pure;
they say that because they are not of the nature of Asuras, they are not to be pressed.
Indeed, this world was formerly among the Asuras.
The gods, having conquered it, took it for themselves.
Therefore, one should press [the Soma] while it is still fresh.
If they cannot find that, they should press *ūtīka* plants.

Indra, having struck Vṛtra with his thunderbolt, thought, "I have not slain him," and he entered into the *ūtīkas*. They found protection for him; indeed, the protection of one whose king is carried off perishes.
They indeed find succor for him. When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its vital essence that flowed out became the *ūtīkā* stalks.
Thus, when they press the *ūtīkā* stalks, they are pressing the sacrifice itself visibly before them.
If they should not find him,
they should press white *śyāmāka* grains.
King Soma, indeed, when he came to this world, dwelt right there;
that very [place] is his *nyaṅga*.
It is him whom they press at that time.
If they should not find it, they should press the *parṇa* leaf.
Indeed, when the king Soma was carried away by the Suparṇa bird, that which was his feather (*parṇa*) fell down; that very thing became the *parṇa* tree.
That indeed is its corresponding part.
They press that very [Soma] at that time.
If they should not find it, they may press whatever plants are available.
Indeed, when Suparṇa brought King Soma, he tore him apart; those drops of his that fell became these very plants.
All plants, indeed, are full of Soma;
that very part of him is deficient;
they press him [the Soma] for that very purpose.
One should pour fresh milk (*pratidhuk*) at the morning pressing, boiled milk at the midday pressing, and curds at the third pressing.
They consume that very Soma directly when it is milk,
for milk is indeed the essence of plants.
One should give five sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
The sacrifice is fivefold;
in as much as is the measure of the sacrifice, in that very [measure] they thus find firm support.
Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, he should undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*) again.
He should give whatever he intended to give [at the first initiation].
That itself is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) in that case. 14-353 (Ed.: 1,355)
That which has been chanted before its time is as if it were not chanted at all;
that which has been over-chanted is a bad chanting.
That which is [performed] at the present time is the *stuta*.
If they were to chant before that, they should either introduce the subsequent *stotra* with as many verses as there are in it, or they should chant with verses containing more syllables.
In this way, they place what was deficient into what is redundant, for the sake of pairing and procreation.

If they should praise with fewer verses than the subsequent *stotra*, or if they should not praise at all with that many, or if they should praise with verses containing fewer syllables, they place what is deficient into that which is redundant, or what is redundant into that which is deficient, for the sake of pairing and procreation. He who knows thus is procreated through a productive union.
If they should praise [the *stotra*] earlier than that, they should perform the *agniṣṭomasāman* on the third day;
thus they close two gaps in the sacrifice, while one [verse] remains in its own proper place.
If they should over-praise, they should make the *svāra* tone the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
The *svāra* tone is deficient;
thus, when they over-praise, they cause this [deficiency] to overflow.
That which is praised with one [verse] is the Virāj; that is the hairy [skin]. That which is [praised] with two [verses] are the two breasts.
That which is [praised] with three [verses] is the milking.
For the milker is indeed the third;
what [is done] with four [verses] are the udders;
what [is done] with five is the milking.
The milker is indeed the fifth;
by the sixth or the seventh [verse], it has been sung beyond measure.
Then Prajāpati desired to procreate.
He performed austerity.
He reflected: "Come now, let me produce a foundation."
"Then those creatures whom I shall create will find their support in this very [world]; they will not be consumed by fire while wandering without a foundation.
He generated this world, the intermediate world, and that world.
Having generated these three worlds, he exerted himself.
He heated them. From them, being thus heated, three pure essences (*śukra*) arose: Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, and Āditya from the sky.
He heated those pure essences once again.
From them, as they were being heated, three pure essences (*śukra*) emerged: the *Ṛgveda* from Agni, the *Yajurveda* from Vāyu, and the *Sāmaveda* from Āditya.
He heated these pure essences once again.
From them, as they were being heated, three pure essences emerged: "bhūḥ" from the *Ṛgveda*, "bhuvaḥ" from the *Yajurveda*, and "svar" from the *Sāmaveda*.

That indeed is the radiance (*śukra*) of the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*). This entire world is just this much. Whoever knows thus, he gains that world which belongs to one who knows the threefold knowledge. 16–355 (Ed.: 1,357)
Prajāpati, having created the sacrifice, indeed ascended upwards.
He said to the gods, "With this threefold Veda, you must extend the sacrifice."
Those gods, sacrificing with this threefold Veda, struck away evil and came to know the heavenly world.

They said: "Now, since we, sacrificing with this threefold Veda, have struck away evil and have come to know the heavenly world, what if this sacrifice of ours were to meet with failure today? With what might we heal it?"
Prajāpati said to them: "Whatever brilliance, sensory power, vigor, and essence belonged to this triple Veda, I shall now gather it all together.
Giving him these *vyāhṛtis*, he said: "With these, you shall heal him.
If the sacrifice should suffer a failure regarding the *ṛc* verses, you should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire with the words: "bhūs svāhā!"
That itself is the expiation in that case. Now, if [the sacrifice] fails on account of the Yajus formula, one should offer with "Bhuvaḥ svāhā" in the Āgnīdhra fire;
that itself is the expiation in that case.
Now, if by chance [the fire] goes out, one should offer into the Āhavanīya with the words "Svaḥ svāhā";
that itself is the expiation in that case.
Now, if it should go out during the *iṣṭi* or animal sacrifices, or during the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should offer into the Anvāhāryapacana fire with the words "Bhuvaḥ svāhā."
That itself is the expiation for that case.
Now, if [the source] is not remembered—thinking, "From where was this born?"—one should offer an oblation into the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā.
That itself is the expiation for all of that.
Just as a physician would heal a fracture by joining joint to joint, even so does one who knows this heal all that [is broken].

Now, if one who does not know this performs an expiation for it, it is as if one were to join a fracture with what is already fractured, or as if one were to place poison upon a wound; such is that act.
Therefore, one should indeed have an expiation performed only by one who possesses such knowledge.

Regarding this, they say: "Since the office of the Hotṛ is performed with the Ṛgveda, that of the Adhvaryu with the Yajurveda, and the Udgītha with the Sāmaveda, then by what is the office of the Brahman performed?
One should reply: "By means of this triple Veda.
Therefore, one should appoint as Brahman priest whoever he considers to be most learned in the Vedas (brahmiṣṭha).
He indeed becomes a Brahman who knows this.

Regarding this, they say: "Men press [the Soma] during the first fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), and the gods during the latter fortnight (*aparapakṣa*); yet those performing the sacrificial session (*sattra*) sit pressing it during both the first and the latter fortnights. Now, whoever presses [Soma] together with even a single man, him indeed they despise.
Then, what [is the case] for those who are honored by both gods and men?
How is it that for them this [honor] becomes unshared?
He should say: "In the bright fortnight, men cause that world to increase, they cause it to swell, and they cause it to be reproduced."
During the fortnight of the waxing moon, the sacrificer should know: "I am increasing that world, I am nourishing that world, I am procreating that world;
I am the follower of the gods.
For he who is the follower of one who is superior does not come to harm.

The gods indeed cause this world to increase during the waning fortnight; they cause it to swell; they cause it to be born. During the waning fortnight, the sacrificer should know: "I am increasing this world here; I am swelling it; I am causing it to be born.
He is the one who follows the lineage of men.
He who indeed follows after the superior does not come to harm.
Now Bhāllabeya used to say: "In the dark fortnight, the gods cause this world to increase; they cause it to swell; they cause it to be born."
"Therefore, the earlier offspring—the cattle, the plants, and the trees—wither away, while later ones are established as ever more beautiful.
Knowing this, he spoke thus.

Regarding this, they say: "When they consider a day to be one of Rathāhnī, or a river, or a mountain-pass, or a place where there is no joint libation (*asaṃsava*), yet many performers of a sacrificial session (*sattrin*) sit together in a common hall pressing the Soma—if they think, 'We are sacrificing separately here,' then they press the Soma together."
But if they think, "Let us cause this householder to sacrifice," then they become excluded from the sacrifice.
How is it that for them that [sacrifice] does not become performed separately, and how is it that it is not a *saṃsu*?
He should say: 19-358 (Ed.: 1,360).

King Soma is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Now, when they have pressed King Soma with the pressing-stones in the oblation-hall (*havirdhāna*) and draw the various cups (*graha*), choose the various *pravara* priests separately, and sacrifice separately, by that very act their sacrifice becomes separate.
Moreover, because this deity, though being one and the same, is established separately among various creatures, for that reason it is not a joint pressing (*asaṃsuta*).
Indeed, he who knows the joint pressing (*saṃsava*) in the context of a joint pressing overcomes the two who are pressing together.
This very wind which blows here—that indeed is the joint pressing in the joint pressing.
For all the gods follow after this [wind].
Therefore, in whichever direction it blows, in that same direction the plants and trees bend down after it.
This very [wind] is indeed the waters.
For when he desires it, then rain stands [in the air].
That very space between them is the interval; that same river becomes a mountain-breaker for the sake of non-mingling.

Therefore, indeed, one who knows this may also undergo consecration even when there is a sneeze. He surely overcomes those two who are pressing the Soma together. He should worship this deity with the formula: "Be auspicious; I fall down before you; homage be to you; do not harm me; let him who hates me meet with misfortune."
Whoever indeed hates one who knows thus meets with misfortune. 20-359 (Ed.:
1,361) *Avakīrṇaprāyaścitta* (Bar: 360; Ed.: 3,362) |c360 (Ed.: 1,362)
Regarding this, they ask: "In how many ways does he who spills [the oblation] enter?
One should say: "In four ways.
For indeed, he who spills enters in four ways: Indra with his strength, the Maruts with his breath, Bṛhaspati with his spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and Agni with all the rest.
Now, if the *aśukra* remains over,
this is the expiation for it:
having kindled the fire on the night of the new moon, having strewn grass around it and poured water around it, he should offer these two oblations.
"I am beset by desire, I am beset by desire; O Desire, to Desire, svāhā!
I am assailed by desire, I am assailed by desire; O Desire, to Desire, svāhā! Having thus spoken, let him join his palms in reverence and stand before [the fire] three times.
"May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra sprinkle me; may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me; may this Agni sprinkle me with long life and with strength; may he grant me a long life.
When he says, "May the Maruts sprinkle me," he thereby gives breath back to him who knows thus.
When he says, "May Indra [sprinkle me]," he thereby gives strength back to him who knows thus.

When he says, "Bṛhaspati has united," Bṛhaspati himself bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) upon him who knows thus. When he says, "Agni has united," Agni himself endows him with all other things by which, when being scattered, one might be deprived. He recites the mantra three times.
These three worlds exist.
He who [performs this] attains these three worlds, reaches his full lifespan, strikes away evil, and goes to the heavenly world. 21-360 (Ed.:
Now, it is said that the performers of a sacrificial session (sattrins) belonging to Naimiṣa, with Ayasthūṇa as their householder, were engaged in a long sacrificial session.
While they were so engaged, Mahendra, intending to frustrate them, crushed their sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in the form of a monkey.
Now, Śitibāhu Aiṣakṛta was their Adhvaryu priest and a learned scholar.
He indeed recognized this pure essence, the swelling sap of the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), as the expiation for everything by means of these *vyāhṛtis*: "bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ.
These *vyāhṛtis* are indeed the expiations for all [transgressions].
Just as that ocean is infinite, shoreless, inexhaustible, so too are these *vyāhṛtis*—heaven and earth, and all these worlds—inexhaustible.
Brahmatva (Bar: 362; Ed.: 1,364) |c362 (Ed.:
1,364) |p1 "Unmilked, infinite, and boundless," [it says].
Now, that which is "bhūḥ" is this world;
that which is "bhuvaḥ" is this intermediate space;
and that which is "svar" is yonder world.
These indeed are the *vyāhṛtis*; these are the deities.
"These deities are these *vyāhṛtis"—this was said by a monkey to Śitibāhu Aiṣakṛta Naimiṣeya when he, being learned in this, had stepped upon a sacrificial cake.
He said, "Having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter, do you take it away or offer it?"
He said, "If you have indeed recited it in this way and that way, then a monkey will tear apart the sacrificial cake; [tell me] the expiation for that.
He said, "In that case, may I become even wealthier than before, since I have recited it. Either bring the expiation for what is unknown, or I shall offer it myself.
"I shall bring it," he said. "Do not offer it yourself."
And he indeed took it away.

Thus, for whomsoever there is a Brahman priest who knows this, his sacrifice inclines toward the north from the south; for whomsoever there is a Brahman priest who knows this, and whoever else knows this, his sacrifice concludes inclining toward the north from the south. 23-362 (Ed.: 1,364)
JB 2.1 | Speech is these *pṛṣṭha* chants.
They disjoin this [chant];
they distribute it.
Having reached the first day, it becomes the *rathantara*.
This very earth;
speech indeed is the *rathantara*;
it is this [earth] that speaks.
On reaching the second day, it becomes the *bṛhatī*, as it has been said: "That speech which the lord speaks.
For that [speech] is heard from afar.
On reaching the third day, it becomes the *vairūpā*, as this speech [is used] horizontally: "Come here! Go away!"
"Bring it, serve it, eat it, drink it!
On reaching the fourth day, it becomes the Virāj.
One should sit silently.

This indeed is the sovereignty of speech: that which consists in sitting silently; for it is this very [power] which they seek to discern in the leader when he sits in silence. Having reached the fifth day, that [speech] becomes the Śakvarī, by which one who is commanded is able [to act].
Having reached the sixth day, that [verse] becomes the *revatī*, by which food is bestowed.
It should not be consumed month after month.
This is the ancestral tradition of Leḷibha, which the Leḷibhas speak as this speech.
"Indeed, he spoke this yesterday, this the day before, and this the previous year.
Alas, he speaks the same speech; alas, it does not pass him by.
This is the significance of the fact that they perform the *pṛṣṭha* days month after month. (1)
JB 2.2 |va Then, as if having remained silent, she would utter whatever is auspicious and meritorious.
vb "She has indeed uttered it! Oh, she has uttered it! [they would say].
Thus, as for the fact that they perform the *pṛṣṭha* stotras above the year:
with the *rathantara*, he indeed makes [the embryo] cry out; with the *bṛhat*, he pours forth the seed; with the *vairūpa*, he establishes the embryos;
with the *vairāja*, he brings them to birth; with the *śakvarī* verses, he causes them to grow; and with the *revatī* verses, he provides nourishment.
It is given. Wherefrom, then, will it be born month after month?
Indeed, they say of that embryo which falls away month by month, "It has miscarried."
Just as internal embryos might fall away, or as desirable plants might wither away once they have been cut down, even so it is when they perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants month after month.

Now, as when one who has carried [the fire] for a year gives birth to a fetus at the proper season, they would gather ripe herbs and fulfill their desires from them—even so it is when they perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants after the year. Now Citra Gāṅgyāyani used to say: "This [fire-altar] is a cow that yields much milk; it is the *pṛṣṭhas* that cause her to flow."
Who will seek to sustain them for their daily trembling?

Indeed, these do not yield milk when the [Dasha-ratra] has not been arranged; nor do they yield milk after being arranged at the end of the ten-night period, unless they have been encompassed by the Gāyatrī.

Just as one might milk [cows] by pulling them down with ropes from a cart, so do these [days] yield their milk when they are arranged above in the ten-night period, having been surrounded by the Gāyatrī.
Just as one would approach [them], so is that three-day period which has the Gāyatra at its beginning; just as one would place [something] upon [them], so is that.

If it has the *gāyatrī* in the middle, it is just as if one were to milk [the cow] after having already removed [the calf]; so it is when it has the *gāyatrī* at the end. Therefore, one should approach [the sacrifice] from above.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "He who is this moon is indeed the year, he is Prajāpati, he is..."
"Month"—
this [year] is indeed as much as a month;
having reached this [month], it indeed returns again.
He rises for fifteen nights and descends for fifteen. Those [nights] which fill up, he rises during them; and those which diminish, he descends during them.
As he is being filled, he goes to that world.
Having been touched by that world, he becomes food. Whatever is savory for him there, he relishes that; having departed, he comes to this world.
He enters these waters and these plants.
Having entered these waters and plants, and having deposited himself within these waters and plants, he goes to that world while being filled up. 3.

In this very manner, as he proceeds again, he completes the year. Indeed, whatever one obtains in twelve years, that same amount he obtains in a single year— he who, knowing thus, undertakes the *pṛṣṭha* chants month by month.
They undertake these four *abhiplava* periods.
There are twenty-four nights for them;
the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
Thus, after that year, for them there is an attainment month by month throughout the year.
They enter upon the *pṛṣṭhya* as the fifth;
thus, after that year, for them the *pṛṣṭha* days are entered upon month by month.

Now Mahittha Śainmiṣi used to say: "As for this one they call 'the unasked, the one without a turban,' who wraps himself around as the piercer of every clan— this very [rite] is indeed that unasked one without a turban,
which is the six-day period (ṣaḍaha) from which the pṛṣṭhya has been removed."
Should they, while performing only the *stomas* of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, pay heed to them?
Or rather, having approached these five *abhiplava* days, should they approach the *pṛṣṭhas* only after them?
Yonder sun was here at the beginning, where this *cātvāla* pit now is.
He scorched all this world.
The gods were afraid of his burning.
They said, "This one will surely burn up everything here. "Let us carry him upward," they said.
They carried him upward in six months.
They placed him upon the twenty-first, the Viṣuvat day.
He, being thus placed upon the twenty-first, the Viṣuvat day, shines forth.
Therefore, he belongs to both these sets of worlds: those that are above this [world] and those that are below that [world].

At the Viṣuvat. Because it belongs to both [classes of days] at the Viṣuvat, therefore it is called the Viṣuvat. Just as all the spokes are gathered together in the nave of a chariot wheel, even so all the worlds are gathered together in this one.
Now, some perform these very six-day periods as upward-extended after the Viṣuvat day.
Just as they perform them prior to the Viṣuvat, so too do they perform them as directed away from it.
For the heavenly world is indeed turned away.

"Let us ascend this heavenly world in a forward direction. "If we were to descend in a backward direction, that would be a descent; therefore, let us not descend. Now, those who proceed in that manner while saying, "Thus it is not descended," [fall]. Therefore, those who proceed in that way...
The worlds are directed hitherward from the sun; they indeed attain those very worlds.

Even if they perform [the rites] for many years, they nevertheless attain those very worlds. Now, those who perform these six-day periods both forward and backward—they indeed attain both these kinds of worlds.
"They attain [him] as he goes away and as he comes hither.
He brooded over this world from close at hand.
They enclosed him from below with wind;
by that they appeased him.
For he indeed carries these waters.
They extinguished him with water.
He scorched that world beyond. They surrounded him on the far side with the moon.
With that they pacified him.
Prajāpati, indeed, is the moon;
it was by means of Prajāpati that they then pacified him.
Indeed, this [wind] blows here in three worlds. From those three [come] the sun, and from those three, the stars; therefore they are the smallest, for these indeed are the twelve worlds of the gods.
Now, just as it is with the dawn, or rather, other worlds are exactly like this.
Knowing this world to be his dwelling place, he pierced it through with three [staves].
They placed the Svarasāman chants below.
He beheld that other world;
he pierced it upward with three strings;
they placed it above with the Svarasāman chants.
They found satisfaction in this here.
Because they found satisfaction (*aspṛṇvan*), that is the essence of the *svarasāman*s; hence their name *svarasāman*.
There are seventeen *svarasāman*s.
The seventeenfold is indeed food;
they thus place him upon food.
Moreover, Prajāpati is the seventeenfold.
By means of Prajāpati itself, they thus placed him upon the food-eating power.
For he, having been placed upon the food-eating power from of old, shines forth.
These Svarasāman days, being fifty-one in number, result in thirty-one Virājs; twenty-five...
Twenty-five below and twenty-five above. Now, that which is the fifty-first—in it, this one shines, having been placed as a superimposition after being arrayed in the middle.
Therefore, there is neither grief, nor cold, nor hunger, nor thirst; for him, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
Indeed, he who knows this does not hunger, does not thirst, and no obstacle whatsoever arises for him.
(JB 2.7) Just as a jar of clarified butter or a jar of honey might be carried away while its contents are held up by a net, so [is it].
Thus, this [sacrifice] is encompassed by these Virāj verses;
it is held fast by them, extending both eastward and westward.
Now, some perform these Svarasāman days as Agniṣṭomas, thinking, "We are performing this so that the Stoma becomes large."
They say: "Those three Agniṣṭomas indeed consist of thirty-six stotras;
twelve for one, twelve for another, and twelve for another—that makes thirty-six."
The *bṛhatī* indeed consists of thirty-six syllables;
the *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world;
it thus touches that [heavenly world].
"By means of the Bṛhat-sāman, let us go to this heavenly world," they said.
And so they indeed went; it was just as if one were to go without food.
Now, as for the fact that there are Ukthya-stotras...
The *ukthas* are indeed cattle;
cattle are food.
Just as one might approach a superior person who is greeting him with food, even so does he [the sacrificer] approach him [the deity] by means of these *ukthas*.
They proceed with the Svarasāman chants; for these two, the Viśvajit and the Abhijit, are indeed the very essence of the deities, and the Svarasāmans are food.
Just as one might place food on a slaughter-ground and offer it to a superior person,
even so does he offer this food to him by means of the Viśvajit and Abhijit sacrifices.
Moreover, this is indeed performed as a propitiatory rite.
The *agniṣṭoma-sāman* should be the *āgnimāruta-śastra*; this is the *viṣuvant*.
Whoever, having approached these three fires, burns them on both sides, will surely lie there consumed. Therefore, the *ukthas* occur in between.
The *ukthas* are indeed cattle;
cattle are food; with food they quieted him.
Having appeased him by means of the Nārmedha [sāman] alone, they finally approach it.
These two, moreover, are the Viśvajit and the Abhijit.
One [set of] Virāj verses consists of thirty-eight syllables, and another [set] consists of thirty-eight. This world is indeed the Abhijit, and yonder world is the Viśvajit;
the Svarasāman chants are cattle.
Therefore, when they praise with the Abhijit and then praise with the Svarasāmans, they establish cattle in this very world.
Then, because they praise with the Viśvajit after praising with the Svarasāmans, cattle [return] from that gift above.
They live. Now, for this very Vaiṣuvata day, there are ten twenty-five-fold stotras and two stotriya verses.
Then, those twenty-five stotras which [make] ten [sets of] five-and-twenty, that is the Mahāvrata.
By means of them, on his Vaiṣuvata day, the Mahāvrata becomes attained.
Now, those two stotriyas are the Āditya [stotra]; he is established upon this day.

Now, indeed, in former times they used to perform the Mahāvrata three times: on the Ārambhaṇīya day, on the Vaiṣuvata day, and on the Mahāvrata day. Of that very Ārambhaṇīya day, there are fourteen Pañcaviṃśa stotras.
And there are ten *stotriya* verses.
Then, those fourteen twenty-five-fold hymns (*stotra*) constitute the Mahāvrata;
by means of them, the Mahāvrata becomes attained on this introductory day (*ārambhaṇīya*).
Now, those which are the ten *stotriya* verses are the ten-syllabled *virāj*; the *virāj* is food. Thus, they proceed by means of this food until the *vaiṣuvata* day.
Now, those two *stotriya* verses which exceed the *viṣuvat* day are indeed food and drink.
For there are two forms of food: that which one eats and that which one drinks.
Just as one would go along eating and drinking, even so do they proceed by means of these two until the *mahāvratīya* day.
Of the day:
*vu*. They come to this heavenly world.
*vv*. This is the Mahāvrata day.
This very day of the Mahāvrata is indeed the heavenly world.
He who knows this thus—his Mahāvrata becomes threefold and he goes to the heavenly world.
Regarding this, they say: "The opening verse (*pratipad*) for this day should be *tam īṃ hinvanty agruvaḥ*. [And] *tam arkebhis taṃ sāmabhiḥ* is for the head; *tad id āsa bhuvaneṣu jyeṣṭham*.
Of the self.
With this day they proceed as if [thinking], "This and that.
Thereupon, indeed, Prajāpati [arose].
Then, indeed, this [Agni] is the father of all the deities;
that day is the father, and the other days are the offspring.
Just as a son, having come to his father, might call out, "Father! Father!", so is that.
Or rather, it possesses both forms:
“*tam*” (him) is indeed the form of a man, and “*agruvā*” (with the maiden) is that of a woman. Having become both of these, Prajāpati procreated.

Regarding this, they say: "This introductory verse (*pratipad*) belongs to the *abhyudita* [chanting]. But when the *yoga* has arrived, the introductory verse should be performed with the words: "Flow on, O foremost of speech.
For Prajāpati is indeed the mind.
Mind is indeed the foremost of speech;
thus they seize him by his own form.
He indeed becomes a pair.
"Flow on" (*pavasva*) is the form of the male; "of speech" (*vācaḥ*) is the form of the female.
Thus, this procreative union is brought about. He who knows thus is born through that union.
Therefore, this very path should be followed.
"Sing forth to him, O men! is the second [verse].
From that day, they do not depart.
The third [verse], "With flashing luster," is the manifest form of this day.
The fourth, "They urge him on, the maidens," is the *pratipad* (opening verse) which has already been recited; [they use it] so as not to let that [day] slip away.
"O Soma, win with the ancient [songs] and conquer!"—this hymn of ten verses comes into being.
Indeed, the seers, desiring prosperity, beheld this "rising" (upotthāna), the beloved of speech:
"And so make us more prosperous; and so make us more prosperous. With that they praised.
Then indeed they all prospered. All indeed prosper who, knowing thus, praise with this ten-verse hymn.
Regarding this, Śakti used to say: "The Virāj is to be sung: 'O Soma, conquer and win, O Pavamāna, great...'"
"Śrava! One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, *huṃbhā oi bhūr*.
Regarding this, they say: "This Virāj is indeed artificial; it is merely something to be recited. It tempts one toward the attainment of the full number."
"Om"—this very syllable is to be sung.
Indeed, this entire world is this syllable;
just as leaves might be pierced by a needle, so too are these worlds pierced by this syllable.
This [sāman] flows tenfold when it pierces through, a hundredfold when it flows, and a thousandfold when it flows.
Therefore, this very syllable should be sung; thus there is the *paryāsa*.
Whatever desire is contained in the *paryāsa*, that has not yet been attained; [thinking] "it shall be," [he sings].
These amount to twenty-five *stotriyas*.
Prajāpati is indeed the twenty-fifth; the Mahāvrata belongs to Prajāpati. Thus, it is performed as having the same characteristic mark as him. 10.
JB 2.11 |va| Now, Āryakacin used to say: "This entire day should indeed be made twenty-four-fold;
they should perform this single chant as twenty-five-fold. |vb|
This is indeed an ascent of a single *stotra* when they perform the entire [sacrifice] as a twenty-five-fold one. Thus, this *stotra* remains unascended.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "This is like the ruin of a house; for it is as if a single *stotriyā* verse were torn away."
If it is cut from two, or if it is cut from three—people find an expiation for that, or they do not; but what if it is cut from eleven? What is the expiation for that?

This day indeed belongs to a single deity, namely to Prajāpati alone. Verily, by means of this day, he serves Prajāpati. Therefore, this entire day should be performed as consisting of twenty-five [verses].
It has three hundred and sixty-two *stotriya* verses. Of these, the three hundred are the *virāj*,
and the sixty are the udder.
Now, those two [cups] are indeed the two breasts for the milking of this very day. 11.
The *ājya* offering consists of the *āprī* verse: "Well-kindled, bring hither to us... 12. *Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa* 2.12.
Wherever there is indeed an *aprī* hymn for clarified butter (*ājya*), that belongs to Prajāpati alone;
by means of it, they gratify Prajāpati.
"May [the gods] be able for us on earth"—this is for Mitra and Varuṇa.
In that same way, it becomes so.
For the undefined indeed belongs to Prajāpati;
on the day belonging to Prajāpati, that which has the same characteristic mark as that is performed.
The verse "Great is Indra by his might" belongs to Indra;
for this is the form of the *niṣka* amulet.
Therefore, they wear the *niṣka* amulet and a garland in front.
"‘That indeed was the eldest among the worlds’—this is the form of the chariot;
therefore, they stand having mounted it.
‘O thou praised by the great, O wielder of the stone’—this is the form of the elephant."
Therefore, they mount it as if from the side.
These indeed become great forms;
Prajāpati is indeed of a great form.
The Mahāvrata belongs to Prajāpati; it is performed with the same characteristics as that [sacrifice]. These forms stand un-purchased for him who knows thus.
"This [song] of yours, O you two, from this thought"—with these words, there is a hymn to Indra and Agni.
"O Indra and Agni, the ancient praise has been born like rain from a cloud.
They say, "It has been born," for it is indeed born on this day.
Just as here on earth eggs might burst open, even so do they burst open from this day.
"Listen to the caller's invocation, O Indra and Agni; accept the songs! As lords, cause our prayers to swell."
"O King of Men and Agni, do not deliver us to evil, nor to calumny;
do not subject us to reproach"—this is the repelling of evil itself. 12.
JB 2.13 |va:
"High is thy birth for the sake of the soma-juice"— these *gāyatrī* verses of the midday *pavamāna*, beginning with the word *andhas* (soma-juice),
belong to Prajāpati.
On the day belonging to Prajāpati, that which possesses the same characteristic mark is performed.
Among those [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa already stated.
Now, the Āmahīyava Sāman belonging to Prajāpati is performed on the day belonging to Prajāpati.
They thus cause the day itself to prosper through its form;
by means of that prosperity, it becomes successful for them among their own people. Then, having milked the *dohādohīya* [verse], one should milk it for the sake of this day's milking.
Now, *hariśrī* is the *nidhana*. Indeed, *śrī* (prosperity) is *hariśrī-nidhana*.
By means of this, Indra attained the prosperity of all the gods.
By this, they attain prosperity itself.
Those ten *stotriya* verses amount to a *gāyatrī*;
the *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
Food is the Virāj;
the Gāyatrī is the face of the meters. Thus, they place food for themselves at the very beginning.
"Being purified, O Soma, for the sake of support"—this *bṛhatī* verse possesses both forms. Indeed, this [verse] uplifts both *sāmans*.
Therefore, they perform it; those who use the *bṛhat-sāman* perform it, as do those who use the *rathaṃtara-sāman*.
"By the ancient common dwelling-place and by the supporting foundation," "Drink the Soma, O Indra, for you are placed within the womb of the Ṛcs"—
wherever this Bṛhatī is employed, indeed, Indra has no power over that [place], nor would he come to it. 13.
In those [verses], the Raurava is known as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
"The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is well-known; let us not cause an interruption," [they thought].
Now, the *arka* is either the *arkapuṣpa* (Arka flower) or food; its flower is that which is wild (*āraṇya*).
For it grows in the forest; [he does this] for the attainment of wild food.
Then, for the sake of satisfaction, [they offer] the *abhīśu*; indeed, they satisfy him with this.
Then follows the *āṅgirasa* chant, which has twenty-five syllables in its *nidhana*.
The Aṅgirases, desiring prosperity, performed austerities. They saw this Sāman;
with it, they praised.
Then indeed they all prospered. All indeed prosper who, knowing thus, praise with this *sāman*.
Its *nidhana* consists of twenty-five syllables.
Prajāpati is indeed twenty-fivefold;
the Mahāvrata belongs to Prajāpati, and thus it is performed as having that same characteristic.
Now, the Naudhasa is the well-known Brahman-sāman.
"The Brahman-sāman is well-known; let us not interrupt it.
Now, *pṛśni* is indeed food; [he sings it] for the attainment of food.
Then, the *rauhiṇaka*.
By means of this, Prajāpati indeed ascended to the desire of one-hoofed animals. Because he ascended to his desire (*kāma*), that is the reason for the *rauhiṇaka*’s name being *rauhiṇaka*.
He who knows thus ascends to the desire of animals.
Just as these wild animals and beasts are, so were these one-hoofed animals in the beginning.
He brought them to the village by means of these very "kiṭ-kiṭā" sounds of Rauhiṇaka.
That [sāman] has thirteen *nidhanas* for the attainment of the thirteenth month.
Or rather, it is endowed with eighty [syllables].
By this, they indeed cause him to breathe. Now, there is the Dairghaśravasa [chant]; the Dairghaśravasa is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
*vad*—now, [he sings] *samantam*, [thinking] "May we be surrounded on all sides by offspring and cattle";
*vae*—now, the *triṇidhana* *yaudhājaya* for the fulfillment of the pressings;
*vaf*—now, the *auśana* as the final *sāman*.
"By means of the final *sāman*, may we attain the final world, heaven," [they say].
Regarding this, they say: "The *pṛṣṭha* of this day should indeed be performed with the *tavaśśāvyam*."
This is merely a praiseworthy eulogy for it; however, two [priests] do not perform this together.
They say, "It is indeed the Vāmadevya," for it is the Vāmadevya.
That *rājana* chant is indeed the *vāmadevya* directly perceived;
he begins the *prastāva* with its breath;
he begins the *vāmadevya* with a *ṛc*.
For by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they utter "hiṃ hiṃ hiṃ," thinking, "The vital breath is non-existent.
Just as there is a dwelling for a bird, so is the Vāmadevya-sāman for the Rājana-sāman.
Prajāpati is indeed the father; Āditya is the son.
Prajāpati is the Vāmadevya; Āditya is the Rājana.
Therefore, he burns more intensely than these two, for from him this splendor was separated.
That [sāman] is indeed perfected by means of eighty [syllables].
In each *stotriyā* verse, two sets of eighty are produced;
those amount to fifty sets of eighty.
There are indeed two eighties: day and night.
With these two they cause him to lie;
with these two they indeed cause him to lie.
Whatever its *nidhana* may be, those are indeed the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].
15. JB 2.16. "Speech" (*vāk*) is the *rathantara*.
*iḍā* is the *vairūpa*;
that is the *śakvarīs*, that is the *revatīs*; *svar* is the *vairāja*.
*Ve*: "The Great" (*bṛhat*) means the Great.
*Vf*: "Light" (*bhā*) is yonder sun. *Vg*: "Light" (*bhā*) is indeed its *nidhana*.
He who knows this attains harmony with it. This [Sāman] expresses all the *pṛṣṭha* chants by means of this Sāman-concluding formula (*sāmanidhana*).
Furthermore, these indeed amount to five sets of twenty-five when the Sāman-concluding formulas are chanted together.
The Hotṛ recites these very verses with the *nidhana*s. Regarding this, they say: "One should proceed first with the body, then with the head";
for the body comes first, then the head.
Now, that would be just like a piece of pottery falling apart; it would be the same if they were to descend from the twenty-fivefold self back toward the threefold as the head.
One must proceed by means of the head alone.
Indeed, all these deities attend upon the *stotra*, each thinking, "He shall begin with me; he shall begin with me.

If he begins with the head, he prospers through that very deity who is the presiding deity of the head. If he begins with a wing, he prospers through that very deity who is the presiding deity of the wings.
If by means of the tail, he prospers through that very deity who is the *pratipad* (opening verse) of the tail;
if by means of the body, he prospers through that very deity who is the *pratipad* of the body;
the other deities become excluded.

Indeed, all the deities are in the head. These Vasus are these [breaths]; these Rudras, these Ādityas, these Viśve Devas. 16.
