This very world here, this intermediate space, that world yonder, and these quarters are the ear;
this is the *Rathantara*, this the *Vāmadevya*, this the *Bṛhat*, and this the *Yajñāyajñīya*.
Thus, by entering [the sacrifice] through the head, one proceeds with all the deities, with all these worlds, and with all [these chants].
By means of the *sāman*s, he proceeds without obstacle.
For if he were to proceed by means of any other limb, he would merely strengthen that deity which is the presiding deity of that particular mode of proceeding;
the other deities would be excluded.

Now, by beginning with this [head], he begins without interruption by means of all the deities indeed. Moreover, it is dear to the deities that he begins with the head, thinking, "May none of us fail. (17)
JB 2.18 |va| Semen indeed enters first, namely that which is the *gāyatra*;
thereafter the other limbs are developed. |vb|
This *gāyatra* indeed enters as the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
other limbs settle down toward it.
It churns out these vital breaths and spaces.
The Gāyatra is indeed the vital breath;
the Gāyatra is the head itself; for the vital breath has its abode in the head.

Therefore, one should begin with the head consisting of the *trivṛt* [stoma], then with the wing consisting of the *pañcadaśa*, then with the wing consisting of the *saptadaśa*, then with the tail consisting of the *ekaviṃśa*, and then with the body consisting of the *pañcaviṃśa*. Thus, they ascend to renown, to prosperity, and to the heavenly world, all directed upwards.
Moreover, this day of theirs is praised around with those very auspicious and peaceful *stomas* of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
Furthermore, these very auspicious and peaceful *stomas* of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* become for them the vessel that wards off misfortune.
JB 2.19 |va This is the day [of the sacrifice] which possesses all the *pṛṣṭha* [laud-sāmans] and all the *stomas*.

In that he addresses all the *pṛṣṭha* chants with this *sāman*-finale, it is therefore the *sarvapṛṣṭha*. And in that these *stomas* of the *jyotiṣṭoma*— which are auspicious, peaceful, and the vessel for warding off calamity— are employed, it is therefore the *sarvastoma*.

By means of this very perfection, the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa Stomas are brought into correspondence. For him who knows thus, the praise on this day is performed with the Sarvapṛṣṭha and the Sarvastoma.
Some indeed perform the praise by making even this [the third], saying, "This Sāman is truly one."
In that world, neither their heads nor their other limbs are discerned; for they become like mere lumps, lacking ritual purpose. 19.
They are indeed like lumps, being devoid of sacrifice.
One should indeed praise according to the limbs [of the body].
It is they who, in that world, come into being immortal with their limbs and their bodies intact.
Now, some indeed utter the *hiṃ* sound only once for the head, saying, "The head is this which is turned away."
Three times each for the other limbs;
thus those *hiṃkāras* amount to thirteen.
In this way, there is the attainment of the thirteenth month.
But that is certainly not so;
for they utter the *hiṃ* three times for the head, and three times each for the other limbs. Thus, those *hiṃ*-utterances amount to fifteen.
Indra is indeed fifteenfold; the Mahāvrata belongs to Indra, and thus it is performed with that same characteristic mark. 20.
Regarding this, they say: "The *brahmasāman* for this day should be the *naudhasa*. This indeed accords with that [previous] position. [But others say:
"The *rathantara* or the *śyaita* should be performed."
That indeed merely restates the position [of the opponent].
"The Bṛhat alone, with five nidhanas, should be made the Vāmadevya"— this indeed merely restates the self [of the system].
One should perform only the Śrāyantīya; indeed, one does not repeat anything else that is Śrāyantīya.
One should perform the Mahāvaiṣṭambha;
that has the quarters as its *nidhana*.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the quarters.
This eastern quarter is the *rathantara*; this is the *bṛhat*; this is the *vairūpa*; this is the *vairāja*;
those [stars] are the *mahānāmnī*s; these are the *revatī*s.
From the quarters, indeed, they bring food to him; from the quarters, indeed, food is brought to him who knows thus.
Moreover, by this very means, all their *pṛṣṭha* chants become possessed of the *brahmasāman*.
Therefore, this *sāman* must not be omitted from this day. And it occurs in *satobṛhatī* verses, for the sake of transition and to prevent falling away.
Regarding this, they say: "The *ilānda* should be made the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* for this day.
This is its truly auspicious praise. That which exceeds [the norm] is that which they would cut away; it is that which is there on the wing.

"The *ilānda* should be performed for the *pavamāna* of the *ārbhava* [laud] in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; since it has been prescribed, we must not omit it. "The *vāravantīya* alone should be performed," [he said].
This is indeed a beautiful praise of it:
however many times he performs the sacrifice, for that long he desires to prosper and for that long he yearns,
thinking, "May I become better and better."
Therefore, that which was prescribed for the *gāyatrī* of the *ārbhava-pavamāna* should indeed be performed; [they think], "Lest we should exclude what has been recited.
Regarding this, they also say: "Whatever speech does not speak beyond itself—that should be made the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* for this day."
Indeed, no other speech surpasses the *yajñāyajñīya*;
for the *yajñāyajñīya* is speech itself.
How indeed could speech surpass speech?
Therefore, for this day, the Yajñāyajñīya alone should be made the Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
Now, they perform this on an Anuṣṭubh verse measured by thirty-four syllables;
for there are indeed thirty-three deities.
Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth.

By this [rite], the gods together with Prajāpati attain success. Now, as for the fact that on the introductory day it is commensurate with the thirty-three, it is the deities themselves [that are thus honored].
With this they attain prosperity.
Now, by means of this very [sacrifice], having finally attained and reached the deities together with Prajāpati, they rise up.
Regarding this they ask: "Which deity do those being consecrated sit down after, and which deity do they rise up after?
He should say: "They sit down after Agni, the deity among the gods, as they are being consecrated; they rise up after Āditya.
Therefore, even if those who have been consecrated should lie down, people still say of them, "They are sitting [in session]. Even if they were to rise up, [they are still said to be sitting].
For Agni was the best of the gods while they were seated;
for at that time they have Agni as their deity. Therefore, even if they are sitting or lying down, when they have risen, people say, "They have stood up."
For Āditya is the best of the gods when they have arisen;
for then they have Āditya as their deity. Regarding this, they say: "Becoming what do they arise?"
He should say: "Becoming human beings, they undergo initiation; becoming gods, they rise up.
Thus, they go while depositing seed in the womb of the Brahman, which has the *ṛc* as its seed and the *yajus* as its seed.
It is indeed into Agni that they go, offering oblations with those very offerings.
Therefore, during the consecration (dīkṣā) and the Upasad days, they become as if exhausted;
at that time, the semen is as if fresh.
For this reason, a woman who is pregnant becomes as if exhausted.
For at that time, the seed is as if young.
They proceed, listening while thrice strengthening those [seeds] with hymns of praise and recitations;
therefore embryos develop without eating. 23.
JB 2.24 |va They become composed of the *Ṛgveda*, composed of the *Yajurveda*, composed of the *Sāmaveda*, composed of the *Brahman*, composed of gold, and immortal. vb Indeed,
one becomes composed of the *Ṛgveda*, composed of the *Yajurveda*, composed of the *Sāmaveda*, composed of the *Brahman*, composed of gold, and immortal.
The bones of one who knows thus consist of the *ṛc*s.
Having generated them before the year [begins], the *udgātṛ* hands them over to the *hotṛ*;
the *hotṛ* brings them forth with hymns (*sūkta*).
That is the "hymn-ness" of the hymns (*sūkta*). He praises them with the *śastra* recitations;
that is the "recitation-ness" (*śastratva*) of the *śastra*s.
He raises them up with hymns;
that is the reason for the name of the *ukthas*.
To them he offers this divine honey and food by means of the eighty [verses].
He who knows this becomes honey in this world and food in the other world.
By means of each syllable, all branches of knowledge milk for him all his desires.
Therefore, it is indeed in the year that one should praise, and in the year that one should proclaim.
Therefore, a Brahmin who has been killed does not become a thief; therefore, semen once discharged does not become a thief; and therefore, indeed, one who knows this does not become a thief.
By means of eighty [verses], indeed, the gods reached these worlds and these paths.
That is the reason for the "eighty" of the eighty.
By three [verses] they reached this world, by three the intermediate space, and by three that [upper] world; by four [they reached] the quarters.
With four [verses] they pervaded the four quarters; with one, the intermediate directions; with one, the upward direction. There were ninety-two [verses].
There are nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
He pervades the vital breaths.
He comes into being with his vital breath;
he reaches a full lifespan;
he does not die against his will. 24.
Now this is the royal throne-seat made of Udumbara wood.
Of it, the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* [Sāmans] are the two front legs; the *Vairūpa* and *Vairāja* are the two rear legs; the *Śākvara* and *Raivata* are the side-boards.

The *ṛc* verses were the longitudinal warp, the *yajus* formulas the crosswise woof, the *sāman* chants the covering, the dialogues the side-boards, and prosperity the pillow. Prajāpati and Bṛhaspati supported its two front feet, while Soma and Varuṇa [supported the other two].
And two others.
Upon her they consecrated this Āditya:
the Vasus for kingship, the Rudras for overlordship, the Ādityas for self-sovereignty, the Viśve Devas for paramount sovereignty, and the Maruts...
For universal sovereignty, for those to be accomplished and those to be attained, and for the supreme state.
Indeed, nothing has been conquered by any deity as much as it has been by the Sun.
For those who were the pressed juices of the gods, they pressed him out.
The quarters sought kinship with him, just as people seek kinship with a victorious king.
He said to them, "Offer me a gift.
This eastern quarter offered itself to him, saying, "I am thy rising; I am day and truth."
"Come toward me," said the upward direction; it bestowed upon him sovereignty and the kingdom.
"Depart from me," said the southern direction; it bestowed upon him food and a chariot. "Depart from me," said the northern direction; it bestowed upon him form and color.
"Come to me with equanimity," the intermediate space gave him, bestowing both light and freedom from obstruction.
"Set in me as you go to rest," the western quarter gave him, bestowing both cosmic order (*ṛta*) and night.
"Heat me along," the earth gave him. (25)
JB 2.26 |va Security and liberation.
vb Then they thought themselves superior.
"May we warm ourselves toward them," they said, and they bestowed upon him both the journey and the departure.
For he goes by means of the waters, following the path of the waters;
therefore, their shadows, rising upward, warm him from that side.
In this way, he attains these directions.
He rises for this eastern direction;
he rises toward this upward direction.
|vi Thus he goes for six months; |vj thus he goes for another six. |vk He goes through the intermediate space to the setting [of the sun], toward this western direction.
It heats across this entire earth;
just as a husband might follow after his wife, even so does he follow after these [worlds] here. He thought: "Let me encompass all this myself."

He took from the sky sovereignty alone; from the stars, the self; from the intermediate space, form; from the wind, command; from men, sight; from cattle, vigor; from the waters, sap; from the plants, movement;
from the trees, the male organ; from birds, brilliance; from fire, the heart; and from the earth, fragrance.

The thundering of gold, the gathering of speech, the radiance of the fathers, and the brilliance of the moon—because he took these from those beings, that is the *ādityatva* (nature of the Āditya) of the Āditya.
He who knows this thus, becoming this very Āditya, sits upon this royal throne. 26.
JB 2.27 |va One should not say, "I shall sit for the sacrificial session" (sattra);
rather, one should simply say, "I shall exert myself. vb.
Verily, there are two deities who sit at a sacrificial session (*sattra*): namely, Prāṇa and Apāna. That is their ascent.
Because they both sit for this sacrificial session, therefore they are called *sattrasadau* (the two who sit at the session).
Therefore, one should simply say, "I shall exert myself.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"The seven seers, O Subhūti, were appointed as messengers."
|vi “Seven see [him] as he is established in many ways. |vj “These seven waters go to this world.
|vk “[They are] those who do not sleep, who sit at the sacrificial session where the gods [dwell].”
Thus:
"The seven seers, O Subhūti, are the deputies. Man indeed is Subhūti;
these seven seers who are the deputies are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

“They see him established in many ways,” for they see these two, namely the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, as established in many ways. “Seven waters go to this world,” that is, these two kinds of waters, these two kinds, these one kind, and these two kinds.
"Those two who do not sleep, seated at the sacrificial session where the gods [are],"—these indeed are those two deities. He who knows this thus [attains them]. 27.

Whether he sits for the sacrificial session (*sattra*) or not, his session indeed becomes one that has been performed. Furthermore, he who, knowing this, undergoes the toil—the two deities themselves sit for his session;
he remains unharmed and reaches the completion of the year.
That which shines yonder is indeed the year. Of that [year], what shines is the *saṃvat*, and that black circle in its center is the *sara*; thus with respect to the deities.
Now, with respect to the self.
This very year is this person who is in the eye.
That which is white in him is the *saṃvat*; that black circle in the middle is the *saras*. Regarding this, there is this verse:
"From me alone the sun rises, and into me it sets.
"All the gods are dependent upon me; nothing whatsoever transcends me.
Thus [he said].
"The sun rises from me alone"—for one who knows thus, indeed, the sun rises. "And it sets into me"—for one who knows thus, indeed, it sets.
"All the gods are dependent upon me"—for one who knows thus, indeed, all the gods are dependent.
"Nothing indeed ever passes beyond me"—for one who knows thus, nothing indeed ever passes beyond him. 28.
Regarding this, they ask: "What is the *saṃvat*, what is the *sara*, and what is the *ayana*?"
He should say: "The triple knowledge itself is the *saṃvat* (the year), for all the gods have blown together (*saṃvāntāḥ*) into it. Day and night themselves are the *saras*."
For they indeed move toward all this.
The sun is the path;
for it moves through these worlds.
Thus with reference to the deities.
Now with reference to the self:
food indeed is the *saṃvat*.
For all this is indeed moving.
Speech alone is the flow;
for by means of speech, a person moves.
Breath alone is the way;
for it moves through this entire universe.
He who thus knows this "way of the year" with respect to both the deities and the self is indeed unharmed.
He reaches the conclusion of the year. Regarding this, they say: "How does the year become a single-metre [verse] consisting of Bṛhatīs?
"By days," he should say.
"How, by days?
"The two *atirātra*s, the *ārambhaṇīya* day, the *mahāvratīya* day, the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [six-day periods], the *abhijit*, the three..."
The three Svarasāmans face westward; the Viśvajit, the Go and Āyus, the ten-night rite, and the Vaiṣuvata as the thirty-seventh—this is established upon this heavenly world.
Of this there is this verse:
They say that it consists of twenty and seven hundred [syllables];
the Bṛhatī, comprising thirty-six [syllables], when being fashioned,
becomes the Anuṣṭubh and is of the same womb as the cattle.
"They bestow [sacrifices] upon the gods, the ancestors, and human beings"—
thus it is said. "They say that those are twenty and seven hundred"— these are indeed the days and nights.

"By arranging the *bṛhatī* as a thirty-sixfold [verse]," thus indeed is that *bṛhatī* arranged by means of the days. "Having become an *anuṣṭubh*, it is of the same womb as the cattle"— this very world (the earth) brought the cow, this [world] the horse, and this [world]...
"This is the unborn ewe.
Indeed, they brought the quarters as the price for this true Anuṣṭubh; such indeed was that. "He gives to the gods, to the ancestors, and to men."
The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech;
for all this that exists here is from speech.
Thus, the year becomes a single-metre *bārhata* [verse]. 30.
JB 2.31 |va This very one who blows here is the *spṛṣṭya*; for by him all this is touched (*spṛṣṭa*). vb.
This [sacrificial session] is indeed called *spṛṣṭya*. They call it *pṛṣṭhya* cryptically.
He who knows thus touches all desires.
That which shines yonder is indeed the *abhiplava*;
for it overspreads (*abhi-plavate*) all this. Regarding this, they say: "As for what they call the *pṛṣṭhya* and the *abhiplava*, they actually enter upon the *abhiplava* first."
[Question: How is it that the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] is entered first? [Answer:
He should say: "Because this lower wind blows and the sun is above.
Moreover, they enter the lower *abhiplava* while it is actually higher for the sake of interlocking, for the sake of non-omission, and for the sake of attaining full life.

Regarding this they say: "Since there are four *stomas* for the *abhiplava* and six for the *pṛṣṭhya*, how is it that [the former] possesses the same burden (*sabhāra*)? He should reply: "Because these two deities are similar—Vāyu and Āditya—therefore it has the same burden.
Furthermore, because the *abhiplava* is the *brahman* and the *pṛṣṭhya* is the *kṣatra*, it is for that reason as well. 31.

Regarding this they say: "Since these are the uneven *stomas* of the *pṛṣṭhya*— namely, the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, the *saptadaśa*, the *ekaviṃśa*, the *triṇava*, and the *trayastriṃśa*— how is it that they have attained equality from what is equal?"
He should say: "The *brahman* is indeed the *trivṛt*;
the *kṣatra* is the *pañcadaśa*. The *brahman* is indeed superior to the *kṣatra*."
Therefore, it becomes equal to the equal.
The *viṭ* (the common people) is the seventeenth; indeed, the *kṣatra* (the ruling power) is superior to the *viś*.
By that, it becomes equal to the equal.
(vi) The Śūdra follows the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*).
(vj) The Vaiśya is indeed superior to the Śūdra.
By that, it becomes equal to the equal. The domestic animals correspond to the twenty-seven-fold hymn-form (*triṇava-stoma*). The Śūdra is indeed superior to the domestic animals.
For the self belongs to them;
therefore, it becomes equal with the equal.
The wild animals follow the thirty-threefold *stoma*.
Domestic animals are indeed superior to wild animals.
The others roam about in fear, while the other has the power to kill them.
Therefore, it becomes equal to that which is equal.

Regarding this they ask: "Why is the *abhiplava* of one form while the *pṛṣṭhya* is of two forms—both being essentially the same, yet one being expanded (*vyūḍha*) and the other contracted (*samūḍha*)?
He should reply: "Because this Brahman is indeed Brahman."
Now, because one who is a Kṣatriya becomes a Brāhmaṇa, therefore the Abhiplava is of one form and the Pṛṣṭhya is of two forms.
Regarding this, some perform the sixth day of the Abhiplava as an Ukthya, thinking, "In this way it possesses a burden."
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "Those who perform it in that manner cause confusion regarding the *abhiplava* [six-day period].
In that case, it becomes devoid of the sacred formulation (*brahman*).
Therefore, it should not be performed in that way."
Now, some indeed extract the *dvipadā* verses from the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭhya* ṣaḍaha, [thinking] "thus it is with its burden.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "This *pṛṣṭhya* ṣaḍaha is the heavenly world;
these *dvipadā* verses are, by their very nature, the sacrificer."

They cause him to fall from his abode. If one were to say of those who have acted in this manner, "They shall fall from their abode, or they shall fall from this world," it would surely happen exactly so.
"Therefore, it should not be done in that way. (JB 2.33) Regarding this, they say: "As for this day called the *prāyaṇīya*, which they call the *prāyaṇīya*, it is [actually] the *trivṛt*."

"How is it that this twenty-fourfold [stoma] becomes prepared by means of the ninefold (trivṛt)? He should reply: "Because these forty-ninefold [stomas] result in being twenty-fourfold, thereby it becomes prepared by means of the ninefold."
"Moreover, because the *gāyatrī* has twenty-four syllables, it is for that very reason [so]. Regarding this, they say: "How does this *vaiṣuvatīya* day come to possess the *chandomas*?
He should reply: "As many as are the syllables of the seven meters increasing by four, so many are the syllables of this day."
The *stotriyas*. By this, the *chandomas* are established. Regarding this, they say: "Since they perform the *chandomas* after the *viṣuvat*, how is it that they are performed before the *viṣuvat*?"
Regarding the statement, "The Chandomas are obtained," he should say: "By means of that very twenty-four-fold stoma of the Chandomas which belongs to the *ārambhaṇīya* day,
the Chandomas are obtained prior to the Viṣuvat."
Moreover, because two days at a time of the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] are combined, they thus result in the *chandomas*.

Regarding this, they say: "Since they perform the *pṛṣṭhya* days six times before the *viṣuvat*, but only once—the seventh—after the *viṣvajit*, how is that [the sacrifice] 'equally balanced' (*sabhāra*)?
He should reply: "That which is prior to the *viṣuvat* is this world; that which is subsequent to the *viṣuvat* is yonder world."
That world is near,
as it were; this world is close at hand,
while that other one is, as it were, set apart.
For this second world is indeed [the counterpart]. Therefore, when they perform the seven *pṛṣṭha* days at the end of the Viśvajit, it is thus "with its burden.
Moreover, he who knows the Viśvajit as having the *pṛṣṭhas* in this very way...
The *rathaṃtara* is indeed the cow, the *bṛhat* the horse, the *vairūpa* the goat, the *vairāja* the sheep, the *śakvarīs* the rice,
and the *revatīs* the barley.
This very thing is the chariot joined together, which is the *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
The axle of that chariot is the *bṛhat* which serves as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* upon the *gāyatrī* verses; it is for the sake of preventing this chariot from falling into ruin.
Now, those who perform this sacrifice with the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* removed have their chariot stuck; they approach the *viśvajit* sacrifice empty-handed.
They do not attain anything at all;
therefore, the Viśvajit should be performed as consisting entirely of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
Now, some perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants of the *svarasāman* days as the *svaras* themselves. For the day is designated by its *pṛṣṭha*, and these [days] are designated as *svarasāmans*.
Therefore, the *pṛṣṭhas* of the *svarasāmans* should indeed be performed as the *svaras*.
If they should perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants with the *svaras*, those which are [ordinarily] in the *ṣaṣṭha* [meter] they should perform in *ekabṛhatī*s.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "We indeed perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants with the *svaras* directly, we who perform the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara*."
"This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara, and "that" [sky] is the Bṛhat. By means of these two, indeed, all this world is encompassed.
Therefore, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara alone should be made the Pṛṣṭha stotras."
Now, they perform these *svarasāman* chants in a disjointed manner when they perform three;
indeed, all [the *svarasāmans*] must be performed.
In this way, the day is extended by two [sāmans] at a time.
"In this way, they are gathered together by their own inherent nature, uninterrupted, through the turning away from the inversion of evil.
Now, some perform the *bṛhat* *pṛṣṭha* chant on the *bṛhatī* verses at the *viṣuvat*.
The Viṣuvat day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre, and that Āditya [the sun] also belongs to the Bṛhatī;
he shines resting upon this Bṛhatī.
Therefore, the Bṛhat-pṛṣṭha stotra should be performed in Bṛhatī verses alone.
Now, some indeed perform the *divākīrtya* *pṛṣṭha-stotra* on *bṛhatī* verses;
for the *pṛṣṭhas* have the *bṛhatī* as their abode,
and this intermediate space is indeed the *bṛhatī*.
In that [metre], this wind blows within;
that is its back. Furthermore, because there is a twelve-syllable foot, it becomes established among the Jagatī verses.
In this way, the third pressing is performed as one whose strength is undiminished.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "The Viṣuvat day belongs to the Jagatī;
this Sāman is of the Jagatī meter; and yonder sun is of the Jagatī meter."
For when this [sun] rises, then the world follows after his very departure. Therefore, the *divākīrtya* *pṛṣṭha* should be performed in *jagatī* verses alone.
Thus, those three *jagatīs* become four *bṛhatīs*.
By that, it becomes established in the *bṛhatī* meters.
When they are chanted together, those twenty-eight verses result in *bṛhatīs*.
Thus, the *bṛhatī* is indeed preserved.
Now, this *divākīrtya* is indeed the created seed of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
the *jagatī* is procreation;
and that is yonder sun.
In that they perform the Divākīrtya Pṛṣṭha-stotra in Jagatī verses, they thereby endow it with its own proper abode.
Through that which is thus successful, it becomes prosperous for them within their own community. 36.
Regarding this, they ask: what is it that is performed on the Divākīrtya day by which one procreates offspring and by which one sustains offspring?
He should say: "The *divākīrtya* is fashioned from the very seed of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
the *jagatī* is procreation;
by means of it, he procreates offspring."
Now, in that he, having become the breath (*prāṇa*), supports both the later and the earlier days, by that very act he supports offspring.
The *divākīrtya* is indeed the breath; the *bhrāja* and *abhrāja* are the two eyes.
The ear is Vikarṇa;
speech is Daśastobha. These vital breaths (prāṇas) are placed in the middle.
Regarding this, some take the *ājya* cups only after [the sun] has risen;
they commence the *prātaranuvāka* after [the sun] has risen;
for this day is indeed named the *divākīrtya*.
"Therefore, they should not join it with the night.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "The days are praised by means of the Sāmans, and the nights by means of the Ṛks. Thus, for them, that night remains unpraised and empty."
Now, this morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) is Prajāpati.
They cause it to fall from its abode. If one were to say of those who have acted thus, "They shall fall from their abode, or they shall fall from this world," so indeed it would be.
They should indeed be so. Therefore, it should be performed in the same manner as for the other days.
The *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* [libations] are the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*).
Some offer [the oblation] when the sun has risen, others before it has risen.
Indeed, they live upon the out-breath (*prāṇa*) which is outside, and upon the in-breath (*apāna*) which is inside.
Thus, when some offer after sunrise and others before sunrise, they live upon the out-breath that is outside and the in-breath that is inside.
"Peaceful is the out-breathing," he says.
Now, those who offer these two oblations when the sun has risen tear away the out-breathing and in-breathing.
If one were to say of those who have acted thus, "They have torn away their out-breathing and in-breathing; they will die," it would indeed happen exactly so.
Or they may be [different]. Therefore, it should be performed just as it is for the other days. 37.

Now, these indeed depart from one who is being consecrated: the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Cāturmāsya offerings, the animal sacrifice, the Pitṛyajña, the Gṛhamedha, the Brahmaudana, and the pair.
Therefore, when he consumes his fast-food with the utterance "Svāhā" during the Dīkṣā and Upasad rites, by that means these [sacrifices] are not separated from him during the Dīkṣā and Upasads.
The Agnihotra is established.
In that they offer one [libation] after sunrise and the other before sunrise, by that it is the Sutyā;
in that there is the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), by that it is the Paurṇamāsa.
In that there is curd, by that it is the New Moon sacrifice; in that there is clotted milk, by that it is the Four-Monthly sacrifices;
in that they immolate an animal, by that it is the Animal Sacrifice.
In that he performs the meditations, thereby [is fulfilled] the Pitṛyajña;
in that there are parched grains and gruel, thereby [is fulfilled] the Gṛhamedha;
in that he brings the Soma-oblation, thereby [is fulfilled] the Brahmaudana.
In that he causes the wives to be counted, thereby [he produces] a pair. Regarding this, some say: "One should breathe over the response with the words, 'I have united with you through the breath'.
But Śāṭyāyani said: "This is like a form that has been spilled."
There is indeed only one man; by means of knowledge alone this [world] is made continuous. Moreover, it is that which they cause to be counted during the Yajñāyajñīya hymn. 38/ JB 2.39
Regarding this they say: "Since they praise with various different *sāmans* and recite various different [verses], why then are the houses the same?
He should reply: "The *sāman* is indeed food."
Food is the *ṛc*;
the vital breaths are the *gṛha*s;
for they bring various kinds of food from other sources than the vital breaths themselves.
Therefore, they praise with various different *sāmans* and recite various different [verses], thinking, "The houses are indeed the same.
The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are the *sāman*;
that is its root.
Now, just as the trunks, branches, or leaves of a tree, so too are the other Sāmans. He who knows this thus—indeed, all the Sāmans become known to him.
Speech itself is the Ṛc.
That is its root.
Now, just as a tree has trunks, or branches, or leaves, so too are the other *ṛc*s. He who knows this thus—indeed, all the *ṛc*s become known to him.
The mind alone is the Yajus;
that is its root.
Now, just as a tree has trunks, branches, or leaves, so too are the other Yajus formulas.
He who knows this thus—verily, all the *yajus* formulas become known to him.
(39) JB 2.40 Regarding this, they say: "Why do they not chant beyond [the norm]? Why do they not recite beyond [the norm]? Why do they not take up beyond [the norm]?"
He should say: "They do not over-praise breath alone;
when breath is praised, breath alone remains.
They do not over-commend speech alone."
When speech is grasped, indeed, speech alone remains;
they do not grasp the mind beyond that;
when the mind is grasped, indeed, the mind alone remains.
That which is neither over-praised nor over-censured, and is not excessively grasped—such a sacrifice becomes truly perfected for one who knows this.
Now, indeed, a sacrifice should be performed only when it is complete. That which one performs while studying and without causing failure leads to heaven.
"One should understand this thus: 'This of mine is conducive to heaven; by means of this, I shall attain the heavenly world.
Now, when one who studies poorly performs [the recitation] while being distracted, stumbling, or spilling [the text], that is nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and procreation (*prajananam*).
One should understand this thus: "This is my nourishment and procreation; I shall become abundant and I shall procreate. (40)
JB 2.41 |va Now, indeed, there were formerly three Agnis: Bhūpati, Bhuvanapati, and Bhūtānām pati.
Now, this one was named Bhūti. Their *vaṣaṭ*-utterance cut off their heads,
and they entered these three earths.
Therefore, if anything of the Agnihotra or the clarified butter should spill, he should touch it with: "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā!
To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā!
In these very fires of his, what has been offered becomes as if unspilled.
Now, indeed, there were formerly three seers: Śūrpaṇyava, Aśvānām Antarvān, and Kṛṣi Saurvālā.
They saw the flaws of the sacrifice;
they saw these expiations for it: "May there be peace for me, and may there be prosperity for me, and may there be long life for me, and may there be abundance for me."
"O Sacrifice, may you be well-established for me; O Sacrifice, may you be well-sacrificed for me; O Sacrifice, may you be unharmed for me.
Therefore, these [formulas] are used with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, or with the Four-Monthly sacrifices, or with the Animal sacrifice, or with the Soma sacrifice.
Having sacrificed with the *vadhry-aśva* [oblation], he should mutter [the following] after the conclusion.
Whatever defect occurs in the sacrifice here, that very thing he pacifies by means of this.
Prāṇa is indeed before the *viṣuvat*, vyāna is the *viṣuvat*, and apāna is that which follows the *viṣuvat*.
The *apāna* indeed brings all this hither;
therefore, we approach the six-day periods from beyond the *viṣuvat* towards it. 41.
Regarding this, Kratujit Jānaki asked Iyāpin Saumāpa: "By what does a mortal live here—by the out-breath (*prāṇa*) or by the in-breath (*apāna*)? "Tell that to the assembled Brāhmaṇas of the Kurus."
He said, "I shall answer you right here.
He replied to him: "It is not by means of the out-breath (prāṇa), nor by the in-breath (apāna).
While this mortal being lives, the diffused breath (vyāna) is the overseer of the animal; it is that which moves it in all directions."
The person (*puruṣa*) is indeed the sacrificial animal (*paśu*); that [person] is an animal because he is an animal.
Indeed, the vital breath (*vyāna*) impels him in all directions.
Regarding this, some indeed perform those six-day periods as exclusively subsequent to the *viṣuvat* day. [They say:
"By that very *pṛṣṭhya* which we performed previously, we have become distinguished;
moreover, it is thus [performed] so that there is no kinship."
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "Both these [classes of days] are indeed upward-moving—both those that are upward and those that are downward.
By means of the *savana*s (pressings), they become upward-moving; thus they attain that desire which is in the turnings.
Regarding this, they say: "Just as there is a turning back of the waters, so it is with these, namely the *go* and *āyus* [stomas]."
“Of which days are these?
“Of the later ones or the earlier ones?
“One should say: of both.”

Indeed, these two sets of days stand together, encompassing both the subsequent and the preceding; therefore, one part is extended over three days and the other over three days. Thus, being a two-day period, it becomes a six-day period.
Then the *go* and *āyus* [sacrifices] come after that; the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*) comes after them.
Now, some perform the *go* and *āyus* in an expanded form: the *āyus* after the *viśvajit*, and the *go* before the ten-night rite.
"Thus [it is] 'unrelated' (ajāmī). Furthermore, this was indeed their prior approach. Then the Naimiśīyas passed by in negligence.
They should join together here before the ten-night rite, or they may do so later;
from there they proceed with this [rite] that follows.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "The Go and Āyus are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath."
*vac*—those who dwell [thus] cut off food and drink for them;
*vad*—this indeed is the path leading to the gods, namely the Cow and Life;
*vae*—this world is heaven, namely the ten-night sacrifice.
They go to this heavenly world by means of this path that leads to the gods. But those who disperse [their fires] cut off this path that leads to the gods; they do not attain anything at all.
"Therefore, one should approach [the sacrifice] together. Thus [ends the section].
Śāṭyāyani said to Gobala Vārṣṇa: "O venerable one, you have a father; you have a grandfather."
"I shall undergo initiation for the sake of the year; instruct me," [he said]. "So be it," he replied.
"I will tell you the way of life by which one who knows it reaches the completion of the year without harm, having risen."
"He becomes one who provides security and prosperity, and is worthy of honor.
"Indeed, these twelve months pass," he said;
"therefore, those four months that pass, they go by means of the path of Agni."
And by that [path], they attain Agni among the deities and this world.
Now, those four other months which they pass, they go by way of Vāyu; and by that [path], they attain Vāyu among the deities and the intermediate world (antarikṣaloka).
Those other four months which they pass, they pass by means of the course of the sun alone; and by that means they reach Āditya among the deities and that world beyond. 43. JB 2.44.
"This indeed is the way," he said.
"Now, as for what they say here, 'He has come by a way that is not a way'— those who, being ignorant of this, undergo initiation for the sake of the year, they go by a way that is not a way."
Now, he who knows this thus reaches the completion of the year unharmed; rising up, he becomes one who possesses security and prosperity, and one worthy of honor.
They come to this heavenly world.
This is the day of the Mahāvrata.
Indeed, this day of the Mahāvrata is the world of heaven. It consists of twenty-five [stomas].
Then, that which is the twentieth is the Virāj.
Now, those which are the four are these very four quarters. And that which is the twenty-fifth is this very upward quarter.
Where the quarters indeed rose up together, there this world named Atyagra came into being—that which shines yonder.
It is to this very [world] that they ascend by means of the twenty-fifth [verse];
they attain co-residence (*salokatā*) with it.

Regarding this they say: "Since they desire most abundantly by means of this day and by means of the Mahāvrata, why then is this *vāraṇa* performed with a twenty-five-fold hymn-form (*pañcaviṃśastoma*)? One should reply: "For the sake of securing all food."
By five *stotriya* verses he wins the man; by five, the cow; by five, the horse;
by five, the goat; by five, the sheep.
Thus, this twenty-five-fold hymn-form (*pañcaviṃśastoma*) is performed at the end for the sake of securing food in its entirety.
Now, those two Atirātras are indeed the foundation.
Having established themselves in this world by means of the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, they set forth;
having established themselves in yonder world by means of the Udayanīya Atirātra, they rise up.
They, too, as it were, desire to become [something] and stand as it were facing [it]. 44.
Now this is the royal throne made of Udumbara wood. 45. JB 2.45.
Some indeed place it facing east;
one should rather place it facing north.
Its two front feet are these two intermediate regions, and its two hind feet are these two [other] ones.
Regarding this, some indeed ascend facing eastward. But Śāṭyāyani said: "The Sāman-chanters perform the priestly office facing north; the Udgātṛs have the north as their deity."
"Having ascended by means of the northern [formula]," it is said. Some indeed ascend it with a salutation alone: "Homage be to thee, O Blessed One; we know thee; mayest thou be auspicious to us."
Some indeed ascend in silence.
Mind is Prajāpati;
this day belongs to Prajāpati.
He should mount it first with this [formula]: "Now with this, now with this, now with this, may I cause him to go to the immortal.
Then, for him who has mounted, they bring a lute (*vīṇā*) with a hundred strings.
He makes it resonate with this continuous sequence.
*bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* | *vadā vadā vadā vadī vadā vadoruḥ* | *pṛthuḥ sugaḥ sugantuḥ*
Action, instrument, and agent, about to act; speak forth, O divine lute, the Aindra speech, which is lofty and multiform, granting a lifespan of a hundred years.
Thus [he says].

Then, with an *iṣīkā* reed that has been made crooked by Indra, and with a branch of the cane (*vetasa*), he scrapes [the heart], saying: "The mind is the light," "Speech is truth," and "The mind is auspicious."
He gives that [to him]. 45.
Then he performs these other *parimāda* chants. 46. JB 2.46.
Then, when the Stotra has been chanted: first with the head, then with the right wing, then with the left wing, then with the tail, and finally with the body.
That is for the sake of its being hairy.
The Udgātṛ begins with the head, while the Hotṛ begins with the self. For he begins with that very [verse] which he has recited;
but if he were to begin with one [verse] different from the one he has recited, that would be contrary to the natural order.
Now, some indeed enter [the path] first by means of the self alone.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "That is just as if a blind man were to stumble toward a door.
Now, some, having praised, descend and sit gazing at this day as it is being recited.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "He who acts in such a manner is liable to become worse off.
The *sāman* is indeed the *kṣatra*, and the *śastra* is the *viṭ*."
One should remain seated right there;
one should descend only after the king has been brought down.
In this way, the king becomes one who has been made to descend.
The descent for her [the offering-spoon] is:
"May the great heaven and the earth sprinkle this sacrifice for us;
may they fill us with nourishments."
Thus [it is said].
Having carried that very throne around to the north, they set it down.
Regarding this, they say: "Since this day is recited as expanded (*vihṛta*), should one chant on the expanded [verses] or on the unexpanded (*avihṛta*)? One should say, "On the expanded ones.
For those deities which belong to the Rājanya, by means of them the day becomes expanded.

Now, as for the fact that the head consists of *gāyatrī* verses, the two wings of *bṛhatī* and *kakubh* verses, the tail of *dvipadā* verses, and the body of *triṣṭubh* verses— how is it expanded from this?
There are one hundred and twenty-five *triṣṭubh* verses for this body.
Then, that which is the hundred [years] of life—that is this. Now, those which are twenty-five are the person (puruṣa).
These five, these five, these five, these five, and four limbs.
The self is the twenty-fifth. This person has a lifespan of a hundred years.
Regarding this, they say: "Why do they chant with other *triṣṭubh* verses that have complete syllables?"
He should say: "Man is indeed of the *triṣṭubh* nature; his womb is the *triṣṭubh*.
These [syllables] of man are not deficient. Therefore, they have fewer syllables."

Now, as for the fact that they are complete in syllables because the unequal is made equal by the equal—regarding this they say: "The person (*puruṣa*) consists of twenty-five [parts]; this is the hymn of praise (*stotra*) of the person. But why are these *sāman*s performed in an uneven manner for the sake of the person's wholeness?
He should say: "Mind, indeed, is Prajāpati;
Prajāpati is the person (puruṣa).
This [person] is his inner self, namely these twenty-five stotriya verses."
Moreover, it is just as a man’s hair, nails, body hair, and beard;
for when these uneven *sāmans* are performed, it serves for the wholeness of the person.
Regarding this, they say: "Since the *pṛṣṭha* stotras have the *bṛhatī* as their foundation, how is it that they are thereby established upon *bṛhatīs*?
There are one hundred and fifty-two *bṛhatīs* for this self, plus one *kakubh*;
by that, they are established upon *bṛhatīs*.
"Therefore, it does not fall away from the *kakubh* meters as its back.
Regarding this, they ask: "What is the metre of the twenty-fivefold hymn-form (*pañcaviṃśastoma*)? One should say: "The *paṅkti* is its metre."
This, indeed, is the manifest metre of the twenty-five-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), namely the *paṅkti*.
Of this self, there are one hundred and thirty-seven *paṅkti*s and a half-*paṅkti*.
Therefore, the metre is the *paṅkti*.
Those same [verses] are ninety-two *aticchandas* verses. Indeed, the *aticchandas* surpasses all other meters;
thus, for him, all the meters are thereby attained.
Regarding this, they ask: "How does this entire day become twenty-fivefold? One should reply: "By way of correspondence. [They ask:
"How by way of correspondence?"
In the *padya* [arrangement], there are nine *gāyatrī* verses of the head;
their total number of *padas* is twenty-seven.
There are one hundred and six *padas* in the two wings, and forty-two in the tail.
|vs Now, of these twenty-seven footprints of the head, having taken two from there, they lay down six hundred.
vt Then one remains as the twenty-fifth.
vu From that, those four hundred are the twenty-fives.
Now, those eight which remain over, they place them upon the forty-two;
those two are twenty-five-fold;
indeed, the twenty-five-fold is the twenty-five-fold.
"Everything becomes twenty-fivefold.
This Agniṣṭoma is indeed the equinox among sacrifices.
Those *havis*-sacrifices which proceed eastward from the day of preparation (*aupavasatha*)—they pass away by that.
And those subsequent sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) which take place at the soma-pressing (*sutyā*)—they pass away by that.
Since the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is threefold, and since the *stomas* are threefold, they pass away by means of that.
In that there are fifteen *ājya* chants, the midday pressing is fifteenfold, and there are fifteen *stomas*, by these they go forth.
In that there are seventeen *pṛṣṭha* chants, the third pressing is seventeenfold, and there are seventeen *stomas*, by these they go forth.

In that the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the twenty-onefold [stoma], and the stomas are twenty-onefold, by that they enter into it. In that all the stomas converge upon the twenty-onefold, by that all the stomas enter into it.
This very Agniṣṭoma is he who blows here (the wind).
Those sacrificial rites which are directed eastward have Agni as their foundation; those sacrificial rites which are directed northward have Āditya as their foundation.
Indeed, when Agni goes out, he enters into Vāyu.
When the sun sets, it enters into the wind alone. Now, for this very Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, there are likewise twenty-four *stotra* and *śastra* hymns;
in the same way, there are twenty-four [winds]: the east wind, the south wind, the west wind, the north wind, and the upward wind.
Thus:
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself is the *agniṣṭoma* stoma.
Those sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) which are directed forward are, by their fundamental cause (*nidāna*), speech (*vāk*); and those sacrificial rites which are subsequent are sight (*cakṣus*).
By way of the introduction:
when one sits in silence, speech indeed enters into the breath.
When he sleeps, his sight indeed goes into his breath. Thus, when one who knows this speaks, his sacrifice has been performed by means of the *haviryajñas*;
when he breathes, his sacrifice has been performed by means of the *agniṣṭoma*.

Whatever he looks at with his [other] eyes, that becomes for him as if sacrificed by the other sacrificial rites (yajñakratu). Therefore, when one who knows this speaks, breathes, or looks, it becomes as if all those sacrificial rites have been performed by him.
This very year has a common departure and a common connection. Its mind is the departure, and its speech is the connection.
This very year thus results in Agniṣṭomas.
Six exceed the *atirātra*: three *ukthas* and the *sandhi* consisting of three deities.
Three exceed the introductory day (*ārambhaṇīya*). Now, wherever there is an *abhiplava*, those seven are *agniṣṭomas*.
They perform the *pṛṣṭhya* six times;
they exceed it by six in two [periods], and by six in two [others].
That is the *agniṣṭoma*.
Two [bricks] for each of the six; thus he lays down these six.
That is the Agniṣṭoma.
The Agniṣṭoma is the Abhijit. Nine Svarasāman days pass by. Then he lays down those three bricks.
That is the Agniṣṭoma.
The Viṣuvat is an Agniṣṭoma.
They pass nine [verses] beyond the Svarasāmans of the western direction.
They perform the *pṛṣṭhya* six times;
they exceed two [days] by six, and two [days] by six. That is the *agniṣṭoma*.
Three for one;
he places those nine upon these [bricks];
that is the Agniṣṭoma.
|vae Agniṣṭoma Viśvajit |vaf Go and Āyus, six [sacrifices] pass by |vag Twelve Agniṣṭomas, the Daśarātra.
The Agniṣṭoma is the Mahāvratīya day;
indeed, six [stomas] exceed the Atirātra;
that is why he lays down these six bricks.
*vak*—that is the Agniṣṭoma;
*val*—twelve times they perform the Ṣoḍaśin;
*vam*—that is the Agniṣṭoma.
If, however, they perform the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*, they confuse that perfection of the *virāj*;
it exceeds this perfection of the *agniṣṭoma*.
That [excess] is a thunderbolt without a foundation, and it strikes down.
Or rather, the thunderbolt is without support.
This very year has a common departure and a common connection.
Of it, the mind is the departure and speech is the connection.
This very year culminates precisely in the Agniṣṭoma.
Indeed, through this correspondence, it becomes a journey by means of the Agniṣṭoma. Furthermore, those days which are distinctive within the year have been fully attained.
By this path, indeed, one attains both desired objects: that which belongs to the Agniṣṭoma path and that which belongs to the monthly Pṛṣṭha path. The three Mahāvrata sections are completed.
JB 2.51 |va| Indeed, in former times there were two kinds of seasons: the breath-seasons and the divine seasons.
vb| But now, these are simply the [ordinary] seasons.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) was the spring; speech (*vāc*) was the summer;
the eye (*cakṣus*) was the rainy season.
The eye is indeed like the moist; the rainy season is like the moist.
The ear is the autumn;
the mind is the winter.
|vi The waters that are in man are the cold season.
|vj Now, the divine seasons: |vk Vāyu alone was the spring.
Agni is the summer;
Parjanya is the rainy season;
Āditya is the autumn.
The moon was the winter season;
those waters in heaven were the cool season (*śiśira*);
that which was the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was the spring season, and the wind that was the spring season is this very spring season here now.

Now, that speech which was the summer and Agni who was the summer, he is this very summer here now. Now, that sight which was the rainy season and Parjanya who was the rains, those are these very rains here now. Now, that hearing which was the autumn and Āditya who was the autumn, she is this very autumn here now.
Now, that which was the mind became the winter season; and that which was the moon became this winter season as it exists now.
Now, those waters which were in the person became the cool season (*śiśira*); and those waters which are in the sky became that cool season as it exists now. 51.
These six seasons are the six directions. These seasons are in union with the directions: this eastern direction is in union with spring; this [southern direction] is in union with summer.
"This is for the rains, this for the autumn, that for the winter, and this for the cool season.
Just as a wife gazes at her husband without blinking, even so do these [seasons] gaze upon him who knows this as he undergoes consecration.
Because he is looked upon by the quarters (*diś*), therefore he is consecrated (*dīkṣita*).
When he is about to be consecrated, he should worship the sun, saying: "O Goddess, you are the consecrated one.
As such, you take away the splendor, sensory power, vigor, and fame of one who is being consecrated."
"Do not take away my brilliance, sensory power, vigor, and fame;
follow your consecration with my consecration"— thus he speaks,
and then he ascends after the seasons.
Those seasons which existed from the seasons themselves,
prior to the sun and the moon,
by which one discerns the intermediate points and the cardinal directions.
"I ascend after them with austerity and with the sacred word," thus he ascends after the vital breaths and the seasons— "those seasons which were prior to the moon."
"They have brought forth the Ṛc, the Vāc, and the Brahman"—
for they brought forth one who knows thus— "by whom, perceiving, [he knows] the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions."
"I ascend after them with austerity and with the sacred word (*brahman*).
With this, he ascends after the divine seasons.
"He who is the one season and the three seasons..."
vv Those which are the six and twenty-four seasons;
vw those which are the twelve and seventeen, and also the twenty;
vx may I ascend after them with fervor and with the sacred word.

Thus he ascends after these seasons. Being thus encompassed by these seasons, just as one who is encompassed by those seasons [survives], so indeed does he, unharmed, reach the completion of the year.
Season after season indeed falls into alignment for one who knows thus.
Keśin Dārbhya consecrated himself with two darbha leaves.
Then, having heard this, Yājñasena became a golden swan and perched upon the sacrificial post.
Keśin addressed him by name, saying, "O Keśin!
He (Yājñasena) became enraged, thinking, "I am an elder, the king of the Pañcālas."
"I am indeed consecrated.
"Who then would dare to address me by my name?
He said, "Do not be angry."
I have been saluted by him because I was the king of this people before you. Indeed, I have been saluted by him because you are not yet consecrated.
You know the imperishability of sacrifices and charitable works.
"I know initiation," he said. "Let us both explain it.
He replied: "Agni is initiated; the earth is initiation. Vāyu is initiated; the intermediate space is initiation. Āditya is initiated..."
The sky is consecration; Prajāpati is the consecrated one; the mind is consecration.

He should consecrate himself with that consecration by which Agni was consecrated; he consecrates himself with that consecration by which Vāyu was consecrated; he consecrates himself with that consecration by which Āditya was consecrated; he [consecrates himself] with that...
"By means of initiation Prajāpati was initiated; through that initiation he became 'the Initiated'.
Then the other said:

When giving to the Brahman priest, he should say: "O Brahman, I give you the mind; I redeem that with this; O Brahman, I give this. Whatever he intends to give, if it be the mind, the mind is indeed the moon; thus he gives the moon to him.

As long as the moon does not wane, so long does that which has been given to him not wane. When giving to the *hotṛ*, he should say: "O *hotṛ*, I give you speech; I redeem it with this; O *hotṛ*, I give this," whenever there is something he intends to give.
When he gives speech, since speech is indeed Agni, he thereby gives Agni to him.
As long as Agni is not exhausted, so long does that which has been given to him remain unexhausted. When giving to the Adhvaryu, he should say: "O Adhvaryu, I give you breath; I redeem it with this."
"O Adhvaryu, I shall give this," he says when he intends to give something.
When he gives the breath, since the breath is indeed Vāyu, he thereby gives Vāyu to him. As long as Vāyu does not perish, so long does that which has been given to him not perish.

When giving to the Udgātṛ, he should say: "O Udgātṛ, I give you the eye; I redeem that with this; O Udgātṛ, here I give this. Whatever he intends to give, if it be the eye—since the eye is indeed the sun—he thereby gives the sun to him.
As long as the sun does not perish, so long does his *sattva* not perish.
When giving to the *sadasya*, he should say: "I give myself to you; I redeem him with this; I give this to the *sadasya*.
This refers to whatever one might have to give.
When he gives himself, the self is indeed space; it is space that he thus gives to him. As long as space is not exhausted, so long is what has been given to him not exhausted.
When giving to the *hotraka*s, he should say: "O *hotraka*s, I give you the ear; I redeem this with this [gift]."
The *hotṛ*s [should think], "I shall give this," regarding whatever he intends to give.
When he gives the sense of hearing (*śrotra*), the quarters (*diś*) are indeed the sense of hearing; it is to the quarters that he thus gives it.
As long as the quarters do not perish, so long does what has been given by him not perish.
While giving to the *prasarpakas*, he should say: "O *prasarpakas*, I give you hair; I redeem it with this;
O *prasarpakas*, I give this. Whatever he intends to give, when he gives hair—hair being indeed the plants and trees—it is the plants and trees themselves that he gives to them.
He gives that.
As long as the plants and trees are not exhausted, so long does what he has given remain inexhaustible for him. This is the imperishability of his sacrificial and charitable works.
He who thus knows this imperishability of sacrifice and pious works—his sacrifice and pious works are not exhausted.
Regarding this, they say: "Speech indeed is the consecrated one; speech is the consecration; speech sustains all this.
"In speech, indeed, all this is sustained"—thus did those two converse with each other.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyanī said: "One should undergo initiation with the thought, 'I am initiated with the *Rathantara*, I am initiated with the *Vāmadevya*, I am initiated with the *Bṛhat*.
Then one should release [the vow] with the thought, 'I release with the *Bṛhat*, I release with the *Vāmadevya*, I release with the *Rathantara*.'"
This is both the application and the release of the consecration (*dīkṣā*).
He who thus knows this application and release of the consecration becomes truly more prosperous.
Va. Hṛtsvāśaya Āllakeya was a pupil of Dhaumya Dantāla. Vb. Now, Dhaumya Dantāla had mastered the three Vedas up to their very foundations.
Vc. Therefore, having taught him the Sāmaveda, he declared: "I shall undergo initiation for a year."
Then, indeed, they used to go about from that city asking one another, "We shall undergo initiation for the sake of the year.
And so, having gathered together, they would sit, reproaching one another's choice of partners while inquiring after their private conduct.

They used to undergo initiation for as many [days] as they could manage. Indeed, this was always their very wish. That becomes a sacrificial session (*sattra*) when they rise after having made that very man a Brahmin, together with one who has not been addressed as a non-Brahmin.
They undergo initiation.
Therefore, one should undergo initiation together with one who has not been addressed by a Brāhmaṇa.
Indeed, for this kinsman of the Rājanya, a tiger skin, a gem, and gold are placed [as sacrificial gifts].
Having sent it to a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), he would say: "I shall undergo initiation for the sake of the year; instruct me.
They used to consider that [instruction] as something to be imparted to that kinsman of the royal class (rājanyabandhu).
He, wandering in that very manner, came to Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi.
He said to him, "O Prācīnayogya, I shall undergo initiation for the year-long rite;
O venerable sir, instruct me."
"So be it. Having spoken thus, he pleased him;
then he approached him.
When he had taught him this arrangement, followed it with the *abhyūha*, and performed the *prastāva* and *pratihāra*,
he then instructed him further,
saying: "This, indeed, is the year."
"This is his very path leading to the gods; these are the two tracks, this is the goal.
When he knows this thus, he indeed reaches the completion of the year unharmed. Prajāpati is indeed the Person.
Prajāpati is the year.

That person who is this very space in the intermediate region—that indeed is that person. Because it is full, he does not find rest in the intermediate region; because it is full, he does not find rest therein.
Moreover, because one looks within this entire [space], it is called *antarikṣa*. Moreover, because this all is joined (*yuta*) together, it is *vāyu*.
Moreover, because this all blows (*vāti*), it is *vāta*.
Of this very space, that which is the sun is its self, being well-concealed;
he is this person in the sun. Now, that which is the space beyond that, of that the moon is its self, being well-concealed.
This is that person in the moon.
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani used to say: "He is not to be thought of as distinct;
for he who is this person in the eye, he is indeed this one in the sun and he is this one in the moon."
One attains him by this very same human method. 56.
The Prāyaṇīya Atirātra is indeed breath. 57. JB 2.57.
For breath indeed causes all this to breathe; because it caused [all] to breathe (*prāṇayat*), therefore it is called *prāṇa*.
The day of the *ārambhaṇīya* (opening) rite is speech itself.
For by speech indeed the entire year and all sacrificial rites are undertaken; therefore, on the day of the introductory rite (*ārambhaṇīya*), all forms are performed,
for all forms are in speech.
This is one *abhiplava*, this is one, this is one, this is one.
Of this *abhiplava*, this is the first day;
of it, this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing.
This indeed is the second day.
Of that [day], this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing.
This indeed is the Vairūpa, the third day.
Of that [sacrifice], this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing.
This indeed is the *śākvara* fifth day.
Therefore, by embracing it with this, one is able [to perform it].
Of this [sacrifice], this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing.
This indeed is the Raivata, the sixth day.
Therefore, he eats with this [verse].
Of this [Abhiplava], this indeed is the morning pressing, this the midday pressing, and this the third pressing.
Thus belongs to this Abhiplava, thus to this, and thus to this.
This very [Pṛṣṭhya] is the self.
These indeed are the nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The introductory day (*prāyaṇīyam ahar*) is threefold; for the vital breath has caused all this to breathe.
Because it has caused [them] to breathe, therefore also this is called the introductory day.
These very necks are the fifteenth day;
the necks are indeed vigor and strength.
The necks are vigor.
*vac*: vigor is the fifteenfold [stoma]. *vad*: therefore animals carry burdens with their necks.
*vae*: these eight clavicles, these eight upward-tending clavicles—the seventeenfold [stoma].
That indeed is the seventeenth day.
This very belly is the twenty-first day;
for all the *stomas* are perfected in the twenty-first.
All food is established within the belly.
57. There are these thirteen *pariśavas*; these thirteen are the egg-*pariśavas*, making twenty-seven.
That very [rite] is the Triṇava day.
These thirty-three Pṛṣṭha-sections, together with the Kiṃkālukās,
constitute that very Trayastriṃśa day.
This is the Abhijit; this is the Viśvajit; the white and the black are the pupils.
These three are the Svarasāmans; these three are [the others]; this is the Viṣuvat.
The Go and Āyus are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath.
These very ten vital breaths are the Daśarātra;
the mind itself is the Mahāvratīya day;
and the upward-breath (udāna) is the Udayanīya Atirātra.
These are the ten vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the ten *stomas*, and the ten meters (*chandas*).
These indeed are the seven principal vital breaths; two are downward, and the tenth is in the navel.
These indeed are the *stomas* of the six-day *pṛṣṭhya* sacrifice.
The Chandomas are the twenty-five-fold [stoma].
These seven meters, increasing by four syllables each, together with the Virāj of two feet and the Atichandas, are divided into four groups.
The Gāyatrī is indeed the vital breath; the Uṣṇih and Kakubh are the two eyes; the Jagatī is the ear; the Anuṣṭubh is speech; and the Bṛhatī is the mind.
The self is the *paṅkti*, strength is the *triṣṭubh*;
stability is the *dvipadā*, the flesh is the *virāj*, and the bodies are the *aticchandas*.
Of these seven meters, each increasing by four syllables, they amount to twelve sets of twenty-one.
/58/ JB 2.59 |va The *gāyatrī*, the *uṣṇih*, and the *anuṣṭubh* have eighty-four syllables.
Those four [groups] consist of twenty-one [verses] each.
There are eighty-four syllables in the *paṅkti* and the *triṣṭubh*;
those four [groups] consist of twenty-one [verses] each.
The Bṛhatī and the Jagatī have eighty-four syllables.
Those four [stomas] are twenty-one-fold.
Now, there are one thousand syllables in three meters.
A verse of twenty syllables is the *dvipadā*;
one of thirty syllables is the *virāj*;
and one of sixty syllables is the *aticchandas*.
Those [syllables] amount to one thousand and ten;
from that, he takes two;
thus, they become twelve *trivṛt*s.
He places these twelve threefold ones upon the twenty-one-fold [stoma] of the twelfth month.
These become twelve months consisting of thirty days each; thus, these meters attain the threefold stoma. 59.
JB 2.60 |va The twenty-first, the breath, the fires, and the sun;
vb And as for the two syllables, they are the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*, they are day and night.
That [becomes] half a month, that a month, that a season, that a year.
Regarding this they say: "The vital breaths are the meters, and the meters are the *stomas*"; they say this—how then does the sacrificer attain the meters through the vital breaths?

Through the meters, through the *stomas*, through the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* [sāmans], through day and night, through the half-month, through the month, through the season, and through the year. From where is the year born? Where is it established?
He should know: "I am indeed the year; I am established in myself. For one who knows thus, the year is truly born, and it is established in one who knows thus.
Moreover, they say that the sun itself is the year.
For all glory is indeed this, all fame is this, and all the gods are gathered here; therefore, the sun alone is the year.
Of that [year], what shines is the *saṃvat*, and that black circle in its center is the *sara*; thus with respect to the deities.
Now, with reference to the self:
this very person who is in the eye is the year.
That which is white in him is the *saṃvat* (the first part of the year); that black circle in the middle is the *sara* (the second part).
Now they say: "The year is indeed the Āditya, and the moon is the *saras* (lake/flow). He (the sun) flows toward it;
he reaches it on the full moon day."

Regarding this, they say: "The breath (*prāṇa*) is the *saṃvat* and speech (*vāk*) is the *saras*, for by means of these two one attains [the goal]. Now, the path leading to the gods for this very year-sacrifice (*saṃvatsara*) consists precisely of the *agniṣṭoma-sāmans*. 60.
These, indeed, are called the Rauhiṇakas;
by means of these, the gods ascended to the heavenly world.
Because he ascended, they are called *rohiṇaka*s;
therefore, we perform the *agniṣṭomasāman*s every single day.
Now, as for the two paths, they are the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*.
By means of these two, indeed, this [Sāman] proceeds.
Therefore, we perform both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara at the Atirātra; thus our Sāman is complete, it carries the sacrifice when joined, and by means of the complete Sāman, may we attain the Ṛc.
Now,
as for the goal: that person who is there in the sun and this person here within the self— one should venerate this very thing as the "attainment of Prajāpati."
By this very path, Prajāpati attained this prosperity and achieved this distinction.
He who knows this attains that same prosperity and achieves that same distinction which Prajāpati attained and achieved. 61.
JB 2.62 |va This one who shines yonder is indeed the consecrated one.
vb He, having been consecrated, has attained sensory power, preeminence, and excellence.
Those rays of his that go downward are his beard; those that go upward are his hair.
Day and night are the form of the black antelope skin:
day is the form of the white one, and night is the form of the black one.
Now, that which is this orb is water, it is food, it is the immortal.
Within this very orb is the person consisting of splendor and consisting of the Vedic meters.
He is the vital breath; he is Indra; he is Prajāpati; he is the consecrated one.
This is indeed encompassed by the consecration (dīkṣā) itself. Then he releases food for these creatures;
these very quarters were his wives.
The three golden directions surpassed it;
this southern direction is indeed the one most devoted to him. Therefore, he turns back toward this very direction.
Even if it rises from the north, it nevertheless turns back toward this very [south]. Therefore, one should place the wife whom he loves on the southern side. 62/ JB 2.63.
He girds the first [wife], makes her recite the first [formula], and she comes to the full vessel first;
"You are the wives who do not exclude," [he says].
Thus the sacrificial rite is completed toward the north.
Thus with reference to the deities.
Now with reference to the self:
this very person who is in the eye is the consecrated one.
Those eyelashes of his that are directed downward are the beard; those that are directed upward are the hair of the head.
That which is white and black is the form of the black antelope skin;
the white is the form of the white, and the black is the form of the black.
Now, that which is this orb is water, it is food, it is immortality.
Within this very orb is a person consisting of splendor, consisting of the meters;
he is Prāṇa, he is Indra, he is Prajāpati, he is the consecrated one (dīkṣita).

When one who knows this undergoes initiation, he becomes initiated for the sake of that very power, preeminence, and excellence which this [sun] here possesses; even so does he become initiated for the sake of power, preeminence, and excellence.
Therefore, when one who knows this is initiated, it is possible for kingdoms to tremble before him, for he is like a hole in the ground that has been filled with dust.
He becomes equal [to them].
For thus he, having been consecrated, attains this preeminence, this excellence of the sense-organ.
Therefore, indeed, he addresses everyone—the teacher, the father, and the kṣatriya—with the same [respectful] speech.
For thus does he become consecrated for this faculty, which is preeminent and supreme. 63.
He speaks speech that is full of insight. JB 2.64.
Food is indeed *vicakṣaṇa*.
Thus he speaks speech that possesses food;
he speaks speech that possesses *vicakṣaṇa*.
Soma, indeed, is the far-seeing; Soma is food. Thus he utters speech that possesses food.
He speaks speech that is discerning. The discerning one is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
speech is its mate.
Thus he speaks speech that possesses a mate;
he speaks speech that possesses discernment; for food is indeed discernment.
For by means of food these creatures see;
therefore he bestows food upon these creatures. When he should give him the vow-food, he should consume everything indeed, for the sake of securing all food.
If, however, there should be a remainder, he should say to the one who has administered the vow, "Eat it or drink it. If, however,
the one who has administered the vow is accustomed to eating without leaving remnants, or if there should be a remainder, he should sprinkle it with water and say, "Pour it out in the shade."
He should say, "It must be completely covered with herbs. He then sprinkles the roots of the herbs.
Where one who knows thus is consecrated, Parjanya becomes rain-giving.
"The consecrated ones have indeed yearned for water," so they say here.

When the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice has been completed, when the Adhvaryu has anointed him, and when he has purified himself, then he should worship this Āditya, saying: "Thou art the deity of the consecrated."
"O Vx, you take away the sensory power, the seniority, the preeminence, and the glory of one who is being consecrated.
O Vy, do not take away my sensory power, my seniority, my preeminence, and my glory.
O Vz, following your consecration, may I be consecrated."
For him, as he undergoes initiation, that deity does not take away his sensory power, his seniority, his excellence, or his glory.
Having anointed him and led him forward, the Adhvaryu offers the *audgrahaṇa* oblations.

When he offers the Audgrahaṇa oblations, when he hands him the Udumbara staff, and when he stands before this Āhavanīya fire, he should pray: "By my speech, may my consecrated speech be united with Agni;
by my breath, may my consecrated breath be united with Vāyu; by my eye, may my consecrated eye be united with Sūrya."
"May my mind, consecrated by my mind, be united with Prajāpati.
Thus, by means of these uninjured deities, he consecrates these very deities.
Then he says: "Agni is consecrated; the earth is the consecration. May that consecration consecrate me; through that consecration, may I be consecrated."
Vāyu is consecrated; the intermediate region is the consecration. May that consecration consecrate me; by that consecration I am consecrated.
Āditya is consecrated; the sky is the consecration. May that consecration consecrate me; by that consecration I am consecrated.
Prajāpati is consecrated; the mind is the consecration. May that consecration consecrate me; by that consecration I am consecrated.
"May my speech be consecrated along with the *ṛc*s; may my mind be consecrated with the *yajus* verses; may my breath be consecrated with the *sāman* chants. May King Soma consecrate my faith.

I am consecrated by the *ṛc*, I am consecrated by the *yajus*, I am consecrated by the *sāman*; I am consecrated by the earth, I am consecrated by the intermediate space, I am consecrated by the sky."
In this regard, the consecrated one is the whole. Now, for him whose these worlds are unconsecrated, whose meters are unconsecrated, and whose King Soma is unconsecrated— 65/JB 2.66.
One should fulfill that desire of his. Now, indeed, one who knows this attains all desires even while being consecrated;
therefore, during the consecrations, one should not serve the king [with food].
