Thus, consecrated by Soma, he becomes radiant and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasin).
They cry out three times; these worlds are indeed three. Thus they establish his fame in these very worlds. There are one hundred and eight *stotriya* verses for it.
Then, that which is the hundred is the Virāj;
the Kṣatra is the Virāj;
and those which are the eight are the Gāyatrī.
*Ve*: Radiance (*tejas*) and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) are the *gāyatrī*. *Vf*: Thus he places radiance and spiritual luster before the *kṣatra*;
therefore, the *brāhmaṇa* is the domestic priest (*purohita*) of the *kṣatriya*.

He who desires the office of a domestic priest (*purodhā*) should sacrifice with this; he attains the office of a domestic priest. Some, indeed, perform it with only a single *chandas*, namely the *gāyatra* alone throughout; for Bṛhaspati is *gāyatra*.
The *gāyatrī* is indeed the sacred word (*brahman*).

"Brahman is Bṛhaspati; through the Brahman, may we prosper in Brahman-splendor. Those who perform it in this manner indeed thereby attain Agni among the deities, the Gāyatrī among the meters, and this world.
For them, the other deities are excluded, as are the other meters, the other gods, the other worlds,
and the other desires. Therefore, one should perform [the ritual] according to the meter for all the deities and all the meters.
For the attainment of all the gods, all the worlds, and all desires;
for him, the *bṛhat* of Bṛhaspati becomes the prescribed *sāman* during the *ārbhava-pavamāna*.
For this is indeed the *Bṛhaspatisava*.
In this way, they bring the *stoma* into harmony with its proper form.
Now, this is the nest of Indra and Agni.
Indra and Agni desired: "Being equal among the gods, may we attain preeminence;
through this common sacrifice, may we achieve common prosperity.
They beheld this sacrifice.
They two brought it; they two sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, indeed, while remaining among their equals, they two attained preeminence among the gods by means of that which was common.
Through sacrifice, they two attained equal prosperity.
That Brahman is indeed Agni;
Indra is the Kṣatra.
This [stoma], indeed, becomes both the threefold (*trivṛt*) and the fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*).
The threefold is the Brahman;
the fifteenfold is the Kṣatra.
By means of the *trivṛt* [stoma], Agni attained preeminence; by means of the *pañcadaśa*, Indra.
Both the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* *sāmans* belong to him.
The *rathaṃtara* is indeed the *brahman*, and the *bṛhat* is the *kṣatra*.
By means of the *rathaṃtara* alone, Agni attained preeminence; by means of the *bṛhat*, Indra.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya should both desire, "May we attain preeminence among our own equals who are alike;
may we prosper through a common sacrifice and achieve equal prosperity," then they [should perform] this [sacrifice].
The two of them should sacrifice;
being equals among their own kin, they attain preeminence, and through this common sacrifice, they achieve equal prosperity.
By means of the *trivṛt* [stoma] alone, the Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; by means of the *pañcadaśa*, the Rājanya.
By means of the *rathantara* [sāman] alone, the Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; by means of the *bṛhat*, the Rājanya. Thus, these *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* stotras become interwoven. 132.
Therefore, it is the nest of Indra and Agni. Regarding this, they say: "In the sacrificial session (sattra), that which consists of the Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa [stomas] is interwoven."
These stotras are interwoven as "the threefold" and "the fifteenfold.

There should be exactly six threefold stotras and six fifteenfold ones. Those that are prior to the midday pressing should be the threefold ones, and those that follow it should be the [fifteenfold ones].
Regarding the fifteenfold [stomas]:
the midday pressing should indeed be fifteenfold, with the *trivṛt* as the *pṛṣṭha* chant for the Hotṛ.
Upon that fifteenfold midday pressing, they arrange the *rathantara*.
The *rathantara* is indeed the *brahman*, and the fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*) is the *kṣatra*.
Thus, they establish the *brahman* upon the *kṣatra*.
Now, as for the fact that the threefold (*trivṛt*) is the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ—the threefold is the *brahman* and the *bṛhat* is the *kṣatra*; thus, it is the *kṣatra* itself [that is established].
They establish that as Brahman.
Thus, these two, having established themselves in one another, attained preeminence.
Of these two, this [Brahman] is indeed invincible.

He who knows this indeed conquers unconquerable fame, unconquerable prosperity, and the unconquerable heavenly world. Furthermore, because these two *stotras* of the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* stomas are interwoven, offspring and cattle are born from an interwoven union; it is for the sake of procreation.

Moreover, the *stomas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); these vital breaths are interwoven so that there may be no wandering away from them. Therefore, these *stotras* consisting of the threefold and fifteenfold [verses] should be interwoven.
For him, the *aindrāgna-sāman*, the *ādiṣṭa-sāman*, occurs during the midday *pavamāna*.
For this sacrifice belongs to Indra and Agni;
thus they bring the *stoma* into fulfillment by means of its corresponding form.
Now follows this Agniṣṭut. Indeed, all beings turned against Indra, saying: "He slew Tvaṣṭṛ’s three-headed son;
he gave the Yatis to the hyenas; he slew those with mouths of wounds; he struck back at Bṛhaspati; he overstepped the compact that had been made."
"He cut off the head of Namuci, the Asura"—from these sins against the gods.
He wandered about in the forest alone, not descending among the gods.
He then said to the gods, "Sacrifice for me!"
"No," they said.
"These bonds have indeed been passed by you; these offenses against the gods have been committed. We will not perform the sacrifice for you.
Now, among the gods, Agni alone was his most intimate friend.
He then said to Agni, "Sacrifice for me. "So be it," he replied. "In that case, I wish to find among the gods one with whom I may sacrifice for you."
He did not find among the gods that one with whom he might have caused him to sacrifice.
He said, "Indeed, I do not find among the gods anyone with whom I might cause you to sacrifice. [The other replied,] "Then you yourself must cause me to sacrifice."
"So be it," he said.
That Agni then extended this Agniṣṭut sacrifice for himself; with it, he caused him to perform the sacrifice.
It instantly burned away all his evil. Just as a snake might cast off its slough, or as one might pull a reed from its sheath, even so was he released from all evil.
This very one, having its evil struck away, shines; this indeed is Indra. He who has been spoken against, or against whom something has been said, should sacrifice with this [offering];
instantly it burns away all his evil.
Just as a snake might free itself from its slough, or just as one might pull out a blade of grass from its sheath, even so does he free himself from all evil. 134/ JB 2.135
He who, having committed a sin with his mouth, might think, "I shall sacrifice with the Trivṛt Agniṣṭut"—
for he indeed commits a sin with his mouth who speaks what should not be spoken;
the Trivṛt, among the Stomas, is indeed the mouth.
By that very means, they strike away evil from the mouth itself.
Now, he who, having committed evil with his two arms, might think, "I shall sacrifice with the fifteen-fold Agniṣṭut"—
he indeed commits evil with his two arms who strikes down one who should not be struck down.
The arms, indeed, are the fifteen-fold hymns (*pañcadaśa-stoma*).
By means of them, they strike away evil with their very arms. Now, if one should think that he has committed sin with his belly, he should sacrifice with the seventeen-fold *agniṣṭut*.
Verily, he who eats the food of one whose food should not be eaten commits sin with his belly.
The belly, indeed, is [the essence] of the seventeenfold hymns;
by means of that, they strike away evil from the belly itself.
Now, if one should think that he has committed a sin with his feet, he should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut consisting of twenty-one [verses].
For he indeed commits a sin with his feet who goes among the people;
the twenty-one-fold is the firm foundation of the *stomas*.
By that very act, they strike away evil with their feet.
Furthermore, they say: "One should sacrifice by means of this very Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma.
In that regard, because its *bahiṣpavamāna* chant consists of nine verses (*trivṛt*), one strikes away evil from the mouth itself by means of it.

Now, in that there are fifteen *ājya* stotras and the midday pressing consists of fifteen [verses], they thereby strike away evil by means of the two arms. And in that there are seventeen *pṛṣṭha* stotras and the third pressing consists of seventeen [verses], they thereby [strike away evil] from the belly.
They strike away evil.
Now, in that the twenty-one-fold *agniṣṭomasāman* occurs, they strike away evil by means of the feet themselves. 135.
One desiring splendor and desiring sacred luster should sacrifice with the *trivṛt*; one desiring vigor with the *agniṣṭut* [stoma]; one desiring cattle with the *pañcadaśa*;
one desiring procreation with the *saptadaśa*; and one desiring a firm foundation with the *ekaviṃśa*.
One desiring vigor [should sacrifice] with the twenty-sevenfold [stoma], one desiring glory with the thirty-threefold.
Regarding this, they say: "This fourfold-stoma Agniṣṭoma is indeed the mouth of all;
one should sacrifice with that alone."
"This indeed is the Trivṛt; this is the Pañcadaśa; this is the Saptadaśa; this is the Ekaviṃśa.
For Agni is dependent upon these vital breaths. He who, though being learned in the Vedas, does not shine forth, should sacrifice with this [rite]."
Just as a gold ornament (*niṣka*) seized by impurity does not shine, even so it is with one who, though learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*), does not shine.
Indeed, they throw him into the fire who officiates for another with the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice.
It is just as if one were to throw a gold ornament seized by impurity into the fire and burn away all its impurity with a hammer.
In this way, they indeed strike away all his evil;

he becomes one whose evil is struck away, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*). Furthermore, they say: "If cattle do not thrive in a place that is otherwise suitable for cattle, one should perform this sacrifice there."
Just as indeed Jaratkārṣa was, so is he in whose possession cattle do not find delight while they are there.
For him, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is performed upon the *revatī* verses.
The *revatīs* are indeed the waters.
Verily, they throw this man into the fire who they cause to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut.
It is as if one were to set Jaratkakṣa ablaze with fire and then douse him with water; in that [fire], there would be no beauty.
Herbs would grow, and in them cattle would find delight; even so do all cattle find delight in this [fire-altar].
"O Agni, purify our lives"—this verse addressed to Agni Pavamāna becomes the opening (pratipad).
Regarding this they say: "Those who begin with the verses addressed to Pavamāna are indeed deprived of these vital breaths."
In that this *agnipāvamānī* serves as the introductory verse (*pratipad*), and since Vāyu is indeed breath, they thus prosper through the vital breaths.
With the words, "O Agni, purifier, for thy radiance," food is indeed the purifier; thus they endow him with the eating of food.
Moreover, Vāyu is indeed the purifier (pāvaka), and Vāyu is breath; thus they cause him to prosper with his vital breaths in due order.
"Agni, most pure in his vows"—for he who is falsely accused becomes, as it were, impure.
By this [verse], they make him pure, purified, and fit for sacrifice.
For that [laud), there are these *bṛhatī* verses of the midday *pavamāna*: "O Agnis, at every sacrifice (*yajñā-yajñā vaḥ*)."
Indeed, they cast him into the fire who cause him to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut.
With the words, "And [he is] the protector of our bodies," the sacrificer thus entrusts his body to Agni Vaiśvānara.
For this sacrifice, the Rathantara serves as the *pṛṣṭha* stotra upon the Nārmedha verses beginning with "Protect us, O Agni, for our unity."
With these [verses], Nṛmedha Auśija indeed drove away the flames of Agni.
By means of these very [verses], he drives away the flames of Agni.
For this [sacrifice], the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is performed upon those Aponaptrīya verses beginning with "śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye."
The waters, indeed, are the Aponaptrīyas.
For they throw this man into the fire whom they cause to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut.

Just as one might sprinkle water upon what has been burnt by fire, so too is that for the sake of pacification. Regarding this, they say: "If one sprinkles water upon what has been burnt by fire, it either spreads further or becomes a skin disease (*kilāsa*)."
"O Vāyu, come to our sacrifice that touches the sky with your benevolent thoughts"—in these very verses addressed to Vāyu, the rite should be performed;
for Vāyu is peace, and it is for the sake of peace, so that there may be no burning by fire. Regarding this they say: "If one fans a kindled fire with wind, it indeed burns even more intensely."
"Or rather, this is indeed radiance. Regarding that, they say: "The sacrificer should desire that he might shine;
for it is Vāyu alone who shines for the sake of radiance."
And as for [the fact that] Vāyu is indeed for peace,
therefore this [rite] should be performed with these very verses containing [the word] "Vāyu.
Its sacrificial fee consists of a goat and gold.
The goat belongs to Agni, and gold does not belong to Agni; moreover, they say that the draft-ox is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
for the draft-ox carries, and Agni carries the oblation to the gods.
In this way, they bring the *stoma* into perfection through its corresponding form.
Now, this is the *Indrastoma*.
Indra, indeed, desired: "May I attain preeminence among all the gods.
He saw this sacrifice;
he took it up.
He sacrificed with it. Thereupon, he indeed attained preeminence among all the gods.
He who knows this attains preeminence among his own people.
In the beginning, the sacrifice indeed belonged to Indra;
prosperity indeed resided in him.
For the sacrifice is truly the prosperity of the gods.
Vṛtra indeed grew stronger against him.
He fled to the gods, saying, "With your strength, let me slay this Vṛtra. They said to him, "In that case, you must offer to us that sacrifice which is exclusively yours alone."
Therefore, when the king desires to conquer, they seek the surrender of the subjects;
and so the king, desiring to conquer, grants the surrender of the subjects themselves.
He gave the morning pressing to the Vasus and the midday pressing to the Rudras.
The third pressing belongs to the Ādityas and to the Viśvedevas;
with them, Indra slew Vṛtra by his strength;
the gods conquered the Asuras.
Having slain Vṛtra and conquered, he saw these splendors of theirs shining separately. Misfortune found him.
He thought: "How indeed might I gather these splendors of theirs together?"
He sacrificed with this very sacrifice.
By it, he appropriated all the prosperity of those [others].
He who knows thus appropriates the prosperity of his hateful rival. 139.

JB 2.140 |va He becomes entirely connected with the verses dedicated to Indra |vb The morning pressing takes place with verses dedicated to Indra, the midday pressing with verses dedicated to Indra, and [the third pressing] with verses dedicated to Indra.
The third pressing. Now, in that the morning pressing, though it belongs to the Gāyatrī, is performed with verses addressed to Indra, he thereby secures for himself the sacrifice of the Vasus.

Now, in that the midday pressing, though it belongs to the *triṣṭubh* metre, is performed with verses addressed to Indra, he thereby appropriated the sacrifice for the Rudras. And in that the third pressing, though it belongs to the *jagatī* metre, is performed with verses addressed to Indra, he thereby appropriated the sacrifice for the Ādityas.

He appropriated [the portion] of all the gods. Then the Viśas, having taken possession of the sacrifice, approached him, saying, "Grant us a share in the sacrifice; we shall be your subjects. They approached him just as wives approach their husband.

He assigned the Vasus to the morning pressing, the Rudras to the midday pressing, the Ādityas to the third pressing, and all the gods to [all of them]. Just as a king, having conquered, would assign shares in his own wealth to his dependents, even so did he assign them.
Therefore, they recite: "For Indra, accompanied by the Vasus, accompanied by the Rudras, accompanied by the Ādityas, accompanied by the Viśve Devas.
That [stoma] becomes the fifteenfold;
for the fifteenfold is indeed the thunderbolt.
Indra is the vajra;
this sacrifice belongs to Indra, and it is performed with his characteristic marks;
it is an Ukthya sacrifice.
The *viṭ* (the people) are indeed the hymns (*ukthas*). They thus place the ruling power (*kṣatra*) above the people. Therefore, the *kṣatriya* is placed above the people.
If one should desire prosperity (*śrī*), he should sacrifice with this [rite]. Prosperity is the ruling power (*kṣatra*); he attains prosperity through this sacrifice of the ruler. 140/ JB 2.141
Now this is the Vighana [stotra].
Prajāpati created the gods— the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas—
and he bestowed upon them both the sacrifice and these worlds.
He gave the morning pressing to the Vasus, the midday pressing to the Rudras, and the third pressing to the Ādityas.
He gave this world to the Vasus, the intermediate space to the Rudras, and yonder world to the Ādityas.
Then he created Indra.
He saw all this [world] divided among them.
He said: "Since all this has been divided among them, for what purpose then have you created me? They replied:
"We have created you for preeminence and sovereignty over these."
"How shall I become their chief and sovereign? he thought.
"Go and tell them," he said, "that Prajāpati did not create you for preeminence or sovereignty.
He went and said, "Prajāpati did not create you for preeminence or sovereignty."
They said, "We alone are the best; we are the lords, for we are the eldest," and so they did not understand. He returned and said, "These [others] do not know what you say.
He saw this sacrifice.
He fetched it;
with it, he caused him to sacrifice.
Having sacrificed, he indeed struck down all his adversaries.
That which was struck down is the "striking down" (*vighana*) nature of the *vighana*. Indeed, he who knows this strikes down his hateful rival. 141.

When he had conquered, all the gods gathered around him on every side: the Vasus in front, the Rudras to the south, the Ādityas behind, the Maruts to the north, the Viśve Devas above, and the Sādhyas, the Āptyas, and the Aṅgirasas below. This indeed is the divine glory, the divine assembly, the divine congregation.
He who knows this attains that divine glory, that divine assembly, that divine congregation.
This very [sacrifice] amounts to six *bṛhatī* verses.
There are six seasons; the year is prosperity.
Verily, he has thus bestowed prosperity upon him.
This very one, having ascended to this glory among the seasons and the year, shines forth.
For him, there are these *satobṛhatī* verses beginning with "The ancient nectar, that which was first worthy of praise," which serve as the portion for the *gāyatrī*.
The *gāyatrī* is indeed the sacred formulation (*brahman*).

The *bṛhatī* is the nobility (*kṣatra*). Thus, he anoints the spiritual power (*brahman*) with glory. For one who knows this, although he is spiritual power, his manifestation becomes like that of nobility. 142.
They chant while those [verses] are interwoven; for from an interwoven pair, offspring and cattle are produced—this is for the sake of procreation. Moreover, a man is indeed interwoven with evils.
By means of these very interwoven [verses], he strikes away the interwoven evils.
Regarding those [verses], the *gāyatra* has its Brāhmaṇa explained;
now follows the *āmahīyava*, whose Brāhmaṇa has also been explained.
Now follows the *sauparṇa* [sāman], whose Brāhmaṇa has been stated.
Now follows the *satrāsāhīya*, for the sake of victory: "May he completely overcome him who is to be overcome by him."
|vi Now, elevation and suppression are for the sake of elevating and suppressing what is bad and what is superior, respectively.
|vj Now, the *viśoviśīya* and the *sadoviśīya*.
|vk By means of the *viśoviśīya*, Indra ascended over the gods.
With the [verse] "Enter the assembly," he indeed made them enter the assembly by means of the *sadoviśīya* chant.
Now, these [verses] are *triṣṭubh*s; upon them the *brahmasāman* is chanted.
The *brahmasāman* is indeed the *brahman*;
the *triṣṭubh* is the *kṣatra*.
This *brahmasāman* is indeed the desire of the sacrificer.
In its own very abode, they thus satisfy the sacrificer with his desires.
These [verses] are the *padabrāhmaṇas*.
"That indeed was the eldest in the worlds"— for he is Prajāpati;
"from whom was born the fierce one of brilliant valor"— for he is Indra.

"Born at once, he strikes down his enemies"—for as soon as he was born, he indeed struck down all adversaries. "Him whom all the helpers (ūmāḥ) rejoice in"—the helpers are indeed the seasons; they thus rejoice after him.
"Increasing in strength, possessing abundant power, he, the enemy, instills fear in the Dāsa"—he is indeed Indra.

"Both the in-breath and the out-breath, the winner; they have shouted together at thy offerings in the exhilarations"—for both that which breathes out and that which does not, all this is for the sake of his glory; that is his station.
"In thee they choose wisdom, when these helpers become twice and thrice"—the seasons are indeed the helpers; it is they who become twice and thrice.
"O sweet one, with the sweeter, mingle with the sweet"—progeny is indeed the sweet; progeny is the sweet of progeny.
"Yonder honey, fight with honey! Honey is indeed offspring; that which is offspring is the honey of honey. He who knows this indeed sees offspring within offspring.
Upon these [verses] is the Śyaita [sāman], whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
JB 2.145 |va| Now, these are the names of cows; the names of cows are indeed cattle. [This is] for the sake of obtaining cattle.
vb| The first [verse] consists of a single foot, while the two following ones consist of three feet each.
These amount to seven steps;
the *śakvarī* verses consist of seven feet,
and cattle are associated with the *śakvarī*.
It is for the sake of securing the animals in their proper sequence. Regarding this, they say: "The *apāvamānī* verses should not be used during the *pavamāna* [laud].
To this, however, others say: "They are indeed *pāvamānī* verses; these are the *ṛc*s of that moon."
|vi This indeed is Pavamāna; this is King Soma. |vj Therefore, it must certainly be performed. |vk "O benevolent one, wealthy one, delightful one, noble one, O beautiful bull, come hither!"
"These two noble draft-oxen approach these [cows];
lower your heads; he stands in the midst of the waters, pointing with his ten horns."
"Vo"—these rays of the sun are indeed its horns.
And in the midst of these waters, this [sun] is present;
in them is the *vāravantīya* chant.
"Whatever we have obstructed by this rite, let that be removed by the Vāravantīya; it should stand at the very end," they say.
But they also say: "That which another speech does not surpass—that should be made the Agniṣṭoma-sāman for this day.
Indeed, the Yajñāyajñīya is that which another speech does not surpass.
The *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed speech (*vāk*).
For how could speech speak beyond speech?
Therefore, on this day, the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* should be performed as the *yajñāyajñīya* alone. 145.
JB 2.146 |va Now this is the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
vb One who desires offspring should indeed sacrifice with this.
Prajāpati indeed desired: "May I multiply through offspring and cattle; may I create offspring belonging to all the gods.
He saw this sacrifice.
He took it; he sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle; he created offspring belonging to all the gods.
If he should desire, "May I be propagated with many offspring and cattle; may I create offspring belonging to all the gods," let him sacrifice with this [offering].
Verily, he is propagated with many offspring and cattle; he creates offspring belonging to all the gods.
In that this [offering] belongs to the Viśvedevas, it is for the sake of the creation of offspring belonging to the Viśvedevas.
It is entirely performed with verses addressed to the Viśvedevas, for the sake of the procreation of offspring belonging to the Viśvedevas.
It consists of the *trivṛt* stoma; indeed, the *trivṛt* is deficient.
That which is deficient is procreation; [he thinks], "May that which is procreative cause me to procreate.
For him, the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant; the *rathantara* is indeed procreation; [he thinks], "May that which is procreative cause me to procreate."
He becomes one for whom the *uktha* hymns are recited; the *ukthas* are indeed offspring and cattle.
Offspring and cattle are procreation; [he does this] thinking, "May that which is procreation procreate me.
Now they say: "It should consist of seventeen [verses]," for Prajāpati is seventeenfold;
Prajāpati is procreation, so [he thinks], "May he procreate me. Now they also say: "It should consist of twenty-seven [verses]."
These three are indeed triplets;
the triplet is indeed a deficiency, and a deficiency is procreation.
"May that which is procreative cause me to procreate.
Now they also say, "It should consist of thirty-three [verses]," for Prajāpati is indeed the thirty-third.
Prajāpati is procreation.
"May he who is procreation cause me to procreate"—thus [one should think].
Regarding this, they also say: it should indeed be seventeenfold.
This seventeenfold [stoma], indeed, is Prajāpati;
therefore, it should be seventeenfold. And that very same [stoma] attains both the Trivṛt stoma and the Gāyatrī metre.

This indeed is the divine couple, the source of procreation: the *trivṛt* chant and the *gāyatrī* metre. [Thinking] "May that which is the divine couple, the source of procreation, procreate for me," it becomes an *ukthya* sacrifice; for the *ukthas* are the people (*viś*), and this is for the procreation of subjects belonging to the All-Gods.
This very sacrifice is indeed named Bhūḥ.
Having sacrificed with this sacrifice, Prajāpati became (abhavat);
because he became (yad abhavat), it is therefore called Bhūḥ.

He who knows thus becomes so. This sacrifice belongs to the Vaiśya; the Agniṣṭut belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, and the Indrastoma to the Rājanya. Indeed, when men sacrificed with these [sacrifices] thus distinguished, they were recognized as such by their speech.

"A Brahmin speaks, a Rājanya speaks, a Vaiśya speaks"—this is what they say. Now, because they perform these sacrifices at this time according to their respective designations, they are not recognized as such unless they have been explained. 147. JB 2.148.
Now follows this Upahavya sacrifice. Prajāpati created offspring;
once they were created, those offspring did not know whether they had been created by Prajāpati or not.
He reflected: "How indeed might I create these creatures, so that I may not be without knowledge of them once they have been created?
He saw this sacrifice;
he took it up.
With it he performed the sacrifice.
Then, with that very [offering], he invited those [gods]. Because he invited them, that is the reason for the name "Upahavya" (the Invited).
That [sāman] becomes the seventeenfold among the undefined verses.
Just as a thicket of forest, so indeed is the seventeenfold among the undefined verses.
Just as one might emerge after having circled around a thicket of forest, even so did he manifest himself by means of these [verses] that had seen him.

When the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is performed upon these verses containing the words "That which was seen, O best finder of the way," then indeed they recognized him, thinking: "We belong to him; he has been ours. And so, having become food itself, he appeared to them.
Desiring food, the subjects turned toward him.
Therefore, if subjects should depart from a *rājanya* or *brāhmaṇa*, or if his kinsmen should do so, he should sacrifice with this [rite].
He should cause the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to invoke him therein.
These officiating priests (ṛtvij) are indeed the subjects (viś) of the sacrificer. For him, the Rathantara becomes the Pṛṣṭha-stotra.
The Rathantara is indeed food;
therefore, one should give him much cooked food.
Thus, offspring longing for food turn toward him.
Prajāpati created the sacrifice;
he gave it to the gods.
Having given away the sacrifice, he felt himself depleted.
He reflected: "How indeed might I summon this sacrifice back again?
He sacrificed with that very same sacrifice;
by means of it, he summoned it back again.

That which he invoked—that indeed is the reason for the *upahavya* being called *upahavya*. Now, if a sacrifice should not approach one who has performed only a single *iṣṭi*, he should perform this [sacrifice].
For the sacrifice has indeed departed from him.
If the sacrifice does not approach one who has sacrificed but once, it is by means of this very [rite] that he calls it back again;
the sacrifice approaches him who knows thus. 149.
In the beginning, there were two classes of offspring of Prajāpati: the gods and the asuras.
Then the gods were more successful, while the asuras were less successful.
Prajāpati desired, "May the gods alone prevail; may the asuras be defeated."
He saw this sacrifice;
he took it up; with it, he sacrificed.
In that [space], he invited the gods with "upāhvaya" (invite hither); then he enclosed the Asuras within with a long bamboo pole with "antaragṛhṇāt" (he enclosed).
Thereupon, the gods indeed prevailed and the Asuras were defeated.
He prospers in himself; his hateful rival is defeated—he who knows thus.
He who has a rival, he who would practice sorcery, or he who would compete, should sacrifice with this [rite].
He should invite as officiating priests those who are, as it were, desirous of his success.
Then he should take up the others with a long bamboo pole.
Following their very invocation without seeking a response himself, his hateful rival perishes, and he enjoys prosperity for himself.
JB 2.151 |va Now follows this Tīvrasoma sacrifice; one who desires offspring should perform it with this. vb.
Verily, he who is without offspring is like a mere body.
A man is indeed intense and abundant through his offspring. [One should think: "May I be intense and abundant through offspring."
Now they say: "One who desires cattle should indeed sacrifice with this.
For he who is without cattle is, as it were, like a mere body;
but a man, through cattle, becomes powerful and abundant.
[Vi] "May I be intense and abundant through my cattle.
[Vj] That [Stoma] becomes seventeenfold.
[Vk] For this seventeenfold [Stoma] is indeed intense and abundant.
"May I be intense and abundant in offspring and cattle"—
for him, both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara Sāmans are used;
for these two, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, are indeed intense and abundant.
"May I be intense and abundant in offspring and cattle," [he thinks]. A mare pregnant with a foal is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for him;
for the mare is indeed intense and abundant.
It is intense because it is abundant, in that she is pregnant;
it is intense because it is abundant, in that she has teeth on both jaws;
it is intense because it is abundant, in that being one, she is worthy of many cows.
"May I be intense and abundant in offspring and cattle," [he thinks].
Now, they say: "A hundred cows of various calves should be his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). For that which is a hundred cows is indeed intense and abundant.
|vx It is intense and abundant because of that which is its hundredfold [portion].
|vy It is intense and abundant because of that which is its milk. |vz It is intense and abundant because of that which are its calves.
"May I be powerful and abundant in offspring and cattle.
Indra, having struck Vṛtra with his thunderbolt, thinking "I have not slain him," went to the furthest distance.
The gods sought it;
they did not find it.
They said, "Let us press [the Soma] indeed."
"He will come from there.
They pressed [the soma].
Of them, the entire morning pressing did not arrive.
They used to draw the cups up to their chests, holding them close, thinking, "Lest we should consume Soma that has not been offered to Indra.
Then he arrived at the midday pressing.
They raised a clamor, just as people raise a clamor when a chief has arrived.
Regarding this, they say: "It indeed came to the *acchāvāka*’s chant at the morning pressing.
For had it been at the *acchāvāka*’s chant at the morning pressing, it would have been excluded from the sacrifice.
"He would not have come.
Therefore, they consume [the soma] during the chant of the Acchāvāka at this sacrifice.
And therefore, both Adhvaryus and all the Camasādhvaryus respond to the Acchāvāka.
They indeed raise a cry of lamentation.
Therefore, he for whom prosperity might depart should sacrifice with this [offering]. Prosperity indeed departed from them when their preeminence departed.
They found her by means of this very [hymn].
He who knows thus finds prosperity; that prosperity does not depart from him.
Tvāṣṭra, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, indeed had three heads. He had one mouth for drinking Soma, one for drinking Surā liquor, and one for eating food.

With one [mouth] he would chant the *prastāva*, with another he would sing the *gāyatra* chant, with another he would perform the *pratihāra*, with one he would call for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and with the other he would respond with the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*.
With one [verse] he praises, with one [he praises].
He used to complete the entire sacrifice by crawling around all alone. Indeed, he was possessed of such power.
Now there was one who was the son of an Asura woman.
He used to speak directly to the gods, but indirectly to the Asuras. And to whomever he desired more, to him he spoke indirectly.
Therefore, indeed, Indra was afraid, both because he was the son of an Asura and because he possessed such great power. He reflected:
"This one is truly not of the nature of the gods (asurya), for he is the son of an Asura;
he speaks directly to us, but indirectly to the Asuras."
"Come now, let me kill him!
He indeed split his heads apart with the thunderbolt.
They became those very birds.
That which was the drinking of soma became the kapiñjala; therefore, it is as if brownish-red.
For Soma is indeed tawny (*babhru*). Now, that which was the drinking of *surā* became the *kalaviṅka* bird;
therefore it cries out like one intoxicated.
Then, that which was the eating of food became the partridge;
therefore it is, as it were, multiform,
for food is, as it were, multiform.
Therefore, for him, the scorpion and the *śaṅkuliṣṭha*—this is his food.
That Tvaṣṭṛ, whose son had been slain, offered Soma without Indra. Indra reflected: "If he indeed excludes me from this sacrifice, then I shall be excluded from the sacrifice."
"O Bhavānī, slay him! Let me slay him! /154/ Then he, with the thunderbolt in hand, rushed toward him. JB 2.155. va.
Tvaṣṭṛ, having flown back, sought refuge with the wives.
He did not, however, enter among them there.
Therefore, they sacrifice to Tvaṣṭṛ together with the wives.
Therefore, one should not strike a woman who has approached [her husband]. Indra went forth;
he went toward the *droṇakalaśa* of the two *havirdhāna* carts in order to purify King Soma with the strainer.
Having set it down with the *droṇakalaśa* vessel itself and having drunk from it, he departed.
Tvaṣṭṛ followed after him and asked: "Is there anything remaining?"
"This is a flow," they said.
He cast it into the fire with the words, "O enemy of Indra, grow strong, svāhā!
As soon as he cast it forth, it became Vṛtra.
While still existing as such, he united with Agni and Soma;
therefore they say, "Agni and Soma are of the nature of Asuras.
He indeed rises up as high as an arrow's length.
Then, indeed, the earth was [established] for him.
He became possessed of the entire threefold knowledge, all prosperity, and all food, as well as that which is called the "thousand" in the three-night sacrifice.
Indeed, all this was his offering. The rivers used to flow for him with sweet drink.
Now, there were eight companions of the gods named Abhiyugvānas, eight of the Pitṛs, and eight [of the Asuras].
There are eight for humans and eight for the Asuras.
Of these, Indra indeed becomes the eighth through his *māyā* when he desires to slay Vṛtra.
Therefore, it was Indra himself who slew him [Vṛtra] with the words: "O thou whose enemy is Indra, grow strong! Svāhā!"

He set it in motion. Now, had he indeed set it in motion [with the words], "O enemy of Indra, grow strong, svāhā! [this would have been another instance of the interruption of a syntactically connected sentence by chapter numbering in the JB, as noted by Parpola 1981, p. 216].
[The text] supplements [this]:
"He would certainly not have struck him. (JB 2.156)
This King Soma, when drunk, impelled this Indra even though he had not been invited.
He indeed departed through all his apertures except for his mouth;
therefore, he was a physician.
That which went downward from him became the *surāvāriṭakā* plant;
that which [went out] from the penis became the *parisruk*;
he spat out thrice.
That which he spat out first became the *karkandhu*; that which he spat out second became the *badara*; and that which he spat out third became the *kvala*.
Therefore, these possess both food and juices.
Making a sound like *khāṭ*, he spat out a fourth [piece];
that became a mango tree.
While it was thus, the gods sat down all around it.
"This was not the only hero. He replied thus: "Where shall we be?"
He said, "We truly do not know where we are.
"What? [he asked].
"I am indeed seeing," he replied.
Now, it is said that in former times people would die immediately after sneezing.
They said to him, "Sneeze! We shall say 'Live' to you. He then sneezed.
They said to him, "Live!
He lived.
Therefore, even now, when someone has sneezed, people say, "Live!"
Therefore, indeed, whomsoever one considers to be well-seeing, one should say to him, "Live! That which went from his nose—
Those two became lions;
what was in the eyes became the two tigers, what was in the ears the two wolves, and what was in the armpits the two *vailūṣas*.
Therefore, these are the most powerful among birds.
For Indra was their place of origin.
Then, that which went downward became these small predatory beasts. He lay there, scattered.
He was indeed covered over with grass.
They said to him, "Where indeed are you? Where indeed shall we treat you?
Therefore, even now, when someone is afflicted, they ask, "Where does it hurt you? Where shall we treat you?"
Pointing to some grass, he said, "He is right here; heal him from this very side! Heal him from this very side!
Then they said to Agni, "Burn this!"
Agni burned it.
They said to Parjanya, "Rain upon this!
Parjanya rained upon it.
Then, O auspicious ones, the plants were born. They milked them with cows; they milked that milk.
They saw this sacrifice;
they took it;
with it, they performed the sacrifice for him.
They poured out *pratidhuk* (fresh milk) for him at the morning pressing;
"He has indeed been set against [the enemy] by this," therefore it is called *pratidhuk*.
They heated it at the midday pressing; "He has indeed been made to boil by this," therefore it is called *śrita*.

There is curd at the third pressing; for by means of this, one has indeed become as it were "curdled" (adādhīvat), therefore it is called *dadhi*. Just as he was before, so indeed did he become even more so than that. He who is either a seeker of Soma (*somavāmī*) or one who has over-poured Soma (*somātipavitaḥ*) should sacrifice with this.
And as he was before, so indeed he becomes even more so.
Therefore, one should not despise one who has vomited Soma or one who has passed Soma;
for even Indra was thus. 157.
The oblation of Soma indeed departed from them;
it was that very Virāj.
Those gods said, "Let us search for this Virāj."
They performed fervent austerity.
They beheld this Virāj sacrifice;
they brought it forth.
They consecrated him. For one day they did not eat. They beheld its path of departure.
They said, "Let us perform even more austerity.
They did not eat for a second day;
they heard its sound.
They said, "Let us perform even more austerity.
They did not eat for a third day.
They beheld it from afar, like a great mountain rising up, or like a vast cloud.
He pursued it, advancing and retreating.
For indeed, he who pursues a wild animal only from behind does not capture it;
but he who pursues it by advancing and retreating—he alone captures it.
They won it on the tenth day itself.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* is food.
The Virāj [is used] for the attainment of food. Its vow consists of water and clarified butter.
"Water is bodiless; ghee is bodiless; *svadhā* is bodiless. With that which is bodiless, may we restrain the bodiless *svadhā*.
Thus much he observes as his vow.
"Truly, this much is the measure of a person, lest one should exceed the person.
Moreover, by this he joins together the limbs of his own self joint by joint. It contains clarified butter within for the sake of unification.
The *stoma* consists of seventeen [verses].
Prajāpati is indeed the seventeenfold;
Prajāpati is the finder of what has been lost.

"He who is the seeker of what has been lost—through him may we find this our own portion. For him, both the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans are used: "If we find it in this world, let us do so with the Rathantara;
if in the intermediate space, with the Vāmadevya; if in yonder world, with the Bṛhat."
An offering-cup of *udumbara* wood for Soma is its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The *udumbara* is indeed vigor and food; it is for the attainment of vigor and the eating of food.
Furthermore, Soma is bodiless, and the *svadhā* (ancestral offering) is bodiless; [he thinks], "May we obtain the bodiless *svadhā* by means of the bodiless."
He gives it to the Brahman priest.
For the sacrificial fee for Brahman consists of a single cow. Regarding this, they ask: "Is it to be given as an offering (huta) or as a non-offering (ahuta)? They say, "As a non-offering."
"It would indeed be as if [the gift] were spent when one gives what has already been offered.
To this they say: "It should be given only after it has been offered;
for this is the portion of the gods."
Who is worthy to give a portion to the gods?
Therefore, one should give only that which has been offered into the fire.
Whatever kind of food one gives in this world, such will be the food for him in that world.
Indeed, that which is the supreme food in yonder world is the drinking of Soma.
This very offering of Soma becomes his food in yonder world;
speaking the *ṛta* and the truth, they consume it.
For by means of *ṛta* they indeed found that through truth;
he says, "The *ṛta*, the immortal," for by means of *ṛta* they indeed found that immortality.
“*Oyi jvarā oyi jūhe*”—these are the *sāman*-concluding formulas, the truth of speech.
For they found that [truth] of speech by means of the truth.
By this very [means], Gārgya Ātharvaṇa, Keśin Dārbhya, Ṛjiśvan, and Vātavāta performed sacrifice from heaven.
Arjiśva Vātavāta was performing the *avattana* ceremony.
Now, they sat down with him, accompanied by his son, the youth Vṛṣaśuṣma Arjiśvana, whose eyes were anointed, thinking: "If he should perish, we will complete this [sacrifice] with him."
He became exhausted.
Being exhausted, he went to the other world.
He came to his father in that world. 160.
JB 2.161 |va His world was indeed auspicious. vb He said: "In that case, whose world is this?"
"It is mine," he said.
Then there was another world that was more beautiful.
"Whose is this? [he asked].
"Yours," he said.
He replied, "Since you have given me more than I gave you, I have taught you more than you taught me;
so how is it that this world belongs to you and that one belongs to me?"
He said: "My dear son, that world was indeed one to be entered through a vow. You have been initiated into the vow for us both.
Therefore, this world is mine, and that one is yours."
"Go," he said; "you shall surely obtain whatever desire you may wish for, and that desire of yours shall be fulfilled.
"But let him bend his fingers," [the other said]. He then approached him.
Having finished [the sacrifice], he said, "Let this man indeed be one whose vessel is not empty among the Brāhmaṇas.
He indeed became one whose vessel was not empty among the Brāhmaṇas.
From that time on, therefore, those who are not empty-vesselled have descended from Ārjiśvana. 161.
JB 2.162 |va Now follows this Citistoma sacrifice. vb One who desires offspring should perform it.

The *stomas* of that *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* are the seasons, for the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the seasons; the year is the seasons, and the year is procreation. [He performs it] thinking, "May he who is procreation cause me to procreate."
Both types of *stomas* belong to it: the odd ones and the even ones. Indeed, these two kinds of *stomas* constitute a divine couple, a source of procreation.
[The sacrificer thinks: "May that which is a divine couple, a source of procreation, cause me to procreate."
For him, both the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans are used.
Indeed, these two—the Bṛhat and the Rathantara—are a divine couple, a source of procreation. [He thinks:
"May that divine couple, that source of procreation, cause me to procreate."
It has twelve *stotras*; the year consists of twelve months.
The year is procreation; [he performs it] thinking, "May he, who is procreation, cause me to procreate.
It has twenty-four *stutis* and *śastras*; the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
The year is procreation; may he who is procreation cause me to procreate—so [it is said].
Moreover, they say: "One who desires heaven should sacrifice with this.
The *stomas* of that *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* are the seasons, for the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the seasons.
The year is the seasons;

the year is the heavenly world, for the sake of attaining the heavenly world. Its *stomas* are directed upwards, for the heavenly world is indeed directed upwards, for the sake of attaining the heavenly world.
For the sake of attaining the totality.
Both the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans belong to it; they are for the sake of heaven, indeed for the attainment of the heavenly world. There are twelve Stotras for it; the year has twelve months.
The year is the heavenly world; it is for the attainment of the heavenly world itself. There are twenty-four *stotra* and *śastra* hymns for it; the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
The year is the heavenly world; it is for the attainment of the heavenly world itself. (162)
JB 2.163 |va His subsequent stotras consist of [verses] increasing by two.
vb For the sacrificer is indeed two-footed.
He thereby establishes the sacrificer himself in the heavenly world.
Now, they say: "These two should be laid down as bricks";
furthermore, they are heaven and earth, furthermore, they are the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*, furthermore, they are day and night, furthermore, they are the two outflows.
Only on the two *avacchada* [bricks].
For this sacrificial rite is indeed like a roof-covering (*chadis*). Truly, rain does not fall upon houses that have a roof-covering.
Rain does not fall upon him who knows this.

Furthermore, they say: "Verily, he is one of the sacrificial rites of the *anviṣṭis*. Therefore, whoever—whether having maintained the fire for a year or not—should sacrifice with the built-up fire-altar (*agni-citi*), let him sacrifice with this [rite].
Immediately, indeed, his year becomes sought out according to its seasons, months, half-months, and nights.
Now, as for the fact that the *stomas* of the six-day *pṛṣṭhya* period are used: the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the seasons, and the seasons are the year; thus it is [sought] according to the seasons.

Now, as there are twelve stotras, and the year consists of twelve months, it is thereby [attained] month by month. And as there are twenty-four stotras and śastras, and the year consists of twenty-four half-months,
it is thereby [attained] half-month by half-month.

Now, as there are three hundred and sixty stotriyas, so many are the nights of the year; therefore it is [perfected] by night. Indeed, for one who knows this, the year is immediately sought after. 163.
Now, these two are the Rāśi and the Arāyi. One desiring offspring should sacrifice with these two.
Prajāpati indeed desired, "May I be multiplied through offspring and cattle."
"May I create offspring and cattle in pairs.
He saw these two sacrifices; he brought them forth.
He sacrificed with those two.
Thereupon, indeed, he multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle;
he created offspring and cattle in pairs.
He who should desire, "May I be propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle; may I create offspring and cattle in pairs," he should sacrifice with these two [offerings].
He indeed becomes propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle; he creates offspring and cattle in pairs.
That *rāśi* becomes the forty-four-fold, having the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*.
The *Rathantara* is indeed the *brahman*, and the forty-four-fold is the *kṣatra*. Through both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*, joined together, he is propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle.
And because these chants (*stotra*) arose as it were in great abundance, therefore he is called *rāśi*. He is the forty-eight-fold [Stoma], having the *Bṛhat* as his *Sāman*.
The forty-eight-fold is indeed the Brahman, and the *Bṛhat* is the Kṣatra.

For those two Gāyatrīs which constitute the forty-eightfold [stoma] are indeed the Brahman and the Kṣatra; through these two joined together, one is born abundantly with offspring and cattle. And because these stotras are, as it were, superior, therefore they are called *marāyaḥ*.
For indeed, that which is more abundant than the *rāśi* becomes immortal.
These two, moreover, are the very foundation of the *stomas*.
Those two which are the abundance of the *stomas*—by means of them, one is multiplied with offspring and cattle, [thinking] "May I be multiplied with offspring.
For those two, there is a simultaneous consecration (*dīkṣā*), a simultaneous purchase (*kraya*), and simultaneous *upasad* rites.
However, having purchased [the Soma], they put on their sandals separately.
They do not have separate officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Regarding this, they say: "This is indeed a confluence (*saṃsava*) that there are no separate officiating priests.
For that which is celebrated from afar is unpleasant."

Now, what about the fact that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be from the same lineage? Indeed, they should not be so; otherwise, the two rites would conclude simultaneously, and the officiating priests would have to be different.
However, they indeed choose the same *pravara* (ancestral invocation) and pronounce the same benediction (*āśis*).

Therefore, there should not be different officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Now, some say that having sacrificed with the *rāśi* [oblation] as before, one should emerge from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) and undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the sake of immortality (*marāya*).
But these two [cases] would indeed be so.
"For the origin of twins is indeed common; they are born together and grow up together.
Therefore, they should remain together.
With these two [verses], Ugrāyudha Mānacitti performed a sacrifice.
Now Alanda Vātsya had more than a hundred sons in one [lineage] and more than a hundred in the other.
Thus they were born in great numbers.
He who knows this is born in great numbers through offspring and cattle. 165.
JB 2.166 |va| Now these *stomas*— Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyuḥ— come into being.
vb| Gauḥ leaped away from Āyuḥ.
From that, light was born.
This world is indeed *āyu*, that [heavenly] cow is *gauḥ*, and this intermediate space is *jyotis*.
They placed him in front just as one would a son.
Either from here this world extends upward, or from there that world extends downward. This light between them has been raised up; by means of it we see.
As they approached their union, they pushed aside the darkness at the end of the light.
Just as parents might follow behind a son who has gone ahead, so it is with that. These chants (*stoma*) become a pair when they are joined;
for the son lies between the husband and wife.
Just as a couple, about to unite, might pass their son back and forth from this side or that side, even so is this.
These deficient and redundant chants are pairs that procreate.
He who desires, "May I be propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle," should sacrifice with these.
Verily, he is multiplied manifold with offspring and cattle.
Now follows this Śunaskarṇastoma.
Śunaḥkarṇa Vārṣṇyaka was indeed a doer of merit and a non-doer of evil.
He desired: "Having performed only merit in this world and having avoided evil, may I go to the heavenly world.
He beheld this sacrifice.
He brought it; he sacrificed with it.
Then indeed, having performed merit in this world and having cast off evil, he went to the heavenly world.
Now, he who is a doer of merit and should desire, "Having performed only merit in this world and having cast off evil, may I go to the heavenly world"— he should sacrifice with this [rite].
Having performed only merit in this world and having cast off evil, he goes to the heavenly world.
It consists of the *trivṛt* [stoma].
Indeed, this [stoma] is, as it were, turned away;
for the *trivṛt* stoma is one that has reached out toward the heavenly world itself.
By this [rite], one goes to the heavenly world turning away from here.
Its stotras are directed away, its śastras are directed away, its pṛṣṭhas are directed away, and its viṣṭutis are directed away.
Everyone indeed turns away.
They chant on the *pravatī* verses; they thus cause him to go away toward that world.
For him, the Vāmadevya becomes the *pṛṣṭha* chant with the *svāra* intonation. They arrange all the *sāmans* with the *svāra* intonation; for the *svāra* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
By means of his own vital breaths, the Udgātṛ thereby expels the vital breaths of the sacrificer.
Regarding this they say: "At the chanting of the Yajñāyajñīya, one should lie down behind the Gārhapatya fire, turning toward the south;
from that very place, one goes to the heavenly world."
Regarding this, they say: "If one were to sit down while the sacrifice is not yet completed, there would indeed be a dragging away of the sacrifice.
Therefore, only when the entire ritual action has been concluded, or when they proceed with the cow (*vaśā*), should one sit down behind the Āhavanīya fire, turning toward the south.
"From that very [place] he goes to the heavenly world.
Now, yonder sun is indeed the Āhavanīya fire;
this is truly the heavenly world.
In this very world of heaven, O dear one, he finally finds firm support.
Now, this is the Man-stoma.
Manu and Yama, the sons of Vivasvat, were both [kings]. Manu desired: "May the gods appoint me for this world and its sovereignty, and Yama for that [other] world.
He saw this sacrifice.
He brought it; he sacrificed with it.
Then indeed the gods bestowed upon him sovereignty over this world, and [bestowed] Yama upon that [other world].
This indeed is a *sadaśa*.
For this *sadaśa* is a pair of tongs (*saṃdaṃśa*).
Just as one might carry something away after pinching it with a pair of tongs, even so does he [carry it] by means of this pair of tongs.
Having seized him, he carried him from this world to that world.
For him, the *rathaṃtara* serves as the *pṛṣṭha* chant;
the *rathaṃtara* is indeed a thunderbolt.
By means of that very thunderbolt, he struck him from this world to that world.
Therefore, whoever has a rival, whoever would practice sorcery, or whoever would compete, should sacrifice with this; by means of that very thunderbolt, he strikes him from this world to that world.

In that [sacrifice], they prescribe these formidable *sāmans*: the *jamadagneḥ saptāha*, the *vidratha*, and the *cakṣūṃṣi*. 169/ JB 2.170. 1va. Jamadagni’s seven-day [rite], the *vidratha*, and the eyes.
Those *sāman*s which have the form of rites for malevolent magic—by means of their form, they thus bring the *stoma* into correspondence.
Furthermore, they say: "One who desires food should sacrifice with this."
Indeed, everyone else praises the *virāj* beyond [its limit];
but he alone does not praise the *virāj* beyond [its limit] who praises with ten [verses].
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
Food is the Virāj;
it is for the attainment of food from the Virāj.
Its Pṛṣṭha-stotra is the Rathantara; the Rathantara is indeed food.
It is for the attainment of food itself. Upon that [fire-altar], they arrange these Sāmans: the *arkārkapuṣpa* and the *dairghaśravasa*.
Those Sāmans which are the form of food, those they place there.
In this way, they bring the *stoma* into perfection through its corresponding form.
Now, this [hymn] belongs to the *gāyatrī*.

In that threefold [sacrifice], the morning pressing has the fifteen-fold stoma; the *acchāvāka*’s *ājya* chant has the fifteen-fold stoma; the midday pressing has the seventeen-fold stoma; and the third pressing has the twenty-one-fold stoma.
It is an *ukthya* sacrifice with both *sāmans*.
One who desires the office of domestic priest (*purodhā*) should sacrifice with this [offering].

Now, as for the fact that at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), which is threefold (*trivṛt*), there is the *ājya* chant of the Acchāvāka consisting of fifteen verses (*pañcadaśa*): the threefold is indeed the Brahman, and the fifteenfold is the Kṣatra; he thus places the Brahman before the Kṣatra.
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is the domestic priest of the Kṣatriya;
moreover, he thus makes the Kṣatra follow the path of the Brāhmaṇa.
The midday pressing consists of seventeen [stotras].
The *viḍ* (the people) is indeed the seventeenfold [stoma].
This, moreover, is the second king, namely the domestic priest (*purohita*). Indeed, he who attains prosperity attains the sovereignty and overlordship of the people.
"May I enter into sovereignty and lordship"— therefore the midday pressing consists of seventeen [stotras].
Moreover, by this he makes the people obedient to both the priesthood and the nobility.
For him, the Rathantara becomes the *pṛṣṭha* chant and the Bṛhat the *brahmasāman*.
The Rathantara is indeed the Brahman.
The *kṣatra* is the great. He thus places the *brahman* before the *kṣatra*;
therefore, the *brāhmaṇa* is the domestic priest (*purohita*) of the *kṣatriya*.
Moreover, he thus makes the kṣatra follow the path of the brahman. That [sacrifice] is the Ukthya;
for the hymns (ukthas) are indeed the people (viś).
For this second king is indeed the domestic priest (purohita).

Now, he who attains prosperity attains the sovereignty and lordship over the people (viś); thinking, "May I attain sovereignty and lordship over the people," for that reason the Ukthya sacrifice is performed.
Moreover, this makes the people subordinate to both the priesthood and the nobility.
These [stomas] become twenty-one-fold.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first.
This, indeed, is prosperity (*śrī*). Thus, at the very end, he ascends to this very prosperity.
And that same [laud], when fully praised, results in the *gāyatrī* meter.
The Gāyatrī is indeed the Brahman.

When one prospers in the splendor of the Brahman (*brahmavarcasa*), then he attains the office of the domestic priest (*purodhā*). When he has attained the office of the domestic priest, if he should then desire: "May I be irremovable from this office of the domestic priest; may I not..."
Thinking, "May he fall away," one should perform for this very same [sacrificer] the *ājya* chant of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin as the fifteenfold [stoma].
The Trivṛt is indeed the Brahman;
the Pañcadaśa is the Kṣatra.
Thus, he encloses the kṣatra on both sides with this brahman.
He becomes one who cannot be displaced from the office of the domestic priest; he does not fall away.
Now, this is the Catuṣṭoma of Gautama.
Gautama indeed desired, "May I restrain cattle for myself; may I attain abundance of cattle.
He beheld this sacrifice.
He fetched it;
he sacrificed with it. Thereupon, indeed, he secured cattle for himself and attained abundance of cattle.
He who should desire, "May I restrain cattle; may I attain abundance of cattle," he should sacrifice with this [offering].
Verily, he restrains cattle and attains abundance of cattle.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* chant for him takes place in four [verses]. Horses, indeed, are four-footed and have four hooves;
those animals which are four-footed and have four hooves, these he wins by this very means.
There are eight portions of clarified butter for each [set].
Cattle indeed have eight hooves;
thus, by this very means, he wins those cattle that have eight hooves.
The midday [pressing] consists of twelve [stotras].
The *jagatī* indeed has twelve syllables;
the *jagatī* is cattle.
That which is small among the animals is connected with the *jagatī* meter;
by this [rite], he obtains that very thing.
There are sixteen *pṛṣṭha* chants.
The sixteen parts (*kalā*) are indeed the cattle, both those we know and those we do not; by this [rite], he secures them part by part. The *ār-bhava* *pavamāna* [laud] consists of twenty verses.
These two sets of ten, making twenty, are indeed two *virāj* verses.
Cattle have twenty as their support and are of the nature of the *virāj*.
Those cattle which have twenty as their support and are of the nature of the *virāj*, those he wins for himself by this very means.
Now follows the twenty-fourth *agniṣṭomasāman*.
Cattle are four-footed and belong to the *vairāja* [meter].
Those cattle which are four-footed and *vairāja*, those he wins by means of this.
Now, the year consists of twenty-four half-months;
by means of the year, he thus encompassed them and placed them within himself.
Indeed, this is neither an Agniṣṭoma nor an Ukthya, but rather something like both.
These cattle are neither domestic nor wild; they are, as it were, both.
By this [rite], he wins them.
Now this is the *apūrva* [offering]. One desiring offspring should sacrifice with this.
Prajāpati indeed desired: "May I be multiplied through offspring and cattle; may no one other than I be first."
It might be so. He beheld this sacrifice;
he brought it.
He sacrificed with it. Thereupon, indeed, he was multiplied through offspring and cattle;
no one else existed before him.

If one should desire, "May I be propagated abundantly; may no other be before me," let him sacrifice with this [offering]. He is indeed propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle; no other becomes prior to him.
It is the Trivṛt-stoma, having the Rathantara as its Sāman.
Indeed, there is no other Stoma prior to the Trivṛt; there is no other Pṛṣṭha prior to the Rathantara;
there is no other deity prior to Prajāpati. Because these are without predecessor, he is therefore "without predecessor" (apūrva).
Now, Prajāpati is indeed the mind. There is nothing whatsoever prior to the mind;
therefore, he is indeed without predecessor.
It consists of the *trivṛt* stoma; the *trivṛt* is indeed deficient. Deficiency is procreation; [he does this] thinking, "May that which is procreative cause me to procreate.
Its *pṛṣṭha* chant is the *rathantara*; the *rathantara* is indeed procreation; thus, that which is procreative—
"May he not procreate for me.
There are twelve stotras for it; the year consists of twelve months.
The year is procreation; [he thinks], "May he who is procreation procreate for me."
It has twenty-four *stuta-śastra* hymns; the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
The year is procreation; [he performs it] thinking, "May he, who is procreation, procreate me.
Now follows this Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice. The Maruts, indeed, desired: "May we be the strongest, the most powerful, the most numerous, and the most heroic among the gods;
may we conquer the heavenly world."
They saw this sacrifice;
they took it up; with it, they sacrificed.
Then indeed those gods became the strongest, the most powerful, the most numerous, and the most heroic; they conquered the heavenly world.
He who is the strongest, the most powerful, the most numerous, and the most heroic among his own people conquers the heavenly world.
Thus he knows.
This, indeed, is the sacrifice of the people (*viś*). The Maruts are the people; therefore, it is the sacrifice of the people.
With this very [sacrifice], Aikayāva Kāndama performed a sacrifice.
He became the most vigorous, the strongest, the most abundant, and the most heroic among his own people; he either conquered the world or did not.
It consists of seventeen [verses]. Prajāpati, indeed, is seventeenfold. Prajāpati is procreation; may he, who is procreation, cause me to procreate.
For it, the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant; the *rathantara*, indeed, is procreation. That which is procreation—
"May he not procreate that [offspring]," so [they think].
Therefore, it becomes an Ukthya; for the Ukthas are indeed offspring and cattle. [He does this] thinking, "May I be procreated with offspring and cattle.
For five autumns, five consecrated bulls roam about.
Because for five autumns five consecrated bulls roam about, it is therefore called the Pañcaśāradīya. And they are all dappled.
"O Maruts, whose mother is Pṛśni," so they say; moreover, it is recited in a verse: "O Maruts, whose mother is Pṛśni. Therefore, they are spotted (pṛśnayaḥ).
|vg The oblation of the gods is indeed vigor.
|vh They took that for themselves. |vi In that it belongs to the Maruts, they thereby place vigor within themselves.

"To the Maruts, the victorious," "to the Maruts, the well-drinkers," "to the Maruts, those possessing their own wealth," "to the Maruts indeed, the Maruts," "to the Maruts, the helpers"—this [is the formula].
Now, as for "to the Maruts, the victorious": it is so that he may achieve that victory which he desires when he sacrifices with whatever desire.
Now, as for the [offering] "to the Maruts, who drink their own portion, svāhā": it is so that he may obtain whatever desire he has obtained for himself, whatever desire he might sacrifice with.
And as for the [offering] "to the Maruts, who possess their own portion, svāhā": the Maruts indeed possess all this as their own.
He thus gratifies them with their own [share].
Being gratified, they yield up their own [power] to him.
With that which has been yielded up, he performs the sacrifice. Now, as for [the formula]: "To the Maruts, indeed, to the Maruts... (176).
"The Maruts are indeed many—both those we know and those we do not. May they all be pleased with us."
Now, as for the [offering] "to the Maruts, the Abhiṣṭis," one who desires that he may attain his own desired object should sacrifice with that desire. He should immolate these very animals.
One [animal] for the consecration, one on the day of fasting, one at the pressing, one for the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice, and one for the *udavasānīyā* offering; thus he should immolate these animals.
Now, some say that this [rite] should consist of exactly five nights.
"In that very place, one should sacrifice these animals day after day.

Regarding this, Udara Śāṇḍilya once questioned the elder Ekayāvāna: "Since they are disputing this—some saying 'it should consist of five nights,' others saying 'it should be an Ukthya with seventeen [stomas] in each case'—how should it be performed?"
He said, "They have indeed presented that Ukthya as a seventeen-fold one-day sacrifice for us.
Now, some say, "This should rather be an Atirātra;
how could the sacrifice, having been commenced, last five years without being an Atirātra?"
But that is not so;
some say it should be an *agniṣṭoma*,
for from the *agniṣṭoma* all sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are extended.
That, however, is not exactly so for us.
That [sacrifice] should indeed be an Ukthya with seventeen [verses].
For the Ukthya-stotras are the people (viṭ).
The *viṭ* (the common people) is seventeenfold; the sacrifice belongs to the *viś* (the common people);
therefore, it should be an *ukthya* sacrifice with seventeen [stotras].
The *arkya* of the Maruts and the *saṃstobha* of the Maruts—these two are the *ādiṣṭasāmans* belonging to the two *pavamāna* lauds.
By means of these, they bring the *stoma* into harmony with its corresponding form. 177.
JB 2.178 |va Now this is the Abhijit.
vb The gods and the Asuras contended for these worlds, for this world.
Those gods desired: "May we conquer these worlds; may we conquer the Asuras, our rivals and enemies.
They saw this sacrifice;
they brought it.
With it they sacrificed.
With it they conquered these worlds; they conquered their rivals, the Asuras.
Because they conquered these worlds, that is the reason for the name of the Abhijit sacrifice.

He who knows this conquers these worlds; he conquers rivalry and the hateful enemy. For him, there are *stomas* increasing by three; for these worlds are three, and it is for the conquest of these worlds.
They consist of four repetitions; for there are four quarters, and it is for the conquest of the quarters.
They chant on the *abhivatī* verses for the conquest of these very worlds.
The *ābhīka*, the *abhinidhana*, the *abhīvarta*, and the *ābhīśava*—these are the *sāmans*; they serve for the conquest of these very worlds. 178.
For this [sacrifice], the Rathantara is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra, the Vāmadevya is the Maitrāvaruṇa-sāman, and the Bṛhat is used for the Ārbhava-pavamāna.
This indeed is the Rathantara;
the intermediate space is the Vāmadevya;
yonder [heaven] is the Bṛhat.
For the unobstructed conquest of these very worlds. In that [sacrifice], they arrange these forms of the *pṛṣṭha* chants in secret for the purpose of counter-attacking the Viśvajit.
Indeed, Indra slew Vṛtra.
Darkness covered that Vṛtra, who had been slain, from these worlds.
He desired, "May I drive away this darkness.
He saw this Abhijit sacrifice.
He brought it; with it he sacrificed.
For him, the *stomas* increase by three.
There are indeed these three worlds;
by means of them he drove away the darkness from these worlds.
But the darkness enveloped him from the fourth world.
He desired, "May I indeed dispel this darkness.
He saw this Viśvajit sacrifice;
he performed it.
With that he sacrificed. For him there are the fourfold-increasing *stomas*;
there are four directions.
This, indeed, is the fourth world, namely the quarters.
By means of that, he struck away the darkness from the fourth world.
Then, having struck away the darkness—the evil—from all these worlds, he [ascended] to the heavenly world.
Having struck away the darkness and evil from all these worlds, he who knows this ascends to the heavenly world. 179.
JB 2.180 |va| Now follows this Viśvajit sacrifice. |vb| Indra conquered the Asuras.
He did not conquer them as if they were his own.
The gods caused him to sacrifice with this [rite];
he conquered the universe.
Indra is indeed the All-conqueror. Because he conquered by means of this craft, that is the "all-conquering" nature of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
The gods, fearing the Asuras, gathered all this together and ascended upward to the heavenly world.
He who, while acquiring everything, does not give everything away, is a thief of everything.
Now, he who, finding everything, gives everything, is the possessor of all wealth (*sarvavedasī*).
Indeed, he finds everything: he finds all the *stomas*, all the *grahas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, and all the *chandas*.
Its stomas increase by four each time. By means of the first three, he conquers these very worlds;
that which is the fourth, by it all the *saṃbhāryā* verses become fulfilled.
There is indeed a conjunction of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras; they have various deities, and thus they are joined by that connection and by that form.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who begin with the *pāvamānī* verses go, as it were, upon a wrong path.
The final verse (*paryāsa*) is: "O Pavamāna, [of] thee..."
|vs Further, they traverse the paths. |vt There are not four from six.
|vu By that, they prevail. /180/
JB 2.181 |va Now these *āprī* butter-portions come into being. vb Prajāpati created offspring.
Having created [the world], he felt himself emptied.
He perceived these *āprī* verses and *ājya* offerings;
with them, he gratified himself for the sake of freedom from exhaustion.

For he who gives everything is, as it were, emptied out. Therefore, in that these *āprī* butter-offerings exist, the sacrificer gratifies his very self with them, so that there may be no loss of vigor.
Regarding this they say: "Verily, those who,
in a single sacrificial rite, transpose these [verses] which have different forms, different deities, and different meters, are indeed deprived of their vital breaths."
Now, as for the fact that the *bṛhat* occurs in *gāyatrī* verses: the *bṛhat* is indeed breath, and the *gāyatrī* is breath; thus they prosper through the vital breaths.
If they were to perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants in their regular order, they should make the *revatī* verses the final ones; these verses have the form of the *revatīs*.
For that very reason, they do not depart from the forms of the Revatī verses.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who perform the thirty-three-fold hymn-form (stoma) indeed depart from the Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
These *ṛc* verses consist of twenty-one syllables.
Therefore, they do not depart from the Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who make the Bṛhat the Agniṣṭoma-sāman indeed depart from the Yajñāyajñīya.
In that there is [the verse] "O Agni, you, the invoker of sacrifices," by that very means they do not depart from the form of the Yajñāyajñīya.
They go by means of it; they do not depart from the third pressing.
Regarding this, they say: "He indeed fails to prosper with cattle who gives away everything.
He puts on a reddish-brown complexion. Indeed, that which is reddish-brown is the beloved form of cattle;
thus he prospers through the beloved form of cattle.
He digs with a spade; he overcomes lack of subsistence.
The spade is sharp-edged on both sides; verily, from both sides he fashions for him food.
He dwells in the forest for three nights; verily, by means of these [nights], he wins whatever forest food there is.

Three [steps] neither in the village nor in the forest—with those, he obtains that food which is neither in the village nor in the forest. Three among the people—with those, he obtains what belongs to the people.
Three among the assembly—with those, he obtains what belongs to the assembly.
These amount to twelve;
twelve months are a year;
verily, from the year he obtains food.
He puts on the Rohiṇī skin.
Indeed, this was formerly the skin of animals; that which belonged to the human was [the skin] of humans, while that which belonged to the animals remained with the animals.
Those animals could not endure the heat, the rain, the gadflies, or the mosquitoes.
They approached the Puruṣa and said, "O Puruṣa, let this skin be yours; [give] this to us. He asked, "What would come of that?
They replied, "We would be your eaters."
They gave him a garment, saying, "This is your garment.
In that he puts on the ruddy skin, he prospers through his own form;
thus, cattle do not devour him in yonder world.
In that world, indeed, the animals devour the man.
Therefore, one should not stand naked at the edge of a cow-pen; for it is possible that the cow might leap upon him, thinking, "I am wearing his skin! (182)
It has a tail for the sake of completeness;
moreover, all these indeed belong to Prajāpati.
Among sons, he who is the most wretched causes his father's heart to wither. He who gives everything enters into a state of wretchedness; thus one goes to the realization of Prajāpati.
Therefore, those [days] which one would spend in the forest—one should indeed spend them under an Udumbara tree.
When Prajāpati distributed strength and food for his offspring, that which remained as a surplus became this tree, the Vanaspati.
Indeed, the Udumbara is strength; it is food.
The forest is indeed the food that has been taken away by him who gives everything.
Whatever there is here that belongs to Prajāpati, namely the food— that very thing he secures for himself by means of those [cows].
Now, those [beasts] that dwell neither in the village nor in the forest—verily they dwell among the Niṣādas;
for these Niṣādas indeed dwell neither in the village nor in the forest.
Through these [beasts], one obtains both kinds of food, that which is domestic and that which is wild.

Whatever member of Prajāpati is here, whatever food there is—that indeed he wins by means of those [cows]. Now, she might dwell among the *jana* (the people), or among a Vaiśya, or indeed among an enemy; for this Vaiśya or this enemy is indeed the *jana* of the Brāhmaṇa.
The food of that man indeed becomes lost who gives everything away.
That which is the body of Prajāpati here, and that which is the food—verily, he wins that by means of those [cows].
Now, as for those that would dwell among people, they would indeed dwell with the king.
This indeed is the "possessing of kin" (sajana): that there is a king.
Prosperity is indeed at the end of food-eating; thus, he establishes himself at the very end in the prosperity of food-eating. 183/ JB 2.184.
Prajāpati created living beings.
By means of this very [sacrifice], he created this universe through the Viśvajit.
Because these introductory verses (*pratipad*) are of diverse forms, therefore indeed this entire world (*viśva*) exists.
It is of various forms.
Indeed, this is the application of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].
The *rathantara* is joined precisely with the *upavastī*.

With [the verse] addressed to Sarasvatī, the Vairāja; with one addressed to Sarasvatī, the Mahānāmnīs; with one addressed to Bṛhaspati, the Vairūpa; with one addressed to Savitṛ, the Revatīs; with one addressed to Agni-Pavamāna, the Bṛhat.
That is why these [verses] are of various forms.
The *pṛṣṭha* stotras become the opening verses (*pratipad*) at the morning pressing; thus they are harnessed there.
At the midday pressing, they ascend upon them.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who begin with the *pavasvinī* verses are indeed deprived of their vital breaths."
In that this opening verse belongs to Vāyu, and Vāyu is indeed breath, they thus prosper through the vital breaths.
Now these [verses] are for Sarasvant and Sarasvatī.
This indeed is the divine couple, the procreative pair, namely Sarasvant and Sarasvatī.
[He offers] with the thought, "May I be procreated through the divine couple."
Regarding this, they say: "The [oblation] for the man should be performed first, and that for the woman afterwards;
thus the offspring of the sacrificer is born undaunted. On this point, however, they also say: "Vāyu, indeed, is the depositor of seed."

Sarasvatī is procreation; those two produce Sarasvant from their union. Moreover, the female indeed runs first, and the bull follows after her; therefore, the [image of] Sarasvatī should be made first.
Indeed, this [verse] should first be dedicated to Sarasvatī.
Now, this verse addressed to Bṛhaspati serves as the introductory invocation (*pratipad*):
