"Those creatures whom Prajāpati created without the Brahman perished."
He saw this opening verse addressed to Bṛhaspati; with it, he created subjects endowed with sacred knowledge (*brahman*);
once created, they did not perish.
In that this opening verse belongs to Bṛhaspati, he creates through it offspring endowed with spiritual power (*brahman*);
once created, they do not perish for him.
(va) Now, those generated by Savitṛ:
(vb) "Whatever is of diverse forms here, these various forms we have approached as the *pratipads*; may that be for us, impelled by Savitṛ."
Now follow the *agnipāvamānya* verses.
For it is said: "Those who begin with the *pāvamānī* verses go as if along a path.
Indeed, Agni is the deity among the gods who makes the path.

By whatever fire one goes, one goes indeed making a path. Therefore, since this *agnipāvamānī* serves as the introductory verse (*pratipad*), they traverse the path by means of Agni himself, the path-maker.
"O Sage, of thee who art being purified..."—this becomes the *paryāsa* (concluding verse).
By this, they again traverse the path.
Verily, he who knows the leader of the *pṛṣṭha* chants becomes a leader among his own people.
The Vairāja is indeed the leader of the Pṛṣṭha-stotras. He who knows thus becomes a leader among his own people.
Regarding this they say: "This is indeed like a reversal of the proper order (*pāpavasyasa*), that the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are on both sides while the Pṛṣṭha-stotras are in the middle.
Just as one who is superior would sit below while one who is inferior sits above, such is the case with these.
"The Bṛhat and Rathantara are on both sides, and the Pṛṣṭhas are in the middle.

"The Bṛhat and Rathantara should indeed be in the middle, and the Pṛṣṭhas on both sides, for the sake of distinguishing between the superior and the inferior. Moreover, it is just as when one of lower status sits below while one of higher status sits above; such is that [arrangement]."
"The Bṛhat and Rathantara are in the middle, with the Pṛṣṭhas on both sides.
But in that case, it would not be a performance of all the Pṛṣṭhas;
for indeed, among all the Pṛṣṭhas, the Vairāja alone first attained its proper application.
Moreover, even if they should ask him as he is departing last, "Have you performed the *pṛṣṭha* chants? he should simply say, "No.
The *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* should be on both sides, with the *pṛṣṭhas* in the middle, for the sake of achieving the state of having all *pṛṣṭhas*.
This world is indeed the *rathaṃtara*, and yonder world is the *bṛhat*.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are cattle.
By means of these two worlds, he thus encloses cattle on both sides for the sake of non-loss.
His wealth is not lost by one who knows thus. 187.
JB 2.188 |va| Now, as the father and the mother, so are the Bṛhat and Rathantara; as the sons, so are the Pṛṣṭhas.
For whatever a son transgresses, the father is indeed his pacifier and the father is the restrainer. |vb|
In that the Bṛhat and Rathantara are on both sides, it is for the sake of peace and for warding off [evil].
Moreover, just as two parents might lie down around their children, such is the case when the Bṛhat and Rathantara are on both sides with the Pṛṣṭha-stotras in the middle.

Just as, for instance, bulls or wild asses might stand there in a state of great fury, so it is with these *pṛṣṭha* chants that are placed in the middle; and as for the fact that the *śyaita* and *naudhasa* are on both sides—
verily, the *naudhasa* is the *brahman*.
Having thus pacified them from the front by means of the *brahman*, they cause them to become tranquil from behind by means of the *śyaita*.
Therefore, the *naudhasa* should be at the beginning and the *śyaita* at the end.
Regarding this, they say: "Since the *pṛṣṭha* stotras have the same *nidhana*, how are they made non-identical?"
The Vairāja, the Mahānāmnīs, the Vairūpa, and the Revatīs—by this designation they are "not of the same womb.
Moreover, because these have their *nidhana* in the middle, it is for that very reason so.
In that [sāman], there are three seventeen-fold stomas.
Those are fifty-one *stotryās*.
That is the morning pressing of the cow. One hundred and eighty-nine [verses] belong to the night; that is the night of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
Thus this pair is produced for procreation. He who knows thus is propagated through a pair. These two kinds of stotriya verses amount to two hundred and forty.
That is the Virāj.
Food is the Virāj. Thus, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, he becomes firmly established in the Virāj, which is food. 188.
The gods and the Asuras were contending.
Now, at that time, these crafts belonged only to Prajāpati, and not to the other gods.
That Indra ran to Prajāpati, saying, "I shall conquer the Asuras. He gave that very craft to him;
he fastened it upon him.
Just as one would fasten on a golden coin, a gem, or a garland, so did he raise up his body.
From that, he fashioned this craft: these *pṛṣṭha* chants.
Now, as for the other brilliance with which he shines here—
Those Asuras, recognizing this form [of the sun], cried out, "He is our father who slays us! He is our father who slays us! and thus they were defeated.
Then indeed the gods prevailed, and the Asuras were defeated.
He prospers by himself, and his hateful rival is defeated—he who knows thus.
Regarding this, they say: "It should not be praised excessively."
"Just as if one were to fasten on a gold necklace, a gem, or a garland, and then remove them again— such is he who sings the *agniṣṭoma* chant.
"But indeed, he wins both of these worlds."
The day and night indeed comprise the entire universe.
Moreover, it is just as if one were to climb to the top of a great tree and find no way to descend; such is that which constitutes the Agniṣṭoma.

In that there are descending stotras, this Atirātra is indeed the complete foundation; by it he finds firm support on this earth. Regarding this they say: "Those who perform the Atirātra fall away from this world."
Now, as for the fact that the Bṛhat occurs in Gāyatrī verses: the Gāyatrī is indeed this earth; thus he finds firm support on this very [earth].
(JB 2.191) Furthermore, just as one might fasten a chariot wheel to a chariot axle, even so, having brought together all these arts...
Those who establish the *brahman* in the *gāyatrī* verses perform the *bṛhat* as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
Therefore, the *bṛhat* should indeed be performed as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* on *gāyatrī* verses.
Regarding this, they say: "One should give a thousand [cows]; that itself is the universe."
Now they say: one should give as many [cows] as there are verses for the Viśvajit-stotra; for that indeed is the "all.
But they also say: one should give whatever else may be his own property.
"That which he leaves over is evil," they say.
Just as it flows away from him because of [the lack of] a mate, even so does evil flow away from him because of that which he leaves over.
"Therefore, everything indeed should be given. 191. JB 2.192.
Now, this is the Vājapeya sacrifice.
One who desires food should sacrifice with the Vājapeya. Indeed, this Vājapeya is a "food-sacrifice" (annapeya).
For *vāja* is indeed food.
When indeed a cow, a horse, or a man is well-fed with food, then he becomes vigorous.
One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with the *agniṣṭoma*; for the *agniṣṭoma* is indeed Brahman, [and thus it serves] for the attainment of spiritual luster itself.
Indeed, he who is consecrated is consecrated for the sake of the desires of both the seasons and the animals.
For him, they should perform five stotras consisting of thirty-four verses each; all the *pavamāna* chants and both *brahmasāman*s should be [of that same measure].
There are that many verses to be chanted in the *ukthya* sacrifice.
They obtain that desire which is [attained] at the Ukthya;
nor indeed do they depart from the Agniṣṭoma.
Truly, this is neither an Agniṣṭoma, nor an Ukthya, nor a Ṣoḍaśin, nor an Atirātra.
This sacrifice is indeed redundant;
Prajāpati is indeed redundant;
this sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati.
For the attainment of Prajāpati itself. Its [verse] contains the word *bṛhat* and the word *śipiviṣṭa*. Cattle indeed are *śipiviṣṭas*.
"The Kṣatra is great.
"This world belongs to the Kṣatriya.
"May cattle attend upon the world of this Sāman which possesses a world for us."
They chant the Bṛhat Sāman in Triṣṭubh verses.
The Triṣṭubh is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
[The priests do this] thinking, "May he be consecrated with the ruling power as he is being consecrated."
They praise with the Vaiṣṇava verses; Viṣṇu is indeed the supreme among the deities, [thinking] "May he, being consecrated by the supreme deity, consecrate me.
They run the race for the attainment of Prajāpati and for the conquest of the heavenly world.
Seventeen [priests] run forward in a race.
Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold;
this sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati, for the attainment of Prajāpati himself. 192.
Regarding this, they say: they should run forward even when only three [verses] have been chanted.
For there are indeed three vital breaths: the out-breath (prāṇa), the in-breath (apāna), and the diffused breath (vyāna).
"So that their continuity may not be interrupted.
Now they say: "They should run toward one [of the fires] alone while it has not yet been praised. For what indeed is this, other than the prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna?"
Regarding this, they say: "They should run [the race] even when all the stotras have not yet been chanted, so that these two *ājya* offerings may not become mixed.
Regarding this, they also say: "Those who cause [the chariots] to run outside the sacrificial altar after the Soma has been pressed indeed depart from the sacrifice;
for the sacrifice is only as large as the space within the altar."
"One should have him run right up to the edge of the altar," they say. "Alternatively, having placed his foot on the seat of the chariot itself, one should bring him back again;
that is both 'run' and 'not run'."
Regarding this, they say: "They should indeed cause [the horses] to run.

For by means of the *rathantara* one wins the divine race, and by means of a chariot one wins the human race. Therefore, they should certainly cause them to run for the sake of winning these two races."

Brahmā, seated on the chariot wheel, chants the Sāman: "O Agni, bring us strength, O you who possess strength!"—"They, the possessors of strength, have come for strength"—"Strength is indeed immortality; it is for the attainment of food."
He sings while it is present;
for by means of that which is present, he goes to where he desires to go; he gives a horse of the same age.
Or rather, this is established by Vayaśva; or rather, all this belongs to Prajāpati;
this sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati, for the attainment of Prajāpati himself.
From each age (*vayas*), he gives seventeen [cattle]. Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold;
this sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati; it is for the attainment of Prajāpati himself.
Its morning pressing is unexpressed (*anirukta*).
Prajāpati is indeed unexpressed;
this sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati, for the sake of attaining Prajāpati himself.
*vad*: the midday pressing is possessed of strength;
*vae*: for this is indeed the Vājapeya; *vaf*: the third pressing is variegated.
For this sacrifice is most variegated.
With the words, "High is thy birth for the sake of the soma-juice," there are *gāyatrī* verses containing the word *andhas* (soma-juice) for the midday *pavamāna*.
Food indeed is *andhas*.
Therefore, they satisfy him, while he is being pressed at the very beginning of the *pavamāna*, with food.
In those [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa already explained.
Now follows the Āmahīyava;
the Āmahīyava belongs to Prajāpati.

This sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati; it is for the attainment of Prajāpati itself. Now follows the Saindhukṣita, the Kṣatra-sāman. Being consecrated with the power of the Kṣatra, he should be consecrated.
Now, *athābhīkam* is the form for consecration (*abhiṣiktyai*).
"O Soma, being purified, flow in a stream"—this *bṛhatī* verse possesses a dual form. This [verse] is the *udyayāma* which has both *sāmans*.
Therefore, they perform these very [verses]: they perform them for those using the *bṛhat* as the *sāman*, and they perform them for those using the *rathantara* as the *sāman*.
Among them, the *raurava* is well known as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
[They do this] so that the well-known *agniṣṭoma-sāman* may not be interrupted.
Now, the *vājajit* [verse]: *vāja* is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
Now, the *dairghaśravasa*: *dairghaśravasa* is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food. Now, the *arkapuṣpa*: *arka* is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
Then [the hymn] *samanta*;
"May glory be on every side for him"—thus [it is].
Then the *yaudhājaya* with three *nidhanas*, for the satisfaction of the pressings (*savana*).
Now, as for the *Auśana*, the final *sāman*: "By means of the final *sāman*, may we attain the final heavenly world.
Then there is the *Rathantara*;
the *Rathantara* is indeed the *brahman*.
This is the *brahmasava*. Being consecrated by means of the *brahman*, may he be consecrated.
Now, may they follow the *vāmadevya* chant, which is auspicious, peaceful, and well-sounding.
Now, the Vāmadevya is indeed cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
Then there is the Naudhasa, the well-known Brahman-sāman.
"The Brahman-sāman is well known; let us not exclude it," [they thought].
"Now, what does he obtain by pressing the *kāleya*? [He replies: "He obtains the *kāla* (time/measure), and furthermore, he attains that which is his own *kālya* (proper time).
Regarding the verse "The exhilaration of yours, most excellent," there are *gāyatrī* verses containing the word *andhas* belonging to the *pavamāna* of the *ārbhava* [stotra].
*Vae* is food, or rather, *andhas* (the soma-juice).
*Vaf*: thus they satisfy him, while he is being pressed, with food at the very beginning of the *pavamāna* chant.
In them, the Gāyatra [Sāman] has its Brāhmaṇa explained;
and also the Saṃhita.
The Saṃhita is indeed Brahman.
This is the Brahmasava.
"Being consecrated by the *brahman*, may he be consecrated," [he says].
Then come the *vājadāvaryas*.
"Vāja" is food; "vārya" means "giver of food. These [verses] are for the attainment of food itself.
Then there is the Vāravantīya chant, [performed with the thought]: "May prosperity attend him through water."
Now, the Vāravantīya is indeed cattle;
it is for the attainment of cattle.
Then, the Sabhā.
"May he obtain the assembly for one who has pressed [the Soma]," and "Furthermore, may he who has pressed [the Soma] obtain the assembly.
Now follows the *śrudhīya* chant, the *kīrtimat* melody.
"May fame arise after him as he has arisen through merit.
The *anuṣṭubh* verses beginning with "purojitī vo andhasaḥ" contain the word *andhas*;
for *andhas* is indeed food.
Thus, they endow this very [Soma] as it is being pressed with food.
In these [verses], there is the *nānada* chant; for here too, the *ṣoḍaśin* is performed.

Now, the *viśoviśīya* is the *kṣatrasāman*; [it is used] for one being consecrated with royal power, thinking, "May he be consecrated. Furthermore, this [sāman] is the people when pressed; [it is used] with the thought, "May he become the king of the people."

Now, the Śyāvāśva is a *sāman* leading to heaven; it serves for the complete attainment of the heavenly world. Now, the Āndhīgava is food; it serves for the acquisition of food. Now, the Kāva is "Happiness indeed for him who has pressed [the soma]."
"Moreover, may he who presses [the Soma] obtain the Kava [laud]," so they say.
Then there is the Yajñāyajñīya, the well-known Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
"The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is well known; let us not omit it," they say.
*vae*—now, regarding preeminence: *vaf*—the Yajñāyajñīya is indeed preeminence;
*vag*—he thus establishes him in preeminence.
Now, the Sākamaśva is a *sāman* leading to heaven; it serves for the complete attainment of the heavenly world.
Now, the Saubhara is the splendor of the Bṛhat;
[it is used] with the thought, "May our praise be performed with the Bṛhat endowed with splendor."

Now, as for the Nārmedha: "The Nārmedha is the *atirātra-sāman*; let us not exclude the *atirātra-sāman*. Furthermore, the Nārmedha is indeed cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle. Now, as for the *ṣoḍaśin*: "May whatever desire there is in the *ṣoḍaśin* be attained by me."
Now, there is [a verse] containing the word *bṛhat* and the word *śipiviṣṭa*. The *bṛhat* is indeed the mind;
Prajāpati is the mind.
This becomes the seventeenth of the hymns;
this is the seventeenfold *stoma*;
Prajāpati is indeed the seventeenfold.
*vat* is Prajāpati; *vau* is the heavenly world (*svarga-loka*); *vav* is glory (*śrī*).
Thus, they finally establish him in Prajāpati himself, in the heavenly world, within glory. 195.
JB 2.196 |va Now follows this Rājasūya sacrifice.
vb Varuṇa indeed desired: "May I be consecrated for the kingship over all the gods."
He saw this sacrifice;
he took it up; with it, he sacrificed.
Then indeed, he was consecrated for the sovereignty of all the gods.
He who knows thus is consecrated for preeminence among his own people. His *pavamāna* chants consist of thirty-four verses each.
The world of the gods is indeed self-ruling (*svarāj*);
the thirty-four-fold [stoma] is self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).
Thus, they endow him, while he is being pressed at the beginning of the *pavamāna*, with the world of self-sovereignty.
The *anuṣṭubh* is the opening verse;
speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*,
and speech is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
"Being consecrated with the power of the ruling class (*kṣatra*), may he be consecrated!
Now, these five *saṃbhāryā* verses have various deities.
Indeed, it is for the sovereignty of five types of men that one being consecrated is consecrated—for a king, for a nobleman (*rājanya*), and so forth.
To the charioteer, to the village headman, to the Śūdra, and to the slave.
They draw forth from here the threefold *stoma* and the verse addressed to Agni from the *saṃbhāryā* verses.
Therefore, the wife of a Brāhmaṇa is not to be conquered by a Rājanya; she is not to be treated as a common woman, nor punished, nor slain.

If they were to perform the *trivṛt* stoma here in the *saṃbhāryā* verses dedicated to Agni, the Rājanya would indeed be one who oppresses the Brahmins; he would conquer the Brahmins and kill them without having committed the slaying of a fetus.
Regarding this, they say: "A *rājanya* should not cause this to be known.

For just as a chief (*śreṣṭhin*) does whatever he desires, so [the *rājanya*] acts. If he were to say, "Make the *stoma* the *trivṛt* indeed; [make the verses] addressed to Agni in the *saṃbhāryās*," he would be a violator of the *brahman*.
"A kṣatriya may overcome brahmins; he may kill them even for the murder of an embryo.
Regarding this, they also say: "He who knows this, that very kṣatriya should overcome those who do not honor the brahmins;
he should kill them even for the murder of an embryo."
Regarding this, they say: "Those who depart from the *trivṛt* stoma indeed depart from the vital breaths.
One should perform the sacrifice first with the *trivṛt-agniṣṭoma*;
for the *trivṛt* is indeed the vital breath.
By that very [means], they do not depart from their vital breaths.
Brahman is indeed generated in front as the *kṣatra*;
moreover, they say that the sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) is the "covering" (*apiciti*).
"One should sacrifice with that very [soma].
Because it has two *trivṛt* stotras, by means of that very [fact], they do not depart from the vital breaths; thus, the one who presses [the soma] attains honor.
Regarding this, they say: since this opening verse belongs to Vāyu, and Vāyu is indeed breath, they thus prosper through the vital breaths.
"O Vāyu, the bright [oblation] is offered to you"—thus it contains the word *śukra*.

"Verily, he who is pressed out shines forth among other men like light; this one being pressed thinks, 'May I become like light. With the words, "The first of the honey in the heavenly rites," they thus make that very [Soma] the foremost of what pertains to the honey.
"Come for the drinking of Soma"—this verse belongs to Soma;
by it, the *pāvamānī* [verse] is performed;
"O God, desirable one, accompanied by your team of horses."
The *kṣatra* is indeed desirable;
the *viś* are those with teams of horses (*niyutvatīḥ*). Thus, they make the *viś* follow the path of the *kṣatra*.
Therefore, the people (viś) follow the path of the ruling power (kṣatra). 197/ JB 2.198 |va Now, these [are] of Sarasvant and of the Sarasvatī.
This indeed is the divine couple, the source of procreation: Sarasvant and Sarasvatī.
[The purpose is] "through the divine couple, may we procreate.
Regarding this, they say: "The offering for the male should be made first, and that for the female afterwards."
Likewise, for one who presses [the Soma], a son is born who is not timid. Regarding this, they also say: "Vāyu is indeed the depositor of seed;
Sarasvatī is procreation."
The two produce Sarasvant from the pair. Now, the female indeed runs first, and then the bull follows; therefore, the female of Sarasvatī should be made first.
But this [other view] says that the male of Sarasvant should indeed be made first.

Now, the verse addressed to Bṛhaspati is for one who desires that his spiritual power (*brahman*) should produce sovereign power (*kṣatra*). Then, the verse addressed to Savitṛ is for one who desires that he, impelled by Savitṛ, should be consecrated.
Now, these two are the introductory verses (*pratipad*).
For here both *sāmans* are performed.
There is a nine-verse hymn addressed toward [the sun], which is the form of consecration;
moreover, by means of that very [hymn], they do not depart from the *trivṛt* stoma.
It consists entirely of six verses; it should be pressed with verses containing the word "sāman";
it contains the word "vṛṣan."
"This bull, being consecrated, may he consecrate us"—thus [it is said]. There are four verses for the acquisition of four-footed cattle.
They are cryptically expressed in two-footed [verses] for the acquisition of two-footed cattle.
That which is a reversal (*paryāsa*) is the desire for that reversal; that has been attained by me as "non-existent" (JB 2.199).
The final [verse] is an *anuṣṭubh*: "Then, O Night, adorned... (adha kṣapā pariṣkṛta).

Indeed, that Udgātṛ priest should officiate for a king with the Rājasūya sacrifice who, at the very Bahiṣpavamāna [laud], causes him to ascend the gods’ throne. The Anuṣṭubh is the introductory verse, and the Anuṣṭubh is the final verse.
In those two, there are sixty-four syllables;
of these, the sixty are the *āsandī*,
and the four are the legs of the *āsandī*.
Indeed, at the very *bahiṣpavamāna*, the *udgātṛ* causes the King [Soma] to ascend the gods’ throne.
There are both kinds of *ājya* chants; for here both *sāmans* are performed.

Regarding this, they say: "Only the *bṛhatī*-verses should be performed; for the clarified butter portions belong to the people (*viś*), while the *vājina* belongs to the nobility (*kṣatra*), so that the nobility might be consecrated by means of the people.
But on this point they also say: "Both [types of verses] should indeed be performed."
Indeed, he who is being consecrated for the sovereignty of all [the gods] is consecrated;
therefore, both sets [of rites] must be performed.
These amount to fifteen.
The fifteenfold [stoma] is indeed the kṣatra.
[He thinks: "May he who is being consecrated be consecrated with the kṣatra.
a) Upon emerging from the *avabhṛtha* bath, he fastens a garland of twelve lotuses upon himself.
b) The Waters were indeed the wives of the gods; they desired sexual union. c) They sought a mate.
The gods approached them;
they deposited the embryo;
from that, lotuses were born.
|vg Water is truth. |vh The consecration is truth.
|vi That which is the lotus leaves is indeed the truth of truth.
By means of truth itself, he thus binds for him austerity and consecration through truth.
That [consecration] consists of twelve *puṣkara*s;
there are twelve months in a year.
The year is the sacrifice;
thus he fastens the sacrifice onto this [altar].
Now, they also say that it should consist of seven lotuses.
There are indeed seven meters; by means of the meters the sacrifice is extended.
He thereby fastens the sacrifice onto this [person].
Now they say: "It should have six *puṣkaras*.
For the year consists of six seasons, and the sacrifice is the year.
He thereby fastens the sacrifice onto this [altar].
Now they say: "It should have five hollows," for the sacrifice is fivefold.
Animals consist of five parts;
the sacrifice is animals;
thus he fastens the sacrifice onto this [altar].
Now they say it should have four *puṣkaras*,
for there are four directions;
cattle are four-footed.
"Vae! The sacrifice is cattle.
"Vaf! He thereby fastens the sacrifice onto this [person].
"Vag! Now they also say, "It should have three *puṣkaras*."
The sacrifice consists of three pressings;
verily, he thus fastens the sacrifice upon this [altar].
Now, they also say that it should have twelve cups (*puṣkara*).
"Or rather, all these [syllables] are in twelve [stomas];
therefore, it should consist of twelve *puṣkaras*. (JB 2.201)
Now, these *saṃsṛp* offerings take place.
Indeed, when Varuṇa was pressing the Soma, the waters struck away his splendor with sixteenfold [blows].
That [splendor] fell toward this direction.
That [soma] became fourfold: Bhṛgu was one quarter, Sarasvatī was one quarter, Daśapeya was one quarter, and Śrāyantīya was one quarter.
Therefore, for this sacrifice, the descendant of Bhṛgu (Bhārgava) becomes the Hotṛ; the waters are the consecrating Sarasvatīs; and it is the Daśapeya.
The *Śrāyantīya* is the *brahmasāman* for the sacrifice. Those gods said, "Let us find this splendor (*bharga*). They saw these *saṃsṛp* offerings.
With them they crept after it. Because they crept after it, that is the nature of the *saṃsṛps* (creepers).
They recovered it by means of Viṣṇu as the deity and by means of the ten [fingers].
Therefore, for this sacrifice, an oblation to Viṣṇu is offered as the tenth;
for they found [it] on the tenth day,
and he has entered upon the tenth.
For on the tenth day they found them;
there are ten cups,
for on the tenth day they found them.
Ten men each attend to a cup;
for it was on the tenth day that they found [the Soma].
He whose lineage of ten ancestors has not been cut off from the drinking of Soma is the one who performs the consumption.
For on the tenth day they found it; having found it, they enclosed it with fire, and the Maruts blew upon it.
They mixed it with the Śrāyantīya [sāman]. That is why the Śrāyantīya has its name "Śrāyantīya.
Its *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is performed upon the verses of the Yajñāyajñīya.
Agni, indeed, is the verse of the *yajñāyajñīya*.
By means of Agni, they thus enkindle it.
The Śrāyantīya is the Brahman-sāman; thus they thoroughly prepare it. They chant the Yajñāyajñīya over *anuṣṭubh* verses.
The Yajñāyajñīya is indeed speech;
the Anuṣṭubh is speech.
By means of speech, they thus bring it to fulfillment.
The Vāravantīya is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman. The Vāravantīya is indeed power and vigor;
with power and vigor they thus endow it.
The *stoma* consists of seventeen parts; Prajāpati, indeed, is seventeenfold.
Prajāpati is the finder of what is lost; through him who is the finder of what is lost, may we find this splendor (*bharga*).
The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is the year; for this Agniṣṭoma is indeed the year.
By means of the year itself, they thus enclosed them and placed them within themselves.

At that [sacrifice], these sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) are led forth according to their respective forms: a garland for the Udgātṛ, a golden plate for the Hotṛ, two mirrors for the Adhvaryu, twelve six-year-old cows for the Brahman, a milch-cow for the Maitrāvaruṇa, and a bull.
Two garments for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; a one-horsed cart laden with barley for the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ; an ox for the Acchāvāka; and [an ox] for the Agnīdh.
Now, as for the fact that there is a wreath for the Udgātṛ: the wreath belongs to Sūrya, and the Udgātṛ belongs to Sūrya; thus, a common mark is established between them.
That becomes the *paṭariṇī*.
For that sun is indeed like a piece of cloth.
Now, as for the gold plate belonging to the Hotṛ: these three things are joined together in alignment—the gold plate, the Āhavanīya fire, and yonder sun.
Because these [spoons] are joined together, it is for the sake of prosperity;
indeed, prosperity comes to him who knows this. Now, as for the two *prākāśa* spoons belonging to the Adhvaryu, they say that they invoke them by means of their form.

Furthermore, because those two move by means of light alone, that [sacrifice] is made to correspond with them. Now, as for the fact that there are twelve six-year-old cows for the Brahman; the six-year-old cow is indeed procreation.

Procreation is the Brahman; thus, that which shares its characteristic mark is performed. Now, as for the fact that there is a cow for the Maitrāvaruṇa: a cow is indeed milk, and these two, Mitra and Varuṇa, partake of milk; thus, that which shares its characteristic mark is performed.

Now, as for the fact that there is a bull for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin: the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin belongs to Indra, and the bull belongs to Indra; thus, that which is his characteristic mark is made to correspond with him.

Then, as for the two garments belonging to the Neṣṭṛ and the Potṛ: the two garments belong to the Maruts, and the Neṣṭṛ and the Potṛ belong to the Maruts; thus, that which is theirs is made to correspond with them.
It is made to have the same marks as that.
Now, the Maruts are indeed abundance, and the cloth is abundance through its threads.
Furthermore, as for the fact that there is a single-yoked cart covered with barley for the Acchāvāka, this Hotrā-offering is indeed like a worn-out woman whose vitality is exhausted.
That which belongs to the Acchāvāka—them they cause to swell with these very barley grains.
That [cart] becomes one-horsed; it is the form of security.
"The *hotṛ*s are to be unyoked at the end," so it is said. Now, as for the fact that the ox belongs to the *āgnīdhra*: the ox draws, and Agni carries the oblation to the gods;
thus, they are made to share the same characteristic mark.
In that these sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) are led forth according to their proper form, it is for the sake of success;
indeed, it succeeds for him who knows thus.
Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, he shaves only his beard, not his hair.
For the head is indeed prosperity (*śrī*);
and indeed, the prosperity of one who has pressed the Soma departs to the head.
If he were to shave his hair before the year [is complete], he would shave his prosperity itself, not his hair.
But since he shaves his hair after the year has passed, he first encloses prosperity within himself by means of the year and then shaves his hair, not his prosperity.
Therefore, one should shave [the hair] only from above. That [sacrifice] is an Atirātra;
for the Atirātra is indeed the form of the hair.
Those [days] of the day which are white are its form; those which are black belong to the night.
Therefore, there is an Atirātra sacrifice.
Its [days] proceed in reverse order.
"Then he indeed mounts Śreyāṃsa (the More Excellent), he who is about to be born.
Its morning pressing consists of twenty-one stotras.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first.

This is indeed Varuṇa. This is the consecration of Varuṇa (*varuṇasava*). He who now mounts [the throne] is one who, having mounted upon a superior, does not yield to him; by whatever affliction he desires that [superior], by that very means he causes him to fall.
In that these *stomas* proceed in reverse order (*pratiloma*), they are indeed concealing themselves and departing; then the *stomas* return again hitherward.
For he who, having overtaken a superior, then seeks to deceive him, says to him: "Go away! Do not depart!"—so indeed does he speak.
In that the *kratavaḥ* of the Aśvins rise upward again, it is just as if one were to say to someone who is hiding, "Come out! Do not flee! Such is that.
For him, the *Rathantara* is at the midday pressing.
This, indeed, is the Rathantara;
verily, he thus finds firm support in this [earth].
Now follows this two-night sacrifice. One desiring offspring should perform it with this.
Both types of *stomas* are used in it: those that are odd and those that are even.
This indeed is the divine pair, the source of procreation, namely both types of *stomas*.
[Thinking] "May that which is the divine pair, the source of procreation, procreate me," for it,
both the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* *sāmans* are employed.
These two, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, are indeed a divine pair, a source of procreation. [He thinks:
"May that divine pair, a source of procreation, procreate me.
For this [sacrifice], the Pañcaviṃśa becomes the Brahman-sāman.
The person, indeed, is the twenty-fifth.
This *brahmasāman* is the desire of the sacrificer; thus, he causes offspring to attain the state of the person.
It has seven hundred and twenty hymn-verses (*stotrīya*);
there are just as many days and nights in a year.
Indeed, it is the days and nights that generate all this.
"May those who generate all this [universe] generate me," [he says].
Now, this Agniṣṭoma is a Triṣṭubh. 206. JB 2.206.
One who desires a firm foundation should bring this [sacrifice].

Regarding this, they say: "He who is about to give birth indeed falls away from this world. In that there is a *triṣṭubh* [stoma], and since these worlds are three, he thereby finds a firm foundation in these very worlds.
Now, this sacrificial rite is indeed named Dhṛti.
Its Pṛṣṭha-stotra is the Rathantara;
with this very [rite], King Abhipratāraṇa performed a sacrifice.
He indeed performed [the sacrifice] ending with the *dvirātra*.
A Brahmin said to him: "The Kurus will conquer Kurukṣetra;
take away only the offspring, not the fields."

These Kurus, having conquered Kurukṣetra, roam about; all these [deities] are in Kurukṣetra. Indeed, this Agniṣṭoma Triṣṭoma is carried away for the very sake of maintaining the sacrificial fields. 206. JB 2.207.
Now, these are the *nākasad* [sacrificers].
Indeed, the gods ascended to the heavenly world.
Having reached the heavenly world, they remained there together, having reached a firm resolve.
They desired: "May we settle in the vault, in the heavenly world. They saw these *nākasad* stoma-chants;
they took them up.
They sacrificed with them. Then indeed they settled in the vault, in the heavenly world.
Because they settled in the vault, in the heavenly world, that is the reason for the *nākasads*' being called *nākasats*.
"Indeed, he dwells in the vault of the sky, in the world of heaven, who knows thus," so said Jānaśruteya.
Then Vaitahavya used to say, "In this very world, in the beginning, Prajāpati created the gods.
Now, these worlds above were indeed the wild tracts; they were without chariots or vehicles, just like forest thickets.
They were unbound.
Those gods desired, "May we go to the heavenly world. 207/ JB 2.208.
Those Vasus were the first to go forth. By means of three threefold [stomas] they extended this world; with one fifteenfold [stoma] they settled upon it.
By means of three threefold [stomas] they extended this intermediate world.

They descended by means of one [stoma] consisting of seventeen verses. By means of three [stomas] each consisting of nine verses, they ascended to that world. They descended by means of one [stoma] consisting of twenty-one verses.
Just as the axe is sharp, and as Agni is among the deities, so is this Trivṛt Stoma. Just as one might go cutting ahead with an axe and smoothing behind with fire,
even so did the Vasus, by means of the Trivṛt Stoma, impel these worlds forward.

Because they extended (*prāyuvan*) these worlds, therefore these *stomas* are also called *prayujas*. Just as one would go toward a place where there is good pasture that has been burnt by fire, even so did the Vasus go.
Therefore, they are the most excellent among the gods.
For they were the first to go. Then the Rudras saw a more prepared path.
By means of one threefold [stoma] alone, they extended this world;
by means of three fifteenfold [stomas], they settled upon it.
By means of one threefold [stoma] alone, they extended this intermediate world.
With three [sets of] seventeen they settled down;
with one threefold [set] they strove toward that world;
with three [sets of] twenty-one they settled down.
Just as, indeed, on that triple-jointed path of what was made,
the Rudras went along making it even at the rear;
then the Ādityas [went] by means of four *trivṛt*s, four *pañcadaśa*s, and three *saptadaśa*s.

Then the Aṅgirases traveled separately by means of three triplets each: by three fifteen-fold, three seventeen-fold, and three twenty-one-fold stomas, along with the Virāṭsvarāja. They proceeded by way of the single twenty-one-fold stoma. Then the Aṅgirases proceeded by means of three triplets each: by three fifteen-fold, three seventeen-fold, and three twenty-one-fold stomas, along with the Virāṭsvarāja. Then the Aṅgirases proceeded by means of three triplets each: by three fifteen-fold, three seventeen-fold, and three twenty-one-fold stomas, along with the Virāṭsvarāja. They proceeded by way of the single twenty-one-fold stoma. Then the Aṅgirases proceeded by means of three triplets each: by three fifteen-fold, three seventeen-fold, and three twenty-one-fold stomas, along with the Virāṭsvarāja. They proceeded by way of the single twenty-one-fold stoma. Then the Aṅgirases proceeded by means of three triplets each:
By means of the twenty-sevenfold [stoma] alone, the Maruts went;
for the Maruts are indeed might and vigor; the Maruts are might and vigor.
The Triṇavas went by means of vigor and heroism alone.
The Viśvedevas went by means of the Trayastriṃśa [stoma] alone. Having gone to the heavenly world, they remained there together, having reached a firm resolve.
They desired, "May we also sit upon the firmament, in the heavenly world.
Then all the gods perceived this thirty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*).
They brought it.
Regarding that, they ask: "Who are the Viśve Devāḥ?
One should say: "These very five deities, having become complete, become the Viśve Devāḥ."
The All-Gods sacrificed with this thirty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*).
There are indeed thirty-three deities and thirty-three divine worlds. From that, they settled in the firmament, in the heavenly world.
They said, "We shall indeed sit upon the firmament in the heavenly world.
Because they said, "We shall indeed sit upon the firmament (nāka) in the heavenly world," that is the reason for the Nākasads' name, their being "Nākasads" (sitters on the firmament).
Indeed... [so it must be read, if one consults 2.209 (250.28)].
He who knows this sits in the firmament, in the heavenly world.

In these [verses] there are both Sāmans; for by means of both he goes to where he desires to go. Among them, those Sāmans which have *suvar* as their finale and those which have *jyotis* as their finale, they arrange as leading to the heavenly world.
For the attainment of the heavenly world in its totality and for the prosperity of the forms of the days.
Now, these are the Ṛtuṣṭomas. JB 2.211. va.
The seasons indeed desired: "May we attain prosperity through a common sacrifice;
may we obtain food; may we become ever new, ever renewed.
They saw these sacrifices.
They brought them;
with them they sacrificed.
Spring was the first to sacrifice.
He sacrificed with this [offering]. He attained that very prosperity and secured that food, as well as this state of renewal which belongs to spring.
Then Śiśira thought: "By the very same means by which these [ancestors] of old sacrificed and prospered, by that same means shall I sacrifice.
He sacrificed with this very [rite]. He attained that same prosperity and secured that food; he also attained this state of renewal which is this [renewal].
Of the cool season.
For among these, this very one is always the most prosperous.
For having reached this very [breath], one descends into this same form of the cow, the horse, and the human.
This is that infinite wheel of the gods, undecaying and ever-renewed, which revolves both hitherward and thitherward.
He who knows this thus wins this very infinity, this undecaying state, and this ever-renewed nature.
He who should desire, "May I attain prosperity through a uniform sacrifice; may I obtain food and nourishment;
may I become ever new, ever renewed," he should sacrifice with these [offerings].
He should sacrifice with the first [offering] in the spring.
He attains this very prosperity, secures this food, and achieves that renewal which belongs to spring. In summer, he should sacrifice with the second [offering].
In the rainy season, one should sacrifice with the third [offering];
in autumn, one should sacrifice with the fourth;
in winter, one should sacrifice with the fifth.
In the cool season (śiśira), he should sacrifice with the sixth [offering]. He thus attains this very prosperity, secures this food, and obtains that freshness which belongs to the cool season. 212.
He becomes one with the seasons alone;
he attains the seasons themselves, and his merit becomes inexhaustible and uninterrupted.
"Ever new, ever new indeed he goes, swelling with his good deeds.
There are five *stotriya* verses; for the sacrifice is fivefold, cattle are fivefold, food is fivefold, the seasons are five, and whatever there is—[all that is fivefold].
And five by five; this is the entire supernatural power (ṛddhi) of that [sacrifice], its attainment.
Of each of those, there are sixty stotriya verses;
so many nights are there in the seasons.
Therefore, they do not praise the seasons.
Of all those [stomas], there are three hundred and sixty verses for the stotras;
so many are the nights of the year.
Indeed, they reach that year by means of the nights alone. Regarding this, they say: "The *pṛṣṭha* chants themselves should be undertaken.
For one should indeed proceed from one *pṛṣṭha* to another *pṛṣṭha*.

"For the *pṛṣṭha* chants are the seasons. Thus, the first [day] should have the *rathantara* as its *sāman*, then the one with the *bṛhat* *sāman*, then the one with the *vairūpa* *sāman*, then the one with the *vairāja* *sāman*, then the one with the *śakvarī* *sāman*, and the last should be the one with the *revatī* *sāman*.

Regarding this, they say: "The *pṛṣṭha* chants should be separated from the *sutyā* by means of the *dīkṣā* and *upasad* rites. If they were to do so, they would indeed approach the *pṛṣṭhas* as if from a great distance;
for one *pṛṣṭha* alone is capable of carrying another *pṛṣṭha*.
These *sāmans* are indeed the offspring of the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*.
The *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* are the two means of continuity for a sacrifice that has been interrupted.
Therefore, they should consist of the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* alone.
The Rathantara-sāman should be first, then the Bṛhat-sāman, then the Rathantara-sāman, then the Bṛhat-sāman, then the Rathantara-sāman, and the Bṛhat-sāman should be last. Among these,
those Sāmans which have the seasons as their *nidhana*— those Sāmans with the seasons as their *nidhana*— they arrange as leading to heaven.
For the attainment of the heavenly world and for the prosperity of the forms of the days.
Now, these are the *stomas* of the quarters. JB 2.214. v.
The quarters desired: "May we attain equal prosperity through a common sacrifice;
may we be firmly established; may we conquer the infinite world of heaven.
They saw these sacrifices.
They brought them;
they sacrificed with them. This eastern direction was the first to sacrifice.
He sacrificed with this [sacrifice]. He attained that very prosperity, that very foundation, and he conquered this infinite heavenly world.
This very infinite heavenly world has been conquered by him.

Indeed, even if one were to travel for many days toward the east, one would not find its end. Then this upward direction thought: "By that very means through which these [other directions] have sacrificed and succeeded, by that same means shall I sacrifice.
It, therefore, sacrificed with that very [means].
He attained this very prosperity, this support, and he conquered this infinite heavenly world.
This is that infinite heavenly world which has been conquered.
Indeed, even if one were to go upward for many days, one would not find its end. 214.
Regarding this they say: "One should indeed approach the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. For from the *pṛṣṭha*, one should indeed approach the *pṛṣṭha*.

"For the *pṛṣṭha* chants are the directions. Thus, the first [day] should have the *rathantara* as its *sāman*, then the *bṛhat*-sāman, then the *vairūpa*-sāman, then the *vairāja*-sāman, then the *śakvarī*-sāman, and the *revatī*-sāman should be the last.
Regarding this, they say: "The *pṛṣṭha* chants should be separated from the consecration (*dīkṣā*), the preliminary offerings (*upasad*), and the soma-pressing (*sutyā*).
If they were to do so, they would approach the *pṛṣṭhas* as if from a very great distance;
for indeed, one *pṛṣṭha* ought to carry another *pṛṣṭha*.
These *sāmans* indeed arise from the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*.
The *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* serve to reconnect a sacrifice that has been interrupted.
Therefore, they should consist of the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* alone.
The Rathantara-sāman should be first, then the Bṛhat-sāman, then the Rathantara-sāman, then the Bṛhat-sāman, and the Rathantara-sāman and the Bṛhat-sāman should be the last. 215/ JB 2.216.
Now, those indeed become five sets of twenty-five.
Of these, the twenty that remain are the Virāj;
and as for the four, they are these very four quarters.
Now, that which is the twenty-fifth is this very upward direction.
The directions indeed milk the sky, and the sky milks the directions.
He who knows this attains the milking of both the directions and the sky.
He who should desire, "May I attain prosperity through a common sacrifice; may I be firmly established;
may I conquer the infinite world of heaven"—he should sacrifice with these [offerings].
He should indeed choose a very large sacrificial ground for the gods.
He should say, "Five halls are to be built: one here, one here, one here, one here, and one in the middle. He should sacrifice with this *Rathantara* Sāman;
he attains this very prosperity, this foundation, and wins this infinite heavenly world.

<ahīna> JB 2.235 | Now,
these are the two-night sacrifices (dvirātra).

Haviṣmān and Haviṣkṛt were two Aṅgirasas. While they were wandering about heedlessly in this world, practicing the conduct of women, the seers of the Aṅgiras clan, the fathers, and the grandfathers who had performed meritorious deeds abandoned them and departed for the heavenly world.

When they had performed that practice for a long time, they both desired: "How indeed might we go to that same world where the seers, the Aṅgirases, our fathers and grandfathers who were doers of good deeds have gone to the heavenly world?
They both practiced austerity.
The two of them saw this two-night sacrifice;
they took it up; they sacrificed with it.
Then indeed, those two went to where the seers of the Aṅgiras clan, their fathers and grandfathers who had performed good deeds, had gone to the heavenly world.
He who should desire: "Where my fathers and grandfathers who performed good deeds have gone to the heavenly world, [there may I go]."
Thinking, "May I follow after them," he should sacrifice with this [rite].
Indeed, wherever his fathers and grandfathers have gone to the world of heaven through their good deeds, there he follows after them.
Now they say: "He who is superior to his rival should sacrifice with this.
For he who is superior is like one who has departed before;
indeed, by means of this [sacrifice], those two reached them as if they were those who had departed before.
Having attained what is better, he becomes more prosperous in himself.
Moreover, they say: "One who desires offspring should sacrifice with this [rite].
Indeed, the first day is the self, and the subsequent day is offspring.
By the first day he prepares himself; by the second day, his offspring.
Indeed, this sacrificial rite consisting of two nights is very difficult to perform.
If the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma is the preceding day and the Sarvastoma Atirātra is the subsequent day, they discontinue the stotras.
Alternatively, if the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma is the preceding day, the subsequent [day] is indeed the Sarvastoma Atirātra.
They interrupt the hymns.
Now, if the first day is a Jyotis Ukthya, the second day is indeed an Atirātra with all the Stomas;
they thus ruin the opening of the sacrifice.

In that there is a *jyotis* (light) [stoma], they do not cause the opening of the sacrifice to fail by means of it. And in that there is an *ukthya*, they do not interrupt the *stotras* by means of it.
Indeed, this sacrificial rite which has attained the *virāj* is truly as if already accomplished.
That [rite] is to be undertaken again.
That which is the twenty-four-fold *bahiṣpavamāna* of the subsequent day is the year,
for the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
The year is the sacrifice; thus they take hold of the sacrifice itself at the very mouth of the sacrifice.
Moreover, the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables;
it is the Gāyatrīs that extend the sacrificial rite once it has been attained.
For no other [meter] than the Gāyatrī is capable of raising up a sacrificial rite that has been attained.
Regarding this they say: "How is it that neither the forty-fourfold nor the forty-eightfold [stoma] can become the mouth of the even-numbered stomas?"
“How is it that there are exactly twenty-four?
He should reply: “The Gāyatrī indeed has three feet;
thus they begin with that which has three feet.”
The Atirātra consists of all the Stomas; it serves for the conquest and the overcoming of all the worlds.
For indeed, all this is nothing but Stomas.
Moreover, having prospered through those individual Stomas which we have approached one by one, and having established ourselves in them, we have risen upward.
"May we attain," [they say].
Indeed, this sacrificial rite that is the *dvirātra* (two-night sacrifice) is, as it were, interrupted. JB 2.237. va.
The Gāyatrī is attained on the first day, and the Triṣṭubh on the latter.
Now, they ask: "Wherein are the Jagatī and the Anuṣṭubh?
One should effect the attainment of the Gāyatrī on the first day, as well as the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and the Anuṣṭubh.
And furthermore, it is for the continuity and non-interruption of the meters.
"High is thy birth for the sake of the food-stuff (*andhas*)," he says; it contains the word *andhas*, for the *jagatī* has the form of containing *andhas*;
thus they do not depart from the form of the *jagatī*.
The *vaikhānasa* is a *jāgata* *sāman*. By that very means, they do not depart from the form of the *jagatī*.
Of the two *sāmans*, one or the other is used; it is like one who would stand firm with both feet.

*vi*: It becomes *suvar-jyotis* (the light of heaven). *vj*: Heaven (*suvar*) is indeed the former day, and light (*jyotis*) is the latter; [this is] for the continuity of the days and for the commencement of the day.
*vk*: The two *sāmans*, *hāviṣmat* and *hāviṣkṛta*, belong to the heavenly realm; they serve for the complete attainment of the world of heaven.
Regarding this they say: "If they were to perform both [Sāmans] as *kṣipra*-sāmans, they would be liable to strike down the sacrificer before his full span of life;
for, disregarding this world, those two would have gone over to that world alone.
Therefore, on the subsequent day, they should perform the *brahmasāman* upon the *uktha*s of the *hāviṣmat* [stotra].
In this way, he reaches his full lifespan and goes to the heavenly world.
(237) Now, for him whose first day is the Jyotir-ukthya and whose subsequent day is the Āyus-atirātra, by this [rite]—

Hābhipratāraṇa performed a sacrifice, desiring offspring; and Khalati Daivodāsi, being about to cut [the hair], [did so]. Then indeed he cut off his baldness, Daivodāsi; he obtained this much offspring.
Three [bones] exceed in the other; the other is deficient by two.
Those three are excessive in the male, by which he procreates;
those two are deficient in the female, from which she gives birth.
Thus, this pair is created for procreation. He who knows thus is procreated by means of that pair and procreation.
Those two become the stotriya verses: seven hundred and twenty-one; so many [are they].
The days and nights of the year.
Indeed, Prajāpati is the whole day and night; "May we prosper through the whole Prajāpati; may the whole Prajāpati be attained by us. Thus [they say].
Now, that one *stotriyā* verse which remains over is indeed the world of the sacrificer.

A Brahmin once said to him: "In your offspring, no other hero such as this will ever be born. He created the world for himself alone, not for his offspring; for he has entered into this very world. (238)
Having realized this, he said: "Let his offspring be according to the divine [fate]. I am a god among gods; I have cut away the divine wind."
For thus they both threatened him and thus they tormented him.
This is that very same thing.
These two are indeed deceivers; such another hero as we were shall not be born again.
Now, as for this [sacrifice] which has a reversal of the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* [stomas]:
the first day is an *agniṣṭoma*,
and the subsequent day is an *atirātra* with all the *stomas*.
One who desires offspring should sacrifice with this [rite].
There are the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* *stomas*, which are deficient and redundant, forming a pair for procreation;
one is deficient and the other is redundant.
From a pair that is indeed deficient or excessive, offspring and cattle are produced;
thus, that act of procreation is performed.
For this, the Rathantara becomes the Pṛṣṭha-stotra.
The *rathantara* is indeed procreation; thus, that procreation is performed. It has twelve stotras.
Twelve months are a year;
the year is procreation;
thus, that procreation is performed.
For that [sacrifice], there are twenty-four *stuta-śastra* hymns;
the year consists of twenty-four half-months;
the year is procreation.
That very procreation is performed in successive order.
He who knows thus is propagated with offspring and cattle. There is an Atirātra sacrifice consisting of all the Stomas, for the conquest and the overcoming of all the worlds.
For all this is indeed the *stomas*. Moreover, those individual *stomas* which we have approached, having prospered together with them— in them [we abide].
"May we attain the *ṛc* by means of the *pratiṣṭhā*," [so they say].
Now, for this [sacrifice], the first day consists of the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, and the *saptadaśa* stomas, while the [next] day is the *ekaviṃśa*. 239/240. JB 2.240. va.
The *triṇava* and the *trayastriṃśa*: one who desires heaven should sacrifice with this latter [set].
These *stomas* are directed upwards;
for the heavenly world is indeed directed upwards.
For the attainment of the heavenly world itself.
They possess surpassing *stomas*;
indeed, by means of what is surpassed, they enjoy the sacrifice.
By this very means, indeed, Haviṣmān and Haviṣkṛt both went immediately to the heavenly world.
For him, the *stotras* are directed forward, the *śastras* are directed forward, the *pṛṣṭhas* are directed forward, the *viṣṭutis* are directed forward; he becomes entirely directed forward.
Therefore, one should perform this sacrifice only in the latter part of life, when one no longer desires this world, when one no longer wishes to deposit anything in this world,
and when one intends to depart from this world for that other world.
One should indeed sacrifice with this.
Having sacrificed, he indeed goes to the heavenly world.
At that time, they should perform both [offerings] as having oblations and as having the oblation made manifest, for the attainment of the heavenly world, for the sake of reaching the heavenly world.
Regarding that, they say: "They should perform seven hundred and twenty stotriyās.
There are as many days and nights in a year;
thus, they do not depart from the year itself.
Furthermore, they say: "As many *stotriya* verses as there are for this three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus, so many *stotriya* verses should they effect for this [Sāman].
By this, they do not depart from the form of the three-day period.
Now they say: "One should complete his *stotriyās* as exactly one thousand.
There are indeed one thousand *stotriyās* for the three-night rite;
thus, they do not depart from the very form of the three-night rite.

This two-night rite is indeed successful when it is performed according to the perfection of the three-night rite, or when the three-night rite [is performed according to the perfection] of the four-night rite. 240.
Now, these are the three-night rites (*trirātra*).
By means of the three-night rite, indeed, the gods prospered in these worlds; by means of the three-night rite, they went to the heavenly world.
Speech, indeed, is the three-night rite.
By means of the form of speech, the *ājya* chants and the days are divided.
Speech, indeed, consists of one syllable, while the imperishable (*akṣara*) consists of three syllables. By means of the form of the imperishable, they are divided.
There are three Gandharvas. Their respective domains are these: the earth belongs to Agni, the intermediate space to Vāyu, and that [heaven] belongs to Āditya; just as that sky is, so is he.
Regarding this, the following verse is recited:
"Three create seed within the worlds; three noble progenies have light as their foremost element.
"Three heats accompany the dawn; all these the Vasiṣṭhas know."
Thus:

Regarding that which he says, "Three create seed in the worlds," Agni creates seed upon the earth, Vāyu in the intermediate space, and Āditya in heaven. "The three noble progenies have light as their foremost. (241)
The Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas—
of them, that light which is yonder sun goes before.
"Three heats accompany the Dawn"— Agni accompanies the Dawn, Vāyu accompanies the Dawn,
Āditya accompanies the Dawn.
"The Vasiṣṭhas know all of that"— the Brāhmaṇas who have heard [the sacred texts] are indeed the Vasiṣṭhas.
For they indeed know all this.
This much, indeed, is the three-night sacrifice:
the Gāyatra is breath, the Triṣṭubh is sight, and the Jagatī is hearing.
There are three pairs; among these, two become a pair, and that which is born from the pair is the third.
Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra.
Viṣṇu entered into him.
He said, "Indeed, there is this splendor, sensory power, and vigor in him;
let me take that away from him."
"Do not strike me," he said. "So be it," [the other replied],
and he gave it to him.
Viṣṇu accepted that. He offered a second to him;
Viṣṇu stood by it.
He said, "Indeed, this splendor, sensory power, and vigor exist within me;
let me bring that to you. Do not strike me."
"So be it," he said; he gave it to him;
Viṣṇu accepted it.
He raised it up for him a third time.
Viṣṇu supported it.
He said, "Is there indeed this splendor, sensory power, and vigor in that [third part] of yours?"
"Or rather, I shall bring that for you. "Do not strike me," [he said].
"So be it," [the other replied].
He gave it to him. Viṣṇu accepted it. Regarding it, they disputed: "It is all mine," said Indra; "The third part is mine," said Viṣṇu. (242)
"Let us two indeed ask him," they said.
They both asked Prajāpati.
With this [verse], he spoke apart from those two:
"Both of you have conquered; you are not defeated. Neither of these two has been defeated. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you contended, you divided the thousandfold [booty] into three parts."
"Thus," he said. "Two shares for you," he told Indra; "the third for you," he told Viṣṇu.
He then bestowed that thousand upon those two.
Regarding this, there is this attainment: one should give it on the first day to a man who has kinsmen and is learned in the Vedas.
Just as this earth is, so is he;
for this earth is firmly established, and he is firmly established.
Now, if there should be one who is not a kinsman but is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*), to him he should give on the second day.
Just as this intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is, so is he;
for they know this [gift] as "the intermediate space," and they know it as the Veda.
Now, if there should be one who possesses kin but is not a learned reciter (*ananūcāna*), to him one should give it on the third day.
For as is that sky, so is he;
indeed, they know that sky as "the sky" (*dyauḥ*), and they know its kinship (*bandhu*).
They are given ten by ten every day;
the Virāj consists of ten syllables;
the sacrifice is of the nature of the Virāj.
That very [gift] is given as a distinct unit.
A hundred are given day after day. This, indeed, is the measure of the sacrifice: that it be a hundred.
That very [portion] is given as separated.
On the first day, one should give three hundred and thirty-three;
on the second day, one should give three hundred and thirty-three.
On the third day, one should give three hundred and thirty-three [cows].
Now, this thousandth cow is three-colored and dedicated to two deities;
of her, two shares go to the Brahman priest and one to the Agnīdh. 243.
JB 2.244 |va Prajāpati indeed was this universe in the beginning.
vb Seeing no other second being, speech alone was his own; speech was his companion. He reflected.
"Come now, let me release this speech.
"This speech, once released, will pervade everything and depart," [they said]. He released it as "Vāc" (Speech).
He blew upwards, just as a continuous stream of water [flows].
He approached it; he cut off one syllable from it.
That became this.
|vh “This indeed came into being” (abhūd vā idam)— this is the reason for the earth’s name, *bhūmi*.
|vi “What [was there]?”— this is the second.
That became this intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
[He thought: "Verily, both of these have become between (*antara*). That is the essence of the intermediate space's being "intermediate" (*antarikṣatva*).
With "Ho! he raised it up for the third time;
that became the sky. "That, indeed, seemed to shine," they said.
That [is] the divinity of heaven. Prajāpati, indeed, in the beginning, divided this speech consisting of a single syllable into three parts.
These worlds came into being; they were barren and not fit for subsistence.
He grieved; he suffered.
He reflected: "How might these worlds take root? How might they possess means of subsistence?
He saw this three-night sacrifice.
He brought it; with it he sacrificed;
he caused it to extend through these worlds.
From that, these worlds grasped the hair (lomā); from that, they became possessed of livelihood.
Indeed, this abundance and this extraction of the three-night sacrifice is what exists upon these worlds. He who knows thus goes to the abundance of cattle, both two-footed and four-footed. 244.
Just as a gem-string might be strung upon a gem, even so is the three-night rite strung upon these worlds. The face of one who knows this shines with splendor.
This indeed is speech manifest: that which one utters with the tip of the tongue, when [one says] *e*; that which one utters with the middle of the tongue, when [one says] *ai*;
and that which one utters as the essence of all speech rising upward, when [one says] *o*.
For "Ho" is indeed all speech. Therefore, in that these forms are employed both in the *ājya* chants and on the days [of the sacrifice],
they release speech from the very beginning, and from the very beginning they perform the sacrificial rite.
When Prajāpati emitted speech, it indeed flowed forth: *sā*, *kṣarat*, *eva*. Of that, the first syllable is *eti*, the second is *kṣeti*, and the third is *raditi*.
Whatever form Prajāpati emitted through speech, in that very form the *ājya* oblations [came into being].
By means of this or that, the days are undertaken and completed. Indeed, this three-night sacrifice is firmly established in the syllable.
The syllable consists of three syllables.
The three-night rite consists of three syllables;
the three-night rite consists of a single syllable.
Indeed, he truly knows it who knows it as commensurate with the person; for the person is the three-night rite. 245.

By means of the first day, he differentiated this very world; by the second, that which has its root dependent upon this [earth]; by the third, that which breathes, moves, rains, consists of the stars, and belongs to yonder world.
This three-night rite is indeed a great vow (*mahāvrata*).
Those which are the *bahiṣpavamāna* chants of these days constitute the head; those two days on either side are the two wings.
That which is the midday [pressing] is the self;
the Agniṣṭoma-sāmans are the tail. Moreover, they say that what rises there is the head.
The two days on either side are the two wings;
the middle day is the self;
Agni himself is the tail.
Now they say: that which rises yonder is the head; the two days on either side are the two wings;
that which is the middle day is the self (ātman).
"That which sets is the tail," [so it is said].
The first day of the three-night rite has Vāc as its deity; the second has Prāṇa as its deity.
The third [night] has the eye as its deity.
Regarding this they ask: "How long is the three-night rite? One should say: "It is this long."
"For this is indeed just so much," he says; "and furthermore, it is of such a measure," he should say,
"for this is indeed just so much."
Regarding this they say: "Is the three-night rite directed hitherward or awayward? One should say, "Awayward.
For one speaks awayward, breathes awayward, looks awayward, and hears awayward.
Then one might say: "Both hitherward and thitherward.
For he speaks both hitherward and thitherward; he breathes both hitherward and thitherward; he sees both hitherward and thitherward;
and he hears both hitherward and thitherward.
Regarding this, they say: "Are there one three-night rite, or two, or three? One should reply: "One. For this is indeed one, namely the prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna.
Regarding this they say: "Which is more numerous, one or a thousand? One should say, "One. For in calculation, one indeed becomes more than a thousand.
JB 2.248 |va: "Speech indeed [is it].
vb: The first day of the three-night rite is indeed in the *gāyatrī* metre, the second is in the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the third is in the *jagatī* metre.

Or rather, that which is the reverse of another three-night sacrifice is the same order for this one, and that which is the same order for this one is the reverse for another. Therefore, when this subsequent day is made prior, they thereby cause cattle to be born for the sacrificer; it does not [harm him].
In that world, indeed, cattle are born. Now, these two among the meters are truly the most powerful: the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh.
Therefore, since the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh are on both sides and the Jagatī, which consists of cattle, is in the middle, [the cattle] are enclosed by the two powerful ones.
Thus, by means of these two meters, they enclose cattle on both sides for the sacrificer so that none may be lost;
his wealth is not diminished, he who knows thus.
That which shines yonder is indeed this three-night rite.
As it rises, so is its first day; as at midday, so is the second;
as it sets, so is the third.
He who knows this thus attains union with and absorption into it. 248.

Indra, indeed, [is] the Maruts; by means of this thousand he conquered his own people after having announced it to King Soma. (JB 2.249) va.
