In imitation of that, even today, after announcing it to the king, they cause the people to prosper.
Yama perceived this: "May these two win a thousand.
He came.
He came and said, "Invite me to share in this thousandfold gift. "So be it," they replied, and they invited him.
That Yama saw a cow even in this thousand, one that bore the milk of a thousand cows. He said to her, "This one is mine; this other belongs to you two.
The other two said, "Whatever indeed you see in her, that we two also see. He replied:
"Let us transform these very [beings] by means of her," they said. They transformed them by means of her. They said, "Let us bring portions; to whichever among us it shall come first."
They brought portions:
first that of Soma,
then that of Indra, and then that of Yama.
They caused her to enter the waters. They said to her, "Go forth for Soma with a third of yourself and a third of a thousand."
She arose as a brown cow with reddish-brown eyes, consisting of one-third of herself and one-third of a thousand.
She is this very cow for purchasing the Soma.
Indeed, it is with one-third of her and one-third of a thousand that King Soma is purchased.
They sent her back again into the waters.
They said to her, "Go forth for Indra with a third of yourself and a third of the thousand.
Thereupon Śabalī, the six-year-old cow, emerged with a third of herself and a third of the thousand.
That very [cow] was given to Indreṣya.
And indeed, by means of one-third of it and one-third of a thousand, she became given along with that [thousand].
They caused her to enter the waters once again.
They said to her, "Go for Yama with one-third of yourself and one-third of the thousand.
She went forth as a smoky-colored cow, shorter in front and taller behind, old, with ears like horns—
with one-third of herself and one-third of the thousand.
This very one is the cow for the funeral pyre.
And indeed, with a third of her and a third of the thousand, she becomes provided with the cow for the funeral pyre. One should not think that they have failed to do so. 250.
JB 2.251 |va | Regarding this, they say: "In that world, there is no space for a thousand.
vb | [It is] for oneself indeed... {The whole is not entirely clear; in any case, the separation of the [sentences] results in...}

"Indeed, this [world] belongs to the self alone, and not for the sake of the self, nor even for the sake of the self"— thus they say. "How large is this heavenly world?"— "As large as a thousand cows standing upon a cowhide," one should say.
And furthermore, as many as a thousand breaths they breathe together; and furthermore, as many as a thousand horse-teams;
and furthermore, as many as a thousand leagues; and furthermore, as many as a thousand days' journeys—it is by means of a cow that one obtains all this.
This very brindled heifer that stands here— she stands as a cow of plenty for him in yonder world who knows thus.
Having cast down a garment of silk, he leads her as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of providing a common womb for the thousand.
When he created the thousand, its womb was indeed the *tārpya* garment.
Therefore, having cast down the *tārpya*, he leads it as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); thus he makes the thousand have its proper womb.
A thousand [cows] with their proper wombs stand ready for him who knows this and has given the thousand.

Regarding that cow which is the thousandth, he should whisper into her ear: "O *Iḍā*, O *Rantī*, O Great One, O Far-Famed One, O Radiant One, O Shining One, O Invocable One, O Desirable One, O Aditi, O Sarasvatī—these are your names, O inviolable one. Proclaim us among the gods as doers of good deeds.
Thus, he indeed proclaims him among the gods as a doer of good deeds.
He causes him to smell that jar [with the verse]: "Smell the jar; may the drops enter thee, O Great One. May she yield for us a thousandfold, broad-streamed, full of milk.
To one who knows thus, a thousand [cows] stand ready when he has given a thousand. 251.
JB 2.252 |va Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning. vb He desired: "May I become many; may I procreate; may I attain abundance."
He performed austerity.
He emitted speech.
From speech, he fashioned the cow.
He reflected: "It is indeed enough for me that I am; what would I gain by creating?

Whatever food I might create, I would surely obtain it. Come now, let me create! (This same phrase also occurs at 2.2.8 [257.30f], which the editors, as can be seen from their footnotes, appear to have overlooked).

The form *sṛjeyet* is strange, which the editors explain at 2.228 as *sṛjeya* + *id* in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇārthe*); it is more probable, however, to explain *et* as a dittography and assume the simple *yat sṛjeya*.
He created the Vasus, he the Rudras, he the Ādityas. The Vasus sat down near him, saying, "Let this be ours.
To them, he gave this cow.
They guarded her for a year.
At the end of that year, she brought forth three hundred and thirty-three offspring belonging to the Ibhas.
She was born again.
The Rudras approached him, saying, "Let her be ours.
He gave this cow to them;
they guarded it for a year.
In the course of a year, Saibhya brought forth three hundred and thirty-three [calves].
He was born again;
the Ādityas waited upon him, saying, "Let it be our own."
He gave this cow to them. They guarded it for a year.
At the end of that year, she brought forth three hundred and thirty-three [calves] for them.
That became a thousand;
she herself was the thousandth;
he begot her again.
Whoever, knowing thus, guards the cows, a thousand [cows] indeed come to him. Therefore, one who knows thus must certainly guard the cows.
They said, "We are indeed sufficient for him; let us sacrifice with a thousand."
"Come, let us sacrifice with a thousand," they said.
Then they gathered together that thousand along with [the other] half.
Even counting them by the thousands, there was not enough for even one cow.
They said, "Let us beg this thousandth [cow] from Prajāpati himself.
They begged that thousandth cow from Prajāpati himself.
Prajāpati reflected: "If I give these [cows] to them, I shall be left empty; if I do not give them to them, their thousand will remain incomplete.
Come, let me approach them together with this very [cow]."
He said to them, "I shall go with you together with her.
They replied, "So be it," and he approached them along with her.
He saw this three-night sacrifice.
They brought it.
He said, "Shall we sacrifice with this equal [sacrifice], or with an unequal one?"
They said, "Let us come together.

In that they said, "Let us come together," they made the rain even; in that they made the rain even, they brought about concord in the kingdom; in that they said [this], they established common understanding.
Now, had they said, "Unevenly," the rain would have been uneven, the kingdom would have been unsettled, and there would have been a lack of consensus. They asked, "With what shall we become even?"
"By means of the *yajñāyajñīya* [sāman].
Therefore, they proceed by means of the *yajñāyajñīya* alone.
Speech, indeed, is the *yajñāyajñīya*.
Speech is these worlds. By speech alone they ascended to speech. On the first day, they gave three hundred and thirty-three.
By means of that, he prospered in this world with the Vasus.
On the second day, they gave three hundred and thirty-three;
by means of that, he prospered in the intermediate world with the Rudras.
And on the third day they gave three hundred and thirty-three;
by that he prospered with the Ādityas in yonder world.
Verily, he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with this sacrificial rite, prospers among these very deities and attains these [worlds].
And he attains the worlds. 253.
When Prajāpati first created a thousand, he bestowed it upon his offspring, saying, "This is yours. 254. JB 2.254. va.
Because he said, "Together" (*saha*), that is the reason for the thousandfold nature of the thousand.
Therefore, one should indeed be like a thousandfold sacrificer;
for he said, "Together."
If someone were to say to him while he is being settled there, "May you grant me the milk of a thousand," it would surely be so.
Those gods said to the god Īśāna, "You indeed are the best among us."
"Extract that extraction," [he said].
He extracted these three *sāmans* as the essence of the thousand: the one with the *ṛtunidhana*, the one with the *īnidhana*, and the one with the *triṇidhana*.
These very *sāmans* are to be performed at the thousand-night sacrifice; they have been extracted as the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the Lord God.
One who knows thus carries away the extraction; he becomes one whose extraction is carried away.
Therefore, these *sāmans* are to be performed at the thousand-night sacrifice as the extraction of the Lord God Akhala.
"The Sāmānīśvara [priest] intends to harm the cattle of the sacrificer. However, his thousand [cows] should be given as if they were inferior;
for the thousand must indeed be maintained for the sake of stability.
Prajāpati gave a thousand [cows] to the gods; they ate them without even looking back. As they were being eaten by the gods, it vanished from sight. They then addressed it with a mantra.
He said, "I am indeed afraid of exhaustion.
They said, "No;
we shall consume you in such a way that you will not be exhausted while being eaten and drunk by us."

"Perform for me the *ṛta* (cosmic order) for him," he said. For him they performed the *ṛta* with the *ṛta*-finale; they caused it to shine forth with the *ī*-finale; they generated it with the threefold finale; and they established imperishability for him.
The thousandfold [offering] of one who knows thus, even while being consumed, is not exhausted.
Every day there are milkings for the race.
The *ājīdohas* are indeed the vital breaths.
In that there are *ājīdohas* on each successive day,
he thereby establishes himself in the vital breaths.
The *ājīdoha* offerings take place day by day.
The *ājīdoha* offerings are indeed cattle.
In that the *ājīdoha* offerings take place day by day, one thereby establishes oneself firmly in cattle.
The milkings for the race-course (ājidoha) occur day by day. These worlds, indeed, are the milkings for the race-course.
In that the milkings for the race-course occur day by day, he thereby establishes himself in these very worlds.
Agni is the milk-yielder of the race-course; Vāyu is the milk-yielder of the race-course; yonder Āditya is the milk-yielder of the race-course.
In that there are these milk-yielders of the race-course day after day, he thereby finds firm support in these very deities.
These worlds are indeed called the race-courses.
These are their milk-yields:
he who knows thus milks these worlds.
Every day there are *arkas*; the *arka* is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
The *svāśiras* [stotra] becomes the *arkasāman* on the first day.
Indeed, the *svāśiras* is water;
and water, moreover, is food.
Or rather, he does not traverse the path without a resting place.
On the second day, there is the *arka* of Agni;
for the second day has the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) as its abode.
The intermediate space itself is the setting [place]; the *rakṣases* are masses of darkness. Agni is indeed the repeller of the *rakṣases*;
it is for the repelling of the *rakṣases*.
The *arka* of Dīrghatamas occurs on the third day.
The *arka* of Dīrghatamas is indeed in the *jagatī* meter; the third day is in the *jagatī* meter; they thus cause the day itself to prosper by means of its own form. 255.
Day after day there are the Sauparṇa chants; they lead to heaven and serve for the complete attainment of the heavenly world.
Regarding this, they say: "The Sāmans are rapid; they might cause the sacrificer to perish before his full span of life."
"There are indeed two purposes for falling," they say; "they truly accomplish it for him. "There is indeed one purpose: for the sake of unification."
How much more so those who would crush him—even all his undertakings [would fail].
By means of the three-night rite, the gods indeed ascended to the heavenly world;
yet it was not held fast for them, and it fell away.
They propped it up with the Gāyatrapārśva; they made it continuous with the Saṃtanin;
they made it uniform with the Saṃkṛti; they joined it together with the Triṣandhi; they mixed it with the Śrāyantīya; and they brought it to safety with the Ariṣṭa.

In that these *sāmans* are performed, it is for the support of the three-night rite (*trirātra*), for its continuity, for its preparation, for its cohesion, for its reliance, and for the safety of the three-night rite. [The *aiḍa* is on the *kakubh*, the *svāra* on the *uṣṇih*.]
They interweave these three nights in the middle for the sake of non-laxity.
Indeed, six Gāyatrīs and ten stotriyas constitute the first day.
And the second day amounts to six *triṣṭubh*s and one *stotriyā*. Now, as for the third day, two of its pressings amount to *jagatī*s and *anuṣṭubh*s.
The third pressing consists of the twenty-one-fold [stoma] and the *ṣoḍaśin*.
The Ṣoḍaśin indeed desired companionship with the two preceding days;
the two preceding days desired companionship with the Ṣoḍaśin.
They met him with these eleven stotriya verses.

That *ṣoḍaśin* became an *ānuṣṭubha*. He who knows that the *ṣoḍaśin* is not a "non-participant" (*apitvin*) on the two preceding days— on those two preceding days the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed a non-participant— becomes a non-participant wherever he desires, thinking, "May I be a non-participant."
Regarding this they say: "By means of the *stomas* one obtains the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period; by means of the [verse] correspondence, the *chandomas*; and by means of the night, the tenth day.
He who knows thus obtains whatever is obtained through the twelve-day sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Now, this is the thousandth [cow]. If he were to give her away, the [other] thousand would be deficient and the embryos would wither;
if he were not to give her away, his thousand would have been given incomplete.
He should neither give a fraction nor a substitute.
That is a pair;
after that, offspring is produced.
Regarding this they say: "In that way, it truly becomes unappropriated; moreover, one conquers even a mere fraction [of the enemy]."
[If he does not give her back], she may go after him for as many years as there are parts [of the body]—that is, for a thousand years.
Having given her back along with a thousand parts—that is, having given her back while she is ignorant [of her husband's sin]—he should redeem her with a cow that has been eaten.
Regarding this, they also say: "In that case, it truly becomes as if she had been given away."
[The teacher says: "One cow for the other [debt], one cow for the other; he should redeem it with as much woolen thread from sheep as he deems sufficient. [The student asks:
"Is there not indeed some woolen thread belonging to the cow? [The teacher replies: "Yes, indeed."
A thousand is given to him; he is not depleted of his own self.
Just as one might enclose a pen with a rope or a cord, even so does he encompass these cattle to prevent their loss.
The wealth of him who knows thus is not diminished.
(JB 2.259) O Śabalī, you are the ocean, the imperishable abode; the goddess of Brahman, the first-born of *ṛta*, you flow as the one imperishable syllable (*akṣara*).
O Night, you who look upon these worlds, milking out immortality—such as you we know you to be, O Saramā, shining and imperishable, burning with light for the sake of the gods.
You are brilliance; you are pure; you are immortality; you are food; you are great; you are this greatness; thus do I know you.

"In her, I place for you this imperishable sacrificial fee—undecaying prosperity, the great light of the gods, clothing herself in it, the most powerful among creatures; may I follow her in accordance with her turn.
For that which is yonder sun is indeed the most powerful turn.
Of her there are these two feet: day and night, and truth and falsehood.
Of her, that foot which is the day is the foot of truth;
this is called "Transcending Life."
He who knows this foot of his named *atyāyu* (exceeding life) indeed surpasses others in offspring, cattle, prosperity, fame, and lifespan.

Now, this spotted and variegated footprint of hers is the night. He who knows this spotted and variegated footprint of hers becomes, through offspring, cattle, prosperity, fame, and long life, as spotted and variegated as that very footprint.

Just as one would fan a blazing fire with a bellows, even so does this Brahmin polish himself by speaking the truth. He should speak only the truth, he should act only according to the truth, he should desire to accomplish only the truth; thus he becomes truth itself.
Or rather, he might find him out through the desire for untruth, or out of a desire for livelihood, or a desire for a wife, or a desire for amusement,
or a desire for friendship.
Or one might speak of him at night, or in the shade.
For thus it does not injure him; it injures [him who speaks otherwise].
For he speaks it in its own abode:
"The broad one, the sprouting one."

Heti! Hesini! From obstruction, O Aditi, may your mind be born; you two are the youth of the sacrifice; you are the clarified butter. You are the dwelling-place; you stand in the cosmic order (*ṛta*), you stand in the mind; enter the village of the mind. I am your sustenance; you are delight;
you are the source of delight. O Śabalī, rich in heaven, full of vigor, full of milk, come hither! I am the one who does not grasp; I scatter the sand before me; [I am] the calves.
"I bear the one who has a thousand mothers; we know you, O Puruṣa, as the mark. Tell us this: how will this come to be? (JB 2.260)

"O Agni, Hotṛ of the gods, you are the Hotṛ of the gods; I am the Hotṛ of men. Tell this for us: how this shall come to pass. Neither the *sāman* comes together with it, nor the *stotriyā*; my worlds do not pass over to him, but the world of the sacrificer becomes more spacious.

If the *sāman* were to coincide with the [verse], or if the hymns (*stotrya*) were to coincide, or if these worlds were to coincide, the world of the sacrificer would be diminished. It coincides with the *gāyatra*.
The *gāyatra* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
for the vital breath extends everywhere; the *yajñāyajñīya* extends [therein].
The *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed speech.
For everywhere, speech and breath are joined together.
Two *sāmans* are joined; the sacrificer has two feet—for the sake of stability.
He who knows thus finds firm support. 260.
Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning. JB 2.261. va.
He desired: "May I be many; may I propagate; may I attain abundance.
He grieved;
he practiced austerity.

As he was grieving and suffering, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) said to him, "We indeed have seen this sacrifice; let us perform the sacrifice for you with it. He said to them, "How did you see it? Which one did you see?"
They said: "Make us hear!"— "Let there be *śrauṣaṭ*!"— "We sacrifice for the sake of sacrifice!"— "*Vauṣaṭ*!"— thus we have seen this.
He thought, "I have either known it or seen it.
Since there are five [seasons], the sacrifice is fivefold;
therefore he thought, "I have either known it or seen it."
Now, as for those five beings, there were seventeen syllables; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and the sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati. By that very means, they perceived: "We have indeed seen it."
He said, "With what shall we sacrifice? In what shall we sacrifice?
They replied, "Having extracted your own omentum, we shall sacrifice it as a complete offering in the fire of your own heart."
They extracted the omentum from Prajāpati himself.
Of them, speech alone caused the *āśrāvaṇa* call, breath caused the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* response,
and mind was the *hotṛ*.
Prajāpati himself sat as the fourth Brahman priest to the south.
They offered that [oblation] entirely into the fire within the heart of Prajāpati.
Because they cast it [into him], that is the origin of the name "vapā" (omentum/fat).
When they offered her [the earth] to you, they sowed her;
therefore, one must indeed sow.
For from what has been sown, all this is born. When she had been offered, the goat... 261.
A white, hairy, hornless, and spotted goat with teeth on only one side was born as a four-footed creature;
in it they beheld all forms.
They said, "Indeed, all these forms are in him;
let us sacrifice this very one. They sacrificed it.
Of them, the out-breath (*prāṇa*) alone made the call for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and the in-breath (*apāna*) responded with the *pratyāśrāva*.
The mind (*manas*) was the *hotṛ* priest; Prajāpati himself sat as the fourth, the *brahman* priest, to the south.
They offered him as a complete oblation into the fire that is the very heart of Prajāpati.
From that oblation, Agni was born as a deity;
that is the Rigveda.
After [it], Vāyu was born as the deity;
that is the Yajus, the Veda. After [it], Āditya was born as the deity.
That is the Sāmans, the Veda. Following these three, the most excellent of the gods, were born these three branches of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Indeed, this much alone was created by Prajāpati from the beginning.
Then, by means of these very deities, all this other [universe] was produced.
They said, "Let us sacrifice with that same sacrifice by which our father Prajāpati, having sacrificed, attained success.
They brought that [sacrifice].
Vāyu alone called for them; Āditya responded.
Agni was the *hotṛ*.
Prajāpati, as the moon, sat as the fourth *brahman* priest to the south. 262.
JB 2.263 |va They themselves sat as the Caturhotṛs.
vb These indeed are the Caturhotṛs which they call the Caturhotṛs.
At the thousandth oblation, a cow was born.
In her, they beheld all enjoyments—whatever enjoyments exist in a cow. They said, "Indeed, all these enjoyments are in her."
"Come here; let us speak thus: 'Procreate for us!
They said to her, "Procreate for us!
She [procreated] three hundred and thirty-three [gods] for Agni.
He generated three hundred and thirty-three for Vāyu;
he generated three hundred and thirty-three for Āditya.
That became a thousand;
she herself was the thousandth;
he begot her again.
Whoever, knowing thus, guards the cows, a thousand [cows] indeed come to his possession. Therefore, one who knows thus must certainly guard the cows.
They said: "We are indeed sufficient for him; let us go away in different directions and remain as sacrificers."
"Having gone apart in different directions, let us sit as sacrificers," they said.
Having gone apart in different directions, they sat down as sacrificers.
They became neither better nor worse.
They said, "We have neither become better nor worse;
let us perform this sacrifice with a thousand.
Va: They were gathering them up by the thousands. Vb: That thousand of theirs did not suffice for even one cow.
Vc: They said, "Let us beg this thousandth one from Prajāpati himself."
They begged Prajāpati for that very one who was the thousandth.
Prajāpati reflected: "If I give her to them, I shall be left empty; if I do not give her to them, their thousand will remain incomplete."
"Let me go with them together with her.
He said to them, "I shall go with you together with her. "So be it," they replied.
He approached them with that very [vessel].
They saw this three-night sacrifice;
they brought it.
He said, "Shall we sacrifice with this equal [sacrifice], or with an unequal one? They replied, "With an equal one.
Because they said, "With an equal one," they thereby made the rain equal, and they thereby established equality in the kingdom and in common understanding.
They performed [the ritual]. Now, had they said, "With an uneven [number]," the rain would have been uneven, the kingdom would have been uneven,
and there would have been a lack of consensus.
"With what shall we unite?
"With the *yajñāyajñīya*.
Therefore, they unite with the *yajñāyajñīya* alone.
The *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed speech;
these worlds are speech.
By means of speech, they thus ascend to speech.
They gave three hundred and thirty-three on the first day.
By that, Agni attained success in this world.
They gave three hundred and thirty-three on the second day.
By that, Vāyu attained success in this world, the intermediate space.
On the third day, they gave three hundred and thirty-three;
by that, Āditya attained success in yonder world.
He who, knowing thus, performs this sacrificial rite, prospers in these very deities and attains these worlds. 264/ JB 2.265
That which was the thousandth became lightning itself and entered Prajāpati. Regarding this, it is recited:
"This is that which bellows; by it the cow is covered; she lowing like a mother rests upon the mist."
"By her powers of thought she indeed made the mortal [her own]; becoming lightning, she cast off her covering.
Thus, having concealed her form within this very cow and having become lightning itself, she entered Prajāpati once again.
This is indeed lightning. When it thunders, "dadadadada," as it were, it is saying, "I give, I give! Thus it bestows rain and food upon creatures.
This deity bestows rain and food upon him who knows this. 265.
JB 2.266 |va Now follows this Aśvamedha. vb One who desires offspring should sacrifice with it.
Prajāpati indeed desired: "May I be multiplied through offspring and cattle; may I attain these worlds; may I win power and vigor.
He beheld this sacrifice.
He took it; he sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle; he attained these worlds and gained sovereign power.
He restrained his vigor.
He who should desire, "May I be propagated with abundant offspring and cattle; may I attain these worlds;
may I win power and vigor," he should sacrifice with this [offering].
He indeed is born again with offspring and cattle; he attains these worlds and secures power and vigor.
This sacrifice, indeed, is vigor itself.
Or whenever they proceeded with this [sacrifice] in former times, everything was indeed full of vigor: a seer, a composer of mantras, and a Brahmin would be born;
an archer, a hero, and a nourishing Kshatriya; a wealthy and industrious Vaishya; a capable and diligent Shudra;
and auspicious women devoted to their husbands.
Grain ripened even without being ploughed.
Indeed, a single vessel of cooked rice would suffice for an entire household. At that time, everything was full of milk.
Indeed, even in the forest, powerful beings are born: fierce lions, fierce tigers, fierce bears, fierce hyenas, fierce serpents, and fierce pythons.
Truly, tiger-like men stand in the forests seizing [their prey].
Indeed, there was once a single porpoise who protected many sacred bathing places (tīrtha).
Truly, it was by virtue of his prowess that they were thus.

From the forehead of this very [being], the lion was born; from the chest, the tiger; from the belly, the leopard; from the eyes, the apāṣṭhis; from the ears, the aśvakarṇas; from the hair of the mane, the bears and the ṛkṣīkas; from the body-hair, the dūrvā grass;
from the backbone, the porpoise; from the tail-hair, the aśvavālas; from the thighs, the two krauñcas; and from the testicles, the two boars.

From his two mouths the cakravāka birds were produced; from his *vaniṣṭhu* (rectum) the *udra* (beaver); from his *guda* (intestines) the *ahayaḥ* and *ajagarāḥ* (non-venomous and venomous snakes); from his *kuṣṭhikās* (knees) the *vartakās* (quail);

from his hooves the *śalyakās* (porcupines); from the balls of dung the *kūśmās*; from his *uruvadhya* (undigested food in the stomach) the *urvāru* (cucumber), the *tantisantadūla*, the *śyāmāka* (millet), and the *lohitaka*—thus this small variety of food was born.
JB 2.268 |va Regarding this they say: "How is he to be sacrificed?
|vb They say: "He who is heard from afar is to be sacrificed."
"He is indeed renowned for his vigor;
vigor is this sacrifice.
Furthermore, they say: "Whichever of the two draft animals draws better, that one should be sacrificed."
By its vigor, it is indeed the swifter of the two;
for this sacrifice is vigor. Regarding this, Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratāraṇa were once disputing as to what its form was.
"Having seized [it]," they said. They prepared two [animals], one black-spotted and one tawny-spotted.
That which is white yet has black, or black yet has white—that indeed is it.
The limb of Prajāpati swelled;
his eye burst forth,
and it fell away.
It entered the waters;
from that, the horse was produced. Because it moved (*aśvayat*), therefore it is called a horse (*aśva*).
That which arose from the swelling became putrid; that which entered the waters became white (śvetanaḥ)—that is, white in color.
Indeed, of the eye that was white, there is a black part; or of that which was black, there is a white part.
That very one is Prajāpati with his limbs;
they immolate him at this time.
With this very [sacrifice], Mauṇḍibha Audanyu performed the sacrifice; he was the king of the Audanyus. Then Yavakrī Saumāstambiya sat down at the place of praise (*āstāva*).
For him, they made these [verses] the introductory stanzas (*pratipad*): "This wealth, Pūṣan, Bhaga."
He said, "O Śambaṇa, do not stand there! O Mauṇḍibha, you have failed to sustain your vital breaths.
This was indeed the reproach at that time.
Now, Mauṇḍibha Audanya was a seeker of knowledge from the three Vedas.
He said: "Demolish my *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds; having sealed my cups with clay, set them aside.
When this Brahmin who speaks against us dies, then you shall be sacrificers. They then set his cups aside after sealing them with clay.
Now, Yavakrī, the son of Soma, was brilliant and possessed of the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*).
Whomever he addressed with the words "Come here," if she desired him, she would die;
and whomever did not desire him, she would likewise die.
He [Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana] desired the wife of [the sage] Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana. She reflected: "If I desire him, he will surely die; therefore, let me desire him. So she desired him.
"Even for a Brahmin, one might die after performing a service that is pleasing [to him].
He said to him, "Wait here; then we shall come to you. 269.
JB 2.270 |va His husband came upon her as she was adorning herself and weeping.
vb He said to her, "Why do you adorn yourself? Why do you weep?"
She said, "You will surely die; you have merely shown pity for yourself. "Yavakrī indeed spoke thus to you," [he replied].
He said, "Bring clarified butter from here."
Having purified that [milk] with two strainers, he offered it as an oblation:
"O Agni, bring to me that woman who today protects us, who has been prepared by the descendant of Bharadvāja— the beloved of Agni— Svāhā!"
"Vi.
Thus [he spoke]. He then raised up against her the Gandharva Īrṣyu, who held a braid of hair in his hand.
He said to him: "That wife of yours has gone to Yavakrī."
"Come here," he said.
He approached her as she was lying there.
She smiled.
He said, "Indeed, you must not laugh at me. [The other] said, "But I am laughing. [The first] asked, "Why?"
"You will die," he said.
She, lifting up her foot, said: "Surely you have never seen a woman with feet like this before. Indeed, her feet were hairy underneath.
They sat down, either together or separately.
Then the Gandharva, with an iron club in his hand, stepped forward toward them.
He said: "Homage be to you!"
"What is the expiation for this?
[he asked]. "It either exists or it does not," he replied.
"Whatever belongs to your father, cut off the head of all that before the sun rises. "Whether it be that very thing or something else," he replied. He then proceeded to cut it off.
They said, "Yavakrī has not faltered; let us bind him. "No," his father said, "my son acts as one impelled by the gods."
"Only he knows what is truly beneficial in this matter. Now, a deaf carpenter in the village did not hear him being forbidden.
As he was striking [the wood], he passed away.
"Which person among us has struck [him] down?
"It was he himself who struck him down," some say.
As he was being struck down, the sun rose over him.
Some say that as soon as he had risen, that very Gandharva struck him down; however, it was exactly as [the text] says: "He died.
Indeed, that very Gandharva struck him down perpetually. (271)
JB 2.272 |va | Then Mauṇḍibha, having understood it, said: "Prepare my *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds; O Brahmins, perform the sacrifice for me."
"Truly, that Brahmin who recites after [the teacher] will drink nectar.
They did exactly so for him.
Then Saumastambi, having understood this, arrived.
He sat down in the *āstāva* in that very manner.
They made these very [verses], "This wealth is Pūṣan, Bhaga," his introductory verses (*pratipad*).
He said, "Surely this kinsman of the royalty did not know this sacrificial rite."
"He certainly did not kill my son by saying this. "Indeed, that was all the life-span his son had," he said.
He then cursed him: "This kinsman of royalty shall die immediately; let there be baldness upon his head!"
"They will come to pass.
These very defeated Gotamas wander about proclaiming this.
For that same [sāman], the *pratipad* verses are those containing the word "crossing," beginning with "Crossing over, the gladdening one runs."
Therefore, the horse crosses the path. They contain the word "running";
therefore, the horse reaches its destination by running along the path.
The *samaya* consists of a single foot;
therefore, the horse stands with each foot raised upward.
The *bahis-pavamāna* chant for him consists of four [verses].
Horses are indeed four-footed and have four hooves;
those animals which are four-footed and have four hooves, these he wins by means of this.
There are eight oblations of clarified butter for each [set].
Cattle indeed have eight hooves;
those cattle which have eight hooves, it is these he wins by this very means.
The midday [pressing] consists of twelve [stotras].
The *jagatī* indeed consists of twelve syllables;
the *jagatī* is cattle.
That which is small among the animals is the *jāgata* [meter];
by this, he secures that very thing.
The *ārbhava-pavamāna* consists of twenty verses.
These two sets of ten, making twenty, are indeed two *virāj* verses.
Cattle have twenty as their support and are of the nature of the *virāj*.
Those cattle which have twenty as their support and are of the nature of the *virāj*, those he wins by means of this very [rite].
Now follows the twenty-fourth Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
Cattle are four-footed and belong to the Vairāja [meter].
Those cattle which are four-footed and belong to the Vairāja—verily, by this [sāman], he wins them.
Moreover, the year consists of twenty-four half-months; by means of the year itself, they take hold of it. Having thus enclosed it, they immolate it on this second day.
This second day consists of the twenty-one-fold stoma; it is a single-stoma day.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first.
Just as a firm pillar is firmly set, so is the twenty-one-fold among the stomas; it is just as if one were to set up a firm pillar, for the sake of non-decline.
In that [sacrifice], they immolate these animals: the elephant as the highest, and the louse as the lowest.
Having carried fire around them, they immolate some and release others.
For this [rite], the Mahānāmnī verses constitute the *pṛṣṭha* stotra.
For nothing else besides the Mahānāmnī verses is worthy of lifting up the *pṛṣṭha* chants for cattle.
(b) They consist of seven steps; there are indeed seven domestic animals, for the sake of securing domestic animals.
(c) There is a step beyond the seventh, for the sake of securing wild animals.
For him, there is the *pārthuraśma* *brahmasāman*, which is perfected by the syllable *atha*. For indeed, a horse gallops as if saying "athag, athag.
Moreover, only a broad rein (*pṛthu-raśmi*) is capable of restraining a horse.
That [sāman] is fivefold;
for the *brahmasāman* of the Mahānāmnīs is fivefold.
For that sacrifice, there are twenty-one sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), each twenty-one cubits (*aratni*) in length.
For these twenty-one sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) are not capable of supporting the animals.

There are six made of *bilva* wood, twelve of *khadira* wood, and two of *pūtudru* wood on either side of the fire; for the *pūtudru* and the *rājjudāla* are indeed the body of this fire. Thus, there are twenty-one.
That [post] which stands nearest the fire is the *agniṣṭha*.
This *rājjudāla* wood is indeed Prajāpati among trees. Its fruits are his sexual organs,
and its sap is his semen.
Prajāpati is indeed the father, and Āditya is the son. There is an Atirātra sacrifice with all the Stomas for the conquest and mastery of all the worlds;
for all this is indeed nothing but Stomas.
"Moreover, those individual *stomas* which we have approached—one by one—having increased them together and having established ourselves upon them, may we attain the highest limit. 274.
Now this is the *Govinata* *Chandomapavamāna*.
One who desires cattle should sacrifice with this.

For him, there are both types of *stomas*: the odd-numbered and the even-numbered. Now, those *stomas* which are odd-numbered, after them follow the domestic animals; and those which are even-numbered, after them follow the wild animals.
The *Chandomas* are indeed cattle.
He who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice with the *Chandomapavamāna*, secures both kinds of cattle—both those that are domestic and those that are wild.
Now, this second day has the twenty-one-fold *pṛṣṭha* chant.
Whatever praise was given to the twenty-one-fold chant— that it is "not attained"—
that indeed is its *brāhmaṇa*.
On that [day], they immolate this sacrificial horse. Furthermore, because this consists of twenty-one *pṛṣṭha* chants, it is therefore called the *govinata*.
On the third day, there is again a repetition of the thirty-three-fold chant.
There are indeed thirty-three deities and thirty-three worlds of the gods;
it is by reaching these very ones at the end that they ascend. Now, for him whose Agniṣṭoma is fifteenfold, whose Ukthya is fifteenfold, and whose Atirātra is fifteenfold—
One who desires sovereign power (*kṣatra*) should sacrifice with this [rite]. The horse is sovereign power; the fifteenfold [stoma] is sovereign power; the sacrifice is sovereign power.
Thus, that [sacrifice] is made to have the same characteristic as that [sovereign power].
With this very [sacrifice], Ṛṣabha Yājñatura Śvaitna, a king desiring to be a sole ruler, performed the sacrifice. Having sacrificed, he indeed became a sole ruler of the Śvitnas.
Whoever should desire prosperity, let him sacrifice with this.
*vu* Sovereignty is prosperity; *vv* this is the sacrifice of sovereignty; *vw* he attains prosperity. /275/

JB 2.276 |va| Now, one who desires heaven should sacrifice with this [rite] which has a *trivṛt* day and a *pañcadaśī* night, a *trivṛt* day and a *pañcadaśī* night, and a *trivṛt* day and a *pañcadaśī* night.
Datva Sautemana and Mitravid Daṃṣṭradyumna were both students of Brahman (brahmacārins) under King Pratidarśa Vaibhāvata Śvaitna.
Of the two, Mitravid Daṃṣṭradyumna performed the duties of a teacher.
He used to guard the cows;
then the other devoted himself solely to his study.
Every evening, having come together, they would say to one another, "Bring [the fuel], my dear; we shall place our hands together after what has been recited."
"Come, my dear, take my hand; we two shall set it down [in the fire].
Then the teacher instructed Datta Sautemanasa.
Having come together in the evening, the two said to each other: "Come, my dear; since we have not yet recited the texts, let us set our hands [in the fire]."
"Come, my dear, take my hand; we two shall go together.
"No," he said, "I am already released from you, for I have been instructed by my teacher."
He spent that night pierced by what was unpleasant. When morning came, he went after the cows.
As soon as the cow saw him, she recognized him, thinking, "There is something unpleasant about this man."
She said, "I indeed know what is displeasing to you; may nothing displeasing happen to you."
"Come, I shall tell you the path leading to the gods. "So be it," he replied.
He then spoke to him.
The two of them met in the evening.
He said, "Come here; you say this because you have been instructed by your teacher. Do you see the path of the gods?"
"No," he said.
"But I see it myself.
"Then tell it to me," [the other] said.
"So be it," he said.
He then spoke to him.
Therefore, indeed, a kinsman of the royal class is more affectionate toward a Brāhmaṇa than [his own] heart.
Datva Sautemana said to him: "Do you indeed see the path of the gods? Come, let us go to the heavenly world. (JB 2.278)
"No," he said.
"One approaches that [world] knowing it through either giving or through toil.
Come now, let us either give or toil."
Mitravid Daṃṣṭradyumna went to the world of heaven by means of the Go and Āyus [sacrifices] for a year;
he indeed went to the heavenly world at the very end of that year.
Then Datva Sautemanasa, having sacrificed with this very three-night rite, went to the heavenly world.
By means of this very [sacrifice], having sacrificed, one indeed goes to the heavenly world.
By means of this very [sacrifice], Veda Hiraṇyadan, desiring pairs, performed the sacrifice.
That which consists of cattle and horses, elephants and gold, goats and sheep, rice and barley, sesame and beans—this, indeed, became much for him.
He was. He who, knowing thus, performs this sacrifice desiring pairs, indeed obtains many such pairs for himself.
Now, this is Antarvasu.
Khaṇḍika Auddhāri and Keśin Dārbhya contended for supremacy among the Pañcālas;
Khaṇḍika indeed overcame Keśin.
Bound by Khaṇḍika, Keśin went to Uccaiḥśravas, the son of Kuvaya, King Kauravya, who was his mother’s brother. He said to him, "Perform a sacrifice for me."
"So be it," he said.
"How shall I provide for you?
So that you may prosper in this world, and so that you may prosper in yonder world?"
"Vi. "As in this," he said.
He replied, "Now, does he ask about the sacrifice who does not know the sacrifice together with its companion? "How so? he asked.
"For the sacrifice is for that world alone, not for this one," [he said].
"No," he replied.
"Khaṇḍika Audbhāri indeed surpassed him."
"Act for me in such a way that I may overcome him. He established for him this *antarvasu* sacrifice:
the *sarvastoma* *agniṣṭoma*.

From this point forward, the middle day is characterized by the *chandomas*: the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) consists of the twenty-four-fold stoma, the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) consists of the forty-four-fold stoma, and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) consists of the forty-eight-fold stoma.
Following this is the *sarvastoma* *atirātra*, performed in the reverse direction.
The Brahman is indeed the twenty-fourfold; the Kṣatra is the forty-fourfold; the Viś is the forty-eightfold. The year is indeed the Sarvastoma.
By means of these two Sarvastomas, having encompassed this threefold people, he established it within himself.
He went to her for the sake of that splendor.
Then indeed, he caused Khaṇḍika to be expelled.
Then indeed Keśin became the son of Dārbhya, while Khaṇḍika was cast aside.
He who knows this prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is cast aside.
He who desires prosperity should sacrifice with this [rite].
By means of these very two *sarvastoma* rites, having encompassed this threefold people (*trayī viś*), he places it within himself;
indeed, he attains the splendor of that [people].
Now follows this *parāka*.
One who desires heaven should sacrifice with this.
Its *stotras* are directed away, its *śastras* are directed away, its *pṛṣṭhas* are directed away, its *viṣṭutis* are directed away;
indeed, everything becomes directed away.
With this very [sacrifice], Uccaiḥśravas, the aged king of the Kauravyas, descendant of Kuvera, performed a sacrifice. Having sacrificed, he went to the heavenly world.
By sacrificing with this very [sacrifice], one goes to the heavenly world.
Now, for this sacrifice— the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, the Jyotis Ukthya, and the Jyotis Atirātra— one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with it. Indeed,
he who attains spiritual luster shines like light.

Verily, by this he prospers; he becomes endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). Now, that sacrifice of Prajāpati which has a seventeen-fold *agniṣṭoma*, a seventeen-fold *ukthya*, and a seventeen-fold *atirātra* is the Horse Sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
One who desires offspring should sacrifice with this [rite]. Now, that which has a twenty-one-fold Agniṣṭoma, a twenty-one-fold Ukthya, and a twenty-one-fold Atirātra is the Aśvamedha of Āditya.
One who desires heaven should sacrifice with this [rite]. 280.
Now, these are the four-night sacrifices. 281. JB 2.281.
Atri, indeed, desired: "May four heroic sons be born to me.
He saw this four-night sacrifice;
he brought it [into practice].
With it he sacrificed. From that, indeed, four heroes were born to him.
Four heroes are born to him who knows thus.
The Atri seers, indeed, desired: "May four sons be born to each of us.
They saw this four-night sacrifice;
they took it up.
They sacrificed with that.
From that, indeed, four heroes were born for each of them; for him who knows thus, four heroes are born for each of his [descendants].
Indeed, the productive union is up to four; beyond that, it is no longer a productive union. One and one, two and two, three and three, four and four—this indeed is the productive union up to four.
"Five and five" is not indeed the name [of the days]. That which is a productive pair, may that produce me.
Its *pavamāna* chants are twenty-four-fold; the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
"The year is procreation; may it procreate me.
For this [sacrifice], both the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans are employed.
Indeed, these two—the Bṛhat and the Rathantara—are the divine couple that is procreation.
"May that divine couple, the procreative power, procreate for me.
For it, there are both types of *stomas*: the odd-numbered and the even-numbered. Indeed, this is the divine couple, the procreative power, namely the two kinds of *stomas*.
"Therefore, may that divine couple, which is procreative, procreate me. (JB 2.282) Furthermore, the subsequent *stomas* are uneven.
The odd-numbered seasons are indeed the seasons;
the seasons, indeed, procreate all this.
"May they, who procreate all this, procreate me," [he thinks].
vg They proceed releasing the *stoma* day by day;
vf they bring forward the *stoma* day by day.
vg The *stoma* is indeed a hero.

Generating the vigor of each very day, they proceed; they bring forth the vigor of each very day, proceeding while ascending by means of each syllable. On the first day there is a *nidhana* consisting of one syllable; on the second day, a *nidhana* consisting of two syllables.
The *nidhana* consists of three syllables in the third [round] and four syllables in the fourth: "akṣareṣṭhā vīro 'sad" and "akṣareṣṭhā vīro 'sad.
There are various *agniṣṭoma-sāmans* for the sake of providing various heroic powers (*vīrya*) to the heroes themselves.
He indeed is not a hero who is a hero only by following the heroism of another;
he alone is truly a hero who is a hero by following his own heroism.
Therefore, the fact that there are different *agniṣṭoma* chants serves to provide various kinds of heroism for heroes.
JB 2.283 |va They say: "They should make the *yajñāyajñīya* the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* for each day of the sacrifice;
for the *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*). vb.
"Let the hero not fall away from his preeminence. Therefore, if the *stotras* were equal, they would attain strength equally;
but since they are unequal, they place the strength all at once in the eldest.
In that the *pavamāna* chants are equal, they thereby attain equal vigor.
Then, in that they proceed ascending by means of the subsequent *stotras*, they go while bestowing greater vigor upon the most excellent [seasons].
Indeed, this sacrifice is performed as a two-night rite (*dvirātra*).

On the third day, they should perform the *rathantara* as the *pṛṣṭha* stotra upon these verses beginning with "O bull, toward you, the pressed [juice]" (*abhi tvā vṛṣabhā suta*), while using the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans].
In that they proceed with "Abhi tve," they do not depart from the form of the *rathantara*.
The third day is extended by means of the *gāyatrī* which has not lost its potency.
The *maitrāvaruṇa-sāman* is [chanted] with "Kaḥ tam indra tvāvaso."
Of these, the syllables here become complete:
those which are *gāyatrīs* remain *gāyatrīs*, those which are *kakups* remain *kakups*, and those which are *bṛhatīs* remain *bṛhatīs*. Thus the meters are joined according to their proper places.
The first day is indeed performed with the Gāyatrī, the second with the Triṣṭubh, the third with the Jagatī, and the fourth with the Anuṣṭubh.
On the fourth day, they should perform the Bṛhat-pṛṣṭha using these verses beginning with "taṃ tvā yajñebhir īmahe."
In that they [sing] "taṃ tvā," they do not depart from the form of the Bṛhat.
The fourth day is extended by means of an Anuṣṭubh verse with its syllables arranged in a specific order (āyātayāman).
The Maitrāvaruṇa-sāman is [chanted on the verse]: "vayam u tvām apūrvye."
Of these, the syllables here become complete:
those which are *gāyatrīs* remain *gāyatrīs*; those which are *kakups* remain *kakups*; those which are *bṛhatīs* remain *bṛhatīs*. Thus the meters are joined according to their proper place. 283.
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the first day, the Ukthya the second, the Ṣoḍaśin the third, and the Atirātra the fourth.
The days possess various powers for the sake of providing various powers to the heroes themselves.
Now, Takṣaka Bhāgerathi used to say that King Mātsya [performed] the four-night sacrifice; it encompasses the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
Indeed, the two-night sacrifice is extended by means of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans].
On the third day, they should perform the Vairūpa and the Mahānāmnī hymns; these two belong to the Rathantara [Sāman],
for the third day is a Rathantara day.
They should perform the Vairāja and the Revatī [stomas] on the fourth day; for these two belong to the Bṛhatī [meter],
and the fourth day is of the Bṛhatī [meter].
"Thus indeed the four-night sacrifice pervades the *pṛṣṭha* chants," so he used to say.
Regarding this, they ask: "Which among the sacrifices is the most exalted (*varṣiṣṭha*), which is the most extensive (*variṣṭha*)?
He should reply: "The three-night sacrifice alone is the most exalted among the sacrifices."
These worlds indeed are the three-night rite; the quarters are the four-night rite.
Now follows this [rite] of Jamadagni.
One who desires offspring should sacrifice with this.
Jamadagni, indeed, desired: "May I be propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle.
He saw this four-night sacrifice.
He took it; he sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he was multiplied through offspring and cattle.
Furthermore, two Aurvas were not born among his offspring, [each asking], "Who are you? Who are you?
Thus he was born here in great abundance.
Therefore, even now, two grey-haired Aurvas, having come together, do not recognize one another.
He who knows thus is propagated with many offspring and cattle.
Regarding this, they say: "The consecration (*dīkṣā*) for him should indeed last for a year.
For the year is procreation.
This sacrifice is procreation; thus, that very act of procreation is performed. Therefore, one who desires offspring should indeed sacrifice with this.
Now they say: "There should be exactly forty-eight [verses].
For the *jagatī* consists of forty-eight syllables, and cattle are the *jagatī*.
This sacrifice belongs to the Jagatī;
therefore, one who desires cattle should indeed perform it with this.
Now, they also say that there should be exactly thirty-six [verses].
The *bṛhatī* indeed consists of thirty-six syllables.
The *bṛhatī*, indeed, attained the heavenly world.
That, verily, is his [attainment of] the heavenly world.
Therefore, indeed, one who desires heaven should sacrifice with this [sacrifice].
Those [verses] are three *jagatī*s.
There are three *jagatī* feet.
By that, they do not depart from the forms of the Jagatī.
Now, some say there should be exactly twenty-four;
for the year consists of twenty-four half-months and is a source of procreation.
This sacrifice is procreation;
that very act of procreation is performed.
Therefore, one who desires offspring should indeed sacrifice with this.
That single *jagatī* foot exists;
by that very means they do not depart from the form of the *jagatī*.

Regarding this they say: "Since the first day is performed with the *gāyatrī*, the second with the *triṣṭubh*, the third with the *jagatī*, and the fourth with the *anuṣṭubh*, then why is this sacrifice designated as belonging solely to the *jagatī*?
He should reply: "When one who possesses many horses or many mares comes along, yoking various [animals] one after another, it is in this manner..."
Thus, they ascend from one metre to another, reaching the Jagatī; and furthermore, because these Stotras, once fully chanted, culminate in the Jagatī, they are therefore of the Jagatī nature.
Moreover, the Jagatī is indeed the eldest among the metres.

Therefore, they call them *gṛhyas* by virtue of their seniority; those who know thus call them *gṛhyas*. Indeed, this sacrifice is performed as a two-night rite (*dvirātra*) when [the *rathantara*] is used with the verses beginning "O bull, for you the pressed juice...
on the third day; they should perform the *rathantara* as the *pṛṣṭha* chant.
In that they proceed with the verse beginning "Abhi tvā," they do not depart from the form of the *rathantara*.
The third day is extended by means of the *gāyatrī* which has not lost its strength.
The *maitrāvaruṇasāman* is [chanted] on the verse: "Who, O Indra, will aid thee? (Kaḥ tam indra tvāvāsaḥ).
The syllables of these [verses] are thus accomplished here.
On the fourth day, they should perform the *bṛhat* as the *pṛṣṭha* stotra upon these verses beginning with "We implore you with sacrifices" (*taṃ tvā yajñebhir īmahe*).
Since it begins with "that you" (*taṃ tve*), by that they do not depart from the form of the *bṛhat*.
The fourth day is extended by means of an *anuṣṭubh* verse that has reached its full measure (*āyātayāmnī*).
The *maitrāvaruṇa-sāman* is [chanted] on the verse beginning, "We indeed you, O matchless one.
The syllables of these [verses] here come together to form a total. 286.

JB 2.287 |va This four-night rite indeed has its meters arranged in a wide array (vyūḍha). vb The first [day] is the application of the Bṛhatī among the Pṛṣṭhas; the latter [day] is that of the Gāyatrī. Or rather, the first [day] is that of the Uṣṇih and Kakubh in the Ārbhava [Stotra].
The *uttara-yoga* verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. Now, as these meters are interwoven, so indeed from an interwoven union are offspring and cattle produced; it is for the sake of procreation.

Moreover, man is indeed interwoven with evils; by means of these very interwoven metres, he thus drives away the interwoven evils. Regarding this, they say: "What is the basis for the four-night sacrifice?"
"One should say, 'day and night.
For the four-night rite indeed follows day and night.
By the first day he spreads out the day; by the second, the banner of the day; by the third day, the night."
He who spreads [the sacrifice] as the banner of the forenoon—him [he serves] with the fourth [offering].
Indeed, day and night produce all this;
"May those two who produce all this produce me," [he thinks].
Then he might say: "The four-night rite follows the quarters.
There are four quarters;
the upward quarter is the fifth.
These are four days;
the night is the fifth.
By this, he prospers in the quarters.
Having established himself in the quarters, he goes to the heavenly world.
For him, these are the *upasad* rites accompanied by sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
Indeed, the sacrificial cake is the womb, and the clarified butter is the seed.

In that, having offered the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), he makes an oblation over it with clarified butter (ājya), they thereby establish the seed within the womb. He who knows this, his emitted seed is produced in due order. Moreover, he thus prospers in those very deities for whom he prepares these oblations.
Having established himself upon them, he goes to the heavenly world. 287.
Now this [sacrifice] belongs to Prajāpati. 288. JB 2.288.
One who desires offspring should sacrifice with this.
Prajāpati indeed desired, "May I be multiplied through offspring and cattle. He beheld this four-night rite and performed it.
He sacrificed with it.
For him there are these *stomas*: the ninefold (*trivṛt*), the fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*), the seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*), and the twenty-onefold (*ekaviṃśa*).
They are deficient and redundant, forming pairs for procreation.
One is deficient, the other is redundant. From a union that is both deficient and redundant, offspring and cattle are produced.
The *trivṛt* and the *pañcadaśa*—that is the productive union.
The seventeenth and the twenty-first—this is a productive couple. Since this is a productive couple, may it procreate me.
From that, indeed, he was multiplied through offspring and cattle.
He who knows thus is indeed multiplied with offspring and cattle. Now they say: "He was afraid of the loss of those very creatures that had been created. He beheld this four-night sacrifice.
He brought it; with it he sacrificed.
For that sacrifice, there are two *agniṣṭoma*s on both sides and two *ukthya*s in the middle.
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the Brahman, and the Ukthya-stotras are offspring and cattle. By means of the Brahman, he thus encompasses offspring and cattle on both sides, so that they may not be lost.
He whose wealth is not lost is he who knows thus. 288.
JB 2.289 |va Now this is the *saṃsarpa* of Vasiṣṭha. vb Vasiṣṭha indeed desired, "May I glide over these worlds."
He saw this four-night sacrifice;
he brought it; with it he sacrificed.
Then indeed he glided over these worlds.
Because he glided over these worlds, that is the reason for the *saṃsarpa*’s name, *saṃsarpatva*. He who knows thus glides over these worlds.
Three triple-stomas are yoked to it and carry it through the day.
Indeed, among those that are yoked, three by three are the most effective carriers. By means of what is thus yoked, one goes to wherever one desires to go.
Now they say: "One who desires offspring should sacrifice with this. Indeed, this *stoma* becomes joined with a *stoma*.
From a union that is joined, offspring and cattle are produced; it is for the sake of procreation.
Day after day they release the *stoma*, and day after day they bring the *stoma* back again.
JB 2.290 |va| Now follows this Catuṣṭoma of Gautama.
vb| They indeed did not have faith in Gautama.
"The royal sage is not to be trusted," they said.
He desired, "May they place faith in me; may I become trustworthy.
He saw this four-night sacrifice.
He brought it;
he sacrificed with it. Then indeed they placed faith in him, and he became one worthy of faith.
One who knows thus becomes worthy of faith.
Indeed, this [sacrifice] is one whose *stoma* has been performed;
for faith is indeed what has been performed.
Whatever they carry away here after having won it by means of a ritual performance (*kṛta*), they indeed carry it away through faith alone;
therefore, it is the *kṛtastoma*. This very [stoma] of the Aṅgirases increases by four [syllables].
By [the verse] with two more syllables, the Ādityas went to the heavenly world; by [the verse] with four more, the Aṅgirases.

He who knows thus goes to the heavenly world by [the verse] with four more syllables. Regarding this they say: "The sacrificial rite is prone to fall away; it is liable to depart for that world before one's full lifespan."
In that the stotras are descending, it is therefore free from ruin; it is therefore conducive to long life.
Now follows this Viśvajyotis (All-Light) [sacrifice]. The gods indeed desired, "May we all be like light."
They saw this four-night sacrifice;
they took it up and sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, indeed, they all became as if light itself.
Therefore, even now, when people see the gods, they say, "We have seen them like a light.
He who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with this [rite]. Indeed, he who attains spiritual luster shines like a light.

Verily, by means of this he prospers; he becomes possessed of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). 290. Now, these are the five-night rites. 291. *vā* (or). *ṛdhnoti hainena brahmavarcasaṃ brahmavarcasī bhavati*. 290. There are indeed five victories.
By means of the five *vyāhṛtis*, the gods conquered this world.
[The sacrificer thinks: "May I conquer as much as the gods conquered."
The sacrifice is fivefold;
[he does this] thinking, "May I attain whatever is the measure of the sacrifice";
cattle are fivefold.
"May cattle, in their full measure, attend upon me as something already acquired.
Food consists of five parts;
"may food, in its full measure, attend upon me as something already acquired."
These [days] are five; the year consists of five seasons;
the year is Prajāpati, the sacrifice.
By this, one attains Prajāpati, the year, and the sacrifice.
The gods and the Asuras contended;
they did not conquer each other by means of clubs nor by means of arrows.
They said, "We shall not conquer by means of clubs nor by means of arrows;
rather, O Brahmin, let our victory be through speech alone. They reflected, "Whichever of us speaks first, they will overcome those others."
Those gods said to the Asuras, "You speak first!
The Asuras said to the gods, "You indeed [speak first]!
Then those gods perceived this pair of speech. 291.
"Let us be one," said the gods; "let us be one," said the Asuras.
The gods spoke of the mind, the Asuras of speech.
Those gods, by means of the mind alone, appropriated the speech of the Asuras.
Therefore, whatever one conceives with the mind, that one speaks with speech.
"Two are ours," said the gods; "Two are ours," said the Asuras.
The gods spoke of out-breathing and in-breathing; the Asuras, of day and night.
Those gods, by means of out-breathing and in-breathing, excluded the Asuras from day and night.
Therefore, one who lives long breathes through many days and nights.
"Three are ours," said the gods; "Three are ours," said the Asuras.
The gods said, "These very three worlds"; the Asuras said, "The three branches of knowledge.
By means of these very worlds, the gods appropriated the three branches of knowledge from the Asuras.
Therefore, these branches of knowledge are proclaimed in these very worlds.
Regarding them, the gods said, "Four are ours," and the Asuras said, "Four are ours.
The gods claimed the four-footed animals, while the Asuras claimed the four quarters.
Those gods, by means of four-footed animals, appropriated the four quarters from the Asuras.
Therefore, whichever direction one brings an animal toward, he follows it as already conquered, prepared, and firmly established.
"Five are ours," said the gods, referring to the seasons (*ṛtu*).
Then the Asuras could not find [a match],
for there is nothing whatsoever that is fivefold.
Those Asuras, finding no foothold, were defeated while merely crying out, "Five! Five! Then indeed the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated.
He who knows this prevails by himself, and his hateful rival is defeated. 292.
JB 2.293 |va: These utterances (vyāhṛti) are indeed victory;
vb: the five-night rite is victory.
Victory! Victory! He who knows thus wins.
Indeed, this [knowledge] is the victory over everything else, and the defeat of everything else.
By means of this, the gods conquered all the asuras.
The Asuras were utterly defeated.
He who knows this conquers every hateful rival; his hateful rival is utterly defeated.
Now, these [days] are continuous. Just as wooden planks are held together by a leather thong on a chariot or a wagon, even so is the five-night rite (*pañcarātra*) held together by the *stomas*.
The *stomas* are indeed the vital breaths; man is continuous through his vital breaths.
He who knows this is woven together.
Two by two, the *stomas* are yoked and carry that day.
Indeed, among those that are yoked, two by two are the best at drawing. By means of what is yoked, one goes to wherever one desires to go. 293.

JB 2.294 |va| Now, one who desires food should sacrifice with this [sacrifice] which consists of the three-day period beginning with Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus, followed by the Pañcaviṃśa Mahāvrata and the Sarvastoma Atirātra.
Regarding this they say: "The Mahāvrata should not be undertaken before a year has passed.
Now, as for the fact that there is a three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus—this world is indeed Jyotis, this [atmospheric] world is Gauḥ, and yonder world is Āyus.
These worlds are the seasons, and the seasons are the year.
The seasons are the year; it is the year that ripens all food. Thus, they partake of that very food which has been won by the year.
The Mahāvrata chant consists of twenty-five parts; the twenty-fivefold is indeed food, [performed] for the sake of securing food.
The *atirātra* sacrifice consists of all the *stomas*, for the conquest and mastery of all the worlds;

for indeed, all this is simply the *stomas*. Moreover, having prospered together with those individual *stomas* which we have approached, and having established ourselves upon them, we have risen upward.
"May we obtain," he says. Now,

for one who desires food, he should perform this sacrifice which consists of a three-day period of the Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, and Saptadaśa stomas, a Mahāvrata with the twenty-five-fold stoma, and an Atirātra with all the stomas.
Regarding this they say: "The Mahāvrata should not be undertaken before a year has passed.

In that regard, as for the fact that there is a three-day period consisting of the Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, and Saptadaśa stomas—it is because this world is Trivṛt, this [atmospheric] world is Pañcadaśa, and yonder world is Saptadaśa.
These worlds are indeed the seasons, and the year is the seasons. The year ripens all food; they thus partake of that very food which has been won by the year.
The twenty-fifth [stoma] is the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*); the twenty-fifth is indeed food, for the sake of securing food.
There is an *atirātra* with all the *stomas*, for the conquest and overcoming of all worlds;
for all this is indeed the *stomas*.
"Now, those individual *stomas* which we have approached, having prospered together and being established in them, may we attain the beyond. (JB 2.295)

Now, he who desires, "May my Mahāvrata be endowed with the indirect," should sacrifice with this [sacrifice] which consists of the three-day period of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus, the Caturviṃśa day, and the Sarvastoma Atirātra. In that there is the Caturviṃśa day, by that very means his Mahāvrata becomes endowed with the indirect.

Moreover, whatever *hiṃkāra*, *prastāva*, or *pratihāra* occurs there, by that very means his twenty-fifth [element] becomes attained. The *atirātra* sacrifice consists of all the *stomas*; it serves for the conquest and the overcoming of all the worlds.

"Indeed, all this is nothing but the *stomas*. Moreover, having prospered together through these individual *stomas* which we have approached, and having established ourselves within them, may we attain the highest world."

Now, for one who performs this sacrifice consisting of the three-day period— the Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, and Saptadaśa— and the twenty-four-fold day, the Jyotis Atirātra, he who should desire, "May my Mahāvrata be endowed with the indirect," he should sacrifice with this.
In that there is a twenty-four-fold day, by that very means his Mahāvrata becomes endowed with the indirect.
Furthermore, whatever there may be in that [sacrifice]—whether it be the *hiṃkāra*, the *prastāva*, or the *pratihāra*—by that very means his twenty-fifth [stotra] becomes attained.
The *jyotir-atirātra* is this well-known ford of the deities; because the *jyotir-atirātra* is well-known, [it is performed].
"By the divine ford, by the unharmed, may we, unharmed, reach the highest point.
Now, for this [sacrifice] where there are two *jyotis* *agniṣṭomas* on both sides and two *go-āyus* *ukthya*s in between, there is *jyotis*. 296. JB 2.296. va.
One who desires offspring should perform this sacrifice with the Atirātra in the middle;
for that which is the Jyotir Atirātra is indeed complete procreation,
and procreation is indeed in the middle of the self.
In that there is an Atirātra with light in the middle, he thereby places the organ of procreation in the very middle of his self;
he becomes many and is propagated.
The two Ukthya sacrifices, Go and Āyus, are the ones in between.
The *ukthas* are indeed cattle;
there are five hundred *stotriyas* in those two.
Thus, by means of cattle itself, he encloses offspring on both sides.
The two *jyotis* *agniṣṭomas* are on both sides.
The *agniṣṭoma* is indeed the light, and the *brahman* is the light.
By means of the *brahman*, he thus encloses the offspring and cattle on both sides so that they may not be lost.
The wealth of one who knows this is not diminished. Now, for him whose two *jyotiṣ* *agniṣṭoma*s are on both sides, with the *go* and *āyus* *ukthya*s in between,
and a *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* in the middle— he who should desire, "May a son endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) be born among my offspring," he [should perform] this [sacrifice].
He should sacrifice.
Splendor indeed is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and light is the *agniṣṭoma*.
Moreover, the organ of generation is in the middle of the self.

In that the Agniṣṭoma with its light-element occurs in the middle, he thereby places the light in the very center of his self; consequently, a son endowed with spiritual luster (brahmavarcas) is born among his offspring.
The two Ukthya sacrifices, Go and Āyus, are placed within as the intermediate ones.
The *ukthas* are indeed cattle;
there are five hundred *stotriyas* in those two [services].
Thus, by means of cattle on both sides, he encompasses offspring endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*).
There are two *atirātra* sacrifices on both sides [of the central part].
These two *atirātras* are indeed these two worlds.
By means of these two worlds, he thus encloses offspring and cattle on both sides, so that they may not be lost.
The wealth of one who knows thus is not diminished.
Now, these are the six-night sacrifices. 297. JB 2.297.
The Maruts, indeed, desired: "May we be the strongest, the most powerful, the most numerous, and the most heroic among the gods;
may we conquer the heavenly world.
They saw this six-night sacrifice.
They brought it;
they sacrificed with it. Thereupon, indeed, those gods became the strongest, the most powerful, the most numerous, and the most heroic among the gods; they conquered the heavenly world.
He who knows this becomes the most powerful, the strongest, the most abundant, and the most heroic among his own people; he conquers the heavenly world.
They proceed by means of the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed prosperity and the summit;
thus, he ascends to that very prosperity and summit which are the *pṛṣṭhas*.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed vigor and strength; it is by means of that very vigor and strength that they proceed.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the heavenly world.
They go ascending indeed to that world of heaven. Their consecration takes place at the immersion in the Sarasvatī;
they undergo consecration on the southern bank.
The two *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds are shaped like wheels; the sacrificial post has its base in a mortar (*ulūkhalabudhna*). This is for the sake of transcendence and to prevent falling away.
For if they were to act as if they were performing [the rites] there, that would indeed be their downfall.
They go by casting the *śamyā* (wooden pins). These castings of the *śamyā* are indeed the strides of the heavenly world;
thus, they go taking strides across the very strides of the heavenly world.
They go along striking and shouting;
for that which is struck and shouted at is indeed the form of strength.
They go along with the Sarasvatī.
vii Speech is indeed Sarasvatī. viii And speech is the path leading to the gods.
ix By that very path leading to the gods, they go.
They go against the current;
for the heavenly world is, as it were, against the current;
thus they attain the heavenly world.
They go eastward and northward;
for the heavenly world is, as it were, toward the northeast;
thus they go ascending to that very heavenly world.
They go as far as the *prakṣa* and the *prāsravaṇa*.
Indeed, this *prakṣa-prāsravaṇa* is the very end of speech.
And where there is the end of speech, that is the heavenly world.
They go to the heavenly world itself.
For by means of this very [rite], the Maruts, when Indra and Agni looked upon them, [thought]: "If these indeed complete this [sacrifice]..."
"The Maruts alone are all this," they said.
They both won a thousand [cows] at the distribution of the sacrificial session;
however, they caused them to be lost.
They indeed struck away evil from them; therefore, one should not desire anything belonging to a *vimathin*, lest one share in evil.
They indeed prospered through the superior power of those two.

When ten cows become a hundred, that is one [unit]. When a hundred cows become a thousand, that is one [unit].
By means of this very [calculation], the Purāyus, with Sthūra as their householder, [performed the sacrifice].
They rose up against those who were either three-pronged or barbed and defeated them. Then they killed their householder.
As they sat weeping all around that slain householder, they said:
The guardian of the sacrificial post (dhruvagopa) recognized him as he was running away by his very appearance.
He ascended from the Āhavanīya fire directly to the heavenly world.
He said, "Do not grieve."
"Or rather, this one for whom you feel compassion— this indeed was he who ascended from the Āhavanīya fire to the heavenly world.
Those among them whom they slew there went to the heavenly world.
Now, those who remained are these very ones who at this time appear as it were more worthy of reward among the wealthy;
for previously they were, as it were, more wretched villagers.
Therefore, they cause the wealth of a wealthy man to be proclaimed by means of a yoke-pin.

Now, for this [sacrifice], there are the Viśvajit and Abhijit as the two Atirātra rites on either side; in the middle there are four Ukthya rites, namely Gaur-āyus, Gaur-āyus. Those desiring cattle should perform this.
This world, indeed, is the Abhijit; yonder world is the Viśvajit.
Now, these four Ukthya offerings occur in the middle;
for the Ukthas are cattle.

There are a thousand stotriya verses for them. By means of both this world and that world, they encompass these cattle on both sides; thus they secure cattle. Indeed, they become possessed of many cattle.
By this very [sacrifice], indeed, Indra and Agni and the Maruts conquered a thousand;
Indra, indeed, won a thousand for the Maruts.
Agni is the conqueror of the near, Indra is the conqueror of all.
Now, these four Ukthya-stotras are performed in the middle;
for the Ukthas are indeed cattle,
and they consist of a thousand Stotriya-verses.
Indra and Agni indeed carried this away, having enclosed it on both sides with a thousandfold enclosure.
And for one who knows thus, cattle attend upon him from both sides, enclosed by these two worlds and by Indra and Agni.
"Of them, indeed of them, the *parīṇah*," [this is] at the rear half of Kurukṣetra; that is for the consecration (*dīkṣā*).
They go eastward across Kurukṣetra. Kurukṣetra, indeed, is the place of sacrifice for the gods.
By means of that sacrificial ground of the gods, they go to the very gods;
for them, the Yamunā is the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Indeed, this Yamunā is the world of heaven.
They go indeed to that world, the heavenly realm.

Now, regarding this sacrifice for which there is a three-day period upwards and a three-day period backwards: he who should desire, "May I go to the heavenly realm, yet may I remain established in this world," he should perform this sacrifice.
In just three days from here he goes upward to the heavenly world; in three days he descends back from there.
He goes to the heavenly world and stands firm in this world. Moreover, he knows: "He who was that, I am this one. Thus he is born again in this very world. 300.
JB 2.301 |va Now follow these seven-night [sacrifices].
vb There are indeed seven meters.
All speech is indeed the meters. He attains the sovereignty and lordship of speech who attains prosperity.
[He thinks: "May I attain the sovereignty and lordship of speech."
Therefore, he sacrifices for seven nights.
There are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*). By means of the vital breaths, offspring and cattle are encompassed and sustained.

"May the offspring and cattle that are encompassed by those vital breaths attend upon me with those same vital breaths. Indeed, it was by means of the vital breaths that the gods went to the heavenly world.
"Therefore, by means of those vital breaths (*prāṇa*) by which the gods went to the heavenly world, may I go to the heavenly world by means of those vital breaths.
Now, there are indeed seven principal vital breaths;
these principal vital breaths are indeed those that have struck away evil.
"Let us extend the sacrifice by means of those vital breaths which have had their evil struck away, according to their measure.
The Seven Seers, desiring prosperity, performed austerities;
they saw this seven-night sacrifice.
They brought it; with it they sacrificed. 301.
They were sharers of the day.
Then, indeed, by means of the day alone one among them prospered, by the day alone another, and by the day alone another.
That, truly, is the most excellent of prosperities and the most meritorious of worlds, which the seven seers attained through this.
They prospered.
That which is the most excellent of prosperities, that which is the most meritorious of worlds— that which the Seven Seers prospered by means of this—
may I prosper in that.
Therefore, he sacrifices for seven nights.
These days are seven; there are seven *stomas*. Indeed, the day carries the *stoma*; the *stoma* is the day, the *stoma* is the day.
Indeed, that is the prosperity of the days, namely that these carry various *stomas*.
That which is the prosperity of the days is precisely what is performed here.
And all of them, amounting to seven, result in the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*), namely the nine-fold (*trivṛt*) and the thirty-three-fold (*trayastriṃśa*).
Those two twenty-one-fold [stomas] and the fifteen-fold; those two twenty-one-fold and the seventeen-fold and the twenty-five-fold;
those two twenty-one-fold and the twenty-one-fold itself is the twenty-one-fold.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-one-fold.
Indeed, those who perform the seven-night sacrifice attain co-residence (*salokatā*) with him. Having attained this [sacrifice], their world prospers.
He who knows thus goes to him and attains co-residence with him. 302.
JB 2.303 |va With this very [sacrifice], Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice.
vb When the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas said to him, "We shall cause you to sacrifice with this sacrifice; we shall cause you to sacrifice with this," [he replied: ...
"Let us perform the sacrifice for you," [they said].
"No," he replied.
