"That Brahmin was not more learned in the Veda than I, who arranged this sacrificial rite for me."
"Let him perform the sacrifice for me with this very [offering]," he said.
"So be it," he replied.
They had him perform the sacrifice with that.
This indeed is the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha itself, with the twenty-five-fold Mahāvrata as its [concluding] day.
From that very point they proceed to the night.
Prosperity, indeed, is the pinnacle; the Pṛṣṭha-stotras are the pinnacle.
Verily, he ascends the heights and the back-sides of glory itself.
The Mahāvrata is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
Regarding this, they say: "One should not undertake the Mahāvrata before a year has passed."
In that there is the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the seasons;
the seasons are the year. The year ripens all food; thus, it is the food won by means of the year.
They approach the twenty-fifth, the Mahāvrata; for the twenty-fifth is indeed food, [and it serves] for the attainment of food. 303.
Regarding this they say: "This is indeed the place of day and night; the Agniṣṭoma is this day. And regarding this they also say: "The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the year. (Also at 2.202 [247.31])
Prajāpati is the year. The Mahāvrata belongs to Prajāpati; thus there should be twenty-five stotras for the Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
Then they should descend to the night with the twenty-one-fold Ukthya chants.
In this way, these two sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are distinguished.

Now, for this *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the *stomas* on the fifth day consist of the *mahāvrata*, the *viśvajit*, and the all-*pṛṣṭha* *atirātra*. With this very rite, Kārīrādi, desiring prosperity and desiring food, performed the sacrifice.
The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is indeed the self, and the *mahāvrata* is food.
He thinks, "I shall place food for myself in the very middle of my self; thus I will become an eater of food and the best among my own people.
Furthermore, the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is the year.
"May that food, gathered over the course of a year, attend upon you.
A Viśvajit Atirātra with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras takes place;
for the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed prosperity and the highest form.
"Thinking, 'I shall ascend to the heights of glory and the back-sacrifices,' he [the king] said this.
But a Brahmin said to him: 'As long as he lives, he will be the best among his own people, an eater of food; however, he will die headless.'"
The Mahāvrata is indeed the head of the sacrifice.
It is as if one were to cut off the head and hide it under the armpits; it would not adhere, for he said, "He has done such a thing."
"They know full well who will cut off his head. And so it indeed came to pass.
For as long as Kratu Kārīrādi lived, he remained a consumer of food and the most excellent among his own people.
But he died indeed headless.
However, his kinsmen, knowing [the truth], cut off his head.
This very sacrifice is auspicious for one who would perform it with him as a supervisor. 304.
JB 2.305 |va Now follows this Babara-saptarātra.
vb Its first day is indeed the seventeenfold (stoma), then the ninefold, then the fifteenfold, then the twenty-onefold.
Then the Triṇava, then the Trayastriṃśa, and the Jyotis Atirātra. With this [sacrifice], he indeed sacrificed, desiring prosperity and desiring food.
"The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha is indeed the self," [it is said].

"The Trivṛt is the mouth, and the Saptadaśa is food. He thinks: 'From the very beginning, I shall place food in my mouth; thus I shall become an eater of food and the most excellent among my own people.'"
Moreover, the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is indeed the year; thus, he thinks, "May I not be overtaken by the food-obtainment that has been secured before the year.
[The rite is] the *jyotis* *atirātra*.
"This indeed is the well-known divine ford, namely the Jyotir Atirātra.
Thinking, 'By means of this well-known divine ford, which is secure, I shall reach the conclusion without harm,' he set out. But his own pupil called him out from behind. (305)
The son of Khālāti, Govarṇa, will become more wicked;
from the very beginning, he has placed food in his mouth.
"When food indeed reaches the mouth, it certainly becomes putrid there; whether one swallows it, it becomes putrid, or whether one spits it out, it becomes putrid.
'If I have not made this food putrid, I shall become worse off,' [he thought].
And so it was exactly thus.
He became worse off. They said to him, "This very pupil of yours, Govarṇa Khālateya,
has indeed contradicted you."
He said to him, "Do you indeed perform this sacrifice for me.
He replied, "So be it.
[The other said,] "I shall restore you, just as one would repair a broken chariot or a damaged cart."
For him, he indeed made the first day Trivṛt, then Pañcadaśa, then Ekaviṃśa, then Triṇava,
then Trayastriṃśa, then Saptadaśa, and then Saptadaśa again; two Saptadaśas follow one after the other.
By this very means, Govarṇa Khālateya caused his teacher to perform a sacrifice.
The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite is indeed the self, and the seventeenfold chant is food.
Thus, he will rise up from the self toward the attainment of food.
"That food which you have secured above will attend upon you; from each of the seventeen [stomas], food shall come from food. "Your offspring will become eaters of food," he said. (306)
These Bābaras among the Kurus are indeed worthy of being honored.
He used to attend upon that sacrificial ground, saying, "I have sacrificed here; I have not sacrificed there."
Now, for this [sacrifice] consisting of the Jyotis, Go, and Āyus [days], there is a three-day period, a Viśvajit with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, an Ukthya with the *ṣoḍaśin*, a Chandoma-pavamāna,

an Ukthya with all the *stomas*, a Mahāvrata with the Pañcaviṃśa [stoma], and a Jyotis Atirātra— for one who should desire: "Having approached the Abhiplava, having approached the *pṛṣṭhas*, having approached the Chandomas, may I [attain] the Mahāvrata."
Thinking, "May it be attained," he should sacrifice with this [rite].
Having indeed attained the Abhiplava, having attained the Pṛṣṭhas, and having attained the Chandomas, the Mahāvrata becomes attained for him;
for the Mahāvrata is food, and it is for the attainment of food.

Regarding this, they say: "The Mahāvrata should not be undertaken before a year has passed. In that regard, as for the fact that there is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period—the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the seasons, and the seasons are the year.

The year ripens all food; they thus partake of that food which has been won by the year. The Mahāvrata is the twenty-fivefold [stoma]; the twenty-fivefold is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
The Jyotir-atirātra.
This Jyotir-atirātra is indeed the well-known ford of the gods. [Thinking: "By means of this well-known ford of the gods, being unharmed, may I reach the conclusion unharmed. (307)
The Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha; then as for the seventh day, its Bahiṣpavamāna is the Caturviṃśa-stoma,
the subsequent stotras are Trayastrimśa, the Mahāvrata is Pañcaviṃśa, and [the Agniṣṭoma-stotra] is Catustriṃśa.
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman. This Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha sacrifice is indeed like something that has been obtained; it is as if the sacrifice has been obtained.
Therefore, on the seventh day, the Bahiṣpavamāna-stotra consists of the Caturviṃśa-stoma.
Twenty-four half-months make a year;
the year is the sacrifice. Thus, they take hold of the sacrifice itself at the very beginning of the sacrifice.
Moreover, the Gāyatrī indeed consists of twenty-four syllables.
The *gāyatrī* verses indeed extend again the sacrificial rite that has been attained;

for by means of them, another [verse] is able to lift up the sacrificial rite attained through the *gāyatrī*. The subsequent stotras consist of thirty-three [verses]; for there are thirty-three deities, and it is for the attainment of the deities themselves.
The twenty-fifth is the Mahāvrata; the twenty-fifth is indeed food, for the attainment of food.
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the thirty-fourth;
there are indeed thirty-three deities.
Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth. Thus, he establishes the sacrifice at its conclusion within these very deities, including Prajāpati.
The first six days are the *pṛṣṭhya* ṣaḍaha; as for the seventh day, its *pavamāna* stotras consist of twenty-four-fold verses.
The thirty-third day is the *abhyāvartin*; the twenty-fifth is the *mahāvrata*; and the thirty-fourth is the *agniṣṭomasāman*.
This *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* sacrifice is, as it were, replenished; indeed, it is replenished.

In that the *pavamāna* stotras of the seventh day consist of twenty-four verses at each opening of the pressings, [it is so] thinking, "May our sacrifice be commenced at every opening of the pressing.
The *trayastrimśa* [stotra] recurs; for there are thirty-three deities, [and it serves] for the attainment of the deities.
The twenty-fifth is the Mahāvrata; the twenty-fifth is indeed food, for the sake of obtaining food.
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the thirty-fourth;
there are indeed thirty-three deities.
Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth. Thus, he finally establishes himself among these deities, including Prajāpati, at the conclusion of the sacrifice. 308/ JB 2.309
It is indeed the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period; then, as for that seventh day, it is entirely the twenty-fourfold, the twenty-fivefold, the *mahāvrata*, and the thirty-fourfold *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
This *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is, as it were, a sacrificial session that has been attained; it is indeed attained.

In that the seventh day is entirely the Caturviṃśa, the sacrifice has been commenced with the whole day; thus it becomes so. The Mahāvrata is the Pañcaviṃśa; the Pañcaviṃśa is indeed food, for the sake of obtaining food.
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the thirty-fourth.
There are indeed thirty-three deities;
Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth.
Thus, at the very end of the sacrifice, he establishes himself upon these deities together with Prajāpati.

It is indeed the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period; then, as for the seventh day, its *chandomas* and *pavamānas* are the thirty-four-fold [stoma], the twenty-five-fold *mahāvrata* which returns again, and the thirty-three-fold [stoma].
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman. He who should desire, "May the Pṛṣṭhas come to me, may the Chandomas come to me, and may the Mahāvrata come to me," he should sacrifice with this.
Having approached the *pṛṣṭhas*, having approached the *chandomas*, the *mahāvrata* becomes approached for him;
the *mahāvrata* is indeed food, [and this is] for the attainment of food.
The thirty-four-fold [stoma] returns again.
There are indeed thirty-three deities;
Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth.
Thus, he establishes himself among these deities together with Prajāpati.
The twenty-fifth is the Mahāvrata; the twenty-fifth is indeed food, for the sake of obtaining food.
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the thirty-third; there are thirty-three deities, for the sake of attaining the deities. 309/ JB 2.310.
Now, these two are to be recited together.
Jamadagni was indeed the domestic priest of the Mahenās;
he surpassed them in wealth.
They indeed began to plot against him.
He reflected: "How might I kill seven of these domestic animals each day?"
He saw these two sacrifices; he took them up;
with them he sacrificed.
Then indeed, on each successive day, he struck down seven by seven of their domestic animals.
This, indeed, is that flawless thunderbolt.
With this very flawless thunderbolt, he used to drive them away.
Just as one would crush sesame seeds with a millstone, even so does he utterly crush these [enemies] when they have been driven away.
He who has rivals, he who would practice sorcery, or he who would compete, should sacrifice with these two [offerings].

By this very unbroken thunderbolt, he strikes down his hateful enemy and adversary. Moreover, they say that one who desires offspring should sacrifice with these two; for the *stoma* becomes joined with the *stoma*, and from such a union, offspring and cattle are produced.
They are born through procreation itself.
Now, this seventh day consists of seventeen [stomas];
on that day they perform the Mahāvrata.
Prajāpati is indeed the seventeenfold [stoma].
The Mahāvrata is food; thus, in its own abode, they cause Prajāpati to prosper with food.
Now, these are the eight-night sacrifices.
Bṛhaspati indeed desired: "May I be radiant and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge; may I attain glory among the gods.
He beheld this eight-night sacrifice.
He brought it; with it he sacrificed.
Thereupon, indeed, he became radiant and possessed of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*), and glory went to the gods.
For glory indeed went to him who attained their priesthood. He becomes radiant and endowed with spiritual luster; glory goes to the gods for him who knows thus.
Moreover, they say: "One who desires long life should sacrifice with this very [offering]."
The Gāyatrī is indeed the vital breath;
this sacrifice is perfected through the Gāyatrī.
Therefore, one who desires long life should perform this sacrifice.
Now they say: "One who desires cattle should indeed sacrifice with this.
The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables;
cattle have eight hooves.
The cattle are the *gāyatrī*;
this sacrifice is perfected through the *gāyatrī*.
Therefore, one who desires cattle should indeed perform this sacrifice.
Prajāpati desired, "May I go from this world to that world.
He beheld this eight-night sacrifice;
he took it up.
He sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, he indeed went from this world to that world. Because he went from this world to that world, that is the reason for the eight-night sacrifice being called the *aṣṭarātra*.
He who knows thus departs from this world to that world. Regarding this, they ask: "What is the basis for the eight-night rite? One should reply: "The quarters."
The eight-night rite, indeed, follows the directions:
four directions, four intermediate directions,
and the upward direction is the ninth.
These eight days come to be; the night is the ninth.
By this, he prospers in the quarters; having established himself in the quarters, he goes to the heavenly world.

Now, for one whose [sacrifice] consists of a Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and a Jyotis Agniṣṭoma—if he should desire, "May I be radiant and endowed with spiritual luster in this world; may I go to the heavenly world;
may I be radiant and endowed with spiritual luster in that world"—he should sacrifice with this.

In that there is an Agniṣṭoma with light at the beginning, light is indeed splendor and spiritual luster; by means of that Agniṣṭoma, he becomes splendid and possessed of spiritual luster in this world.
There is a Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha; the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha is indeed the heavenly world; by means of it, he reaches the heavenly world.

He goes. The *jyotiṣṭoma* Agniṣṭoma occurs at the end; light indeed is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the Agniṣṭoma is light; by that very means, he becomes possessed of spiritual luster in yonder world.

Now, he for whom this sacrifice consists of a Jyotis Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and a Jyotis Atirātra— if he should desire, "May I stand firm in this world, may I go to the heavenly world, and may I stand firm in that world"—
let him sacrifice with this.

In that there is an Atirātra with light at the beginning, this indeed is the complete foundation; since the Atirātra with light is the foundation, by that very means he finds firm footing in this world.
There is a Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha; the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha is indeed the heavenly world; by it, one reaches the heavenly world itself.
He goes forth. The Jyotir-atirātra is at the end; this Jyotir-atirātra is indeed the complete foundation. By means of it, he finds firm support in that world. 312.
JB 2.313 |va| Now, for him whose [sacrificial sequence] consists of the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and the Jyotis Atirātra— whoever should desire:
"May I be radiant and endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) in this world, and may I go to the heavenly world in yonder world"— [for him this is prescribed].
"He who thinks, 'May I abide in this world,' should sacrifice with this [rite].
In that there is a Jyotis Agniṣṭoma at the beginning, and since the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma is indeed splendor and spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa),
by means of it he becomes possessed of splendor and spiritual luster in this world."
There is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period. The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is indeed the heavenly world; by means of it, he goes to the heavenly world.
There is a *jyotis* *atirātra* at the end; this *jyotis* *atirātra* is indeed the complete foundation.
By that very means, he becomes firmly established in yonder world.
Now, regarding this sacrifice which consists of a Jyotis Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and a Jyotis Agniṣṭoma—for one who should desire:
"May I be established in this world and go to the heavenly world, being radiant and endowed with spiritual splendor"—[this is the sacrifice for him].
Thinking, "May I be in that world," he should sacrifice with this [rite].
In that the Jyotir Atirātra occurs first, this Jyotir Atirātra is indeed the complete foundation;
by it he finds firm support in this world.
There is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period; the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is indeed the heavenly world. By means of this, he goes to the heavenly world itself.
There is a *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* at the end; the *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* is indeed splendor and spiritual luster.
By that very means, he becomes radiant and endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) in that world. 313.
Now follows this *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the twenty-five-fold *mahāvrata*, and the *sarvastoma* *atirātra*. 2.314. va.
One who desires food and drink should sacrifice with this [rite].

Regarding this, they say: "The Mahāvrata should not be undertaken before a year has passed. In that regard, as for the fact that there is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the seasons.
The seasons are the year;
the year ripens all food; thus they partake of that very food which has been won by the year.

The twenty-fifth [stoma] is the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*); the twenty-fifth is indeed food, for the sake of securing food. The *atirātra* sacrifice consists of all the *stomas*, for the conquest and overcoming of all worlds;
for all this is indeed the *stomas*.
"Furthermore, those individual *stomas* which we have approached, having increased them together and having established ourselves in them, may we attain the upward path.
Now, the *stomas* of this *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period are: the twenty-four-fold on the first day, and the *viśvajit* [on the last].
The Atirātra with all [the Stomas] at the end is for one who desires, "May my Mahāvrata be endowed with the unperceived. He should sacrifice with this;
in that there is the twenty-fourth day, by that very means his Mahāvrata becomes endowed with the unperceived.
Furthermore, whatever there may be in that [sacrifice]— whether it be the *hiṃkāra*, the *prastāva*, the *pratihāra*, or anything else— by that very means his twenty-fifth [verse] becomes attained.
The Viśvajit sacrifice is an Atirātra with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
The *śrīs* are indeed the heights and the back-songs (*pṛṣṭhas*). It is thus that they ascend to the heights and the back-songs, which are *śrī*.

Now, regarding this *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), he for whom there is a *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma* in the middle and a *jyotis* *atirātra* at the end— should he desire, "May a son endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) be born among my offspring," let him sacrifice with this.
Indeed, the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite is the self.
Luster is indeed spiritual splendor, and the Agniṣṭoma is light.
Now, the generative organ is in the middle of the body;
therefore, in that the Agniṣṭoma is light in the middle, he thereby places light in the middle of his own self.
One who laughs is born among his offspring as one possessing the splendor of Brahman.

A Jyotir-atirātra is performed at the end; this indeed is the well-known path to the gods, namely the Jyotir-atirātra. [They perform it] thinking, "By means of this well-known path to the gods, by that which is unharmed, may we, being unhurt ourselves, reach the conclusion."

Now, for this sacrifice, the Viśvajit and Abhijit Agniṣṭomas are on both sides, with a six-day period containing light on both sides in the middle; one who desires cattle should perform this sacrifice.
These four intermediate days are Ukthya sacrifices.
The *ukthas* are indeed cattle;
they have a thousand *stotriya* verses.
Moreover, there are these four *agniṣṭomas* on both sides.
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the Brahman, the light.
By means of the Brahman, he thus encloses the cattle on both sides so that they may not be lost. His wealth is never lost for one who knows this.
Indeed, whatever kind of person one is when one sacrifices, such one becomes.
When he thinks that his prosperity has reached its end, then he should sacrifice with this [rite].
Having sacrificed, he indeed goes to the heavenly world. 315.
JB 2.316 |va Now, these are the nine-night sacrifices (navarātra).
vb One who desires splendor should sacrifice with this nine-night rite.
The *trivṛt* stoma is indeed splendor.
This sacrifice has attained the *trivṛt* stoma;
therefore, one who desires splendor should perform this sacrifice.
Now they say: "One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with this.
For the *trivṛt* hymn-form is indeed the Brahman;
this sacrifice is fully accomplished through the *trivṛt* hymn-form.
Therefore, one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should indeed sacrifice with this.
Now, they say: "One who desires long life (*āyuṣkāma*) should sacrifice with this.
For the threefold hymn-form (*trivṛt-stoma*) is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
These days do not consist of nine; the tenth is the night.
There are nine vital breaths in a person, and the navel is the tenth.
By this [rite], he conquers the vital breaths and attains the vital breaths.
Regarding this, they say: "In accordance with what is the nine-night rite?
One should reply: "In accordance with the quarters.
For indeed, the nine-night rite is in accordance with the quarters.
There are four quarters, four intermediate directions, the zenith as the ninth, and the nadir as the tenth.
By this, he prospers in the very quarters;
having established himself in the quarters, he goes to the heavenly world. 316.

JB 2.317 |va Now, he for whom there is this [sacrificial session] consisting of a three-day period of Jyotis, Go, and Āyus; a three-day period of Jyotis, Go, and Āyus; and a three-day period of Jyotis, Go, and Āyus, followed by an Atirātra—should he desire, "May I ascend to these worlds without interruption," let him sacrifice with this.
In that there is a three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus—this world is indeed Jyotis, this [middle] world is Gauḥ, and yonder world is Āyus;
by means of this, he ascends these worlds without interruption.
There are two Atirātras, and the three-day period is not the last.
These worlds are indeed of such a nature: this world is like the Agniṣṭoma, this [intermediate] world is like the Ukthya, and that [highest] world is like the Atirātra.
Thus, in accordance with the nature of these worlds, he goes ascending toward them.
Now, for him [the sacrifice] consists of Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus, Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus, Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus.

The Atirātra: he who should desire, "May I ascend to these worlds without interruption," let him sacrifice with this. Now, in that the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus are the Atirātras—this world is indeed the Jyotis, this [middle] world is the Gauḥ, and yonder world is the Āyus—it is by means of this that he ascends to these worlds without interruption.

The three-day periods are accompanied by *atirātra*s. Moreover, these worlds are indeed of such a nature: this world is like an *agniṣṭoma*, that one like an *ukthya*, and yonder world like an *atirātra*.
Just as these worlds are constituted, so indeed does he go, ascending them in this manner.
(JB 2.318) There are indeed three equinoctial points among these worlds: Agni is the equinoctial point of this world, Vāyu [is that of the intermediate world], and...
The Āditya [cup] belongs to the intermediate space, and the [cup] of the sky belongs to heaven; by means of this, he overcomes them.
It consists of three series for the sake of Indra’s victory.
By means of the threefold array, indeed, the gods conquered the Asuras with the seat of the gods.
Therefore, even now, whatever army is formed in a threefold array, it surely conquers.
Just as one would advance with a threefold arrayed army intending to conquer, even so does he advance with this [sacrifice] intending to conquer heaven.

He who knows this attains the world and conquers the heavenly world. Now, for him whose [sacrifice] consists of a Jyotir-atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, a Pañcaviṃśa Mahāvrata, and a Jyotir-atirātra, one desiring food should sacrifice with this.

Regarding this they say: "The Mahāvrata should not be undertaken before a year has passed. In that regard, as for the fact that there is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period—the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the seasons, and the seasons are the year.

The year ripens all food; they thus partake of that very food which has been won by the year. The Mahāvrata is the twenty-fivefold [stoma]; the twenty-fivefold is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.

The Jyotir-atirātra—this indeed is the well-known ford of the gods, namely the Jyotir-atirātra. [Thinking: "By means of this well-known ford of the gods, which is unharmed, may I reach the conclusion unharmed. //318// JB 2.319
Now, they speak disparagingly of this, saying that they consider it merely a *sattra*; for they used to enter upon it as a *sattra* in former times.
But it is by means of this alone that the *stomas* belonging to the *sattra* and those accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are distinguished.
The sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) have *atirātra* rites on both sides; those with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have *atirātra* on one side only.

He who should sacrifice with this [session] that has sacrificial fees should perform an *agniṣṭoma* first and then sacrifice. Now, regarding this *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, the *mahāvrata* [is performed] on the fifth day.
The Viśvajit-stoma is an Atirātra.
Indeed, those who sacrifice and those who sit for a sacrificial session (sattra) employ speech here and there. They bring it to completion on the tenth day alone.
The Mahāvrata has been undertaken for speech that is perfected, unimpeded, and firmly established.
The Mahāvrata is indeed food;
it is for the attainment of food.
The *viśvajit* stoma is an *atirātra*.
Indeed, this [sacrifice] is as if turned away;
for when the *viśvajit* stoma is an *atirātra*, it has effectively wiped away [all] toward the heavenly world.
By this [sacrifice], he goes to the heavenly world facing away from here.
Now, as for the fact that the fourth Stoma is the twenty-one-fold: the twenty-one-fold is a foundation; by means of it, he finds firm support on this earth. 319.
JB 2.320: Now, one who desires offspring should sacrifice with this [rite] in which there is a three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Go, and Āyus in the middle of this Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha.

The Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha is indeed the self; these Stomas are the means of procreation. In that there is a three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus in the middle, it is from the very center of the self that this [procreation] occurs.
He obtains procreation; he becomes many, he is propagated.

Now, for him for whom this six-day period is upward and the three-day period is downward—should he desire, "May I go to the heavenly world, yet may I remain established in this world," let him sacrifice with this.
By means of the six-day rite alone, he goes from here upward to the heavenly world; by means of the three-day rite, he descends back again from there.
He goes to the heavenly world and remains established in this world. Moreover, he knows: "He who was that, I am this one," and thus he is born again in this world.

Now, for one who has this three-day period upwards and the six-day period directed downwards—if he should desire, "May I go to the heavenly world, yet may I remain established in this world," let him sacrifice with this [rite].
By means of the three-day period, he goes upwards from here to the heavenly world; by means of the six-day period, he descends back again from there to this world.
He goes to the heavenly world, yet he remains in this world;

moreover, he who knows "I am that which was," is indeed born again in this world. Now, for one who desires heaven, he should sacrifice with this six-day rite, which is upward-tending, or with this three-day rite, which is upward-tending.
These *stomas* are upward-pointing; for the heavenly world is indeed upward-pointing. It is for the attainment of the heavenly world.
Now follows this Vivadha sacrifice:
its [sequence] is the Jyotir Agniṣṭoma, the Gauḥ Ukthya, the Āyus Ukthya, the Jyotir Agniṣṭoma, the Āyus Atirātra,
the Jyotir Agniṣṭoma, the Gauḥ Ukthya, the Āyus Ukthya, and the Jyotir Agniṣṭoma.
One who desires cattle should sacrifice with this [rite]. For him, there is another connection: the *go* and *āyus* [stomas] are the two *ukthya* chants in the middle;
for the *ukthas* are indeed cattle.
There are five hundred stotriya verses in those two.
On both sides there are Jyotis Agniṣṭomas;
the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma is indeed the Brahman.
By means of the *brahman* alone, he encloses the cattle on both sides so that they do not escape;
he whose wealth does not perish is he who knows thus.
The *atirātra* sacrifice occurs in the middle as life itself.
Just as, for example, a crossroads is broad in its center so that it cannot be crushed, such is that.
This, indeed, is its other attachment. (So *mu* should perhaps be read here, as it is the counterpart to what is on the other side.)
Hanging down from the side of the shoulder-yoke, what line 13 calls *tasyaiṣo 'nyatassaṅgo goāyuṣī* etc., refers to the *goāyuṣī*: "The *ukthya* verses are the two inner [cups];
the *ukthas* are indeed cattle."
There are five hundred *stotriya* verses in those two.
On both sides there are *agniṣṭoma*s characterized by light (*jyotis*).
The *agniṣṭoma* is indeed the light of the Brahman.
By means of the *brahman* alone, he encloses the cattle on both sides so that they do not escape;
his wealth is not lost by one who knows thus.
Now, these are the ten-night rites.
One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should perform this sacrifice, for it is a ten-night rite;
there are these ten days.

There are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person. By means of the day alone he encompasses the vital breath; by the day he encompasses the vital breath, by the day the vital breath. Therefore, his vital breath does not exceed that [limit], so that he whom one might strike down with malevolent magic would not survive.
Now they say: "One who practices sorcery should indeed sacrifice with this.
These days are ten in number;
there are ten vital breaths in a person.
By the day alone he lays low the breath of his enemy; by the day the breath, by the day the breath.
There remains no breath of his enemy beyond that by which he who is being struck down might live.
This indeed is the preeminence among rites: this Soma sacrifice of ten nights according to its rule.
That which is the preeminence of ritual actions, by that our sacrifice is ordained as "being" (asad).
"Daśa"—this indeed is the highest stride of speech; "daśa"—so far has speech stridden.
[He thinks: "May I attain all that which is the highest stride of speech."
Now they say: "One who desires food should sacrifice with this.
Indeed, everyone else praises the Virāj;
but he alone does not over-praise the Virāj who praises when ten [verses] have been chanted.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* is food.
By means of the tenth day, he indeed secures the *virāj*; by the tenth day, the *virāj*; by the tenth day, the *virāj*. Through that tenth day alone, he [secures] the whole.
Having obtained the Virāj as food, he rises up at the end.
Indeed, the Puruṣa surpasses the Virāj.
These [days] are ten; the night is the eleventh.

In the person there are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*), with the self (*ātman*) as the eleventh. Indeed, this person is mounted upon the *virāj* for the sake of non-destruction. Neither a cow, nor a horse, nor a mule mounts the *virāj*.
Verily, man presides over the Virāj;
therefore, man is the eater of animals.
He who knows this becomes the eater of animals and presides over the Virāj. 323.
Indra, having hurled his thunderbolt at Vṛtra, thought, "I have not struck him down," and he was filled with wonder.
He, the tawny one, being amazed, grew old.
He reflected: "How indeed might I pass beyond the tenth day of this stain of evil? He beheld this ten-night sacrifice.
He took it;
he sacrificed with it. Thereupon, he indeed reached the tenth day beyond the reach of that stain of ill-fortune.
He who knows this reaches the tenth day of the period of impurity for the stain of evil, having passed through the ten days.

Therefore, whether it be a pierced fetus, one born dead, or one that has fallen, people ask, "Has it become one that has passed the ten days? Indeed, they reach that tenth day of the period of impurity for the stain of evil for him.
He who knows this goes beyond the tenth day of the period of impurity, having passed through the ten days of the stain of evil.
Now follows this *trikakubh* [chant].
One who desires offspring should sacrifice with this [offering].
The Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa stomas are employed;
being deficient and redundant, they form a productive pair.
One is deficient for one, the other is redundant for another.
Indeed, from a pair that is both deficient and redundant, offspring and cattle are produced.
With these two, they construct the *trivṛt* hymn-form.
Those two procreate that very [fire].
The seventeenfold and the twenty-onefold *stomas* come into being; deficient and redundant, they form a productive pair.
One is deficient for one, the other is redundant for another. Indeed, from a union that is neither deficient nor redundant, offspring and cattle are produced.
With these two, they enclose the seventeenfold *stoma*.
Those two procreate that very [fire].
There are the *triṇava* and *trayastrimśa* *stomas*;
deficient and redundant, they are a pair for procreation.
One is deficient for one, and the other is excessive.
From a pair that is both deficient and excessive, indeed, offspring and cattle are produced.
With these two, they surround the twenty-sevenfold hymn-form (*triṇava-stoma*).
Those two produce that very [six-day period].
Regarding this they say: "The *stomas* are indeed obtained here, the *chandases* are obtained, the deities are obtained, and the seasons are obtained when this *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* is obtained."
They should chant on the seventh day upon verses addressed to Agni that are not exhausted in their power.
For Agni is indeed among the gods the one whose power is not exhausted. Thus, perceiving Agni among the gods as the one whose power is not exhausted, they sacrifice.

They should chant on the eighth day with the *aindrī* verses that are not exhausted in their power (*ayātayāmnī*). Indeed, Indra is among the gods the one who is not exhausted in his power; thus, perceiving Indra—the one among the gods who is not exhausted in his power—they sacrifice.
On the ninth day, they should chant praises with the *vaiśvadevī* verses which are not exhausted;
for the All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*) are indeed the ones among the gods who are not exhausted. Thus, perceiving the All-Gods as those among the gods who are not exhausted, they sacrifice.
The *atirātra* sacrifice consists of all the *stomas*, for the conquest and mastery of all the worlds;
for indeed, all this is nothing but *stomas*.
Moreover, having prospered through those individual *stomas* which we have approached one by one, and having established ourselves in them, we have risen upward.
"May we obtain [it]," [they say].
Now, this is the sacrifice consisting of five rites (pañcayajñakratu).

Those five divine coverings—their prosperity is this: the fivefold sacrifice, the fivefold cattle, the fivefold food, the five seasons, and whatever else is five by five; this is the prosperity and attainment of all that. The parallel is 2,341 (307,79).
They do not perform this very [sacrifice] for a night, lest they should overstep the Virāj.
Regarding this, they say: "The ten-night sacrifice indeed exceeds the measure of the sacrifice.
In that this fivefold sacrificial ritual (*yajñakratu*) exists, and it is heard of as being within the five-day period, may I fulfill that desire which [I have].
"The ten-night [sacrifice].
It is an Atirātra with all the Stomas, for the conquest and the overcoming of all the worlds;
for all this, indeed, consists of the Stomas alone.

"Furthermore, those single-fold *stomas* which we have approached, having prospered together and being established in them, may we attain the upward limit. Now, this is the sevenfold sacrifice (*yajñakratu*).
Those seven divine coverings—of them this is the prosperity:

the seven *śakvarī* meters of seven feet, the seven domestic animals, the seven meters increasing by four syllables, the seven vital breaths in the head, and the twenty-seven celestial lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). What [is that]...?
The twenty-sevenfold hymn-form (*stoma*)—whatever consists of sevens—is the prosperity of all this; it is the attainment thereof.
Regarding this, they say: "The ten-night rite (*daśarātra*) indeed exceeds the measure of the sacrifice.
Therefore, since this sevenfold sacrificial performance (*yajñakratu*) is heard of as lasting seven days, [one performs it] so that one may fulfill that desire.
Regarding the "ten-night" [sacrifice]:
it consists of an *atirātra* with all the *stomas*, for the conquest and mastery of all worlds;
for indeed, this entire universe is nothing but *stomas*.
"Furthermore, those individual *stomas* which we have approached, having combined them together and having established ourselves in them, may we attain transcendence.
Now follows this Mahātrikakup. He who desires prosperity and desires the office of domestic priest should sacrifice with this.
There are three heights, three prosperities, and these three worlds.
By this very means, he secures that.
They chant the *pañcadaśa* stoma surrounding the *trivṛt*.
The *trivṛt* is indeed the Brahman, and the *pañcadaśa* is the Kṣatra.
By means of the *brahman* alone they encompass that *kṣatra*.
With the seventeenfold [stoma] they chant around the twenty-onefold;
for the seventeenfold is indeed the *brahman*, and the twenty-onefold is the *kṣatra*.
By means of the *brahman* alone, they encompass that *kṣatra*.
With the *triṇava* [stoma], they chant around the *trayastrimśa*.
The *triṇava* is indeed the *brahman*, and the *trayastrimśa* is the *kṣatra*.
By means of the *brahman* alone they encompass that *kṣatra*.
For when one encompasses the *kṣatra* by means of the *brahman*, then he attains its leadership; he attains leadership, for they place him at the front. 327.
JB 2.328 |va This [sacrifice] indeed becomes a great *trikakubh*.
vb For there are three peaks (*kakubhaḥ*) of these worlds.
Agni is the peak of this world, Vāyu of the intermediate space, and Āditya of the sky.
He who knows thus becomes the one among the peaks.
The Viśvajit is an Atirātra sacrifice characterized by all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed prosperity and the summits; verily, he thus ascends prosperity,
the summits, and the *pṛṣṭha* chants, which are strength and vigor.
By means of vital force (*ojas*) and heroism (*vīrya*), he thereby secures the office of the domestic priest (*purodhā*).
There are various *agniṣṭoma* chants so that they do not follow one after another.
And the *yajñāyajñīya* chant [is performed] with the verses: "May the goddesses be for our aid; praise him, the one who bestows light."
And the *sākamaśva*.
"O Agni, guest of every clan, [lord] of booty consisting of cattle"—this is both the *śrudhīya* and the *viśoviśīya*.
"O Agni, we kindle thee, the head of heaven, the messenger of earth"—this is the *saṃjaya*.
And [he recites] the Dairghaśravasa hymn;
and the *bṛhat* and *samanta* hymns addressed to Agni, beginning with "The men [kindle] Agni with their insights from the two fire-sticks" and "O Agni, you are the lord of the house."
"Sing to the kindled Agni with fuel and with song; [bring] our sacrifice that touches heaven"—thus [he recites] the Rājovājīya and the Bṛhat.
With this very [sacrifice], Āruṇi caused Jābāla to perform a sacrifice.
He attained the priesthood over three rival claimants: one from Kāśī, one from Kosala, and one from the Ikṣvāku line.
He had a beautiful wife.
Seeing her beauty, Śvetaketu once argued with his father: "O gray-haired one who desires sacrifice, you consort only with others for wealth and fame; you do not honor yourself."
"No," he said,
"do not say that to me, my son;
the sacrifice as a ritual act was already known to me."
O you who are a mere nominal Brahmin, you sought to know that [truth] as if it were something evil.
He indeed remained exactly as they had described him to me;
or rather, he was even more so.
This sacrifice, indeed, is the very subterfuge of Death.
The gods were afraid of Death in the heavenly world; therefore, they ran to Prajāpati for refuge.
For them, he prepared this ten-night sacrifice. They took it up; they sacrificed with it. /329/
They praised with the *trivṛt*.
"They are praising with the *trivṛt*," thought Death; he approached the *pañcadaśa*, thinking, "He will depart from here."
They followed him on the fifteenth day. They then obstructed him from there. He stepped up toward the seventeenfold [stoma].
Then the others, having praised with the fifteenfold [stoma], praised again with the threefold [stoma].
"They are praising with the threefold," thought Death, and he rushed toward the fifteenfold itself, thinking, "From this very point they will escape.
Then the others stepped beyond the seventeenfold.
They praised with the seventeenfold [stoma].
Regarding this, Death, having approached the twenty-onefold [stoma], stood waiting, thinking, "They will depart from here after praising with the seventeenfold.
He followed them to the twenty-onefold.
They then obstructed him from there.
He ascended toward the Triṇava;
then the others, having praised with the Ekaviṃśa, praised again with the Saptadaśa.

"Verily, they praise with the seventeenfold [stoma]," said Death; he rushed toward the twenty-onefold, thinking, "They will surely come to this one. Then the others stepped beyond toward the twenty-sevenfold.
They praised with the twenty-seven-versed hymn.
"They praise with the twenty-seven-versed hymn," [said Death]; Death approached the thirty-three-versed hymn and stood over it, thinking, "They shall depart from here.
They followed after him at the thirty-three-versed hymn.
They then released him from there. He ascended toward the *chandomas*.
Then the others, having praised with the thirty-threefold hymn, praised again with the twenty-sevenfold hymn.
"They praise with the twenty-sevenfold [stoma]," they said; Death then rushed toward the thirty-threefold [stoma], thinking, "They will come to this one from here.
Then the others took refuge with Prajāpati, the Father, in the Viśvajit sacrifice which possesses all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
Thereupon, having cut off death, they became immortal.
Indeed, he who knows this cuts off death and becomes immortal.
Now, these ten days are indeed *agniṣṭoma*s.
For it was from these *sāman*s that Prajāpati bestowed the Soma-drink. These *sāman*s, having been granted the Soma-drink, are indeed free from evil.

Having struck away evil, he who knows this becomes superior. Indeed, these *sāmans* are full of desires; just as a leather bag might be filled with curds, or ghee, or honey, so too are these *sāmans*.
The desires are fulfilled. Kuṃstha used to sing these verses as an accompaniment for the Kālāśas:
"Always moistening the ruddy horses from the goal..."
"Full jars of flowing liquor [are] at Janamejaya’s dwelling.
Thus it is said; indeed, whatever desire one desires by means of these Sāmans, that very thing one attains.
Now, these are the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*).
Indeed, those days of the twelve-day rite are full of vigor.
Thinking, "May that which is full of vigor not be left unstudied," [he recites them].
Now, various *stomas* carry these [days].
This indeed is the perfection of the days, that they are carried by various *stomas*.
That which is the perfection of the days is thus produced here. 331.
Now follows this Kusurubinda ten-night rite.
It consists of three *agniṣṭoma*s with the *trivṛt* stoma, three *ukthya*s with the *pañcadaśa* stoma, and three *ukthya*s with the *saptadaśa* stoma.

The Jyotis Atirātra: he who should desire, "May I be radiant, possessed of spiritual luster, powerful, heroic, an eater of food, and firmly established," let him sacrifice with this. For the Trivṛt Stoma is indeed radiance and spiritual luster; the Pañcadaśa is power and heroism; the Saptadaśa is food.

The *atirātra* is the foundation and the light; by means of this, one prospers in those desires which are contained within it. Therefore, since the *atirātra* is heard of in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, [one thinks]: "May I fulfill that desire which is in the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*).
Regarding this, two Brahmins who had set out on their way used to converse together: "O gentle friend, what sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*)..."
Regarding the phrase "when they had set out":
one of them said, "If indeed this very thing will happen tomorrow, then we shall both surely spend ten days with you as Agniṣṭomas."
Those two indeed considered this very [sacrifice] to be the Agniṣṭoma; for those which are the Stomas of the Agniṣṭoma are these very ones.
Now, this spade is sharp on both ends.
Its Agniṣṭoma at the beginning is the Trivṛt; its Agniṣṭoma at the end is the Trivṛt; in the middle there are eight Ukthyas, which are the Saptadaśa.
One who desires food should sacrifice with this.
Agni is indeed the former *trivṛt*, and Āditya is the latter. Agni is the spade of this world, and Āditya is that of yonder world.
Now, one should sacrifice with this very food.
There are eight Ukthya-stomas, seventeen-fold, in the middle.
This very Agni here procures this food for him from this side, and the Āditya yonder bestows rain from that side.
These two procure food for him from both sides; he who knows thus becomes an eater of food.
Now they say: "One who desires cattle should sacrifice with this.
Of that [sacrifice], there are two *agniṣṭomas* on both sides and *ukthyas* in the middle.
The *agniṣṭoma* is indeed the Brahman, and the *ukthyas* are cattle.
By means of the *brahman* alone, he encloses the cattle on both sides so that they do not escape;

his wealth is not lost by him who knows thus. Now, for one who performs this six-day period [of the *ṣaḍaha*] upwards, the three-day period upwards, and the *jyotis-atirātra*, he does so when desiring heaven.
He should sacrifice.
These *stomas* are directed upwards; for the heavenly world is indeed directed upwards. This is for the sake of attaining the heavenly world.
Now, regarding this [sacrifice] which consists of Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus, Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus, Atirātra, and Jyotis Atirātra—whosoever [performs it]...

If one should desire, "May I conquer the luminous worlds," let him sacrifice with this. For there are indeed four lights of the gods that are as if most manifest: Agni on earth, the sun in heaven, the moon among the stars, and lightning in the waters.
He who, knowing this, performs this sacrificial rite, and he who knows it thus, wins these very worlds which possess light— yea, he wins them, he who knows it thus.
(333) [The Sattra]
JB 2.334 |va Now follows this thirteen-night sacrifice.
vb Yonder sun was indeed equal to the other gods— equal to this fire, to Vāyu, to the moon, and to the others.
By the gods. He desired: "May I attain preeminence among all the gods; having become the thirteenth month, may I ascend upon this entire universe."
He saw this thirteen-night rite;
he undertook it. Thereupon, he indeed attained preeminence among all the gods.
Having become the thirteenth month, it ascended over all this.
Verily, the year is all this.
It is indeed all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, all the *chandas*, and all those [other things].
All the pressings belong to you; all the worlds belong to you; all desires belong to you.
Having reached twelve months by means of exactly twelve days, he became the thirteenth month by means of the thirteenth day itself and ascended to this entire universe.
Those who, knowing thus, undertake the thirteen-night rite, they cause this very [year] to prosper and go to share the same world as it. 334/ JB 2.335
This sacrificial session indeed belongs to the month; whatever prosperity is attained through it, that is true prosperity.
For the month, revolving again and again, surely attains the year.
For they desire this year, they seek to obtain the year, when they sacrifice and when they sit for a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever outside of the year.
These fourteen nights are indeed self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).
Seven days beyond, seven below. Now, that world which is in the middle is the self-ruler (*svarāṭ*); it is the heavenly world (*svarga*).
To that realm of the sun (*bradhnasya viṣṭapaṃ*) they go; to that sovereignty (*svārājya*) they go.
They do not follow after anything else.
These very nights amount to the Virāj and the Gāyatrī;
for these two, the Virāj and the Gāyatrī, are indeed the most powerful among the meters.
"Those two which are the most powerful among the meters—may we succeed through them, may we be established in them; through them may our hymn of praise be effective. Thus they approach the Virāj.

Thus they attain the sovereignty and lordship over the Virāj and over food. The Virāj is deficient by two; those two are deficient in the woman, for it is from that deficiency that she gives birth; therefore, it is a source of procreation. The Vaiśvānara Atirātra is the opening sacrifice.
For the Ahīna Soma sacrifices have the Vaiśvānara [rite] as their opening;
now this Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha occurs.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed prosperity; the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the summit.
Thus, they ascend to prosperity, the summit, and the *pṛṣṭhas*.
Furthermore, they become performers of a sacrificial session (*satra*).
Regarding this they say: "Those who undertake this *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) are indeed ascending toward something superior.
Now, as for the fact that the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period occurs later, directed westward, it is for concealment, to prevent injury, for auspiciousness, and for peace.
Now, they criticize this very point: that they undertake the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period while [already] having undertaken [the sacrifice].
The *vaiśvānara* *atirātra* serves as the concluding rite;
for the *ahīna* Soma sacrifices have the *vaiśvānara* as their conclusion.
Now, these *stomas*—the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus—come into being.
Indeed, these *stomas*—the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus—are auspicious, peaceful, and wholesome.
[The thought occurs: "May our praise not be performed with those *stomas* that are auspicious, peaceful, and wholesome."
These [stomas], having become the Virāj,
they thus undertake the Virāj as food. Indeed, he who mounts upon one who is superior without being in harmony with him surely harms him.

With that very distress by which he desires him, he leads him away. Now, he who, having reached a common understanding with him, climbs up after him—surely he does not exclude him from that prosperity.
Thus, as these *stomas*—Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus—are employed, it is just as when one follows a superior person with a common understanding.
Having approached it in this manner, one should ascend; such is that [practice].
336/ JB 2.337 |va | Now, this is the Pṛṣthya ṣaḍaha.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed prosperity; the *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the summit.
Thus, they ascend to prosperity, the summit, and the *pṛṣṭha* chants;
and so they become performers of a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Regarding this, they say: "Those who undertake this *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite indeed climb as if to the very top.
For he who, having climbed to the top of a great tree, does not know how to descend, surely meets with a breakage; for he either falls down or withers away from above.
In that there is a three-day period facing westward at the end, it is for concealment, for freedom from affliction, for auspiciousness, and for peace.
They rise from the Jyotis day, from the well-known *jyaiṣṭhya* stoma.
[They do so] thinking, "May we reach the conclusion, being established upon the well-known *jyaiṣṭhya* stoma."
It has twelve stotras; the year consists of twelve months.
The year is preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*); he has no rival in that preeminent stomas which is the foundation. "May we attain the highest point," [he thinks].
The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the concluding rite;
for Soma sacrifices that do not form part of a multi-day sequence (ahīna) conclude with the Vaiśvānara [offering].

Now, these [days] consist of twelve-day periods; for this twelve-day rite is indeed the sacrificial session of the gods, the sacrificial session of Prajāpati. By means of this very sacrificial session, Prajāpati prospered—namely, that sacrificial session by which Prajāpati prospered.
"Therefore, one should desire to obtain wealth.
Regarding this, they ask: "What is the preeminent form (*varṣman*) of the sacrificial sessions (*satra*)?
One should reply: "The twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*)."
The twelve-day rite is indeed the summit of the sacrificial sessions (*satra*s), for in no other session is there a forty-four-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), nor a forty-eight-fold one. Therefore,
they thought, "May that which is the summit of the sacrificial sessions be attained by us."

Indeed, it is here that they separate their speech, both those who sacrifice and those who sit for a sacrificial session (*sattra*). They bring that speech to completion on the tenth day itself, thinking:
"May we reach the summit of speech that has been completed, unseparated, and firmly established."
And with one sacrificial session they enter two sacrificial sessions: the twelve-day rite and the fourteen-night rite. The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the concluding rite;
for the Ahīna Soma sacrifices have the Vaiśvānara as their conclusion. 338.
This sacrificial session indeed belongs to the month; whatever prosperity is attained through it, that is true prosperity.
Indeed, the month, revolving again and again, attains the year.
For they desire the year when they sacrifice, and they seek the year when they sit for a sacrificial session (*sattra*);
for there is nothing whatsoever outside of the year.

These nights are indeed self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), namely the fifteen [days]. Seven days are beyond them, and seven are below them. Now, that day which is in the middle is the self-ruling one (*svarāṭ*); it is the heavenly world.
They go to that world of the sun; they go to that self-sovereignty.
They become such that no one else follows after them.
Indeed, this fifteen-night rite is truly a thunderbolt.
By means of the fifteen-night sacrifice, indeed, the gods overcame the Asuras with the thunderbolt.

Those who might feel themselves as if seized by evil should undertake this very fifteen-night sacrifice. By means of the fifteen-night sacrifice, indeed, they overcome their hateful, evil rival with the thunderbolt and rise up.
Regarding this, Yāmana Bhrātalāyana said: "As for that Sarasvatī whom I conquered with the fifteen-night sacrifice as a thunderbolt—who else is capable of settling upon her?
Indeed, it was with a thunderbolt that I conquered her.
"Vajrajit is indeed difficult to conquer.
These nights, indeed, amount to the Virāj and the Gāyatrī.
For these two, the Virāj and the Gāyatrī, are truly the most powerful among the meters.
"Those two which are the most vigorous of the meters—in those may we succeed, in those may we be established; by means of those two, may our hymn be effective. Thus they approach the Virāj.
Thus, they attain the sovereignty and lordship over the Virāj and over food.
The Virāj is deficient by one; that which is deficient belongs to the woman, for she gives birth from that deficiency; therefore, it is a means of procreation.
The Vaiśvānara Atirātra is the opening sacrifice.
For the *ahīna* Soma sacrifices have the *vaiśvānara* as their point of departure.
Now, these [sacrifices] consist of the *stomas* called Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus.
These indeed are the auspicious, peaceful, and wholesome *stomas*, namely: Jyotis, Go, and Āyus.
"May we not have praised with those *stomas* that are auspicious, peaceful, and wholesome"—thus [they thought].
And they became the *virāj*.
They thus undertake the Virāj as food.
For he who mounts upon one superior to himself without his knowledge, he indeed harms him; with that very injury he desires him, and with that he brings him low.
Now, if someone approaches and mounts him after having reached a common understanding with him, he certainly does not shake him off.
In that these *stomas*—namely Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus—occur, it is just as if one were to approach and mount a superior person after having reached a common understanding with him; such is that.
Now, this Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is threefold (*trivṛt*).
The *trivṛt* is indeed the Brahman;
the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha is the Kṣatra.
In that they perform the Agniṣṭut before the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, he thereby places the Brahman before the Kṣatra. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is the domestic priest (purohita) of the Kṣatriya.

And by means of one *sattra*, they enter into two *sattras*: the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) and the fifteen-night rite (*pañcadaśarātra*). The *vaiśvānara* *atirātra* serves as the concluding rite (*udayanīya*).
For the *ahīna* Soma sacrifices have the *vaiśvānara* as their conclusion. 340.
This sacrificial session lasts for two months;
whatever prosperity is attained through it, that is indeed prosperity.
Indeed, two months are a season (*ṛtu*), and a season is the prosperity (*ṛddhi*) of the year;
for the year is visibly the prosperity of the year.
Verily, when they sacrifice and when they sit for a sacrificial session (*sattra*), they strive for the year; they desire to obtain the year.

For there is nothing whatsoever outside of the year. These nights are indeed self-sovereignty (*svārājya*): the twenty-one-fold [stoma] consists of ten days beyond and ten days below; and that which is the day in the middle is the self-ruling one (*svarāṭ*), that is, the heavenly world.
They go to that world of the sun; they go to that self-sovereignty.
They become such that no other follows after them.
Indeed, these nights amount to the Virāj itself.
Thus, they attain the sovereignty and lordship over the Virāj and over food.
There are five [verses] and the Virāj; whatever five divine coverings there are, this is their perfection.

The fivefold sacrifice, the fivefold animals, the fivefold food, the five seasons, and whatever else is fivefold—this is the perfection and attainment of all that. (TSUCHIDA 1979 overlooked the parallel at 2,326 [300,46]. /341/
These ten days are on the far side; the *viṣuvat* day, the twenty-one-fold, is below.
Indeed, there are ten fingers on a man's hands and ten toes on his feet; the self is the twenty-first.
This person, indeed, is mounted upon the Virāj for the sake of non-falling. Neither a cow, nor a horse, nor a mule mounts the Virāj;
it is only the person who mounts the Virāj.
Therefore, man is the eater of animals. He who knows this becomes the eater of animals and stands above the Virāj.
They should perform these nights during the month of Naidāghīya.
In the month of Naidāghīya, Prajāpati bestowed radiance upon Āditya.
Therefore, in the month of Naidāghīya, he burns most intensely, even though double shadows approach him. Hāgradeva Rājani approached this [rite] desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
A Brahmin said to him: "As long as you have not secured spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), you will remain white. He became just like a white horse.
These nights were thus full of splendor, full of spiritual luster, and full of heroic power.
Those who, knowing thus, undertake these nights, all indeed prosper; all become endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*).
At those [sacrifices], they should immolate an animal for Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed peace (*śānti*); it is for the sake of peace, so that there may be no burning.
The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the opening rite.
For the Ahīna Soma sacrifices have the Vaiśvānara as their beginning.
Now, this is the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha.
The Pṛṣṭhas are indeed prosperity; the Pṛṣṭhas are indeed the summit.
Thus, they ascend to prosperity, to the summit, by means of the Pṛṣṭhas.
Now, they are indeed performers of a sacrificial session (*satrin*).
Then these seventeen *svarasāman* days occur; they are days belonging to Prajāpati—three at the end and three at the beginning.
This Prajāpati, indeed, being thus expanded in two ways, bestows radiance upon the Āditya. Therefore, he who is the giver of radiance, by whom radiance was bestowed, may he bestow radiance upon us.
Now, this [day] is the twenty-first Viṣuvat.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first.
Indeed, they attain co-residence with this [sun] and ascend unto it.
Regarding this, they say: "They indeed ascend unto one who is superior—namely, unto this sun."
In that there is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period facing westward after [the central part], it is for concealment, for the absence of affliction, for auspiciousness,
and for peace.
The *vaiśvānara* *atirātra* serves as the concluding rite (*udayanīya*).
For the Ahīna Soma sacrifices indeed begin with the Vaiśvānara [stotra].
Now, regarding this Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, that which is the seventeenth day in its middle is placed above.
They pile up the altar for the Trayastriṃśa day. Those desiring procreation should undertake this; for the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha is indeed procreation.
By means of the sixfold increase, the *stomas* procreate; by means of the fourfold increase, the *chandas*.
Now, this seventeen-fold *stoma*, separated in the middle by the sixfold-increasing *stomas*, stands as if having placed a barrier between itself and procreation.
When they pile it above the Trayastriṃśa layer, it is so that they may procreate from an unseparated source of generation;
indeed, it is for the sake of being the third of two seventeen-fold layers.
Now, these two, the Viśvajit and the Abhijit, are on both sides the vigor of the *stomas*.
Indeed, by means of their vigor, these two support the Viṣuvat day.
Truly, the Viśvajit and the Abhijit are the two doorposts of the sacrifice.
By these two, indeed, the sacrifice is supported.
Now, the Viśvajit and Abhijit are truly the couch of the gods, and that sun yonder is the kṣatra.
Thus, they place the kṣatra upon the very couch of the gods.
Therefore, the Kṣatriya is superior to the Vaiśya.
Now, this Viṣuvat day is the twenty-first:
twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first.
Indeed, they go to share the same world as this one; they ascend unto him.

Regarding this, they say: "They are indeed ascending unto one who is superior—unto this Āditya. In that the six-day period (ṣaḍaha) occurs later, facing westward, it is for concealment and to prevent injury.
For the sake of auspiciousness and peace.
The Vaiśvānara Atirātra is the concluding rite.
For the Soma sacrifices of the Ahīna class conclude with the Vaiśvānara [rite]. 344.
JB 2.345 |va Now this [sacrifice] consists of five-day periods.
vb Indeed, that which has a central day (*viṣuvant*) is not truly a twenty-one-night sacrifice.
Who indeed is that Viṣuvat day upon which the Viśvajit and Abhijit do not occur? [The answer is:
Because the Viśvajit and Abhijit occur, we shall perfect the entire Viṣuvat; thus the Viṣuvat will be fully attained by us.
Regarding this they say: "Those who undertake these nights indeed ascend toward something superior.

In that the five-day period (*pañcāha*) occurs subsequently facing westward, it is for concealment, for the sake of non-affliction, for auspiciousness, and for peace. The *vaiśvānara* *atirātra* serves as the concluding sacrifice.
For the Ahīna Soma sacrifices are indeed characterized by the rising of Vaiśvānara.
This sacrificial session (sattra) lasts for two months.
Therefore, prosperity is indeed prosperity.
Now, the two months that constitute a season are indeed prosperity;
and the season is visibly the prosperity of the year.
For they desire the year; they seek the year when they sacrifice and when they sit for the sacrificial session (sattra).
For there is nothing whatsoever outside the year. These nights are indeed self-sovereignty (svārājya): twenty-four in total, consisting of twelve days beyond and twelve below.

Now, that world which is in the middle is the self-ruler (*svarāṭ*), that is the heavenly world (*svarga-loka*). They go to that realm of the sun (*bradhna*), they go to that sovereignty (*svārājya*).
There, they become those who do not follow after another.
These nights indeed amount to the *jagatī* meter;
the *jagatī* is cattle; therefore, this sacrificial session (*sattra*) is conducive to cattle.
They go toward the Virāj;

indeed, they attain sovereignty and overlordship over the Virāj, which is food. The Virāj is deficient by two; since it is deficient by two [syllables] from the female, she gives birth, and thus it is a means of procreation.
The Gāyatrī is completed by means of the consecrations (*dīkṣā*), the attendant rites (*upasad*), and the soma-pressings (*sutyā*).
The Gāyatrī is indeed breath; therefore, this sacrificial session (*sattra*) bestows long life.
The Gāyatrī is indeed splendor; thus, they become splendid and endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*).
The Gāyatrī is indeed preeminence; thus they become established in that preeminence which is free from rivals. Now, these are the seven-day periods; for there are seven meters.
"The meters are indeed the world of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). As great as the world of self-sovereignty is, so great a world of self-sovereignty shall we perfect.
There are seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

By means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), indeed, offspring and cattle stand encompassed. Therefore, with those very vital breaths by which offspring and cattle stand encompassed, may offspring and cattle stand encompassed for us.
By means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the gods indeed went to the heavenly world.
Thinking, "By those very vital breaths by which the gods went to the heavenly world, may we go to the heavenly world," [they performed this rite].
There are seven principal vital breaths.

These vital breaths (*prāṇa*) which are in the mouth are indeed those whose evil has been struck away. Thinking, "Let us extend the sacrifice by means of the measure of those vital breaths whose evil has been struck away," there are more *agniṣṭoma* [sacrifices] than *ukthya* ones.
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed Brahman;
they thus attain spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and so they become possessed of spiritual luster.
The Agniṣṭomas are on the far side, the Agniṣṭomas are on the near side, and the Ukthyas are in the middle.
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the Brahman, and the Ukthyas are cattle.
Thus, by means of the Brahman, they enclose the cattle on both sides so that there is no loss; his wealth does not perish.
He who knows thus is propagated.
The *vaiśvānara* *atirātra* serves as the opening rite.
For the *ahīna* *soma* sacrifices have the *vaiśvānara* as their commencement. 347.
Now, these are the *stomas* of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.
The *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed prosperity; the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed the summit.
They ascend to that glory, those heights, and those ridges;
thus they become performers of a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Now, this is the thirty-third day.
From the Trayastriṃśa heaven itself, [they take] the Trayastriṃśa; for that is the end.
For from where else could they bring anything?
Its *bahis-pavamāna* chant consists of thirty-four verses.
There are indeed thirty-three deities;
Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth.
Prajāpati is indeed the sixth sense-base (*ṣaṣṭhāyatana*) among the deities; now, that which is the seventh day is self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), and that is the world;
moreover, the thirty-four-fold hymn is self-sovereignty.

In that the *bahiṣpavamāna* of the seventh day consists of the thirty-four-versed hymn, they [think]: "May we attain as much of the world of self-sovereignty as there is"; and also for the sake of not following in immediate succession the three *trayastrimśa* days.
These nights are indeed the form of the *proṣṭha*.
This six-day period is upright from here, transverse in the middle, and directed hitherward from yonder;
these nights are indeed the form of the *upariṣadya*.
He indeed attains the position of presiding over an assembly who attains prosperity;
[thinking] "May we attain the position of presiding over an assembly, the state of being the eldest, the state of being the best,
and prosperity," they therefore undertake these nights.
Regarding this they say: "Those who undertake these nights indeed ascend to something superior.
In that the *stomas* of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* proceed westward from the end, it is for concealment, to prevent affliction, for auspiciousness, and for peace.
They rise from the *jyotis* [sacrifice] into the day, according to the stated Brāhmaṇa. The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the concluding sacrifice (*udayanīya*).
For the Soma sacrifices of the Ahīna type have the Vaiśvānara as their conclusion. //348//
JB 2.349 |va Now, as for him for whom every day is indeed a thirty-fourfold [stoma], he thinks: "By means of this entire day, may we attain sovereign power in the world."
And indeed, it is for the sake of the non-sequential arrangement of the three sets of thirty-three [deities].
Now Bhāllaveya used to say: "The Mahāvrata should not be undertaken before a year has passed;
if they should undertake it, they should undertake it on the twenty-fourth night."
These twenty-four nights are indeed the year;
for the year consists of twenty-four half-months. Thus, this very year is encompassed on both sides.
That which is the seventeenth day in its midst—on that very day one should approach [the Mahāvrata].
Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold;
the Mahāvrata belongs to Prajāpati.
Prajāpati is indeed the central abode among the deities. Therefore, they think: "Where Prajāpati is the abode among the deities, there we shall cause Prajāpati to prosper.
For food that is eaten nourishes when it is in the middle.
Thus, when they proceed in this manner, they rise after having driven away hunger from the very center.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who undertake these nights indeed ascend to something superior. In that regard, the *stomas* of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* occur subsequently, directed westward.
For concealment, for freedom from distress, for auspiciousness, and for peace.
From the light they arise during the day, according to the stated Brāhmaṇa.
Indeed, this metre which is the Gāyatrī is truly that very [light].

If they were to rise from the *gāyatrī*, they would be liable to wander about without a firm foundation. Therefore, at the *vaiśvadeva* [śastra], one should recite the *sāvitra* verse, "Savitar has firmly established the earth with his supports," as the invitatory formula for the Hotṛ.
They rise from that which is firm and established.
The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the concluding rite;
for the Soma sacrifices of the Ahīna type have the Vaiśvānara as their conclusion. 349.
JB 2.350 |va Now, these are the *saṃsads*. vb For this indeed is the essence of the *saṃsads*, namely that these *stomas* and *chandas* are in the middle.
They were exhausted.
Indeed, the *stomas*, the meters, and all the deities—
for the gods were afraid of death in the heavenly world.
Therefore, they ran toward Prajāpati.
Prajāpati said to them, "Do not fear;
I shall lead you across that death which is in the heavenly world."
He established them in the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period. Indeed, the *pṛṣṭhas* are the seasons;
the seasons are the year.
The year is death.
Indeed, standing upon the back of death, he established them;
by means of this undefined [stotra] consisting of thirty-three [verses], he led them across.
He thought, "Let them not be undefined. He defined them by means of the Nirukta.
They went forth, stepping toward the *stomas* and the *chandas*.
They went forth indeed making that a stepping-stone for Death; for this reason these *stomas* and *chandas* are turned in all directions from the middle.

Just as one might stand not knowing which of two footprints placed apart—one here, one there—was the one by which [the traveler] came, so indeed does this become a stepping-stone for Death, in order to avoid being overtaken by evil.
Verily, death does not overtake him again; he strikes away evil and goes to the heavenly world.
Having reached the further limit, they were again afraid.
He led them beyond that by means of this very same thirty-threefold [stoma] which is unexpressed; he proclaimed it with the expressed one.
Thereby, indeed, they conquered that death which was in the heavenly world.
Verily, he who knows this conquers death; he indeed conquers death who knows this regarding the world of heaven.
These nights are indeed the year; they are the womb of the year.
Verily, it is from the womb of the year that creatures and cattle derive their livelihood.
These nights are indeed pregnant.
Just as a python, having swallowed its prey, so are these nights.
Moreover, when a python has swallowed its prey, both ends become thin while the middle remains thick.
These nights are indeed the form of well-being. He who attains prosperity attains well-being;
thinking, "May we attain well-being, preeminence, excellence, and prosperity," they therefore undertake these nights.
JB 2.352 |va | Then Āṣāḍha Sāvayasa, the son of Yadu-vaśa, used to say: "In whichever year my kinsmen..."
The maidservant brought water and boiled rice; in that very same year, twenty-four attendants with gold neck-ornaments followed after the serving of food.
We do not see those who were without gold ornaments.
These nights are indeed full of splendor, full of sacred luster, and full of heroic power.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who undertake these nights indeed ascend toward something superior.
In that regard, the *stomas* of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* occur subsequently, directed westward.
For concealment indeed, for freedom from distress, for auspiciousness, and for peace.
They rise after the *trivṛt* stoma of the day;
the *trivṛt* is indeed the Brahman.
It is by being established in the Brahman that they attain the *udgītha*. The *trivṛt* is the attendant of the *trivṛt*;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa becomes the attendant of a Brāhmaṇa.
He finds followers; many become his followers [he who undertakes these nights]. Indeed, this Gāyatrī does not find rest on the earth.
Verily, she goes upward to the heavenly world together with the sacrificer.
Verily, for one who knows this, his fame rises upward, his prosperity rises upward, and he goes upward to the heavenly world. The Vaiśvānara Atirātra is the concluding rite;
for the Soma sacrifices of the Ahīna series conclude with the Vaiśvānara. 352.
This sacrificial session lasts for two months;
whatever prosperity is attained through it, that indeed is prosperity.
Indeed, two months are a season;
a season is visibly the prosperity of the year.
It is for the sake of the year that they strive when they sacrifice, and it is the year they seek to attain when they sit for a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
For there is nothing whatsoever outside of the year.

These nights are indeed self-sovereignty (*svārājya*): twenty-five in total, consisting of twelve days beyond and twelve below. Now, that day which is in the middle is the self-ruling one (*svarāṭ*), that is the heavenly world (*svarga-loka*).
They go to that world of the sun; they go to that sovereignty.
They become such that no other follows them.
Indeed, these nights amount to the Jagatī meter itself.
The Jagatī is indeed cattle;
therefore, this sacrificial session is conducive to cattle.
They attain the Virāj.
Thus, they attain the sovereignty, the lordship, and the mastery over the Virāj and over food.
The Virāj is deficient by one; that deficiency belongs to the woman, for she gives birth [from that deficiency]; therefore, it is a means of procreation.
Furthermore, they complete the Gāyatrī through the consecration days (*dīkṣā*), the attendant days (*upasad*), and the days of pressing (*sutyā*).
The Gāyatrī is indeed breath; therefore, this sacrificial session (sattra) bestows long life.
The Gāyatrī is indeed splendor; therefore, they become splendid and endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcas).
The Gāyatrī is indeed preeminence; therefore, they are established in that preeminence which is free from rivals. 353.
JB 2.354 |va This twenty-five-night rite is indeed the concentrated essence of the year.
vb For all this is performed in the form of the year.
These two are the Atirātras; these two are the Ārambhaṇīya and Mahāvratīya days; these two are the Pṛṣṭhya periods; these two are the Viśvajit and Abhijit;
these are the Svarasāmans; this is the Viṣuvat day.
Those who might think they are beginning every single desire should perform this very twenty-five-night sacrifice.
They should enter upon it; having indeed completed this sacrificial session (*sattra*), they rise from it.
For this twenty-five-night sacrificial session is truly commensurate with man.
A person has ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, four limbs, and the self as the twenty-fifth.
These six sets of six joints each— the self being the twenty-fifth— make up the body.
These twelve enclosing-stones and these twelve [days]—the self is the twenty-fifth.
Verily, by this they perfect the person; they procreate the person.
Regarding this, they say: "They indeed ascend to something superior who undertake this twenty-five-night rite."
In that there is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period facing westward after [the preceding period], it is for concealment, for the sake of non-affliction, for auspiciousness, and for peace.
They rise from the day of the *mahāvrata*; the *mahāvrata* is indeed food; thus, it is for the sake of obtaining food.
By means of the *pratiṣṭhā* (firm foundation), they attain the *ṛc*.
The *vaiśvānara atirātra* serves as the concluding sacrifice (*udayanīya*).
For the *ahīna* Soma sacrifices have the *vaiśvānara* as their conclusion.
This sacrificial session lasts for two months;
whatever prosperity is attained through it, that indeed is prosperity.
Indeed, two months are one season;
a season is visibly the prosperity of the year.
Verily, when they sacrifice and when they sit for a sacrificial session (*sattra*), they strive for the year; they desire to obtain the year.
For there is nothing whatsoever outside of the year.

These nights are indeed self-sovereignty (*svārājya*): thirty-three [nights], sixteen days beyond, and sixteen below. Now, that day which is in the middle is the self-ruling one; it is the world of heaven.
