They go to that world of the sun; they go to that self-sovereignty.
They become such that no other follows after them.
Indeed, these nights amount to the Virāj itself.

Verily, they attain the sovereignty and lordship over the Virāj and over food. There are three [metres] and the Virāj; those which are the three divine coverings, their prosperity consists of these three metres and these three pressings.

The three vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna—are these three worlds. Whatever is triple, this is the perfection and attainment of it all. Indeed, this thirty-three-night sacrifice is truly a divine sacrificial session.
There are indeed thirty-three deities. The deities, desiring prosperity, performed austerity.
They saw this course.
They approached that. Then, indeed, by means of the day alone one of them prospered, by means of the day another, and by means of the day yet another.
Now, that prosperity which the deities attained by this [sacrifice] is indeed the most excellent of prosperities and the most meritorious of worlds.
They prospered.
That which is the most excellent prosperity among prosperities, that which is the most meritorious among worlds— that which the deities prospered by means of this—
may we prosper in that.
Therefore they perform these nights.
Now there are these five-day periods; for there are indeed five victories.
"By means of the five *vyāhṛtis*, the gods indeed conquered this world; let us conquer as much as the gods conquered. The sacrifice is fivefold.
"May we attain whatever measure belongs to the sacrifice," he says.
"Cattle are fivefold;
by as much as is the measure of cattle, by so much may cattle be secured and attend us."

"The food of the Paṅkti is as much as there is of food; by that much may our food be obtained and attend us. Now, the Kāpeyas said: "This six-day period is indeed established in what is not the proper season."
Or rather, it is established in the five seasons.
Spring is indeed the first of the seasons, summer the second, the rainy season the third, autumn the fourth, winter the fifth, and the cool season the sixth.
This very one is the best of the seasons, namely the winter, with a fat cow and a fat calf;
following it, the five-day period proceeds, finding its firm foundation.
Now, this cold season is indeed to be looked upon with aversion, having a lean cow and a lean man.
Following that, the six-day period becomes firmly established.
Since winter is the best of the seasons, they go forth, becoming established by following its firm foundation.
Therefore, they undertake this five-day rite.
The *vaiśvānara* *atirātra* serves as the opening rite (*prāyaṇīya*).
For the *ahīna* Soma sacrifices have the *vaiśvānara* as their point of departure.
Now, these chants (*stoma*)—the *jyotis*, the *go*, and the *āyus*—come into being.
Indeed, these are the auspicious, peaceful, and wholesome chants, namely the *jyotis*, the *go*, and the *āyus*.
"May our praise not be performed with those chants that are auspicious, peaceful, and wholesome"—[so they think].
These [verses] become the Virāj;
thus they take hold of the Virāj as food. They should not release that [Virāj] until the end.
The *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are the *sāmans*. For that is prosperity, that is the path.
The *śyaita* and *naudhasa* are the *brahmasāmans*.
"Clearly we shall win the battle, O boar!
(Thus they say). Now, if on the third day the *rathantara* were to coincide, they should resort to the *vairūpa*.
This world is indeed the *rathantara*, yonder world is the *bṛhat*, and this very intermediate space is the *vairūpa*.
In the absence of these two *sāmans*, however, [the following occurs].
Now, indeed, the Brāhmaṇas of old who were called Niṣkaraṇīyas once sat down for a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Among them, Sātyahavya Vāsiṣṭha used to run away after sitting down and consuming the *soma*.
They then brought a curse upon themselves, saying, "How can those who are not initiated consume the Soma while we are initiated?
They approached this one day with the Vairūpa chant.
Having returned, he sat down silently, merely looking on.
They said to him, "Why do you not move? Why do you not eat?
He replied, "You have indeed become performers of a sacrificial session (*satrin*), or rather, you have previously been performers of the *Dīrghasoma*.
Therefore, when they employ the *Vairūpa* chant on the third day, it is for the sake of the sacrificial session itself.
These two *sāmans*, occurring on different days from this point onward, reach their fulfillment in the cow where the *rathantara* is realized. 357/JB 2.358.
He should say to the Hotṛ: "Recite both forms, that which belongs to the *rathantara* and that which belongs to the *bṛhat*.
Where the *bṛhat* is completed within the lifespan [of the chant], he should say to the Hotṛ: "Recite both forms, that which belongs to the *bṛhat* and that which belongs to the *rathantara*."
If both days should consist of the *rathantara* [sāman], they should perform the *saubhara* as the *brahmasāman* for the *ukthya* chants of the first day.
If both days should consist of the *bṛhat* [sāman], they should perform the *kaṇvarathantara* for the second day.
They should chant the *pavamāna* at the midday pressing.
These two *sāmans*, the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*, are indeed offspring;
therefore, when they proceed in this manner, it is for the sake of avoiding sameness (*ajāmitā*).
Now, this Viśvajit sacrifice is an Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras; it is a day dedicated to Prajāpati. For Prajāpati is the entirety of day and night.

"May we prosper through the complete Prajāpati; may the complete Prajāpati be attained by us," they think. Regarding this, they say: "Those who undertake this Viśvajit Atirātra indeed ascend to something superior."
For they approach Prajāpati directly. Now,
as for the fact that there are three five-day periods facing westward at the end, it is for concealment, to prevent distress, for auspiciousness, and for peace.
The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the concluding rite.
For the Soma sacrifices of the Ahīna class have the Vaiśvānara [offering] as their conclusion.

Now, these [days] are like those of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*); whatever praise there is for those twelve-day rites has been attained here as well. However, it is this [following] that is specifically applied here.
They should indeed approach them either before or after [the tenth day].
If they were to approach them before, it would be for the sake of avoiding failure on the very day of the *prāyaṇīya*.
However, in this case, they criticize that which they have exhausted their speech, failing to complete it until the tenth day.
They reach the ultimate limit of speech that is drawn out and lacks a firm foundation.
Whatever they consider to be the form of the *prāyaṇīya* (opening rite) there, that very thing they should perform there. [Thinking:
"May we reach the ultimate limit of speech that is ancient, gone forth, perfected, not drawn out, and firmly founded."
Now, this Viśvajit sacrifice is an Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras; it is a day dedicated to Prajāpati. For Prajāpati is the day and night in their entirety.

"May we prosper through the complete Prajāpati; may the complete Prajāpati be attained by us," they think. Regarding this, they say: "Verily, those who undertake this Viśvajit Atirātra ascend to something superior."
"For they approach Prajāpati directly.
Now, as for the fact that there is a five-day period (*pañcāha*) facing westward at the end, it is for concealment, for the absence of affliction, for auspiciousness, and for peace.
The *vaiśvānara* *atirātra* constitutes the concluding day.
For the *vaiśvānarodayana* are indeed the *ahīna* Soma sacrifices.
Now, this [sacrifice] consists of three days (*tryaha*).
"There are indeed three seasons that are true, while the others are untrue.
Summer, the rainy season, and winter—these indeed are the prosperous seasons, while the others are like those who have come into contact [with them]. May those prosperous seasons be attained by us."
There are indeed three *chandas*, three pressings (*savana*), three vital breaths—out-breath, in-breath, and diffused breath—and these three worlds.
Whatever is threefold, this is the perfection and attainment of it all. These five days that follow are [the same] as those five that precede.
They do not go [to the other side] for the sake of its fivefold division.

Now, this Viśvajit becomes an Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas; it is a day belonging to Prajāpati. Day and night indeed constitute the whole of Prajāpati. "May we prosper through the whole of Prajāpati; may the whole of Prajāpati be attained by us," [they think].
Regarding this they say: "Those who undertake this Viśvajit Atirātra indeed ascend to something superior;
for they are approaching Prajāpati himself directly.
Now, as to why there are five three-day periods (tryaha) directed backwards from the end: it is for concealment, to prevent misfortune, and for auspiciousness.
For the sake of peace.
The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the concluding rite;
for Soma sacrifices belonging to the Ahīna class conclude with the Vaiśvānara. 360.
This sacrificial session (*satra*) lasts for three months; whatever prosperity there is in it, that is indeed prosperity. For the two months that constitute a season are indeed prosperity.
The season (*ṛtu*) is the manifest prosperity of the year;
and that which is the third month is the prosperity of the thirteenth month.
Indeed, they strive for the year when they sacrifice, and they seek to attain the year when they sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
For there is nothing whatsoever outside of the year. These nights are indeed self-sovereignty (*svārājya*): forty-nine in total, twenty-four beyond [the central day] and twenty-four below.
The year consists of twenty-four half-months. This very year is encompassed on both sides.
That which is the day in its middle is the self-ruling [svarāṭ], the heavenly world.
They go to that summit of the sun; they go to that self-sovereignty.
They become such that no other follows them.
Indeed, these nights amount to the Jagatī meter itself.

The *jagatī* is indeed cattle; therefore, this sacrificial session (*sattra*) is conducive to cattle, and they attain the *virāj*. Indeed, they attain sovereignty and overlordship over the *virāj*, which is food.
The *virāj* is deficient by one; that which is deficient belongs to the woman, since she gives birth [thereby], and thus it is a means of procreation.
They complete the *gāyatrī* through the *dīkṣā*, the *upasad*s, and the *sutyā*s.
The *gāyatrī* is indeed breath; therefore, this sacrificial session (*sattra*) is life-prolonging.
The Gāyatrī is indeed splendor; therefore, they become splendid and endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcas).
The Gāyatrī is indeed preeminence; thus, they find firm standing in preeminence that is free from rivals.
The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases contended for the world of heaven.
Those Ādityas desired, "May we go first to the world of heaven.
They perceived this course.

They approached that [knowledge]. From there, indeed, the Ādityas went first to the heavenly world, while the Aṅgirases were left behind. That which the Ādityas reached by means of this is truly the most excellent of prosperities and the most meritorious of worlds.
Thinking, "Let us go to that which is the most excellent of prosperities, the most meritorious of worlds, to which the Ādityas went by means of this [rite]," they therefore perform these nights.
The introductory Atirātra sacrifice belongs to Vaiśvānara.
For the Ahīna Soma sacrifices have the Vaiśvānara as their opening point.
Now, these Stomas consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus come into being.
These indeed are the auspicious, peaceful, and wholesome *stomas*, namely: *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*.
"May we have praised with those *stomas* which are auspicious, peaceful, and wholesome," they [think]. And these [stomas] are perfected as the *virāj*.
They undertake the Virāj as food;
the Bṛhat and Rathantara are the two Sāmans, for that is prosperity, that is the path.
The Śyaita and Naudhasa are the *brahmasāman* chants. "Clearly we shall win the battle," [he says]. Now, these are the six *atirātra* sacrifices.
There are indeed six evils in man and six equinoctial points: sleep and drowsiness, anger and hunger, the desire for dice, and the desire for women.
By means of these [chants], they strike away those [evils] and pass beyond them.
Now, these consist of three tri-days;
that makes nine days.
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person.
This is indeed the perfecting of the vital breaths; this is the prosperity of the vital breaths.
Now, this tenth day has the Vairāja as its *pṛṣṭha* chant.
That is the navel; and that day, being established, is joined to these days.
Since this day, being *ākṣit*, is joined among these days, therefore the *nābhi* (navel), being *ākṣit*, is joined among the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
For, following it as it breathes out, one breathes out; following it as it breathes in, one breathes in.
Of these days, the tenth belongs to them; the Virāj consists of ten syllables. Food is the Virāj; it is for the attainment of food from the Virāj. 363/ JB 2.364.
That has the Vairāja as its *pṛṣṭha*; the Vairāja is indeed food, for the sake of securing food.
That is an *ukthya* sacrifice; the *ukthas* are cattle, and cattle are food—for the sake of securing food that precedes [all other] food.

That [sacrifice] consists of the *ṣoḍaśin* (sixteen-fold cup). The *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the *virāj* is food; by means of the thunderbolt, they thus encompass the enjoyment of food.
That [sacrifice] consists of twenty-one [parts]: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun.
Twenty-one.
This indeed is the divine sovereignty;
the Kṣatriya is indeed the giver of food.
"May he who is the giver of food bestow food upon us.
Now, these four three-day periods constitute twelve days.
Indeed, there are twelve full-moon nights in a year.
This is indeed the perfecting of the full-moon sacrifices; this is the prosperity of the full-moon sacrifices. Now, there is this six-day *pṛṣṭhya* period.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed glory; the *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the summit.
They ascend to that glory, to the height, to the back-regions;
and thus they become performers of a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Now, these four subsequent three-day periods consist of twelve days.
There are indeed twelve new-moon days in a year;
this is the perfect measure of the new-moon days, the prosperity of the new-moon days.
These twelve days that follow the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period are there, and twelve are before it.

Therefore, there are equal full-moon and new-moon days of the year. The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the concluding rite; for Soma sacrifices that conclude with the Vaiśvānara are Ahīna sacrifices. 364.
The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases indeed contended for the world of heaven.
Those Ādityas went first to the world of heaven.
Those Aṅgirases desired, "May we also go to that world which the Ādityas have gone to.
By whichever path they set out, from there they were repelled by them.
They indeed pushed them back for forty years.
They saw this path; they settled upon it. They approached it as if it were something already familiar.
Then indeed the Aṅgirases went to that world which the Ādityas [went to].
Indeed, that is the most excellent of prosperities and the most meritorious of worlds which the Aṅgirases went to by this [means].
That which is the most excellent of prosperities, that which is the most meritorious of worlds, which the Aṅgirases went to by this—[that is it].
"Let us go," [they said].
Now, those rays of the sun that point upward are the Ādityas; those that point southward are the Aṅgirases.
Now, these Ādityas and Aṅgirases are co-resident (saloka). Indeed, he who knows this becomes co-resident with the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases.
Now, these two three-day periods constitute six days.
Or there are six seasons;
thus they find firm support in the seasons.
Now these two subsequent three-day periods consist of exactly six days.
In this way, they establish themselves successively within the seasons. Now, there are these six *atirātra* sacrifices, whose *brāhmaṇa* explanations have already been stated.
Then, there are these three *tryaha* periods, whose *brāhmaṇa* explanations have already been stated.
Now, these four three-day periods constitute twelve days.
Twelve months make a year. Having thus become the months themselves, they passed through the middle of the year and ascended to the heavenly world. 366.
JB 2.367 |va| Now, these [days] consist of twelve-day periods; whatever praise there is for those consisting of twelve-day periods, that has not yet been attained here.
Now they proceed with these meters that increase by four syllables.
For the ascents of speech indeed increase by four;
it is speech itself that they ascend.
For cattle are indeed four-footed; thus,
in that they employ these meters increasing by four syllables, it is for the attainment of four-footed cattle.
Now they bring these two-antithetical [verses]. These are the two-antithetical verses, each increasing by four syllables.
Indeed, one does not attain prosperity as long as one does not possess mastery over bipeds and quadrupeds.

They do not attain sovereignty. Now, when they bring forward these two-interval [verses]— the two-interval verses increased by four— in order that they might attain lordship and sovereignty over two-footed and four-footed animals.

Then they bring these eight intermediate spaces, which consist of four pairs with two intervals between them; all of them represent the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions. "May we, having established ourselves in all directions, go to the heavenly world—that world above which is meritorious"—with this intention they do so.
Now, there are these five *sandhi-sāmans*: the *rathantara*, the *jarābodhīya*, the *śrudhīya*, the *nānada*, and the *gaurīvita*.
Indeed, this one *sandhi-sāman* is well-known: it is the *rathantara*; that which is well-known as one...
"The *sandhi-sāman* was not praised by him; it was non-existent."
Moreover, the *rathantara* is indeed speech, and the *āśvina* is speech; for speech is indeed capable of manifesting itself through speech, because this speech manifests itself through speech.
This, indeed, is the second well-known *sandhiṣāman*, namely the *jarābodhīya*.
Now, that second [sāman] which is known as the *sandhiṣāman* was not chanted by him, thinking, "It is non-existent.
Then there is the *śrudhīya*, the *kīrtimant*. And the *sandhiṣāman* is indeed the *sāmavṛkti*.
"Therefore, since we have obtained [the Sāmans] from these two joints, may cattle attend upon our world as a consequence of this world-possessing Sāman.
Then [he says], "May the Nānada and Gaurīvita, the two world-possessing Sāmans, attend upon a more abundant world for us."
Regarding this, they say: "The *āśvina* [śastra] should be recited three times," for speech is indeed threefold in truth (*triṣatyā*).
These worlds are three;
if one were to recite the *āśvina* at an *atirātra* sacrifice when it is not an *atirātra*, that would be a dragging away of speech.

He should say to the Hotṛ: "Recite the Āśvina-śastra for those other Atirātras whose sacrificial rites are dedicated to the Aśvins; the Āśvina must be recited exactly three times—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
This Āśvina is indeed successful when it is brought to completion with the Rathantara Sāman.

If it should be accomplished with one [verse], then the Rathantara alone is used for the commencement, the middle, and the conclusion; if with two, then the Rathantara alone is used for the commencement, the middle, and the conclusion; if with three, then the Rathantara alone is used for the commencement, the middle, and the conclusion; it is not accomplished with four, nor indeed with five.
Now, these are the *eṇya* [nights], each with one black [mark].
Indeed, these nights are called *eṇya*.
In those [days], Kṛṣṇa also [is present] for the sake of pairing and procreation.
He who knows thus is born through pairing.
They should indeed approach him either from the front or from behind.

If they were to approach from the front, [thinking] "they would be male-guides"; if from above, [thinking] "for behind a woman, a man deposits seed for the sake of procreation. Indeed, in the beginning, Prajāpati alone was created here; he did not see any other second being.
He reflected: "I alone have been born first; I am the most excellent. Is there indeed anyone else besides me here?
He looked around.
He saw another who stood higher than himself and was superior.
He asked him, "What is this that you are? He replied, "I am indeed Brahman.
He said, "Since we two were indeed born first, and we two are the best, let us unite together."
"Come here," he said. "No," he replied. "For you are seized by evil."
"Where is that evil of mine?
"It is in your head.
"Then remove it from me."
"So be it," he said.
He drove him [there].
He struck him on the neck with a sword.
He squeezed it.
He cast off that which was like something grasped. He drove it away.
He fastened it upon his waistband;
he pressed it together;
thus, one casts it off as if it were something already grasped.
He drove him away; he struck him with his feet; he bound him at the ankles; he crushed him.
"Kill this very thing, as if it were seized! He drove it away.
"Trample it with your foot! he said.
He stepped upon him with his foot.
This very thing is the "leaping over" (ucchlaṅkha) of the feet.
"Cut it into three parts," he said.
He cut it into three parts.
That very thing became his glory: the cow was one third, sleep was one third, and shadow was one third.
Therefore, these [parts] belong most abundantly to the best.
Most abundant are cattle; the shadow is the eldest; it sleeps.
He reflected: "That evil which has been declared concerning me—come now, let me cut this away entirely."
He divided this very Brahman into eight parts.
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables;
the Gāyatrī is Brahman.
Brahman itself divided that into eight parts.
With eight threefold [stomas] he drove it away from him.
With eight fifteenfold [stomas] he drove it away from him.
With eight [verses] of seventeen [syllables each], he drove it away in a backward direction;
with eight [verses] of twenty-one [syllables each], he drove it away in a backward direction;
with eight [verses] of twenty-seven [syllables each], he caused it to go to the furthest distance.
He cut him away with eight [stotras] and thirty-three [stotras].
This very one is the Atirātra at the end; thus, evil has been removed from him.
Now, this very one who shines yonder is Prajāpati.
He shines as one whose evil has been struck away;
he has no shadow.
Therefore, one should indeed spit upon and urinate upon one's shadow; thus one strikes away evil. Having slept, one should sip water.
Verily, he strikes away evil. Let him strike a cow that has been licking [the calf].
Verily, he strikes away evil thereby.
Those who, knowing thus, perform these nights, rise having indeed struck away all evil.
They are liable to become non-animals; for the *ukthas* are cattle, and he struck away cattle even there. Those who may be desirous of prosperity should perform these nights.
In former times, indeed, the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas used to approach these [cows] when desiring prosperity.
Those cows were not auspicious;
their cattle were found only among their own kinsmen.
"Vai"—then, indeed, they would tie up a cow for Gauruhā when he arrived;
"vaj"—then they gave [it] to one to whom it should not be given;
"vak"—regarding that, Śāṭyāyani said: "One should not speak of that which is censurable."

"If cattle were indeed subject to one's will regarding prosperity, and if wealth were subject to one's will, then thinking, 'We shall become possessed of cattle, we shall be the best, and we shall succeed,' they should undertake these nights. And so it indeed comes to pass.
The Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the concluding rite;
for the Soma sacrifices of the Ahīna class conclude with the Vaiśvānara [offering]. (This is a supplement to the Gavām Ayana.)
On the preceding day, they immolate an animal sacrifice for Savitṛ. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, they take hold of the year.
For who indeed, being unborn, is worthy of undertaking this?
On the following day, they immolate the animal dedicated to Prajāpati;
for the gods have Prajāpati as their chief.
It is precisely by means of the best that they thus gratify the deities.
For if one, having failed to propitiate the best, then seeks to win others, all of them indeed remain unpropitiated for him.
But if, having propitiated the best, he then also honors the others, all of them indeed become his most desired and gratified.
They exist.
For the gods are indeed the best of progenitors.
Thus, by means of excellence itself, they gratify all the deities.
A white, hairy, hornless goat, a *lapsudya*, and one with teeth on both sides—these are four-footed.
That which is white and hairy is the form of sheep; that which is hornless is the form of horses.
That which is spotted belongs to the *pruṣa* deer; that which has teeth on both sides belongs to the cattle;
that which is hornless belongs to the goats.
This is indeed the fat of all animals.
By means of the fat of all these animals, they gratify their father Prajāpati for a year.
He, being gratified, gratifies them in return.
The gods, desiring prosperity, performed austerity.
Indra saw this eightfold [offering].
He consecrated himself in that [night].
He prospered by means of one [night]. Because he prospered by means of one, that is the reason for the name "Ekāṣṭakā" (the One-Eighth).
Those who, knowing thus, undergo initiation—all of them attain [the goal], all of them become equinoctial (viṣuvant).
For this one has indeed become the equinox.
If they were to undergo initiation beforehand, they would undergo it in the world of the fathers; they would be liable to die prematurely.
If they were to undergo initiation later on, it would be as if he wished to flee as before; he might either attain that [goal] or not—it is not like that.
Therefore, they should undergo initiation on this very Aṣṭakā day.

Just as one would mount a chariot that has been brought near, or an elephant that has been seated; when they ask, "In what direction are the performers of the sacrifice? one should say, "Neither toward this side nor toward that side," just like that sun.
Indeed, these do not go forward nor do they go backward; indeed, these go crosswise.
Indeed, yonder sun does not go forward nor does it go backward; indeed, it goes crosswise.
Indeed, this [sun] goes south for six months and north for six months.
Those [days] which it goes south belong to the Pitṛs as their deity; those which it goes north belong to the Devas as their deity.
Indeed, having set out from this very place, they proceed toward Indra, Prajāpati, the Sage, the Footstep, the Vessel of the Seasons, the All-Gods,
and the heavenly world. Indeed, they turn back following the turning of this very place.
Indeed, they turn back following its turning back; they are released following its release.
This is the explanation of it: that they go to the Soma-pressing while [the moon] is waning, and they reach the conclusion while [it] is waning.
They should perform twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*) and three *upasads*;
by this they obtain both of these.
Regarding this, however, they say: "Indeed, by this very means they do obtain both."
But that which they declare as a fault is when they enter the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the cold season without taking pleasure in the waters.
The frost indeed agitates them as it were. If someone were to speak ill of those who have acted thus, saying, "It will be so" or "It will not be so," it would indeed happen exactly so.
On the fifth or sixth day after that very new moon of Phālguna, they should undergo initiation.
Indeed, he who proceeds by the path of one who is superior thinks, "I have gone this way, I have gone that way," yet he does not come to harm;
for those who proceed by the path of one who is superior go to the sun, and being unharmed, they reach the end of their journey; it is to that they go.
Wherever this sun goes, having gone there, they return again by its very path.
The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session (sattra) in the beginning, desiring to win food. JB 2.374. va.
Then, in the tenth month, they arose, thinking, "We have obtained all kinds of food.
These are those horned ones.
To them, Tvāṣṭṛ said, "Let us complete all these twelve months together."
They applied themselves excessively;
in the twelfth month, their horns grew out,
and thus they became hornless (tūpara).
Therefore, even in the twelfth month, those performing a sacrificial session (sattrins) shave their topknots;
for then they become conformable to the cattle. They rose up, saying, "We have succeeded," having completed the sacrificial session and having attained all food.

Therefore, all these [seasons] rise for twelve months— the rains as well as the two winters— for they have won the sacrificial session (*sattra*) and have secured it. Those who, knowing thus, complete the twelve months, [secure] all food indeed.
Having enclosed [the fire], they rise.
Indeed, the sacrificial session has the self as its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
By the first two *upasad* days, they preserve the hair; by the second two, the skin; by [the third two], the flesh.
With the third [verses] they satisfy the bones; with the fourth [verses], the marrow; with the fifth [verses], the marrow.
Whatever of these remains unsatisfied there, that they satisfy with the sixth [verses]. Having become pure, cleansed, fit for sacrifice, and bright, they enter the world of the gods. 374.
JB 2.375 |va Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning. vb He desired: "May I become many; may I procreate; may I attain abundance."
He performed austerities.
He beheld this Vaiśvānara Atirātra as the opening rite.
From it, he brought forth day and night.
He established himself in day and night. Therefore, in that this Vaiśvānara Atirātra serves as the opening sacrifice (prāyaṇīya), they procreate from him in day and night,
and they find firm support in day and night.
He desired, "May I indeed be born forth.
From this very Vaiśvānara Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, he fashioned out a three-day period; from the Agniṣṭoma, he fashioned out the Jyotis; from the Ukthyas, the Gāyatrī; and from the night, life.
From that three-day period he generated the three seasons; he found support in the three seasons.
Therefore, in that this is a three-day period, they generate the three seasons from it and find support in the three seasons.
He desired, "May I indeed be born."
He pushed this very six-day period further out.
Those two became two six-day periods. By means of those two six-day periods, he generated twelve months; in twelve months [he completed the year].
He established himself.
Now, as to why there are these two six-day periods (ṣaḍaha): by means of these two, they generate twelve months;
in twelve months they find firm support.
He desired, "May I indeed be born.
He pushed back those very two six-day periods to the further side;
they became four six-day periods.
From those four six-day periods, he generated twenty-four half-months;
in those twenty-four half-months, he found firm support.
Thus, in that these four six-day periods exist, it is from them that he generates the twenty-four half-months.
They procreate in twenty-four half-months and find firm support therein. Having generated this entire world, he placed it within himself by means of the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite.
In that this Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha occurs, they place the entire world, which has been procreated by it, within themselves.
The Pṛṣṭhas are indeed the summit.
Verily, they find support in height;
the *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed prosperity;
verily, they find support in prosperity.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed preeminence;
thus they find firm footing in preeminence.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed splendor; thus they find firm footing in splendor.
The Abhiplava six-day period is indeed cattle, and the Pṛṣṭhya is the self.
When they enter upon the Pṛṣṭhya after entering upon the Abhiplava six-day period, they thus place the person upon the cattle.
Therefore, the man stands as it were above the animals. Indeed, the Abhiplava six-day period is the root, while the Pṛṣṭhya is the top.
Because they approach the Pṛṣṭhya after having reached the Abhiplava six-day period, therefore plants [grow] from the root.
They are born first and ripen later;
these five six-day periods come into being; the sacrifice is fivefold.
In whatever measure the sacrifice consists, in that very measure they find firm support.
That becomes a month;
for the month is indeed the year.
In this way, they indeed attain the year month by month.
It consists of thirty nights; the Virāj has thirty syllables, and the Virāj is food. Thus, they proceed while firmly established in the Virāj, that is, in food. 376.
JB 2.377 |va The opening day (prāyaṇīyam ahar) takes place. vb By means of the opening day, the gods went to the heavenly world.
Because they went forth (*prāyan*), that is the reason for the *prāyaṇīya* (opening) nature of the *prāyaṇīya* [offering].

In that there is this opening day, it is for the sake of attaining the heavenly world. Therefore, one should indeed desire to be the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) on this day, for it is the nearest [approach] to the heavenly world.
That makes twenty-four;
for the year consists of twenty-four half-months;
thus, by means of the half-months, they indeed attain the year.

Now, some performers of the sacrificial session (*satrin*), having reached this day, rise [from it], saying, "We have completed the year. Those who might be as if beginning each desire one after another should rise on this very day;
for them, the year becomes truly attained.
There are three hundred and sixty *stotriya* verses for it;
there are that many nights in a year.
Thus, by means of the nights, they indeed attain the year.
Regarding this they say: "Since those who sit for a year-long session perform the Soma-pressing during the days of the year, by what means do they attain the nights?
He should reply: "As many as are the *stotriya* verses of the opening day (*prāyaṇīya*), so many are the nights of the year."
"Having reached the nights by means of the *stotryās* of the *prāyaṇīya* day itself, they sit pressing the Soma during the days.
Thus it becomes an *ukthya*; for the *ukthas* are cattle, and it is for the attainment of cattle.
It has fifteen *stotras*.
There are indeed fifteen nights in a half-month;
thus, by means of the half-months, they reach the year.
There are thirty *stotra*s and *śastra*s.
There are thirty nights in a month; in this way, they reach the year month by month. 377/ JB 2.378
Regarding this they say: "The Acchāvāka is, as it were, a sore among the Hotṛ-offices; if one were to conclude the rite with the Acchāvāka, they would be like those who have praised over a sore.
For him, the Traikakubha is the Brahman-sāman, and the Udvaṃśīya is the Acchāvāka-sāman.
The *udvaṃśīya* is indeed the sense-organ, the vigor, the triple-heaven, and the form of all the *pṛṣṭha* hymns.
Thus, they finally find firm support in the sense-organ, in vigor, and in the entire form of the *pṛṣṭha* hymns.
That is what he praised.
Regarding this, they say: "The Agniṣṭoma alone should be performed.
It has twelve stotras;
the year consists of twelve months.
This month is indeed the preeminent joint of the year. [He thinks:

"Since this is the preeminent joint of the year, may we thus have the year commenced for us. However, they are liable to become devoid of cattle; for the *ukthas* are cattle, and from them [the cattle] depart.
They should perform for it three stotras consisting of forty-eight [verses] each; both Pavamāna stotras and the Brahmasāman should be likewise.
There are as many verses for the Ukthya stotras as there are for those;
they attain that desire which is [attained] in the Ukthya, or they do not depart from the Agniṣṭoma.
The Agniṣṭoma is the summit, and the Hotṛ is the summit; by means of the summit they thus join the summit together, and by means of the summit they become established upon the summit.
The Agniṣṭoma is prosperity, and the Hotṛ is preeminence; by means of preeminence they thus join preeminence together.
By means of preeminence, they find firm standing in preeminence. Regarding this, they say: "The Jagatī metre is like a boat; it is not for the beginning."
In that place, they should perform six thirty-six-versed hymns and six twenty-four-versed hymns.
The *bṛhatī* indeed consists of thirty-six syllables;
the *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world and sovereign power (*sāmrājya*).
Verily, they go forth establishing themselves in the sovereignty of the heavenly world within the Bṛhatī itself.

Indeed, the Bṛhatī pervades all these worlds by means of its syllables: it pervades this world with ten syllables, the intermediate space with ten, yonder world with ten, the quarters with four, and the two [worlds] with two.
[It is] day and night.
She pervades these worlds; [thinking] "may we pervade these worlds," they should therefore perform exactly six thirty-six-fold stotras and six twenty-four-fold stotras.
Now, the year consists of twenty-four half-months;
thus, by means of the half-months, they indeed attain the year.
They should take "These drops have been poured forth" (*ete asṛgram indavaḥ*) as the introductory verse (*pratipad*), for it contains many forms.
For many indeed undergo initiation here.
Regarding this, they say: "The introductory verse (*pratipad*) should be performed as 'Flow on, the foremost of speech' (*pavasva vāco agriya*)," for this one is indeed multiform.
In this [verse], indeed, all forms are present.
Both [verses] serve as the *pratipad* (opening verses), for two *sāmans* are performed here.
Then, like two most vigorous, strongest, swiftest, and successful carriers, they carry one across the great path.
Having united, he would pass away; such is that.
They cause everything to turn back toward the form of the back, just as one would cause the calves to turn back toward both the father and the mother; such is that.
Regarding this, they say that the Agniṣṭoma-sāman should be performed upon these verses beginning with "O Agni, yoke those which are yours.
For the year is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara;
by means of its very yoking, [the verse] "O God, the excellent horses" serves for success, and [the phrase] "the swift ones carry well" is employed.
For the sake of unification.
Regarding this they say: "Those who cause the *yajñāyajñīya* to fall away from the verses of the *yajñāyajñīya* indeed go against the sacrifices with their sacrifice."
Now, those who cause the *yajñāyajñīya* to fall away from the verses of the *yajñāyajñīya* chant do not find firm standing in the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice.
Therefore, the *yajñāyajñīya* should be performed only upon its own [verses]. //379//
The *abhīvarta* becomes the *brahmasāman*.
By means of the *abhīvarta*, the gods indeed turned toward these worlds.
Because they turned toward it, that is the reason for the *abhīvarta*’s name as the *abhīvarta*.
In that the *abhīvarta* serves as the *brahmasāman*, it is for the purpose of turning toward these very worlds. Indeed, the *abhīvarta* is Prajāpati, and the meters are the creatures.
This very Prajāpati goes about depositing the embryo among the creatures. They praise with various [verses] using the same *sāman*;
they thereby pour forth semen.
Therefore, being the same, he deposits seed in many [women].
The verses (*ṛc*) are the same up to a certain point, while the melodies (*sāman*) are different from one another;
thus they bring forth the seed once it has been emitted.
Therefore, the same [melody] produces many [verses]. They chant with different verses while using the same *sāman*;
for those who are moving toward their goal see various things as distinct.

The *ṛc*s are uniform beyond [this world], while the *sāman*s are different from one another. Just as they ascend to these worlds from here by means of the *pragāthas*, so do they descend again from there to these [worlds] by means of the *sāmans*.
The *ṛc* is this world, and the *sāman* is that world. When they proceed from here having commenced the *sāman*, they proceed having commenced that world.
If they were to omit [the *sāman*] before the *viṣuvat*, they would be cut off from that world.
When they come from there, having begun with a *ṛc*, they take hold of this world.
If they were to omit [the *ṛc*] before the twelve days of the sacrificial session (*dvādaśāha*), they would be severed from this world.
Va: Once they turn over the *abhīvarta* on the other side. Vb: Therefore, embryos being born turn over.
Vc: Indeed, formerly, up until the fifth month, the *bārhata* *pragāthas* were obtained.
Having combined the two meters, the *uṣṇih* and the *triṣṭubh*, they should complete five months;
having combined the two meters, the *anuṣṭubh* and the *paṅkti*, they should complete six months, leaving one meter remaining.
They should resort to the *jagatī* at the *viṣuvat*. For the *viṣuvat* is indeed *jāgata*;
thus they perfect the *viṣuvat* in its own proper abode.
The meters are indeed the heavenly world.
Thus, they go ascending to that very heavenly world.
Regarding this, they say: "Verily, one enters into these meters as it were, when one joins them two by two."
For how could the day of today and the day of tomorrow ever coincide?
One should approach all seven meters, each increasing by four syllables:
one should approach the *gāyatrī* on the first day, the *uṣṇih* on the second, the *anuṣṭubh* on the third, and five [verses] of the *bṛhatī* on the fourth.
They should complete six months having approached the *paṅkti* on the first day; they should complete six months with the *triṣṭubh*, leaving behind only one metre.
They should resort to the *jagatī* at that central day (*viṣuvat*). For the central day is indeed *jāgata*. Thus, they bring the central day to fulfillment in its own proper abode.
The meters are indeed the heavenly world;
thus they go ascending to that very world, the heaven. 381/ JB 2.382
Regarding this, they say: "One yokes these meters as if they were not yet exhausted, even though they are indeed exhausted.
They employ them all again and again. Having selected whichever *pragāthas* one considers most powerful, one should proceed with thirty-six of them."
The *bṛhatī* indeed consists of thirty-six syllables;
the *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world and sovereign rule (*sāmrājya*). Thus, they proceed while firmly established in the *bṛhatī*, in the heavenly world, and in sovereign rule.
He performs six *utsargas* and then returns with thirty [verses] for the sake of non-exhaustion. Now they say that one should stop at thirty-three;
for the thirty-three are indeed all the deities.
Thus they proceed, finding firm support in all these very deities.
They perform three utsargas with thirty [verses], turning back again for the sake of non-exhaustion;
moreover, some say that one should stop at exactly thirty.
The *virāj* consists of thirty syllables; the *virāj* is food. Thus, they proceed while firmly established in the *virāj*, that is, in food.
Moreover, some say that one should approach [the sacrifice] with twenty-four [syllables].
The year indeed consists of twenty-four half-months;
thus, they proceed while firmly establishing themselves in the year by means of the half-months. Moreover, some say that one should approach [the sacrifice] with only twelve.
Twelve months make a year;
thus, they proceed while finding firm support in the year month by month.
Moreover, some say that one should undertake only six.
Or there are six seasons; thus they go while finding firm support in the seasons. Moreover, some say that one should approach [the fire] at four [seasons].
The four quarters are four-footed cattle;
thus, they proceed while establishing themselves both in the quarters and in cattle. Moreover, some say that only three should be approached.
Or these worlds are three;
they proceed while finding firm support in these very worlds. Moreover, some say that one should approach two [verses] at a time, namely the *pragāthas* of the Śyaita and the Naudhasa.
Indeed, the two *pragāthas* of the Śyaita and Naudhasa are most powerful;
the sacrificer is two-footed for the sake of stability.
Indeed, he who returns along the path does not reach him;
but he who goes toward him without returning—he alone reaches him.
Those two who enter [the fire] go as if they were returning.
"One should approach [the *stotras*] with those of the *triṣṭubh* and *bṛhatī* meters.

For the midday pressing (*mādhyandina*) indeed consists of the *triṣṭubh* and *bṛhatī*. Therefore, if the day were of the *rathaṃtara* type, they should approach it with a *bārhata* [*stotra*]; if the day is of the *bārhata* type, they should approach it with a *traiṣṭubha* [*stotra*].
Neither *triṣṭubh* nor *bṛhatī* *pragāthas* are obtained for these [days]. The meters are joined according to their proper place, and they dwell for a year that is not exhausted.
Regarding this, however, they say: "Only two *pragāthas* are to be approached, namely those of the Śyaita and the Naudhasa."
Now, indeed, these two—the Bṛhat and the Rathantara—are the most powerful; they are truly the straight paths leading to the heavenly world.
Of these two, the Śyaita and the Audhaṣa are the straight paths.
Day after day, they thus go directly to the heavenly world.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"When a man awakens from the great path, he [attains] all life."
"Having run that very race, being exhausted, he desires to run it again.
Thus [it is said].
Or rather, those who employ other *pragāthas* set out upon the path of truth along the great road.
Now, those who employ the *pragāthas* of the Śyaita and Naudhasa [sāmans] go directly to the heavenly world day after day.
Therefore, one should employ only these two *pragāthas*, namely those of the Śyaita and Naudhasa. 383.
The other *sāmans* have the *anuṣṭubh* as their food;
the *anuṣṭubh* itself is the food of the other *sāmans*.

Or rather, those *sāman*s which consist of advancing and retreating are the *anuṣṭubh* and food. With these, she speaks out against those who deprive her—this speech being unadorned, displeased, unknown, and unpalatable: "They have violated the seasons; they have sacrificed without faith; they have not succeeded."

Now, those who fulfill her with these [offerings], to them this Speech—satisfied, pleased, and recognized—speaks favorably: "They have performed the seasonal rites; the faithful ones have sacrificed; they have succeeded. Day by day, it becomes well-known.
Indeed, that Udgātṛ priest should initiate those performing a sacrificial session for the sake of the session,
so that he may cause them to ascend to the gods' field of the gods.
Having ascended to the gods' field of the gods, he truly fears nothing, he does not hunger, he does not thirst, and he does not suffer distress.
He approaches. Indeed, the *sujñāna* is the gods' field of the gods.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who go to the *sujñāna* day after day truly fall away from this world."
Therefore, if there should be a day connected with the *rathaṃtara*, they should perform the *pauṣkala* on that; on a day connected with the *bṛhat*, the *sujñāna*.
Regarding this, they also say: "In the *sujñāna*, indeed, all these forms are contained.
"Suvarvid" is the form of this world; "e" is the form of the intermediate space; "suvar" is the form of yonder world.
That [nidhana] consists of seven syllables. JB 2.385 va.
There are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*). It is by means of the vital breaths that they proceed, becoming successful and finding firm support in the vital breaths.
Day after day, there is the *Gaurīvita* chant.
The Gaurīvita is indeed something in excess of the *brahman*.
These days of the *ahīna* sacrifice are themselves in excess.
Thus, they proceed placing that very excess—the essence of the *brahman*—into the excess.
Day by day it becomes a raft for the attainment of the heavenly world itself. Thus they leap across the intermediate space.
"May we cross over all difficulties"—whatever in the sacrifice is ill-praised, ill-recited, or defective, that [they cross over].
They transcend it.
That [chant] has a *nidhana* consisting of twelve syllables.
There are twelve months in a year.
They proceed while finding firm support in the months themselves, and thus in the year.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who undertake these six-day periods in forward succession indeed fall away from this world. On the sixth day, they should perform the *okonidhana* chant.
This world, indeed, is the dwelling-place of man;
it is in this very world that they find firm support.
And so they say: "The one sent forth is the fetter."
Day and night are indeed sent forth;
for these two move as if sent forth. Now, indeed, these six-day periods are as if cut asunder when they reach the sixth day.
Just as one would harness a horse with a halter, even so they proceed, harnessing the six-day periods with this *sāman*.
Regarding this, they say: "Should the *okonidhana* be performed on the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period? "Yes," they say; "No," they say.
"No," he should say.
"For this *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite is indeed the foremost; it is the end.
Verily, by means of this they seek him, by means of this *abhīvarta*, by means of this *plava*, and by means of this *sujñāna*."
Or rather, it would be like a repetition, as they might do this here;
therefore, this should not be done here. 385/ JB 2.386.
Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the sun with darkness.
The gods and the seers healed him;
they saw these *svaras*.
With them they healed him.
Because they healed (*aspṛṇvan*), that is the *svaratva* (the state of being a *svára*) of the *svaras*. Therefore, when these *svaras* occur, it is by means of them that they heal the sun.
In whatever manner a man indeed acts toward the gods, in that same manner the gods act toward him. Therefore, in that these *svarasāman* chants occur, they thereby secure their own selves.
There are seventeen *svarasāmans*; the central day (*viṣuvant*) is the twenty-one-fold.
Prajāpati is indeed the seventeenfold; yonder Āditya is the twenty-onefold. Thus, by means of the father, they encompass the son.
For the father is dearest to the son, and the son is dearest to the father.
If they were to insert another *stoma* here, Agni Vaiśvānara would consume it with his brilliance, and he would take away the offspring. These six are the Svarasāman chants.
There are six seasons.
They thus place him upon the seasons; therefore he goes south for three seasons and north for three. Just as a son would follow after his fathers, so it is for the sake of non-repetition (ajāmitā).
For the son follows after his fathers, who are not of the same womb.
Now these two, the Viśvajit and the Abhijit, are on both sides the strength of the Stomas; indeed, by their strength they support the Viṣuvat day.

Regarding this, they say: "This is like a cutting away of the *stomas*; the *stomas* go astray when one proceeds from the thirty-threefold (*trayastrimśa*) to the seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*). [The answer is:
Having first reached the *Abhijit* before the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, one proceeds by means of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* itself.
The seventeenth day is in the middle; they should place it above the thirty-third.
Thus, because they proceed from the seventeenfold stoma to the seventeenfold stoma, they go from the same to the same; the stomas do not suffer mutilation, nor do they meet with ruin. 386.
Regarding this, they say: "The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is indeed the self, and the seventeenfold stoma is food.
If they were to extract the seventeenfold from the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, they would cast food outside and become hungry."
They should be. One should approach from the thirty-three alone;
for the thirty-three are indeed all the deities.
Indeed, all the deities, having come together, either reach Prajāpati or they do not;
yet they approach him from that very same equality as equals,
for he is the summit of the summit.
For the father is the height;
moreover, he is indeed the transcendence,
for the father is superior to the son.
They are Ukthya sacrifices; for the Ukthas are cattle, [and this is] for the attainment of cattle.

Regarding this they say: "Is it not as if the sacrifice is performed in a reversed manner, when there are two Agniṣṭomas—the Viśvajit and the Abhijit—while the Viṣuvat is an Agniṣṭoma and the Svarasāmans are Ukthyas?"
All [the days] should indeed be performed as Agniṣṭomas.
The Agniṣṭoma is the summit, and the Viṣuvat is the summit; thus, by means of the summit itself, they join summit to summit.
By means of height they ascend to height.
The Agniṣṭoma is brilliance; the Viṣuvant is brilliance. Thus, by means of brilliance they join brilliance together; by means of brilliance they ascend to brilliance.
Now, those known as the Kāmyakīyas, having Ayasthūṇa as their householder, sat for a sacrificial session (*sattra*).

Indradyumna Bhāllaveya set out to run after them, thinking, "I shall cause my son to be praised with the Viṣuvat day. He arrived while they were still performing the praise of one day of the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha.
He said, "You have indeed done well that you performed [the sacrifice].
However, had I been here, I would have arranged the Viṣuvat day differently.
The son said to him, "How, O Venerable One, would you have arranged it?"
He said: "Having first reached the Abhijit after the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, I shall proceed from the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha itself to the Svarasāmans.
The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite is indeed the self; the *svarasāman* days are offspring.
"Offspring indeed depart from us," [they say]. "We are indeed speech."
"Speech has departed from us.
Now, because this *abhijit* occurs in between, it stands having placed a barrier between itself and procreation.
When they pile it up before the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, it is from that which is not separated by a barrier from procreation.
"Let us procreate!
Thus they say; and indeed, they are seventeen in number.
Prajāpati, verily, is seventeenfold.

*vi*: Prajāpati is the progenitor of creatures. *vj*: "He who is the progenitor of creatures—through him may we, who have been procreated, be procreated. *vk*: And these [verses] are indeed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech is procreation; it is from the procreative power of speech [that this occurs].

"Let us procreate," they said. Now, these [stotras] are indeed the *ukthas*; the *ukthas* are cattle, and cattle are food. [They did this] thinking, "Lest we exclude offspring from the eating of food for the sake of cattle."
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said, disregarding the speech of Bhāllabeya: "One should resort to the Abhijit itself.
For that which is this Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha is indeed the Abhijit;
by its very nature, these stomas of the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha are those very [stomas] of this [Abhijit]."
In the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite, there is indeed one *saptadaśa* [stoma];
but in this [twelve-day rite], there are three *saptadaśa*s.
It is by making that very *stoma* into this [threefold form] that they cause it to be born.
In that they produce the seventeen-fold from the seventeen-fold, the seventeen-fold from the seventeen-fold, and the seventeen-fold from the seventeen-fold;
indeed, beyond that, in the Viśvajit, there are three seventeen-fold stomas.
These two, having come together, procreate;
for them, this is the foundation.
One should strive toward victory alone. 388.
The Viṣuvat day is the twenty-first;
for the twenty-first is the Viṣuvat of this world.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first. Indeed, he is established upon all this;
therefore, "Upon that in which he is established, upon all this may we be established."
Therefore, the opening verse belongs to Vāyu and is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
Speech and Vāyu are indeed those two deities among the gods who have not yet attained this [sacrifice].
Thinking, "Since these two among the deities have not yet attained it, may we attain it through them," they proceed.
If Vāyu were not to blow, Agni Vaiśvānara would burn this world with his heat and consume all creatures;

therefore, there is a *pratipad* addressed to Vāyu for the sake of appeasing Agni Vaiśvānara and preventing him from burning. Regarding this, they say: "Those who begin with the *pāvamānī* verses are indeed deprived of their vital breaths."
In that this opening verse is addressed to Vāyu, and since Vāyu is indeed breath, they thus prosper through the vital breaths.
"O Vāyu, the bright [oblation] is offered to thee"— thus it contains the word "bright" (śukra),
for this day is the Śukriya day.
"Of the honey, the first portion, in the heavenly rites"—thus they become foremost in sweetness, possessed of sacred luster (*brahmavarcas*).

"Come for the drinking of Soma"—this is addressed to Soma; by it, the verse becomes one dedicated to Pūṣan. "Desirable, O god, with thy team"—the desirable is indeed food, and the team-borne is food; thus he [attains] this very thing.
They approach him with food and drink.
Indeed, he who approaches a superior bringing [something] welcomes him;
but he who approaches him not bringing [anything] does not welcome him at all.
In that this opening verse is an *anuṣṭubh* addressed to Vāyu, [it is because they think]: "May he greet us; may we succeed in this.

Regarding this, however, they say: "The opening verse should be performed as 'Flow on, the foremost of speech' (*pavasva vāco agriya*). For this world, which consists of these worlds, is indeed speech spread out.
The tip of that [speech] shines forth, which is yonder sun. Therefore,
since this opening verse is "Flow on, O foremost of speech," they proceed toward that very [sun] by means of it.
Just as one would take hold of oneself by means of oneself, even so do they take hold of him by means of his own form. Furthermore,
because this word "pavasva" (purify yourself) is placed below, by that means this wind blows from below, covered over, so that it may not burn [the earth].
Svarbhānu, the son of Asura, pierced the sun with darkness.
The gods and the seers healed him.
They saw these *divākīrtya* sāmans;
with them they struck away his darkness. Therefore, in that these are the *divākīrtya* [sāmans], it is by means of them that they strike away the darkness of the sun.
In whatever manner a human indeed acts toward the gods, in that same manner the gods act toward him.
Therefore, insofar as these *divākīrtya* hymns exist, they drive away the darkness from themselves by means of these very hymns.
The two [hymns] *Bhrāja* and *Abhrāja* occur at the beginning of the two *pavamāna* sections.
They drive away that darkness from his very limbs;
the Mahādivākīrtya is the *pṛṣṭha* chant and the Vikarṇa is the *brahmasāman*;
they drive away that darkness from his very center.
The *daśastobha* *bhāsa* is the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*;
they thus strike away the darkness from his very head.
Yonder sun is the twenty-first, the *viṣuvat*; its rays are indeed the *divākīrtya* hymns.
Now, as these *divākīrtya* hymns come to be, they encircle this very [Agni] with them and cause him to prosper.

Regarding this, they say: "By what means does one who sits for a year-long sacrifice reach the heavenly world? One should reply: "The *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is 'The head of heaven, the messenger of earth'."
"By that"—this one who shines yonder is indeed the head of heaven; it is him they ascend by means of this [chant].
Regarding this, they say: "Verily, those who ascend this [altar] fall away from this world."
"Discontent with the earth," it is said. This world is indeed the discontent of the earth; thus they find firm support in this very world.
The *bhāsa* becomes the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* with ten *stobhas*; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is food. Thus they obtain the *virāj*.

This is for the attainment of food. However, there is a danger that someone else might take away the food from the head of one who performs the Agniṣṭoma-sāman on these verses containing the word "head."
That should be performed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*, and food is the ten-fold *stobha*.
Speech is at the beginning; thus they place this food for themselves at the very beginning of their being. Therefore...
"It should indeed be performed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter," [so it is said].

The *viṣuvat* day is the self of the year, and the two wings are on either side of it; by whichever *abhīvarta* they go, [by that they proceed]. JB 2.391. va. ātmā vai saṃvatsarasya viṣuvān pakṣāv abhito yena ceto 'bhīvartena yanti yena.
From there they descend with the *pragātha*; they should perform both of these at the *viṣuvat*.
They thus attach two wings to themselves for the purpose of flying to the heavenly world; therefore, the wings are attached to the self.

Regarding this they say: "Verily, those who undertake these six-day periods in a forward direction, the *stomas* in a forward direction, the *pṛṣṭhas* in a forward direction, and the *chandas* in a forward direction, fall away from this world.
Therefore, when they undertake the six-day periods in a backward direction after the *viṣuvat*, they thereby establish themselves firmly in this very world.
"Day by day, tomorrow and tomorrow, we [invoke] him; for today, for yesterday, O men, where are you going? Where are you?
O Indra, the threefold shelter! Thus there are *saṃtanaya* *pragāthas*, for the sake of continuity from today and tomorrow.
They continue [the ritual] both today and tomorrow.
They remain for a year that is not exhausted.
Regarding this, they say: "One should praise with these [verses] beginning with *indra kratuṃ na ā bhara*, which are similar [to the ritual], by means of the form of the day.
[As it says: "Just as a father [bestows] upon his sons..."
"Teach us, O much-invoked one, on this path; living, may we attain the light," he says.
Indeed, those who reach the end of the year attain the light of life.
"May unknown, evil-minded, and unpropitious powers not step upon us.
"O Hero, with you we shall cross over the eternal downward-flowing waters.
These eternal downward-flowing waters are indeed the year, the seasons, the months, and the half-months.
The dawns are the days and nights;
by means of this [sacrifice], they indeed overcome them.
The Saudāsas indeed cast Śakti Vāsiṣṭha into the fire.
As he was being cast in, he said: "O Indra, bring us the power of will, just as a father [brings it] to his sons.
This much indeed was the utterance from him.
Then they threw him into the fire.
Then Vasiṣṭha arrived and said,
"What did my son say as he was being thrown?"
They said to him: "O Indra, bring us wisdom, as a father brings it to his sons. This much alone was uttered by him;
then they cast him into the fire. He said:
"Teach us, O Much-invoked, on this path, so that we, living, may attain the light"—this is what he said regarding that which was [offered] to me.
If the son had obtained the latter half-verse, he would not have cast him into the fire, and he would have attained a full lifespan.
He approached that very deity which was the most excellent among the gods.
"Those performers of a sacrificial session (*satrin*) who praise me with this *pragātha* of my son have prospered. This is that *pragātha* preceded by prosperity.
Those who praise with it indeed become prosperous.
The *gauḥ* and *āyuḥ* stomas are employed for the sake of stability;
they are deficient and redundant for the sake of procreation;
they are *vairāja* stomas for the sake of securing food.
There is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed prosperity and the summit;
thus they ascend toward prosperity, the summit, and the heights.
The Chandomas take place; the Chandomas are indeed cattle, for the very purpose of obtaining cattle.
The tenth day takes place; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food—for the very purpose of obtaining the Virāj and the eating of food.
"This one, the thousandfold man" (RV 8.69.3)—they say that before the silent hymn (*tūṣṇīṃstoma*), one should chant these *aticchandas* verses.
The *aticchandas* indeed surpasses all other meters;
those who sit for the year-long sacrifice (*saṃvatsarasad*) surpass others;
thus they find firm support in their own meter.
The *ekākṣaranidhana* Sāman is used.
Speech, indeed, consists of a single syllable.
It is by means of this tenth day that they bring speech to completion.
"Go! is the *nidhana*; for the cow is indeed all food;
it is for the attainment of all food. Regarding this, they say: "The *anuṣṭubh* would be left unstudied if they were to perform this here."
"Let us not surpass speech with our praise"—thus they praise silently with the mind by means of the *tūṣṇīṃ-stoma*.
"In this [case], it is indeed perfected through speech.
Therefore, this [silent praise] should not be performed here. //392//
"Should we release [the fires] or should we not release them? they deliberate.
Regarding this, they say: "One must certainly release them."
He who goes without release either cuts himself off or perishes.
Those who do not let go proceed as if toward non-release. Therefore, when they let go of the full-moon sacrifices, it is for the sake of safety.
Whatever one pours out when it is full, that indeed either falls apart or is shattered. This year is full; therefore, when they omit the full-moon sacrifices, it is for the sake of safety.

For from what is deficient, semen is emitted; from what is deficient, offspring are born. This year is full. Therefore, when they omit the full-moon sacrifices, they thereby create a world out of semen for the sake of procreation.
From what is deficient, the vital breaths depart.
This year is Prajāpati;
its vital breaths are the full-moon sacrifices.
When they omit the full-moon sacrifices, they omit the vital breaths of Prajāpati.
For the full-moon stomas are indeed the gods.
When they omit the full-moon sacrifices, [they think]: "Who is fit to chant the praises for the gods? (393)
JB 2.394 |va On the day they should release [the sacrifice], they should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Vasus in the forenoon.
At midday, they should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Rudras;
in the afternoon, they should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Ādityas.
These deities indeed possess the pressings as their share; thus, they do not depart from the pressing, nor from the deities.
They enter within.
Prajāpati is this year;
its out-breaths and in-breaths are the full-moon and new-moon sacrifices.
In that the full-moon and new-moon sacrifices are omitted, they omit the out-breath and in-breath of Prajāpati himself.
They undertake this twenty-four-night rite at the end of the year. Moreover, some say that only the full-moon sacrifices should be omitted.

The full moon night is indeed the vessel for the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and the new moon night is the vessel for the in-breath (*apāna*). People live by means of the out-breath which is external, and by means of the in-breath which is internal.
Therefore, when they omit the full moon sacrifices, they live by means of the out-breath which is external and the in-breath which is internal.
Thus it is said.
They perform this very [rite] after the twelve-night period.
Regarding this, Āruṇi said to Aṣāḍha Sāvayasa, who was letting loose [the sacrificial animal]: "The Hotṛ remained in the breach for a year.
He replied: "Do not speak thus to me; we indeed approached him from above for twelve nights.
He then recited that [verse] to him.
"For whether it be greater or smaller, it is indeed not equal to that"—
"In another way, the skull is laid down so as to be without a gap"—
thus, indeed, do I consider this regarding the Hotṛ priest.
I consider a year to be a flaw for those who omit [the *sattras*];
moreover, their sacrificial session (*sattra*) thus becomes as if undertaken in a contrary manner.
Indeed, the sacrifice is just like a hare.
He who seeks to obtain the release of the hare does not catch it;
but he who seeks to obtain it without releasing it, he indeed catches it.
Those who release [the animal] seek only its release.
"Therefore, it must not be omitted at all.
Then Kusurubinda Auḍālaki used to say: "It may be omitted, and yet it may not."

Whatever [stotras] they might omit on this day, they should calculate them and perform them on the following day; thus, what was omitted is indeed not omitted. Furthermore, however many days they might omit, having counted those, they should perform them after the Atirātra.
[The view is: "They should indeed be omitted, and not [performed].
Now Bhāllabeya used to say: "The *ukthas* alone should be omitted;
for the *ukthas* are indeed offspring and cattle."
They thus release the offspring as cattle. Moreover, it is just as if one were to let air out of a leather bag with the foot; such is that.
Regarding this, they say: "It must indeed be released."
This year is Prajāpati.

Its joints are these vital breaths, namely the full-moon and new-moon days. Just as a leather bag might burst when overinflated, even so does this Prajāpati burn up the cattle if he is not released [at these times].

In that they omit both the full-moon and the new-moon sacrifices, they thereby extend his limbs, his vital breaths, and his joints, thinking: "Lest the year, burning against us, should injure us. On the following day, they should perform the *pratipad* with the verse, "They urge him on, the maidens.
That is just as one would re-inflate a leather bag that has been emptied.

“They blow the *bākura* skin-bag; there is honey of three kinds from the bees. The *bākura* skin-bag is indeed the year, the threefold [honey] is the sacrifice, and the Brāhmaṇas are the bees; they are the ones who produce this honey.
Now Sirinda Pālāli used to say: “One should indeed release [the sacrifice] on the new moon day alone.”
On the new moon night, indeed, the deities released this [sacrifice], thinking,
"Let us release it following the release of the deities.
For these two nights of the year— the full moon and the new moon— are indeed the sacrificial nights of the year.
If they were to omit both the full-moon and the new-moon sacrifices, they would diminish the year by the sacrifice.
Therefore, the Agniṣṭoma should be performed as the Trivṛt;
because its stotras are deficient, it is neither omitted nor not omitted.
Now, Nagari Jānaśruteya used to say: "Having approached by means of the *ekatrika* alone, [the sacrifice] is both abandoned and not abandoned.
This is because its hymns (*stotra*) are, as it were, marked with dog-prints; thus it is both abandoned and not abandoned.
Then Āruṇi used to say: "By means of these two *stomas*, the *go* and the *āyus*, it is both abandoned and not abandoned."
Of those two, that which has fewer hymns is the one by which it is abandoned; that which has more is the one by which it is not abandoned.
Therefore, they say, "One should approach these very two.
The Adhvaryu, having taken the cup, runs forward.
He says, "Turn back!
Having uttered the *hiṃ* sound, they go out toward the east and stand in front of the Āgnīdhra shed for the sake of the Viśve Devas.
They praise with the *vrata* chant.
They thus announce to all the gods, "We have succeeded. Having stepped forward toward the east while looking at the *cātvāla* pit, they praise with the *krośa* chant.
When the gods had reached the end, their sensory power and vigor departed.
They recovered it by means of the *krośa* chant alone.
Those who reach the conclusion of the year go, as it were, to the very end.
Now, as for the fact that they chant with the *krośa* [chanting method], it is for the sake of securing sensory power and vigor.
Then follows the *anukrośa*.
When the gods reached the heavenly world by means of the three-day rite, this was their third day.
The Vairūpa is the Vyāra.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"The gods, dwelling together in the Vairūpa, took their stand upon it; that indeed became their Vyāra."
"Having uttered the *hiṃ* sound, they ascended again and all shook off old age from their bodies.
This is a verse concerning that very [sacrifice].

"When they stood together on their journey, crying out 'hiṃ' while striking at what was struck down in the Vairūpa [chant], they created that Sāman which is the abode of the gods; by means of it, the gods attained immortality.
Thus.
When they had gone to the heavenly world, the Creator said to his sons, "Do not be concerned; I shall provide for you right here. (JB 2.399)
He established the city of Vaidhatra in this eastern direction; Prācīnayogya is said to have been his domestic priest. He established Adharāhi Vaidhatra in this southern direction.
His domestic priest was Dakṣiṇāhuryāyaṇa.
He established the Pañca Vaidhātra in this western direction. His domestic priest was Pratīcīnāhuryāyaṇa.
He placed the Vaidhātra [sacrifice] in this northern direction, toward the north.
Udiyāyana was his domestic priest (purohita) in the north.
Those gods said to Vidhātṛ: "If you have established this in such a way, then look after us accordingly."
"May we go safely to the heavenly world," he thought;
with this cry, he looked after them.

"O Indra, at the pressed Soma juices, *hoyi-hūho*!"—with these words he drove them away. They said, "He has indeed surpassed us completely; look upon us in such a way that you may grant us a share in this world."
With this very cry of "O Indra, come hither! Come hither! he assigned them a share in this world.
Thereupon, indeed, they became firmly established in both these worlds. By the *krośa* they went to the heavenly world, and by the *anukrośa* they became established in this [world].
Those who, knowing thus, chant with the *krośa* and *anukrośa*, find firm support in both of these worlds:
by the *krośa* they go to the heavenly world, and by the *anukrośa* they find firm support in this world. 400.
They praise with the *apipakṣa* of Agni for the success of the sacrificial session.
It is thus that they announce to the gods, "We have succeeded," for the sake of Agni himself.
On both sides of the two *havirdhāna* sheds [they chant] with the two wings of the vow (*vratapakṣa*).

Indeed, those who consecrate themselves for the year-long rite consecrate themselves for the sake of the heavenly world. Therefore, when they chant with the two wings of the vow, they place the two wings upon their own self for the sake of the heavenly world.
For the falling of the world;
therefore, two wings are placed upon the self.
They praise with the out-breath and the in-breath.

By the out-breath (*prāṇa*) in front, by the in-breath (*apāna*) behind. Regarding this they say: "Those who [neglect] that which belongs to the sacrifice (*yajñīya*) indeed fail in their vital breaths. The parallels at 1,164 (69,57) and 3,301 (479,2527) have *yajñīyasya*, although *yajñiyasya* with a short vowel [is also attested].
It is also stated: "Whether they cause the *karman* to fall or do not cause it to fall—who indeed knows whether they cause it to fall or not?
When they praise with the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*), they thus prosper through the out-breath and the in-breath.
They praise with a *śloka* and an *anuśloka*:
with the *śloka* in front and the *anuśloka* behind.

Now, when they praise with the *śloka*, [they do so thinking], "May we obtain the merit of a *śloka*. And when they praise with the *anuśloka*, [it is so that] "the merit of an *anuśloka* may arise following those who have arisen.
They praise by means of concealment and non-concealment.
By concealment in front, and by further concealment behind.
Regarding this they say: "Those who perform the year-long rite indeed ascend toward something superior.
In that they praise with concealment, they thus conceal themselves from what is superior; and by means of further concealment, they ascend toward it.
"Whatever we have done here, may we not be deprived of that"—thus it is;
in this way, their [act] becomes approved.
They chant within the *sadas* with the twenty-six-syllable *nidhana* of the Aṅgirases.

Behind the Udumbara post they announce this to the Aṅgirases and to the gods: "We have succeeded! Having made it twenty-fivefold, they chant for the sake of not failing the vow; and furthermore, because of the *prati*.
They praise with the *bhūtecchandas* and the *saṃvrata*:
"O Indra, thy two bay horses are tawny; even so are thy beard and thy two bay steeds.
"The poets, those men who dwell in the forest, praise thee."
"O Indra, eat with supernatural power! O Maghavan, O Indra, eat!
"Indra is purified by the *trasara*.
"The buttocks again and again, the *trasara*-buttocks."
Thus it is said.
Indeed, one limb of this [sacrifice] remained unstudied, namely the buttocks. With that unstudied limb they praise him.

Those who praise with this indeed become possessed of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Regarding this, they say: "For what purpose are these exhilarations (*parimāda*) performed? Indeed, the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*) is like an autumnal bull.
Just as they would immolate an autumnal bull after surrounding it with spears, even so do they immolate the Mahāvrata with the Parimarīs, so that the vow may not be exhausted.
And just as there are here on a man’s hair, nails, body hair, and beard, so too is this [the Parimarīs] for him.
"Moreover, that which is here around a person— cows, horses, goats, sheep, rice, and barley— that indeed is this of his.
There are eighty-seven stotriyas of the Mahāvrata and thirteen parimādas; that makes one hundred.
Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years, a hundred powers, and a hundredfold vigor; [this is] for the attainment of that very power and vigor.
Then these voices resound: the small drums,
the *parimādas*, the *karkarī*, the *alābu*, the *vakrā*, the *kapiśīrṣṇī*, the *aiṣīkī*, the *apāghāṭalīkā*,
the lute (*vīṇā*), the *kaśyapī*, the earth-drum (*bhūmidundubhi*) struck with a bull-hide, and the arrow.
The hundred-stringed lute;
the drums are stretched out in the intermediate space and resound;
the water-jars move about.
They utter these words for the attainment of all speech, so that they may attain the entirety of speech, thinking, "We shall attain the whole of speech.
Now, when the earth-drum, covered with a bull's hide, resounds, the bull is indeed the supreme speech.
It is for the attainment of this very supreme speech.
The drums stretched out in the intermediate space resound; by this, they attain that speech which is in the intermediate space.
The water-jars with their mouths turned upward go around; for the head is indeed the manifest form of heaven.
Whatever speech is in that [lute], they obtain that very thing by means of it.
They strike a lute with a hundred strings; for man has a lifespan of a hundred years, a hundred faculties, and a hundredfold vigor;
it is for the attainment of that very faculty and vigor. 404.
At the southern edge of the altar, they cause a Māgadha man and a harlot to unite for the sake of pairing and procreation.
He who knows thus is born through a pair.
