They cause the noble class and the Śūdra class to exert themselves one above the other upon the Cātvāla mound, either on the skin of a goat or on a bull's hide.
Of these two, the noble class remains within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), while the Śūdra class remains outside the altar (bahirvedi).
By means of the noble class, they cause the Śūdra class to be surpassed.
The gods and the asuras contended for that sun in yonder world.
The gods wrested it from the asuras.
When they cause the Śūdra caste to be surpassed by the Ārya caste, they thereby wrest this very [sun] from their hateful rival.
Of these two, one reviles while the other praises. He who reviles purifies them;
then he who praises bestows power and vigor upon them once they have been purified.
They run the race. The race is indeed the highest greatness; it is for the attainment of that highest greatness.
They become equipped with armor.
For when one is girt for battle, splendor is indeed supreme;
thus they place supreme splendor within themselves. They carry full jars around the Mārjālīya fire-altar, for the attainment of the full.
"Great, great, great!"—this is for the attainment of greatness.
"This is honey, this is honey"—for the Mahāvrata is indeed made like honey for the gods;
honey is the highest essence, and it is for the attainment of that very highest essence.
Regarding this, they say: "The masters were about to eat when [the singers] went around singing, 'O great one, this honey!
"They went around singing only 'O great one!
Śāṭyāyani, however, said: "When one truly exists, when one is present, then one becomes one who may be eaten."
"What would they sing for if [the Soma] were non-existent? "They should go around singing, 'O great one, this is honey! Thus they went around. 405/ JB 2.406.
They go forward, intending to chant the stotra. The Adhvaryu, intending to chant with the Trivṛt head-formula in the Gāyatra meter, sits down in front of the two *havirdhāna* carts.
The Maitrāvaruṇa, intending to chant with the Pañcadaśa side-formula in the Bṛhat meter, sits down to the south.
The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin sits down to the north, intending to chant with the Rathantara-stotra on the seventeen-fold side;
the Neṣṭṛ sits down in the midst of the wives, intending to chant with the Bhadra-stotra on the twenty-one-fold tail;
and the Udgātṛ mounts the Udumbara post, intending to chant with the Rājana-stotra on the twenty-five-fold body—for food is indeed vigor.

[He prepares] an udumbara [branch] for the attainment of vigor and the eating of food. He consecrates it [with the mantra]: "The *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] are your two front feet; the *vairūpa* and *vairāja* [sāmans] are the two hind feet;
the *śākvara* and *raivata* [sāmans] are the side-pieces; the meters are the covering; the *yajus* formulas are the weaving; sit upon the pleasant seat."
"May he sit upon the well-seated seat.
This is the descent for that [altar].
"May the great heaven and earth sprinkle this sacrifice for us."
"May they ferry us across with their supports," so [it is said].
They all utter the *hiṃ* sound at once.
Therefore, a person is born fully conscious.
Indeed, they utter the *hiṃ* sound following the *hiṃ* sound of the Udgātṛ priest.
Therefore, the limbs come under the control of the self.
The Adhvaryu chants the *udgītha* with the threefold head in the *gāyatra* meter;
he thus restores that head.
Therefore, this head is set back.
(v) By means of [the verses] directed away, [it is placed] so as not to turn back again.
(vi) Therefore, this head indeed turns away; "not this, not this."
He chants the *udgītha* with nine [syllables].
Therefore, this head does not become fat when [the body] becomes fat, nor does it become thin when [the body] becomes thin.
The *maitrāvaruṇa* chants the *bṛhat* [sāman] with a fifteen-fold [stoma] as the *udgītha*.
He replaces this arm;
therefore, this arm is restored. With verses directed away [from him], so that there is no returning again.
Therefore, this arm bends back and stretches forward. He makes three into fifteen;
therefore, this arm becomes fat when one becomes fat, and it becomes thin when one becomes thin.
The *bṛhat* is indeed vigor; the fifteenfold [stoma] is vigor.
Therefore, when one chants the *bṛhat* with the fifteenfold [stoma] as the wing, for that reason this [right] arm is more vigorous.
And for that reason, birds fly along following the right wing.
This, indeed, is the form of man, namely the Bṛhat; this is the form of woman, namely the Rathantara.
Because they chant with the Bṛhat from here [the right] and with the Rathantara from here [the left], therefore a man lies on the right side of a woman.
The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin chants the Udgītha with the seventeenfold Rathantara-stotra.
He replaces this arm;
therefore, this arm is replaced.
With verses directed away [from him], so that there is no returning again.
Therefore, he bends this arm and extends it.
He makes three [fingers] seventeen.
Therefore, this arm becomes fat when [the body] becomes fat, and it becomes thin when [the body] becomes thin. 407.
The Neṣṭṛ chants with the twenty-one-fold tail as the auspicious [Sāman];
he thus restores that tail.
Therefore, this tail is firmly fixed.
Because [he recites] with verses directed away, there is no returning again; therefore, this tail both bends together and extends forward.

He makes the three *satī*s into twenty-one. Therefore, this tail becomes fat when [the body] becomes fat, and it becomes thin when [the body] becomes thin. The Udgātṛ sings the *udgītha* with the twenty-five-fold self by means of the *rājana* chant.
He restores this very self;
therefore, this self is restored. With verses directed away [from him], he does not turn back again.
Therefore, this [body] contracts itself and expands itself.
It makes the three [breaths] into twenty-five;
therefore, as this self grows fat, it follows along and grows fat, and as it becomes thin, it follows along and becomes thin.
With each of these stotras, they approach the Udgātṛ;
with them, the Udgātṛ sings the *udgītha*;
thus, he restores the limbs to his very self.
Therefore, the limbs are established within the self.
Thus, he sings the *udgītha* within the self.
Therefore, this [self] lies, as it were, within the self. 408.
Prajāpati, while creating offspring,
became exhausted; from him the deities departed.
Indra alone among the deities did not abandon him.
He said to Indra, "How indeed might I return from here? Indra replied, "What, pray, do you still possess?"
"Indeed, these two, prāṇa and apāna, are mine," he said. Because he said, "They are mine (me)," that is the origin of the name *stoma*.
His own people praise him, thinking, "He is the best among us. He who knows thus [attains this].
He said to him: "Praise the year with these very two. To him who had praised it with these two, all the deities descended from above at the end of the year.

He praised for a year with these two [sāmans]. While he was praising with these very two, at the end of the year, all the deities approached him from above, having extracted the essence of the quarters, the essence of the waters, the essence of the Veda, and the essence of food.
"Let us take up the great vow! Let us take up the great vow!"—saying this, they took it up.
Because they said, "Let us take up the great vow," that is the reason for the Mahāvrata's name, "the Great Vow.
They then bestowed it upon him.
He performed the Mahāvrata rite for them.
They rejoiced, saying, "He has performed the Mahāvrata! He has performed the Mahāvrata!
Therefore, on this day they indeed rejoice.
For the deities indeed rejoiced in this.
Regarding this, they say: "One should approach the Viṣuvat [day] in the middle of the year.
Food, indeed, is the vow.
For food, when eaten in the middle, satisfies. Regarding this, they also say: "Those who [perform it] in the middle of the year obtain only half of the food."
At the equinox, they perform the Mahāvrata rite. The year ripens all food;
therefore, it should be performed at the end of the year for the sake of securing all food.
Now, Nāgarī Jānaśruteya used to say: "This Mahāvrata is indeed fierce and of middling power.

For when one is fierce and of middling power, he overthrows all others and then lies alone. Therefore, it should be undertaken only at the end of the year, for the sake of securing the entirety of food."
That [brick] becomes the twenty-fifth.
For the year consists of twenty-four half-months;
the twenty-fifth is food; thus, by means of the twenty-fifth, food itself is placed [therein].
Just as one might approach a cow that is full uddered and milk her, even so do they milk food from this twenty-fifth [syllable].
Regarding this, they say: "The *tvaṣṭṛ-śāviya* should indeed be made the *pṛṣṭha* chant of this day.
For when the gods first gathered their vow (*vrata*), that became the *tvaṣṭṛ-śāviya*. Thus, when the *tvaṣṭṛ-śāviya* serves as the *pṛṣṭha* of this day, it is the vow itself made manifest.
They approach.
Regarding this, they also say: "The *stobhas* of Taṇu Śāvyāya are indeed of poor intelligence; the *padavṛttis* are the *prastāvas*, the *devatās* are the *pratihāras*, and the *nidhanas*."
"The Vāmadevya-sāman alone should be made the *pṛṣṭha* of this day. Now, the Vāmadevya is indeed the self of the vow.
Just as one might arrive at home and not find it, such is that which is the *pṛṣṭha* of this day other than the Vāmadevya.
They should perform it.
Regarding this, they say: "The *svāra* [sāman] is not for the sake of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra].
Therefore, the *rājana* [sāman] alone should be made the *pṛṣṭha* of this day; that is its proper place.
By means of the *rājan* [sāman], Prajāpati attained sovereignty, lordship,
and overlordship over his subjects. Thinking, "By that same means by which Prajāpati attained sovereignty, lordship, and overlordship over his subjects,
may we also attain sovereignty, lordship, and overlordship over our subjects," [they performed it].
Indeed, this *vāmadevya* [sāman] is, as it were, hidden when it is the *rājana*.
The *rājana* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*;
the *vāmadevya* is the *maitrāvaruṇa-sāman*.
The *vāmadevya* with five finales is the *brahmasāman*. They proceed having joined the self in the middle by means of the *vāmadevya*, preceded by the *sāman*. 411/ JB 2.412.
That [sāman] has five *stobhas*, five metrical feet, five deities, five *pratihāras*,
and five *nidhanas*. Whatever is fivefold— whether it be the sacrifice, the cattle, the food, the five seasons, or whatever else— is [encompassed by it].
And five by five; this is the supernatural power of all that, its attainment.
The *vāmadevya* with five *nidhanas* becomes the *brahmasāman*;
for they praise with the vow in five ways indeed.
That [metre] occurs among the *aticchandāḥ* verses, namely in those beginning with “The buffalo at the *trikadruka* [sacrifices], drinking the barley-mash.
For the *aticchandas* indeed surpasses the other metres;
and these [who perform the *saṃvatsara-sattra*] surpass others.
Verily, they find firm support in their own metre.
Now, that [verse] becomes *aticchandas* (exceeding the metres), containing the words "here" (*iha*) and "hither" (*ehi*); it is the form of the end, for this day is indeed the end.
Regarding this, they say: "The *ilānda* should be made the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* for this day.
Indeed, by means of the *ilānda*, Prajāpati bestowed *irā*—that is, food—to be eaten—upon his offspring. Therefore, by that same means, one bestows *irā*—that is, food—to be eaten.
"Let us rise up after having enclosed [the fire]," they said. Therefore, it occurs in the *aticchandas* verses;
for the *aticchandas* indeed surpasses all other meters.
These surpass others who sit for a year-long session;
they thus find firm footing in their own very *chandas*.
That occurs in the verses addressed to Vaiśvānara;
for this is indeed the hymn of Vaiśvānara. It occurs in verses consisting of eighty syllables, [with the thought]: "May we attain."
The Atichandas metre is indeed like the ocean, like something inexhaustible. [Thinking], "May we praise with this which is like the ocean, like something inexhaustible," they praised.
That becomes the bird.
For the bird is indeed the vow (vrata) of this day.
He says, "The vow," for the vow is food; it is for the attainment of food. He says, "Svarga," for the attainment of the heavenly world.
"O birds," he says; for these very vital breaths, having become birds, attain the heavenly world.
Regarding this, they say: "The Vāravantīya should be made the Agniṣṭoma-sāman for this day.
Prajāpati created cattle.

Once created, they departed from him. He cut off a branch of the *varaṇa* tree and warded them off with the *vāravantīya* chant. Because he warded them off (*avārayata*), that is the reason for the name *vāravantīya*.
Therefore, they say that choosing [the priests] is healing.

Now, when the Vāravantīya becomes the Agniṣṭoma-sāman of this day, [it is because they think: "That which we have warded off by means of this rite, may that be propitiated for us at the end by means of the Vāravantīya."
That which is "ehi-vat" (containing the word "come") becomes "iha-vat" (containing the word "here"), for this is the form of the end;
for this day is indeed the end.
Moreover, they say: whatever other speech does not surpass [this], that is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman to be performed on this day.
Indeed, no other speech surpasses the *yajñāyajñīya*.
For the *yajñāyajñīya* is speech;
how indeed could speech surpass speech?
Therefore, for this day, the Yajñāyajñīya alone should be made the Agniṣṭoma-sāman. The vow is indeed food; the vow is indeed prosperity.
"By means of the vow (*vrata*), food is eaten; by means of the vow, prosperity (*śrī*) is attained.
Regarding this, they say: "One should undertake it only at the end of the year;
for the vow is known to be difficult to maintain from the moment one is born."
That becomes the twenty-fifth.
For the year consists of twenty-four half-months, and food is the twenty-fifth; thus, by means of the twenty-fifth [brick], food itself is established.

The person (*puruṣa*), indeed, consists of twenty-five parts. They say this is the hymn of praise (*stotra*) of the person: there are ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, four limbs, and the body itself as the twenty-fifth; these six sets of joints [make up the remaining parts]. These six, these six, these six...
These [limbs] are the self as the twenty-fifth; these twelve are the enclosing-stones, and these twelve are the self as the twenty-fifth.
Verily, by this they consecrate the person and produce the person.
Regarding this, they say: "This entire day should be approached as consisting of twenty-five parts."

They would resort to the twenty-fifth as the head, the twenty-fifth as one wing, the twenty-fifth as the other wing, the twenty-fifth as the tail, and the twenty-fifth as the body; such is the attainment of the vow: "May we attain the vow limb by limb."
Therefore, Harjjishva Vātavāta used to say: "This is indeed one single *stotra*; having spread it out fivefold, they should chant it.
They should chant the head with five [verses], another wing with five, the other wing with five, the tail with five, and the body with five."
In the same way, the twenty-fifth alone does not exceed [the others];
thus is the attainment of the vow.
Now Āruṇi used to say: "Indeed, no other limbs are equal to the self;
nor is the self equal to the other limbs. For a person is fashioned by what is unequal, yet he is equal through that which is unequal."
"In whatever manner this [Vrata] is, in that very manner it is to be approached.
"The Brahman is indeed the head of the Vrata; heaven and earth are its two wings; the intermediate space is its body; the Sāman is its tail.
"The Gāyatra is indeed the head of the Vrata, for that is the Brahman."
The Bṛhat and Rathantara are the wings, for they are heaven and earth; the Vāmadevya is the body, for that is the intermediate space;
the Yajñāyajñīya is the tail, for that is the Sāman.
They praise the head with nine [verses].
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person;
this is the complete measure of the vital breaths, the prosperity of the vital breaths.
Upon it they place the Gāyatra-sāman. The Gāyatra-sāman is indeed breath;
thus they place breath in the head.
Therefore, the vital breath is placed in the head. Having crept out toward the west, they praise with the hymn "The head of Arka.
Those [verses] are indeed the necks; thus, it is as if he sings while describing these worlds.
And thus he joins the head with the self; therefore, the head and the self are joined together.
Regarding this, they say: "It becomes non-twenty-fivefold; it exceeds [the proper number]; therefore, this should not be performed here. 415.
JB 2.416 |va They approach the Rathantara with this threefold (trivṛt) stoma.
vb The threefold is indeed the Brahman, and the Rathantara is food.
By means of the *brahman* alone they secure that food.
Upon it they superimpose the fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*).
The fifteenfold hymn-form is indeed a thunderbolt, and the *rathantara* is food.
By means of the thunderbolt itself, they thus encompass that food.
They approach the seventeen-fold [stoma] by means of this fifteen-fold [stoma].
The fifteen-fold is indeed the thunderbolt; the seventeen-fold is the clan (viś).
With the thunderbolt itself they thus strengthen that people;
upon it they superimpose the *brahmasāman*;
the *bṛhat* is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*).
They thus place the ruling power (*kṣatra*) over the people (*viś*). Therefore, the *kṣatriya* is placed over the people.
Regarding this, they say: "One should chant the *bṛhat* [sāman] from here, and the *rathantara* from there."
"This entire world indeed moves toward [the sacrificer] as if toward his own breath," so [it is said].
Regarding this, Kīja Vākāyana used to say: "Those who chant the Bṛhat from here and the Rathantara from here perform their food-eating from behind."
The *rathantara* is indeed food.
From the south, one approaches having obtained food.
Therefore, they chant with the *bṛhat* from here, and with the *rathantara* from here, for the sake of obtaining food.
And that which is this fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*), it is indeed for the purpose of counter-attack. Therefore, birds fly around following the left wing.
By means of all this, they reach the twenty-onefold hymn-form as their firm foundation.

There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first. Indeed, he is established upon this whole world; therefore, he attains a firm foundation upon that whole world upon which he is established.
They establish this; upon it they superimpose the Bhadra Sāman. JB 2.417.418. va.
Offspring indeed is prosperity. From the tail offspring are born.
It is from the very tail that they thus bestow offspring upon the organ of generation for the sake of procreation.
In that regard, they say that what is beneficial (*śreyas*) should be performed. Offspring indeed is the auspicious; offspring is what is beneficial for offspring.
Moreover, he who knows this beholds offspring within his own offspring.
Regarding this, they say: "One should praise with the entire [Sāman] all at once, having made it conform to one's age.
For when a bird flies away, it flies away having joined all its limbs together;
and when it settles down, it settles down having drawn all its limbs into itself.
In that they chant with the whole [hymn] all at once, it is just as when a bird flies away: it flies away having joined all its limbs together; such is that.
Then, in that they approach with each individual verse of praise, it is just as when a bird settles down: it settles down with all its limbs individually.
Having composed himself, he should sit down; such indeed is that.
Now Bhāllabeya used to say: "On this day, no one other than the Udgātṛ should perform the priestly office with the Sāman.
For this day is prosperity, and the Udgātṛ is prosperity."

"O you! If on this day another should perform the priestly office of the Udgātṛ with the Sāman, one should address those [verses] without being interrupted; one should ascend [the chant] without having already ascended it; otherwise there would be a confusion of the good and the bad. Therefore, one should conclude by moving around in succession, or one should approach with each individual hymn of praise."
In this case, however, they point out that it results in the twenty-nine-fold hymn-form (*stoma*).

Regarding this, they say: "The twenty-nine-fold *stoma* is accomplished; [the cow] lowing follows her own herd, O Jānañjaya; the bull [goes] among the cows of the performer of the thousand-fold sacrifice, as if the stalks of the *śalaka* grass were scattering. Indeed, these [verses] proceed according to their respective order.
“They attain,” he says.

Indeed, one attains the head in the head, the wings in the wings, the tail in the tail, and this self in the self. Thus the twenty-ninefold *stoma* is accomplished; it is indeed to be performed in this manner. 417.
The Udgātṛ ascends the throne-seat (āsandī), the Hotṛ the swing (pleṅkha), and the two Adhvaryus the two mats (kūrca); the other Hotrakas likewise sit upon mats.
Regarding this they say: "The consecrated one must not mount the throne-seat.
For on this day they indeed arrive having already risen.
And that which is the tenth day is the *avāva* (the day of non-singing); it is precisely there that the *uktha*s [are performed].
"Having mounted this very [chariot]," they say; for prosperity indeed moves through the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*);
thus is the attainment of prosperity.
The lute (*vāṇa*) has a hundred strings.
Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years, a hundred faculties, and a hundred powers; [this is] for the attainment of those very faculties and powers.
Regarding this, they say: "A lute with a hundred strings should not be made, for when the Brāhmaṇas did not know its continuity."
"Or rather, this continuity is broken; I enter the assemblies of kings now speaking as I used to, so what would they do now that it is not as it was before?
To this they say: "Why indeed is it now not as it was before?"
In ancient times, it is said, they used to go to the heavenly world after praising with a single *sāman*; moreover, one should emerge from the final ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) in this very manner.
Thus, the lute (*vāṇa*) has a hundred strings for the sake of the completeness of speech.

Its lineage is this: *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, "speak, speak, speak, speak, speak! O wide one, broad one, easy path, easy traveler, action, instrument, agent, about to act! Speak forth the Vedic speech of Indra, which is lofty, multiform, and grants a hundred-year life, O divine voice!"
Then Indra scraped with that blade of grass and a branch of cane, saying: "The mind is light," "Speech is truth," and "The mind is auspicious.
The sons of Ahīnasa Āśvatthi approached him and said, "O Venerable One, we are indeed performing a sacrificial session; please instruct us.
He said, "Do not speak thus.
The year is indeed difficult to master."
"Just as the spokes are fixed in the nave of a chariot wheel, even so all deaths are fixed in the year.
"Then you should speak thus," he said.
They said, "You alone are indeed our physician; you are the expiation; instruct us accordingly.
That was pleasing to him.
He said, "If you say this, then establish yourselves upon the six foundations."
Go forth from these six green-hued [regions]!
Ascend the four-wheeled, rescuing chariot! Go forth along the direct paths to the heavenly world!
Do not leap over the year’s extent;
enter into the divine pair;
do not be left behind by the visible caravans.
|vo Do not cause the sacrifice to fall from the infallible.
|vp Approach the future of the sacrifice. |vq Approach speech that is endowed with truth.
Yoke the most excellent [steeds] for battle; attain ever-increasing prosperity. Establish yourselves in the heavenly world;
go from the village to the forest.
From knowledge, may I not fall away;
from divine marriage, may I not fall away; from sacrifice, may I not fall away.
He instructed them in these [matters].
They said, "You have instructed us in this as if it were something obscure. Teach us in such a way that we may understand it. 419.

He said: "What I told you was: 'Establish yourselves in the six foundations,' and 'Do not cause me to fall away from the openings of the *pavamāna* chants that possess the *nidhana*. That is exactly what I told you."
This, indeed, is the foundation of the Sāman, namely the *nidhana*.
These six [Sāmans] have a *nidhana*; the year consists of six seasons.
Just as one might ascend a tree by means of steps, even so does one reach heaven by means of these *nidhanas* of the Sāman.
They go ascending to the world.
Therefore, the *nidhana*s should not be displaced from the openings of the *pavamāna* [laud].
Now, as for what you said—"Do not step beyond the six golden-footed ones"—that was indeed your *iḍā*-division.
"I said, 'Grasp the great *iḍā*s!'—that is exactly what I said to you.
These are those six *ḍharitmatī*s.
Just as one would go wherever he wishes to go after yoking six female mules (*aśvatarī*s) that are *ḍharitmatī*s, so it is.
Thus, by means of these *iḍā*-divisions, they attain the heavenly world.
Therefore, one should begin with the *bṛhatī* verses using the *iḍā* formulas alone.

Now, as for what I said to you: "Mount the four-wheeled ship that carries across. I spoke these very four *bṛhatī* verses to you: "O Soma, flow forth for the feast of the gods; pour out the pressed juice on every side"; "The living Somas [flow] toward [the goal]"; "Being purified, O Soma, [flow] in a stream. These are those four *bṛhatīs* I spoke.
These Bṛhatī verses are indeed a four-wheeled vehicle that carries one across.
Just as one would go wherever one wishes to go by means of a four-wheeled vehicle that carries one across, even so do they go to the heavenly world by means of these Bṛhatīs.
Moreover, this indeed is the chariot of the gods.
Just as one would go wherever one wishes to go by means of a well-yoked chariot of the gods, even so do they go to the heavenly world by means of these *bṛhatī* verses.

Therefore, these very [verses] should be made into *bṛhatī*s. Now, as for what I said to you— "Do not lead me astray from the direct paths to the heavenly world"— that was indeed the *auśanaka* and *kāva* [verses] that I spoke to you.

This indeed is the direct path to the heavenly world, namely the Auśanaka. The Auśana hymn is at the beginning, and the Kava hymn is at the end. These two, like a father and son, have fashioned this ship.

Just as a father and son, steering a boat, might cause it to reach the other shore safely and without harm, even so do these two, Auśanaka and Kāva, reach the end of the journey safely and without harm. Therefore, Auśanaka and Kāva are let loose [as sacrificial victims]. 421.

JB 2.422 |va| "Now, as for what I said to you: 'You have overstepped the span of the year; either perform the *abhīvarta* during the *pavamāna* [laud], or [use] a raft'—that is exactly what I said to you."
This indeed is the pervasion of the year: namely, the seasons, the months, and the junctions of the seasons.
Regarding this, they say: "The seasons, the months, and the junctions of the seasons—these are indeed just day and night. Day and night, verily, are the pervasion of the year.
Therefore, a raft must be made.
Indeed, the cow floats, the elephant floats, and the man floats; but the raft does not float. Thus, by means of this non-sinking raft, we shall cross over that which has been pervaded by the year.
Regarding this, they say: "There is a reproach; they indeed censure one who is 'floating and submerged'.
For whoever is defeated or loses, of him they say, "He has been scalded.
Therefore, the *abhīvarta* alone should be performed.
Its finale consists of a single syllable.
Speech, indeed, consists of a single syllable;
and speech is the entirety of Brahman.

Thus, with this entire Brahman, just as one might pass over thorns by covering them with a hide, even so they pass over this [year] having covered it; for it is pervaded by the year. Moreover, it is just as if one were to pass over heated dust while wearing shoes.
Therefore, one must indeed perform the *abhīvarta* chant.

Now, as for what I said to you regarding approaching the divine couple: when I said, "O lofty one, [the Soma] born with the juice, most sweet, most intoxicating," these two *gāyatrī* verses were what I spoke to you.
This indeed is the divine couple: that which is these [verses] in the Gāyatrī meter—“*uccā te*” is the form of the male, and “*svādiṣṭhyā*” is that of the female.
Thus, this procreative couple is brought about.
He who knows thus is born through a pair.
Therefore, these two alone should be made into *gāyatrī*s.
Now, as for what I said to you— "Do not fall away from the manifest caravan"— I was speaking of the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* when I said that.
For these two, the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*, are indeed the manifest caravan.
These, indeed, are the forest-tracts that lead beyond these very forest-tracts of the *savana*s. That which is "six villages" is the *trivṛt* stoma;
that which is "further beyond" is the *pañcadaśa*.
"Is there something further beyond? is the seventeenfold [stoma].
"There certainly is something further beyond" is the twenty-onefold [stoma]. "One who is weary should go toward this" is the twenty-sevenfold [stoma].
"Having approached this," thus [ends] the thirty-third [section].
Now, as to why there are the Chandomas after having stayed for one or two nights in between:
these Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are indeed the Kṣatra among the Sāmans.

The Kṣatriya is indeed the leader through the wilderness. When one goes through the wilderness by means of the Kṣatriya, whatever wild honey or sweet there may be that the robber knows of, he manifests it to him.
Then those other predatory bandits who are opponents and turn away flee into thickets and dense forests.
Just as one would pass through a forest without fear accompanied by a kṣatriya,
even so do they pass beyond [the dangers] by means of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans].
Moreover, this very Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha is indeed the path leading to the gods.
Having gone to this heavenly world by means of this path leading to the gods, those gods were afraid that humans might follow after them.
They said, "Find out how it is that men do not follow after us.
They drove back those *rakṣas* who were obstructing the sacrifice. Therefore, when one who is consecrated dies or is seized, these very ones perform that [act].
They lead those two, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, across.
Those whom they strike down while blind, they indeed strike down; therefore, one should not let go of the Bṛhat and the Rathantara. 423.
JB 2.424 |va| Now, Nāgarī Jānaśruteya used to say: "The slithering of a prowling wolf.
|vb| "What is a wolf? he asked.
"Prajāpati.
"Who is Prajāpati?
"The year."
What is its gliding?
Day and night. What are day and night?
*vi* "The Bṛhat and the Rathantara.
*vj* By means of these two, indeed, he moves along this [world].
*vk* These two are out-breath and in-breath; they are these two worlds, which constitute the divine couple.
These two, indeed, set out by grasping the very feet of the year;
they reach the goal safely and unharmed.
Now, as for what I said to you—"Do not cause the unshakable [part] of the sacrifice to waver"—that is the Vāmadevya for you.
I have said this to you. Indeed, the Vāmadevya is that which is unshakable in the sacrifice;
for the Vāmadevya is the vital breath.
"Lest we should cut off our vital breaths.
Then, as for what I said to you, "Prepare the provisions for tomorrow's sacrifice," it was the Gaurīvīta chant that I meant by that.
This, indeed, is the "tomorrow" of the sacrifice, namely the Gaurīvīta hymn; offspring is the tomorrow, cattle are the tomorrow, and the heavenly world is the tomorrow.
Just as one who knows the land might direct someone toward a village, saying, "By this way we shall go to that good path; by this way to that easy ford."
"We shall cross over this [obstacle], O Suvasa; we shall dwell there"—thus do these two *udāsa*s of Gaurīvīta perform their recitation, showing the place of rest.
Moreover, just as the *somapravāka* announces the *soma*, so do these two *udāsa*s of Gaurīvīta [announce] for the gods.
They both spoke to Soma.
He whose *gaurīvita* chant occurs on that day dwells that night as one for whom Soma has been announced.
Moreover, the gods look upon him, saying, "Run! You shall sacrifice tomorrow!"
Therefore, they do not perform the Gaurīvīta chant on the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), thinking, "Lest we cause the gods to be mocked.
Now, as for what I said to you: "Approach speech that is endowed with truth"—that refers to this [verse]: "With your foremost conquests of the soma-juice... (*purojitī vo andhasaḥ*).
"Thus have I spoken this to you as the Anuṣṭubh.
This Anuṣṭubh is indeed speech that possesses truth. The Anuṣṭubh comes first, and the Gāyatrī follows.
The Anuṣṭubh is speech, and the Gāyatrī is breath.
Indeed, that which is breath is the truth of speech; thus, this speech is possessed of truth.
Moreover, just as one would mount two other newer wheels, even so they carry this *anuṣṭubh* around at the openings of the three-day periods for the attainment of the heavenly world.
Therefore, this very *anuṣṭubh* should be performed.
Now, as for what I said to you, "Yoke the most excellent ones for the battle," I was speaking of the *agniṣṭoma-sāmans* themselves;
these indeed are the most excellent things yoked for battle, namely the *agniṣṭoma-sāmans*, which are those days that are to be passed over.

Now, as for what I said to you, "May you attain prosperity that is ever-increasing," I was speaking of the *pṛṣṭha* chants themselves. This indeed is prosperity that is ever-increasing: the *pṛṣṭhas*—the ninefold, the fifteenfold, the seventeenfold, the twenty-onefold, the twenty-sevenfold, and so on, ascending up to the thirty-threefold. They rise upward through these.
"Now, as for what I said to you—that you should find firm footing in the heavenly world—I meant that the *yajñāyajñīya* should be your *agniṣṭoma-sāman*; that is exactly what I said to you.
Indeed, this *yajñāyajñīya* is the heavenly world, and yonder sun is the twenty-one-fold [stoma].
In this very heavenly world they finally find firm footing.
Now, as for what I said to you: "From the village to the forest—let me go"—those were the *sāmans* that were to be brought back.
"I told you, 'Do not covet,' and that is what I said to you.

Just as one would travel from village to village without fear, so it is with those who perform the Agniṣṭoma chants. But just as one traveling from forest to forest might come upon being pierced by a thorn or a splinter, so it is otherwise.
"May so many protect us; so many have we missed while being pierced"—this is what he means when he says, "The *sāmans* are to be brought forward.
Therefore, the *sāmans* that are to be brought forward must not be destroyed.
Now, as for what I said to you, "Do not step over me from knowledge," I have indeed told you something very well known.
And as for what I said to you, "Do not step over me from the divine wedding," I have told you that very thing which is the Śyaita and Naudhasa [sāmans].
"Now, as for what I said to you: 'Do not exclude me from the sacrifice,' and 'May faith not depart from you'—that is precisely what I said to you.
For faith, indeed, is the queen among the gods."
This very [cow], having set out in the morning, stands still.
The gods attend upon her, thinking, "In whatever direction she will go, in that same direction we shall go.
All the gods follow after her and enjoy her in the evening.
He enters it; he offers the oblation; he performs the sacrifice. Upon this the gods subsist.
He has thus declared to them this security for a year.
Those who, knowing thus, undertake the year-long rite, reach its conclusion safely and unharmed.
For they indeed sit upon the Person himself that is the year.
Man is indeed Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year.
Desiring him, they sit performing this [rite], having made themselves the sacrifice.
Of that [sacrifice], the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra is indeed his two feet.
Of those two, that which is white below is the form of the day; that which is black above is the form of the night.

The nails are the stars. These very four "urvaṣṭhīvas" are the opening day, this is the Abhiplava, this is the Pṛṣṭhya, this is the Abhijit following from here, this is the Viśvajit—these are the three.
These three are the Svarasāmans; this is the Viṣuvat day; this is the Mahāvratīya day; this is the Udayanīya Atirātra.
This is the form of the day, this is the form of the night; the nails are indeed the form of the stars.
They reach this very Person, Prajāpati, who is the year, as their own self, limb by limb.
They arise as consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of speech, consisting of the *Ṛg*, consisting of the *Yajuṣ*,
consisting of the *Sāman*, consisting of the *Brahman*, consisting of gold, and immortal. The gods and the Asuras contended.

Those gods ran to Prajāpati, saying, "We have conquered the Asuras. He said, "Indeed, neither you nor the Asuras know me. If you were to know me, then you would truly exist and the Asuras would be defeated."
"Tell us that," they said. He replied, "The Person, Prajāpati, is the Year; worship him as such.
Then indeed you shall prevail, and the Asuras shall be defeated."
The Puruṣa, Prajāpati, is the year—thus they venerated him. Thereby the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated.
He who, knowing this, venerates the Puruṣa, Prajāpati, as the year, will prevail by his own self, and his hateful rival shall be defeated. 428.
JB 2.429 |va| Now, with respect to the deities: vb| This very world is the *prāyaṇīya* *atirātra*.
That which is white in it is the form of the day; that which is black is the form of the night; the variegated stars are the form of the constellations.
The year itself is the heavenly world; the introductory day is the Brahman; the *abhiplava* is the Kṣatriya; the *pṛṣṭhya* is Agni;
the *abhijit* is the Viśvedevas; the *svarasāmans* are Āditya; the *viṣuvat* is Indra; and the *viśvajit* is day and night.
The *go* and *āyus* [sāmans] are indeed the days of the twelve-day sacrifice; Prajāpati is the day of the *mahāvrata*; yonder world is the concluding *atirātra*.
This is the form of the day, this is the form of the night; the stars are indeed the form of the stars. 429.
JB 2.430 |va| Now,
some are indeed sattrasads, while others are satrasads. vb| Those who, having reached the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, dwell [there], they dwell in this very world.
Whatever food there is in this world, that they obtain by means of it. Moreover, they would know: "We are now in this world; for us there is no affliction whatsoever.
Then, the day they enter upon which they dwell as the *ārambhaṇīya* (opening day), that very day they place in the heavenly world within the year.
They dwell [there].

That food which exists in the year-long heavenly world—that very thing they obtain by this means. Moreover, they know: "At this time we are in the heavenly world; for us there shall be no affliction whatsoever."
"It exists.
Now, when they dwell having approached the *abhiplava* [six-day period], they dwell in the *brahman* itself. Thus, whatever food there is in the *brahman*, that very thing they obtain by means of it.
"Then indeed they would know: 'We are now possessed of this Brahman; for us there is no affliction whatsoever.

Now, when they dwell having reached the *pṛṣṭhya* [rite], they dwell in the *kṣatra* (the ruling power) itself. Thus, whatever food-eating capacity exists in the *kṣatra*, that very thing they secure by means of it.
Then they would know: "Now we are indeed the ruling power (kṣatra); for us there is no affliction whatsoever.
Now, when they dwell having reached the Abhijit [lunar mansion], they dwell in Agni himself. Thus, whatever food-eating power (annādya) is in Agni, that very thing they obtain by means of it.
Then they would know: "Now we are here in Agni; for us there is no affliction whatsoever.
Now, that which they dwell upon having approached the Svarasāman, they dwell upon it among all the gods.
Thus, whatever food-eating power exists among all the gods, that very thing they secure by means of it.
"Then indeed they would know: 'Now we are among all these gods; for us there is no affliction whatsoever.
Now, when they dwell having reached the Viṣuvat day, they dwell in the Āditya himself.
Whatever food-eating power is in the Āditya, that very thing they obtain by means of this [day].
Then indeed they would know: "The Ādityas are here now; for us there is no affliction whatsoever.
Now, when they dwell having reached the Viśvajit, it is Indra whom they dwell with.
Whatever food-eating power is in Indra, that very thing they thereby win.
"Then indeed they would know: 'Indra is here now; for us there is no affliction whatsoever.
Now, when they dwell having approached the [days called] Go and Āyus, they dwell in the very days and nights.
Thus, whatever food-eating power exists in the days and nights, that they obtain by means of this.
"Then they would know: 'This is now [the time] of day and night; for us there is no affliction whatsoever.
Then, those days which they spend having reached the twelve-day sacrifice, those they spend indeed in the worlds. Whatever food there is in the worlds, that they thereby obtain.

*vae*—Then they would know: "In these worlds, we are now here; for us there is no affliction whatsoever. *vaf*—Now, when they dwell having approached the day of the Mahāvrata, they dwell in Prajāpati himself.
*vag*—Whatever food-eating power exists in Prajāpati, that very thing they obtain by means of this.
"Then indeed they would know: 'Now we are here in Prajāpati; for us there is no affliction whatsoever.
Furthermore, when they reach and dwell in the *udayanīya* Atirātra, they dwell in that very world. Whatever food there is in that world, that they secure for themselves by means of it.
"Then indeed they would know: 'Now we are in that world; for us there is no affliction whatsoever. 430.
Some are indeed *satisada*s, others are *satrasada*s.
While some sit as *sat* [in the sacrificial session], others sit for the *sattra*.
Those who, knowing thus, undergo consecration (*dīkṣante*), are indeed the *satisads*; for it is while sitting upon these very deities that they proceed.
They indeed strike away all evil.
Now, those who, having had their topknots cut, coil themselves around while desiring to move forward, they truly are the performers of the sacrificial session (*satrasad*).
He who reviles one who knows thus—just as one would lead these deities astray, so it is for him—for he [reviles] these very ones.
He indeed speaks ill of him who has entered into these deities and dwells among them; for him who knows this, there is no affliction whatsoever, while he who speaks ill of him meets with distress.

Now, these indeed are the ten days of the year: the two *atirātra*s, the *ārambhaṇīya* day, the *mahāvratīya* day, the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [six-day periods], the *viśvajit* and *abhijit*, the *svarasāman* days, and the *viṣuvat*.
Pravati Kauśānteya was a student of Kusurbinda Auḍālaki.
He said to him, "My dear Sūtaputra, how many days of the year did your father consider there to be?
"He said, 'Ten.
"There are indeed ten," he said. "The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the Virāj is food; the sacrifice is of the nature of the Virāj."
“How many did he think? “Nine,” he said.
“Indeed, nine,” he said.
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person;
by means of the vital breaths, the sacrifice is extended.
How many did he think?
"Eight," he said.
"Indeed, eight," he said.
"The Gāyatrī has eight syllables."
"The sacrifice is based on the Gāyatrī.
"How many [verses] did he think of? "Seven," he said.
"Seven indeed," he said.
"The sacrifice is performed by means of the seven meters.
How many did you think [there were]?"
"Six," he said. "Six indeed," he said. "Six indeed; for the year consists of six seasons."
"The year is the sacrifice.
"How many [parts] did he think it had? "Five," he said.
"Five indeed," he said. "The sacrifice is fivefold; cattle are fivefold."
"Pa-śa-vo ya-jñaḥ" (The sacrifice is cattle).
"Vaṃ—how many did he think? "Van—four," he said.
"Four indeed," he said.
"There are four quarters; cattle have four feet; there are four meters that carry the sacrifice: the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and the Anuṣṭubh."
“How many did you think?
“Three,” he said.
“Indeed, there are three,” he said.
The sacrifice has three pressings; there are three vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna—and these worlds are three.
"How many did you think [the gods] were? he asked. "Two," he replied.
"Two indeed," he said.
"The day and night.
"These two worlds are as if entered by them; there are the two breaths, prāṇa and apāna; the person has two feet."
“How many did you think [were there]?
“One,” he said. “Indeed, there was only one,” he said.
"Day indeed. This day has been; tomorrow it will be.
Therefore, this very thing is called "day after day."
This day is indeed the foundation of the year. He who knows this foundation of it becomes firmly established.
This, verily, is its unity.
He who knows this oneness of his—having become one, prosperity attends him.
Regarding this they say: "Was it more, or will it be more? One should reply: "The past was indeed more than what is yet to be."
These worlds are real; this fire is real, that wind is real, yonder sun is real, Indra is real, and the moon is real.
These indeed rule over what has been and what is yet to be.
Therefore, what has been is truly more [substantial] than what is yet to be. 431.
Now this Vaiśvānara Atirātra is the opening sacrifice;
its arrangement directed upwards leads to heaven.
For this [sacrifice], the Rathantara is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra; the Vāmadevya is the Maitrāvaruṇa-sāman; and the Bṛhat is in the Ārbhava-pavamāna.
Indeed, this world is the Rathantara, the intermediate space is the Vāmadevya, and yonder world is the Bṛhat.
This indeed is the upward-arranged Sāman that leads to heaven.
By means of this very arrangement, they ascend to the upward world of heaven.
Moreover, it is this very Sāman, thus arranged, complete and yoked, that carries their sacrifice. 432.
For him, the *hiṃkāra* is indeed the *gāyatra*, the *prastāva* is the *rathantara*, the *udgītha* is the *vāmadevya*, the *pratihāra* is the *bṛhat*,
and the *nidhana* is the *yajñāyajñīya*.
Verily, each one of these is capable of [attaining] the heavenly world.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world. Moreover, this indeed is the *arkya*, this is the *mahāvrata*.
The Gāyatra is its head, the Bṛhat and Rathantara are its wings, the Vāmadevya is its body, and the Yajñāyajñīya is its tail.
He who knows this obtains as much as one obtains through the Arkya and the Mahāvrata.
Moreover, this is indeed a preparation for long life:
the Gāyatra is life; the Rathantara is all-encompassing life; the Vāmadevya is equal life; the Bṛhat is universal life;
and the Yajñāyajñīya is surpassing life.
The venerable ones indeed became long-lived by praising with this [hymn].

Moreover, these very five lights of theirs are established and shine upon these worlds: Agni on the earth, Vāyu in the intermediate space, Āditya in heaven, Candramas among the stars, and lightning in the waters.
Agni belongs to the *rathantara*, Vāyu to the *vāmadevya*, Āditya to the *bṛhat*, Candramas to the *gāyatra*,
and lightning to the *yajñāyajñīya*.
For the waters indeed are the *yajñāyajñīya*.
These very five kindled lights shine in these worlds. 433/ JB 2.434.
Now, of this very Agniṣṭoma which possesses the Ukthas, there are two hundred and fifty-three stotriya verses.
Now, with the night together with the *rāthaṃtara* *sandhi*, there are one hundred and eighty-nine *stotriya* verses.

Of these, three are redundant in the male, by which he procreates; two are deficient in the female, from which she gives birth. Indeed, the day is the form of the male, and the night is that of the female.
This surplus of the man he places in that deficiency of the woman for the sake of pairing and procreation. He who knows thus is propagated through pairing.
Now, those two *stotriya* verses which remain over are indeed the two testicles that remain over.
The *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans], when yoked, carry the sacrifice.
If they were to perform the *ṣoḍaśin* [stotra] at that point, hemorrhoids or a swelling would surely arise among them;
for if a fourth son were born after these three sons have already been born, one says, "Hemorrhoids or a swelling has arisen for him."
They would say:
"In exactly the same way, it will happen to her who gives birth to a female child.
Furthermore, regarding this, whoever should say of those performing the *ṣoḍaśin* rite, "Hemorrhoids or a swelling will be born to them," it will indeed be so.
They would indeed be so.
Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśī* [stotra] should not be performed here. 434/ JB 2.435
This very Atirātra, excluding the Ṣoḍaśin cup, amounts to twenty-one Ekaviṃśas and one Stotrīyā verse.
Now, that which consists of the twenty-one Ekaviṃśas is the Sun itself.
The sun indeed possesses sovereignty and lordship over that world.
Those who know thus attain sovereignty and lordship over that world.
If they were to perform the *ṣoḍaśin* here, the twenty-two [stotras] would become twenty-one, and there would be one [left over].
The *stotryā* [verse]—
it would entice him toward perfection. That very [number] becomes forty-nine *trivṛt* [stomas] and one *stotryā*.
Then, that which is the forty-ninefold threefold fire is indeed Agni himself. Verily, he attains sovereignty and lordship over this world;
he who knows thus attains sovereignty and lordship over this world.
If they were to perform the *ṣoḍaśin* here, there would be fifty-one *trivṛt*s and four *stotryā*s;
they would thus cause the perfection to be disturbed.
One would attain neither prosperity nor the other.
This Vaiśvānara Prāyaṇīya Atirātra is indeed a divine ford;
in it, this pillar is established, which is the Ṣoḍaśin.
The sixteenth [stotra] is indeed the Vairāja; it is established in each Virāj.
Whenever one considers this [sixteenth stotra] as becoming the Virāj, at that very moment it should be praised with this [Vairāja-stotra].
Now follows this twenty-fourth day, the *ārambhaṇīya* (inaugural) day.
Its arrangement directed upwards leads to heaven.
For it, the *rathantara* is performed at the midday pressing, then the *dairghaśravasa*, and then the *naudhasa*.
This indeed is the *rathantara*;
the intermediate space is that of Dīrghaśravas;
for this is the *vāmadevya* by way of its foundation.
|vg This very [verse] is the Naudhasa;
|vh for it is the body of the Bṛhatī; |vi this is the upward-arranged [chant], leading to heaven.
By means of this very desire, they indeed ascend upward to the heavenly world.
Regarding this day, some perform the *rathantara* as the *pṛṣṭha* chant, just as the *rathantara* serves as the *pṛṣṭha* for the *atirātra*.
The heavenly world is indeed turned away; we would thus ascend to that heavenly world turned away. That which is the *rathantara* [sāman] at the midday pressing is a descent back [to earth].
"Now, those who say that it is thus not returned [to the earth]—
that indeed is as if turned away, as if not conducive to long life.
If one were to speak ill of those who have performed it in that manner, saying either 'It will be so' or 'It will happen,' it would indeed come to pass exactly so."
Therefore, the *pṛṣṭha* at the midday pressing should indeed be the *bṛhat*, while the *rathantara* [is used] for that [other time].
This is its body;
this is the well-ordered arrangement leading to heaven. 436.
For this [sacrifice], the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant, the *vāmadevya* is the *maitrāvaruṇa-sāman*, and the *śyaita* is the *brahman-sāman*.
Indeed, yonder [heaven] is the *bṛhat*, the intermediate space is the *vāmadevya*, and this [earth] is the *śyaita*.
This is the body of the *rathantara*. This is that well-ordered arrangement leading to heaven;
by means of this very arrangement, they indeed ascend straight to the heavenly world.
The out-breath, the in-breath, and the diffused breath are indeed directed rightly; they move both hither and thither without becoming exhausted.
Those who praise with this [hymn] become long-lived.
There are two types of hymns for it: some are twenty-four-versed, and some are thirty-six-versed.
Now, as for those that are twenty-four-versed—the year indeed consists of twenty-four half-months; thus, by means of them, they attain the year half-month by half-month.
Now, as for those thirty-six [verses]: the *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables;
the *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world and universal sovereignty (*sāmrājya*). Thus, they proceed while firmly established in that very *bṛhatī*, in the heavenly world, and in universal sovereignty.
Moreover, by means of this very thirty-sixfold *stoma*, the year is grasped by them limb by limb.
There are indeed twelve full-moon days in the year, twelve *aṣṭakā* days, and twelve new-moon days.
Thus, by means of this thirty-sixfold *stoma*, they grasp the year limb by limb.
Regarding this, there are these two verses:
"The odd-numbered [breaths] draw forward first; thereafter, the even-numbered ones follow along."
They completed one year with the *chandases* (metres) for twelve months.
On the final day of the twelfth month, they established the thirty-sixfold [stoma] as their distinction.
Then they separated by pairs: some went upward toward heaven, while others went away.
Thus it is said. It has twelve stotras;
therefore, it is the Agniṣṭoma.

Those [stomas] indeed are twelve, yet they become fifteen and twenty-four-fold chants (*stotra*). Therefore it is an *ukthya*. This very sacrifice, being an *agniṣṭoma*, is an *ukthya*; being an *ukthya*, it is an *agniṣṭoma*.
He who knows thus obtains both those desires: that which is in the Agniṣṭoma and that which is in the Ukthya.
Now, these Stomas—Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyuḥ—come into being.
The cow leaped up as life-force;
from that, light was born.
This world, indeed, is life-force; yonder world is the cow; this very intermediate space is light.
The two of them placed him in front just like a son.
From here, this world is upward; from there, that world is downward.
Therefore, this light of theirs is enveloped in front.
Therefore we see it.
Those two, as they were approaching the union, pushed aside the light at the end.
Just as two parents might follow behind their son who is walking ahead, so was that.
Thus, these *stomas* become a pair when they are joined. Indeed, the son lies between the wife and the husband;
just as those two, about to unite, would carry the son around either from this side or that side, so too is this.
These deficient and redundant *stoma*s are paired for procreation. Now, there were indeed certain Asuras named Paṇis who were the cattle-herders of the gods.
With them they stood firm against the days.
They, having confined them within the Rasā river, sealed it shut with power.
Those gods said to Aliklavasuparṇa, "Search for these cows of ours."
"So be it.
He descended;
he arrived at the Rasā, which was covered within by power.
When he had arrived, they set before him clarified butter, milk, curds, and whey. He ate his fill.
They said to him, "This very Suparṇa shall be your tribute; this is your food. Do not reveal us."
He flew back again.
They said to him, "O knower of the *suparṇa*, where are the cows?
He replied, "What fame is there in cows?"
"This is indeed the fame of cows," said Indra to him, pressing his throat, "for you have surely placed your mouth among the cows. He then spat out either a drop of curd or some whey.
This very person became he who is born as Bhūmikapaṭhu in the spring.
He cursed him, saying, "O wretch, may your livelihood be foul, you who, having discovered our cows, did not tell us!
And his livelihood was that which is the most wretched part of this village, located at its rear end. 440.
They said to Saramā, "Saramā, you must seek out these cows of ours.
"So be it," she replied, and she set out after them.
She came to the Rasā.
This, indeed, is that Rasā which flows toward the ocean. He said to her: "I shall either burn you, or you shall become shallow for me."
"Jump over me," he said, "and I shall not provide you with a ford. She, having spoken thus, ran along while her ears were being scorched.
She then reflected: "How indeed can this bitch jump over me? Come now, I shall provide her with a ford."
He said to her, "Do not scorch me; I shall provide a ford for you. She said, "So be it.
And there was indeed a ford for her.
She swam across by means of a ford.
He followed after her to where she had entered the Rasā river, hidden by its power.
When she had arrived there, they placed for her exactly these things: clarified butter, milk, curdled milk, and curds.
She said, "I am not so very unloved by the gods that I would eat of yours.
Indeed, you have been living after having committed theft against the gods; I am merely a tracker of these cows. You will not cause me to swear an oath, nor will you offer Indra’s cows to him."
She lay there for a long time without eating.
She perceived that the afterbirth had been cast off; she ate it.
Some sang this verse concerning her: "Saramā, as if striking, was indeed eating the afterbirth.
Even now, this remains a proverb: "Saramā, as if striking, was indeed eating the afterbirth.
For she did indeed eat that afterbirth.
She ran back again.
They said to her, "Saramā, did you find the cows?
"I found them," he said, "hidden within this river by means of power.
"Take them away just as you think best," [he said].
Then Indra said to her: "O Saramā, I make your offspring eaters of food, since you have found our cows."
These are the Mācalas, the dogs of Vidarbha;
they even kill tigers. The gods brought together this Abhiplava.
Therefore, they leaped upon them; because they leaped upon them, that is the reason for the name *abhiplava* (leaping-towards) of the *abhiplava* [sacrifice].
They scorched Vala with fire alone and shattered it with the thunderbolt.
That light which is here in front is Agni; and that fifteen-fold *gobahiṣpavamāna* is the thunderbolt.
They drove it away by means of life itself.
Because they made it long-lived by means of life itself, that is the "life-nature" (*āyuṣṭva*) of life. They enclosed it on both sides with this very light.
These four *ukthya* offerings become situated in the middle.
The *ukthas* are indeed cattle;
they have a thousand verses for the *stotra*.
The *agniṣṭoma* is indeed the Brahman, the light.

They recited [the hymns], having grasped them on both sides with this very *brahman* as their light. Those who, knowing thus, undertake the *abhiplava* [six-day period], truly become established as winners of a thousand.
Regarding this they say: "Since this four-day period is interwoven in the middle—'Gauḥ-Āyuḥ, Gauḥ-Āyuḥ'—then why [is it so called]?"
"If the two luminaries are overturned," he should say, "it is for the sake of pairing, for the sake of procreation. He who knows thus is procreated through pairing. 442.
JB 3.1 |v1 Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning.
He desired: "May I become many; may I propagate; may I attain abundance. He performed austerity.
He beheld the seasonal power within himself.
Then he created the three seasons—these very worlds.

Because he created them from the seasonal (*ṛtviya*) [source], that is the reason for the "seasonal" nature (*ṛtutva*) of the seasons. Because he generated them from the seasonal [source], they are called *ṛtvij* (sacrificial priests).
When he first performed austerity, from that he created summer; therefore it burns most intensely. When he first performed austerity, from that he created summer.
Therefore, it burns most intensely.
When it heated itself for a second time, from that it emitted the rains.
Therefore, they perform both functions: they burn and they rain.
When he heated himself for the third time, from that he created the winter season;
therefore, it is as if the coldest of all. He heated himself over the three existing [seasons].
He divided them into two.
They became the six seasons. From the summer alone he fashioned spring; from the rainy season, autumn; and from the winter, the cool season.
Therefore, these were indeed fashioned as if they were the attachments of the seasons. Being six, he brooded over them; he divided them into two groups.
They became twelve months.
He heated himself for twelve [months].
He divided them into two parts.
Those became twenty-four half-months. He brooded over the twenty-four *sat*s. He thought: "If I divide them into two parts, they will not come into being; well then, let me create them."
From them, he fashioned seven hundred and twenty days and nights.
He differentiated all this;
for indeed, prior to that, it was like unrefined gold.
He knows all this; in him all the arts are understood, both those that are modified and those that are unmodified, for one who knows thus.
JB 3.2 |v1 That very Prajāpati became the year.
|v2 Having propped up and pervaded all this, he remained.
He reflected: "By what self-power (*svadhā*), by what food, and by what vigor (*ūrj*) has this [universe] been pervaded?
In that regard, he beheld this self-power, this vigor, this imperishable food: twelve full-moon days, twelve eighth-days (*aṣṭakā*), and twelve new-moon days.
He desired to win her over.
She said to him, "You shall not win me while I am exhausted by my fast.
He performed austerities.
He saw this twelve-day sacrifice;
he performed it.
He desired, "May the consecrated priests perform the sacrifice for me while I am consecrated."
He said to the months and the seasons, "Sacrifice for me. They did not say anything to him.
He said, "Eat [the offering] while remaining right here with us."

Therefore, all these full-moon, eighth-day, and new-moon sacrifices belong to Māsi alone. Then the seasons, as if having recognized him at his consecration, said, "He has indeed given [the sacrifice] to us. They said to him, "Give us a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as well!"

He bestowed upon them food and sustenance. Thus, this food is produced according to the seasons: by means of the consecrations (*dīkṣā*) he won the full-moon days; by means of the attendant rites (*upasad*) the eighth-day offerings (*aṣṭakā*); and by means of the pressed soma-juice (*prasuta*) the new-moon days.

He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the twelve-day rite, secures for himself this very self-sustenance, vigor, food, and imperishability. The seasons accepted [the sacrifice], but the months did not desire to accept it.
Therefore, the months are as it were more like verbs; for he who does not accept gifts becomes more like a verb. Therefore, the seasons are superior.
For he who receives [the gift] indeed becomes superior.
These, then, are indeed those three nights: the full moon, the eighth day, and the new moon.
JB 3.3 |v1 The gods did not yield the preeminence to Indra.
|v2 He ran to Prajāpati, saying, "Bestow these [powers] upon me."
He gave these two to him: the full moon and the new moon. He established the Aṣṭakā in this very [third] one.
Then indeed the gods stood firm for Indra’s preeminence.
They remain for his own preeminence, for one who knows thus.
Therefore, on this night, everyone dwells well-satisfied;
indeed, they dwell in Prajāpati as their father.
Therefore, one should not offer the oblation on that night; if one were to offer it, one should not recite [the formulas].
Prajāpati is indeed unexpressed (*anirukta*). Whatever three-fold hesitation he makes there, and those who dwell well in his house—that indeed belongs to him.
Prosperity. Those months and seasons said: "Let us sacrifice with that same sacrifice by which our father Prajāpati, having sacrificed, attained success."
They brought it to him.
Prajāpati reflected: "If these people complete this work, they will become just as I am."
He said to them, "Be consecrated with me as the householder. They replied, "We shall indeed designate you as such. He said, "May I [be] for you."
Therefore, by means of four months they designate a year; and by means of a year, the seasons and the months.
Therefore, by means of a son they designate a father, and by means of a father, sons.
Those who know this say that by means of this [rite], one obtains the domestic fires.
They performed sacrifice. Those months and the seasons became established in the year,
and the year in the seasons and the months.

Therefore they say: "The prosperity of those for whom they officiate and the prosperity of those who officiate for them are indeed equal in measure. One should reflect: "My prosperity is indeed equal in measure," [thinking], "As it is for him, so it is for me."
Therefore, one should sacrifice with this very [rite] alone;
for Prajāpati alone indeed prospered. However, if more should sacrifice—whether twelve or thirteen—they should sacrifice as these four and these [others].
These four [priests] might create [the fires], thinking, "This one is one of the four.
Whomever they should desire, thinking, "May this man's failure in the sacrifice follow [him]," his failure in the sacrifice indeed follows him.

But if more should sacrifice—whether sixteen or seventeen—they should arrange them thus: "These four, these four, these four, these four, and this one. Whomever they might desire, thinking, "May the prosperity of the sacrifice attend him," upon that very person the failure of the sacrifice attends instead.
But if more should sacrifice— whether twenty-four or twenty-five should sacrifice—
they should separate them out, saying, "These five, these five, these five, these five, these four, and this one.
Whomever they should desire, thinking, "May the failure of the sacrifice follow him," that very person the failure of the sacrifice follows.
All others prosper.
He who indeed knows the master of the house and the mistress of the house of the sacrificial session (*satra*) attains the status of the *gārhapatya* fire and prevails.
He attains the status of the *gārhapatya* fire.
The year, indeed, is the householder (*gṛhapati*), and this earth is the housewife (*gṛhapatnī*).
He who knows thus partakes in the *gārhapatya* and attains preeminence in the *gārhapatya*.
JB 3.5 |v1 He who knows the sovereignty of the meters attains sovereignty; he reaches the world of sovereignty.
|v2 The Bṛhatī, indeed, is the sovereign among the meters.
They subsist upon this very [year]—facing it, turning away from it, and moving across it—for the sake of food.

Therefore, they live upon the animal facing them, turning away from them, and moving across them. Indeed, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) possesses as much power and vigor as the year, for there are twelve full-moon nights.
There are twelve Aṣṭakās and twelve new-moon days; by this very means, he wins them.
He who knows the Virāj established in the seasons, and the seasons established in the Virāj, attains a firm foundation and secures food.
The Virāj consists of thirty syllables;
there are six seasons.
Thus, the Virāj is established in the seasons, and the seasons are established in the Virāj.
He who knows this attains a firm foundation and secures food. Indeed, they sit for this twelve-day rite using the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
the *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables.
Four-footed are the animals;
speech is the *anuṣṭubh*;
by means of speech he sustained the animals.
Therefore, cattle are accomplished through speech; summoned by speech, they come.
JB 3.6 |v1 The first three-day period indeed has the Gāyatra as its beginning.
|v2 Therefore, this Agni shines upward.
The second three-day period has the Gāyatra at its middle;
therefore, this wind blows crosswise.
The third three-day period has the Gāyatra at its end.
Therefore, that sun shines hitherward.
Indeed, the Gāyatrī supported the first three-day period with its brilliance (*tejas*), the second with its feet (*padāni*), and the third with its syllables (*akṣarāṇi*).
The Gāyatrī is indeed the threefold (*trivṛt*) brilliance.
The first day is the *trivṛt* [stoma].
By it, the first three-day period (*triyaha*) is sustained.
The *gāyatrī* has three feet; the three-day period is in the middle; by it, the second three-day period is sustained.
The *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables; the seventh day consists of twenty-four [stomas]; by that very means, the third three-day period (*triyaha*) is sustained.
How is it that they say the *gāyatrī* is the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*)?
Just as the rim encompasses the spokes on all sides, so does the Gāyatrī encompass the twelve-day rite from all sides,
for the sake of non-slipping.
Just as the spokes are held fast in the nave of a chariot wheel, so is the twelve-day rite held fast within the Gāyatrī, for the sake of non-overlapping.
The Gāyatrī is indeed a ray or a support;
upon it the twelve-day rite is sustained for the sake of non-disturbance.
This twelve-day rite is extended as an Anuṣṭubh.
With eight syllables one raises up the first day by means of the *anuṣṭubh*, with eleven the second,
and with twelve the third. Thus, only one syllable remains over as a tri-syllable.
He performs that very same [rite] for the next three days.
The meters indeed carry her fourth part.
They attend upon her— her who faces west, who faces away, and who is transverse— for the sake of food.
Therefore, they subsist upon the animal from the front, from behind, and from the side.
Prajāpati, as soon as he was born, was born together with evil. He desired, "May I strike away this evil."
He beheld this twelve-day sacrifice with its meters arranged in expanded form (*vyūḍhachandas*);
he took it up and sacrificed with it.
By means of that, he drove away evil in all directions.
He who considers himself as if seized by evil should sacrifice with this twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha) whose meters are expanded;
indeed, he drives away evil in all directions.

For offspring, indeed, tend to be like those who creep away. Therefore, the fact that the subsequent *ājya* chants are in the *gāyatrī* meter is for the sake of preventing the creeping away of offspring.
For the *gāyatrī* is indeed a supporting beam or a foundation.
On that [occasion], the twelve-day rite is performed for one who has not yet undergone the *saṃsarpa* ceremony.
By means of ten days, Prajāpati indeed created offspring. Once created, they became dispersed in all directions.
He saw these two Vaiśvānara Atirātras;
with them he enclosed them on both sides— from this world above and from that world below—
and by means of these very two, he caused them to halt.
Because he warded off all that has come into being, that is the *vaiśvānara*-ness of the two *vaiśvānara* [cups].
This Udgātṛ is Prajāpati;
by means of these ten days alone, he creates offspring.
He wards them off by means of these two Vaiśvānara [bricks]: with this one from below and with that one from above, for the support of creatures and to prevent their loss.
The wealth of him who knows thus is not lost.
The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the former Vaiśvānara, and the in-breath (*apāna*) is the latter.

By means of these very out-breath and in-breath, they attain prosperity and reach the conclusion of the chant (*udṛc*). Therefore, one should sleep during the chanting of these two [stotras], thinking, "Lest I should cut off the vital breaths."
Regarding this, they say: "Who indeed has mastery over sleeplessness?
For that which the breath (*prāṇa*) keeps awake is itself the state of waking.
One may sleep at will."
Regarding this, they say: "Since this Atirātra is indeed the supreme sacrificial rite (yajñakratu), why do they perform it first, even though it is the supreme?
One should reply: "It is for the sake of attaining the sacrificial rites themselves."

All these sacrificial rites—namely the Agniṣṭoma, the Uktha, and the Atirātra—are indeed attained by this [rite], as is he who knows the ten-day sacrifice as being structured according to the Agniṣṭoma. For him, the first three-day period is made successful by the morning pressing alone; it is made successful by the midday pressing.
The second [day] is by means of the midday pressing, the third by means of the third pressing, and the tenth day is fashioned by means of the Agniṣṭoma-sāman alone.
He who knows thus is successful.
The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the first Vaiśvānara, the in-breath (*apāna*) is the latter; and that which exists as the sacrificial session (*sattra*) constitutes the other days.
This twelve-day rite is indeed a *gāyatrī* with light for its wings.

The two Atirātras are the wings, and the two Agniṣṭomas are the eyes; the two outer Atirātras are the outer [eyes], and the two inner Agniṣṭomas are the inner [eyes]. Therefore, there are the pupils within the eyes. Now, those eight days constitute the Gāyatrī.
By means of it, the gods went to the heavenly world.
He who knows this goes to the heavenly world.
"There is a repetition (*jāmi*) in the twelve-day sacrifice," they say.
Regarding these eight days which are *ukthya*s in the middle, one should say: "There is no sameness (*jāmi*) there. The *ukthas* are indeed cattle;
thus, he unites cattle with cattle.
"Furthermore, cattle indeed shine when they are gathered together with other cattle.
The Jyotiṣṭoma Atirātra results in the Virāj;
the Virāj is the year, and the year is procreation.
Two *stotriya* verses of the first day exceed the *virāj*, and two of the second day [exceed it].

Those *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* chants which are on both sides of the *virāj* of the first day are yoked and carry the sacrifice; then those *virāj*s of the second day are its milking and its foundation.
One who desires heaven should perform the Āyuṣṭoma sacrifice;
the Stomas proceed upwards so that there may be no falling away.
One who desires vigor should perform the Goṣṭoma sacrifice;
for the fifteenfold [stoma] is indeed sensory power and vigor.
As long as they live, they remain full of vigor;
but once they have passed away, they become subject to the power of the Lord,
for they depart from their vital breaths.
Those who have sacrificed with the *trivṛt* [stoma] have prepared their portion; those who have not sacrificed have not prepared theirs.
If the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*, they chant for the Aśvins with the *rathantara*.
This world is indeed the *rathantara*; that world is the *bṛhat*.
They do not step upon this [earth], but they step upon that [other world]. They become short-lived or suffer from exhaustion.
Furthermore, it is as if one were to fill [a vessel] through an opening at the far end; indeed, it is filled from the far side, but one does not drink from it.
If the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant in such a manner, they praise with the *rathantara* for the Aśvins.
"JB 3.11 |v1 They say, 'That which has been milked is to be approached.
|v2 One should say, 'There is nothing there that has been milked which is to be approached.'"
The *rathantara* is indeed speech, and the *āśvina* is speech; for from where else could one endure?
This, indeed, is the milk of the single *chandas*, namely speech—whether by those who have sacrificed or those who have not sacrificed.
Regarding this, they also say: "Flow on, O foremost of speech! Sing to him, O men! Of you, the purifying one... etc.
They become the *pratipad*s.
They chant the *rathantara* on the *pavamāna* [laud].
The *bṛhat* becomes the *pṛṣṭha* [laud].
They chant the *jarābodhīya* for the Aśvins. This *jarābodhīya* is indeed the *sāman* of the god Rudra.
By means of this, the god Rudra attained sovereignty and lordship over cattle; that by which Rudra [attained it]—
The god attained sovereignty and overlordship over cattle; [they thought], "By that means may we attain sovereignty and overlordship over cattle.
Regarding this, they say: "It is cruel and unappeased; it is liable to destroy the cattle of the sacrificer."
Regarding this, they say: "This Āśvina [laud] is indeed the entire Vāc-Brahman. "By means of this very speech, by means of the Brahman, and by means of the Āśvina, they bring it to rest," they say.
They chant it as the *aurdhvasadmana* among the *āpiśarvara* verses.
By means of the *aurdhvasadmana* [chant], the gods, having driven the Asuras away from these worlds, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) in their own abode.
By means of the *aurdhvasadmana* alone, one should drive away the hateful rival from these worlds and [establish oneself] in one's own abode.
He who knows thus sits at a sacrificial session.
JB 3.12 |v1 The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the Brahman.
|v2 The Prāyaṇīya day is the Brahman.
This, indeed, is the measure of the sacrifice: namely, the Agniṣṭoma.
By that very measure of the sacrifice, they thus proceed in this sacrificial session; as is the contact at the beginning, so is it at the conclusion.
Therefore, they set out with the Agniṣṭoma and conclude with the Agniṣṭoma. Mind is indeed prior, and speech follows after it;
mind is the Bṛhat, and speech is the Rathantara.

The *bṛhat* is indeed ancient, and the *rathantara* is near. In that these [verses] contain both the word "ancient" (*pratna*) and the word "near" (*upa*), the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* are thus yoked together for the sacrificial session (*sattra*).

"Going forth" (*preti*) and "coming back" (*eti*) are the form of the Gāyatrī. In that there is both "going forth" and "coming back," they set out by means of the very form of the Gāyatrī; they do not fail, nor do they falter.
By this very connection, the *ṛc* and the day are joined together, just as one would fasten the pins of a harnessed team.
Such is that.

They say: "Those who break up the *ṛc*s of the *prāyaṇīya* day are indeed deprived of their vital breaths (*prāṇa*). They possess common characteristics; for the vital breaths are indeed characterized by commonality. This is for the sake of the continuity of the vital breaths.
For the sake of non-interruption:

"O Agni, come for the feast; O Mitra and Varuṇa, come to us; O thou for whom we have pressed [the Soma], come; O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed [Soma]"—thus the *ājya* offerings consist of [verses] beginning with "come, come."

"Come hither, come hither!"—with these words they proceed in front of the harnessed [steeds]. Just as one might go in front of the harnessed [steeds] saying, "Come hither, come hither," such is that. The *stoma* is the *trivṛt*.
The Trivṛt is indeed Brahman;
it is thus while remaining established in Brahman that they proceed.
"O Soma drops, wise ones! O Soma, forward for the feast of the gods! Run forth and sit down within the vessel!"—these are the *pravatī* verses used on the day connected with the *rathantara* chant.
This day is indeed to be led forward.
*Pra* is the form of the Gāyatrī;
it is by the very form of the Gāyatrī that they proceed.
That which has five *sāmans* is contrary and unsuccessful.
The *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *vyāna*—that is the *ṛc*.
They interrupt it.
They cut off themselves, their offspring, their wife, and these worlds.
There are three Sāmans;
that is the *kḷpta* (the prepared), consisting of three triplets and three Sāmans.
Then there is the horse [chant] with the *padanidhana* finale, without a *stobha*, belonging to the *rathantara* [sāman]. Therefore, it is performed on the day of the *rathantara*.
