The *pavamāna* is performed as the *soma-sāman* accompanied by the *iḍā*.
Indeed, one is able to traverse the year by means of the *pañcasāman*.
In that regard, the *yaudhājaya* has the *ṣaḍakṣaranidhana*; for there are six seasons, [this serves] for the purpose of yoking the year itself.
"Towards the wooden vats, the brown ones [have flowed]"—the word "towards" (*abhi*) occurs; this is a form of the *rathantara*.
This day belongs to the *rathantara*.
"Pressed for Indra, Vāyu, Varuṇa, and the Maruts"—these verses are addressed to the Maruts.
The form of the midday pressing indeed belongs to Marutvat. Thus, they do not depart from the very form of the midday pressing.
Regarding these [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa explained.
JB 3.14 |v1 Now, concerning the horse: |v2 Prajāpati created living beings.
He created them by means of the horse, having himself become a horse.
Because he created them by means of the horse, having become a horse, that is the horse-nature of the horse.
That is the *sāman* of procreation.
It is performed on the day of procreation.
He who knows thus is propagated with offspring and cattle.
Therefore, this *sāman* must not be omitted from this day.
This Sāman is indeed procreation;
this day is procreation.
Thus, procreation is performed within procreation itself.
Regarding this, they also say: "The Sāmudri chants of the horse.
Indeed, the horse was Sāmudri; he desired, "May I acquire cattle; may I attain abundance of cattle."
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
Thereupon, he indeed acquired cattle and attained abundance of cattle.
This is a Sāman pertaining to cattle.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and attains abundance of cattle.
Because the horse from the sea saw it, it is therefore called "Āśva" (belonging to the horse).
Now they say: "By means of the horse, indeed, the gods, having become horses, went to the heavenly world. That, then, is the horse-nature of the horse; that, indeed, is its heavenly nature.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
JB 3.15 |v1 Now follows the Soma-sāman. |v2 King Soma, as it were, shared a feast with the other deities.
He desired, "May I be consecrated for the sovereignty of all the gods.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
Then indeed he strove for the sovereignty over all the gods. He who knows thus is consecrated for preeminence among his own people.
He disappeared from them.
They sought after it. It appeared to them in this form, namely that which belongs to the moon.
They approached it, saying, "It has been seen! It has been seen!"
Therefore, when he shows himself, they then gather around him; when he does not show himself, they say, "He is not seen.
They consecrated him with this [rite].
He thought this:
This is the Śrīsava Sāman. He who knows this attains prosperity and attains kingship.
Because King Soma saw it, it is called the Somasāman.
Now, regarding the Vajra [Sāman]:
Vajra Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, performed austerities. He beheld this Sāman and praised with it.
He resorted to this *iḍā*. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
from it, he indeed obtained cattle.
This is a *sāman* pertaining to cattle;
he who knows this secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Furthermore, because Aṅgiras saw it as a thunderbolt (*vajra*), it is therefore called "the Thunderbolt."
Then there is the Yaudhājaya with three *nidhanas*, for the fulfillment of the *savana*s.
Then there is the Auśana as the final *sāman*; [they think], "By means of this final *sāman*, may we attain the final world, heaven.
Then there is the Rathantara.
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed Brahman, and the Rathantara is Brahman;
thus they proceed while firmly established in Brahman.
Then follows the Vāmadevya.
The Vāmadevya is indeed cattle;
those who praise with it become possessed of cattle.
Now follows the Naudhasa.
The *saloka* and the *kāleya*, as well as the *rathantara*.
"O Soma drops, flowing with exhilaration"— these *pravatī* verses in the *gāyatrī* meter belong to the *pavamāna* laud of the *ārbhava* section on the day connected with the *rathaṃtara*.
This day is indeed to be led forward;
"pra" (forth) is the form of the Gāyatrī;
it is by the very form of the Gāyatrī that they proceed.
These [verses] contain the word *mada*. Now, *mada* is indeed essence (*rasa*). This third pressing is, as it were, solidified.
In that these [verses] contain the word "madhu" (honey), they thereby bestow essence upon him;
with this, they cause him to swell. Regarding them, the Gāyatra [stotra] has its Brāhmaṇa already explained.
Now, the *saṃhita* [chant] has two syllables as its *nidhana* for the sake of stability;
for the sacrificer is two-footed, for the sake of firm standing.
"Flow on with zeal, seeking the gods," and "The beloved, tawny one flows"—these are the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* [metres].
The two *gāyatrī* verses, by their form, belong to the *rathantara*; they are for victory in the assembly in the first [day].
Now, there is the syllable with the *pada* as its finale, without a *stobha*, belonging to the *rathantara*.
Therefore, it is performed on the day connected with the *rathantara*.

Prajāpati indeed created this sacrifice, which is the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). Of it, the other days were fashioned with triplets of verses (*tṛca*), but this [day] was with single verses (*ekarca*).
Consequently, that part of it became, as it were, collapsed.
He saw these two *sāmans*.
With them he struck out this day, just as one would strike a hide with two wooden pins.

With the *āśva* [sāman] in front and the *ākṣāra* above; thus, when these two *sāmans* are performed, it is for the support of the day itself. "O, press out the juice for the one who pours the soma-plant!"—thus there are *anuṣṭubh* verses with a downward motion on the day belonging to the *rathantara*.
This day is indeed to be led forward.
*Pra* is the form of the Gāyatrī;
it is by the very form of the Gāyatrī that they proceed.
In those [verses], the Gaurīvīta [is chanted].
Just as two who see the place of rest find a place of rest here on earth, even so are these two udāsa syllables of the Gaurīvīta.
They find their sustenance for tomorrow from the gods.
"May there be sustenance for us tomorrow," they think as they sit at the sacrificial session (sattra).
Indeed, there is sustenance for them tomorrow.
This Gaurīvīta is indeed the "tomorrow's horse" (*adyaśva*) of the gods. It becomes an inexhaustible "tomorrow's horse" for him who knows thus.
Of these two [melodies], one is the beholder of the resting place (*avasāna*), while the other is the one who causes the other to rest.
It was just as if one were to settle down by clear grass and water;
for just as the Soma-proclaimer here announces the Soma, even so did these two announce the Soma to the gods from the heights of Mount Gairivīta.
On whichever day the Gaurīvita occurs, he who has performed the Soma sacrifice dwells that night as one for whom the Soma has been proclaimed.
Then the gods look upon him, saying, "Run! Tomorrow you shall sacrifice!
Therefore, they do not perform the Gaurīvita on a one-day (ekāha) sacrifice, lest they should cause the gods to reproach them.
Just as these footholds are made upon a tree, so have these footholds of Gaurīvīta been made for the attainment of the heavenly world.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Just as one would proceed toward a place of rest after having traveled along this path, so is the Gaurīvita;
it should be sung in that very manner.
The Śākyas, performing the Tarasapuroḍāśa sacrifice, sat for a sacrificial session.
That Gaurivīti Śākya killed a deer.
Tārkṣya Suparṇa swooped down upon him from above;
he offered it to him.
He said to him, "O seer, do not stand before me."
"I shall tell you about tomorrow.
"But today indeed you know, not tomorrow.
To him he spoke this Gaurīvīta.
Then indeed he saw the morrow.
Now, the morrow is offspring, the morrow is cattle, and the morrow is the heavenly world.
In that there is the Gaurīvīta [Sāman], it is for the attainment and acquisition of all this.
The essence of speech indeed flowed away;
it became the Gaurīvīta. In that the Gaurīvīta occurs on each successive day, they proceed while bestowing the essence of speech on each successive day.
If those who would release the Gaurīvīta chant during the Ahīna sacrifice, he should say to them: "You shall be without provisions for the morrow and without offspring.
And indeed, they become without provisions for the morrow and without offspring.
Now, the Tvaṣṭṛtīya Sāman has its *nidhana* in the middle; it serves for stability.
Indeed, those who undertake the Ārbhava Pavamāna launch themselves upon the ocean as their support.
In that it has its *nidhana* in the middle, it is for the sake of stability.
They perform the *pratihāra* before its *nidhana*;
indeed, by means of the *prastāva* and the *pratihāra*, the sacrificer is supported.
This day, which is the Trivṛt, is as if it were running away.
Therefore, they perform the *pratihāra* before the *nidhana* for the sake of preventing it from slipping away.
Having struck Vṛtra with his thunderbolt, Indra entered the cows, fearing, "I have not slain him."
They desired, "May we bring Indra into being.
They saw these Sāmans, the Tvaṣṭṛ-sāmans;
with them, they brought Indra into being.
These, indeed, are the *sāmans* that produce heroes.
A hero is born to him who knows this.
Moreover, the [verses] belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ are indeed cattle.
In that these *sāmans* are performed, it is for the very purpose of securing cattle.
That [first] one is the *aiḍa*; for the *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and it is for the securing of cattle.
Furthermore, because Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughters saw them, they are therefore called the "Tvaṣṭṛ-sāmans."
"He flows toward what is dear, for the sake of delight"—thus it contains the word "toward" (*abhī*), which is the form of the *rathantara* [sāman].
This day belongs to the *rathantara*.
Regarding those [verses], the *kāva* [laud] has its Brāhmaṇa explained.
Now follows the Yajñāyajñīya, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.
JB 3.20 |v1 “Flow on as the foremost of speech,” these are the opening verses (*pratipad*).
When the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* were created, the *Bṛhat* was created first, and then the *Rathantara*. |v2 [End of section]
Therefore, the introductory verses (*pratipad*) begin with: “Flow on, O foremost of speech.
Some seers saw [the hymns] as moving forward (*pra-iti*), others as coming toward them (*ā-iti*). But this [particular verse] remains fixed as neither moving forward nor coming toward.
Bharadvāja, the seer, beheld the Bṛhatī form of speech.
This Bṛhatī is indeed the ancestral lineage of Bharadvāja;
the mind is the Bṛhatī.
Prajāpati is the Bṛhat. He who knows thus attains the state of Prajāpati. [He recites:
"O Soma, with thy wondrous aids, [overcome] all poetic insights; thou [winnest] the waters of the ocean."
"Thou"—this is a form of the *bṛhatī*;
this day belongs to the *bṛhatī*.
"Leading forth the voice..."—for this day is indeed the foremost.
This second day is indeed that which is called "the beginning" (*agram*). [The verse:
"O Sage, these worlds have stood for the sake of the seasons; O Soma, for the sake of greatness.
For this day, being connected with the *bṛhatī* meter, is as if already run forth.
For this [Sāman] is indeed the Bṛhat.
Now, the words "O Soma, you have stood for greatness" serve to propitiate the day. The words "The milch-cows run for the seasons" serve for completeness.
These verses are *gāyatrīs* with the color of the *triṣṭubh*, perfected by the form of the day. Indeed, wherever they perfect [the rite] by means of the form of the day, there they prosper.
Everything succeeds for him who knows thus.
"Flow on, O Indu, as a bull, pressed!"—thus the *anurūpa* verse contains the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*).
This day indeed belongs to the Bṛhatī metre.
The *traiṣṭubha* is the form of the *kṣatra*.
Regarding this, they say: "They begin with the day's very form, by means of the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa* of the *sāman*.
There are both the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa*.
"Verily, they begin with the *stotriya* as the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and with the *anurūpa* as the *sāman*.
There are both the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa*.
The *stotriya* is indeed the out-breath, and the *anurūpa* is the in-breath (*apāna*).
Verily, having thus made them prosper through the out-breath and the in-breath, they proceed.
The *stotriya* is indeed the mind, and the *anurūpa* is speech;
the *sāman* is the *stotriya*, and the *ṛc* is the *anurūpa*.
The day is indeed the *stotriya*, the night is the *anurūpa*.
This [earth] is indeed the *stotriya*, yonder [sky] is the *anurūpa*.
The self (*ātman*) is indeed the *stotriya*, offspring is the *anurūpa*.

Indeed, this is the characteristic form of the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa*: because whatever excellent speech the superior one speaks, the inferior one repeats after him; and because both the agent and the instrument are perceived as being similar.
It is for the sake of the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa* that offspring are born resembling their parents.

One who knows thus is born with offspring corresponding to that. Regarding this, they say: "Those who break up the *ṛcas* of the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*) are indeed deprived of their vital breaths. Therefore, they employ five continuous *ṛcas* here, for the sake of the continuity and non-interruption of the vital breaths.
All [the verses] contain the word *vṛṣan*. This day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre; the Triṣṭubh is the form of the Kṣatra.
The paryāsa is for the support of the subjects and for the presence of cattle.
There is a fifteenfold stoma; the fifteenfold [stoma] is indeed power and vigor. Thus, they proceed while establishing themselves in power and vigor.
JB 3.22 |v1 “We choose Agni as the messenger”— with these words, there is an *ājya* (offering) for Agni.
|v2 Some seers saw [the verses] after departing [from this world], while others [saw them] by coming [to this world].
Now, this [hymn] stands as "not thus" and "not so.
Bharadvāja, the seer, beheld the Bārhata form of speech.
Indeed, that which is the Bṛhat[-sāman] is the ancestral lineage of Bharadvāja.
The mind is the *bṛhat*.
Prajāpati is the *bṛhat*.
He who knows thus attains the state of Prajāpati.
"Hotāraṃ viśvavedasam" (The Hotṛ, the all-knowing). The syllable "ho" is the form of the Bṛhatī;
this day belongs to the Bṛhatī.

"‘We invoke Mitra; we, the singers of hymns, [invoke] Indra greatly; great homage to Indra and Agni’—these are the *ājya* verses consisting of a single form, all of which are indeed in the *bṛhatī* meter.
This day is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*)."

Therefore, all the kings were of one counsel and one voice. There are two verses containing the word *mahat* (great) and two containing the word *bṛhat* (vast). This indeed is the manifest form of the *bṛhat* [sāman]: that which is great and that which is vast.
They approach this very Bṛhat directly.
There is a fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśastoma*); the fifteenfold is indeed power and vigor. Thus, they proceed while establishing themselves in power and vigor.
"Flow as a bull in your stream"— thus the *gāyatrī* verses of the midday *pavamāna* chant are characterized by the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*).
This day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre;
the Triṣṭubh is the form of the Kṣatra. "And for the one accompanied by the Maruts, the exhilarating [Soma]"—thus there are verses addressed to the Maruts.
The form of the midday pressing indeed belongs to the Maruts;
thus they do not depart from the very form of the midday pressing.
With the words, "Thee, the supporter, in the two bowls," it is for the support of the day itself.
"O tawny one, with inspired thought and through purification, flow forth in your stream"—thus they become "possessing the tawny ones" (harivatīḥ).
For the *triṣṭubh* has the form of the tawny ones;
this day is indeed of the *triṣṭubh* nature.
Among those [sāmans], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa already explained.
Now, the Yauktāśva, which has the Bṛhatī as its nidhana, was praised around [the fire].
Therefore, it is performed on the day of the Bṛhatī.
Vasiṣṭha was indeed the domestic priest (*purohita*) of King Sudās Paijavana of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
That Sudās Paijavana entrusted his mares to Vasiṣṭha, just as one entrusts them to a domestic priest.
As Vasiṣṭha set out for the prize-winning race, he said to his younger brother Yuktāśva: "Of these [mares], ours..."
He thought, "I shall be the overseer of my wives.
Having yoked the horses, he carried off the newborn foals of the king's mares;
those that were beautiful, he kept for himself.
Those who were more wicked, [he placed] in the royal mares.
They realized then: "He has carried off the newborn infants. They assailed him, saying, "You are a thief, you are no seer!"
He desired, "May I find faith; may they summon me.
He saw this Sāman;
with it he praised.
He reached the *nidhana* with "O, Jvara! (o i jvare). From that, he indeed obtained faith (*śraddhā*) and an invitation (*upahava*).
"We wish to find faith," they say as they perform the sacrificial session;
verily, they find faith.
This indeed is the truth of speech: "Oṁ, he burns."
"Ṛju" (straight) is indeed the truth of speech.
By means of truth, he found the faith and the invitation of that speech. He who knows thus becomes worthy of faith and finds an invitation.
That indeed is a Sāman that is productive and conducive to cattle.
"O i jvare" is its Nidhana.
They say of a beast being led forward, "It is being anointed."
The cattle of one who knows this are free from fever and are prolific.
Because he saw [the verse] while his horse was yoked (*yuktāśva*), it is therefore called the *Yauktāśva*.
"O Soma, being purified, flow in a stream"—this *Bṛhatī* verse possesses a dual form.
This [Sāman] indeed raises up both Sāmans. Therefore, they perform this very [Sāman]: those who use the Bṛhat-sāman perform it, and those who use the Rathantara-sāman perform it.
Among these, the Somasāmans are chanted; the *pariṣṭobha* belongs to the Bārhata.
Therefore, they are performed on the Bṛhatī day. Soma is indeed a bull, Indra is a bull, and this day belongs to Indra.
Soma is indeed the ruling power (kṣatra), Indra is the ruling power, and this day belongs to Indra.
Soma is indeed seed; this day is procreation.
In that these two *sāmans* are performed on this day, seed is thereby infused into procreation.
He who knows thus has his seed infused in due order by Prajāpati.

The other [sāman] has its *iḍā* at the beginning; it is the form of the *bṛhat*, for this day belongs to the *bṛhat*. The other is based on the *bṛhat* and has three *nidhanas*; it is the form of the midday *pavamāna* for the sake of stability.
And because King Soma saw them, they are called the "Soma-sāmans."

"The red bull has bellowed towards the cows"—thus they contain the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*). This day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre, yet it is of the Triṣṭubh nature, which is the form of sovereignty (*kṣatra*).
In those [stotras], the *pariṣṭobha* consisting of the second day’s form, the Bārhata, was applied to the Pārtha with a double repetition. Therefore, it is performed on the Bārhata day.
Pṛthu Vainya indeed desired, "May I be consecrated for sovereignty over all cattle.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
Then indeed he was consecrated for the sovereignty over all cattle. This is the Śrīsāman. He who knows thus is consecrated for the sovereignty over all cattle.
And that becomes a *svāra* [chant] with a *stobha* in the *prastāva*, for the differentiation of the *svaras*.
For this day has a *svāra* [chant] in which the *prastāva* contains a *stobha*;
this day is, as it were, elevated, and this *sāman* is, as it were, elevated.
By praising with this [hymn], one ascends to the day itself;
and because Pṛthu Vainya saw it, it is therefore called the "Pārtha."
JB 3.26 |v1 They say, however, that the Vāsiṣṭha is more effective.
|v2 This is the kṣatra which is the Pārtha; this is the kṣatra which are the Soma-sāmans; this is the kṣatra which is this day.
By that which is related to Indra, it is the *kṣatra*; by that which is related to the *triṣṭubh*, it is the *kṣatra*; by that which is related to the *bṛhatī*, it is the *kṣatra*;
by that which is the fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśastoma*), it is the *kṣatra*.
Thus, the *kṣatra* becomes unified.
In that there is the *yauktāśva* [Sāman] in front and the two *ṛṣisāmans* of the Vasiṣṭhas behind, it is for the sake of the Brahmin’s expansion.
"I unite the Brahman with the Kṣatra; may it be so," [he says].
Vasiṣṭha, having been defeated and his sons slain, desired: "May I be propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle. He beheld this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Then indeed he multiplied through offspring and cattle.
This is that generative *sāman*.
He who knows thus multiplies through offspring and cattle.
Because Vasiṣṭha saw this, it is therefore called the Vāsiṣṭha. Now, as for the Bṛhat:
the Bṛhat is indeed the summit.
Verily, they proceed while finding firm support in the very height.
Then follows the Vāmadevya;
the Vāmadevya is indeed cattle.
Those who have praised with this [hymn] become possessed of cattle.
Now follows the Śyaita; it is the wedding of the two Sāmans and the continuity of the sacrifice.
Indeed, there is only one vehicle, namely that which consists of the verse: "O heroes, today and yesterday... (RV 7.32.26).
By that very same [rite], the second day is performed.
JB 3.27 |v1 Regarding those [verses], there is the *mādhucchandasa*.
|v2 Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra indeed desired: "May I be foremost, preeminent, and possessed of sacred splendor (*brahmavarcas*)."
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it. Thereupon, indeed, he became preeminent, chief, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcas).
Thinking, "May we be foremost, preeminent, and possessed of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*)," they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
They indeed become foremost, preeminent, and possessed of spiritual luster.
Furthermore, because Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra saw [this], it is called the *Mādhucchandasam*.
That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
thus, they find firm support in cattle.

JB 3.28 |v1 “Oṁ! That exhilaration of yours which is most excellent”—thus there are *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "exhilaration" (*madvatī*) for the *pavamāna* of the third *pavamāna* (the Ārbhava).
|v2 Exhilaration, indeed, is essence (*rasa*).

This third pressing is, as it were, like something that has been drunk up. In that these [verses] contain the word "madvat" (possessing exhilaration), they thereby place essence into it; they cause it to swell with this very [element].
"Flow with truth for the sake of the soma-juice"—thus [he says], for the juices become full of soma; "soma-juice" (*andhas*) is indeed food, and it is for the attainment of food.
"The slayer of Vṛtra, the enemy"—this is the form of the Triṣṭubh.
That which contains the word "striking" (ghnadvat) is indeed the form of the Triṣṭubh;
for the Triṣṭubh is the ruling power (kṣatra). [The verse:
"The ruddy one has become mingled with the cows that are easy to approach"—this is indeed like something that has rushed forth.
The day belongs to the Bṛhat [Sāman],
for that [day] is indeed the Bṛhat.
When [he says] "with those that are well-established," it is for the sake of the day’s establishment.
In those [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa already explained. Now, the Bārhata [Sāman] with the *aviṣmat* [verse] has the *pariṣṭobha* [chanting] and the *bahirnidhana* [finale].
Therefore, it is performed on the day belonging to the Bṛhatī metre.
Haviṣmān and Haviṣkṛt were two Aṅgirases; when the Aṅgirases were departing for the heavenly world, they were left behind.
They both desired: "May we fly after those who are departing for the heavenly world," yet they were left behind.
The two of them desired, "May we fly up after [the sun] to the heavenly world.
They performed austerity;
they saw these two *sāmans*.
The two of them praised with these [verses]. Having praised, they flew up toward the heavenly world, saying, "To the one possessing the oblation! To the preparer of the oblation!
Indeed, cattle are those who possess the oblation; cattle are the preparers of the oblation.
Verily, by means of these two [Sāmans], they then secured cattle;
having sacrificed with those cattle, they went to the heavenly world. These two are the Sāmans pertaining to cattle and leading to heaven.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and goes to the heavenly world.
Indeed, these two *sāmans* are truly the proclamation and the explanation of the oblation (*havis*).
Therefore, when the *dhāviṣmat* [sāman] occurs on the second day, it is as if saying "We are possessed of the oblation" to the gods.
They say:
"For at this time they are, as it were, possessed of the oblation (*haviṣmant*).
And as for the fact that there is a call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛta*) on the ninth day, it is [the call] 'O preparer of the oblation! that he makes thus to the gods."
They say:
"For then they are indeed like those who have prepared the oblation. These two *sāmans* are the proclamation of the oblation and the explanation of the oblation.
Because the two Aṅgirases, Haviṣmān and Haviṣkṛt, saw [this], they are therefore called Haviṣmant and Haviṣkṛt.
"Flow on, most honey-sweet!"— thus there are verses in the Kakubh meter that are rich in sweetness.

The exhilaration (*mada*) is indeed sap (*rasa*). This third pressing is, as it were, solidified. In that these [verses] contain honey, they thereby bestow sap upon it; by this [means], they truly cause it to swell.
They cause him to swell.
O Soma, you are the exhilarating drink most skilled in the seasons for Indra;
you are the great, most celestial exhilarating drink.
Thus, they place that essence and intoxication into him in successive order.
JB 3.30 |v1 |v2 Regarding those [verses], there is the *sīdantīya*:
"The gods indeed desired, 'May we sit upon the heavenly world.'"
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it. Thereupon, they indeed settled in the heavenly world.
Thinking, "May we settle in the heavenly world," they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
They indeed settle in the heavenly world. Because the gods settled in the heavenly world by means of this *sāman*, it is called the "Sīdantīya."
Now they also call this the "stake" (śaṅku). For they strengthen that which is the *dadhiṣeṇya* by means of a stake;
this second day is, as it were, like the *dadhiṣeṇya*.
Therefore, it is performed on the second day:
"May these pressed drops, the bay steeds, go toward Indra, the bull;
born for swift hearing, the Soma-drops find the light of heaven."
Thus, by means of the *ṛc*, the first day is made to possess the light of heaven (*svarvat*); this [second day] is done by means of the *sāman*.
For the first day belongs to the *rathantara*, while this one belongs to the *bṛhat*.
Regarding those [verses], there is excellent knowledge:
when the gods and the asuras were about to engage in a contest of calls, they sought to strike down [each other]; with that which was the form of the gods, [they acted].
Having entered them in bodily form, they sought to slay those among the gods who practiced private Vedic study in the forest;

and they sought to slay those who were in the village and practiced private Vedic study in the forest. Then, as for those who were in the village and practiced private Vedic study in the forest, they [sought to slay] them by means of their form.
They sought to kill him.
They sought to kill those very ones by means of mutual discord.
Then the gods became aware of this.
They said, "Let us perform a formal consultation.
They performed the consultation, saying: "Whomever we ask as he wanders, 'To whom are you going? let him say, 'I am going to Indra.'"
Whenever they asked him as he was wandering, "To whom are you going? he would always say, "I am going to Indra.
They said, "You are well-known."

That indeed is the state of being well-known for one who possesses good knowledge. This *sāman* is indeed consciousness (*saṃjñāna*). Through it, he becomes conscious of whatever he desires to be conscious of by means of it, provided that he knows thus.
Among them, whomever was questioned and did not answer, they struck him down with this very [weapon]. That, indeed, is the slayer of rivals. He who knows thus strikes down his hateful rival.
When the gods were departing for the heavenly world, they were afraid of knowledge. They desired, "May we make knowledge manifest.
They saw this *sāman*.
They praised with that.
Then indeed, knowledge became manifest to them.
Knowledge becomes manifest to one who knows thus.
"Here flows Soma, being purified, as Pūṣan, as wealth, as Bhaga;
he, the lord of the entire world, has looked out upon both heaven and earth.
This [verse] is for the commencement of both days.
Just as one might lead this [animal] while letting it hang down, even so do these two days lead this day: the Bārhata [Sāman] into the Rāthaṃtara.
In those [verses], the Gaurīvita [Sāman] is used; its Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
JB 3.32 |v1 Now follows the Krauñca [chant].
|v2 Kruñ Āṅgirasa discovered the day as if it were something to be sought.
This second day is, as it were, something to be desired;
therefore, it is performed on the second day. Indeed, there was only one day.
Kruñ Āṅgirasa desired, "May I fashion day after day. He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Then indeed he fashioned day out of day itself. In that this *sāman* exists, by means of it one fashions day out of day itself.
For it was Kr̥ṅ Āṅgirasa who, they say, thus drank up day from day itself.
As for what they say here, "The curlew has drunk up the milk," the curlew does not indeed drink it up.
It was the curlew Aṅgirasa who drank it up day after day. The curlew Aṅgirasa, desiring heaven, performed austerities.
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it,
and thereby he indeed attained the heavenly world.
This is the *svargya* (heaven-winning) *sāman*.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world. It is the *ūrdhveḍa*, which is a form of the *bṛhat* [sāman], appropriate for the day belonging to the *bṛhat*.
By that [verse], it is indeed rich in form.
Because Aṅgiras Kruṅ saw it, it is therefore called the *krauñca*.
"The bull of thoughts flows forth, the far-seeing one"—thus they contain the word *vṛṣan* (bull).
This day indeed belongs to the Bṛhatī; it is of the Triṣṭubh metre, which is the form of the Kṣatra.
In those [days], there is a watch.
Indeed, this second day is like Yama.

This day is indeed like that by which twins might be born. By means of the twins, [the gods] blocked the worlds of Yamotgamaurava and ascended to this world. He who knows thus, having blocked his hateful rival from the world, ascends to this world.
By means of the mantra the ṛṣis possess a *nidāna*; by means of the *yāma* Yama [possesses a *nidāna*].
"May we possess a *nidāna*," they say, and they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Thus, they indeed come to possess a *nidāna*.
The house is indeed the foundation, offspring is the foundation, cattle are the foundation, and the heavenly world is the foundation.
He who knows this becomes possessed of a foundation. To that world, the gods sent Yama Vaivasvata.
He desired: "May I have a foundation in this world.
He saw these *yāma* chants;
with them he sang praise.
By means of them, he became possessed of a foundation in this world.
Indeed, having that as his foundation and having those as his offspring, he who knows these Sāmans becomes established in this world by means of these very Sāmans.
Therefore, he who knows this becomes possessed of a foundation in this world and attains the status of being a son of Yama.

Regarding this, they say: "The Sāmans have the ancestors as their deity. One is able to go to that world before the end of one's lifespan; thus he utters the *stobha* "āyuḥ" (life), or indeed "vāyuḥ" (wind).
Thus, indeed, before the end of his life, he does not go to that world. Because Yama saw it, it is called the *yāma*.
Now follows the *yajñāyajñīya*, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
"Come, O Agni, I shall truly proclaim these songs to you;
may you grow strong by means of these drops. For this day is indeed increased when it is composed in the Bṛhatī metre.
In these [stotras], the Sākamaśva Sāman, which leads to heaven, is for the attainment of the heavenly world.
"For thus indeed art thou, seeking heroes,"—the word "thus" (eva) occurs; this is a form of the Bṛhat.
This day belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman.
On these [verses], the Āmahīyava Sāman dedicated to Prajāpati is chanted.
Prajāpati is indeed the Kṣatra (the ruling power).
This day belongs to Prajāpati.
It occurs in Gāyatrī verses.
The Gāyatrī is indeed Brahman.
This day belongs to the Kṣatra.
In that the Āmahīyava [Sāman] occurs upon Gāyatrī verses, they thereby cause the Brahman to attain glory. He who knows this, though being Brahman, becomes manifest as it were the Kṣatra.
For this reason, indeed, there is this manifestation for the Brahmins, as it were for kings, in that the *uktha* and the *brahmasāman* occur within the *gāyatrī* verses.
That occurs while they are reciting the same [verses].
Indeed, what many people declare in common is the truth. That which—
"For you are truly heroic, truly brave, and truly steadfast."
"Thus may your mind be successful.
This is for the sake of the prosperity of truth alone.
"All have magnified Indra"—for this day, which belongs to the Bṛhatī meter, is indeed magnified.
Among those [stotras], the *āṣṭādaṃṣṭra* has its Brāhmaṇa explained.
That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka-sāman*.
Cattle, indeed, are the *iḍā*.
Verily, they thus find support among the cattle;
with the sound of the *abhīḍā*, he chants the third day.
JB 3.35 |v1 The *pratipad* verses are "with flashing light" (*davidyutatyā ruce*). |v2 Indeed, "with flashing light" is the form of the *gāyatrī*.
"‘They chant around [thee] with their cry’—this is for the Triṣṭubh;
‘The bright Soma-draughts, mixed with milk’—this is for the Jagatī.
Indeed, this is the form of these metres; by means of the metres, the third pressing is performed."

The third day is indeed like the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). These [verses] are *gāyatrīs* with the character of the *jagatī*; they are perfect in the form of the day. Wherever they are perfect in the form of the day, there one prospers.
Success attends him who knows thus.
"These drops have been poured forth," is the *anurūpa* verse.
These verses proclaim what has already come to be; for it is by means of these that they point back to what preceded them.
By means of the performance of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans], they proceed by way of the Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa Stomas.
Regarding this, they say: "They begin the day with the Anurūpa [verse] as the form of the Sāman itself.
There are both the Stotriya and the Anurūpa verses.
The *stotriya* is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and the *anurūpa* is the in-breath (*apāna*).
It is by means of these two, the out-breath and the in-breath, that they proceed having attained success.
These [verses] contain words for cattle, for nourishment (*iḍ*), for horses, and for livestock; they serve to secure livestock,
for this day indeed consists of livestock.
They contain the word "viśva" (all),
for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas. They contain the word "antarikṣa" (mid-space).
For this day is the intermediate space.
They contain blessings,
for this day contains blessings.
Now, they pour the *āśir* (milk-mixture) at the third pressing;
this day has the third pressing as its share.
It consists of five verses; for there are five directions, and it is for the support of the directions.
Moreover, the sacrifice is fivefold; it serves as the commencement of the sacrifice itself.
It has a final repetition (paryāsa) for the support of progeny and the securing of cattle.
The seventeen-fold chant (saptadaśastoma) is employed.
Prajāpati is indeed the seventeenfold;
it is thus that they proceed, finding firm support in Prajāpati himself.
JB 3.37 |v1 “By Agni is Agni kindled”—this is the *ājya* chant dedicated to Agni, belonging to the *rathantara*. For this day belongs to the *rathantara*. |v2 Indeed, this day is *rāthantara*.
When indeed fire is kindled by fire, that is truly the *vairūpa* [sāman] being kindled by the *rathantara*, or the *rathantara* by the *vairūpa*.
Regarding this, the wife of Sañjāti Ārāḍi said: "Since my husband considered that I had only two *pṛṣṭha* [stotras], how then..."
"Because the donkey brayed at the Udumbara post," they say,
"this day belongs to the Rathantara;
therefore, the Rathantara should be made the *pṛṣṭha* stotra for this day."
Regarding this, they say: "What indeed would man be, or what would he be, if he were only his self (ātman) and not possessed of cattle?
The Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are indeed the self;
the Pṛṣṭha [Stotras] are the cattle.
"Therefore, for this day, the Vairūpa should indeed be made the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra].
In that the Vairūpa serves as the *pṛṣṭha* for this day, they thus establish cattle within their own selves."
"O Mitra of purified will, I invoke him"— with these words the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa occurs;
"hu" is indeed the form of the Rathantara.
This day belongs to the *rathantara* [sāman].
"And they accomplish the prayer for Varuṇa, the destroyer of enemies, which is dripping with clarity"—this is indeed for the sake of success.
"By means of Truth, O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who increase Truth and touch Truth..."
You have attained the vast cosmic order.
"O sages, O Mitra and Varuṇa... (RV 1.23.4)—thus it comes to be "vīti," which is the form of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
This day has the intermediate space as its receptacle.
"‘For you shall indeed be seen together with Indra’—this belongs to Indra. Now, ‘together’ (*sam*) and ‘forth’ (*vi*) are the forms of the intermediate space.
Indeed, from here this world is directed upwards, and that [world] from there is directed downwards."
And this intermediate space is indeed both *sam* and *vī*.
"Meeting together with the fearless one, the two joyful ones of equal splendor"—
the third and fourth days are indeed identical.
Or rather, the fourth day is born from the third day.

[The verse] "From there, according to their own nature, they have again entered the state of being embryos" (RV 10.51.6)— it is for this reason that on the third day they again enter the state of being embryos, for the sake of the birth of the fourth day.
They are called "bestowing" that which is worthy of sacrifice.
O Indra, with those who break even what is firm and who carry you as their vehicle,
you found the ruddy cows even in the cave.
Thus, these verses concerning cattle and possessing cattle serve for the attainment of cattle;
for on this day, there are indeed cattle.
JB 3.39 |v1 “I call upon those two by whom this [world] exists”—this verse addressed to Indra and Agni occurs.
|v2 By saying “they have carried the voice, the sacrifice,” they thus invoke them; and with the words “all that was done formerly has been surpassed,” [the rite is concluded].
For this which has been performed now is indeed just as it was before:
"Indra and Agni do not neglect us."
"O fierce ones, destroyers of adversaries!"—
thus [it is said].
"Vīti" is the form of the intermediate space.
This day has the intermediate region as its vessel:
"O lords of the virtuous, you slay the Āryan enemies; you slay the Dāsa enemies;
you slay all those who hate us."
Thus there is the Vārtraghna [hymn] at the end for the sake of victory.
By means of this three-day period, the gods indeed conquered in the beginning.
Therefore, since this Vārtraghna Ājya-śastra is performed at the end, it is for the sake of victory and for the slaying of the enemy.
He who knows thus triumphs; he slays his enemy and rival.
There is the seventeenfold hymn-form (*stoma*).
Prajāpati is indeed the seventeenfold;
it is by means of Prajāpati that they proceed, finding firm support.
"‘High-born for thee, O Soma, is the plant’— these *gāyatrī* verses containing the word *andhas* belong to the midday *pavamāna*;
for *andhas* is food, [and it serves] for the attainment of food."
"Seated in heaven, bestow [wealth] upon the earth"—these are verses addressed to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivīya*).
This day, namely the *vairūpa*, is as it were unestablished;
therefore, in that these verses addressed to Heaven and Earth are used, they establish this very day by means of them.
"O Indra, for the one worthy of sacrifice, for Varuṇa, for the Maruts"—thus they become verses addressed to the Maruts.
For the form of the midday pressing belongs to the Maruts;
thus they do not depart from the form of the midday pressing.
"Enā viśvāny arya ā"—thus they become *viśvavatī* verses;
for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas. Regarding these, the *gāyatra* [stotra] has its Brāhmaṇa already explained.
Now follows the Vaiṣṭambha [stotra].
The gods indeed ascended to the heavenly world on high;
they did not perceive the quarters.
They desired, "May we see the quarters.
They saw these two *sāmans*; they praised with them.
Then he beheld the quarters;
he stepped upon them;
they seemed to dissolve away.
Just as one would stretch a hide over two wooden frames, so indeed did they intend to stretch [the sacrifice] over these two *nidhana*s.
They resolved upon them.
Thus, when these two *sāmans* are performed, it is for the support of the quarters and for the conquest of the heavenly world.
Indeed, this day is the quarters, and these two *sāmans* are the quarters.
Therefore, when these two *sāmans* are performed on this day, they directly take hold of the quarters.
"O Soma-drops, the living ones..."—it contains the word "toward" (abhi), which is the form of the Rathantara;
this day belongs to the Rathantara.
JB 3.41 |v1 Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, that very same thing the Asuras did after them.
|v2 Those gods said, "Whatever indeed we do at the sacrifice, that the Asuras imitate us."
"Let us unite this triple Veda with the *gāthā*," they said.
They then deposited the triple Veda joined with the *gāthā*.
The Asuras said of it: "This has not truly come into being, which they have united with a *gāthā*."
"Let us abandon this. They abandoned it.
Therefore, from that which had been abandoned, the gods extracted this essence of the Gāthā.
This became the *pragātha*. Because they extracted the essence (*rasa*) from the *gāthā*, that is the reason for the *pragātha*'s name. It is indeed this very essence that was extracted.
It becomes praised with essence for one who, knowing thus, praises with the *pragātha*.
Now, in the beginning, the *ṛc* and the *gāthā* were indeed identical; they surpassed one another.
They entered into a contest.
He extracted the essence from the *gāthā*;
that became this *pragātha*.
Because he extracted the essence from the *gāthā*, that indeed is the reason for the *pragātha* being called a *pragātha*.
This very [Pragātha] is indeed the intensified essence (*rasa*). His praise becomes perfected through the essence when one who knows thus praises with the Pragātha.

In that [fire-altar], the gods indeed beheld the Virāj as food and a productive couple. Since the first [verse] consists of four feet and the two following ones consist of three feet each, those [verses] amount to ten feet.
They become complete.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* is food.
They indeed beheld this.
Now, when they call the former [verse] the *bṛhatī* and the latter the *pragātha*, that is a couple, a procreative pair.
In that very [pair], Vasiṣṭha beheld the *virāj* as food-eating, a fourfold procreative couple.
In that regard, since the first [verse] consists of four feet and the following three consist of two feet each, they amount to ten feet in total.
The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the Virāj is food.
He saw this [formula]:
"One"—that is one; "two"—that is three; "three"—that is six; "four"—that is ten.
That indeed is the Virāj.
"One" means "one," "two" means "two," "three" means "three," and "four" means "four"— this indeed is the couple, the procreative union, up to four.
He who knows thus is procreated through a couple.
In those [verses], the *paurumudga* [is used].
The purifying Soma (*pavamāna*) is performed with the *paurumudga*.
Purumudga Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, performed austerity. He saw this Sāman;
with it, he praised.
He approached this *iḍā*. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
from it, he indeed obtained cattle.
This is a Sāman pertaining to cattle.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Furthermore, because Purumudga Āṅgirasa saw it, it is called the Paurumudga.
The gods and the asuras contended for supremacy over the ocean.
Those gods desired, "May we submerge the asuras in the ocean first.
They saw this *sāman*.
They praised with that.
With it they submerged the Asuras in the east. Because they submerged them in the east (pūrve ’majjayan), that is precisely why the *paurumudga* has its name *paurumudga*.
He who knows this submerges his hateful rival even before him.
Of those [who emerged], whosoever among them emerged last, they struck him down with this very *sāman*. It is indeed a slayer of rivals.

Why is this Sāman called "rakṣohā" (the slayer of Rākṣasas)? Because they [the ancient seers] were indeed slaying the Rākṣasas. He who knows thus slays his hateful rival; he strikes down the Rākṣasa, evil.
Then [he sings] for Gautama.
Both meters are for prosperity: the Bārhata by means of the Prastāva, and the Rāthaṃtara above it.
Gotama Rāhūgaṇa desired, "May I be a winner of gain.
He saw this Sāman;
with it he praised.
From that, indeed, he became a winner of gain. "May we be winners of gain," they say as they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*); they become winners of gain indeed.
Therefore, both those Ṛṣis who are beyond Gotama and those who are below him worship Gotama alone as the Ṛṣi;
for he beheld this greatness.
Both those ancestors who are further removed from him and those who are closer approach him who knows this.
And because Gotama Rāhūgaṇa saw this, it is therefore called "Gautama."
JB 3.45 |v1 Now, regarding the intermediate space: |v2 When the gods had departed for the intermediate space, the Asuras pierced them.
They desired: "May we, having conquered from the intermediate space by means of the intermediate space, ascend to the heavenly world.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Then indeed, having conquered through the intermediate space by means of the intermediate space, they ascended to the heavenly world.
That is the very reason for the "intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*) nature of the intermediate space.
This is that *sāman* which leads to victory and the heavenly world.
He who knows this conquers and goes to heaven.
This day is indeed the intermediate space;
for the intermediate space is, as it were, shimmering.

In that it has its *nidhana* in the middle, it is for the sake of stability. On both sides of it, he chants the *pariṣṭobha* syllable; this is the form of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), for this intermediate space is, as it were, enclosed on both sides by these two worlds.
Therefore, one must not omit this *sāman* from this day.
For this day is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and this *sāman* is the intermediate space. By chanting it, one ascends by means of the day itself.

And because the gods, by means of this *sāman*, having conquered from the intermediate space through the intermediate space itself, ascended to the heavenly world, therefore it is called "the intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*).
JB 3.46 |v1 Now follows [the story of] Kaṇva.
|v2 Kaṇva Nārṣada, indeed, having wandered for a long time without a firm foundation, desired: "May I find a firm foundation."
He saw this Sāman;
he did not see its *nidhana*. He heard it from the cry of a cat.
He saw that;
he praised with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he became firmly established.
This is the *pratiṣṭhāsāman*. He who knows thus finds firm support. Because Kaṇva Nārṣada saw it, it is therefore called the *kāṇva*.
"Three voices the bearer sends forth"—the final verses are *triṣṭubh*s, which is a characteristic form of the third day.
By this very means, the three days are made consistent.
"The thought of Order, the inspired wisdom of the sacred word (*brahman*)."
"The cows go toward the lord of the herd, inquiring; the prayers go toward Soma, lowing.
Thus they contain verses concerning cattle and livestock, for the very purpose of securing cattle;
for on this day, there are indeed cattle.
In them, there is lamentation.
By means of lamentation, indeed, the gods, while lamenting, went to the heavenly world.
Because they went to the heavenly world while crying out, that is the reason for the name *saṃkrośa*.
This is the *Sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows this goes to the heavenly world while indeed crying out by means of this [Sāman].
Therefore, they call it "The Lamentation of the Aṅgirases.
The Aṅgirases indeed desired, "May we go to the heavenly world while being in harmony and crying out together.
They saw this Sāman.
They praised with that.
Then, indeed, being in full agreement and crying out together, they went to the heavenly world.
Because they went to the heavenly world while crying out, that is the very reason for the name "saṃkróśa" (the cry).
This is the *sāman* that leads to heaven. He who knows this goes to the heavenly world, being in harmony with it and crying out together with it. For the heavenly world is indeed prosperity (*śrī*).
He who knows this attains prosperity and goes to the heavenly world.
Furthermore, because the Aṅgirases perceived it, it is called the "Lamentation of the Aṅgirases.
Indeed, these two *sāmans* are the Invocation and the Response: "He ye ho vā hā ho."

In this way the Aṅgirases called out; with "hā vā o vā," they responded. These two *sāmans* are indeed the call and the response; they lead to heaven and serve for the attainment of the heavenly world.
Thus it was said.
O Indra, even if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths belonging to you, O wielder of the thunderbolt, a thousand suns could not equal you.
|v2: Not even a thousand suns can match you, O wielder of the thunderbolt.
Thus, that which possesses hundreds and thousands is the form of the Jagatī;
this day is of the Jagatī nature.
"The two worlds did not [contain] him when born"—these two, indeed, are the two worlds.
It is these very [deities] that it thus praises:
"O Bull, most powerful one, you have filled all [worlds] with greatness and manly vigor for the sake of strength"— thus they become associated with all (viśvavatīḥ),
for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
"O Maghavan, O wielder of the thunderbolt, help us in this cow-filled pen with your wondrous aids"— thus they become verses concerning cattle and livestock,
for the very purpose of securing cattle;
for on this day, there are indeed cattle.
In those [stotras], there is the Vairūpa.
The year, indeed, is multiform (virūpa); the seasons are multiform; the half-months are multiform.
Therefore, that which has five *nidhanas* is because there are five seasons; that which has twelve *nidhanas* is because there are twelve months; that which...

Just as there is an advance in the direction [of the quarters], so it is with this; for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas, like the universe itself. This Vairūpa [sāman] is indeed procreation. Therefore, that which is performed on the third day is for the sake of procreation on the fourth day.
When the gods came into being, the Asuras also came into being.
Those gods became horses; the Asuras did not follow after that.
Thereupon, the gods indeed prevailed, and the Asuras were defeated.
He prospers through his own self, and his hateful rival is defeated, for one who knows thus.
In that it is "horse-like" (aśvavat), it serves for the removal of the enemy.
There is an *iḍā* of one and a half verses on the third day; there is an *iḍā* of one and a half verses on the fifth day.
Just as a frog might croak, so should he croak here.
By that very act, the fifth day is made free from weariness.
Indeed, all speech is attained on the third day.
In that these two *vṛkaṇa* vessels are used, it is for the attainment of both kinds of speech: that which is domestic and that which is wild. (JB 3.50)
Upon them [he places] the Vaiṣṭambha [brick].
By means of the Vaiṣṭambha, the gods, having pinned down the Asuras from these worlds, performed the sacrificial session (sattra) in their own abode.
By means of the Vaiṣṭambha alone, [the sacrificer] pins down his hateful rival from these worlds and [performs the rite] in his own abode.
He who knows this sits as one performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
This [practice] is indeed called *naiṣṭambha*;
it is designated as *vaiṣṭambha*.
This day is indeed the belly;
this Vaiṣṭambha [stotra] is food.
In that the Vaiṣṭambha is performed here, they thereby place food for themselves in the very middle of their being.
Therefore, indeed, this person here is, as it were, propped up by food. The *taraṇiḥ* verses, which desire to win across, are well-known as the *stotriya*s.
In them, the *raurava* hymn—threefold in form and threefold in response—is the characteristic form of the third day.
Agni is indeed the ruru deer; Agni is Rudra.
Because cattle flee from him, it is Agni who causes the cattle to flee from him.
And when cattle approach him, it is Agni who causes the cattle to approach him.
The Sattrins belong to Agni; verily, by their own deity, he secures cattle for them. That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman.
Cattle, indeed, are the *iḍā*.
Verily, they thus find firm support in cattle.
"Three voices have risen up"— these *gāyatrī* verses belong to the *pavamāna* laud of the *ārbhava* section; they are the characteristic form of the third day.
By that very [means], three days are made sufficient.
The cows low as milch-cows;
the tawny one goes bellowing.

Thus, these verses contain the word *go* (cow) and the word *paśu* (cattle); they serve for the attainment of cattle, for on this day cattle indeed [prevail]. "The sacred prayers (*brahmīḥ*) cry out toward [him]"—it contains the word "toward" (*abhi*), which is the form of the *Rathantara*.
This day belongs to the *rathantara* [sāman].
With the words, “For wealth, the four oceans,” there is the attainment of offspring for this very fourth day.
With the words, “O Soma, for us from all sides,” they become possessed of the word *viśva* (all).
For this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
"Flow on, bringing thousands,"—in that it contains "hundred" and "thousand," that is the form of the Jagatī.
This day is of the nature of the Jagatī.
Regarding those [verses], the *gāyatra* has its *brāhmaṇa* already stated. Now follows the *pāṣṭhauha*:
O descendant of Aṅgiras, desiring heaven, one who possesses a six-year-old mare performed austerities.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it;
then indeed he attained the heavenly world.
This is that *sāman* which leads to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Furthermore, because Aṅgiras saw [the verses] consisting of four-year-old mares (*pāṣṭhauhī*), it is therefore called the *pāṣṭhauha*.
Indeed, these two *sāmans* are the call (*hūti*) and the response (*pratiśruti*). With "Ho! Ye! Ho! Vā! Hā! Ho! the Aṅgirasas called out;
with "Hā! O! Vā! O! Vā! they responded.
These two *sāmans* are indeed the call and the response; they lead to heaven and serve for the attainment of the heavenly world.
"O pressers, pour it out all around"—thus there are verses containing the word "around," which is a form of the end.
For this day indeed comes to an end.
In these [days], the Vāc-sāman;
the gods sit for a sacrificial session (sattra) with the Niṣkara.
They did not know the way to the heavenly world; this was the third day.
They desired, "May we come to know the heavenly world; may we recognize this third day. While they were singing the *sāman*, Speech floated down toward them.
They saw that;
they praised with it;
through it, they prospered.
Knowing by means of it the heavenly world, one performs this third day.
This is the *ṛddhi* Sāman that leads to heaven. He who knows thus prospers and goes to the heavenly world.
That which is indeed auspicious and peaceful is the *sāman* of speech.
They say, "He speaks the *sāman*.
When one speaks what is good, that becomes this *sāman*; thus, by means of the auspicious and peaceful [nature] of speech, he [performs] the three-day period.
They pacify it.
Because one leaps up while singing the *vāk-sāman*, it is therefore called the *vāk-sāman*.
[The verse] "O friends, sit down for the one being purified; sing forth! thus becomes the *pravatī* and *parivatī* verses.

In that they are *pravatīḥ* (downward-flowing), it is for the sake of the procreation of the fourth day itself. Now, as to why they are *parivatīḥ* (encompassing): this is the form of the end, for this day is indeed the end; whatever is the end, that is the end, [and thus] "it is non-existent" (*asad*).
They go around the end by saying "around, around."
In them [was] that which pertains to the Śukra.
Indeed, the Aṅgirases, while performing austerity, were grieving.
They desired, "May we strike away the heat of affliction.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
By that, they struck away impurity (*śuc*). Because they struck away impurity, that is the reason for the *śaukta* [beads] being called *śaukta*. He who knows this strikes away misfortune (*śubham*).
Śukti Āṅgirasa, desiring heaven, performed austerities. He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he praised.
Then indeed he attained the heavenly world.
This is that *sāman* which leads to heaven;
he who knows thus attains the heavenly world.
Because Śukta Āṅgirasa saw [this], it is therefore called *śaukta*.
"The pressed Soma juices, most sweet and exhilarating, for Indra"—thus they become verses containing the word *mada*. Indeed, *mada* is essence (*rasa*).

This third pressing is, as it were, like something that has been consumed. Therefore, in that these [verses] contain the word "mad" (intoxicating), they thereby place essence into it and cause it to swell with this very [word].

"Flowing with purifiers, let your exhilarating juices go to the gods"— by saying this, they place the essence and the exhilaration in him in successive order. "The drop flows for Indra," thus the gods have said.
The Lord of Speech exerts himself like a sacrificer, the ruler of all by his might.
Thus they become verses addressed to the Viśvedevas;
for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
"The ocean flows in a thousand streams, stirring the voice"— in that indeed which contains "a hundred" and "a thousand," there is the form of the Jagatī.
This day is of the Jagatī nature.
In those [stotras], the Gaurīvīta has its Brāhmaṇa explained. Next is the Tvaṣṭrīsāman, the Sāman that begets heroes.
A hero is born to him who knows thus; moreover, it is for the procreation of the fourth day itself.
For this Tvaṣṭṛ-sāman is procreation.
It has its *nidhana* in the middle for the sake of stability.
Those who undertake the Ārmava Pavamāna launch themselves upon the ocean as their support. In that there is a *madhyenidhana*, it is for the sake of stability.
Moreover, it is as if obstructed; it has the form of an end.
The end, indeed, is the heavenly world.
This third day, which is being performed, is brought forward for the sake of the heavenly world.
That it is, as it were, suppressed serves to prevent the non-attainment of the heavenly world.
"Thy filter, O Brahmaṇaspati, is stretched out"—thus they contain the filter.
Indeed, this atmosphere is stretched out like a filter;
this day has the atmosphere as its receptacle.
"O Lord, you encompass the limbs from all sides"—thus they contain the word *viśva* (all), for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
"One whose body has not been heated does not partake of that; only those who are cooked, carrying it, enjoy it together"—this is for the sake of complete attainment.
"The filter of the nourishment of Truth is stretched out at the station of heaven; its shining threads have been spread abroad.
The swift ones protect its purifier; they stand upon the back of heaven with splendor.
Thus, it is for the complete attainment of the heavenly world itself.
The dappled bull, the foremost, has shone forth at the break of dawn; seeking strength, he bellows among the worlds.
By his creative power, the masters of illusion have measured him out; the fathers, who behold men, have deposited the embryo.
Thus, on this third day they again deposit the embryo for the sake of procreation on the fourth day.
In these [verses], there is safety for the sake of the safety of the sacrifice itself.
For whatever in the sacrifice is ill-chanted, ill-recited, or defective, this indeed serves as its protection against harm.
Verily,
by this sacrifice one becomes unharmed.
The gods indeed performed this twelve-night rite.
Whatever among them was liable to perish, they made it imperishable by means of the Ariṣṭa.
That is the imperishability of the Ariṣṭa. He who knows this overcomes evil through the twelve-night rite of the Ariṣṭa and attains prosperity.
That *iḍā* consists of three parts; for the *iḍā* is cattle, and cattle are this day. It is for the securing of cattle in their proper order. Indeed, the three *iḍās* are truly medicine.
Indeed, that which consists of three *iḍā*s is the auspicious and peaceful state of speech. In that the three *iḍā*s occur on the third day, they thereby pacify the three days.
Now follows the *yajñāyajñīya*, whose *brāhmaṇa* has already been explained.
"Sing forth to the most generous one" (RV 8.99.1)—this is the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya* hymn, for which the Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.

"We praise that exhilarating drink of yours" (RV 8.99.3)—thus they become verses containing the word *mada* (intoxicating joy). In this way, they place the essence, the exhilaration, at the very beginning of the third pressing.
In them, there is the Hārivarṇa [Sāman] with the Brāhmaṇa already stated. That has four *nidhanas*; for cattle are four-footed.
The *uṣṇih* is cattle; [it serves] for the attainment of cattle in their proper order.
"Listen to the call of Tiraścī," [he says]; this is the Tairaśca [chant].
Other worlds, indeed, are upright; the gods and the seers won them.
Then Tiraścī Āṅgirasa desired: "May I win the worlds of Tiraścī— that by which these waters flow,
by which this wind blows, by which that sun moves, by which the moon [moves], and by which the stars [move]."
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
By means of it, he conquered the horizontal worlds (the intermediate regions), by which these waters flow, by which this wind blows, and by which yonder [sun]...
The sun moves along that path by which the moon and the constellations move.
Indeed, by other rites people conquer the worlds vertically;
but by this [rite], they conquer both worlds horizontally and simultaneously.
He who knows thus conquers both those who move horizontally and those who move upwards.
Tiraścī Aṅgirasa desired, "May I restrain heroes and cattle.
He saw this *sāman*.
He praised him with this [hymn]:
"O Indra, hear the call of Tiraścī, who honors you.
Fulfill me with wealth consisting of heroic sons and cattle; for you are great."
Thus he indeed secures both heroes and cattle;
that is the securing of heroes and cattle. He who knows this secures both heroes and cattle.
Because Tiraścī Āṅgirasa saw it, it is therefore called the *tairaśca*. When the gods were going to the heavenly world, the *rakṣases* followed after them;
they desired, "May we slay the *rakṣases*."
They saw this *sāman*.
Having made it into a fortress for the gods, they enclosed it on all sides. By means of it, they struck away the *rakṣases*.
That, moreover, is the driving away of the Rākṣasas. He who knows thus drives away the Rākṣasa and evil. That becomes the Aiḍa Sāman for the Acchāvāka.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle; thus they find firm support in cattle.
JB 3.57 |v1 When the sacrifice is obtained, when the meters are obtained, when the deities are obtained, and when these worlds are obtained, they ask: "By what means is the fourth day extended?"
One should say, "By speech alone.
Thereby, speech alone remains; the single syllable remains as the three syllables.
That very [speech] conforms to the subsequent three-day period.

As for what he says, "The sacrifice is obtained": the first day has the morning pressing as its share, the second has the midday pressing as its share, and the third has the third pressing as its share; by this, the sacrifice is obtained.
As for what he says, "The meters are obtained": the morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī*, and the midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*.
The morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī*, the third pressing belongs to the *jagatī*; by means of these, the meters are obtained.

When he says, "the deities are obtained," the morning pressing belongs to the Vasus, the midday pressing to the Rudras, and the third pressing to the Ādityas; by means of these, the deities are obtained.

As for what is said, "These worlds are obtained": this [world] is the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), this is the midday pressing (*mādhyandinaṃ savanam*), and that is the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*); by these, these worlds are obtained.
Only the syllable remains as three syllables.
He indeed conforms to that very subsequent day. He who knows Indra on the fourth day becomes possessed of sensory power.
Speech, indeed, is Indra on the fourth day.
One who knows thus becomes possessed of the powers of the senses.

These [verses] are used: "O Pavamāna, these milch-cows of yours for the Aśvins... These are descending verses on the introductory day (prāyaṇīya), for this day is indeed something that must be led forward.
The *prētis* are the form of the *gāyatrī*.
It is by means of this very form of the *gāyatrī* that they set forth.
With the words, "The celestial ones have been released with milk, the sustainers," they thus approach the form of the *virājs*.

For this day belongs to the Vairāja [Sāman]. With the words, "O you who stand firm from the intermediate space, they have been poured forth for you," they become possessed of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Indeed, the third day is the vessel for the intermediate space.
This was produced on the third day.
"O you whom the wise ones cleanse, O seer," [he says]; for they indeed cleanse one who has been born.
And he is born by means of this day.
"From both sides are the rays of the purifying one"— with these two [verses], they indeed generate him by means of these two three-day periods;
they generate him from the former and extend him from the latter.
‘The banners of him who stands firm go around’— the day is indeed the firm one, and the meters are the banners.

Just as one would yoke oxen that have become exhausted and are standing upright by attaching them to the pole in two turns, even so they yoke the meters in two turns when the days have been completed.
"‘If the tawny one is cleansed upon the filter’—they are indeed cleansing him as soon as he is born;
for by this day he is born.
‘He sits in his own womb, in the jars’—this they state directly regarding Soma himself."
"O all-seeing one, your rays encompass all abodes, you who are the skillful master. For Agni, indeed, is the master throughout these worlds;
it is him they thus generate from the morning pressing.
When he has been born, they churn him at the midday pressing:
"O Soma, you flow according to the law, pervading all; you are the lord, the king of the entire world. For he indeed rules over this entire world.
These [verses] are Jagatī meters with the appearance of Gāyatrīs, perfect in the form of the day. For wherever they are perfect in the form of the day, there one prospers.
Success attends him who knows thus.
Indeed, the Arpaṇa of this juncture was not seen.
The first three-day period consists of the Jagatī meters within.
They begin this day with the Jagatī metre; thus they approach it from its very beginning. Verily, he who knows the four-yoked Stoma is carried along by four yoked [horses].
The first three-day period belongs to the Jagatī;
they commence this day with the Jagatī.
Just as one would yoke a side-horse to a side-yoke, even so is the latter [three-day period] joined to the former three-day period.
He yokes [the chants] in succession for three days. Four [cows] yoked together carry him who knows thus.
He whose meters are expanded is indeed one whose meters are contracted; he whose meters are contracted is one whose meters are expanded.
The meters are arranged in expanded form.
The first three-day period occurs within the Jagatī. They begin this day with the Jagatī.
From that very point they proceed in a balanced manner. The second three-day period (tryaha) ends with a *triṣṭubh* verse;
they enter upon the third three-day period with a *triṣṭubh* verse.
From the *sama* they thus pass over into the *sama*, since the third three-day period (*triyaha*) occurs at the end.
They enter upon the tenth day with the *gāyatrī*;
thus, passing from the *sama* into the *sama*, they proceed.
This indeed is the collection of meters.
"The purifying one has brought forth" (RV 9.62.25)—thus the *anurūpa* contains the word "born.
By this, they bring forth the *ṣoḍaśin* from the morning pressing.
They undertake that [laud] at the third pressing once it has been produced.
Regarding this, they say: "They undertake the form of the day itself with the *stotriya* and the *sāman* with the *anurūpa*"; thus there are both the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa*.
The *stotriya* is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and the *anurūpa* is the in-breath (*apāna*).
It is by means of these two, the out-breath and the in-breath, that they proceed having attained success.
"Like the bright lightning-flash from heaven, the great light of Vaiśvānara"— with these words they approach the form of the *bṛhatī* [meter].
For this day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre.
"O Pavamāna, your essence; O Pavamāna, your essence"—thus it strikes the same form as the Vairāja, for the form of the Vairāja is struck.
With the verse, "When they have gone forth like eager cows," they approach the very form of the introductory rite (*prāyaṇīya*),
for this day is indeed the introductory one. With the words, "The impetuous, tireless ones have stepped forth, striking away the black skin," the "black skin" is indeed evil.

By this very [verse], they strike it away. With the words, "We win the gain, crossing over the bridge that is difficult to cross," they indeed cross over that very bridge which is difficult to cross, consisting of three days.
"The roar of the mighty Pavamāna is heard like the sound of rain;
lightnings move in the sky"—
thus they attain the form of the Bṛhat [Sāman].
For this day belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman.
"Flow forth, O Indu, bringing great nourishment, rich in cattle, rich in gold, rich in horses, and rich in heroes, O Soma!"
Thus there are verses containing the word "cow" (gomatīḥ) and the word "cattle" (paśumatīḥ), for the very purpose of obtaining cattle.
Flow on, O thou who art seen by all people; fill the two great worlds, heaven and earth, as the sun fills them with his rays at dawn.
Thus they contain [verses] addressed to Sūrya;
for this twenty-first day belongs to Sūrya, and the Vairāja melody is its foundation.
"O Soma, flow around us on all sides with thy protecting stream."
As rivers flow toward the ocean, so do they flow toward the world.
Thus, these [verses] revolve; they are a form of the end, for this day is indeed the end.
O you of lofty mind, flow swiftly around with your beloved luster,
where they say, "The gods are here."
Making complete that which was incomplete;
"This is he who [comes] from heaven"—
thus it becomes *paripari*, which is a form of the end.
Or rather, the *anuṣṭubh* is the end among the meters;
this day belongs to the *anuṣṭubh*.
It consists of six verses; for there are six seasons, [and it serves] for the attainment of the seasons.
Regarding this, they say: "Since a six-verse hymn is the characteristic form of the sixth day, why then is it performed on the fourth day?"
He should say: "There are six seasons; they are the year. The year is Prajāpati, the sacrifice.

By this, having attained the year, Prajāpati, and the sacrifice, they begin again at the opening of the *savana*s. For this sacrifice is indeed completed when this preceding three-day period is completed.
The subsequent [section] consists of six verses.
By means of this, they undertake the sacrifice in its proper sequence. "They urge on the hero at dawn"—for indeed, they urge on [the one] who has been born.
On this day he is born. "Sisters, female kinswomen [go] to their husband"—these indeed are the sisters; these indeed are the female kinswomen.
"O great one, [you who] desire the great Indra"—these indeed are the "great-desirers. It is they who thus exhilarate him.
"O purifying one, with light for the sake of light"—thus, as the *rukma* (golden ornament), they attain the form of Sūrya.
For this twenty-first day belongs to Sūrya; the Vairāja [Sāman] is its foundation.
"O Pavamāna, [bestow] excellent praise, rain, and service upon the gods; flow for the sake of continuous nourishment."
Thus there is a paryāsa for the support of progeny and the attainment of cattle.
The stoma is twenty-onefold.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first.
These twelve *jagatī*s,
when combined, become twenty-four *gāyatrī*s;
these [twenty-four] *gāyatrī*s become eighteen *anuṣṭubh*s.
This day is in the Ānuṣṭubh metre.
JB 3.62 |v1 “The watchful guardian of the people has been born,” with these words the *ājya* chant for Agni contains the word "people" (*jana*).
|v2 For he indeed is the guardian of the people.
It is him indeed that they thus generate from the morning pressing;
once he has been generated, they churn him at the midday pressing.
By saying "Agni," he thereby calls him forth.
"O you of good skill, for new prosperity"—skill (*dakṣa*) is indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*);
thus they place the vital breaths into him.
"With ghee as his face"—ghee is indeed the beloved abode of Agni; by means of that which is beloved, they [endow] him with it.
They cause it to prosper with its own splendor.
With the words, "With greatness, touching the sky," they approach the form of the Bṛhatī;
for this day belongs to the Bṛhatī.
"Radiant and pure, he shines forth for the Bharatas"—these, indeed, are the Bharata people; for them, he thus shines forth in his purity.
Moreover, because the Bharatas first sacrificed with this [fire], and because he carries the oblation to the gods.
Therefore, it belongs to the Bharatas.
[Verse 13] "Thee, O Agni, the Aṅgirasas [discovered], hidden in secret"—thus it says "thee," which is a form of the Bṛhatī.
This day is connected with the Bṛhatī. [Verse 14]
“‘They found him resting in every wood,’ for they indeed found him resting in every wood.
‘He is born when being churned, a great force,’ for they churn him first from the morning pressing.”
They produce him when he has been born at the midday pressing.
"Thee they call the son of strength, O Aṅgiras"—for they produce him thus as strength.
"The banner of the sacrifice"—for he indeed is the banner of the sacrifice.
Wherever, indeed, one is consecrated, there this very banner is raised up in the east.

"First [they established] the domestic priest"— thus they indeed place him (Agni) right in front. When they establish the fire with the words, "Men have kindled Agni in his threefold seat," these creatures are indeed the men.
These very [verses] kindle him thus:
"Seated on the sacrificial grass with Indra and the gods on the same chariot, the wise Hotṛ sits down for the sacrifice."
It belongs to all the gods;
for this day is connected with the *anuṣṭubh* meter and belongs to all the gods,
and the *anuṣṭubh* indeed belongs to all the gods.
"O Mitra and Varuna, this [is for you]..."—thus there is a cup for Mitra and Varuna.
Indeed, this is a repetition regarding the oblation;
for the sacrifice stands firm when this first three-day period is completed.
"Where now is your sacrifice?"—this, indeed, is what they say to the gods.
Therefore, for this reason, the sacrificer should prepare a second portion of clarified butter (*ājya*).
"O two kings, free from malice, in your firm and most excellent seat."
"The two sit upon a thousand-pillared [throne].
Thus they approach the Virāj in its thousandfold form;
for this day belongs to the Vairāja.
"O sovereign kings, drinkers of clarified butter"— thus they contain the word "sovereign" (*samrāj*),
for they attained sovereignty at that time.
"Indra [conquered] with the bones of Dadhyañc"— this [verse] belongs to Indra.
Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa was indeed radiant and possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*).
Whenever the Asuras caught sight of him from afar, they would lie down there with their heads shattered.
He indeed ascended to the heavenly world.
Indra, being overwhelmed by the Asuras, asked, "Where indeed has that Dadhyañc gone?
They said to him, "O Blessed One, he has indeed ascended to the heavenly world."
He said, "There is nothing at all remaining of this here.
They said to him, "This horse-head indeed existed, by which he taught the Devaveda to the Aśvins; but we do not know where it has gone."
"Seek that," he said. So they sought it. [They found:
"Searching for the horse's head which was hidden among the enemies..."
"He knows that at Śaryaṇāvat. Indeed, this is the name of a lake in the rear part of Kurukṣetra.
Having understood this, they abandoned it;
they gave it to him.
Indeed, he maintained it in the presence of the Asuras.
Whosoever among the Asuras saw him from afar would indeed lie there headless.
With those very bones, he struck down ninety-nine of the Asuras. This, then, is the "Slaying of Rivals" (bhrātṛvyahā), the "Victory" (vijiti).
"Indra, irresistible, struck down ninety-nine Vṛtras with the bones of Dadhyañc.
Thus [it is said].
He who knows this conquers and strikes down his hateful rival.
Here they recognized the secret name of Tvaṣṭṛ’s cow,
even so in the dwelling of the moon.
Thus, these verses concerning cattle and possessing livestock serve for the attainment of cattle.
"This [hymn] of mine for you two" is a verse addressed to Indra and Agni;
"Indra and Agni, with ancient praise... [is another].
"Like rain from a cloud, he was born. "He was born," they say, or "he has been born."
By this day, he is born anew.
"Listen to the call of the singer, O Indra and Agni; accept our songs.
As lords, cause our prayers to swell."
O Indra and Agni, do not deliver us to wickedness, nor to calumny;
do not subject us to reproach!
This is indeed the warding off of evil.
The twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*ekaviṃśa-stoma*) comes into being.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first. Verily, they go to share the same world with him; they ascend unto him.
"Flow on, accomplishing skill," thus there are *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "skill" (*dakṣa*) for the midday *pavamāna*.
By means of these [verses], they strengthen the day; they strengthen the meters; they strengthen the deities; they strengthen the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
With the words, "The golden one for the gods to drink, for the Maruts, for Vāyu, for exhilaration," they become verses addressed to the Maruts (*marutvatī*).
The form of the midday pressing indeed belongs to the Maruts;
