thus they do not depart from the form of the midday pressing.
[The verses] "He shines together with the gods, O bull," contain the word *vṛṣan* (bull) and possess the form of the Bṛhatī.
This day belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman.
"O Pavamāna, impelled by prayer, bellowing toward your dwelling-place"—thus they become verses containing the word "dwelling-place" (*yoni*).
From the dwelling-place, indeed, offspring and cattle are born.

The form of this Vairāja day is like that of a human being. [The verses] "By the law, they have raised Vāyu... contain the word *vāyu*; for Vāyu is peace, and it is for the sake of peace, so that there may be no burning.
In those [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa explained.
Now, the Ātharvaṇa with four *nidhanas* is the form of the fourth day.
The Atharvans went upward to the falcon, the heavenly world.
They did not find firm footing there.
They desired, "May we find firm footing in the heavenly world.
They saw this *sāman*.
With it they praised. Thereupon, indeed, they became firmly established in the heavenly world.
That [sāman] has four *nidhanas*; it serves for support, for they say, "May he be firmly established like a four-footed [animal]."
This is well-established; it leads to heaven and provides a firm foundation. He who knows this goes to the heavenly world and stands firmly established in the heavenly world.
Moreover, that is indeed a remedy and an expiation.
Then they perform a healing rite as if for Arbhu;
by this very means they effect a healing and an expiation.
That [rite] remains unassailed.
From what is not pierced, indeed, offspring and cattle are born.
This non-piercing is the characteristic form of this Vairāja day;
by it, it is truly rich in form.
And because the Atharvans saw it, it is therefore called the *Ātharvaṇa* with four *nidhanas*.
JB 3.67 |v1 Now follows the Vairāja [sāman] for one who desires the *nidhana*.
|v2 The Virāj is indeed like this: it has neither the *svāra* [intonation], nor the *nidhana*, nor the *eḍa*, nor is it equal to the *ṛc*.
That has *vāc* as its *nidhana*.
For *vāc* is indeed the *virāj*; it is for the sake of commencing the *virāj*. By this, they directly commence the *virāj*.
In this very *nidhana* of it, indeed, are all desires.
Whatever desire one may desire, let him meditate upon it while approaching this *nidhana*;
that very desire shall be fulfilled for him.
Or because there were desires (*kāma*) at its *nidhana*, it is therefore called the *Vairāja* "desire-at-the-*nidhana*" (*nidhanakāma*).
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerity. They beheld this *sāman*.
With it they praised. Then indeed they attained the heavenly world.
This is that *sāman* which leads to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Its finale is this very one: that fire which they churn out at the Vairāja-stotra.
"O Soma, I have rejoiced in the truth-bearer"—in the word *tava* ("of thee"), there is the form of the Bṛhat.
This day belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman.
"O Indu, [your] friendships day by day—O tawny one, many [enemies] approach me; pass beyond the enclosures."
Thus they indeed went beyond.
"O Soma, you who flow by day and by night, the brown one, you are milked from the udder"—these two, indeed, are the two udders. He thus addresses these two; these two milk for him all desires.
"Beyond the glowing sun that burns with heat"—thus they contain verses addressed to the Sun;
for this twenty-first day belongs to the Sun, and the Vairāja melody is its foundation.
"Like hawks [they have flown] toward their nests"—for they indeed flew beyond.
Among those [stotras], the one for Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra has already been described in the Brāhmaṇa.
That which follows is the Ūrdhveḍa; it is the form of the Bṛhat, and it belongs to the day of the Bṛhat-sāman.
By this, indeed, the form is made complete.
JB 3.68 |v1 Now, the Abhīśava [stotra] is the forward movement of the sacrifice and the backward retreat; thus, he takes hold of the fifth day and retreats back toward the third.
By means of the twelve-day rite, the gods indeed ascended to the heavenly world from above. That [world] of theirs, not being firmly grasped, slipped away.
They saw these two *sāmans*.
Just as one would mount a chariot after securing it with two reins, even so did he ascend to the heavenly world by securing it with these two.
Having gone to the heavenly world, they said: "These two Sāmans have indeed become the reins of the sacrifice."
That is precisely why they are called *ābhīśava* (reins). These two are the *sāmans* leading to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Therefore, both these *sāmans* should indeed be performed.
For just as one might travel with a single rein, so it is with whichever one [of the two] is used; but just as one might travel with both reins, so it is when both are used.
Therefore, both [rites] should indeed be performed.
In this regard, one might say that on the ninth day, either one [of the two] should take place.
Abhīśu Śyāvāśvi desired: "May the gods be satisfied with my Soma."
He saw these two *sāmans*; he praised with them. Thereupon, the gods were indeed satiated by his *soma*.
Of these two, there is indeed something as if unaccomplished; just as one would satisfy [them], so [it is].
Saying "e-e," they satisfy them while warding [the evil] away.
These two are the *tṛptisāmans*.
The gods are satisfied by the soma of him who knows thus.
And because Śyāvāśva saw [this], therefore they are called "Ābhiśava" (the pressing for Śyāvāśva).
Now, the *caturnidhana* of the *Āṅgirasa* is the form of the fourth day; moreover,
by means of it alone, the four days are made complete.
The Aṅgirases, desiring cattle and desiring heaven, performed austerities. They saw this Sāman;
they praised with it.
Having approached this *iḍā* in the middle, they subsequently ascended to the heavenly world. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the heavenly world is the light of heaven (*svaḥ*).
It was by taking their stand upon cattle that they then went to the heavenly world.
This is a *sāman* that is beneficial for cattle and leads to heaven.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and goes to the heavenly world.
Furthermore, because the Aṅgirases perceived it, it is called the "Fourfold Chant of the Aṅgirases" (*caturnidhanam āṅgirasam*).
Then these [verses] come into being: "Purifying himself, he has stepped forth toward... [and] "He has stepped beyond...

These are for the purpose of stepping beyond. For they indeed step beyond these worlds in an outward direction; [they do so] toward the world of Āditya, for these worlds are indeed [the world of] Āditya.
This is the first three-day period.
The world of Āditya is the fourth day;
it is this very [world] that they now transcend.
"From the womb the ruddy one has risen"—thus they possess a womb;
for from the womb indeed offspring and cattle are born.
This contains the form of this Vairāja day, characterized by "being born."
"Indra, the bull, has drunk the pressed [juice]"—these verses contain the word "bull" (vṛṣan) and are thus the form of the Bṛhatī.
This day belongs to the Bṛhatī.
"Now, O Indra, [grant] great wealth to us; O Soma, [be] for us from every side"—these verses contain the word "all" (viśva).
For this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
With the verse, "Flow on, bringing a thousandfold," they approach the Virāj, which has a thousand forms;
for this day belongs to the Virāj.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who place the final [verse] in the *gāyatrīs* fall away from the *triṣṭubhs* of the *pavamāna*. They consist of verses containing the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*);
for the form of the *triṣṭubh* is indeed characterized by the "bull."
Therefore, they do not proceed with the *pavamāna* verses ending in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
In those [verses], the *satrāsāhīya* is used; its *brāhmaṇa* has already been stated.
That becomes the *uktha-sāman*; for the *ukthas* are indeed cattle, and it is for the attainment of cattle.

Regarding this they say: "The *uktha* and *sāman* are performed during the *pavamāna* [laud]; why is that so? The first day has the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) as its share; the second has the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*) as its share;
the third has the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) as its share.
Now, this is the vessel for the *uktha* hymns.
In that the *satrāsāhīya* chant is performed here, they thereby cause it not to fall away from the *ukthas*.
Thus, they make it prosper in its own proper abode.
By means of that which is thus successful, there is prosperity for them within their own community. Now, the *ukthas* are indeed cattle, and the midday pressing is the self.
Therefore, when they chant the *satrāsāhīya* toward the midday pressing, they thereby place the cattle within their own self.
They establish [them].
The Vairāja [sāman] is indeed procreation. Therefore,
when one begins with two choral responses (*stobha*) that form a pair, it is for the sake of the procreation of the pair.

"Three [bricks] are placed first; from truth itself as a *stobha*, progeny are produced," it is said; "three are placed later: out-breath (*prāṇa*), in-breath (*apāna*), and diffused breath (*vyāna*).
These very [breaths] are thus laid down by that [formula].
He pronounces the word *padam* three times. Two form a couple;
that which is born from a couple is the third.
He pushes it away three times.
From what is pushed away, offspring and cattle are born.
He who knows thus is propagated with offspring and cattle.
Ten times he supports it; he sows those very bones.
There are nine *stobhas*, the *nidhana* is the tenth; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is food.
It is for the attainment of the *virāj* and of the eating of food.
They churn the fire.
Agni, indeed, is the Virāj. Thus they generate the Virāj as food.
Having uttered the *hiṃ* and having chanted the *prastāva*, they churn.
For from the *hiṃ*-utterance, seed is deposited. Moreover, they thus generate the *virāj*—the food-eating power—from the very middle of the *sāman*.
They churn [the fire] on the lap of the Udgātṛ; the Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ hold it steady, so that the Virāj may not be cut off.
They churn on the right lap;
therefore this half of a person is more vigorous.
They churn [the fire] upon a splinter for the sake of peace.
They churn upon *avakā* grass so that it does not burn excessively. Once it has been produced, they carry it to the Āgnīdhra shed.
Therefore, they distribute the fires from here.
Regarding this, they say: "The Āhavanīya fire is indeed the horse; the sacrificer is the Āhavanīya, and this is his offspring.
Thus, they cause the sacrificer himself to prosper with offspring.
Regarding this, they say: "They take away the very food from him from whom they carry away the fire.
One should address that [fire] with the following mantra:
May it return with strength, O Agni, may it return with food and long life;
protect us again from distress.
"Return with wealth, O Agni; overflow with a stream that nourishes all, from every side.
With this, he places food back into himself once again.
They conclude with the same [note] with which they begin.
Therefore, that sun moves both hitherward and thitherward;
from the very place where it has risen today, it will rise tomorrow.
Now follows the Vāmadevya.
The Vāmadevya is cattle;
those who praise with it become possessed of cattle.
"The men, acting in concert, have fashioned and generated Indra, the one who overcomes all hostile armies"—
thus they contain the word "generated" (*janat*).
This form containing the word "generated" is the characteristic form of this Vairāja day.
On them [the *ṛc*s], the *traiśoka* [is chanted]. Indeed,
the *vairāja* [sāman] has almost entirely fled from the sacrifice.
They support it with the *traiśoka* [chant], as if with a longer meter. These worlds, being together, swelled up in three ways.
They grieved, just as one might grieve when a single thing is divided into three.
Those gods said, "Let us drive away the three *cuca*s from these three worlds.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
By that, they struck away the three sorrows of these three worlds.
Because they struck away the three sorrows of these three worlds, that is the reason for the *traiśoka* [hymn] being called *traiśoka*.
He who knows this drives away sorrow.
They deposited those [sorrows] in the eunuch, the gambler, and the unchaste woman;
therefore, these are pierced by sorrow and suffer.
These do not arise for one who knows thus.
Therefore, one should not speak against these [sacrificial portions], lest one share in sorrow.
Kaṇva Nārṣada indeed married the daughter of the Asura Akhaga.
From her were born two sons, Triśoka and Nabhas.
Enraged, she went to her kinsmen,
and they came after her.
The Asuras, smearing themselves with pride, said to him: "Recognize whether the dawn has broken here, if you are indeed a Brāhmaṇa!
But the Aśvins became aware of this;
for the Aśvins are the releasers from bonds among the gods.
While remaining invisible, the two of them came to him and said, "Whenever we strike our lutes together and fly over you one after the other, then know that the dawn has broken.
Thus, they used to fly up during the night, saying, "Arise! The day has failed; yoke the ploughs!"
"It has not dawned yet," he used to say.
Then these two, striking their lutes together, flew over and over him.
He said, "Take this away; the day has now failed. Yoke the ploughs!"
They said, "This man was indeed a brahmin seer;
his wife is difficult to carry off."
"Come, let us give this [cow] to him.
They gave it to him. She said, "They will surely try to kill you again by means of something out of sight;
do not sit down upon her."
They set out.
For him, they placed a golden throne in the shade. He sat down upon it heedlessly.
Then that very rock, having become solid, completely enveloped him.
His two sons, Triśoka and Nabhāka, became aware of this, thinking: "The Asuras have indeed completely enveloped our father with a rock!"
The two of them arrived.
Nabhāka desired, "May I deceive these [enemies].
He saw this Nābhāka hymn.
With that, he praised her;
she appeared within it.
Just as the thread of a gem might be seen within the gem, so it was.
Then Triśoka desired, "May I cast this [sorrow] away from myself."
He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he split her in two.
Her exhaustion ceased.
He desired of him, "May he live. He touched him with the words, "O, may you live!
He lived.
For him, it was as if darkness.
He desired, "May it be for me as if by day.
He touched it with the words, "O light, come from heaven! (o yī diva).
For him, it was as if day had come.
He desired: "May I cause him to go to the heavenly world.
With the words "O, yonder sky," he caused him to go to the heavenly world.
If one should feel as if exhausted, he should conclude with the *nidhana*: "O *yi* jīva.
Now, if for someone it should be as if in darkness, he should conclude with the *nidhana*: "O *yi* diva.
Now, if one should desire offspring, he should conclude with the *nidhana*: "O *yi* divam."
These indeed are the *nidhanas* of this *sāman*, and these are the desires.
He wins these very desires.
Whatever desire one has when he praises with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him; for it was what Triśoka saw.
Therefore, it is called "The Three Sorrows."
"O King of the peoples," they said, for they were then going as if toward royalty;
"he who is unrestrained with his chariots."
The deliverer from all hostile armies, whom I praise as the supreme slayer of Vṛtra.
(Thus they went, as it were, seeking preeminence.
O Puruhanman, adorn that Indra for our protection, he who is the eternal sustainer.
In the hand the vajra has been placed, beautiful to behold like the great god Sūrya.
Thus they contain [verses] regarding Sūrya;
for this twenty-first day belongs to Sūrya.
The Vairāja [sāman] is the foundation.
Among them is the *pṛśni*. Speech, indeed, is the *pṛśni*.
By means of this day, they seek to attain speech;
it is that very speech which they thus bring into harmony.
And regarding this, they say: "The speckled ones of Bharadvāja."
Bharadvāja indeed desired, "May I be propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle.
He beheld this *sāman* and praised with it.
Then indeed he multiplied through offspring and cattle. He [Pṛśni] said, "May I indeed multiply through offspring and cattle. That is the origin of Pṛśni's name.
This Sāman is procreation.
He who knows this is propagated with many offspring and cattle. Moreover, it is said that by means of this very Sāman, Bharadvāja obtained various kinds of food.
That is the *sāman* for the attainment of food. One secures food; he who knows this becomes the best of his kin as an eater of food.
Because Bharadvāja saw it, it is called "Bharadvāja’s Spotted" (*bharadvājasya pṛśni*).
That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman.
The *iḍā*, indeed, is cattle;
thus they find firm support in cattle.
"O sage, [go] around the dear [regions] of heaven"— these *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "around" (*pari*) belong to the *pavamāna* laud of the third pressing; they are a form of the end.
The Anuṣṭubh is indeed at the end among the meters;
this day belongs to the Anuṣṭubh.
With the words, "Forward, forward to the dwelling, more glorious," they thus approach the very form of the Prāyaṇīya [opening] sacrifice.
For this day is indeed the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*).

"He, the pure son, having been born, made his two parents shine as soon as they were born"—thus these verses contain the word "born" (*janat*). By means of them, they generate the *ṣoḍaśin* from the third pressing.
In those [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa already stated.
Now follows the Aurṇāyava.
Indeed, the Gandharva Ūrṇāyu desired the Apsarases.
He saw this *sāman*. He praised with it.
By means of it, whatever he desired, that he attained; whatever he touched, that he reached.
He obtained it. This is that *sāman* which wins desires;
indeed, he desired this very desire.
That desire was fulfilled for him. Whatever desire one praises with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him.
Because the Gandharva Ūrṇāyu saw it, it is therefore called the *aurṇāyava*.
The Aṅgirases, desiring heaven, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
They did not find the way to the heavenly world.

Śvitra Āṅgirasa went forth with the fuel-offering. The Gandharva Ūrṇāyu, from above, descended upon him with this *sāman* and said: "This *sāman* indeed leads to heaven; praise with it! Having praised with it, you shall find the world of heaven."
"But you must say that the Sāman belongs to me alone.
If anyone should ask you, 'Who told this to you?', you must simply say, 'Ūrṇāyu told it to me. Do not speak of it to anyone other than me."
He returned and said, "This Sāman is indeed heavenly.
Let us praise with it;
by praising with it, we shall surely find the heavenly world."
They said to him, "Who told you this? He replied, "I myself saw it. They praised him for that.
By praising with that [verse], they indeed came to know the heavenly world. As they were departing for the heavenly world, he was left behind;
for he had spoken untruth, and thus he became this leper (śvitra).
These variegated snakes are indeed the *ahyaḥ*.
Because they diminished (*ahīyata*), that is the reason for the *ahi* nature of snakes. Now, the others are simply serpents (*sarpa*).
Therefore, indeed, from whomsoever he may have learned it, let him say to that person: "I have learned it from so-and-so.
Moreover, one should desire to speak only the truth;
for this is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows thus attains the heavenly world.
"For you indeed, O friend, in the divine [sacrifice]"—thus it is; this is a form of the Bṛhatī.
This day belongs to the Bṛhatī.
"O Pavamāna, most radiant among births"—thus they become verses containing the word "birth.
By this, they generate the *ṣoḍaśin* from the third pressing.
Among those [stotras], one of the Bṛhats is the Bṛhat-sāman. By means of this, indeed, this day is made to consist of the Bṛhat.
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerities. They saw this Sāman; they praised with it.
So, having become the Bṛhat itself, it carried them to the heavenly world.
Having gone to the heavenly world, they said: "Truly, this Bṛhat has become our bliss (ka), by which we have pervaded the heavenly world."
That indeed is the reason for the *bṛhatka* being called *bṛhatka*.
This is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
For one who knows this, there is wide space (*ka*) for him, and he attains the heavenly world.
"Soma, being purified, flows through the sheep's wool with his wave,
crying out at the forefront of speech as he purifies himself.
Thus it becomes, as it were, the very beginning.
For this day is the foremost, which belongs to the Bṛhatī metre.
With the words, "With prayers they groom the prize-winner," they indeed groom him as if he were born;
for by means of this day, he is born.
The bounteous one has been released toward the jar, like a steed seeking the prize; purifying himself and generating speech, he has flowed forth.
Thus they become verses containing the word *jana* (people).
In this way, they generate the *ṣoḍaśin* from the third pressing;
for indeed, they generate the *ṣoḍaśin* from each and every pressing.
JB 3.79 |v1 Regarding these [verses], there is the *ātīṣādīya*.
|v2 Prajāpati created living beings.
Once they were created, they became exhausted.
He desired, "Let these creatures of mine not become exhausted.
He saw this Sāman.
With that, he touched them;
they became equal. Yet they seem to perish on the fourth day, for they go toward the *anuṣṭubh*.
The *parā* is indeed the *anuṣṭubh*.
By means of this [Sāman], they eat from the far distance.
Therefore, one should reach the *nidhana* of this Sāman at the very end, for the attainment of a full lifespan.
Regarding this, they say: "One should approach [the sacrifice] without becoming exhausted. For when one becomes exhausted, then one dies.
Therefore, one should approach it without becoming exhausted."
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerity. They saw this Sāman; they praised with it.
So, having become a *sāda*, it carried them to the heavenly world.
They said, "It has indeed gone (*eti*) as a *sāda*. Because they said, "It has indeed gone as a *sāda*," that is the origin of the name *etīṣādīya*.
Having gone to the heavenly world, they said, "Ah, we have indeed reached heaven!
That is why the *ātīṣādīya* is called *ātīṣādīya*. This is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.

He who knows this attains the heavenly world. Now, these [verses] are: "O you, the conquerors of the front of the soma-juice... These are Virāj and Anuṣṭubh verses on the Vairāja day, for the attainment of food and nourishment through the Virāj itself.
And just as one would mount two other newer wheels, even so they carry this Anuṣṭubh around at the openings of the three-day periods for the attainment of the heavenly world.
JB 3.80 |v1 In them [is] the Nānada [sāman]. |v2 By means of the Nānada, indeed, Indra slew Vṛtra as he was roaring.
That which does not roar is the non-roaring nature of the Nānada;
by means of this, one who knows thus slays the roaring, hateful rival even as he roars.
He intones the *prastāva* with sixteen syllables.
By this [rite], they directly undertake the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice.
Aupoditi Gaupālaya used to say: "Viśāla placed [the hymn] upon the *libūjā*;
he performed the *nānada* on the *anuṣṭubh* verse; with the *gaurīvīta*, they praised the *ṣoḍaśin*. Thus, they did not fall away from prosperity."
He who knows thus does not fall away from prosperity.
Moreover, that [offering] is prepared as something for the morrow by means of offspring.
Now, the Vairāja Sāman, the Āndhīgava, is performed on the Vairāja day; it is for the attainment of food in the very Vairāja.
They approach this ten-syllabled Virāj from the middle; the Virāj has ten syllables, and the Virāj is food—
it is for the attainment of the Virāj, that is, of food.
Soma flows clear, the progenitor of hymns, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor of earth;
the progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu.
Thus he is called "the progenitor," "the progenitor."
In this way, they generate the *ṣoḍaśin* from the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
Just as one says, "Push! Push! Be born! Be born!", in that very manner they generate the *ṣoḍaśin* from the third pressing in successive order.
JB 3.81 |v1 On these [verses], the Vātsapra hymn is chanted.
|v2 The Pratisattrins oppressed Vatsapri Bhālandana, saying, "Thy father was a thief."
He desired, "May I find faith; may they summon me.
He saw this *sāman* and praised with it.
Then indeed he found faith as an invitation.
"May we find faith," they say, as they sit for the sacrificial session;
verily, they find faith.
This is indeed the *anurūpa* chant of the *vairāja*.
Just as the *stobha* syllables and the metrical movements of the *vairāja* are, so too are the *stobha* syllables and the metrical movements of the *vātsapra*.
This offspring indeed belongs to the Vairāja.
He who knows this is born in his offspring as one who corresponds [to him]. For they offered this to him, thinking, "An offspring corresponding to the Vairāja has been created."
That [day] is unperforated;
indeed, from what is unperforated, offspring and cattle are produced.
This unperforated state is the form of this Vairāja day.
By that [means], it is indeed rich in form.
Because Vatsaprī Bālāndana saw this [sāman], it is called the Vātsapra.
Now follows the Yajñāyajñīya, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.
"‘Agni for you, the increasing’—for this day, which belongs to the Bṛhatī metre, is indeed increasing."
In them [he placed] the Saindhukṣita. Indeed,
Sindhukṣit perceived the end of speech.
By means of this day they seek to perfect speech; it is that very speech which they thus recover.
Sindhukṣit, the Bhārata king, while wandering after having been long exiled, desired: "May I go back to my own home."
He indeed wandered along the Sindhu;
that [land] of his was settled by the Sindhu.
He beheld this *sāman*.
He praised with that [hymn]. Thereupon, he indeed went down to his own abode.
This, then, is the *kāmasani* Sāman.
Verily, he desired this very wish;
that wish was fulfilled for him.
Whatever wish one praises with this *sāman*, that wish is fulfilled for him.
Now, sovereignty is indeed prosperity.
He attained that sovereignty;
he who knows this attains prosperity and attains sovereignty.
Because King Bhārata Sindhuksit saw [this], it is therefore called Saindhukṣita.
"And we you, O Unprecedented One"—for they indeed attained an unprecedented body at this time.
In these [verses] is the Saubhara, the splendor of the Bṛhat.
The Vairāja [sāman] has indeed slipped away from the sacrifice;
they support it with the Saubhara by means of the splendor of the Bṛhat.
Therefore, it has the *ū* as its *nidhana*.
This, indeed, is the perceptible form of the Bṛhat: namely, the syllable *ū* and the syllable *ī*.
By means of these, it is truly rich in form.
[The hymn begins: "O Indra, drink this pressed juice, the most excellent, immortal exhilaration"—for this [soma] is indeed preeminent now.
They were coming;
thus, they place that essence and exhilaration in the third pressing itself.
JB 3.83 |v1 Regarding these [verses], there is a hymn by Vasiṣṭha.
|v2 Vasiṣṭha indeed desired: "May I see the Virāj; may I win it."
While performing the *prastāva*, he beheld this ten-syllabled *virāj*.
He approached it and mastered it. This is the *sāman* that effects the mastery of the *virāj* and of food.
He secures the Virāj and the food of the Virāj; he becomes the best of his kin as an eater of food, who knows thus.
Because Vasiṣṭha saw this, it is called the "Vāsiṣṭha";
and they also call it "the beloved of Vasiṣṭha."
Vasiṣṭha, having been defeated and his sons slain, desired: "May I be multiplied with offspring and cattle. He beheld this *sāman* and praised with it.
Then indeed he multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle.
He said, "Truly, this has become dear to me, since I have obtained dear offspring.
That is the very reason for the dearness of what is dear.
This is the *sāman* of procreation.
He who knows this is multiplied with offspring and cattle.
Because Vasiṣṭha saw it, it is therefore called "the favorite of Vasiṣṭha."
That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
thus they find firm support in cattle.
Now follows the sixteenth [section]. The first day has the morning pressing as its share; the second has the midday pressing as its share;
the third has the third pressing as its share.
Now, this is the vessel for the *uktha*s.
Of all the *uktha*s, this one—the *ṣoḍaśin*—is indeed the single one.
Therefore, when the *ṣoḍaśin* is performed here, they cause him to prosper by means of his own proper abode.
By that very prosperity, there is success among one's own people.
"Flow on, winner of cattle, winner of wealth, winner of gold"— this is the form of the *simāns*. "One who will act, possessing the quality of gold"— this is the form of the *triṣṭubh*.

Therefore, these [verses] are performed on the day consisting of the Triṣṭubh metre. With the words, “O Indu, bestower of seed, thou art established among the worlds,” they insert this very bull, the bestower of seed, into the Mahānāmnī verses at the morning pressing for the sake of procreation.

"O Soma, you are a hero, all-knowing"—this is the form of the *simas*. "To you, the inspired ones (*vipras*), sit down with their songs"—the *vipras* are indeed the Brahmins; they thus worship him with songs.
"O Soma, you are the one who beholds men from every side"— the phrase "from every side" (viśvataḥ) is a form belonging to the Simas.
"O Pavamāna, O Bull, you run through those [worlds]"— thus, at the morning pressing, they insert the Bull among the Mahānāmnīs for the sake of procreation.
"Flow for us, bringing wealth and gold"—wealth (*vasu*) indeed means cattle, and gold means cattle.
For they say that what is not gold is without cattle;
and the *cakvarya* verses are cattle.
"May we be those who live among the worlds"—by this he indeed invokes a blessing.
"O Lord, you pervade these worlds with your vigor"—the word *vīti* (pervading) is the characteristic form of the *simā*s.
"Yoking, O Indu, the bay-winged steeds"—the *śakvarī*s are indeed the bay-winged steeds.
These very [cups] are joined at the morning pressing;
having been joined, they ascend at the midday pressing. With the words, "May these pour for you honeyed ghee," honey indeed refers to cattle—[namely] milk, curds, and clarified butter.
"Beasts and Śakvarī verses flow away from this"—
[with the words] "O Soma, let the seasons and the peoples abide in the vow," for indeed, everything here abides according to the vow of Soma.
These [verses] are *jagatī*s with the color of the *triṣṭubh*, made perfect by means of the form of the day. For wherever they are made perfect by means of the form of the day, there it prospers.
Success attends him who knows thus.
"Of the purifying one, the all-knowing," this is the *anurūpa* (respondent verse).
"The all-knowing" is a characteristic form of the *simāns*.
Regarding this, they say: "They begin with the *stotriya* as the form of the *sāman*, and with the *anurūpa* as that of the day.
There are both the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa*.
The *stotriya* is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and the *anurūpa* is the in-breath (*apāna*).
Verily, having prospered them through the out-breath and the in-breath, they proceed.
"Thy streams have been let loose, like the rays of the sun"—for cattle are indeed released in the manner of streams.
The Śakvarī verses are cattle.
"Making a banner from heaven, you flow toward all the worlds with ease"— this becomes the *abhīti* (overcoming) form, which is the characteristic of the *rathantara*.
This day belongs to the *rathantara*.
"O Soma, swell like the ocean"—thus they contain the word "ocean," for on this day the waters indeed abound. "Being born, you impel speech"—on the preceding day he is indeed born;
being born, he [impels it] by means of this [verse]; therefore, there is the phrase, "Being born, you impel speech."
"O Pavamāna,
in your wide expanse, roar like the god Sūrya!"— with these words they approach the *mahānāmnī* verses, which possess the form of Sūrya.
For the Mahānāmnī verses belong to Sūrya.
The Soma drops have flowed forth, the purifying juices;
being mixed with water, they are gathered together.
The cows have flowed forth like waters going down a slope;
being purified, they have reached Indra. Thus [it is said], "the waters, the waters," for this day consists of water.
"O Pavamāna Soma, you flow forth, exhilarating for Indra;
guided by the men, you are led out. Thus it consists of seven verses.
There are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*). It is by means of these very breaths that they proceed, becoming successful and finding firm support in the breaths.
Regarding this, they say: "Since the form of the seventh day consists of seven verses (*ṛc*), why then is it performed on the fifth day?"

He should say: "The *śakvarī* verses consist of seven feet; there are seven domestic animals; there are seven meters with four additional syllables each; there are seven principal vital breaths; there are twenty-seven celestial lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); this day is the twenty-seventh; [this is] for the securing of all this, for the attainment of this."
The *uttara* consists of seven verses.
Thus they proceed, becoming successively more complete with their vital breaths (*prāṇa*). There is a group of four verses; cattle indeed have four feet.
On this day there are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
There is a *paryāsa* (concluding hymn) for the support of progeny and the securing of cattle.
The *stoma* is the twenty-sevenfold (*triṇava*).
These worlds are the twenty-sevenfold;
it is upon these very worlds that they proceed, finding firm support.
JB 3.87 |v1 *Bhūḥ* is the sacred utterance (*vyāhṛti*).
|v2 This world is its fire, the deity; the *gāyatrī* is its metre, the *trivṛt* its chant, the *rathantara* its *sāman*, and the Vasus [its officiating priests].
The deities are the trees and the plants.
*Bhuvaḥ* is the vyāhṛti. This is the intermediate space; Vāyu is the deity, the Jagatī is the metre, the seventeenfold stoma, and the Vāmadevya [sāman].
The *sāman* is the Rudras; the deity is the *devatāpaś*; the *prāṇabhṛt* [is the meter]. (v5) *Svar* is the *vyāhṛti*.
(v6) That is yonder world; the deity is Āditya; the *chandas* is the *triṣṭubh*; the *stoma* is the fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*); the *sāman* is the *bṛhat*; the [deities] are the Ādityas.
The deities are the moon and the lunar mansions.
These worlds constitute the twenty-seven-fold [stomas].
Regarding this, they say: four days are paired, while the fifth day is unpaired.
Indeed, a pair consists of four; that is procreation.
Therefore, when there is the Āgneya *ājya* chant beginning with "O Seasons, glories, like lightning in the rain," by that very means a fifth day is made into a pair.
"Thine" is for the man; "of Śrī" is for the woman.
"Like the rain" is for the man; "like the lightning" is for the woman.
"Of Agni" is for the man; "like the dawns" is for the woman.
With the verse "When the plants... it is for a woman; with "Impelled... it is for a man.
Thus they establish this procreative union in due order for the procreation of the sacrificer.
When, fanned by the wind and impelled, you spread abroad swiftly through your food according to your will,
O Agni; then your hosts, like chariot-horses, strive apart as you, the ageless one, burn.
Thus it is said.
When the wind fans the fire, then it blazes greatly;
that very blazing is the form of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

[Verse 6] Agni, the creator of inspired thought, the ordainer of the assembly, the invoker, the most pervasive wisdom— [Verse 7] whether it be a small oblation or a great one, they choose you alone, and no other than you.
[Verse 8] Thus, indeed, for whatever oblation there may be, whether small or great, they choose Agni alone for the office of invoker.
He chooses [you].
For even with your wide-extending protection, O Varuṇa, there is indeed help for us now;
O Mitra, may you win your favor.
Thus there is the offering to Mitra and Varuṇa for the sake of averting a badly performed sacrifice.
For whatever in the sacrifice is ill-chanted, ill-recited, or defective, this indeed serves as its atonement.
O you two who are free from guile, may we truly attain your well-ordered nourishment and your abode;
may we be yours, O Mitra and Varuṇa.
"Protect us, O Mitra, with your protections, and save us, O excellent saviors!
May we overcome the Dasyus with our own bodies.
With this, he indeed invokes a blessing.
"Rising up with vigor and power"— this belongs to Indra;
for the Triṇava Stoma is indeed vigor and strength.
They thus recite this very thing directly:
"The two worlds, heaven and earth, follow after you"—for these indeed are the two worlds; he thus addresses these very two.
"‘They bestowed [it] upon him as he was contending’—thus they indeed bestowed it upon him as he was contending. ‘O Indra, when you became the slayer of the Dasyus’—this contains the word ‘slaying.
This, namely the *brahman*’s chant, is indeed the sacrificer’s own hymn of praise."
In their own abode, they destroy every evil of the sacrificer.
"Eight-footed speech, nine-cornered, increasing the cosmic order—
from Indra I have measured out my body."
Thus, speech is indeed the Gāyatrī with eight feet.
Of that [speech], the Trivṛt Stoma is the corners.
This indeed is the supreme divine couple, the source of procreation: the Trivṛt Stoma and the Gāyatrī.
The *chandas* [is used];
they thus establish that supreme divine couple as a source of procreation for the procreation of the sacrificer.
Regarding this, they say: it should be performed from the beginning of the triplet (tṛca).
For seed is indeed emitted from the front; from that, offspring are produced here.
That indeed is semen which is emitted from here.
For semen is emitted from food. Regarding this, they say: "It must be performed above; for this is the organ of generation, and from here offspring are produced."
"Offspring are born from that; therefore, let us procreate.
Therefore, [the offering] must be performed above [the others].
"O Indra and Agni, you two..."—thus there is an offering to Indra and Agni.
"Verses of praise resound toward [him]"— this refers to many verses of praise. Other days consist of single *stomas*,
but this one consists of the *triṣṭoma*.
Therefore, in the phrase "the hymns resound toward [you]," he speaks of many hymns. "Drink the pressed juice, O you two who bring auspiciousness!"
Or those teams of horses, O heroes, which are much-desired by the donor—
O Indra and Agni, come hither with them!
"O Heroes, come with those [hymns] to this pressed libation,
O Indra and Agni, for the drinking of Soma. Thus, while the other hymns of praise are addressed to single deities, this one is addressed to two deities.
It is such that one may stand firm with both feet.
The *triṇava* stoma is employed;
these worlds are *triṇava*.
It is in these very worlds that they proceed, finding firm support.
"O Soma, flow on most brilliantly"— these *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "flow" (*ṛṣ*) belong to the midday *pavamāna*.
"Flow on! is a form of the *rathantara*;
this day belongs to the *rathantara*.
"Roaring toward the vats"—the word "toward" (*abhi*) occurs [here], for that too is a form of the *rathantara*.
"Obeisance to Indra and Vāyu for the waters"— thus they contain the word "waters" (apsumatīḥ),
for this day consists of water.
"To Varuṇa and the Maruts"— thus they contain the word "Maruts" (marutvatīḥ).
The form of the midday pressing indeed belongs to the Maruts;
thus they do not depart from the form of the midday pressing.
With the words, "Bestowing nourishment upon our offspring, O Soma, [bestow it] upon us from every side," they become verses containing the word "all" (*viśva*).
For this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
With the verse, "Flow on, thou who art thousandfold," they approach the Mahānāmnīs, which possess a thousand forms;
for the Mahānāmnīs are indeed cattle.
In them, the *gāyatra* has its *brāhmaṇa* explained.
Now follows the *yaṇvasantani*. Indeed, from the fifth day, the gods fashioned the sixth day.

The fifth day is indeed like a hole. When they chant with the *yaṇvasantani* at the beginning of the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, it is for the continuity of the day and for the absence of a hole in the day.
He who knows thus finds firm support.
Prajāpati created cattle;
once created, they moved away from him.
He desired, "May I bestow cattle upon myself.
He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he bestowed cattle upon himself.
In that he restrained the cattle by means of his own self, that is the "yaṇvat" nature of the *yaṇva*.
This Udgātṛ is Prajāpati;
he restrains the cattle by means of his very self through the *yaṇva*.
This fifth day is indeed the Viṣuvat of the twelve-day rite.

That which is continuous (*santani*) occurs in front, and that which is continuous occurs behind. By means of the continuous [hymn] they continue the first three-day period, and by the continuous [hymn] they continue the latter one.
Indra, indeed, could not master the *simā*s. He desired, "May I master the *simā*s."
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
Thereupon, he indeed mastered the *simā*s.

In that this *sāman* comes into being, it is for the sake of the concord of the *simās*. He chants the *prastāva* three times, he performs the *pratihāra* once, and they proceed to the *nidhana* three times. Thus, they amount to seven.
The Śakvarī verses consist of seven feet;
cattle are characterized by the Śakvarī.
Thus, he has indeed supported them foot by foot.
The Śakvarī verses are cattle.
When there is a *yaṇvasantani* [verse] at the beginning and a *santani* [verse] at the end, it is for the sake of securing cattle.
Just as one might enclose a pen with a wooden bar or a rope, even so does he secure the cattle.
"For the scattering away.
His wealth is not scattered away by one who knows thus.
The waters, indeed, are the *śakvarī* verses.
In that there is a continuous [chant] before and a continuous [chant] after, it is for the sake of encompassing the waters;
therefore the waters flow encompassed.
Indeed, these two are the banks of the waters.

If these two were not present, then everything here would be wiped away, just as one might smear the water used for washing away an enemy; such indeed is this [state] because it has not been wiped away.
In the middle of that very Yaṇvasantani, one should approach the *iḍā*; above it, one should approach the *adhyardhā-iḍā*.
They attain it; for on the Śakvara day, the form of the Śakvarī verses is directly perceived.
By this, indeed, it is rich in form.
JB 3.93 |v1 Now follows the Śākala. |v2 Śakala indeed beheld the fifth day as having the form of the *rathantara*.
Therefore, it is performed on the day belonging to the *rathantara*.
Śakala, desiring food, performed austerity;
he beheld this *sāman*.
He praised with that [verse]. Then indeed he obtained food.
Of this very [sacrifice], there is [the rule]: as one would give, so [should one perform it].
That [sound] becomes like the syllable *hiṃ*. Indeed, the *hiṃ* is food;
for with the sound "hum," food is offered.
This is the *sāman* for the attainment of food. One who knows this secures food and becomes the best of his kinsmen as an eater of food.
Furthermore, whatever harshness is performed on this day prior to the *śakvarī* verses, that very thing [is remedied] by this.
They pacify [the fire] with the *hiṃ* syllable.
Because Śakala saw this, it is therefore called the Śākala rite.
JB 3.94 |v1 Now, as for Vārṣa: |v2 Vṛśa was indeed the domestic priest of King Triyaruṇa Traivṛṣṇa, the descendant of Ikṣvāku.
Now, formerly, the domestic priests used to collect chariots for the kings for the sake of supervision, thinking,
"Lest he should commit some evil.
While they were racing, they cut down with a chariot wheel a young Brahmin boy who was playing on the road.
One ran away while the other pursued him; one went forward while the other came back. Having overtaken him, he was unable to let him go.
They both cut him right there.
In that place they were struck down, each crying out, "You shall kill! You shall kill!
Vṛśa, having unfastened his reins and standing there, said, "You shall kill.
He replied, "No."
"Whoever indeed holds the reins of a chariot, he is the master of the chariot.
"Then you shall be the slayer," [said the other]. "No," said Itara, "I was merely driving away; it was you who intended to strike. You alone shall be the slayer."
"Let us two indeed ask [them]," they said.
So the two of them went to the Ikṣvākus with their question.
Those Ikṣvākus said: "He who indeed holds the reins of the chariot is the master of the chariot.
You alone must slay him! Thus they spoke to Vṛśa. He desired: "May I go forth from here; may I find a path and a refuge."
"May this boy live!"—he saw this *sāman*, and with it he restored him, [chanting]: "O you, the skillful one, who brings bliss... (RV 10.59.4).
The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the *dakṣas*.
He thereby placed the vital breaths within him.
"Today we choose the bearer (*vahni*)."
The protector, desired by many.
To the delightful one, to the excellent one, to the inspired singer, to the wise one;
to the protector, to the one desired by many.
Bring wealth, bring conscious awareness, O you of noble power, bestow it upon us; bring the protector who is desired by many.
Thus.
The person is indeed a protector;
therefore, it set him right. This is the remedy, the expiation, the Sāman.
He indeed performed that medicine as an expiation;
with this [rite], they perform medicine as an expiation. And it is also a means of obtaining desires.
Verily, he desired this very wish;
that wish was fulfilled for him. Whatever wish one praises with this *sāman*, that wish is fulfilled for him.
Enraged, he went among the people, saying,
"They have spoken falsehood to me!"
The vigor of Agni departed from those Ikṣvākus.
Whatever rice-meat they set on the fire in the evening was cooked by morning; whatever they set on in the morning was [cooked] by evening.
They said, "We have indeed encountered a Brahmin who is not an Ārya;
from him the power (*haras*) of Agni has departed from us.
Let us address him with these mantras."
They invited him.
He came just as a brahmin would come when being invited by a king.
Having arrived, he desired: "May I see this power of Agni."
He saw this *sāman*. He sang it. He saw: "This is indeed Piśācī, the wife of Triyaruṇa."
Having covered him with her lap, she sat upon him. Then he uttered these words: "The youthful mother carries the boy hidden in secret; she does not give him to the father."
His form, O people, does not diminish; they behold it placed before them upon the sacrificial ladle.
O young woman, whose son is this whom you, as a handmaid, are fondling? The queen has given birth to him. For the embryo grew through many autumns; I saw him born when his mother brought him forth.
Agni shines with lofty light; he makes all things manifest by his greatness.
He overcomes godless and evil enchantments; he sharpens his two horns to gore the Rakṣasa.

Moreover, let the roars of Agni resound in heaven, with sharp weapons for the purpose of slaying the *rakṣas*. Even in his exhilaration, his splendors shatter [the foe]; the godless obstructors do not hold him back.
Thus, this fire-brand of Agni, leaping upward, completely consumed her.
Then indeed they each took away a portion of Agni’s radiance according to their respective status.
Accordingly, Agni cooked for them.
This is that *sāman* which is brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
By this, they indeed recovered the power that had departed from Agni. He who knows this becomes radiant, possessed of spiritual luster, and brilliant.
That [verse] consists of one and a half iḍās; it is the manifest form of the Śakvarī verses on the Śākvara day.
By that [means], it is indeed rich in form;
and because Vṛś saw it, it is therefore called "Vārśa."
"O Soma, pressed by the pressers"—this is the form of the *simāns*.
"Upon the backs of the sheep"—these verses contain [the words] *go* (cow) and *paśu* (cattle); they serve for the attainment of cattle.
For this day belongs to the cattle. With the verse, "They have gone to the enclosures as to the ocean; the exhilarating one flows for intoxication," the verses contain the word "ocean" (*samudra*).
For this day consists of the waters.
These [verses] have fewer syllables:
some have seven syllables, some nine syllables, and some eleven syllables.
There are twelve syllables each.
Thus, they approach the form of the Śakvarī verses in regular succession.
In these [verses], there is a low-pitched tone accompanied by nudging, which is the form of the *simāns*.
From what is not pierced, indeed, offspring and cattle are born.
He who knows this is propagated with offspring and cattle. Now, Dhītin Anūpa desired: "May I obtain both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*; being a king..."
"May I become a seer," he thought. He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he praised.
Then indeed he obtained both the Brahman and the Kṣatra; being a king, he became a seer. He who knows thus obtains both the Brahman and the Kṣatra; being a king, he becomes a seer.
Or rather, because he saw [the world] from the marshland (anūpa), it is therefore called "Anūpa."
Now follows the *mānava* [sāman] with the *padanidhana*, belonging to the *rathantara* [tune].
Therefore, it is performed on a day connected with the *rathantara*.
Manu indeed desired: "May I multiply with offspring and cattle; may I create offspring belonging to Manu.
He beheld this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Then indeed he multiplied through offspring and cattle. These are the descendants of Manu.
He who knows this truly multiplies through offspring and cattle.
Now they say: "Those very creatures created by him sought to destroy the *rakṣases*.
He desired, "May I slay the *rakṣases*.
He beheld this *sāman*.
He praised him with this:
"O Agni, Manu established thee as a light for all people forever; thou didst shine forth, O Kaṇva, born of the Eternal Law (*ṛta*), strengthened by libations—thou whom the human races revere."
The brilliant, impetuous, and fearsome flames of Agni are not to be withstood;
burn up every *rakṣas*, every sorcerer, and every *atri*! Thus he drove away the *rakṣases*.
That indeed is the driving away of the Rakṣases. He who knows thus drives away the Rakṣas, the evil.
The flood, indeed, polished these worlds.
He thought: "Manu, truly, has come into being here."
He desired, "May I go forth from here; may I find a way and a firm foundation.
He saw these two *sāmans* and praised with them.
The two of them became two golden boats and floated toward him; he stood firm upon them,
and they carried him across.
Then indeed he found a path and a firm foundation.
He who knows thus finds a path and a firm foundation.
And because Manu saw this, it is called "Mānava."
Now, the Vāmra is the undertaking of the sacrifice and the withdrawal from it.
Indeed, by means of the sixth day he undertakes [the sacrifice], and by means of the fourth day he withdraws from it.
For by means of undertakings, the gods indeed excluded the Asuras from the sacrifice.
Vamra Vaikhānasa, desiring cattle, performed austerities.
He beheld this Sāman;
with it, he praised.
He approached this *iḍā* in the middle, and then he approached an additional half-*iḍā* above it.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
the additional half-*iḍā* is the earth.
Then indeed he first obtained abundance among cattle.
This is that *sāman* which is conducive to cattle.
He who knows thus obtains abundance among cattle in due order.
Because Vamra Vaikhānasa saw this, it is therefore called the "Vāmra" [chant].
JB 3.100 |v1 Now follows the *triṇidhana* [sāman] dedicated to Agni, for the fulfillment of the pressings (*savana*).
|v2 By means of the *pavamāna*, food is indeed bestowed upon the gods.
That [sāman] has its *nidhana* in the middle; it serves for the distinction of food-eating.
Agni, indeed, desired: "May I become an eater of food, the best among my own people.
This is the *sāman* that secures food-eating.
He secures food and becomes the best of eaters among his own people, he who knows thus.
And because Agni saw this, it is called the "Agni-related" *triṇidhana*.
JB 3.101 |v1 They also call it the Sākamaśva. |v2 Kakṣīvat asked Priyamedha:
"Is it kindled? Is it not shining? "It is, O Priyamedha! he said. He then learned his name.
He [Priyamedha] said: "Let me answer you back for the sake of offspring."
Now, Kaksīvat had a leather bag belonging to the Nākuli family that was filled with either priyaṅgu grains or sand. Every year, he would throw one grain from it;
such was the lifespan granted to him.
And he, the ninth Sākamaśva, was born from Priyamedha. He desired: "May I go forth from here; may I find a way and a response. He saw this *sāman*.
He sang toward it;
then he saw a response. He rushed toward Kakṣīvat.
Seeing him approaching, he said to him: "Throw this bellows of mine into the water; I shall see that person who will answer back and challenge me.
Then he went straight toward him.
He said: "He who performs only the *ṛc* and not the *sāman* has kindled [the fire], but it did not shine. But he who performs both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, he has kindled it and it shines.
"This is what I say to you; this my father [taught], this my grandfather, this my great-grandfather," he said.
He caused [it] to go from Priyamedha.
This is that splendor, the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), the *sāman*.
By means of this, he indeed drove away the evil from his ancestors of old.

He becomes radiant and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*); he who knows this strikes away the evil of his forefathers and grandfathers. And because Sākamaśva saw it, it is therefore called the *Sākamaśva*.
"O Soma, that which is brilliant and worthy of praise"—thus they become verses containing the word "brilliant" (*citra*). Cattle, indeed, possess various forms;
this day consists of cattle, and it is for the very acquisition of cattle.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who conclude with *gāyatrī* verses at the end of the *pavamāna* chant go astray from the *triṣṭubh* meters."
The verses contain the word *vṛṣan*.
For the *triṣṭubh* has the form of that which contains *vṛṣan*.
By means of this, they do not depart from the *triṣṭubh* verses that end with the *pavamāna* chant.
In them is the state of childhood; for the state of childhood is indeed peace.
When they praise with the *śaiśava* [sāman], it is for the sake of peace. Moreover, they say: "By means of the *śaiśava*, Indra indeed encompassed Vṛtra and slew him with the *śakvarī* verses.
That, then, is the reason for the *śaiśava*'s name "childhood" (*śaiśava*).
That, moreover, is the slayer of rivals. He who knows thus strikes down his hateful rival.
The eye of Prajāpati swelled.
It flew away.
He desired, "May the eye enter me again.
He saw this *sāman*.
He praised him with that [hymn].
Thereupon, indeed, sight entered him again;
having become pure as a horse, it entered him once more.
That light is indeed the eye. That light has entered him.
This is the *sāman* that is beneficial for the eyes.
The eye of one who knows this does not age nor does it perish.
JB 3.103 |v1 Then follow the Mahānāmnīs. |v2 Indeed, offspring are born after the Mahānāmnīs.
Animals have calves that are always with them; these Mahānāmnī verses are to be carried together. Therefore, among humans, those who are pregnant appear more beautiful at an earlier stage.
For that embryo of theirs is eternally to be carried; livestock are born with their young already present;
therefore, pregnant livestock appear more beautiful.
For that embryo of theirs is eternal.
Now follows the Vāmadevya;
the Vāmadevya is indeed cattle.

Those who have praised with this indeed become possessed of cattle. Now, the *bārhadgira* and *rāyovājīya* [sāmans] are performed on each of the five-day periods (*pāṅkta* days); for cattle are fivefold. This day belongs to cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
Now, there are both the *athakāra* and the *adhyardheḍa*; these are the manifest form of the *śakvarī* verses on the day of the *śakvarī*s.
Thus, it is indeed rich in form.
Regarding this they say: "That serpent should bathe today; for he will find a firm foundation and a ford on the further shore of these [waters].
The *śakvarī* verses are indeed cows.
Of these, this is the further shore, the foundation, and the crossing-place: namely, the syllable *atha* and the *iḍā* consisting of one and a half [verses].
One who knows thus crosses over evil through the *niṣṭhā-śakvarī* verses and attains prosperity.
That becomes the *aiḍa* *acchāvāka-sāman*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
verily, they thus find firm support in cattle.
The gods and the Asuras contended.
Those gods ran to Prajāpati, saying, "Grant us that unexhausted metre by which we may overcome the Asuras."
"Let us overcome [them]," he thought.
He performed austerity.
Having performed austerity, he saw himself as a lioness.
When he saw that which was quivering within himself, that became the *simā*-ness of the *simās*.
He said to them, "Be created. They asked, "By what means?"
"By which [path] do you desire to go?
They rose up toward the boundary-line (*simā*) itself and were released;
that, indeed, is why they are called *simā*.
He measured them out;
in them he placed the threefold Veda;
he drew them together.
Into them he placed these three worlds;
he drew them forth.
He said: "Ah, great indeed has this measure of theirs become!"
Because he said, "Ah, great indeed has this measure of theirs become," that is the reason for the 'Great-Measure' (Mahāmānī) bricks being called 'Great-Measure.
Indeed, these are truly named the Great-Measures.
They are called "Mahānāmnīs" (Great-Name[d] Ones) in an indirect sense.
He gave them to the gods.
With them, the gods praised today.
They were unable [to complete it] on the following day.
Because they were unable on the following day after having praised [the Sāman] today, that is the reason for the *śakvarī* verses being called *śakvarīs*.
One who knows thus is able to master what he studies.
The gods did not drive them away;
they gave them back to Prajāpati. Having dwelt in Prajāpati for a year, they departed.
He said, "How have you departed from the conversation?"
They said, "You know our shouts directed toward Indra;
give them to us, by which we may become possessed of shouts."
That brahmin who says, "I know us," is a non-existent one.
To them he gave these sounds belonging to Indra. Whatever was the sound of the fire and whatever was the sound of the chariot, that he gave to her.

Whatever sound belongs to the wind, and whatever [sound] belongs to birds—that he gave to this one. Whatever sound belongs to Parjanya, and whatever [sound] belongs to the drum—that he gave to that one.
These, indeed, are the sounds belonging to Indra among these [cows].
Having dwelt there for a year, they departed. He said, "Why have you departed? They replied, "You know our Aindra games."
"Give us those with which we may play.
"That Brahmin shall play with offspring and cattle who knows this of us," he said.
To them he gave these *aindranikrīḍas*, saying, "Indra! Indra! Indra!"
These, indeed, were their playful sports for Indra. Having lived there for a year, they departed. He said, "Why have you departed?"
They said, "Truly, you know our forms;
give them back to us, so that we may become possessed of form."
That Brahmin who says "I know him" is formless.
He bestowed forms upon them.
That form which belongs to her when she first comes into being during the rainy season, having shed her dust—that [form he gave].
He gave this to her.
And furthermore, whatever is the form of the atmosphere when its dust has been settled during the rainy season,
that he gave to her.
These indeed were their forms.
Having dwelt there for a year, they departed. He said, "How have you departed?"
They said, "Truly, you know our names;
give them to us, by which we may become named.
That Brāhmaṇa shall be nameless who does not know us."
He gave names to them. He said to this one, "Thou art Bhūḥ"; to this one, "Thou art Bhuvaḥ"; and to that one, "Thou art Svaḥ.
These indeed are their names.
Having dwelt there for a year, they departed. He said, "Why have you gone away?"
They said, "You know our calves;
give them back to us, so that we may be possessed of our calves."
That brahmin is a non-existent person who says of us, "I know him.
He gave the calves to them:
he gave Agni to this [earth], Vāyu to the intermediate space, and Āditya to yonder [sky].
These, indeed, were their calves.
Having dwelt together for a year, they went away. He said, "How have you departed?"
They said, "You know our bulls;
give them to us, so that we may become possessed of bulls. That Brāhmaṇa shall be a bull who knows us."
To them he gave these bulls, the *athakāras*.
Indeed, these are their bulls.
Having dwelt with them for a year, they departed.
He said, "How have you departed from the conversation?"
They said, "Verily, you know one form of ours;
grant that to us, by which we may become possessed of form."
That Brahmin who says, "I know him," is formless.
To them he gave this one form: "The waters.
For this indeed is their one form, namely, the waters.
Having lived there for a year, they departed. He said, "Why have you departed? They replied, "You know only one of our names."
"Grant us that by which we shall not be nameless. "That Brahmin would indeed be nameless who does not know us," [they said].
To them, he gave this one name: "Indras."
"Indra" is indeed one name of these [waters].
Having dwelt there for a year, they departed. He said, "How have you departed?"
They said, "You indeed know our satisfactions;
give them to us, by which we may be satisfied."
"May that Brāhmaṇa be satisfied with offspring and cattle, who knows us thus.
To them he gave these satisfactions, these monosyllables.
These, indeed, are their satisfactions.
Having dwelt there for a year, they departed.
He said, "Why have you departed?
They replied, "You know our places for sowing, you know our resting-places, and you know our stalls."
"Give them to us, by means of which we may possess seed-vessels, hearths, and cow-pens. "That Brāhmaṇa would be possessed of a seed-vessel, a hearth, and a cow-pen who knows this of us.
He gave speech to them.
Speech indeed does not exceed this all.
"Evā hy evā" is their speech; "evā hy agnā" refers to cattle; "evā hīndrā" refers to horses.
"Evā hi pūṣan"—this refers to goats and sheep;
"evā hi devā"—this is the enclosing-stick.
JB 3.110 |v1 Now follow the Mahānāmnī verses. |v2 In the beginning, there were seven vital breaths.
For them, he fashioned this seven-footed Śakvarī verse. He who knows thus attains the vital breaths and a full lifespan.
From the seven-footed [verse], he fashioned the six-footed [verse], the Stomas, and the year.
He who knows thus entrusts himself to the seasons.
From the six-footed [verse] he obtains the five-footed; from the five-footed, cattle; from the *paṅkti* [meter], cattle.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of cattle.
From the five-footed [Vāk], he [obtains] the four-footed speech, the *anuṣṭubh*, and the foundation.
He who knows thus speaks with speech.
From the four-footed [Vāk], he obtains the three-footed, the brilliance, the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brāhmavarcasa*), and the *gāyatrī*.
He who knows this becomes radiant and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
From the three-footed [Gāyatrī] he fashioned the two-footed person. He who knows this is not struck down by any human violence.
The one-footed [verse] is for the two-footed; it is indeed the man himself.
For two men are, as it were, following one after the other.
Therefore, a man seeks to win over another man; a man becomes the follower of a man; he gains [him].
"He has many followers; the turn of fate that pertains to man does not find him who knows thus. (1.18)
Having gathered all those meters together, Indra slew Vṛtra with them;
because he slew one who was great (mahāntam), they are called the Mahānāmnīs.
Because she was able (*aśaknot*), they are called *śakvarīs*;
because she made herself firm (*maṭviyam akarot*), they are called *maṭvīs*; because she split the boundary (*sīmānam abhinat*), they are called *simās*.
Then he indeed created them from the very boundary (*sīmā*). They call the best "the boundary" (*sima*).
He who knows this becomes the best among his own people.
These [verses], indeed, have "Indra" as their name.
When Indra desired to form a union with the Mahānāmnīs, they said to him, "He must grant us a share."
"What is it?
"That which is this name of yours.
He gave that to them.
Therefore, these [cups] are called *indrā*. Indeed, "the *indrās*" is their dear, secret name.
Whoever, knowing this, distributes them, his dear [name] comes to him and he beholds it.
"Priyam" (the beloved).
Therefore, they are called "Mahānāmnīs" (those of great names) in an indirect manner.
JB 3.112 |v1 Asā is indeed our great one.
|v2 These are its designations.
He thus deprives it of its name. That which is placed first as a two-footed one is the person;
and those three subsequent feet are the cattle.
The buttocks are the first [part], and the two thighs are the second.
Animals are born facing away;
therefore, the buttocks are designated as the first.
Now, as for the three subsequent steps— the calf being the first, then the udder, then the man—
those which are the next three steps are these two [the shoulders], the head and neck; and that which is the highest step is the *upaśas*.
A second one comes from behind; therefore, one should provide two sucklings for a beloved calf.
This indeed is what has been given to them, what has been studied, and by which they live:
namely, that the calf is first, then the milch cow, then the man; thus indeed has what was given and studied become his own.
It becomes something upon which one can subsist.
Now, if one should desire of someone: "May what has been cooked by him remain unoffered and not be available for subsistence," [he should perform it accordingly].
One should first prepare the udder, then the calf, and then the man.
For his [milk] remains unpressed and undistributed, and thus it becomes unfit for subsistence.
Now, if he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should exclude its calf;
for the calf is indeed cattle.
Thus, he excludes cattle from him.
Now, if he should desire, "May Rudra harm his cattle," he should place [the offering] between the calf and a man. For the man is indeed Rudra.
Thus he places Rudra himself within his cow-pen.
This is the deliberation on the matter.
Now, it should be chanted with that very chant which is well-known for them here.
This indeed is the first Mahānāmnī; its attendant is Agni. This is the second; its attendant is Vāyu.
That [heaven] is the third; its attendants are the Sun and the Moon.
He who knows their heart-cavity (*hṛdāvakina*) thrice over, his houses become satisfied, as it were, and not coarse within. Indeed, the heart-cavity of these [cows] consists of the syllable *ekāra*.
Therefore, by inserting the syllable *ekāra* into the heart, they satisfy the cattle.
Now, those who know their ornaments sit in their houses adorning themselves with the *aṃśu*, the gold plate, the neck-ornament,
the elephant, the mule-chariot, and the horse-chariot. Indeed, the *stomas* are their ornaments.
He should sing as if adorning and as if beautifying it;
for those who know thus, these un-purchased forms stand near him.
The Mahānāmnī verses are indeed the waters;
the sun is their calf.
Now, those waters which flow eastward run toward this very sun as it rises;
and those which flow westward run toward this very sun as it sets.
Therefore, if they should ask: "These waters that flow day after day—toward what do they run? [one should reply: "Toward him."
"In this very one," that is the reply given there.
Furthermore, they say: "Vāyu is indeed the calf of the Mahānāmnīs, for he causes these worlds and these quarters to glow."
These worlds are the Mahānāmnīs.
Therefore, when the east wind blows, they hope for rain.
Just as a cow that has been given away might not yield milk, so it is when the east wind blows but it does not rain.
The Mahānāmnīs are indeed cattle;
the *purīṣa* is the cow-pen itself.
Regarding this, they say: "One should first chant the praise with the *purīṣa*, and then with the Mahānāmnīs."
Either the abode comes first, and then the cattle;
for cattle indeed come together toward the abode. Regarding this, they also say: "The soil is indeed the essence of cattle."
If there were no cattle, there would be no *purīṣa*.
When a man acquires cattle, he then encloses a cow-pen for their protection.
Therefore, one should chant the first *mahānāmnī* verses alone.

Regarding this they say: "Once the [stotras] have been chanted, one should subsequently chant with the *purīṣa* (filling verse); for cattle, though many, come together toward a single common pen from various directions."
For in that way, offspring indeed become twofold. One should chant the stotra with the *purīṣa* in regular succession;
in this way, all [the chants] become possessed of a "fold" (*vraja*).
The layers of loose soil (*purīṣa*) consist of verses addressed to the sheep (*aiḍa*). One should chant the hymns over each layer in succession;
in this way, all of them come to possess a "fold" (*vraja*).
The *purīṣas* consist of *iḍās*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *purīṣa* is the abode.
Thus, they establish these cattle in their very abode.
They chant while placing water nearby for the sake of the completeness of the *sāman*. Water, indeed, is the complete form of the *mahānāmnī* verses;
they should sing them aloud for the sake of the perfection of form.
Regarding this, they ask: "Where should one pour these [waters]?
Concerning them, there is this deliberation: "Having poured them into the *vasatīvarī* waters and having pressed the Soma, they should consume it.
For indeed, for those [who do otherwise], it becomes as if churned and exhausted.
They pour out the used [grains] into those that have not yet been used.

"Let us not pass beyond the six-day period in its forward direction," they said.
"They milked out the beloved honey"— that which was the milk of the Mahānāmnīs became the Revatī verses.
The *revatī* verses are indeed the milked-out milk of the *mahānāmnyaḥ*. With the words, "Thee, the great one, the great [verses] follow," the thirty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*) is indeed "great";
it is that very [hymn-form] which the *revatī* verses [attain].
The waters flow like rivers when you clothe yourself with the rays of light.
The ocean has been purified in the waters, the support and sustainer of heaven; Soma, seeking us, is in the filter. Thus there are verses containing the word "water."
For this day consists of the waters. "The tawny bull has bellowed," they say; thus they contain the word *vṛṣan* (bull), which is a form of the Bṛhatī meter.
For this day belongs to the Bṛhatī.

"Like a great Mitra, he is beautiful to behold"— for this day, the thirty-third, is indeed great. "O Indra, those active *ṛṣis* of yours cleanse themselves with vigor, by means of which they adorn themselves for exhilaration."
We implore you, the world-maker, for exhilaration and for joy; we seek you for the sake of your great glorification.
O Indu, you are the winner of cattle, the winner of men, the winner of horses, and the winner of booty;
you are the primordial soul of the sacrifice.
Thus, these verses concerning cattle and livestock serve for the attainment of cattle and livestock.
For this day consists of cattle.
"O Indu, flow for us with a stream of honey, bestowing power,
like Parjanya pouring down rain."
Thus there are ten verses; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food. This is for the attainment of the Virāj and of the eating of food.
"O Soma, win with thy jaws and conquer!"— this subsequent ten-verse hymn follows;
by means of it, they obtain the *virāj* meter and the eating of food in due order.
The seers, desiring supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), beheld this "rising" as a beloved form of speech: "Then make us better off; then make us better off.
With that they praised.
Then indeed they all prospered. All indeed prosper who, knowing thus, praise with this ten-verse hymn.
They place the *udarka* at the end.
The sixth day is indeed essence. To prevent its overstepping, they place an *udarka* at the end of it, just as one would apply a coating of clay over the breach of water; such is this.
It consists of four verses so that the essence may not be over-distributed. It consists of four verses for the sake of securing four-footed cattle.
The two-footed verses are indirect (parokṣa) for the sake of securing two-footed cattle.
It becomes like the Nārāśaṃsa chant for the attainment of both desires:
that which is divine and that which is human; they place the concluding response (udarka) at the end. The sixth day is indeed essence.
For the sake of its non-excess.
JB 3.139 |v1 Now, Taranta and Purumīḍha, the sons of Vītadaśva, having accepted much from Dhvasra and Puruṣanti,
felt as if they were vomiting.
The two of them used to touch that which was not yet settled with their fingers. They desired: "May this which is not yet settled for us become settled, as if it were already taken up and received.
They saw this four-verse hymn and approached [the sacrifice] with it.
Then indeed, for those two, what was not acquired became acquired; it was as if taken up, yet not formally accepted.

If, having accepted something, one should desire, "May this which is not acquired become acquired for me; may it be as if taken up, yet not formally accepted," he should proceed with these four verses.
What was not his own becomes his own; it is indeed taken up, not merely accepted.
"These Soma juices have been poured forth"—these are the final verses, and they are indeed descriptive of what has come to be.
They describe this very six-day period as it was created.
Being purified, you flow toward the cattle and manly powers for our enjoyment;
winning the prize, flow all around!
Thus there are verses containing the word "around" (pari), which is a characteristic form of the end.
For this day is indeed the end.
"O you who are praised by Jamadagni, flow forth for us all food consisting of cattle, accompanied by all songs of praise."
Thus there is a reversal for the support of progeny and the securing of cattle.
The thirty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*) is employed;
for the thirty-three are indeed all the deities.
Thus, they proceed while firmly established in all these deities.
Regarding this, they say: "The five days are pairs, and the sixth day is non-paired.
In that regard, because there is an *ājya* [stotra] for Agni beginning with "To him who is worthy of this praise, Jātavedas," by that very means...
The sixth day is made into a pair.
With [the verse], "Let us prepare it like a chariot for the sake of inspired thought," a pairing is thereby effected.
Indeed, on the preceding days the Hotṛ invoked a blessing for the sacrificer, but on this day it is the Udgātṛ.
Whoever indeed invokes a blessing with the *sāman* is, as it were, diminished.
Therefore, when [the verse] occurs—"O Agni, may we not suffer harm in your friendship; O Agni, may we not suffer harm in your friendship"—they thereby perform a healing and an expiation.
For thus it is not exhausted for him.
They place a subsequent conclusion above it;
the sixth day is indeed the essence, and this is for the sake of its non-excess.
Just as one would coat the opening of water with clay, so do they place the *udarka* at the end for the sake of not letting the essence flow away.
"‘At the rising of the sun, [we respond] to you both’— this is the verse for the Maitrāvaruṇa;
for at this time the hymns, the meters, the seasons, and the cups turn back toward one another."
And because it contains the words "prati vām" (toward you both), therefore here food is established according to the seasons;
moreover, the other stotras have *udarkas* after them.
And this one has its *udarka* at the end.
The Maitrāvaruṇa verses are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath.

If they were to place the concluding response (udarka) above [the verse], they would obstruct the out-breath and the in-breath. Therefore, they place the concluding response after [the verse] for the sake of releasing the out-breath and the in-breath.
"Break all enmities away"—this belongs to Indra;
"Drive away the oppressors, slay the mockers"—this contains the word for "slaying.
Indeed, this is the singer's own hymn of praise, which belongs to the Brahman priest.
In its own very abode, they destroy all the evil of the sacrificer. "Bring that desirable wealth, by which every person shall know thy abundant gift in succession.
Bring that desirable wealth.
O Indra, whatever desirable wealth has been placed in the firm [chest], in the solid [chest], or in the side-chest, bring that here.
Thus.
Cattle indeed are desirable wealth;
and cattle are food. Thus the Udgātṛ invokes this blessing for the sacrificer; they place the concluding response (udarka) at the end.
The sixth day is indeed essence; it is for the sake of not overstepping that.
With the words, ‘For you two are the officiating priests of the sacrifice,’ there is an offering to Indra and Agni.
|v2: Herein he chooses Indra and Agni for the office of the officiating priests; having thus entrusted the sacrifice to Indra and Agni, he is released [from his burden]."

His [sacrificial power] is not diminished; it remains exactly as it was before. Therefore, Indra and Agni perform the office of the officiating priests (*ārtvijya*) from this point onward toward the east.
"O Heroes, the men have milked out for you both this exhilarating honey with the pressing-stones."
"O Indra and Agni, take note of that!"—
this is the form of both the Śakvarīs and the Revatīs.
"The two leaders, who travel on the chariot, the slayers of Vṛtra, the unconquered..."
"O Indra and Agni, take heed of this!
Thus there is the *vārtraghna* hymn at the end for the sake of victory.
By means of this six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), the gods indeed conquered in the beginning.
In that this *ājya* oblation, which slays Vṛtra, is performed at the end, it is for the sake of victory and for the very destruction of the rival.
He who knows thus conquers and slays his hateful rival.
They place the *udarka* at the end.
The sixth day is indeed the essence; [they do this] so that there may be no overstepping of it.
Just as one would smear the seal of water upon something, even so do they place the *udarka* at the end for the sake of the essence.
For non-differentiation. The thirty-three-fold hymn-form (stoma) occurs;
for indeed, all the deities are thirty-three.
Thus, they proceed while firmly established in all these deities.
"O Indu, for Indra accompanied by the Maruts"— these *gāyatrī* verses belong to the midday *pavamāna*, and they are the form of the *bṛhatī*.
This day belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman.
"The inspired poets, skilled in speech, fashion you, the sustainer, as Truth"— thus there are verses containing the word *pari*, which is a characteristic form of the end.
For this day is indeed the end.
"O Mitra and Aryaman, [your] essence," he says; for this day is indeed essence.
