That essence which flowed away from the fifth day became this very day.
This is indeed the very essence.
"O Sage, let Varuṇa and the Maruts drink of the one who is being purified."
Thus they consist of verses addressed to the Maruts;
for the midday pressing has the Maruts as its characteristic form.
In this way, they do not depart from the very form of the midday pressing.
In those [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa explained.
Now follow the Revatīs.
The Simas are indeed cattle.
Cattle are the Revatī verses;
cattle are this day.
Those who praise with this [hymn] truly become possessed of cattle.
The Śakvarī verses were indeed scorching this world with their brilliance; they were not to be touched because of that brilliance. The gods were afraid of being burned by them.
They said, "These [fires] will surely burn up all this.
Let us pacify them.
They fashioned two feet for one of them and one foot for another.
That for which they fashioned two [feet], they placed that as this two-footed [verse]; that for which there was one, that as the one-footed.
That very [verse] became this three-footed *gāyatrī*.
This metre is indeed uniform;
he divided it into two parts for the sake of abundance and for the sake of peace.
He who knows thus is born abundant in offspring and cattle.
From the fifth day, indeed, the gods fashioned the sixth day.
They sought a support for it.
For him, the Revatī verses indeed found a dwelling-place.
He who knows this becomes possessed of a dwelling-place.
The Revatī verses are indeed cattle.
The self is the midday [pressing]. Therefore, when they chant the *revatī* verses toward the midday, they establish the cattle in the self.
The *revatī* verses are indeed cattle;
the midday [pressing] is the self. Therefore, when they chant the *revatī* verses toward the midday, they place that milk within the self.
They establish [it].
The *revatī* verses are indeed semen;
the midday [pressing] is the self.
In that they chant the *revatī* verses toward the midday pressing, they thereby establish seed within their own selves;
for the *revatī* verses are indeed seed.
The *raivata* chant is indeed semen.

Now, these *nidhana*s of the *raivata* chant are truly thunderbolts. Therefore, if they were to perform the *raivata* *pṛṣṭha* stotra upon the *revatī* verses, they would discharge that semen with a thunderbolt. Thus, [they place it] before...
They perform [the rites] during the Pavamāna [laud], thinking, "Lest we scatter the seed by means of the thunderbolt."
The Revatī verses are indeed milk;
cattle are the fifth day.
If these were separated by another *sāman*, the milk would be separated from the cattle.
Since they are not separated, the milk is thus not separated from the cattle.
Regarding this, they say: "Verily, one acts as if it were a repetition when they approach with these *iḍās* after [the verses] that are themselves *iḍās*."

"It should be commenced with the *iṣovṛdhīya* [sāman] for the sake of non-redundancy," they say. "But in that case, the milk would be hidden from the cattle. One should commence with the *revatī* verses, thinking: 'May we not lose the seed by means of the thunderbolt.'"
Moreover, milk does not disappear from cattle in that way.
This world is indeed the *Ṛc*, and yonder world is the *Sāman*.
Yonder world, the purifying one (*pavamāna*), is indeed the field of the gods.
In that they arrange them in two groups, by that very means they do not depart from these two worlds.
The Revatī verses are indeed the waters;
the Raivata Sāman is the waters.
If they were to perform the Raivata *pṛṣṭha* on the Revatī verses, they would sink into the bottomless and find no firm support.
Therefore, the Vāravantīya serves as the *pṛṣṭha* for the sake of stability alone.
Indeed, these *pṛṣṭhas* seem to wear out when they reach the sixth day.
Indeed, when one has grown old, no semen remains.
Therefore, when the Vāravantīya becomes the Pṛṣṭha-stotra, it is for the procreation of the subsequent sacrificial rites.
They let the cattle rest together with their calves.
For when cattle rest together with their calves, they yield their desires.
The wish-fulfilling cows become wealthy for him.
He who desires, "May there be wish-fulfilling cows for me in yonder world," should have [the cows] low together while the Soma is being purified.
Indeed, for him, there will be wish-fulfilling cows in yonder world.
If one should desire, "May there be cows that yield all desires for me in this world," he should have them stay together when they return.
Indeed, for him, there will be cows that yield all desires in this very world.
If one should desire, "May there be cows that yield all desires for me in both worlds," he should have them stay together in both places.
Verily, for him, cows that yield all desires exist in both worlds.
Regarding this, they say: "The calves should be on this side, and the mothers on that side. For the waters flow toward the north.
"These animals are indeed water," they say.
Regarding this, they also say: "The calves should be on this side, and the mothers on that side. For when a father causes his son to settle down, he causes him to settle down from the north."
Therefore, the calves should be to the north, and the mothers to the south.
The gods and the Asuras contended for the cattle.
The gods stood to the north with the calves, while the Asuras stood to the south with the mothers.
Those mothers, having torn away their calves, fled;
the gods held fast the calves,
and by attacking them, they deprived the Asuras [of the milk].
With them they fled toward the north.
He who knows this appropriates the cattle of his hateful rival.
Therefore, the calves should be to the north and the mothers to the south.
JB 3.147 |v1 Now, regarding the *vājadāvarya*:
|v2 Food indeed is *vāja*, and food is *dāvarya*.
These [oblations] are for the attainment of food itself.
Prajāpati created offspring;
he created them without food.
They ran to Prajāpati for refuge; he bestowed food upon them by means of this very *sāman*.
They said, "He has indeed given us *vāja* as our food.
That is the reason for the name *vājadāvarī* ("bestower of *vāja*") of these [verses].

This is the *sāman* for the attainment of food; he who knows this secures food and becomes the best food-eater among his own people. Now follows the *sauparṇa*, which is indeed the commencement of the sacrifice.
The sacrifice indeed rose up from the gods.
Having become a Suparṇa bird, it flew away.
Those gods desired: "May we seize the sacrifice."
They saw this Sāman;
they praised with it;
they began the sacrifice with it.
On the sixth day, the sacrifice is, as it were, departed.
Therefore, that there is the Sauparṇa hymn here is for the sake of seizing hold of the sacrifice itself;
and because they seize hold of him (the sacrifice) as he becomes the soaring eagle and glides along, therefore...
It is called "The Suparṇa.
They also call it "The Krauñca," for Krauñca Āṅgirasa found the *īṣya* as if it were a hidden treasure.
This sixth day is, as it were, a matter of envy (*īṣya*).
Therefore, it is performed on the sixth day. That [chant] consists of verses addressed to *iḍā*; for *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
On this day there are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
Now,
the *iṣovṛdhīya* has the *bahiḥ* as its *nidhana* and belongs to the *bṛhatī* [meter].
Therefore, it is performed on the day belonging to the *bṛhatī*.
The sixth day is indeed the *iṣ* (impulse), and the seventh is for growth (*vṛdh*).
The seventh day is born from the sixth day;
therefore, by [the word] "impulse," they cause the seventh day to be born from that very sixth day.
"Since they grew," for indeed they grew at that time. Prajāpati created offspring;
he created them while they were fasting.
They, seeking to devour, ate one another.
Prajāpati reflected: "How can these creatures of mine not seek to devour one another? He beheld this Sāman.
With the words, "Therefore, do you grow by means of these arrows," he touched them. They grew, being anointed for him with those arrows. That is why the *iṣovṛdhīya* has its name *iṣovṛdhīya*.
Verily, his wife is well-pleased with food, and they prosper who know this.
That [chant] has the *nidhana* on four syllables; for cattle are four-footed. This day belongs to cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
"Being cleansed by the skillful hand, you send forth your voice in the ocean; O Wealthy One!"—*ru* is the form of the *revatī* verses.
"Tawny, abundant, and much-desired, you flow toward the purifying ones."
|v3 Purifying himself in the sheep’s wool while being cleansed, the bull has bellowed in the wood.
|v4 Thus they contain the word *vṛṣan* (bull), which is the form of the Bṛhatī; this day belongs to the Bṛhatī. |v5 This day is [composed] in the Bṛhatī metre.
"O Soma Pavamāna, anointed with milk, you flow toward the prepared place of the gods"— thus they become possessed of cattle and possessed of livestock;
it is for the attainment of livestock,
for on this day there are indeed livestock.
In those [verses], the *sauṣāva* is characterized by repetition; this is the form of the *simāns*.
Indeed, the *revatīs* are repetitions of the *simāns*. Furthermore, they call that the "pippalī of Vasiṣṭha."
Vasiṣṭha, having been defeated and his sons slain, desired: "May I multiply with offspring and cattle. He beheld this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Then indeed he multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle.
He said, "This was surely a *pippalī* by which I have procreated.
That is the etymology of the name *pippalī*.
This is indeed called *pippalī*; it is designated as *pippalī*.
Offspring are the *pippala*, cattle are the *pippala*, and the heavenly world is the *pippala*.
That it is a *pippalī* is for the sake of securing and attaining all this.

That which is the *ūrdhva-iḍā* is the form of the *bṛhat*, and it belongs to the day of the *bṛhat*. It is indeed rich in form because of that. Furthermore, because Vasiṣṭha saw it, it is called "Vasiṣṭha’s Pippalī."

JB 3.150 |v1 Now, [the verse] "The hole of the bull" (*athaukṣṇorandhram*). |v2 Indeed, Kāvya, the son of Uśanas, desired: "May I ascend to the heavenly world against the current by means of the waters, within the waters."
"May I see my paths and my way of departure," he thought. He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he praised.
Then indeed he ascended to the heavenly world against the current by means of the waters, seeing his own paths and his way of departure within the waters.
He was indeed the son of Romaṇvat.
He is indeed Uśanas Kāvya.
He ascended to the heavenly world by means of the Yamunā itself against the current.
This, then, is the Sāman that leads to heaven.
He who knows this ascends to the heavenly world against the current by means of the waters.
Because Kaavya perceived the hollow of the bull (*ukṣan*), it is therefore called *Aukṣṇorandhra*;
furthermore, it is called *Āponiyāna*, because he perceived its descent into the waters.
JB 3.151 |v1 Now, [the hymn] "winning booty" (*vājajit*). |v2 Food, indeed, is booty.
When indeed a cow, a horse, or a man becomes well-fed with food, then he becomes vigorous (*vājín*).
The gods and the Asuras contended for the eating of food.
Those gods desired: "May we appropriate the food of the Asuras."
They saw this Sāman;
they praised with it. With the words, "O winner of booty, win! they appropriated the food of the Asuras.

That indeed is the "conqueror of strength" (vājajit) nature of the vājajit. This is the *sāman* that secures the consumption of food. He who knows this secures the consumption of food for himself and deprives his hateful rival of the consumption of food.
That [sāman] has the *pañcākṣara* as its *nidhana*. The sacrifice is fivefold.
Indeed, those who come on this day exceed the proper measure of the sacrifice.
In that there is a *nidhana* of five syllables, the sacrifice is fivefold; [this is done] so that we may not exceed the measure of the sacrifice.
JB 3.152 |v1 Now follows the Varuṇasāman.
|v2 King Varuṇa, indeed, was as if sharing a feast with the other deities.
He desired, "May I be consecrated for the sovereignty over all the gods.
He lived as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) with Prajāpati for a hundred years.
To him, he spoke this Sāman: "This indeed is my royal form."
"Go!
The gods will make you king.
He went to the gods.
Seeing him approaching, the gods descended to meet him.
He said to them, "Do not descend to meet me;
you are indeed my brothers."
"Indeed, as you are, so am I," he said.
"No," they replied,
"that which is the form of our father Prajāpati, that we see here in you."
They descended toward him.
For him, they set down this royal throne.
Upon it, they consecrated him: the Vasus for kingship, the Rudras for overlordship, and the Ādityas for sovereignty.

The Viśvedevas [are for] sovereignty; the Maruts, for universal lordship; the Sādhyas and Āptyas, for the highest state. This is the Śrīsāman. He who knows this attains prosperity and goes to kingship.
And because King Varuṇa saw it, it is therefore called the Varuṇasāman.
JB 3.153 |v1 Now follows the *goṣṭha*.
|v2 This, indeed, is the stall of the *śakvarī* verses and the *revatī* verses.
The cow-pen is for the support of cattle;
cattle are supported in it.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of cattle.
Prajāpati created the cattle.
Once they were created, they departed from him.
He sought to restrain them with the first day.
He did not ward them off with the first;
he did not ward them off with the second;
he did not ward them off with the third.
He did not ward them off with the fourth [day].
He did not ward them off at all with the fifth.
On the sixth day, he warded them off with this very *sāman*.
He said, "The cow-pen (goṣṭha) indeed has become this Sāman for my cattle. That is the very reason for the cow-pen's name, "goṣṭha.
This Sāman, the cow-pen, is conducive to cattle.
In this [place], cattle are sustained;
he who knows thus becomes possessed of cattle.
Now, it is as if that [sustenance] here is obstructed by the cry, "iḍā! iḍā! iḍā! (O food! O food! O food!).
Verily, by this [verse], he warded them off from the front. "Him, indeed,
the ten fingers cleanse, him whose mother is the Sindhu"— in that it contains the word "Sindhu" and "samudra," that is the form of this day.
This day has water as its vessel.
Regarding this, they say: "Do these *triṣṭubh* verses go from the end of the *pavamāna* [laud] to those which place the final [verse] among the *gāyatrīs*?
They are those [verses] that contain the word "sūrya."
Then there are the verses addressed to Indra.
Therefore, the *triṣṭubh* verses do not extend as far as the *pavamāna* chants.
In these [verses], the *vāmadevya* chant contains the word "here" (*iha*).
The boundary-stones (*simā*) are indeed cattle;
the *raivata* [sāman] is cattle;
the *vāmadevya* [sāman] is cattle as it were here.
Those who praise with this [hymn] become as if possessed of cattle;

yet it is, as it were, obstructed by the words: "O ten fingers, here they cleanse him, the one whose mother is the Sindhu. For indeed, he thereby warded them off from the front even by means of this very [verse].
"Rich for us in the shared revelry"— thus they become rich;
it is from the very same [source] that they thus attain equality.
The final verses of the midday pressing consist of *gāyatrī*s;
these are indeed *gāyatrī*s.
Just as one might pass from an equal [height] to an equal [height], so is that.
At this time, the other meters have become exhausted in their power, while the Gāyatrī alone remains unexhausted.

Through the exhausted stotras and the exhausted śastras, the vaṣaṭ-call becomes exhausted. Five of the days possess the seasonal character (ṛtumant), while the sixth is without the seasonal character (anṛtu).
In that the Hotṛ-priests offer the *ṛtuyāja* oblations with separate *vaṣaṭ*-cries, by that very means the sixth day is made to possess the *ṛtu*.
In those [verses], there is the *vāravantīya*;
for this indeed is wealthy and related to Revatī, namely the *vāravantīya* sung upon the Revatī verses.
He becomes wealthy, his offspring becomes wealthy, and a wealthy son is born to him who, knowing this, chants the Vāravantīya on the Revatī verses.
This indeed is the Bṛhat-sāman belonging to Revatī, which is the Vāravantīya sung upon the Revatī verses.
The sixth day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre.
By that very [metre], the sixth day is made to belong to the Bṛhatī.
This Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the seasons;
the seasons are the year;
and the year is Agni Vaiśvānara.
That unappeased Lord was about to burn [the world].
Therefore, when the Vāravantīya becomes the *pṛṣṭha* chant, it is for the appeasement of Agni Vaiśvānara and to prevent his burning.
Prajāpati created this sacrifice, namely the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha.
Once created, it ran away.
They sought to ward him off with the *rathantara* [sāman], but they could not ward him off. They sought to ward him off with the *bṛhat* [sāman], but they could not ward him off.
They did not ward him off with the Vairūpa [Sāman].
They did not ward him off with the Vairāja [Sāman].
They did not ward him off with the Mahānāmnī [verses].
They could not turn him back with the Revatī verses.
They turned him back with the Vāravantīya;
because they turned him back (avārayata), that is the reason for the name Vāravantīya.
In that the Vāravantīya is the *pṛṣṭha* [laud], it is for the warding off of the sacrifice.
Prajāpati indeed created this sacrifice, namely the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite;
he then sought a firm foundation for it.
From that, he found the waters.
In them, he sought a firm foundation with the *rathantara* [sāman];
he did not find it.
He did not find [the *sāman*] in them by means of the *bṛhat*. He did not find it in them by means of the *vairūpa*.
He did not find it in them by means of the *vairāja*.

Among them, he did not find [the goal] by means of the Mahānāmnī verses; among them, he did not find it at all by means of the Revatī verses; among them, he found it by means of the Vāravantīya chant.
That which he found is precisely what constitutes the *vāravantīya* nature of the *vāravantīya*.
It is upon this very [earth] that they thus establish the sacrifice.
Indeed, this *vāravantīya* is Agni Vaiśvānara.
The waters are indeed wealthy.
Because the Vāravantīya chant occurs upon the Revatī verses, therefore the waters are the womb of Agni.
Indeed, these Pṛṣṭha-stotras seem to grow old when they reach the sixth day.
Indeed, when one has grown old, no seed remains.
Therefore, that the Vāravantīya is the *pṛṣṭha* chant serves for the procreation of the subsequent sacrificial rites.
Regarding this, Abhipratāraṇa said while lying down, aged and infirm:
"His sons divided his inheritance."
There was a sound.
"What is that sound? they asked.
They said to him, "O Venerable One, your sons are dividing their inheritance."
He said, "I am indeed Suśravas; for it is said that while he is still alive, his sons shall inherit his property. "I am indeed Suśravas," he said.
This is just as one would inherit the property of a living person: when the Raivata day occurs, the Vāravantīya becomes the *pṛṣṭha* chant.
|v9 Now they perform the other [ritual] during the Pavamāna [laud].
|v10 Then Gaireya Āṣāḍhi questioned Aṣāḍha Bhāllabeya: "Since there are so many Sāmans here, how is it that they did not suffice for the sixth day?
|v11 He said: "There were six kings like you in the Pañcālas who were worthy of the sacrificial altar."
He said, "In this way you know it as deficient; we, however, know it otherwise.
Because the Vāravantīya is performed here as a *pṛṣṭha* chant where it is not [ordinarily] a *pṛṣṭha*, by that very fact this day is rendered ineffective.
Then the nine [pupils] questioned Āruṇi: "O Āruṇi, why do the Mahānāmnīs, though being devoid of semen, produce offspring?"
"Why do the *revatī* verses, being true and bestowing seed, not cause procreation?
"Because he utters 'yaḥ' first, it is indeed the seed.
He did not answer that.
By means of that, he conquered him.

Had he replied, "The *revatī* verses are indeed semen; the *raivata* sāman is semen. There is no semen within semen," then at this point the *pṛṣṭha* chants would have reached their end in the son alone.
When they reach the sixth day, offspring are not born from them thereafter.
Therefore, the Retodhas Sāmans give birth through the Mahānāmnīs; and for that reason, the Retodhas Sāmans do not give birth through the Revatīs.
Now follows the Vāmadevya.
The Vāmadevya is indeed cattle;
those who have praised with it become possessed of cattle.
On the sixth day, there are six verses beginning with "suṃrūpakṛtnum ūtaye" (RV 1.4.1), performed by way of repetition;
by that very means, the six-day period is completed.
In those [verses], there is the *ṛṣabha* of the *raivata* [tune].
Cattle indeed are the *simā*s; cattle are the *revatī*s; cattle are the *ṛṣabha*.
Verily, they thus incorporate the bull among the cattle for the sake of pairing and procreation. He who knows this is propagated through pairing.
They cause him to share the greatest portion of the eastern half.
Therefore, cattle consume most of their food with both the forepart and the hindpart;
they carry [burdens] with the forepart and produce [milk] with the hindpart.
He who knows this obtains both kinds of milk: the milk of the cow and the milk of the ox.
On the sixth day, there are six-footed verses beginning with "When both worlds, O Indra.
By means of these very [verses], the six days are made complete.
The gods and the Asuras contended for the cattle.
Those Asuras went down to the sea together with their cattle.
Those gods desired, "May we seize the cattle of the Asuras.
They saw these *aṅkas*, these *ṛc* verses: "The divine mother has brought them forth; the auspicious mother has brought them forth."
This is the form with the mark.
With these [verses], they drove those animals away.
These are the verses pertaining to cattle.
One who praises with these verses secures cattle for oneself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
In these [verses], the Śyena is performed for the sake of successful completion so that there may be no failure;
indeed, the Śyena is capable of bringing this day to a successful conclusion.
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerities. They saw this Sāman; they praised with it.
Then, having become a hawk, he carried them to the heavenly world.
Having reached the heavenly world, they said: "It was indeed the hawk who, having become this, carried us, the Sāman, to the heavenly world."
That indeed is the "hawk-ness" of the hawk. This is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows thus attains the heavenly world.
Indra, indeed, by means of this *sāman*, having become a falcon, struck down the Asuras.
That is the reason for the falcon’s name, "śyena. It is also a slayer of rivals.
He who knows thus slays his hateful rival.
That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*-sāman;
for the *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
Verily, they thus find firm support in cattle.
"Resounding, he stands upon the mountains"— these *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "around" (*pari*) belong to the *pavamāna* laud of the third pressing; they are a form of the end.
For this day is indeed the end.
"Into the filter Soma has flowed;
in the exhilarations, you are the bestower of all."
Thus they contain the word *mada*. Now, *mada* is indeed essence (*rasa*).
This third pressing is, as it were, coagulated.
In that these verses contain the word "mad" (intoxicating), they thereby bestow sap upon him; by this means they cause him to swell.
[The verse] "Thou art a sage, thou art a seer"—the word "thou" is a form of the *bṛhatī* meter.
This day belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman.
"Honey has been produced from the plant-juice; in thy exhilarations, thou art the bestower of all."

"In you, all [gods] are of one accord" (RV 8.27.13); "In you, all [gods] are of one accord" (RV 8.27.14). Thus, they become verses containing the word *viśva* (all), for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
"O gods, you have attained the drink; in your exhilarations, you are the bestowers of all.
Thus they place the *udarka* at the end.
The sixth day is indeed the essence; it is for the sake of not overstepping that [essence].
In those [verses], there is the *gāyatra* chant, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained. Now follow three *vaidanvata* chants.
Śaryāta Mānava performed a sacrifice on the eastern plateau;
the Harṣayas officiated as his priests.
Then both gods and men drank the Soma together.
Thus, that supreme Soma was drunk together by both gods and men. In that [rite], Cyavana Bhārgava took a cup for the two Aśvins.
Indra seized that cup, saying, "What is this unknown cup that is being circulated?"
Vidānvān Bhārgava countered him, saying, "Who is worthy to examine that cup which we might give away?"
Those gods became enraged; the seers became enraged.
Those ninety-nine Maruts, spears in hand, stood [ready], thinking: "Now we shall encompass this; then this..."
"Everything shall be crushed!
Then the Ṛṣis invoked the Asura Madin. Piercing through the intermediate space with his head, he thrust it upward; that became the Great Battle (Mahatī Samad).
That Agni said to Indra: "Let your anger depart; they are indeed superior to us.
For if he should provoke them to anger, nothing here will remain.
Indeed, we were born from them."
Agni alone dispelled his anger.
Indra, freed from anger, fled together with the gods. For them, the sacrifice became devoid of Indra and devoid of the gods.
They desired: "May our sacrifice be accompanied by Indra and the gods.
Having found these, Bhārgava saw these *sāmans*;
he praised with them.
With them he summoned Indra;
with them he dispelled his anger.
Thereupon, indeed, Indra returned to their sacrifice.
Then [the sacrifice] did not depart from them.
Consequently, their sacrifice became one accompanied by Indra and the gods. Indeed, these *sāmans* are those accompanied by Indra and the gods.
The sacrifice of one who knows thus becomes possessed of Indra and the gods; Indra turns toward his sacrifice, and Indra does not depart from his sacrifice.
Cattle, indeed, are full of wisdom (*vidanvant*); these *ṛc*s are full of wisdom.
Into these [cows], they release this bull of Vidanvat for the sake of pairing and procreation. He who knows thus is propagated through pairing.
And because Vidanvat, the descendant of Bhṛgu, saw them, they are called the Vaidanvata chants.
JB 3.161 |v1 Now Mada Āsura was afraid.
|v2 He said, "Do not summon me in vain; do not set me down."

They said, "Let us drink," thinking thus: "Let us bring the *surā* from the plant-juice (*andhas*) of Varuṇa. In that [liquor], not even one among them was affected by distress, owing to its power. Thereupon, they said, "Go further into intoxication!"
This very intoxication of the Asuras was placed within the *surā* liquor.
"He is pressed, he who [is the master] of riches, he who [is the master] of wealth"—this is the form of the *revatī* verses.
In those [verses], one [verse] of the Bṛhatīs is long. By means of this, indeed, this day is made to consist of the Bṛhatī metre.
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerity. They saw this Sāman;
with it, they praised.
So, having become long indeed, it carried them to the heavenly world.
Having reached the heavenly world, they said: "Indeed, having become long, this *sāman* has carried us to the heavenly world."
That indeed is the length of the long [note].
This is the *sāman* that leads to heaven;
he who knows this attains the heavenly world.
"O friends, [sing] the *ṛta* for your exhilaration"—thus they become full of intoxication. In this way, at the third pressing, they place the essence and the exhilaration in their proper order.
"Sing toward him as he is being purified."
"With praises they make him savory like a child with oblations.
(RV 10.79.4) Thus they approach him in the very form of an animal;
for a child is indeed among animals.
"Like a calf with its mothers, Indu is urged forth and anointed"— thus there are verses containing the word "cattle" (*go*) and the word "livestock" (*paśu*),
for the sake of obtaining livestock;
for on this day, there are indeed livestock.
"O gods, the exhilaration that wins the gods, adorned by our prayers"—these verses are *parivṛt* (encircling), for they are the form of the end;
for this day is indeed the end.
JB 3.163 |v1 He [gave] that to Kārṇaśravasa.
|v2 Indra, having struck Vṛtra with the thunderbolt, thinking "I have not slain him," was filled with wonder.
His two ears became closed up;
through them he did not hear. He desired, "May I not be deaf; may I hear with my two ears."
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it. Thereupon, indeed, he became no longer deaf; he heard with his two ears.
He said, "I have indeed heard with my two ears.
That is precisely why he is called Kārṇaśravasa. One who knows this becomes free from deafness and hears with his two ears.
And that, indeed, they call "Gauloma.
Goloma Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, performed austerity. He beheld this Sāman.
He praised with that.
He resorted to this *iḍā*. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle; from it, he obtained cattle.
This is a Sāman pertaining to cattle.
One who knows this secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Furthermore, because Golaoma Āṅgirasa saw it, it is called the Gauloma.
The Soma drops, the best finders of the way for us, flow clear;
they are friends, well-sounding and stainless—
this is the form of the wealthy ones.
In those [verses], the Gaurīvīta has its Brāhmaṇa explained.
JB 3.164 |v1 Now follows the Bārhata [Sāman] which has *madhuścyut* as its *nidhana*.
|v2 Therefore it is performed on a day belonging to the Bṛhatī metre; moreover, honey is the end of flavors, and heaven is the end of the worlds.
"This day is the end; by means of the final *sāman*, may we attain the final world of heaven," [they thought].
Then, regarding the *krauñca*:
Kruñ Āṅgirasa found this day as if it were something desirable.
This sixth day is, as it were, something to be envied;
therefore, these two [rites] are performed on the sixth day. And they call them the "Udvañca" and the "Śāmmada."
By means of the *udvat* [melody], the gods ascended straight up to the heavenly world. Because they ascended straight up to the heavenly world, that is the reason for the name *udvat*.
This, therefore, is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows this indeed ascends to the heavenly world by means of this very [sāman].
Now follows the Śāmmada.
When the gods had conquered, these worlds fled from them in fear.
They desired, "May these worlds turn toward us;
may they not depart from us.
They saw this *sāman*.
With that they praised.
Then indeed these worlds turned toward them;
consequently, they became those who do not depart from these worlds.
They said, "Truly, these worlds have not rejoiced in us.
That is why it is called Śāmmada;
these worlds rejoice for him, and these worlds turn toward him.
These worlds do not depart from him who knows this.
That [sāman] is the *ūrdhva-iḍā*; it is the form of the *bṛhat*, on the day belonging to the *bṛhat*.
By that, indeed, it is rich in form.
Flow with zeal through these riches; O Indu, flow forth into the vessel, you who possess all manly vigor.
Even Bradhna, like the wind, bestows his speed upon him; Purumedhas bestows it upon the swift hero.
This is the form of the wealthy ones.
In them [there is] the *śnauṣṭa* [chant].
By means of this, indeed, Agni Vaiśvānara shone forth.
They sit for the sacrificial session [sattra] with the thought, "May we shine.
Indeed, they cause him to shine by means of this.
Now, Agni Vaiśvānara was exactly like these embers.
He desired, "May grandsons be born to me, not [mere] pupils.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
Then indeed his *śnuṣṭi*s were born as flames (*arcis*). These flames are indeed his *śnuṣṭi*s; that splendor was born as his spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
He who knows this becomes radiant, endowed with spiritual luster, and possessed of vigor.
That [day] is, as it were, excluded, for it is the form of the end;
for this day is indeed the end.

Just as, for example, when leading a horse here, one calls out after it, "Come here, come here, my dear," even so do they call out after the Stomas at the end once they have been obtained by means of this [Sāman].
JB 3.166 |v1 Now follows the Yajñāyajñīya, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been stated. |v2 Then these [verses] consist of two feet, for the sake of securing the freshness of the meters.
At this time, the days and the meters have indeed become exhausted; only the two-footed [verses] are unexhausted.
Since these [two-footed verses] are performed here, by that very means this day is made unexhausted.
Now, Keśin Dārbhya used to sing along with this.
"Always on the mountain, even with leaves one lives happily;
when one finds no dwelling, then one runs toward hope.
Thus [he said].
"O Brāhmaṇas, just as you are, so do you perform this: [chant] 'the two-footed' upon the *chandas* of the *Āptas*.
The six-day *pṛṣṭhya* sacrifice is indeed cattle, and among the *chandas*, the two-footed is the human.
Whatever [rites] are performed here, they thereby place the person upon the animals.
Therefore, the person stands as it were above the animals. Moreover, this six-day *pṛṣṭhya* period is the heavenly world, and the two-footed [human] is the sacrificer by its very nature.
In that they pile them up above the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, they thereby raise the sacrificer himself up into the heavenly world.
When the meters tried to lift up yonder sun, they were not able to lift it up.
They said to the *dvipadā* meters, "Establishing ourselves upon you, let us lift this up."
"May these indeed become food for me," he said.
"We shall become your food," they replied. Thus, the two-footed *brāhmaṇa* is indeed the *chandas*; these [metres] are his food both here and in the hereafter.

These very meters, having established themselves upon the two-footed verse, lift up this sun and these sacrificial rites. Therefore, if they should ask, "Why are the two-footed verses performed on the sixth day? one should reply, "For the sake of stability."
He should say:
"Therefore, these [verses] must not be omitted here.
These verses are: "O Agni, you are our closest [friend]," etc.
The Gaupāyanas defeated Asamāti Rāthaprauṣṭha. They performed a sacrificial session at Khāṇḍava.
Now, two Kirātas named Ākulī, who were masters of *asura*-magic, lived at Asamāti Rāthaprauṣṭha.
They used to place rice on a non-fire and cook it, and meat on a non-fire. These two sorcerers would sow [seeds] here in front and reap them there behind.
The two laughed.
Indeed, having eaten that perpetual food of the Asuras, the Ikṣvākus were utterly destroyed.
The oblations of the Gaupāyanas tormented that Asamāti Rāthaprauṣṭha.
He said, "These two Kirātas are scorching me; these are indeed the oblations of the Gaupāyanas.
They both replied, "We two are indeed his physicians, we two are the expiation;
we shall act in such a way that these [oblations] will not scorch you."
Having gone away, those two took the life-breath (*asu*) from Subandhu, the descendant of Gopāyana, while he was sleeping and unconscious, and deposited it within the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*).
At that time, the fires were indeed possessed of enclosing-sticks.
While Subandhu was still unconscious, they became aware [of him] and said, "We have taken away his life-force (asu) through the power of the Asuras.
They said, "Come, let us restore the life-force of Subandhu.
They set out from Khāṇḍava.
"O Indra, let us not stray from the paths, nor from the sacrifice, we who possess the Soma.
Let not our enemies stand in our way.
"If we have performed this [rite] and if we have sat for the sacrificial session (*sattra*), let us not stray from both of them," they said.
Having crossed the Hvṛṇinī river eastward by means of Subandhu’s ford, which was constructed by Avatantumat, they proceeded toward Asamāti Rāthaprauṣṭha.
They did not recognize his fire even when it was called out to them from afar, saying, "This fire of yours is indeed named Varūthya.
Now, prior to that time, Agni had been proclaimed by the name Varūthya, thinking, "I am indeed named Varūthya."
"Whoever among you succeeds in winning him over, let him say to him, 'Whatever he tells you, do that.
They approached him with the verse: "O Agni, you are our closest kin; be our protector and auspicious shelter.
He said to them, "With what desire have you come?"
"Let us restore the life-breath of Subandhu," they said.
"He is within the enclosing sticks," he replied. "Take him up! [he said].
Calling out to him:
"Here is the mother, here is the father; this life-giver has come.
This is your place of crawling; O Subandhu, come hither, come forth!"
Thus [he spoke].
Life-breath entered Subandhu again;
he became as he was before.
"Therefore, these seers declared of those two Kirātas: 'They have indeed called forth this life-force (asu) and are summoning it away.
Not comprehending this, the two of them ran away;
having perceived their very departure, all the magical powers (māyā) withdrew."
Of those two, that which was the most wretched of forms became their form.

JB 3.170 |v1 Now, formerly, they two had been beautiful by means of their illusory power (*māyā*). |v2 One of them, while floating upon the fire, said: "In this very way indeed does he act who [performs] the true with the untrue."
"He wishes to kill," [he thought].
Then they cut the cattle apart in this manner.
One of them, having approached from below and cutting into the necks, said: "In this very way indeed does he act."
"Truth seeks to destroy falsehood. Those two then perished. These, then, are the verses that slay the enemy and slay the Rākṣasas.

He slays the hateful rival, drives away the *rakṣas* and evil; he who praises with these verses slays [them]. Regarding this, they say: "Since the *vālakhilyās* are distributed [in the *stoma*], how does one praise when these have been distributed?
He should reply: "Because these deficient syllables are interwoven with the words, by that means [it is done]."
In them was Gūrda. The gods and the asuras contended for the eating of food.
Those gods wrested the food of the Asuras from them.
Among those Asuras, a great portion of food named Gūrda alone remained.
Those gods desired: "May we wrest this Gūrda, the food of the Asuras."
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
By means of it, they appropriated the *gūrda*—the food of the Asuras.
In that [Sāman], they shouted for joy. Because they shouted for joy (*agūrdan*), that is the "shouting for joy" (*gūrda*)-nature of the *gūrda*.
This is the Sāman that secures the acquisition of food.
He who knows thus secures for himself food and drink; he appropriates the food and drink of his hateful rival.
Prajāpati created food and drink. All the gods became possessive of it, saying, "It is mine! It is mine!"
That Agni desired, "May I win this food.
He saw this Sāman;
with it, he encompassed it.
He won that.
This entire food-eating [substance] is indeed in Agni.
Therefore, for whichever deity one offers an oblation, one offers it in Agni alone.
He leaped upon it. Because he leaped (*agūrdat*), that is the very reason for the name of *gūrdana*;
it is the *sāman* for the attainment of food.
He secures food and drink; he becomes the best of his kinsmen as eaters of food, he who knows thus.
"May we now establish these worlds, Indra and all the gods,"—these verses addressed to the Viśvedevas are used.
Vṛṣākapi belongs to the Viśvedevas.
This day belongs to the Viśvedevas. With the mantra, “May Indra, together with the Ādityas, accomplish for us the sacrifice, the body, and progeny,” it is for the sake of success.
With the mantra, “May Indra, together with the Ādityas, the troop of Maruts, grant us remedies,” it is for the sake of medicine itself.
They perform an expiation.
JB 3.172 |v1 In them [is contained] the *bhadra* of Gotama.
|v2 Gotama, desiring prosperity (*śrī*), performed austerity (*tapas*).
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it. Thereupon, indeed, he attained prosperity.
That is indeed prosperity (*śrī*); that is well-being (*bhadra*). Well-being is indeed offspring; that offspring which is [further] offspring is excellence (*śreyas*).
Indeed, he who knows thus beholds offspring for his own offspring.
Because Gotama saw this, it is called "Gotama’s Blessedness. The verses beginning with "Forward [sing] to Indra, the greatest slayer of Vṛtra" are the Vārtraghnis; they serve for victory at the end.

The gods, having conquered by means of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), said: "What indeed might be at the end of this [conquest] so that we might not lose what has been won by us, and so that they might be defeated by us?
They then gathered together the very essences of the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
They chanted over them;
it rose upward like a bamboo pole,
and that became the *udvaṃśīya*.
That is the reason for the *udvaṃśīya*’s name *udvaṃśīya*. It exceeded the sacrifice;
therefore, they extracted this son of the *udvaṃśa*.
From that very essence (rasa), they made that essence— the Udvamśīya chant— at the end of the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, [placing it] at the conclusion of the Chandomas.
These two raised thunderbolts stand at the end for the protection of cattle and to prevent the loss of cattle.
The wealth of one who knows this is never diminished.
This is indeed the form, the essence, and the splendor accumulated of all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
It is within this very form, essence, and splendor of the *pṛṣṭhas*, which is invincible, that the sacrifice finds its conclusion in the *chandas*.
They establish themselves.
At its *nidhana*, they perform the *pratihāra*. Indeed, by means of the *prastāva* and the *pratihāra*, the sacrificer is supported.
They are now as if they were past; therefore, they perform the *pratihāra* before the *nidhana* so that there may be no overstepping.
That [chant] is the *svāra*.
On the seventh day, they chant the *svāra* melody;
thus it becomes the *svāra*. On the following day, they begin with the *svāra* melody.
It is such that it would pass from the equal to the equal, as one would join breath to breath; such is that.
Prajāpati indeed created this sacrifice, which is the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*).
He attained everything through the six-day period consisting of the *pṛṣṭhya* stoma.
He reflected: "How indeed may I join these four days together?

He fashioned the twenty-four-fold day from the *gāyatrī* itself; the forty-four-fold day from the *triṣṭubh*; the forty-eight-fold day from the *jagatī*; and he fashioned the tenth day from the *anuṣṭubh* itself.
Or rather, it was from all the days that he fashioned it; because he fashioned it from the meters (chandas), that is the reason for the Chandomas being called "Chandomas.
Regarding this they say: "Verily, here the Stomas are attained, the meters are attained, the deities are attained, and the seasons are attained."
The planets [said], "In that this Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha is obtained...
Now, in that the Bahiṣpavamāna of the seventh day consists of twenty-four verses,
the year has twenty-four half-months.
The year is the sacrifice; thus they take hold of the sacrifice itself at the very mouth of the sacrifice. Moreover, the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables;
it is the Gāyatrīs that extend the sacrificial rite once it has been completed.
For indeed, no other [meter] is capable of undertaking a sacrificial rite that has been mastered by the Gāyatrī.

These [verses] are: "Proclaim the poetic wisdom as Uśanas does" (RV 1.181.1). These are verses containing the prefix *pra*, used on the day of departure (*prāyaṇa*), for this day is indeed one that must be led forward.
"Prehi" is the form of the Gāyatrī.
It is indeed by the form of the Gāyatrī that they proceed [with this verse].
"The god who proclaims the births of the gods"—Soma, indeed, is the god who proclaims the births of the gods.
In this way, they procreate Soma itself.
With the verse, "The one of great vows, the kinsman of purity, the purifier,"—the gods indeed call food "the one of pure vows.
And Soma is the food of the gods.
In this very way, they bring him forth.
"The boar approaches, lowing at the footprints"—for having become a boar, Prajāpati stepped from the sixth day toward the seventh day;
this is indeed a stepping beyond.
"‘The swans, the *tṛpala*s, have gone toward the song’—the *brāhmaṇas* are indeed the swans, the *tṛpala*s;
‘from here they have gone home, the bull-herds’—the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) is indeed from here, the *chandomas* are the home;
the meters (*chandāṃsi*) are the bull-herds."
In this way, they lead the *chandāṃsi* (metres) beyond the *chandomas* for the sake of reaching the completion of the subsequent three-day period (*tryaha*).
With the verse, "The friends together proclaim the purifying, winged, invincible Vāṇa," the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [Sāmans] are indeed yoked at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
When these two are yoked, they mount them at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina savana*).

“He harnesses the speed of the wide-striding one; they measure him as he plays at will like cattle”—thus there are verses concerning cattle; they are cattle-possessing and livestock-yielding for the very purpose of securing livestock, for the Chandomas are indeed livestock.
“He makes it encompassing with his sharp horns.”
"Parīṇasam," he says; "parīṇasam" is indeed food. It is for the attainment of food.
"The bay one is seen by day, the ruddy one by night"—thus the Atirātra is performed with its proper form.
These [verses] are Triṣṭubhs with the form of Gāyatrīs, perfect in the form of the day. For wherever they are perfect in the form of the day, there one prospers.
Success attends him who knows thus.
Regarding this they say: "Since the seventh day is Gāyatra, the eighth is Triṣṭubh, and the ninth is Jāgata, why then do they commence this [seventh day], which is Gāyatra, with Triṣṭubh verses?"
He should say: "For all these Chandomas have the Triṣṭubh as their opening verse. The verses beginning with "Oṁ, like rattling chariots" are descending;
thus they attain the form of the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīya*).

For this day is the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*). The hymn (*sūkta*) becomes the corresponding verse (*anurūpa*); the hymn is indeed cattle, and the *Chandoma* days are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
Now, cattle are indeed abundance;
the hymn is abundance.
Thus, they make the cattle conformable to the cattle themselves.
In this case, they do not produce offspring corresponding to their own form.
Therefore, animals produce various forms: a white one produces a black one, a black one produces a white one, a red one produces a spotted one, and a spotted one produces a red one.
"Like coursers seeking renown,
the Soma juices have stepped forth for the sake of wealth.
With this, they indeed approach that which has the form of the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīya*).
For this day is indeed the *prāyaṇīya* (opening day).

[The verse begins: "Like chariots being urged on. Now, that which contains the word "chariot" (*ratha*) is indeed the form of the *prāyaṇīya*. [It continues: "They have been placed within the two hands."
Like the burdens of those who perform deeds.
"The kings do not [shine] with praises; the Soma-drops anoint themselves with milk.

(RV 9.86.14) Thus, there are verses containing the word "cattle" (*go*) and containing the word "livestock" (*paśu*); this is for the sake of securing livestock, for the Chandoma days are indeed livestock.
With the verse, "The sacrifice [is joined] with the seven creators," they approach the form of the seventh day.
There are nine verses.
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person.
Verily, they proceed thus prospering through the vital breaths, establishing themselves in the vital breaths. Moreover, by that very means they do not depart from the *trivṛt* stoma;
for whatever is the commencement, it is the *trivṛt*.
The departure hymn, moreover, consists of nine verses in the *uttara* [section].
Thus, they proceed, becoming fully endowed with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in due order. "O you, whose skill is bliss-bestowing"—this is the concluding verse, for the support of progeny and cattle.
For the sake of presence.
Regarding this they say: "When the tip of a blade of grass moves, where does its heat reside?
They say: "It rises upward as birds fly."
"How does one split the wings? [The answer is:
"For these [days] are like birds, having a common beginning and a common end.
By means of these, this day is made winged; by means of these, one flies up; by means of these, one reaches the thirty-three-fold hymn-form (*stoma*)."
He rises up;
he who knows thus crosses over evil as one with wings and attains prosperity as one with wings.
"The first of him who goes forward" is the last [verse], for this day is indeed like that.
Therefore, these two [the wings] are properly formed by their two wings.
There is a twenty-four-fold hymn-form (*stoma*).
Indeed, the year consists of twenty-four half-months.
Thus, they proceed while finding firm support month by month throughout the year.
Moreover, the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables;
the Gāyatrī is splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Thus, they proceed while finding firm support in splendor and spiritual luster.
JB 3.177 |v1: "Three Vaiśvānara Atirātras are to be performed in the Dvādaśāha," they say. |v2:
The first Vaiśvānara is the out-breath (prāṇa), the second is the in-breath (apāna), and the third is the diffused breath (vyāna).
This twelve-day sacrifice is indeed speech stretched out.
They would cut that [speech] off from you.
Aryala Kāhoḍi approached it, thinking, "Having conquered the three divisions."
A certain Brahmin said to him: "He has approached the vital breaths in a contrary manner; he has cut off his speech. They would indeed have completely severed that man's lineage.
Aryala Kāhoḍi approached her, saying, "I have conquered the three armies.
A Brahmin said to him, "You have reached the vital breaths through the Anuṣṭubh;
you have cut yourself off from speech."
His lineage was indeed cut off;
however, he lived for a long time.
He then sought to continue his line through a mere glance.
Vaiśvānara should be performed with the verse, “The head of heaven, the messenger of earth,” and so forth.
Thus, one does not interrupt the speech, nor does one pass between [himself and] Vaiśvānara Agni.
The verse, “Bring forth [the offerings] for the bright radiance,” should be performed as one that inclines forward (*pravatī*).
This day is indeed one that they desire to lead forward.
*Pra* is the form of the Gāyatrī;
it is by the very form of the Gāyatrī that they proceed.
Many forms are being transgressed;
indeed, many other forms [are transgressed]. When he says, "The head of heaven, the steward of earth," the Atirātra belongs to Heaven and Earth; [it is] the Atirātra.
In this very form it is performed.
"Vaiśvānara, Agni born from the Truth"—thus Agni Vaiśvānara becomes manifest.
"The seer, the sovereign, the guest of the people"—thus [he refers to] the midday pressing.
With the verse, "The gods produced the vessel when it was near," they approach the third pressing of the sixth day.
For the gods saw that as the lowest part of the sacrifice;
they are, as it were, departed now.
They approach this very [sacrifice] for the sake of continuity.
Those gods said, "Since these two are Atirātra sacrifices without a Sattra, by what means shall we pierce through the body of Agni Vaiśvānara?"
They said, "Let us perform the sacrifice with these very last bodies of ours, which are fresh and most secret.
With [the verse], "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth," they performed the sacrifice with the last [verse] of heaven and earth, which is fresh and most secret.
The secret body:
"O Agni Vaiśvānara, born from the Ṛta..."— this final verse of Agni Vaiśvānara is the supreme, secret body, possessing unexhausted power.
"Vaiśvānara, born from the *ṛta*, Agni"— this final verse of the Vaiśvānara [hymn] is the ultimate, secret, and inexhaustible body of Agni Vaiśvānara.
"The sage, the sovereign, the guest of men"— this final verse among those containing the word "sovereign" (*samrāj*) is the ultimate [verse] of Indra.
The secret body.
"The gods generated the vessel that was near," says [the verse]; this final verse of the Viśvedevas has unimpaired power and is the supreme, secret body.

Just as one who has threshed grain wraps it in a cloth, so do these [verses] wrap this [fire] with their *nidhana*s as a garment; in this very way, the gods, by means of their final, unfailing bodies, entered the body of Agni Vaiśvānara.
In the same way, they depart now as well;
or rather, all [the deities] depart once the Agniṣṭoma has been completed,
while six Ukthas remain behind.
When this six-day period has concluded, those [verses] depart;
they are joined again in this very *ājya* chant dedicated to Agni.
With the verse, "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth," it is thus joined with that which belongs to Heaven and Earth.
With the verse beginning "Vaiśvānara," one is thereby joined with the Vaiśvānara hymn; with the verse beginning "Agni born from the Truth," one is thereby joined with the Jātavedas hymn;
and with the verse beginning "The Seer, the Sovereign, the Guest of men," the Marutvatīya and Niṣkevalya hymns are thereby joined.
With the verse, "The gods produced the vessel that was near at hand," these two *ājya* stotras are joined by means of this [verse]. In this way, these *ukthas* are joined again;
for this three-day period is performed in a forward direction.
Therefore, it says: "The head of heaven, the steward of earth.
Indeed, yonder [sky] is the head of heaven, and this [earth] is the steward of earth.
"Sing forth to Mitra for you who sings," thus there is a verse addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa;
they thereby approach the very form of the introductory rite (prāyaṇīya).
For this day is indeed the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*).
With the verse, "O two sovereigns who have ghee as your womb, both Mitra and Varuṇa," they thus approach the form of both the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* [Sāmans].
In this [rite], both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara are performed.

[The verses] "O Indra, come hither, O you of wondrous luster," "O Indra, come hither, impelled by our prayer," and "O Indra, come hither, hastening"— thus there occurs the repetition "come hither, come hither."

"Come hither, come hither, come hither"— with these words they proceed in front of the harnessed [steeds]. Just as one would go out in front of the harnessed [steeds] saying "come hither, come hither," so it is with that which belongs to Indra and Agni on the third day.
Therefore, the *ājya* stotras of that [day] belong to Indra and Agni together.

Indeed, these two—the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period and the *chandomas*—are like two separate villages. Just as two friends from different villages might live in mutual fear unless they intermarry, so it is when the *ājya* stotras are common to both.
They exist.
Some perform them with unequal [measures];
therefore, they should indeed be performed with equal [measures].
The Stoma consists of twenty-four parts. The year indeed consists of twenty-four half-months; thus, they proceed while finding firm support in the year month by month.
Moreover, the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables.
The Gāyatrī is splendor and spiritual luster;
thus, they proceed while firmly established in splendor and spiritual luster.
JB 3.181 |v1 Indeed,
those *stomas* which are odd-numbered are even, and those which are even are odd.
|v2 Therefore, the domestic animals follow those *stomas* that are odd, while the wild animals follow those that are even.

In that the Sāman of the odd-numbered Stomas is the last among the even ones, therefore domestic animals draw when they are yoked. And in that the Sāman of the even-numbered Stomas is the first among the odd ones, therefore wild animals [behave thus].
They move yoked together.
And because on the tenth day the Pañcadaśa and Trayastriṃśa stomas occur, therefore those two which are the largest among animals— the elephant and the camel— draw yoked together.
"Flow as a bull for the sake of the stream"— these *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "bull" belong to the midday *pavamāna*;
they are a form of the *bṛhatī*.
This day belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman.
With the verse, "And for the one accompanied by the Maruts, O exhilarating one," the verses addressed to the Maruts (marutvatīḥ) are employed;
for the form of the midday pressing is indeed associated with the Maruts.
They do not depart from the very form of the midday pressing.
With the words, "Thee, the supporter, in the two bowls," [he offers], for this seventh day is, as it were, fallen away;
therefore, by saying "Thee, the supporter," it is for the support of Agni himself.
In those [stotras], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa explained. Now follows the Santani.
Just as two people living in separate houses, having become estranged, walk away from each other, so indeed are the sixth and seventh days.
Having cut it off, he departs from it. Just as one might yoke a horse with a harness, so here is the continuity.
He begins it once, performs the *pratihāra* three times, and they proceed to the *nidhana* three times.
These become seven; this is the form of the seventh day, for the sake of continuity and non-interruption of the seven-night rite.
Now follows the Sauparṇa [Stotra], whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
On the seventh day, the sacrifice has now passed beyond [the Soma-pressing].
Therefore, that there is the *sauparṇa* [sāman] here is for the sake of the commencement of the sacrifice.
That it is the *aiḍa* [sāman] is because the *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
The Chandomas are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
JB 3.183 |v1 Now follows the Rohitakūlīya.
|v2 Viśvāmitra, indeed, went against the Mahāvṛṣas with a cart belonging to the Bharatas.
Now, that [yoke] was indeed too large for the Gaṅgā or the Yamunā.
They said, "O Mahāvṛṣas, who indeed are those two oxen now, who can pull such a large load against the current?"
Viśvāmitra said, "Those two red oxen are indeed mine.
For those two red oxen had belonged to him.
They said, "O great bulls, let us carry off our share if those two oxen carry that [load] away."
"Indeed, you shall fill our wagons with goods.
"If you do not give me a bride, we shall win you over by means of goods.
"So be it."
They carried off a portion.
The two of them yoked it to the pole of a cart loaded with barley or a cart loaded with rice. Viśvāmitra desired, "May I win this contest."
He saw these two *sāmans*; with them, he struck down those two as they were moving around him.
They both crossed over.
The two of them won that race. Thus, he indeed won that contest.
Those who omit the *chandomas* after the sixth day go as if against the current.
In that regard, as for the fact that there is [the chant] belonging to Rohitakūla here, it is for the sake of victory.
He who knows thus conquers.
Moreover, it is a means of attaining desires.
He indeed desired that very desire;
that desire was fulfilled for him. Whatever desire one praises with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him.
Because he conquered by means of the two Rohita [horses] at the bank (kūla), they are therefore called the Rohitakūlīyas.
With the verse, "Being purified, O Soma, flow in a stream," there is a Bṛhatī consisting of both forms.
Indeed, this [verse] raised up both Sāmans; therefore, they perform this very [verse], and those who use the Bṛhat-sāman perform it.
Of the Rathantara-sāman.
JB 3.184 |v1 In them [is] the Raurava [Sāman].
|v2 The gods indeed drew out these unwearied bodies for the battle against the Asuras.
Agni alone extracted the Raurava [sāman].
With it, he heated the Asuras. Being thus heated, they cried out.
Because they cried out while being scorched, that is the origin of the name Raurava. He who knows this scorches his rival by becoming superior.
That is a Sāman belonging to Agni; it is performed on a day belonging to Agni.
This day is related to Agni, in that it is the Gāyatra;
for Agni is the Gāyatrī. Therefore, when the Raurava chant is performed here, they bring the day into harmony with its corresponding form.
By means of that same prosperity, there is success for them within their own community.
That [chant] is the *iḍā*; the *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *Chandomas* are cattle;
it is for the attainment of cattle.
Then there is the Rathantara. They say that there is a repetition (*jāmi*) in the twelve-day sacrifice:
the sixth day belongs to the Bṛhat[-sāman], and the seventh day belongs to the Bṛhat[-sāman].
They chant the *rathantara* upon the *pavamāna* [laud] to avoid sameness (*ajāmitā*). They say that a burden should not be carried away from one side or another;
therefore, when both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* are employed, it is precisely for the sake of such balanced distribution (*vivadhatā*).
Indeed, he who wishes to traverse from the root to the tip is not able; but he who passes from tip to tip is able.
Verily, those who approach the *bṛhat* [sāman] from the *bṛhat* pass from tip to tip.
Therefore, the sixth day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre, and the seventh day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre.
Now, as for the Gauṅgava Sāman, it praises the deities. This Sāman praises the deities; by means of it, the sacrificers become possessed of fulfilled blessings.
The gods and the Asuras contended for the cattle.
Those Asuras went down to the ocean together with the cattle.
Then those gods desired: "May we win back the cattle of the Asuras."
They saw this *sāman*; they praised with it;
by means of it, they appropriated the cattle of the Asuras.
They said, "We have indeed won a cow, a cow from the Asuras.
That is why the *gauṅgava* has its name *gauṅgava*.
This is a *sāman* that is beneficial for cattle.
He wards off the cattle of his hateful rival who hates him; he secures cattle for himself and becomes rich in cattle—he who knows thus.
By means of the Gauṅgava, the gods, having slain the Asuras, made Gaṅgaṇi their herald.
That, indeed, is the reason for Gaungava’s being called Gaungava.
And it is a slayer of rivals; he who knows thus slays his hateful rival.
That [song] is sung both as if upwards and as if across.
That which is sung as if upwards is the form of the *bṛhat*, and that which is as if across is the form of the *rathantara*.
Indeed, this twofold form constitutes the perfection of the *chandomas*.
JB 3.186 |v1 Now,
regarding the *samanta*:
|v2 Indra and Agni desired, "May we be equal, may we achieve equal prosperity."
The two of them perceived this *sāman*:
one perceived half of it, the other half.
Having brought together its two ends, they joined them.

That which they two established together is the "samanta" (all-encompassing) nature of Samanta. With that, they two praised. Thereupon, they two indeed became all-encompassing and attained equal supernatural power.
That *brahman* is indeed Agni, and the *kṣatra* is Indra.
He who knows this secures both the *brahman* and the *kṛṣtra*.
Therefore, one should not omit this *sāman* from this day.

This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara, and yonder [heaven] is the Bṛhat. This very atmosphere is the connection between these two; it is for the sake of making these two worlds continuous that they are so. By means of this, these two are indeed continuous.
One who desires cattle should praise with the *samanta* [hymns]. The intermediate region is indeed cattle, and the *samanta* is cattle. By praising with the *samanta*, he becomes possessed of cattle.
A Brāhmaṇa who desires the office of domestic priest should praise with the *samanta* hymns.
The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni, the Rājanya to Indra; the earth belongs to Agni, and the sky to Indra.
These two meet together over the intermediate space.
He makes these two equal—the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya—praising them equally; thus he goes to the office of domestic priest and places him at the front.
Prajāpati indeed desired, "May I be equal in offspring and cattle."
He saw this *sāman*. He praised with it. Thereupon, indeed, he became complete (*samanta*) with offspring and cattle.
That, then, is the reason for the name "Complete" (*samanta*) of that *sāman*.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of offspring and cattle on every side.
Now follows the Āyāsya [sāman], which possesses both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara;
it serves for the prosperity of both social classes.
The nidhana in the middle is for the sake of stability.

The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases once contended with one another regarding the heavenly world. They reflected: "Whichever of us shall officiate as priests for the other, those [whom they serve] shall surpass us."

Those Aṅgirasas prepared the sacrifice in the past; on the eve of the Soma-pressing, they dispatched Agni Āṅgirasa as their messenger, saying, "Announce to the Ādityas that we shall perform the Soma-pressing tomorrow.
He went and said, "O Ādityas, the Aṅgirasas announce to you that they will perform the Soma-pressing tomorrow."
They said to him, "Go away; having consulted together, we shall give you an answer.
Therefore, even now, they say to a messenger, "Go away; having consulted together, we shall give you an answer.
They said, "Find out how it might be that the Aṅgirases might officiate as priests for us, and not we for the Aṅgirases."
"If we officiate at the sacrifice, we shall lose [him]; but if we do not officiate, we shall fall away from the glory of the sacrifice.
Therefore, one should not withdraw from what has been chosen, lest one fall away from the glory of the sacrifice.
One should cause [the sacrifice] to be omitted by means of a verse;
or one should approach one's own sacrifice, saying, "This has been done by you."
The Ādityas prepared this Sadyaḥkrīya sacrifice.
They said, "O Agni, that which is tomorrow is long; we shall announce this very pressing-festival to you today."
"Of us, you are the *hotṛ*; Gaura Āṅgirasa is the *adhvaryu*; Bṛhaspati is the *udgātṛ*; and Ayāsya is the *brahman*.
Thus they chose all of them.
He said, "I travel as a messenger indeed."
With the verse, "We choose that Agni as our messenger," they chose him as their messenger while he was wandering.
Once chosen by them, he did not depart.
Having returned, he said, "O Aṅgirases, the Ādityas have announced to you that today is the day of the Soma-pressing."
"Therefore, our choosing was indeed not in vain," [they said].
"No," he replied, "I was your messenger; I have already been chosen by these people. Indeed, they have now chosen you."
"Those who saw this in the past were either more intelligent or more steadfast.
They did not depart from their chosen path;
they came and performed the sacrifice.

To them, the Ādityas brought this very horse, the white one belonging to the Ādityas, which had become such and was harnessed with a horse-halter; having led the horse to Ayāsya Brahmán, they went to the heavenly world.
The Aṅgirases were left behind.
Having accepted either one who was his equal or one who was superior to himself, he fell away from his goal.
He desired, "May I fortify myself.
He saw this *sāman*.
With that, he mixes himself [with it].
This seventh day is, as it were, fallen away;
therefore, in that there is an Āyāsya here, they mix it with this very thing and heal it with this very thing.
Because Ayāsya saw it, it is therefore called "Āyāsya. With the verse, "The drop has sped forth to Indra's appointed place," they lead forward this day with both the *Ṛg* and the *Sāman*.
Both classes [of syllables] lead to prosperity.
With "pra," the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, and the Ādityas ascended to the heavenly world. By means of this very [syllable], they now ascend to the heavenly world.
JB 3.189 |v1 Now, as for the Bṛhat: the Bṛhat is indeed the summit. |v2 The Bṛhat is the summit.
Verily, they proceed while finding firm support in the very height.
That occurs on the day of the Gāyatrī metre.
The Bṛhatī is indeed the form of the male, and the Gāyatrī is that of the female.
In that the Bṛhat-sāman is used as the Pṛṣṭha-stotra on this day, by that very means a union is brought about for this day.
Then there is the Vāmadevya;
the Vāmadevya, indeed, is cattle.
Those who praise with this [hymn] certainly become possessed of cattle.
With the verses beginning "We indeed, having pressed the Soma for thee," they proceed using *satobṛhatī* meters to avoid falling away from the ritual integrity.
In these [verses], the *kāṇva* [sāman] has its *abhinidhana*.
Regarding this, they say: "It is indeed contradictory that one should utter either form of the *brahmasāman*.
In that it begins with "abhi," they do not depart from the form of the *rathantara*.
Indeed, Indra desired to slay Vṛtra.
He ran to Kaṇva, saying, "O Seer, we run to you; instruct us here.
Kaṇva beheld this Sāman;
with it, he praised.
Then indeed Indra slew Vṛtra;
he who knows thus slays his hateful rival.
Furthermore, because Kaṇva, by means of this *sāman*, roared out the thunderbolt with the words "abhīti," it therefore has the *abhinidhana*.

It is called the Kāṇva. Now these [verses] occur: "May no one reach this deed of yours. At this time, indeed, the Bṛhatī exceeds the Bṛhatī, the Kakubh exceeds the Kakubh, and the Anuṣṭubh exceeds the Anuṣṭubh.
This very [verse], being a *bṛhatī*, becomes a *jagatī*.
Therefore, it transcends [the norm].
It passes beyond the eighth day, takes hold of the ninth day, and moves back toward the sixth day.
JB 3.190 |v1 Regarding these [verses], they saw the Vaikhānasa [Sāman].
|v2 Indeed, the Vaikhānasas saw these Sāmans as the beginning and the conclusion of the sacrifice.
By means of repeated undertakings, the gods indeed excluded the Asuras from the sacrifice.
Now, there were certain seers called Vaikhānasas who were dear to Indra;
Mārimlava, the secret-slayer, caused them to die.
Seeking them, he approached Rahasyu.
He said to him, "Rahasyu, did you not see those Vaikhānasa seers here?
He replied, "O venerable sir, they have indeed died."
He said to him, "This is a secret matter, wherein the killing of an embryo is difficult to justify. Now, how did you make your promise?
He replied, "I have declared both falsehood and the killing of an embryo."
That indeed became untruth;
he then resorted to truth. "He has come to truth," [the teacher] said. He then said to him, "Choose a boon, for you have made a promise."
He said, "Let a Brāhmaṇa alone be born among my offspring.
These, then, are the Takṣavas Rāhasyavās.
Moreover, they say that the deities praised Indra alone at that time; they looked toward Indra, thinking, "In you [is] what exists."
"May the Mārimlava heat [them] away," he said.
He desired, "May I drive them together.
He saw this Sāman.
With that, he set them in motion.
This is the healing medicine, the expiation-sāman.
Indeed, being [the truth], it performed the healing medicine as an expiation.
This seventh day is, as it were, fallen away;
they heal it by means of this [day].
By this very means, they perform a remedy and an expiation.
And that [verse] is a winner of desires. Indeed, he desired this very desire;
that desire was fulfilled for him.

Whatever desire one has when one praises with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him. That [deity] is indeed Indra Vaikhānasa. Because Indra saw this *sāman*, it is therefore called the "Vaikhānasa."
That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
thus they find firm support in cattle.
"O you, that exhilarating intoxication of yours which is most excellent"— these *gāyatrī* verses of the *pavamāna* laud for the *ārbhava* [śastra] contain the word "intoxicating.
The essence is indeed the intoxication.

This third pressing is, as it were, like something that has been sucked out. Therefore, when these verses contain the word "mad" (intoxicating), they thereby place essence into it and cause it to swell with this very [element].
"Flow with truth for the sake of the soma-juice (*andhas*)," he says; thus they become possessed of soma-juice. "Soma-juice" (*andhas*) is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
"The slayer of Vṛtra, the unfriendly," he says; this is the form belonging to the Bṛhatī metre.
That which follows midday belongs to the Bṛhatī metre of this day. [The verse is]:
"The ruddy steed has become mingled with the cows that are easy to approach.
This seventh day is, as it were, fallen away.
In that [he says] "with those well-established," it is for the sake of the establishment of the day.
In them is the *gāyatra* [chant], whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained. Now, the *arka* of Agni is a Sāman belonging to Agni; it is performed on the day belonging to Agni.
This day is related to Agni insofar as it is the Gāyatra;
for Agni is the Gāyatrī. Therefore, when the *arka* of Agni is performed here, they bring about prosperity through the very form of the day.
By that which is thus successful for them, there comes prosperity within their own community. Now, *arka* is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
Then follows the *soma-sāman*.
Soma is indeed procreation;
this day is procreation;
thus, procreation is performed upon procreation itself.
Now, Soma is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
And the Kṣatriya is the giver of food. [One should think:
"May he who is the giver of food bestow food upon us."
That [offering] consists of one and a half *iḍās*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *Chandomas* are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle in their proper sequence.
Now follows the *dakṣoṇidhana*.
This seventh day is, as it were, fallen away.
They complete that very thing with the *dakṣiṇidhana* chant.
Prajāpati created offspring;
he created them without breath.
He desired, "May these creatures of mine possess vital breath.
He saw this Sāman;
with it, he touched them, saying, "For the sake of skill (dakṣa)."
The vital breaths are indeed the *dakṣas*.
He thereby placed the vital breaths within these [bricks].
He who knows thus places the vital breaths both within himself and within the sacrificer.

Regarding this, Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi said: "They know the *mantha* in his family, yet they do not know it; have they perhaps placed the *dakṣiṇidhana* at the beginning of the *pavamāna*?"—"How so? he asked.
"For they do not find the *mantha* in your family.
Therefore, the *arka* for Agni must be performed first on the first day.
"This one, pressed with a stream" (*eṣa sya dhārayā sutaḥ*) is the *pragātha* of the *santanin*; this day is [performed] with the *pragātha* together with its *santanika*.
"We shall heal it.
This seventh day is, as it were, fallen away;
therefore, they heal it with a *pragātha* that provides continuity.
The most intoxicating one flows through the woollen filters,
sporting with the expanses as if with the waters.
Thus, at this time, the *kakubh* exceeds the *kakubh*, and the *anuṣṭubh* exceeds the *anuṣṭubh*.
This very *kakubh*, being so, becomes a *triṣṭubh*.
By means of that, he transcends;
he begins the eighth day.
"O you who belong to the dawn, you have driven out the cows from within the rock by your might; you have spread out the stall of cattle and horses. Like a mailed warrior, O bold one, burst it open!
Thus [these verses] contain words for "cows" and "livestock," for the very purpose of obtaining livestock.
For the Chandomas are indeed cattle.
In those [waters], all beings praised Indra Śārkara.
But Śarkara Śiñcumāra did not desire to praise him.
He said to him, "Praise me. He replied, "I will not praise you.
I move within the ocean, the waters, diving deep; only for such a one as that would I praise you."
Parjanya caused it to overflow upward with rain toward the desert.
He indeed showed him the waters.
Then he dried it up with a north wind.
Lying there, completely parched, he thought: "Since I have behaved in this manner, Indra has indeed treated me thus; come now, I shall praise him alone.
"Once praised by me, he will cause me to plunge back into the ocean," he thought.
He beheld this mantra. With it, he praised him: "Him who in the past brought to us this and that wealth—him indeed I praise for you."
"O friends, [praise] Indra for his aid!
Thus [he said].
He (Indra) said to him, "With what desire do you praise me?"
"Do not let me float back into this very ocean," he said.
Parjanya then caused him to float back into the ocean with rain.
This is that healing medicine, the *prāyaścitti* chant.
He indeed made that medicine his expiation;
with this [rite], they now perform the expiation as medicine. And it is also a means of obtaining desires.
Verily, he desired that very wish;
that wish was fulfilled for him. Whatever wish one praises with this *sāman*, that wish is fulfilled for him.
By that very mantra, he ascended to the heavenly world.
This very same one rises as the pebble.
That, indeed, is his path to heaven.
He who knows thus attains the heavenly world.
The Chandomas are indeed the ocean.
The porpoise indeed is able to cross over the ocean.
Therefore, that which is gravelly here serves for the very purpose of crossing over the ocean.
That, moreover, is the *punarnitunna* metre.
Wherever the gods indeed found the essence of the meters, they made it a *punarnitunna* (repeatedly struck back), and they struck it again.
These *chandomas*, having the third pressing as their abode, are like daughters.
The third pressing is, as it were, like something already churned. In that a metre is repeated (*punarnitunna*), they thereby place essence into the *chandome* chants;
this is the recovery of that very essence.
Now, that [sāman] is the Kākubha Svara. The Svara is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa), and the Kakup metre is the person (puruṣa).
The vital breath is preeminence (jyaiṣṭhya), and the person is preeminence.
By means of preeminence itself he unites that preeminence; through preeminence he becomes firmly established.
And because Śiṃśumāra saw pebbles (śarkara), therefore it is called "the pebbly" (śārkarī).
"O friends, sit down for the one being purified, sing forth!"—thus they become verses containing the word "forward" (pravatīḥ).
They thus approach the very form of the *prāyaṇīya* (opening) rite;
for this day is indeed the *prāyaṇīya*.
With the words, "Adorn him with sacrifices as one adorns a child," they thus approach the very form of the sacrificial animal.
Indeed, the young one is among the domestic animals.
JB 3.195 |v1 On these [verses], there is a boat.
|v2 He who crosses the ocean without a boat does not reach its further shore; but he who crosses with a boat, he reaches it.
He pervades.
The *chandomas* are indeed the ocean;
therefore, by means of this, one who possesses a boat [crosses] as one with a boat.
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerity. They saw this *sāman*;
with it, they praised.
Then, having become a boat itself, it carried them to the heavenly world.
Having reached the heavenly world, they said: "It was indeed this *sāman*, having become a boat for us, that carried us to the heavenly world."
That indeed is the "floating" nature of the boat. This is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Therefore, they call it "Vasiṣṭha’s Raft.
Vasiṣṭha indeed desired, "May I float across all the worlds safely.
He saw this Sāman.
He praised with that [verse].
Thereupon, indeed, he safely floated across all the worlds.
That, then, is the reason for the "floating" nature of a boat.
He who knows this floats safely across all worlds.
The seers reviled Vasiṣṭha, saying, "This man is a Vaiśya, not a Brāhmaṇa.
He desired, "May I cross over misfortune and evil."
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
