By means of it, [with the words] "O, may we cross over all difficulties," he indeed crossed over difficulty, which is evil.
He who knows this overcomes misfortune and evil.
That [chant] has the *nidhana* consisting of twelve syllables; for the *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables, and cattle are the *jagatī*.
The Chandomas are cattle; [they serve] for the attainment of cattle.
And because Vasiṣṭha saw them, they are called "Vasiṣṭha’s Raft. Now, these [verses] occur: "O you who conquer with the juice... etc.
For indeed, these [verses] go forward, conquering evil and striking away evil from the front.
By means of these, what has been conquered and what has been won are settled upon. Moreover, it is just as if one were to mount two new wheels; even so is this *anuṣṭubh* [to be understood].
They carry [the fire] around at the beginnings of the three-day periods for the attainment of the heavenly world. In these [stotras], the Gaurīvīta is performed; its Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.

JB 3.196 |v1 Then [the lineage] of Kārtaveśa: |v2 The kingdom was divided threefold among the Bharatas— the third part among the Vaitahavyas, the third part among the Mitravats, and [the third] with Kṛtaveśa.
The third [chapter]. He desired, "Alas, these two kingdoms are separate; might they become a single kingdom. He saw this *sāman* with two *nidhanas*.
He praised with that [hymn].
Through that, these two kingdoms became, indeed, a single kingdom.
This is the *śrī* (prosperity) *sāman*, which destroys the adversary.
He who knows this attains glory and slays his hateful rival.
Because Kṛtaveśa saw it, it is called the *Kārtaveśa*.
Now follows the *Śyāvāśva* Sāman, which leads to heaven, for the attainment of the heavenly world.

Now, [some say] the *andhīgava* should be an *anuṣṭubh* verse containing the *iḍā* call, thinking, "May it be an *anuṣṭubh* with the *iḍā*. However, the *anuṣṭubh* should be without the *iḍā*, if they were to do this here. Moreover, the *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *chandomas* are cattle; [thus it serves] for the attainment of cattle.
Now these [verses] consist of two feet; their Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
These verses are "pra vājy akṣār" (the prize-seeker has flowed forth); they are characterized by a downward flow (*pravatīḥ*).
Thus, they attain the very form of the introductory offering (*prāyaṇīya*).
For this day is indeed the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*). Regarding those [verses], there is the *sauhaviṣa* [verse].
The gods, having slain the Asuras, considered themselves as if unpurified and impure.
They desired, "May we be purified and fit for sacrifice.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Then indeed they became purified and fit for sacrifice.
They said, "We have truly become excellent offerings.
That is the reason for the name *sauhaviṣa*, the state of being an excellent offering.
He who knows thus becomes pure and fit for sacrifice.
[The verse] "O Soma juices that are in the distance" refers to the sacrifice, for at this time the sacrifice has gone as if to a distant place.
In those [circumstances], there was the *jarābodhīya* [sāman].
The Śākyas, for whom the *tarasa-puroḍāśa* [offering] was prescribed, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Gaurivīti Śākya killed a deer.
Tārkṣya Suparṇa swooped down upon it from above.
He offered it to him.
He said to him, "O seer, do not stand before me!
Whatever desire you have, I shall fulfill that desire for you.
He replied, "What desire indeed do I have?"
"O Dhāmnya Āsita, you desire the daughter of this man.
I shall give her to you.
Then, Dhāmnya Āsita became envious.
He had a palace in the intermediate space.
They guarded his daughter there.
He used to carry him [the child] away from her, having concealed him within a hollow stalk of a leaf, and he would bring him back to her by that very same means.
In the morning he awakens her with a *sāman*, saying, "O lover, wake up! That is precisely why the *jarābodhīya* has its name. This maiden conceived a child.
That boy was born.
The Asuras, having torn him apart and casting him away, said: "This is indeed the offspring of a sibling; this that has been born is a Rakṣas!"
He desired: "May I set him in motion.
He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he thus set him in motion.
He himself became Saṃkṛti Gaurīvīta.
This is that healing, the *prāyaścitti* chant.
Indeed, he thereby performed that healing, that expiation.
This seventh day is, as it were, fallen away;
they heal it by means of this [day].
By this very means, they perform a remedy and an expiation.
That, moreover, is the fulfiller of desires.
Indeed, he desired that very desire;
that desire was fulfilled for him.
Whatever desire one has when one praises with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him. They approach the *iḍā* toward the east;
the *iḍā*, indeed, is cattle.
The Chandomas are cattle;
verily, they thus place seed in cattle.
JB 3.198 |v1 Now follows the Yajñāyajñīya, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.
|v2 The verses beginning with "O Vatsa, may your mind turn toward me" (RV 5.44.1) are those containing the word *ā*.

This section of the sacrifice consisting of the *ukthas* is, as it were, severed. Therefore, because they contain the word "avatī," it serves to ensure the continuity of the sacrifice. In these [verses], there is the *vātsa* hymn.
Vatsa Kāṇva, desiring cattle, performed austerities.
He saw this Sāman;
with it, he praised.

He, indeed, was Triśoka because he drove away those three sorrows; that is his state of being Triśoka. He immediately obtained hornless, earless cattle. This, therefore, is a Sāman conducive to cattle.
One who knows thus secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Because Kaṇva Vatsa saw this [sāman], it is called the "Vātsa. In the verse, "O Indra, you alone [protect us] in battle," the word "you" (tvam) occurs; this is a form of the Bṛhatī.
This day belongs to the Bṛhatī metre.
"O Śatakratu, O Vicarṣaṇi, [bestow] vigor and manly strength;
[bring] the hero who conquers in battles."
Thus, that which indeed possesses hundreds and thousands is the form of the Chandomas;
for the Chandomas are cattle.
In them [the verses], there is the Sauśravasa hymn.
Kutsa, the son of Urva, was indeed fashioned from Indra’s thigh.
Just as Indra is, so was he; he was as if fashioned from his own self.
He made him his charioteer.
His wife Śacī, the daughter of Puloman, took hold of him.
He said to her, "How did you do this? She replied, "I did not understand you.
He said, "I will surely make him bald; let him know it thus."
He indeed made him bald.
He, having put on a turban, sat down nearby.
This very one is the turban of the charioteer.
He indeed seized her.
He said to her, "How did you do this?
She replied, "I did not know; you placed me down after having covered me with a turban."
He said, "I shall scatter dust upon his two inner shoulders; let him know it thus.
He then scattered dust upon his two inner shoulders.
These are indeed those very grains of dust on the two inner shoulders of the charioteer.
He approached them while they were covering themselves;
he seized him,
and said to him, "Why have you done this?"
She said: "I did not recognize you two.
You should have approached me after covering yourselves."
He oppressed him, saying, "You are a wrestler!
He replied, "O Maghavan, let us not be thus."
"Give us that by which we may live;
indeed, we were born from you," they said.
He replied, "Then scatter the dust between my shoulders."
He utterly destroyed them.
From those very [remnants], a great region named Rajas and Rajīyas arose.
They had kings.
Now, Upagu Sauśravasa was his domestic priest.
He said: "Let no one perform a sacrifice. Whoever sacrifices while I am in charge of the sacrifice, he shall be defeated."
"Indeed, the gods do not eat what has not been offered.
There is no such thing as an offering of leaves, nor should it be offered.
Indra went to Upagu Sauśravasa and said to him, "I shall officiate as your priest."
He said: "Indeed, they do not sacrifice here.
For whoever were to sacrifice here, they would surely overcome him. He showed him that world, saying: "By sacrificing in this very world, one conquers it."
He reflected, "Let me indeed conquer him.
Come now, let us perform a sacrifice. He said to him, "Sacrifice for me."
He caused him to perform the sacrifice. The *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds rose up by themselves; he pressed the *soma* in a mortar.
He said, "Come here from the very presence of Kutsa.
He approached Kutsa.
He said to him, "Whom did you sacrifice for?"
"Upagu," [he said].
"Kill this Upagu!"
They defeated him.
Having approached him a second time and a third time, he said to him, "Let me officiate as your priest."
He said: "Indeed, they do not sacrifice here. For if anyone were to sacrifice here, they would surely overcome him.
Twice indeed did this one sacrifice."
"Let them conquer that very one," he said.

He indeed showed him that world as being just this world, saying, "By sacrificing here, one conquers this very world. He then reflected: "Let them also conquer that other; come now, let us sacrifice!"
He said to him, "Sacrifice for me.
He performed the sacrifice for him.
The two sacrificial sheds, the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, rose up by themselves; he pressed the Soma in a mortar.
He said, "For whom did you sacrifice? "For Upagu," he replied.
Then, rising up himself, he cut him to pieces and cast him into the water.
Now, Suśravas Sthaurāyaṇa understood this from his father: "Kutsa Aurava indeed cast his son into the water after having cut him to pieces."
Rushing toward him, he said, "Where have you placed my son?
"He lies here, scattered in the water," he replied.
Then he descended after him.
Indra, having become a red deer, drank the Soma from his mouth. He reflected: "This is indeed Indra;
I shall praise him with this very [verse]."
"Only he will make me even with this," [he thought].
He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he praised him.
The broad-jawed Indra drank of the soma-juice of the skillful,
offering-rich [Indu], that Indu mixed with barley.
Thus [it is said].
He said to him, "With what desire do you praise me?
He replied, "Bring back this very son of mine.
[The other] said, "Come here," and churned him up.
He set it in motion.
This is the healing medicine, the expiation-sāman.
Indeed, he thereby performed that healing medicine, that expiation.
This seventh day is, as it were, fallen away;
they heal it with this very [rite].
With this, they perform a healing and an expiation.
And that [verse] is a fulfiller of desires. Indeed, he desired this very desire; that desire was fulfilled for him.
Whatever desire one has when one praises with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him.
And because Suśravas Sthautāyana saw it, it is therefore called the "Sauśravasa."
JB 3.203 |v1 The seers, having risen from the sacrificial session (*sattra*), were traveling along, yoking their chariots.
|v2 They said, "Let us look for some kind of spirit (*yakṣa*)."
They said, "This Kaśyapa Akūpāra has a great Yakṣa within the ocean;
let us go see him.
They then descended into it after him.
He did not appear to them. They said, "Let us praise Indra alone; he indeed has power over this. He alone will show himself to us."
They said to Atri, "O Seer, you have praised [him].
He, Atri, saw this triplet;
with it, they approached him.
"O Indra, O wonder-worker, whatever gift of yours is not here for me, O wielder of the stone—
O finder of wealth, bring that bounty to us with both hands.
Thus [he said].
He reflected: "Alas, the seers are making great demands of me!
They say, 'Bring [the wealth] with both hands! And they say, 'That which is your celebrated and lofty mind, which has attained preeminence throughout the quarters.'"
"O wielder of the thunderbolt, with that [strength] you shall pierce even the firm [obstacle] to win the prize.
Thus he thought: "Alas, the seers are making a firm request of me!"
They did not know him as the boundless one, even though they desired to behold him.
"O Indra, bring that which you establish as most excellent and celestial;
may we find it from you, the boundless one, in your giving."
Thus [he spoke].
He understood: "They indeed wish to see Akūpāra.
As he was about to step down, he said: "This very one—this great Ṛṣi—I shall bring here, as if with both hands, like a burden."
Thus they spoke. Not seeing him,
these verses are for the attainment of desire.
This was indeed the desire they cherished;
that desire was fulfilled for them. Whatever desire one praises with these verses, that desire is fulfilled for him.
In those [verses], there is Vasiṣṭha’s *vīṅka* (limping); it is as if the *anuṣṭubh* now oversteps the *anuṣṭubh*.
This very *anuṣṭubh*, being such, becomes thirty-three syllables.
By means of that, he transcends.
Vasiṣṭha, having been defeated and his sons slain, desired: "May I pervade these worlds; may I be distinguished by offspring and cattle."
"May I attain," he thought. He beheld this *sāman*;
with it, he praised.
By means of that [syllable] *vī*, he pervaded these worlds; he pervades [them] with offspring and cattle.
This is the Sāman that leads to heaven and brings about procreation. He who knows this pervades these worlds and pervades [them] with offspring and cattle.
And that [chant] is struck by the *stobha* syllables.
From being struck, indeed, offspring and cattle are produced.
The *chandomas* are cattle.
By that [sāman], indeed, it is rich in form.
Because Vasiṣṭha saw it, it is therefore called the "Vasiṣṭha-vīṅka.
That becomes the Aiḍa sāman for the Acchāvāka.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
verily, they thus find firm support in cattle.
"Adorning the lovely infant as he is born"— thus they become verses containing the word *hari*.
For the body of speech is indeed supreme when it contains the word *hari*.
They seek speech through the *chandomas*.
At this point, during the *chandomas*, speech is as if it has been fully attained;
they thus recover that very speech.
"O Maruts, you adorn the sage with your troop"—thus they become verses addressed to the Maruts (marutvatī).
Indeed, the form of the Triṣṭubh is possessed of the Maruts;
this day is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh.

Now, the *triṣṭubh* is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the Maruts are the common people (*viś*). Therefore, in that the *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to the Maruts occur, they thereby make the common people follow after the nobility.

"Therefore, the people follow the path of the ruling power; the seer through his songs, being a sage by his poetic wisdom, Soma goes forth over the filter, chanting"—thus he recites as he passes over.
"He who is of seer-like mind, the maker of seers, the winner of heaven, the leader of a thousand hymns, the pathfinder of the sages"—thus [he recites] regarding the one of a thousand forms.
They approach the *chandomas*.
The *chandomas* are indeed cattle.
[With the verse: "The buffalo, desiring to win the third abode," for this third three-day period is indeed performed as the *chandomas*.
"Soma shines according to the Virāj, he shines according to the Triṣṭubh"—thus they attain the form of the Triṣṭubh;
for this day is indeed Triṣṭubh.
Moreover, this is the sovereignty of the former power.
The Chandomas shine after him in this very way. With the verse,
"The falcon, the bird, the wide-striding, the drop that finds the cattle, bearing his weapons," they become verses containing the word "cattle" and "livestock," for the sake of securing livestock.
For the Chandomas are cattle.
[The verses] contain the word "ocean" (*samudra*), as in: "Accompanying the wave of the waters, the ocean. This is the form of the Chandomas.
The Chandomas are indeed the ocean.
"The buffalo proclaims the fourth abode," for this day, which consists of the Chandomas, is performed as the fourth of the days.

These verses are Triṣṭubhs; they possess the characteristics of the Triṣṭubh and are perfect through the form of the day. For wherever they bring about perfection through the form of the day, there one prospers.
Success attends him who knows thus.
"These Soma-pressings [are] toward the beloved," so it says; the word "toward" (abhi) is the form of the *rathantara*.
This day belongs to the *rathantara*.
"Indra's desire has flowed forth"—this, being addressed to Indra, is a form of the *triṣṭubh* meter;
for the *triṣṭubh* is indeed sovereign power (*kṣatra*). "Increasing his heroic might"—for this forty-four-verse hymn is indeed an increased day.
It is a matching [verse]. The hymn (*sūkta*) is indeed cattle, and the *Chandoma* days are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
Furthermore, cattle are abundance, and the hymn is abundance;
thus they make the forms of cattle corresponding [to the hymns].
In this matter, they do not act in accordance with direct perception.

Therefore, animals produce offspring of various forms: a white female produces a black one, a black female produces a white one, a red female produces a speckled one, and a speckled female produces a red one.
It consists of nine verses.
There are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person.
Thus, they proceed becoming successful through the vital breaths, finding firm support in the vital breaths.
The second [section] consists of nine verses; the third consists of nine verses.
Thus, they proceed in regular succession, becoming fully endowed with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). There are five verses; for the *paṅkti* meter indeed has five feet.
Cattle are fivefold;
the Chandomas are cattle. It is for the attainment of cattle.
Regarding this, they say: "The Pṛṣṭhya six-day period possesses the seasons, while the Chandomas lack the seasons."
"These Chandomas are established as it were in the seasons.
In that these [stotras] consist of five verses and six verses, by that very means the Chandomas are made to possess the seasons.
The *paryāsa* serves for the support of offspring and the prosperity of cattle.
There is a forty-four-fold hymn-form (*stoma*);
the *triṣṭubh* indeed consists of forty-four syllables.
The *indriya* and *vīrya* [verses] are in the *triṣṭubh* meter;
thus, they proceed while remaining established in power and vigor.
JB 3.207 |v1 | "O Agni, the god, with the Agnis, in harmony..."—this is the *ājya* chant for Agni, belonging to the *rathantara*.
For this day belongs to the *rathantara*. |v2 | Indeed, this day is of the *rathantara* nature.
"Make him the most excellent sacrificer and the messenger at the ritual,
he who is steadfast among mortals, the upholder of *ṛta*, whose path is heated, whose food is clarified butter, the purifier. Thus [it is said].
Ghee, indeed, is the beloved abode of Agni. By means of that very beloved abode, they cause him to prosper. [With the words:
"He snorts like a horse seeking pasture," it becomes possessed of the power of a horse, for the purpose of driving away the rival.
"When he has stepped forth from the great enclosure"— for this forty-fourth day is indeed great—
"the wind blows after his flame; indeed, black is your path."
When the wind fans the fire, it then blazes greatly;
that very radiance is the form of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
With the verse, "O you, the newly born bull," they approach the form of the *triṣṭubh* meter.
For this day belongs to the *triṣṭubh* metre. "O Agni, the ageless ones, being kindled, move about;
the ruddy smoke goes toward heaven; for as a messenger, O Agni, you hasten to the gods."
Thus, for the attainment of the heavenly world.
"O Mitra and Varuṇa, whatever today when the sun has risen..."— this is the Maitrāvaruṇa [śastra].
The word "whatever" (yat) is the form of the Rathantara.
This day belongs to the *rathantara* [sāman].
"May Mitra, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Bhaga impel us toward sinlessness."
May that dwelling be well-protected; may those who give good gifts now go forth on their journey, they who carry us across distress.
Having thus recited the verse of transition, he proceeds.
"Or [the gods] who are self-rulers, Aditi, and those of the unassailable law;
the great kings rule over it.
For this forty-fourth day is indeed a great day.
"O Indra, we impel you for strength"—this belongs to Indra. "We [impel] for the slaying of Vṛtra"—this contains the word for "slaying.
Indeed, this is the singer's own hymn of praise, which belongs to the Brahman priest.

In its own abode, they thus strike away all evil from the sacrificer. "He has become a bull, a stallion," it says; thus it contains the word *vṛṣan*. For the form of the *triṣṭubh* meter indeed contains the word *vṛṣan*.
This day is in the *triṣṭubh* metre.
"Indra, he who was made for the gift, the most powerful, he who is placed in strength"—
by means of this third three-day period, the gods indeed went upward to the heavenly world.
He moved about among them unseized.
Into him they placed strength, saying: "In him, O Indra, for the sake of giving, the most powerful one was placed in strength.
With the words, "The thunderbolt was fashioned by song," they fashioned him together.
With the words, "Possessing strength, unshakable," they thus made him strong.
Having consecrated him, they went to the heavenly world by means of that [consecration].
Therefore, this clarified butter (*ājya*) exists for the sake of attaining the heavenly world.
That which belongs to Indra and Agni on the first day is the *rāthaṃtara* [sāman] dedicated to Indra and Agni;
for this day is indeed *rāthaṃtara*. The *ājya* chants are characterized by the *samana* [melody].
These two, namely the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha and the Chandomas, are indeed like two separate villages.
Just as two friends from different villages might live together in safety by intermarrying, so it is when the Ājya-stotras are performed in common.
Some perform [the rites] with uneven numbers;
therefore, they should indeed be performed with even numbers.
There is a forty-four-fold hymn-form (*stoma*).
The triṣṭubh indeed consists of forty-four syllables;
the triṣṭubh is power and vigor.
Thus, they proceed while establishing themselves in power and vigor.
"O Adhvaryu, [the Soma] pressed with stones," they proceed with this verse in the *triṣṭubh* metre;
for this day is of the *triṣṭubh* nature.
O Soma, lead us across the filter; purify yourself for Indra to drink.
"O Indu, those [draughts] of yours with the juice... (v5); thus they become "possessing juice," for *andhas* is food; it is for the attainment of food.
"The gods have partaken of the honey... (v6).
"The Maruts [are the companions] of Pavamāna.
Thus they become verses addressed to the Maruts;
for the form of the midday pressing is indeed associated with the Maruts.
They do not depart from the very form of midday. With the words, "The supreme nectar of heaven," this final three-day period is performed, namely the Chandomas;
among them, the Gāyatra [stotra] has its Brāhmaṇa explained.
Now, the *rāthaṃtara* [sāman] has the *añjaḥpada* as its *nidhana*. Therefore, it is performed on the day of the *rāthaṃtara*.
Indeed, the gods desired, "May we ascend directly to the heavenly world."
They saw this Sāman;
they praised with it. Thereupon, they indeed ascended directly to the heavenly world.
That indeed is the straightness of the straight.
This is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows this ascends to the heavenly world by the very path of the straight.
And so they call it the Vairūpa;
for cattle are indeed diverse in form,
and cattle are the Vairūpa.
In this way, he joins the cattle together with the cattle themselves.
Virūpa Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, performed austerities;
he beheld this Sāman.
He praised with that [verse].
Thereupon he indeed acquired cattle. This is a *sāman* conducive to cattle.
He who knows thus secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Because Virūpa Āṅgirasa saw it, it is therefore called the Vairūpa.
Now,
the *dhur* chant is the *dravadiḍa*, belonging to the *rathantara*.
Therefore, it is performed on the day of the *rathantara*.
The *dhurs* are indeed the meters.
These *chandomas* are, as it were, exhausted;
therefore, because the *dhur-sāman* is performed here, by that very means the *chandomas* become invulnerable (*adhūrvaṃtaḥ*) and possessed of meters (*chandasvantaḥ*).
They are made to be spent with age. Moreover, the yokes are indeed the vital breaths;
the yokes are the cattle.
Thus he finds firm support in the vital breaths and in the sacrificial animals.
Now, the *iḍat* chant with three *nidhanas* is for the fulfillment of the pressings;
for that which is a *gāyatra* chant with three *nidhanas* is indeed successful.
Iḍa Kāvya, desiring heaven, performed austerities.
He beheld this Sāman;
with it, he offered praise.
By means of the first *nidhana*, he ascended this very world; by the second, the intermediate space; by the third, yonder world.
Thus he ascended these three worlds.
Thereupon, he indeed became firmly established in the heavenly world.
This is that *sāman* which leads to heaven and provides a firm foundation. Whoever knows this goes to the heavenly world and becomes firmly established in the heavenly world.
Because Iḍan Kāvya saw this, it is therefore called Aiḍata.
Now follows the Saumitra, a Sāman that slays rivals; it is accompanied by Indra. He who knows this slays his hateful rival, and Indra comes to his invocation.
Now follows the *sauparṇa* [sāman] whose Brāhmaṇa has been stated. It has four syllables as its *nidhana*. Cattle indeed consist of four feet, and the *chandomas* are cattle;
it is for the attainment of cattle.
JB 3.211 |v1 Now,
[regarding] "quickly":
|v2 The gods, indeed, desired, "May we go quickly to the heavenly world."
They saw this Sāman;
they praised with it. Thereupon, indeed, they quickly went to the heavenly world.
That indeed is the blessing (*āśis*), that is swiftness (*āśutva*).
This is the *sāman* leading to heaven.
He who knows this goes swiftly to the heavenly world by means of it.
Therefore, they call him Āśubhārgava.
The gods and the Asuras were contending with one another.
Those gods ran to Bhṛgu, saying, "Conquer the Asuras!"
Bhṛgu saw this Sāman;
he praised with it. Thereupon, the gods indeed conquered the Asuras.
They said, "Truly, this has quickly come from Bhṛgu. That, indeed, is the reason for Āśu's name "Āśu" (the Swift).
It is a destroyer of rivals and a granter of desires.
He slays his hateful rival.
Whatever desire one has while praising with this [hymn], that desire is fulfilled for him.
JB 3.212 |v1 Now, the *mārgīyava* has the *padanidhana* and belongs to the *rathantara*.
|v2 Therefore, it is performed on a day belonging to the *rathantara*.
The divine hunter (mṛgayu) indeed desired: "May I attain sovereignty and overlordship over all animals, both those that are domestic and those that are wild.
He saw this Sāman.
He praised with that [verse].
Thereupon, he indeed attained sovereignty and lordship over both kinds of cattle— those that are domestic and those that are wild.
Then, indeed, the wild animal would bring a wild animal to him. This is that *sāman* which is beneficial for cattle;
one attains sovereignty and lordship over both kinds of cattle—those that are domestic and those that are wild.
One who knows thus—
this very one is indeed that god Mṛgayu.
He does not harm the cattle of one who knows thus.
And because the divine Mṛgayu saw it, it is therefore called the *mārgīyava*.
"O Soma-drops, the living ones..."— it contains the word "towards" (*abhi*), which is the form of the *rathantara*;
this day belongs to the *rathantara*.
"They pour out the intoxicating drink for exhilaration;
upon the surface of the ocean, the wise ones, the exhilarating ones who shed the flow of intoxication.
Thus they contain the word "ocean" (*samudra*); this is the form of the *Chandomas*.
The Chandomas are indeed the ocean.
"O Pavamāna, as King and God, flow with thy wave into the ocean according to the great *ṛta*;
flow according to the law of Mitra and Varuṇa, being urged forward toward the great *ṛta*."
Guided by men, golden-hued, far-seeing, the king, the god of the ocean.
(Thus there is a four-verse hymn. Cattle indeed have four feet;
the Chandomas are cattle. It is for the attainment of cattle.
In those [verses], the Vāmadevya [Sāman] has two *hiṃkāras*.
The *simā* verses are indeed cattle;
the *revatī* verses are cattle.
The Vāmadevya [Sāman] has two *hiṃkāras* and represents cattle.
Those who praise with it become possessed of cattle.
Prajāpati created cattle.
Once they were created, they departed from him, being out of harmony with one another.
He thought, "Let the cattle come back to me;
let them not depart from me."
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it. Thereupon, indeed, the cattle recognized him.
Then they did not depart from him.
That [sound] consists of two *hiṃ*-utterances. Indeed, cattle recognize one another with "hum"; with "hum" the mother approaches her son, and with "hum" the son [approaches] his mother.
This is the *saṃjñāna* (unifying) *sāman* of cattle.
Cattle recognize him [with favor], and cattle do not depart from him who knows thus.
It belongs to *iḍā*; for *iḍā* is cattle, and the *chandomas* are cattle—it is for the attainment of cattle.
JB 3.214 |v1 Now follows the Gāyatrapārśva.
|v2 These worlds indeed are the Gāyatrapārśva.
In these very worlds they find firm support.
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerity. They beheld this *sāman*.
With it they praised. Having become the Gāyatra itself, it carried them to the heavenly world.
Having reached the heavenly world, they said: "The two wings of this Sāman were indeed the Gāyatra."
That indeed is the "Gāyatra-winged" nature of the Gāyatra-winged [sacrifice].
For this [sacrifice] is indeed named "Gāyatra-winged," and it is designated as "having Gāyatra sides."
For it becomes possessed of the *hiṃ* sound for the attainment of food. Indeed, by means of those [sounds] possessed of the *hiṃ* sound, Prajāpati bestowed food upon his creatures.
Food is bestowed upon him who knows thus.
JB 3.215 |v1 Now follows the undertaking of the Pauruhanmana [sāman], which is the withdrawal of the sacrifice. |v2 One indeed undertakes the ninth day and withdraws from the seventh.
By means of undertakings, the gods indeed excluded the Asuras from the sacrifice.
Puruhanman Vaikhānasa, desiring cattle, performed austerity;
he saw this Sāman.
He praised with that [verse].
He resorted to this *iḍā*.
The *iḍā*, indeed, is cattle.
Thereupon he indeed won cattle.
This is a Sāman that brings cattle;
he who knows this wins cattle and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Because Puruhanman Vaikhānasa saw it, it is therefore called the *Pauruhanmana*.
The gods and the Asuras contended with one another.
Those gods desired: "May we slay the Asuras first."
They saw this *sāman*; they praised with it;
by means of it, they struck down the Asuras in the east.
In that they struck him down first, that is why it is called the *pauruhanmana* [hymn], after Pūruhanman.
He who knows this strikes down his hateful rival first.
JB 3.216 |v1 Now follows the Dvaigata, which has *pada* as its *nidhana* and belongs to the *rathantara* [sāman].
|v2 Therefore, it is performed on a day belonging to the *rathantara*.
The gods, having gathered up the entire sacrifice, ascended upwards to the heavenly world.
The men did not recognize the sacrifice;
thus it was lost to them.
Those gods and humans were hungry; for the gods live by offerings from here, and humans live by offerings from yonder.
Consequently, the oblations went upwards, and rain was not bestowed from yonder downwards.

Those gods said to Ayāsya, "Human beings do not understand the sacrifice; therefore, go and arrange it for them. He said, "I shall divide it among them. They said, "Go forth and ordain the sacrifice for them."
Having approached, he established the sacrifice for human beings by means of this very *sāman*. This sacrifice was thus established among human beings.
Having dwelt among human beings, it did not recognize the heavenly world again.
He desired, "May I know the heavenly world.
Having praised with this very *sāman*, he again came to know the heavenly world.
This, then, is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world;
moreover, by means of this very *sāman*, his sacrifice becomes fully established.
When Ayāsya came from that world to this world, and from this world to that world—
He went; he traversed these two worlds twice, and that is the origin of the name *Dvaigata*.
Ayāsya was indeed Dvaigata.
JB 3.217 |v1 Now, concerning Hārāyaṇa:
|v2 The gods and the asuras contended with one another.
Those gods desired, "May we seize the splendor (*haras*) of the Asuras; may we take it away. They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
By that [means], he took away the *hara* (booty) of the Asuras. Because he took away (*aharat*) the *hara*, that is the reason for the name *Hārāyaṇa*.
He who knows this takes away the *hara* of his hateful rival.
Hārāyaṇa Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, performed austerities. He beheld this Sāman;
with it, he praised.
May we prosper, O powerful Indra, through all your aids;
for we follow you, O hero, the glorious finder of wealth, like Bhaga.
"You are the first of horses, the performer of many deeds for cattle; O God, you are a fountain of gold.
With these words, he indeed obtained cattle and horses.
Having sacrificed with those animals, he went to the heavenly world.
This is a *sāman* that is beneficial for cattle and leads to heaven.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and goes to the heavenly world.
Furthermore, because Hārāyaṇa Āṅgirasa saw it, it is called the "Hārāyaṇa."
JB 3.218 |v1 Now,
the *rathantara* [sāman] has its *nidhana* on the word "achidram" (unbroken). |v2 Therefore, it is performed on the day of the *rathantara*.
Prajāpati indeed desired, "May I become unbroken with offspring and cattle. That very thing is the state of being unbroken. He who knows thus becomes unbroken with offspring and cattle.
The gods, indeed, gathered together the speech that had been obtained from these very worlds by means of that which is without flaw.
Now, at this time, during the Chandoma days, speech becomes as if fully obtained;
they gather it together by means of that which is without flaw.
Verily, that which one piles with a gap is not filled up;
but that which one piles without a gap is filled up. There is a superior undertaking: it surpasses the ninth day and reaches the tenth day.
He exerts himself; he runs away up to the seventh [generation].
Prajāpati created cattle;
once created, they departed from him.
He desired, "May the cattle not depart from me; may they remain with me.
He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he turned them back.
He accepted them with preeminence. They found delight in him. Animals find delight in him; he who knows thus becomes rich in cattle.
JB 3.219 |v1 Now follows the Bārhaduktha. |v2 Bṛhaduktha Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, performed austerities.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it;
he approached this *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
from it, he indeed obtained cattle.
Therefore, this is a *sāman* that is conducive to cattle.
He who knows thus secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Furthermore, because Bṛhaduktha Āṅgirasa saw [this], it is called the *bārhaduktha*.
"The supporter of heaven, the sage, flows as the essence"—thus [it serves] for the support of the day.
"May the skillful one of the gods, to be celebrated by men..."— with these words they cause the meters to flourish, for the sake of the day's vigor.
Upon them [the meters] grow upward with threefold sprouting.
For this third growth is produced: namely, this third three-day period, for the attainment of the heavenly world.
Regarding that, they also say: "It is the broad."
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerities. They saw this *sāman*; with it, they praised.
So, having become broad indeed, it carried them to the heavenly world.
Having reached the heavenly world, they said: "It was because this Sāman became broad for us that it carried us to the heavenly world."
That indeed is the vastness of the Viśāla;
that is this *sāman* leading to heaven.
He who knows thus attains the heavenly world.
Just as indeed are the summits of the sun, so are these the summits of Viśāla, for the complete attainment of the heavenly world.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Then [they chant] the Rathantara. The Rathantara is indeed the Brahman;
thus they proceed while firmly established in the Brahman.

That occurs on the day of the *triṣṭubh* metre. The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the form of the male, and the *rathaṃtara* is that of the female. Therefore, in that the *rathaṃtara* serves as the *pṛṣṭha* chant on this day, by that very means this day is made into a union.
Now follows the Vāmadevya.
The Vāmadevya is indeed cattle;
those who have praised with this become possessed of cattle.
"O Indra, whether [you be] in the east, in the west, or in the north"—by this they indeed invoke Indra from all directions;
on the completed days [they say], "If you are in this direction, if in that, if in this."
In these [verses], the *rāthaṃtara* [sāman] has the *vāśa* as its *prastāva* and the *pada* as its *nidhana*;
therefore, it is performed on the day connected with the *rāthaṃtara*.
Those gods desired, "May we seize the power of the Asuras.
They saw this Sāman;
they praised with it.
They chose the *vaśa* of the Asuras by means of the word "vāś. That is the very reason for the name of the *vāśa*.
He who knows this appropriates the *vaśa* of his hateful rival.
"Who knows him when the [Soma] is pressed?"—with these *satobṛhatī* verses they step forward so as not to fall away from the path.
Within them is the *naipātitha* (the hymn of Nipātithi). While the Kaṇvāyanas were performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), their cattle perished.
They desired, "May we obtain cattle.
Then Nepātithi Kāṇva perceived this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Then indeed they obtained cattle.
This is that Sāman which pertains to cattle.
He who knows this obtains cattle; he becomes possessed of many cattle.

Because Kaṇva Naipātithi saw this [sāman], it is called the *naipātitha*. With the words "Listen to both," he undertakes both forms: that which belongs to the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period and that which belongs to the *chandomas*.
Therefore, one should indeed perform the Brahman-sāman on this [day] for two persons who are sacrificing together.
JB 3.221 |v1 Regarding these [verses], there is the Vaiyaśva. |v2 Vyaśva’s father, the seer Gaya, beheld Sākamaśva while he was still in the womb.
"He will be born," [she said]. When he was born, Parāsta said, "Jātakṣeṇa has been born. Shadow did not leave him.
His own two thumbs pressed down upon him.
They reported this to him, saying, "The boy whom you declared to be dead—he indeed lives!
Taking up a mallet, he approached, intending to strike him.
He desired, "May I go forth from here; may I find a path and a support.
He saw this Sāman;
he sang it.
That club of his fell backward and cut off his head.
This is that *sāman* which slays rivals, finds a way, and provides protection. He who knows this slays his hateful rival, finds a way, and finds protection.
Because Vyaśva saw it, it is called the Vaiyaśva.
That is the Aiḍa Sāman for the Acchāvāka;
for the *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
Verily, they thus find firm support in cattle.
With "Flow on, O god, for our life," they proceed with the form of a Triṣṭubh;
for this day has the nature of the Triṣṭubh.
"Let your exhilaration go to Indra;
ascend to Vāyu according to the cosmic law.
Thus, they contain the word "mada" (exhilaration).
The exhilaration is indeed essence.
This third pressing is, as it were, something solidified.
Therefore, when these [verses] contain the word "madvat" (exhilarating), they thereby bestow essence upon this [sacrifice], and thus complete it.
They cause [the worlds] to swell.
O Pavamāna Soma, you bestow wealth that brings renown;
O Indu, enter the ocean.
Thus they descend from the ocean; this is the form of the Chandomas.
The Chandomas are indeed the ocean.
With the verse, "Striking down the adversaries, you flow clear," they strike down the adversaries, that is, evil, by means of this.
Among those [sāmans], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa explained previously.
Now follows the Mādila, which has *pada* as its *nidhana* and belongs to the Rathaṃtara;
therefore, it is performed on a day belonging to the Rathaṃtara.
The gods indeed desired, "May our Soma be intoxicating; may we rejoice in the intoxication of Soma.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.

Then indeed, Soma became intoxicating for them; they became intoxicated by the intoxication of Soma. That is precisely why Mādhvila has his name "Mādhvila. Now, intoxication (*mada*) is indeed essence (*rasa*).
Verily, they made that [sacrifice] with essence. The Soma of one who knows thus becomes rich in essence and full of flavor.
Moreover, if they were to perform this here, their Chandomas would be as if unappropriated.
These Chandomas, having the third pressing as their abode, are like daughters;
for the third pressing is indeed like something churned. Therefore, when there is a *mādila* here, they place essence into the Chandomas and thereby truly sustain them.
They cause [them] to drink.
Then [he offers] the Surūpa [offering] for the sake of the perfection of form. Indeed,
the descendants of Aṅgiras, while performing austerities, were deprived of their beauty and splendor.
They desired, "May we excel in beauty and splendor.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Then indeed they were endowed with beauty and splendor.
They said, "We have become truly beautiful.
That is the reason for the name "Surūpa" (the Beautiful One).
He who knows thus is endowed with beauty and splendor. Surūpa Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, performed austerity;
he saw this Sāman.
He praised with that. He approached this *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
Thereupon he indeed acquired cattle.
This is a Sāman that pertains to cattle.
He who knows this acquires cattle and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Because Surūpa Āṅgirasa saw it, it is therefore called "Surūpa.
Prajāpati created cattle;
once they were created, their forms could not be distinguished.
He saw these *sāman*s called *surūpa*.
With them, he bestowed forms upon these [beings].
That is the reason for the *surūpa*s being called *surūpa* ("well-formed").
He who knows thus secures cattle that possess form.
The Chandomas have the Arka as their *sāman* and possess beautiful forms;
he who knows thus praises with the Chandomas which possess both *sāmans* and form.
That *punarnitunna* chant shines forth;
wherever the gods found the essence of the meters, they made it *punarnitunna* and struck it again.
These Chandomas, having the third pressing as their abode, are like daughters;
for the third pressing is indeed like something thought out (dhīta). In that a metre is repeated (*punarnitunna*), they thereby place essence into the metres.
This is simply the apprehension of the aesthetic flavor itself.
JB 3.224 |v1 Now follows the [sacrifice] of Kakṣīvat. |v2 Kakṣīvat, indeed, desired: "May I be propagated abundantly with offspring and cattle; may I attain prosperity and sovereignty."
"I shall go.
He saw this *sāman* and praised with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle and attained prosperity and sovereignty. There were a thousand sons born to Kākṣīvata;
with those sons, he indeed attained prosperity and sovereignty.
He who knows this attains glory and goes to sovereignty.
Moreover, it is pierced by *stobha*s;
indeed, from what is pierced, offspring and cattle are produced.
The Chandomas are cattle;
thus it is indeed rich in form.
Because Kakṣīvān saw [this], it is called the Kākṣīvata.
JB 3.225 |v1 Now follows the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya* [chant]. |v2 Once, while the seers were performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), their cattle disappeared.
They desired, "May we obtain cattle.
They said, "Let us beg Agni for these cattle;
he indeed is the lord of cattle."
"He alone will grant us cattle," they said.
They saw this Sāman;
with it, they praised him.
Sing forth to the most generous one, the observer of cosmic order (*ṛtāvan*), the great one with brilliant luster;
[sing] praises to Agni.
Thus.
He said to them, "What is your desire?
They replied, "We desire cattle.
To them he bestowed cattle by means of this very *sāman*.
They said, "He was indeed most exultant for us. That is why the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya* has its name *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya*.
This is a Sāman that is conducive to cattle.
He indeed becomes most exultant for him; he secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle—he who knows thus.
That, moreover, is the *punarnitunna* metre.
Wherever the gods indeed found the essence of the meters, there they made it rise up again and struck it again.
These Chandomas are like daughters, having the third pressing as their abode.
The third pressing is, as it were, like something that has been sucked out. In that a *chandas* (meter) occurs again as a repetition (*punarnitunna*), they thereby place essence into the *chandomas*;
this is their attainment of essence.
JB 3.226 |v1 Now, Arka is one who has his own head; Arka is indeed food, [and this is] for the attainment of food. |v2 Svāśiras by name is an Apsaras; she is these very plants.
They desired: "May we become many; may we procreate; may we attain this world.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Then indeed they became many, they procreated, and they attained this world. This entire world, including the mountains, is covered with plants.
This is the Sāman of procreation.
He is multiplied with offspring and cattle; he who knows thus attains this world.
And because they beheld the Apsaras Svāśiras, it is therefore called the *svāśirām arka*.
"Toward great glory and fame"—the word "toward" (*abhi*) occurs here as a characteristic form of the *rathantara* [sāman].
This day belongs to the *Rathantara* [Sāman].

With the words, "Stirring for the sake of seeking cattle, [the prayers]," the verses become rich in cattle and rich in livestock; this is for the very purpose of securing livestock, for the *Chandomas* are indeed livestock.
In these [verses], the Aiṣira has Vāyu as its seer;
for Vāyu is indeed swift (iṣira).
Whatever indeed perishes among those engaged in a sacrificial session (*sattra*), Vāyu causes that to rise up again for them.
Vāyu is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
It is the vital breath itself that heals them.
By this they perform both medicine and expiation.
With the words, "The breath is the child of the great ones," they thus approach the form of the sacrificial animal;
for the child indeed belongs to the animals.

In these [verses], the *traita* has its Brāhmaṇa explained as previously stated. "Obeisance to us, most bestowing of booty"—it contains the word "towards" (*abhi*), which is the form of the *rathantara*;
for this day belongs to the *rathantara*.
Flow forth, O Indu, wealth that is desired by hundreds, bringing thousands of boons, possessing great splendor, and overcoming all adversaries.
Thus.
That which possesses hundreds and thousands is indeed the form of the Chandomas.
The Chandomas are cattle.
[The verse] "This Soma-drop, flowing around, has flowed through the sheep's wool, distilling rapture" contains the word for rapture; thus they become full of rapture.
In this very way, they place the essence and the exhilaration [of Soma] at the third pressing in due order.
"O Vasu, may we be most closely associated with this thy much-desired bounty, O Lord; may we abide in thy favor, O irresistible one."
Thus, these verses are "possessing cows" (*gomatīḥ*) and "possessing cattle" (*paśumatīḥ*), for the sake of securing cattle;
for the *chandoma* days are indeed cattle. In these [verses], the *gaurīvita* chant is used, whose Brāhmaṇa explanation has already been stated.
JB 3.228 |v1 Now follows the Śuddhāśuddhīya.
|v2 Having slain the Asuras, Indra, as it were, considered himself unpurified and impure.
He desired, "May they praise me while I am pure with a pure *sāman*.
He said to the seers, "Praise me!
Those seers then perceived this *sāman*.
With this they praised him:
"Come now, let us praise Indra, the pure one, with a pure *sāman*;
may he, who has grown strong through pure hymns (*uktha*), be exhilarated by the pure libations."
Thus it was said.
Then indeed Indra became pure, cleansed, and fit for sacrifice.
This is that purifying *sāman*.
He who knows this becomes pure, cleansed, and fit for sacrifice.
Now follows the [teaching] of Audala:
Udala Daivarāta indeed desired, "May I be foremost, preeminent, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcas)."
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he became preeminent, foremost, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*).
Thinking, "May we be foremost, preeminent, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*)," they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
They indeed become foremost, preeminent, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge.
That *svāra* chant is performed upon the *anuṣṭubh* meter for the sake of perfection of form.
That which has its origin in the *gāyatrī* is performed in the *anuṣṭubh*.
Indeed, having become paired, cattle exert their vital powers.
The *chandomas* are cattle.
Therefore, it is performed during the *chandome* [stomas].
Because Udala Daivarāta saw this, it is called the *audala*.
JB 3.229 |v1 Now follows the Pāñcavāja.
|v2 By means of this, Pañcavāja Kautsa drank up both kinds of soma-juice: that which is divine and that which is human.
The human [soma].
With this, those two indeed drink separately:
Kautsa Pañcavāja desired to drink separately from both kinds of soma-juice—that which is divine and that which is human.
"Human," he said.
He saw this *sāman*;
with it, he praised.
Then indeed he drank up both those juices, that which was divine and that which was human. Then, having placed a leather bag for liquor, he would hold it for the sake of Soma.
This is the *sāman* that secures the acquisition of food.
Both juices are drunk when one knows that which is divine and that which is human.
Because Kautsa saw this [hymn] consisting of five powers (*pañcavāja*), it is therefore called *pāñcavāja*.
Now follows the *krauñca* [chant].
Kruñ Āṅgirasa found the *īṣya* as if it were hidden;
these Chandomas are like *īṣyas*.
Therefore, this [rite] is performed during the Chandomas.
It has the *svāra* [melody] in its middle.
Breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *svāra*. These *chandomas* are, as it were, like medical treatments.
Two days each are combined.
In that there is the *svāra* [sāman] in the middle, they thereby place the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *chandoma*s; by this they heal them.
Now, there is the *rayiṣṭha* with the *nidhana* in the middle; it serves for support.
Indeed, those who undertake the *ārbhava-pavamāna* launch themselves upon the ocean as their point of support.
In that it has the *nidhana* in the middle, it is for the sake of stability.
Prajāpati created cattle;
once they were created, they departed from him.
He desired, "May the cattle not depart from me; may they remain with me.
He saw this *sāman* and praised with it.
Then indeed the cattle turned back toward him;
then they became those who did not depart from him. He said, "Truly, this wealth has stood upon me."
That indeed is the reason why the *rayiṣṭha* (the one who stands in wealth) is so called.
This is a *sāman* favorable to cattle.
Wealth stands upon him; cattle turn toward him and do not depart from him, he who [knows this].
Thus he knows.
That [Iḍā] consists of one and a half portions; for the Iḍā is cattle, and the Chandomas are cattle.
This is for the attainment of cattle in their proper sequence.
Now, these [verses] consist of two feet; their Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.
They are as follows: "Flow on, O Soma, as a great ocean.
For this forty-fourth day is indeed great.
"The father of the gods shines toward all abodes"—this is the form of the Rathantara;
this day belongs to the Rathantara.
JB 3.231 |v1 Regarding those [verses], Dharma:
|v2 By means of Dharma, the gods, having taken hold of Dharma, rendered the Asuras lawless through lawlessness.
Overpowering;
by means of *dharman* itself, having taken hold of *dharman*, and having rendered the hostile rival devoid of *dharman* (*vidharman*), he overpowers him who knows thus.

For that prosperity is indeed dharma, and sovereignty is indeed dharma; by means of dharma the king is dharma. He becomes dharma for his own people; his own people come to him, and he maintains them through dharma. Regarding this, they say: "It should be performed on the ninth day."

The Bārhata [Sāman] is indeed the *kṣatra* (the ruling power), while this Rathantara is the *viś* (the common people). Regarding this, they say: "Kings are indeed distinct in their laws; they do not share the same laws as other men."
|v9 This very thing, indeed, is the *kṣatra*, namely the forty-four-versed hymn in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
|v10 Therefore, on the ninth day itself there should be a *vidharma* [variation], thinking, "Let this be here.
|v11 "The sisters, the female kin, the dawns, urge the hero, their husband, onward."
[They approach] the great moon, [desiring] the great ones.
For this forty-fourth day is indeed great;
in those [stotras], there is the *viśoviśīya*, for which the Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.
That [verse] belongs to Iḍā;
for Iḍā is indeed cattle, and the Chandomas are cattle—it is for the attainment of cattle.

Uśanas Kāvya, among the gods, desired an immortal world of the Gandharvas. He saw this Sāman;
with it, he praised.

These are the Kāvya hymns.
By praising with this [hymn], one attains among the gods the immortal world of the Gandharvas in the world of Romaṇvat.
Agni indeed dwelt among the gods.
The gods did not gratify him.
Being ungratified, he went to Uśanas Kāvya.
He said to him, "O seer, please me; I am not pleased. He desired, "May I please him.
He saw this *sāman*.
With this he gratified him:
"I praise for you your most beloved guest, dear as a friend, O Agni, who is to be known like a chariot."
In this way, he made him his most beloved guest.
Indeed, having carried the sacrifice, he remains as if displeased at this time;
therefore, they gratify him here.
Being pleased, he carries away whatever remains of the sacrifice there.
Because Uśanas Kāvya saw this, it is called the *auśana* [rite].
"O Indra, come to us, you who are dear, the ever-conquering, the unconcealable!"
Like a mountain broad on all sides, he is the lord of heaven.
"For you, O true Soma-drinker,"—
thus it contains the word "towards" (*abhi*), which is a form of the *rathantara* [sāman];
this day belongs to the *rathantara*.
"Thou hast become both worlds"—these two, indeed, are the two worlds;
he thus addresses these very ones.
"O Indra, thou art the prosperer of the presser, the lord of heaven"—for this forty-fourth day is indeed a prosperous day.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? They are: physical food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of these four nutriments? “Monks, craving is the cause, craving is the condition, for the arising of these four nutriments. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of this craving? “Contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the arising of this craving. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of this contact? “Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition, for the arising of this contact. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of this name-and-form? “Consciousness is the cause, consciousness is the condition, for the arising of this name-and-form. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of this consciousness? “Volitional formations are the cause, volitional formations are the condition, for the arising of this consciousness. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of these volitional formations? “Ignorance is the cause, ignorance is the condition, for the arising of these volitional formations. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of this ignorance? “Monks, when there is no end to this, there is no end to suffering, to aging-and-death, to birth, to becoming, to clinging, to craving, to feeling, to contact, to the six sense bases, to name-and-form, and to consciousness. But with the ending of this, there is the ending of suffering, the ending of aging-and-death, the ending of birth, the ending of becoming, the ending of clinging, the ending of craving, the ending of feeling, the ending of contact, the ending of the six sense bases, the ending of name-and-form, and the ending of consciousness. When this was said, that monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has this been stated by the Blessed One: ‘With the ending of this, there is the ending of that. “Monks, if one were to say: ‘I shall show you the way leading to the cessation of this entire mass of suffering,’ it is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path that one would point out. That is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. “Monks, what is right view? It is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called right view. “What is right intention? It is the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of harmlessness. This, monks, is called right intention. “What is right speech? It is abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter. This, monks, is called right speech. “What is right action? It is abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. This, monks, is called right action. “What is right livelihood? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by right livelihood. This, monks, is called right livelihood. “What is right effort? Here, monks, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. This, monks, is called right effort. “What is right mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, monks, is called right mindfulness. “What is right concentration? Here, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a monk enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in pleasure. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is beyond pleasure and pain, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, monks, is called right concentration. “This, monks, is the Noble Eightfold Path. And this, monks, is the way leading to the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. When this was said, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has this been stated by the Blessed One: ‘With the ending of this, there is the ending of that. “Ānanda, if one were to say: ‘I shall show you the way leading to the cessation of this entire mass of suffering,’ it is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path that one would point out. That is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. “Ānanda, what is right view? It is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called right view. “What is right intention? It is the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of harmlessness. This, Ānanda, is called right intention. “What is right speech? It is abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter. This, Ānanda, is called right speech. “What is right action? It is abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. This, Ānanda, is called right action. “What is right livelihood? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by right livelihood. This, Ānanda, is called right livelihood. “What is right effort? Here, Ānanda, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. This, Ānanda, is called right effort. “What is right mindfulness? Here, Ānanda, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind
In them [the verses], the Sāṃvarta has the *padanidhana* and belongs to the *rathantara*. Therefore, it is performed on a day belonging to the *rathantara*.
Saṃvarta Āṅgirasa, desiring heaven, performed austerities.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
He ascended to the heavenly world with the words, "The lord of heaven, the lord of heaven. Just as one might fall, so it would be if [he were merely] "the lord of heaven";
therefore, this is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Because Saṃvarta Āṅgirasa saw it, it is therefore called the Sāṃvarta. The gods and the Asuras were contending with one another.
Those Asuras spread themselves out over a great distance.
Indra desired, "May I strike down the Asuras while still encompassing them together.
He saw this Sāman.
He praised him with this hymn:
"O Indra, you indeed are the upholder of all the eternal fortresses;
you are the slayer of the Dasyu, the prosperer of Manu, and the lord of heaven."
Thus he struck them together with the *saṃvarta* [formula].
That is indeed why the *saṃvarta* is called *saṃvarta*.
He who knows thus, having struck together, slays his hateful rival.
JB 3.234 |v1 Now follows the *maidhātitha* [sāman].
|v2 The descendants of Vibhinduka, with Medhātithi as their householder, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
|v3 Among them, Dṛḍhacyud Āgasti was the Udgātṛ, Gaurīviti the Prastotṛ, Acyutacyut the Pratihartṛ, and Vasukṣaya the Hotṛ; Sanaka and Navaka, the two Kāvyas, were the Adhvaryus.
|v4 Medhātithi desired cattle, Sanaka and Navaka desired offspring; whatever desire the others had, that was their desire.
In ancient times, people used to perform sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) with various desires. Having indeed fulfilled and attained their respective desires, they would emerge from the session.
While they were doing so, Indra, having assumed the form of Medhātithi’s ram, used to drink the Soma as his sacrificial portion.
They used to drive him away, saying, "Medhātithi’s ram is consuming our Soma!
But he, having assumed his own form, would consume the Soma for them.
Since then, people have called this [ram] here "Medhātithi’s ram."
Medhātithi, desiring cattle, saw this *sāman*. He praised with it:
"The breaker of forts, the youth, the sage"—with these words, he split Vala asunder.
With the verse, "O wielder of the stone, you opened the cave of Vala who possessed cattle," he opened the cave.
JB 3.235 |v1 Then the cattle were created.
|v2 Those which were created first, they are these very cattle that exist today.
Then indeed, the golden-horned cows with two udders followed after them;
then indeed, two Apsarases, wearing golden loincloths, followed after them.
The householder set his mind upon them.
He said, "These are indeed mine; I withheld them for my Gārhapatya fire. "The prosperity of the householder is indeed all-encompassing," they said.
"No," replied Sanaka and Navaka, "you were one who desired cattle when you sat [in office]."
"These animals are yours.
We two are the parents.
These two are the wives of us two."
While they were thus conversing, it entered into one of them;
she indeed seized it.
This is that [vessel] which has this as if a small mouthpiece.
Then one of them was struck with wonder;
she was this very Hariṇikā. Therefore, she frequents cattle; come, let us go to the place where the cattle are.
Then these golden cows with horns of gold and two udders ran back again to the very place from which they had set out, saying,
"The householder has committed an untruth.
We are certainly not his, he who commits an untruth."
Even today, these very *krūrarṣabha* birds, having become embodied forms (*śārīr*) of Vibhinduka, are known [to exist].
Two descendants of Kaṇva, Medhātithi and Triśoka, both devoted to sacred knowledge (*brahmaṇya*), vied with one another. They said, "Come, let us pass over the kindled fire."
The two of them approached the kindled fire.
Triśoka passed right over it; then he scorched the eyelashes of the other.
He said to him, "I have conquered you."
"No," he said, "you are indeed an Asura's son; the deities did not wish to touch you.
"Come, let us both cross over the waters," [the other] said.
They both crossed over the water that had spilled from the chariot.
Triśoka overtook him again and again, while the other two had their wheel-rims (pavī) protected.
That very [chariot] with its moist rim served as a protection for the chariot.
He said to him: "I have conquered you."
"No," he said, "you are indeed the son of an Asura woman. The deities themselves did not wish to touch what was touched by you.
"Then come, let us both release the cattle," they said.
Triśoka immediately released those long-eared animals from the hairless one;
they, being tormented there, perished and were destroyed.
She was able to move forward.
Therefore, they say, "The cows have gone forth.
For this reason, one who does not eat meat should not eat [her] before [the cows have gone forth].
Then some, being scorched, fled westward;
they entered the Indus,
and there it became salt.
Therefore they say, "Cows are salt.
And so, whoever conducts his business by means of salt, it is cows indeed that he obtains.
Now, Medhātithi, desiring cattle, offered the year-long sacrifice.
From that very stronghold, the one called "the Stone" (*aśmābhidhāna*), he released the cattle with [the verse]: "Thou, O Vala, rich in cattle... This is the *Sāman* for the release of cattle.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Because Medhātithi saw this, it is therefore called the "Medhātithi" [sūkta].
Regarding this, they also call it "the Sāman of the Aṅgirases.
For there were indeed sons of the ṛṣis named Aṅgirases.
They desired, "May we attain the heavenly world.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Then indeed they attained the heavenly world. This is that Sāman which leads to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Because they saw [it] as belonging to the Aṅgirasas, it is therefore called the "Sāman of the Aṅgirasas.

Indeed, the Maruts desired: "May we become the strongest, the most powerful, the most numerous, and the most heroic among the gods."
"May we conquer the heavenly world!
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Then indeed those gods became the strongest, the most powerful, the most numerous, and the most heroic; they conquered the heavenly world.
He who is the strongest, the most powerful, the most numerous, and the most heroic among his own people conquers the heavenly world.
Thus he knows.
And because the Maruts saw it, it is therefore called the Māruta.

Now, the Bharatas were indeed on the far bank of the Sindhu, held back by the Ikṣvākus.

"How do you barter for the ocean?
they asked. Thereupon, they indeed found those cattle.
This is a *sāman* pertaining to cattle.
One who knows this secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Furthermore, because Viśvāmitra saw it, it is called the "Vaiśvāmitra."
That *aiḍa* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
thus, they find firm support in cattle.
"‘The ocean has stepped forth in the highest ordinance’— the horse is indeed the highest of animals,
the ocean is the highest, and the ninth day is the highest; therefore, these [verses] are performed on the ninth day."
"Generating offspring, the guardian of the world"—thus they contain the word *jana* (people/offspring). Indeed, the form of the *jagatī* meter contains the word *jana*;
this day belongs to the *jagatī*.

"Vṛṣan (the bull) has grown great upon the sheep’s back in the filter; Soma, being pressed, has increased like a mountain"—thus they contain the word *vṛṣan* and the word *bṛhat*, which is the form of the *Bṛhat*.
This day belongs to the *Bṛhat*.
"Great indeed is that which Soma, the buffalo, has performed"—for this forty-eight-fold day is indeed great.
"When as the embryo of the waters he chose the gods, Pavamāna bestowed vigor upon Indra; Indu generated light in the sun."
Thus they become verses containing the word *jan* (beget).
By means of this, they cause the ninth day to be born from the morning pressing (*prātassavana*).
"Be exhilarated for Vāyu for the sake of sacrifice and for bounty; be exhilarated for Mitra and Varuṇa while being purified."
"Exhilarate the host of Maruts; exhilarate the gods; exhilarate Heaven and Earth, O divine Soma!
(RV 9.101.14). Thus it becomes dedicated to all the gods;
for this day belongs to the All-gods and is in the Jagatī metre.
These [verses] are Triṣṭubhs with the character of Jagatīs, made perfect by the form of the day. Wherever they make [the rite] perfect by means of the form of the day, there it prospers.
Success attends him who knows thus.
The hymn "This god, the immortal" serves as the *anurūpa*; for the hymn is indeed cattle, and the *chandomas* are cattle;
it is for the attainment of cattle.
Now, cattle are indeed abundance;
the hymn is abundance.
Thus, they make the cattle conformable to the cattle themselves.
In this case, they do not produce forms that correspond to what is perceived by direct observation.
Therefore, animals produce offspring of various forms: a white female gives birth to a black one, a black female to a white one, a red female to a speckled one, and a speckled female to a red one.

In these [verses], they have the same beginning but various endings: "This god is immortal," "This god is made wise," and "This god is full of praise. This indeed is the first step, this is the second, and that is the third.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who perform the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) fall away from this world, for they go as if to its very end.
Therefore, these [days] have the same beginning but different endings;
thus, they find firm support in this very world."
On the sixth day, there are verses beginning with different words but having identical endings;
by means of these, they find firm standing in yonder world.
It consists of ten verses; the *virāj* has ten syllables.
The *virāj* is food; [this is] for the attainment of the *virāj*, that is, of food.
It consists of eight verses. By this, he indeed invokes the forty-eightfold *stoma*.
Moreover, the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables, and cattle have eight hooves.
The Chandomas are cattle; [they serve] for the attainment of cattle.
Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra.
When he had slain Vṛtra, all beings followed after him from these worlds, saying: "This one is a hero."
This is the slaying of Vṛtra.
They thus placed heroic power (*vīrya*) into him in succession. Indeed, he who comes on this day becomes as one who has performed a heroic deed, as one who has slain Vṛtra.
Therefore, when they say "this one," they place that very vigor into him in due order.
Regarding this, they say: "The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period possesses the seasons, while the *chandomas* are seasonless. Indeed, these *chandomas* are established as if in a non-season."
In that these [stotras] consist of five verses and six verses, by that very means the Chandomas are made to possess the seasons. That [six-verse stotra] indeed becomes the unsurpassed one.
For when something is manifest, they call it "this" (eṣa), but when it is hidden from view, they call it "that" (sa).
Those who come on this day go as if into the unseen;
therefore, that by which they set out consists of six verses, the most excellent,
and by it they rise up.
The forty-eight-fold hymn-form (*stoma*) comes into being.
The *jagatī* meter indeed consists of forty-eight syllables;
the *jagatī* is cattle.
The Chandomas are cattle;
thus, they proceed while firmly established in cattle, that is, in the Jagatī metre.
"O Agni, we have come with great reverence to you, the youngest," they say; thus the *ājya* offerings contain the word "go.
For those who arrive on this day are, as it were, going.
“Who has shone forth, kindled in his own dwelling”—with this [verse], they cause him to shine.

“Of wondrous luster, between the two wide worlds”—these two indeed are the *rodasī* (heaven and earth), and this intermediate space is the Maruts. “Well-invoked, facing all directions”—for this three-day rite is performed facing in all directions.
"Overcoming all difficulties by his greatness"— thus they contain the word "all" (*viśva*),
for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
"Agni Jātavedas is to be praised in the house."
"May he protect us from misfortune and from blame, both us who praise him and our patrons.
With this, he indeed invokes a blessing.
"O Agni, you are Varuṇa and Mitra," thus there is a verse addressed to Agni and Varuṇa, for the purpose of warding off a poorly performed sacrifice.
Whatever in the sacrifice is ill-chanted, ill-recited, or defective, this [verse] indeed serves as a means for its restoration.
"The Vasiṣṭhas increase thee with their prayers"— for this day is indeed increased.
"May there be wealth for the sacrifice, easy to win; do you protect us always with blessings"—with this, he invokes a blessing.
"O Mitra and Varuṇa," thus there is the verse for Mitra and Varuṇa;
"May our powerful hymn go forth."
"Obeisance to the two of many births.
Thus it contains the word "people" (*jana*).
By this, they cause this ninth day to be produced.
"O gods, who maintain [the world] by means of *dhī*," he says for the sake of support;
for at this time they go as if toward an end, thinking, "Let us not overstep the *Chandomas* and pass beyond them.
"O you of good skill, whose father is Dakṣa..."
For the sake of the Asuras, with great majesty.
O Varuṇa, protectors of our dwellings and guardians of our bodies, and O Mitra, fulfill the prayers of us who sing your praises.
Thus, it is for the sake of success alone.
"‘I am Indra, who [possesses] power’—this is a verse addressed to Indra;
for this forty-eighth day is indeed great.
‘Like Parjanya, rich in rain’—"
"He has grown strong through the hymns of Vatsa. For this day is indeed increased.
"When the Kaṇvas made Indra the accomplisher of the sacrifice with their hymns"—this is for the sake of success.
"Protecting the offspring of the *ṛta*," thus [he says], containing the word "offspring.
By this, they generate the tenth day from the ninth day;
for the tenth day is indeed generated from the ninth day.
That which belongs to Indra and Agni on the second day is the Aindrāgna Bārhata;
for this day is indeed Bārhata. The *ājya* hymns are characterized by the *samaya* meters.
These two— the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha and the Chandomas— are indeed like two separate villages.
Just as two friends from different villages might live together in safety by intermarrying, so it is when the Ājya-stotras are shared between them.
Some perform [the rites] without fixed timing; therefore, they should indeed be performed with fixed timing. The Stoma consists of forty-eight parts.
The Jagatī meter, indeed, has forty-eight syllables.
The Jagatī is cattle;
the Chandomas are cattle.
Thus, they proceed while firmly established in cattle, that is, in the Jagatī.
"Of the purifying [Soma] who strikes down," this is a form of the Bṛhatī; "of the golden-hued steed," this is for the Jagatī.
"The purifying one, the best of charioteers, most bright among the bright, most praised."
Hariścandra is the host of Maruts.
Thus they are accompanied by the Maruts;
for the form of the midday [pressing] is indeed possessed of the Maruts.
They do not depart from the very form of the midday [pressing].
With the words, "O Pavamāna, pervade," they approach the form of the Vaiśvadeva;
for this day belongs to the Viśvedevas.
These verses contain the word "striking" (*ghnadvatī*).
The ninth day is the end.
Having thus reached the end, they strike away all evil with these [verses].
Regarding those [verses], the *gāyatra* has its *brāhmaṇa* already explained.
Now follows the *nidhana* called *gātuvit*.
With the words "May we find the way (*gātuṃ vindāmahai*)," they perform the sacrificial session (*satra*).
