They indeed find a path.
That [sāman] has an *upariṣṭobha* [chanting], a *bahirnidhana*, and belongs to the *bṛhatī* meter.
Therefore, it is performed on a day belonging to the *bṛhatī* meter.
Therefore, they call it "the non-shattering of Bharadvāja.
Indeed, in the battle of the ten kings against Prātardana, ten kings surrounded him on the human plane;
Bharadvāja was his domestic priest.
He ran toward him, saying, "O Seer, we run to you! Guide us here!
Bharadvāja then desired, "May we win this battle."
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
Having praised, he said: "Indra will surely come to our invocation."
"Or shall we be victorious in this battle?"
Now there was a beautiful woman from the Sāvedasa clan, the wife of Kṣatra Prātardana;
they killed her brother.
That [sacrificial vessel] became a churning-stick.
As she was running about, Indra set his mind upon her.
He put on a dried skin and went down after her.
In his house, a cake was hanging on the beam in one half of the room, while curd mixed with clarified butter was placed in the other half.
He resolved to dance near her;
he would lead her about and smear her with clarified butter.
Whenever he would drive her away, she would dance right near him.
Evening came, and they departed.
Her husband asked her: "Did you see anything there during the day?"
She said: "Indeed, nothing else happened then; rather, a *sthavira* (an old man) danced right in front of me today.
In his weaving, a ball of dough became stuck to one half [of the loom], while curds mixed with ghee were attached to the other half.
As for that which had become stuck, he thought: "This very *mathama* (a young man) must have danced right in front of me today."
He said, "Indra has indeed not come to our call;
we shall win this battle."
He indeed became Indra; you must not harm him. Having made him your ally, you should say: "Let us win the battle."
When the next day had come, they set out on their journey.
This one, however, resolved to dance even further away with his very same carrying-pole.
Whenever the other tried to catch up to him, he would always go even further away.
She reflected, "Come now, let me address him.
She spoke to him:
"O my son, what is this that has happened to you?"
Thus [it was said].
“O you who have assumed the form of a dwarf!
Thus spoke Indra.
"O son, may you fall away from the great, joyous, and powerful [state],"—
this is a comparison found in the *Sāvedasa*.
"If, O dear son, you should fall away, the father shall surely gather that back together."
Thus says Indra:
"Let poison be for you, O Mājaka; creep away like clouds," so says Upamā Sāvedasī.
"O dear son, though poison itself, your father struck down the deer with it.
Thus said Indra.
"The other [deer] ran away, following the favorable path."
Thus is this comparison known from the Veda:
"Even the axe, O son, truly yearns for its handle; even the father [longs for his son].
Thus says Indra.
"Dear is Mahira to me to behold; may he touch me with his hand"—this is a comparison known from the Veda. "O friend, you used to do so; you would stretch out your hand to him."
What has become? How has it become? O Mahira, beloved of the word, may he touch me with his hand;
Indra is desired.
"Thus it was; from that it came to be.
Just as your great favor (*mahiraḥ*) is dear, so may he touch [me] with his hand.
Thus said Indra.
"Thus it was, then it came to be; as your great favor, dear one, touched him with its hand—
such is that Vedic simile."
Having run after him, he said, "Let us win the battle!
He, seizing the horse by its halter, said:
"Just as that shining one flies away from this [earth],
so may the enemies fly away from the human ruler.
Thus he caused the hairs of the *eṇī* deer to be shaved off.
Those very horse-chariots stood up for him;
with them, indeed, he won that battle.
Bharadvāja said, "I did not release the *asṛk* in the conflict."
As for what Bharadvāja said, "I have indeed not flowed away in the *dāra*," that very thing is the *adārasṛt*; it is the state of being *adārasṛt*.
This is the *vijiti* (conquering) Sāman, which slays the rival. One conquers and slays the hateful rival; he causes the hateful rival to flow away in the *dāra*, but not himself.
He washes his wife.
Moreover, it is indeed with Indra.
Indra indeed came to their call by means of this; Indra comes to the call of him who knows thus.

Now, that [hymn] has the *nidhana* consisting of eight syllables; for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables. Cattle have eight hooves, and the Chandomas are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
Because Bharadvāja saw this, it is therefore called "the one that does not let the vessel leak" (adārasṛt) of Bharadvāja.
JB 3.249 |v1 Then [he taught] Saindhukṣita.
|v2 Sindhukṣit indeed perceived the end of speech.
They seek speech through the *chandomas*.
Now, at this stage, during the *chandomas*, speech is as if it has been attained;
they thus recover that very speech.
"Moreover, by means of the final *sāman*, may we attain the final heavenly world.
That [final *sāman*] consists of the *iḍā*;
for the *iḍā* is indeed cattle.
The Chandomas are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle. Now follows the Hariśrī-nidhana.
In the beginning, indeed, prosperity resided in Prajāpati.
Indra desired, "May this prosperity that resides in Prajāpati be mine.
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it.
By means of that, O Prajāpati, he took away the glory; hence it is called *hariśrī*. That is why the *hariśrī* finale is called the *hariśrī* finale. This, then, is the *Śrīsava* Sāman.
He who knows this attains prosperity.
The gods and the asuras were in conflict;
prosperity resided among both of them.
Indra desired, "May I seize the glory of the Asuras.
He saw this Sāman;
with it, namely the *hariśrī*, he seized the glory of the Asuras.
That, indeed, is why it is called the *hariśrīnidhana*. This very Sāman is prosperity itself.
He who knows this attains prosperity and appropriates the prosperity of his hateful rival.
That [sāman] has the *nidhana* consisting of three syllables; for these worlds are three, and it serves to sustain these worlds.
JB 3.250 |v1 Now follows the settling of the Aṅgirases.
|v2 The Aṅgirases indeed desired, "May we hold cattle in check."
They saw this Sāman;
they praised with it.
Thereupon, indeed, cattle gathered around them from all directions.
They said, "Truly, these *iḍās* have flowed together for us.
Now, the *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
therefore, there is a flowing together (*saṃkṣāra*) of the *iḍās*.
Now, there is the Bābhrava [Sāman], which has *gvām* as its *nidhana*, has *bahiḥ* as its *nidhana*, and belongs to the *bṛhatī* meter.
Therefore, it is performed on the day belonging to the *bṛhatī* meter.
Babhru Kumbhya indeed desired, "May I be propagated with cattle."
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it;
he took "gvābhiḥ" as its *nidhana*.
Thereupon, he was indeed impelled by cattle.
This is that Sāman pertaining to cattle.
One who knows thus secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Because Babhru Kumbhya saw [this], it is therefore called the Bābhrava.
Now follows the *ṛṣabha* (bull) *pavamāna*.
The *simā*s are indeed cattle; the *revatī*s are cattle; the *ṛṣabha* is cattle.
They thus introduce the bull among the cattle for the sake of pairing and procreation. He who knows this is propagated through pairing.
Moreover, by means of this very [rite], all their Chandomas are made to possess a bull.
JB 3.251 |v1 Now follows the Gauṣūkta, which has its *nidhana* outside and belongs to the Bṛhatī metre.
|v2 Therefore, it is performed on a day belonging to the Bṛhatī metre.
Gauṣūkti and Āśvasūkti were these two.
Having accepted many gifts, they felt as if they had swallowed poison.
They both desired: "May we expel this swallowed poison."
They both beheld these two *sāmans*;
they praised with them.
With one of them—"O Agni, thou art invoked"—he offered this world as a libation.

In this world, indeed, nothing whatsoever exceeds Agni. One [of the two fires], being offered as the *śukra*, has completely illumined that world beyond. And in that world, indeed, nothing whatsoever exceeds Āditya.
Then indeed those two expelled that poison they had swallowed.

Thereupon, their well-being became as that of a healthy child. Whoever might have swallowed poison, or having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten the food of one whose food should not be eaten—let him [be purified] by these two.
One should praise [it].
Verily, he destroys that swallowed poison;
whatever evil has been done by him, that he destroys.
These two, moreover, consist of five syllables each in their *nidhana*. The *paṅkti* consists of five feet; cattle are fivefold;
the *chandomas* are cattle. It is for the attainment of cattle.
As for the fact that Gauṣūkti and Aśvasūkti saw this [hymn], therefore it is called the Gauṣūkta and the Aśvasūkta.
"Pour out the pressed juice on every side"— these verses containing the word "around" (pari) occur; this is a form of the end,
for this day is indeed the final one.
"O Soma, who is the highest oblation"— for this which consists of the Chandomas is indeed made the highest oblation—
"he, the manly archer, within the waters, has pressed out the Soma with the stones."
"Surely, being purified by the waters, flow around us, O most fragrant one, unharmed!
Even when pressed, we exhilarate you with the soma-juice in the waters.
Thus they become possessed of *andhas*; for *andhas* is food, and it is for the attainment of food.
"Mixing [the soma] with cows, the highest..."— these verses concerning cattle and livestock serve for the acquisition of cattle,
for the Chandomas are indeed cattle. "The roaring, god-intoxicating, wise Indu, the power..."— this consists of four verses.
Cattle indeed have four feet;
the Chandomas are cattle, for the very sake of obtaining cattle. Upon these [days], the Pṛṣṭha [stotra] is performed.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* (the back), the gods became the *pṛṣṭha*. Thinking, "May we become the *pṛṣṭha*," they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*). Thus, they indeed become the *pṛṣṭha*.
The gods indeed desired, "May we become the *pṛṣṭha*.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
From that, they indeed became the back (pṛṣṭha).
This Agni is the back of this world; this Vāyu is the back of the intermediate space; yonder Āditya is the back of the sky.
They praise that as the *pṛṣṭha* (back/chapter) and establish it therein.
Indeed, the *pṛṣṭha* is prosperity (*śrī*), and the *pṛṣṭha* is the summit (*varṣman*). He who knows thus attains prosperity and becomes the summit.
That [verse] is the *ūrdhva-ṛk*; it is the form of the *bṛhat* [sāman], on the day belonging to the *bṛhat*.
By this, indeed, it is rich in form.
JB 3.253 |v1 Now, regarding Saṃkṛti:
|v2 By means of the three-night rite, the gods indeed ascended to the heavenly world.
It became detached from them and rolled away.
They raised it up with the Gāyatrapārśva; they joined it together with the Santanī;
they made it whole with the Saṃkṛti; they fixed it with the Triṣandhi; they adorned it with the Śrāyantīya; and they secured its safety with the Ariṣṭa.
They passed [the time]. By means of this three-night rite, the gods went to the heavenly world; by this very means they then departed.
That [rite] was their means of transition.
In that [sacrifice], these Sāmans are performed in the greatest number.
It is this very three-night rite that they heal;
by means of it, they perform a healing and an expiation.
By means of Saṃkṛti, the gods fashioned offspring, cattle, prosperity, and food.
That is the reason for Saṃkṛti’s name as Saṃkṛti.
He who knows this fashions offspring, cattle, prosperity, and food.
For him, these two *vṛkaṇa* [verses] become [the finale]; it is for the attainment of both kinds of speech, that which is domestic and that which is wild.
That [finale] consists of four *nidhanas*; cattle are indeed four-footed;
the *Chandomas* are cattle; it is for the acquisition of cattle.
JB 3.254 |v1 Now, [the sacrifice] of Kaunmalabarhiṣa:
|v2 By means of this, indeed, Kunmalabarhis caused both kinds of cattle to prosper— both those consisting of cows and those consisting of horses.
By this very [means], he wins them.
Kunmalabarhis desired, "May I obtain both kinds of cattle: those of the bovine species and those of the equine species.
He saw this sāman.
He praised him with this verse:
"Come indeed, O finder, for the sake of the singer; bestow wealth for our prosperity.
Pour forth, O Maghavan, for the quest of cattle; pour forth, O Indra, for the quest of horses."
In this very way, he obtained cattle and horses;
having sacrificed with those animals, he went indeed to the heavenly world.
This, then, is the *sāman* that is beneficial for cattle and leads to heaven.
He who knows this restrains cattle for himself and goes to the heavenly world.
Because he saw the *kunmala* grass as sacrificial straw (*barhis*), he is called Kaunmalabarhiṣa.
JB 3.255 |v1 Now follows the Devasthāna.
|v2 By means of this third three-day period, the gods indeed ascended upwards to the heavenly world.
That [Soma] of theirs, not being held fast, slipped away.
They saw this Sāman;
with it, they established him, saying: "He has stood here! He has stood there! Thus they made him stand firm.
They made it firm by means of this very [rite].
Because they established it by means of this, that is the reason for the name *devasthāna* (the station of the gods).
Therefore, when there is a *devasthāna* here, they thereby establish this very three-night rite; they establish this.
They made it firm.
Having prepared that [fire-altar], they went by means of it to the heavenly world.
Because they established themselves there in the heavenly world, that is precisely why the place of the gods is called "the place of the gods."
When they went to the heavenly world, he then guarded all this [world] for them;
such is its *nidhana*.
By means of this very *sāman*, one conquers a great, invincible victory.
Regarding this, there is this verse:

“The gods, dwelling together with the *vairūpa* [chant], attained that; yet it was also divided among them. Having uttered the *hiṃ* sound and having ascended again, they all shook off old age from their bodies.”
Thus it is said.
Having prepared this very three-day period consisting of the *chandomas*, and having ascended the *sāman* that is the abode of the gods,
they went to the heavenly world.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
“When, having struck down Vairūpa, they stood together on their journey, uttering the *hiṃ* sound, they created that station of the gods, the *sāman*; by means of it, the gods attained immortality.”
In this very way, they attained immortality.
Prajāpati created food.
Fearing its exhaustion, it fled in all directions.
He desired, "May I obtain food.
He saw this Sāman;
with it, he obtained food from all directions, [singing]: "Oṁ! It has stood firm here; oṁ! It has stood firm there. Thus, from all quarters, he secured food.
He enclosed [them].
He who should desire food should recite four times;
for there are four directions.
Verily, from all directions he wins food.
Now, if one should desire heaven, he should say it thrice; for these worlds are three, and it is for the attainment of these worlds.
Now, as for the *arka* flower: the *arka* is indeed food.
The wild flower is its blossom;
for it grows in the forest, and it serves to secure the food of the forest. The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerity.
They saw these two *sāmans*; they praised with them,
and thereby they indeed attained the heavenly world.
These two are the *sāmans* leading to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Just as, when it has rained, the two [banks of the river] become visible, even so by means of these two the heavenly world becomes visible.
These two [paths] lead to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Now follows [the hymn] for Dīrghaśravas. The [gift] of Dīrghaśravas is indeed food; it is for the attainment of food.
Dīrghatamas Māmateya, when setting out on a quest for gain, spoke to his younger brother Dīrghaśravas.
"Let this brother of ours be the overseer of our wives. Dīrghaśravas desired, "May I secure food for myself; may these wives of mine not suffer from hunger.
He saw this Sāman.
He praised Agni with this:
"He who distributes all wealth, the delightful Hotṛ of men—
may hymns go forth to that Agni, like the first vessels of honey."
Thus he spoke.
That Agni, being praised by him, made all this food consisting of honey for him.
His wives ate it just as if they were eating honey.
This very [Sāman] is indeed a great essence; this food is indeed great.
By means of this Sāman, one secures great food. And because Dīrghaśravas saw it, it is called the Dairghaśravasa.
JB 3.258 |v1 Now, as for glory: by means of glory, the gods indeed became glorious. |v2 By means of glory, they became glorious.
"They shall be glorious," they say, as they perform the sacrificial session;
they indeed become glorious. Now, glory is indeed prosperity (*śrī*).
He who knows this attains glory.
Furthermore, that *dhana* consists of thirty-seven syllables.
Indeed, the *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables.
The *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world;
yonder sun is the thirty-seventh.
In that very heavenly world they finally find firm support.
At the end, they pronounce this auspicious benediction for him: "May we attain full life, universal life, all-encompassing life.
It is by means of this very [formula] that they reach the conclusion of the verse in prosperity.
Now, as for the *śulka* (purchase-price):
by means of the *śulka*, the gods became the *śulka*.
Thinking, "May we become the *śulka*," they performed the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
They become the *śulka* itself.
Now, the *śulka* is indeed glory (*śrī*). He who knows thus attains glory.
Therefore, they call it "The Horse" (*āśva*).
The gods, desiring heaven, performed austerity. They beheld this *sāman*.
With it they praised. Then indeed they attained the heavenly world.
This, therefore, is the *sāman* that leads to heaven.
He who knows this attains the heavenly world.
Now, as for *bhargas*:
by means of *bhargas*, the gods indeed became *bhargas*.
They sit for the sacrificial session [with the formula], "We are *bhargas*.
They indeed become *bhargas*.
Now, *bhargas* is indeed glory (*śrī*).
He who knows thus attains prosperity.
Now follows the *abhiśava* [pressing] for the sake of having reins on both sides:
just as one might travel with a single rein, so is that which is one-sided; but it is like traveling with reins on both sides.
Thus, that which consists of both [the Dvādaśāha and the Mahāvrata].
By means of these two, the Dvādaśāha is grasped in its integrity. Through this Dvādaśāha, grasped in its integrity and free from harm, one crosses over evil and attains prosperity—he who knows thus.
[The text provided contains only punctuation and line breaks. Thus it was said.
Now follows the *arka* of Dīrghatamas; the *arka* is indeed food, [and it serves] for the attainment of food.
Dīrghatamas Māmateya, desiring food, performed austerity.
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it,
and thereby he indeed obtained food.
This is the *sāman* for the attainment of food. One who knows this secures food and becomes the best of his kinsmen as an eater of food.
Furthermore, because Dīrghatamas Māmateya saw it, it is called "The Hymn of Dīrghatamas" (*dīrghatamaso arkaḥ*).
"Pressed is Soma, the ruddy, the bull, the tawny one"—thus they become verses containing the word "bull," which is a form of the Bṛhatī.
This day belongs to the Bṛhatī.
"Like a king, the wondrous one has bellowed toward the cows."
Being purified, you shall pass through the sheep’s wool filter; like a hawk, you have settled in your nest rich with ghee.
Parjanya is the father of the great-winged bird; he has established his dwelling upon the mountains at the navel of the earth.

The waters, his sisters, have flowed toward the cows; they clothe themselves with the pressing-stones when the sacrifice is prepared. Thus, these verses concerning cattle and livestock serve for the attainment of cattle.
The Chandomas are indeed cattle.
"O Seer, you move around the greatness with wisdom; like a bathed steed, you rush toward the prize.
O Soma, ward off misfortunes and be gracious to us; clothed in clarity, you go around your mantle."
Thus they are recurrent, for this is the form of the end;
for this day is indeed the end.
In those [verses], the Sāmarāja [is chanted].
Sovereignty, indeed, is prosperity.
He who knows this attains glory and goes to sovereignty. Regarding this, they also say: "It is the *saṃvat*.
By means of the downward slope (*pravat*), the gods went to the heavenly world; by means of the upward slope (*udvat*), they descended.
They attain [the goal] by means of the downward slope.

Now, because these *sāmans* exist, they proceed toward the heavenly world by means of the downward slope and ascend by means of the upward slope. They attain [the goal] by means of the downward slope.
Now, these have *vāc* as their *nidhana*.
They seek to obtain the meters through speech;
for at this time, speech is as if it has been fully attained.
In the *chandome* chants, in that these have their *nidhana* in speech (*vāṅnidhana*), they thereby approach that very Speech directly.
JB 3.261 |v1 Now, as for the Bṛhat:
|v2 The Bṛhat is indeed the summit.
Verily, they proceed while finding firm support in the very height.
That occurs on a day of the Jagatī metre; for the Bṛhatī is the form of the male, and the Jagatī is that of the female.
In that the Bṛhat is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra on this day, by that very means a pairing is brought about for this day.
Then there is the Vāmadevya;
the Vāmadevya, indeed, is cattle.
Those who have praised with this [hymn] become truly possessed of cattle.
"Like branches reaching toward the sun, all enjoy Indra's bounty"— thus they contain the word *viśva* (all),
for this day belongs to the Viśve Devas.
"Riches for the generations born for the sake of power"—thus they contain the word "born. Now, containing the word "born" is the form of the Jagatī;
this day is of the nature of the Jagatī.
We meditate upon [thee] as if upon our own allotted share.
Praise the one who bestows wealth, the giver of bounty; auspicious indeed are the gifts of Indra—he who, when his desire is fulfilled, does not grow angry, but impels the mind toward giving.
With this [verse], he invokes a blessing.
JB 3.262 |v1 In these [verses], the Śrāyantīya [sāman is chanted].
|v2 The gods, indeed, when they were about to enter upon a sacrificial session (sattra), said: "Whatever is cruel in our own selves, let us cast it out."
"May no cruel thing come near us.
Therefore, having fashioned out of themselves whatever was cruel within them, they wiped it away and deposited it in two shallow bowls.
Then they entered upon the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Then this wicked god was born. Because he was born from two bowls (*śarāva*), that is his name.
Indeed, it was this very Agni who was thus born.
He who knows this is not harmed by it.
He said to the gods, "For what purpose has he produced me?
They replied, "For the sake of being a witness; you shall slay whoever transgresses."
Prajāpati set his mind upon his own daughter Uṣas.
Having become a red deer, she stood before him;
having become a spotted deer, he leaped upon her.
He reflected: "The gods have indeed created me for this man, so that I may be his overseer. He is surely stepping over me; come now, let me pierce him.
He pierced him.
Pierced by that, he cast off this form and ascended upwards.
This very arrow consists of three joints;
therefore, the spotted antelope is the most delicious of animals.
Therefore, he was as if burning with grief.
When he was pierced, his seed fell away;
it settled upon the Himavat mountain.

That became human. Then the gods and the seers, having approached it, said, "This is difficult to eat. Because they said, "This is difficult to eat" (*medaṃ duṣada*), that is the origin of the name *māduṣa*.
This, indeed, is called "the human" (māduṣa). It is designated as "human" (mānuṣa).
They kindled it all around with fire.
The Maruts blew [the breath] into it; they seasoned it with the Śrāyantīya [sāman].
That is why the Śrāyantīya has its name "Śrāyantīya."
Then the animals were created.
Those that were created first were the red ones; those that were created from [the fire] while it was being heated were the ruddy ones.
Those that were emitted from [the fire] when it was heated became the brown ones;
those that were emitted from [the fire] while it was burning became both white and black.
Therefore, this very fire burns both the white and the black.
From the sparks, goats and lambs were produced; from the embers, the Aṅgirasas were born.
From the ashes mixed with charcoal, three barren cows were produced: one for Mitra and Varuṇa, one for Bṛhaspati, and one for the Viśvedevas.
From the very ashes the donkey was created;
therefore it is the counterpart of the ashes.
Therefore, when it is carried along, it lives.
This is that *sāman* which produces heroes and is beneficial to cattle. Indeed, it was from this that the Aṅgirases were born as heroes;
it was from this that these very cattle were created.
A hero is born to him; he secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle—he who knows thus.
If there should be one who has failed in the sacrifice, they should perform the Śrāyantīya as the Brahmasāman over his *pṛṣṭha* chants.
For both the *pṛṣṭhas* and the hymns shake off that man who has failed in the sacrifice.
And they establish him upon the backs [of the horses] and in those very hymns (*stotra*s):
“O Indra, from whatever we fear, from that grant us freedom from fear. O Maghavan, be gracious; may you be for our protection. Drive away the haters, drive away the adversaries.”
Thus, by this, they strike away the Mṛdhas, that is, evil itself. Regarding those [verses], the Brāhmaṇa has already been stated in its entirety. That is the Aiḍa Acchāvāka-sāman.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
verily, they thus find firm support in cattle.
"O Soma, you are the upholder," he says for the sake of stability;
for at this time they go as if to the end, thinking, "Let us not overstep the *Chandomas* by going beyond them."

"Thou, when pressed, art most intoxicating"—thus they contain the word *mada* (intoxication), for *mada* is indeed the essence (*rasa*). This third pressing is, as it were, cooked food; therefore, in that these verses contain the word *mada*, they thereby place essence into it.
Verily, they cause this [Soma] to swell by means of this [verse]. "O thou pressed out by the stones," he says; the word "thou" (tvam) is a form of the Bṛhatī.
This day belongs to the Bṛhatī.
"Flow toward us, bellowing,
with brilliant and most excellent vigor"—
for this is indeed the final three-day period that consists of the *Chandomas*.
They have the same opening verses but different concluding verses. "This is indeed the first step, this the second, and that the third.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who perform the twelve-day sacrifice fall away from this world, as it were; for [the twelve days] are like an end."
They go.
In that these [verses] have the same beginning but different endings, they establish themselves in this very world.
On the sixth day, there are verses beginning with different words but having the same endings.
By means of these, they find firm support in yonder world.
Among them is a *gāyatra* verse whose Brāhmaṇa explanation has already been stated.
Now follows the *aidāvasu* finale, the *bahirnidhana*, which belongs to the *bṛhatī* metre.
Therefore, it is performed on the day belonging to the *bṛhatī*.
There was once a seer named Asura who was without cattle.
He desired, "May I indeed secure cattle.
He saw this *sāman*;
he praised with it.
He approached the *nidhana* with the words, "This is wealth (*vasu*). That is why the *nidhana* called *aidāvasu* has its name. Now, cattle are indeed wealth.
Then indeed he won cattle.
This is that Sāman which pertains to cattle.
He who knows thus wins cattle; he becomes possessed of many cattle.
And that [sāman] has a *nidhana* consisting of four syllables; for cattle are four-footed, and the *Chandomas* are cattle; it is for the very attainment of cattle.
JB 3.266 |v1 Now, regarding the *kāśīta*: |v2 The *saubhara* chant, known as the *kaśīta*, was seized by consumption during a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
He desired, "May the waters drive away disease.
He beheld this Sāman;
he praised with it.
May the Wind breathe forth healing for us—beneficent and gladdening to our heart;
may he prolong our lives.
O Vāta, that store of immortality which is placed within your house yonder— from that, give us [a portion] so that we may live.
"O Vāta, you are our father, and you are our brother, and you are our friend; as such, grant us life.
Thus, Vāta himself provided healing for him.
This is the remedy; they perform this expiation. Moreover, it is a fulfiller of desires; for he indeed desired that very desire, and that desire was fulfilled for him.
Whatever desire one has while praising with this *sāman*, that desire is fulfilled for him.
They approach its *iḍā* from the west, thinking, "Lest we overstep the meters by going away from them. The *iḍā*, indeed, is cattle.
The Chandomas are cattle; [they serve] for the attainment of cattle.
And because Kaśīta Saubhara saw this, it is therefore called "Kāśīta.
Now follows the Aśvasūkta, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
That [hymn] has the *pañcākṣara-nidhana*; for the *paṅkti* consists of five feet. Cattle are fivefold;
the *chandomas* are cattle. It is for the attainment of cattle.
Now follows the Śāmmada, for which the Brāhmaṇa has been stated.

Now follows the Hāviṣkṛta, for which the Brāhmaṇa has been stated; it is an etymological explanation of *havis*. It possesses a *nidhana* consisting of four syllables, for cattle indeed consist of four feet.
The Chandomas are cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
"For you indeed, O friend, among the divine..."—thus it contains the word "you" (tvam), which is a form of the Bṛhatī meter.
This day belongs to the Bṛhatī.
"O Pavamāna, most radiant among births," so they say; thus they become verses containing the word "birth.
For the form of the Jagatī is indeed characterized by birth, and this day belongs to the Jagatī.
Regarding those [verses], there is the *Sauparṇa* section as explained in the Brāhmaṇa. With the words, "Flow for the feast of the gods," it becomes dedicated to all the deities;
for this day belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*) and is composed in the *Jagatī* meter.
"O drops, moving in the water, you have strengthened Indra for exhilaration"—for this day is indeed increased [in length].
"Hither, O pressed drops"—these [verses] are directed hitherward so that there may be no over-stepping.
In these [verses], the Vaiśvamanasa [Sāman].
Viśvamanas, having been kindled, entered the forest, where a bear found him.
He desired, "May I slay Atri.
He saw this *sāman*;
he sang it.
Indra saw him [Viśvamanas] and thought, "The bear has found him.
He rushed toward him;
as he was rushing, [the bear] was blown away by his breath.
Viśvamanas asked him: "What is that which is beyond this?
He replied: "Call it a *sūrmī*, O Maghavan.
"A *sūrmī*, O Maghavan," he said.
"Strike him with a staff on his limbs," he said. "Cut a blade of grass and strike him gently with it.
Having cut that blade of grass, he struck him gently with it.
Indra poured that very [Soma] as the thunderbolt;
he struck him right there with it.
That, indeed, is the *sāman* which slays the rival and slays the *rakṣas*.
He who knows this slays his hateful rival, drives away the *rakṣas*, and destroys evil.
Because Viśvamanas saw it, it is called the Vaiśvamanasa.
"O Lord, praise that beloved bay horse"— these are the *parivṛt* verses; they possess the form of the end,
for this day is indeed the end.
They purify the tawny one with the strainer;
he who encompasses all the gods—
thus they become possessed of all.

For this day belongs to the Viśve Devāḥ. "She goes with exhilaration," they say; therefore, the verses contain the word *mada* (exhilaration). Thus, they place the essence and the exhilaration at the third pressing in its proper sequence.
"Whom the five sisters, with their own glory, have twice bathed— the one pressed by the stones,
Indra’s beloved and desirable— his waves drench him. With this [verse],
he indeed invokes a blessing.
"O Soma, you are poured out for Vṛtra-slaying Indra to drink"— these are the Vṛtra-slaying verses at the end,
for the sake of victory. Regarding them, there is the Gaurīvīta hymn, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
Now follows the Nihava.
Indra, loathing the third pressing, departed;
for it was, as it were, stale.
With this *sāman*, all the gods called out after him, saying, "Come here! Come here!
Then Indra returned to the third pressing;
from that time on, he did not depart from it.
This is the *sāman* belonging to Indra.
His sacrifice becomes possessed of Indra and possessed of the gods;
Indra turns toward his sacrifice.
Indra does not depart from the sacrifice of one who knows this.
This, indeed, they call "Vasiṣṭha’s Summoning.
Vasiṣṭha, having been defeated and his sons slain, desired: "May I summon offspring and cattle."
He saw this Sāman;
he praised with it.
With it, by saying "Ayihī! Ayihī!", he summoned forth offspring and cattle.
That, indeed, is the nature of the *nihava* (invocation).
He who knows thus invokes offspring and cattle.
Furthermore, it is struck by the *stobha* (chanted interjections).
From what is not pierced, offspring and cattle are born;
the Chandomas are cattle;
thus, it is indeed rich in form.
Because Vasiṣṭha saw this, it is therefore called the "Invitation of Vasiṣṭha."
JB 3.269 |v1 Now, as for the Vāhiṣṭhīya [sāman]: Agni indeed carried the oblation for the gods from the ninth day across to the tenth day. |v2 [He did so] in order to carry it beyond.
He did not desire [it]. Those gods desired: "May Agni carry this oblation for us. They saw this *sāman*.
With this they praised him:
"Sing forth a great song to Agni, O Vibhāvasu, that which is most effective.
Like a mighty queen, from you wealth and from you spoils of war arise."
Your radiant rays resound loudly like the pressing-stones; and your roar has gone forth by itself from heaven like thunder.
Thus we have paid homage to Agni, the powerful one, seeking wealth;
may he, the wise one, carry us across all hostilities as if with a boat.
Thus.
Just as one might cross over by means of a boat, even so did this Agni carry their oblation across from the ninth day to the tenth day.
Indeed, it is he who is capable of carrying this across.

In this regard, that which is the *yadvāhiṣṭhīya* [sāman] serves for the continuity of the sacrifice. For him who knows thus, the sacrifice is performed successfully, and Agni carries his oblation across. That [sāman] is the *ūrdhveḍam*, the form of the *bṛhat*; it belongs to the day of the *bṛhat*.
By that, it is indeed endowed with beauty.
JB 3.270 |v1 Then [came] the black [bird].
|v2 The seers said, "Let us desire to win this highest heavenly world by means of this [bird], since these [birds] are in it."
"Regarding the *Atharvans*:
Preṇi Saubhāhita, Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra, Asita Daivala,
and whoever else performs the consecration (*dīkṣā*) in his presence— for those sacrificers, indeed, they did not hear much for a long time."
For years they remained there.
And indeed, they heard [the sounds]: "He calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*," or "He utters the *vaṣaṭ*.
Then Udvaṃta by name, one of the Atharvans, descended with a *camasa* cup in his hand.
He said to them, "What is your desire? They replied, "We wish to conquer this heavenly world above, the Śyena, in which these Atharvans dwell.
He said to them, "Then [come] behind the village."
"Indeed, these... "For what desire? "The path."
"Om," he said, "is that not indeed conducive to heaven?
Then he looked into the cup.
He said, "Eat me as meat!"
"We eat," they said.
"For what desire?
"For the sake of sight and the vital breaths."
"Om," he said, "that is certainly not conducive to heaven for you.
Then he looked at the cup itself and said,
"Go away, woman!"
"We approach," they say.
"For what desire?
"For the sake of progeny, for continuity, and so that there may be no interruption."
"Om," he said, "but that is certainly not conducive to heaven for you.
Then he spoke only of the cup.
He said, "You have spoken falsely!"
"We speak thus," they say.
"For what desire?
"Out of a desire for women, or a desire for amusement, or a desire for companionship."
"Om," he said.
"Arise! Speak of your desires! There is certainly no hope for you that you shall win that world.
Now, Preṇi Saumāhita was indeed wicked.
He said, "One chooses from among seven goats that are difficult to impregnate;
whichever one I shall name, let that one desire him.
Then Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra said, "I choose the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa."
Then Āsita Daivala said, "I shall look into this very cup.
He said, "This one alone among them observes the vow.
Having looked into it, he saw this Sāman.
He praised him with this:
“O Agni, we kindle thee for great wealth, for the sake of giving. For thou art to be magnified as a bull for the great sacrifice by Heaven and Earth.”
Thus [he spoke].
Heaven and earth—these are all these worlds.
Thereupon, he indeed moved along after all these worlds.
In the forenoon he was present at the assembly of the gods; at midday, at that of men, at Drupada Vārddhraviṣṇa’s; and in the afternoon, at that of the ancestors.
This is the Sāman that leads to heaven.
He who knows this wanders through all these worlds and attains the heavenly world.
Furthermore, because Asita Daivala saw it, it is therefore called "Āsita."
JB 3.272 |v1 Now, the *sādhra* is for the sake of success alone.
|v2 That [sādhra] has its *nidhana* in the middle; it serves for stability.
Those who undertake the Ārbhava Pavamāna launch themselves upon the ocean as their support.
That it has its *nidhana* in the middle is for the sake of stability.
The gods indeed desired, "May everything we do be successful."
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Thereupon, for them, every deed that was done succeeded.
"Let whatever we have done succeed," they say, and so they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Indeed, for them, whatever they do succeeds.
And because whatever they did with this *sāman* succeeded, it is therefore called *sādhra*.
Sadhri Vairūpa, desiring cattle, performed austerities.
He beheld this [sāman] and praised with it.
He approached this *iḍā*.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
from it, he indeed obtained cattle.
This is a Sāman pertaining to cattle.
He who knows this secures cattle for himself and becomes possessed of many cattle.
Furthermore, because Sadhri Vairūpa saw it, it is therefore called the Sādhra.
JB 3.273 |v1 Now, as for Akūpāra: Akūpāra Kaśyapa, together with the Kali ages, entered the ocean. |v2 [End of section]
He desired a firm foundation in it.
He saw this Sāman;
with it, he praised.
Then indeed he found a firm foundation in this very earth, the ocean.
Then, indeed, his descendants used to sit upon its back.
This is the *pratiṣṭhāsāman*.
He who knows thus finds firm support.
The Chandomas are indeed the ocean.
Kaśyapa is indeed able to cross over the ocean.
In that regard, what here is "ākūpāra" serves for crossing to the further shore of the ocean itself. Or rather, because Kaśyapa Ākūpāra saw it, it is therefore called "ākūpāra.
Then these become two-footed verses, as explained in the Brāhmaṇa.
These [verses] are: "Flow on, O Soma, for great skill" (RV 9.86.3).
For this forty-eighth day is indeed great.
Regarding these [verses], there is the Brāhmaṇa passage concerning the Vidharma.
That [sāman] has a *nidhana* consisting of four syllables; for cattle are four-footed, and the *Chandomas* are cattle;
it is for the attainment of cattle.
"O, the well-born, the swift one" (*upo ṣu jātam apturam*)—thus they consist of words denoting birth.
The form of the Jagatī meter indeed consists of people;
this day belongs to the Jagatī.
"Adorned with cattle, [the chariot] that brings destruction..."
The gods have come to Indu.
Flow for us, O Soma, for the welfare of our cattle; milk out swelling nourishment;
increase the ocean that is worthy of praise.
Thus there are verses concerning cattle and livestock, for the very purpose of securing cattle.
For the Chandomas are cattle.
"May our songs increase this Truth"—for this day, the forty-eight-fold one, is indeed increased.
JB 3.274 |v1 Regarding those [verses], there is the *śrudhīya*.
|v2 Prajāpati created the sacrifice.
He gave it to the gods.
Fearing destruction, it fled.
Those gods desired, "May we hear [it]."
They saw this *sāman*;
with it they called out to him, saying, "O Śrotṛ!
He heard them.
They said to him, "Turn back toward us!
He replied, "I am indeed afraid of destruction.
They said, "No."
"Have faith in me for that very reason," he said.
They placed their faith in him with the words, "O learned one!
They called out to him with the words, "Come here!"
Then indeed the sacrifice did not depart from them;
it returned right back to them. At this time, on the ninth day, the sacrifice is as if it has stumbled.

Whatever in this [chant] is characterized by the word *śrudhīya*, with that they truly summon the sacrifice for him. Therefore, one should use *śrudhīya* in the first [verse], and *śrudhema* in the two following ones.
Moreover, for whomever one desires life, one should summon him with this very [formula].
JB 3.275 |v1 Now follows the Yajñāyajñīya, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.
|v2 Now follows the Daivānīka.
The gods and the Asuras contended. Those gods desired, "May we conquer the Asuras by means of Agni as our vanguard. They saw this Sāman.
With this they praised him:
"May Agni, when invoked, be auspicious to us"—with these words he made Agni the vanguard.
"Auspicious is the gift, O fortunate one; auspicious is the sacrifice."
And may there be auspicious praises.

"Make your mind auspicious for the conquest of Vṛtra, by which you may be victorious in battles. Thus, they indeed overcame them in battles. "Stretch out many firm [bows] against those who are arrogant"—by this, whatever heroism and strength they possessed was [taken away].
With this [hymn] they struck them down;
with "O Vanaspati, may these [helps] be for thee," they overpowered them. Then indeed, by means of Agni as their vanguard, they conquered the Asuras.
That indeed is the "divine army" nature of the divine army.
This is the *sāman* called *Vijiti*, the slayer of rivals. He who knows this conquers and slays his hateful rival.
JB 3.276 |v1 Now, concerning Idhmavāha: |v2 When the seers were going to the heavenly world, they left Idhmavāha behind in the forest as he was alone, carrying the kindling wood.
They abandoned him. He desired: "May I fly up to the heavenly world; may I come together with those performing the sacrificial session.
He reflected: "Come now, let me praise those very ones who are performing the sacrificial session."
"Once they have been praised by me, they will act in such a way that I shall listen to them.
He saw this triplet of verses;
with it, he praised them.
O! Those who kindle Agni and spread the sacrificial grass in due order—those whose youthful Indra is their friend.
Great indeed is their fuel, abundant their praise, and wide their sacrificial post—
those whose friend is the youthful Indra.
Without a fight, the hero leads the one besieged by battle with his warriors—
those whose youthful friend is Indra.
Thus [it is said].
When they had been praised, they did for him exactly as he had overheard them doing.
He overheard the sound of their whips as they spoke;
then he saw this *sāman*.
He praised him with this hymn.
"Right here we hear the cracking of their whips in their hands as they urge on the dappled mare during their journeys."

"O you who are adorned with various [ornaments], come! O you who are bright, come! O you who are radiant, come! O you who are brilliant, come!"—with these words they invoked him in the heavenly world.
Then indeed he came together with his rivals.
Having praised with this very *sāman*, he ascended to the heavenly world: "O, those who kindle Agni, who spread the sacrificial grass in due order—
those for whom Indra, the youth, the friend, and the companion, are here a source of protection."
Thus he ascended after the world of heaven;
this is that Sāman which leads to heaven. He who knows this attains the world of heaven.
Because Idhmavāha saw it, it is therefore called the *Aidhmavāha*. Now follows the *Traikakubha*, whose Brāhmaṇa has been explained; it is a Sāman for three sense-organs.
The Ṛc is addressed to Indra, the Sāman is addressed to Indra, and "Indra" is the *nidhana*.
A man has three powers: himself, his offspring, and his cattle.
By this [rite], he secures these very things for himself.
"The singers sing thee; the chanters chant the hymn."
"The Brahmins have raised you up, O Śatakratu, like a pole.
In this regard, that which contains "hundred" and "thousand" is the form of the Chandomas;
for the Chandomas are indeed cattle.
In these [verses], the Vaṃśīya is recited; its Brāhmaṇa has already been stated.
They perform the *pratihāra* before its *nidhana*.
The sacrificer is indeed supported by the *prastāva* and the *pratihāra*.
At this point, they seem as if they have passed away.
Therefore, when they perform the *pratihāra* before the *nidhana*, it is precisely so that there may be no overstepping.
That [day] is the *svāra* chant. It chants the *svara* on the tenth day. This [day] is indeed the *svāra*.
On the next day, they begin with the *svara* chant.
Just as one might pass from level to level, or as one might join breath to breath, such is that [transition].
On the preceding days, they employ speech;
if they were to rise without having brought that [speech] to completion, they would rise with what is unsuccessful.
They thus bring that very thing to completion.
Day by day, indeed, those who sacrifice and those who sit for a sacrificial session (sattra) are bound in the noose of Varuṇa.
In that they proceed while stepping back, they go forth loosening the nooses of Varuṇa by means of the *stotriya* verses.
Or they go forth depositing seed from here; with the *anurūpa* verses they take their stand there, and they bring that forth.
He who knows thus is propagated with offspring and cattle.
By the opening day (*prāyaṇīya*) the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) is yoked, and by the tenth day it is unyoked.
With the very same thong with which they yoke the horse and the mule, with that very same one they unyoke it again.
Thus, those nine stotriya verses which were previously [recited] are now [performed] above.
They throw up the yoke-pins.

Therefore, just as the sacrificial animal is bound, so too is it released. Consequently, the security of what has been acquired (yogakṣema) is established for those who interrupt the triple verses of the Prāyaṇīya day.
"Where do they extend? they ask.
"On the tenth day," he should say.

They connect the single verses on both sides with triplets, for the sake of the continuity and non-interruption of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Indeed, these [classes] meditate upon one another’s world: the *brahman* meditates upon the *kṣatra*, the *kṣatra* upon the *viś*, and the *viś* upon the *brahman*.
Desiring one another's world, they cause desire to be fulfilled.
Whatever desire one has when he brings them, that desire is fulfilled for him. Indeed, the first three-day period consists of *prasṛta* meters.
By that, it is made fresh;
they transpose the meters of the second [day];
by that, the second three-day period is made fresh.
They distribute the meters of the third [day] around;
by that very means, the three-day period of the third [day] is rendered free from exhaustion.
The first three-day period has the Gāyatra as its beginning;
therefore, this Agni shines upright.
The second three-day period has the Gāyatra at its middle;
therefore this wind blows crosswise.
The third three-day period has the Gāyatra at its end.
Therefore, this sun shines hitherward. The gods and the Asuras contended.
They said, "Whosoever among us sings the Gāyatra without taking breath three times, he shall conquer these worlds for us."
And [he won] the out-breath, the in-breath, and the diffused breath. That Ayāsya Āṅgirasa sang the Gāyatra chant three times without taking a breath;
by means of it, he won these worlds, as well as the out-breath, the in-breath, and the diffused breath.
He who, knowing this, sings the Gāyatra chant three times without taking breath, conquers these worlds as well as the out-breath (prāṇa), the in-breath (apāna), and the diffused breath (vyāna).
He who knows the ten-day rite as being fashioned by the Agniṣṭoma finds success for himself through the morning pressing alone.
The first three-day period is established by the midday pressing; the second by the third pressing;
the tenth day is established by the Agniṣṭoma-sāman alone.
He who knows thus is successful.
JB 3.282 |v1 Now, these Āprī-lauds consist of clarified butter offerings.
|v2 Prajāpati created living beings.
Having created [the world], he thought himself emptied.
He saw these *āprī* verses and *ājya* offerings;
with them, he gratified himself for the sake of freedom from exhaustion.
Verily, those who come to this day seem to be emptied out.
Therefore, in that these *āprī* libations of clarified butter occur, the sacrificers gratify their own selves with them, so that there may be no loss of vigor.
The *ājya* verses are unexpressed (anirukta), for the invulnerability of the meters and for the proclamation of the distinction between the good and the evil.
He who knows thus is separated from evil.
He pronounces the final verse as addressed to Indra and Agni, for the non-destruction of the meters and for the illumination of the sacrifice.
By means of this very *anukhyāta* sacrifice, they attain the heavenly world.
Regarding this, they say: "Since they condense the tenth day from all the days, by what means then are their *chandomas* not omitted?"
"One should say, 'By the Stoma.
The seventh day is the twenty-fourfold; the tenth day is the twenty-fourfold.
Moreover, because this single Ājya-stotra is common to both, it is for that reason so."
"Oṃ! *uccā te jātam andhasaḥ*. On the day of rising, the *udvatī* verses are employed; this is for the purpose of ascending to the heavenly world.
For this tenth day is indeed the heavenly world.
With the words, "O Indra, for the one worthy of sacrifice, for Varuṇa, for the Maruts," there are verses addressed to the Maruts;
for the form of the midday pressing is indeed "possessed of the Maruts" (*marutvat*).
They do not depart from the very form of midday.
"Desiring to win all the glories of men, O Noble One, we strive for them through these [songs]."
Thus, they contain the word *siṣāsant-* (desiring to win).
For it is indeed desiring to win that they go to the heavenly world by means of this day.
Regarding these [verses], there is the *gāyatra* hymn, whose *brāhmaṇa* has already been stated.
Now follows the Āmahīyava.
The Āmahīyava belongs to Prajāpati;
this day belongs to Prajāpati.

In that the Amahīyava is performed here on the day belonging to Prajāpati, they thus cause the day itself to prosper by means of its own form. Through that prosperity, there is success for them within their own community.
Furthermore, the Ājīka is for the sake of victory.
The gods and the Asuras went to the sacrificial contest. Those gods desired, "May we win this contest. They saw this Sāman.
With it they praised.
Then indeed they won that race. Those who come on this day go as if toward a race.
Thus, whatever *ājīka* occurs here is for the sake of victory;
he who knows this conquers.
Now, that which is called *ājīka* is the *prājāpatya* sāman, which is complete in the form of the day, just as the *kava* [is].
Wherever they prosper through food and form, there he prospers;
he prospers for whomsoever knows thus.
JB 3.284 |v1 Now, [the rite] called the *abhīka*.
|v2 The gods, indeed, desired: "May the waters touch our heads in a way that is close (*abhīkam*)."
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Then, indeed, auspicious waters touched them closely.
That is the "abhīka-nature" of the Abhīka.
Indeed, auspicious waters touch him who knows this as "abhīka.
The seers, while performing austerity, were distressed.
They desired, "May we touch auspicious waters immediately.
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it.
Then, indeed, it rained upon them in the encounter. That is why the encounter (*abhīka*) is called an "encounter. Now, water is indeed peace (*śānti*).

Those who come on this day become as if burning, as if glowing. Therefore, that which occurs here in close proximity (*abhīkam*) is for the sake of driving away impurity (*śuc*). Now, that which is called *abhīkam* is the *kavat* Prājāpatya Sāman; it is perfect through the form of the day.
Wherever they prosper through food and form, there he prospers;
he prospers for whomsoever knows thus.
JB 3.285 |v1 Now these [verses], “The ancient, primordial, praiseworthy nectar” (RV 8.76.1), are *satobṛhatī*s.
|v2 Anuṣṭubh indeed created the sacrifice.
The Anuṣṭubh is indeed speech;
the Anuṣṭubh is Prajāpati as its meter.
Having created the sacrifice, he said, "O sons, you must establish yourselves within the meters."
They found them by means of these two. Because it has three feet, it is the Gāyatrī;
by means of those two, they found the Uṣṇih and the Kakubh.
Because it has twelve syllables per foot, it is the *jagatī*. For that very reason, it is also the *anuṣṭubh*.
By means of its syllables alone, she found the *bṛhatī*.
In that it contains the word "milking" (*dohavatī*), it is the *paṅkti* meter;
in its abode (*āyatana*), it is the *triṣṭubh*;
and in that it contains the word "all" (*viśvavatī*), it is all the meters.
They found them by means of this very [verse]. He who knows thus finds them.
This [verse] is indeed the gathered essence and splendor of all the meters.
In the essence and splendor of all these meters, in the unconquered meter, they find firm support at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
JB 3.286 |v1 The *ṛta* verses are ancient (*pratnavatī*). |v2 Prajāpati is indeed the ancient one.
Verily, they find support in Prajāpati;
moreover, the ancient world is indeed the heavenly world,
and so they find support in that very heavenly world.
All of these have an equal number of syllables in their feet. In that they have an equal number of syllables in their feet, that is the reason for the *satobṛhatī* verses being called *satobṛhatī*.
Indeed, he who knows this becomes great in every respect.
Regarding this, Yāmana Śrātalāyana said: "When they arrive at this day, they become confused;
therefore, they perform other *bṛhatī*s.
However, the *bṛhatī* should be performed with [the verse]: ‘O Soma, being purified, flow forth in a stream.’"
This indeed is the known *bṛhatī*.
For when many people go along having made a known person their guide, they all indeed become known.
Therefore, because the verse "O Soma, being purified, flow on" is a *bṛhatī*, by that very means this day is made known.
However, many forms are mistaken;
indeed, the other forms are even more numerous.
Regarding this they say: "One who desires to become [prosperous] should not chant with the *bhūtabṛhatī* verses;
one who has already become so should chant with them, not one who desires to become so."
"Verily, those [verses] whose feet consist of twelve syllables are like beings that have already come into existence.

But these [other verses], which are intended to become Bṛhatīs, become Bṛhatīs again by means of re-employment. Therefore, one who has already come into existence should praise with the Bhūtabṛhatīs, but not one who desires to come into existence."
Regarding this, they say: "As many times as one sacrifices, so long does one desire to prosper; so long does one desire, thinking, 'May I become better, may I become better.
Therefore, both kinds [of bricks] must be made, for the attainment of both these desires."
The *utsedha* and *niṣedha* should indeed occur within the *satobṛhatī*s, while the *yajñāyajñīya* should occur in a future *bṛhatī*.
In this way, the repetitions proceed in a non-regressive direction.
Regarding this, they say: "The Mādhyandina Pavamāna is not for a fourth metre;
yet that metre which occupies its place is made as if it were the fourth. In that the other [verse] is a Bṛhatī and the other is a Bṛhatī, by that they become of the same metre.
In them, there are both elevations and depressions.
By means of the elevation, the Aṅgirases, having raised up the cattle, and by means of the depression, having driven them down, they rose up.
In the same way, by means of the elevation, they raise up the cattle, and by means of the depression, having driven them down, they rise up.
Between those two, the *yajñāyajñīya* occurs;
the *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed cattle.
Having raised up and set down these very animals, they rise.
These two are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath of Prajāpati.
In that there is raising up and setting down, they prosper through the out-breath and the in-breath itself.
These two *sāmans* are indeed the means for the displacement of one who is in a state of moral inferiority.
This tenth day of the ten-day period is like a royal assembly;
for in an assembly, they drive away and suppress one who speaks excessively as a wicked person.
In that there are both the rising (utsedha) and the sinking (niṣedha), it is for the sake of the elevation of what is evil and the suppression of what is base.
The Yajñāyajñīya is indeed speech;
therefore, the rising and the sinking occur within it.
Speech is indeed the self;
the out-breath and the in-breath are the rising and the falling.
Therefore, when the *yajñāyajñīya* chant occurs between the rising and the falling, it is the out-breath and the in-breath.
The swelling and the contraction.
In that there are the swelling and the contraction within the *yajñāyajñīya*, he thereby encompasses the self on both sides by means of the out-breath and the in-breath.
Therefore, speech is encompassed by the out-breath and the in-breath.
The Yajñāyajñīya is indeed brilliance, and the midday [pressing] is the self. Therefore,
when they chant the Yajñāyajñīya toward the midday [pressing], they place that brilliance within the self.
They establish [them].
With the *yajñāyajñīya* chant, they proceed on the preceding days depositing embryos;
on the tenth day, they cause them to emerge from the womb.
Therefore, embryos of ten months emerge from the womb for the sake of procreation.
They bring that [Sāman] back toward the midday pressing.
The midday pressing is indeed the self, and this offspring is the progeny.
In that they chant the Yajñāyajñīya toward the midday [pressing], they thereby establish progeny within their own self.
Indeed, by means of the Yajñāyajñīya at the midday pressing, the gods ascended upward to the heavenly world.

Now, as for why the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters come last and the *bṛhatī* comes first: the *kakubh* is the meter of man, and the *bṛhatī* is the heavenly world. Having thus established himself in the heavenly world, he ascends to the heavenly world.
The gods and the Asuras went to the sacrifice as a contest.
[This concerns] the tenth day.
They made the *yajñāyajñīya* their goal.
Those gods desired: "May we win this race."
They directed the *yajñāyajñīya* chant toward the midday pressing, thinking, "From this very proximity we shall win.
Now, the *pavamāna* is indeed the gods' field of play;
from there, they won that race.
Those who arrive on this day go as if to a race.
In that there is the *yajñāyajñīya* chant here, it is for the sake of victory.
He who knows thus wins.
The Yajñāyajñīya is indeed cattle;
the midday [pressing] is the self.
For indeed, one who possesses cattle brings sacrifice after sacrifice.
Therefore, when they chant the Yajñāyajñīya towards the midday pressing, they establish cattle within their own self.
Now, these [verses] are: "O wakeful one, O sage, the truth of thoughts... These are the *āvatī* verses on the day of rising.
If they were to use the *pravatī* verses, they would pass beyond [the sacrifice] in a forward direction. Therefore, since the *āvatī* verses are used, it is for the sake of not passing beyond.
Regarding this, they say: "Those who perform the *āvatī* [verses] on the day of rising (*utthānīya*) surely fall away.
Therefore, the verse "Soma, the bountiful, has shone upon us with light" is used for the sake of advancing forward and to prevent falling away.
In those [stotras], there is the Gaurīvīta. The Gaurīvīta is indeed offspring and cattle; the midday [pressing] is the self.
Therefore, when they chant the Gaurīvīta toward the midday [pressing], they thereby place offspring and cattle within the self.
They establish it.
The Gaurīvīta is indeed the morrow; the midday [pressing] is the self.
In that they chant the Gaurīvīta toward the midday [pressing], they thereby place the morrow within the self.
They establish it.

The Gaurīvīta is indeed the essence (*rasa*), and the midday [pressing] is the self (*ātman*). Therefore, when they chant the Gaurīvīta in response to the midday [pressing], they place that essence within the self.
They establish [them].
JB 3.292 |v1 Then the Rathantara. |v2 The Rathantara is indeed the Brahman.
Verily, they proceed while establishing themselves in the Brahman.
In that the *rathantara* is performed upon the *gāyatrī* verses, they establish this seed in its very womb.
He who knows thus, his emitted seed is procreated in due order.
The Rathantara is indeed the Gāyatra; the Gāyatrī is its metre. Therefore, when the Rathantara serves as the Pṛṣṭha-stotra on Gāyatrī verses, they endow it with its own proper abode.
Through that very prosperity, one becomes prosperous among one's own people.
Indeed, these three are properly joined together: the *gāyatrī* metre, the twenty-four-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), and the *rathantara* chant (*sāman*).
In that these [verses] are joined together correctly, it is for the sake of prosperity;
indeed, prosperity comes to one who knows this.
These two, indeed, are the Arkyodāmanīyas; these are the two syllables of the Rathantara interwoven together.
By means of these very [syllables], they rise up, having overwhelmed their hateful rival.

Regarding this, they say: "Is this day arranged (vyūḍha) or gathered together (samūḍha)? One should reply: "It is both; it is both arranged and gathered together. It is arranged by means of the *sāmans* and gathered together by means of the *chandas* meters.
These [verses] occur: "He proclaims even this other thing" (RV 10.54.3). This refers to the months and the half-months.
Furthermore, through them one is born after Prajāpati.
"Praise Indra, the bull, at the pressing; repeatedly recite the hymns! (RV 8.96.1).
"Like a bull that seeks to strike down, swift as a steed, like a cow that overcomes the people.
(RV 8.45.27) Thus, these verses contain references to cattle and livestock; they serve for the attainment of cattle.
Among them is the *maidhātitha* hymn, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
On the day of rising, there are the *udvatī* verses beginning with "Up have risen those most honey-sweet ones," for the purpose of ascending to the heavenly world;
for this tenth day is indeed the heavenly world.
JB 3.294 |v1 Among those [stomas], there is the *abhīvarta*.
|v2 The gods and the Asuras contended.
Those gods desired, "May we overcome these Asuras.
They saw this *abhīvarta* (overturning) [chant];
with it, they overcame the Asuras.
Because they turned toward it, that is the reason for the *abhīvarta*’s name as *abhīvarta*. Therefore,
when there is an *abhīvarta* here, since the *abhīvarta* is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), they rise up having overcome their hateful rival by means of that very thunderbolt.
Its *nidhana* consists of a single syllable.
Speech, indeed, consists of a single syllable.
Moreover, the heavenly world is, as it were, turned away from here.
For this tenth day is indeed the heavenly world.
In that there is a one-syllable *nidhana*, it is just as if one were to drive in a firm pillar; it serves to prevent falling away.
Now, as for the *kāleya*:
the *rathantara* is indeed Agni;
the *kāleya* is the Viśvedevas.
Now, this is heaven, this is the world, and these indeed are all the gods;
they find firm support in that very world among all the gods.
"Most sweet, most intoxicating"— these *gāyatrī* verses of the Ārbhava Pavamāna contain the word *mada*; for *mada* is indeed the essence (*rasa*).
This third pressing is, as it were, like something that has been sucked out. In that these verses contain the word "mad" (intoxicating), they thereby place sap into it;
by this means, they cause it to swell.
Regarding those [verses], the Gāyatra has its Brāhmaṇa already explained.
Now follows the Saṃhitā, consisting of two syllables, for the sake of stability;
for the sacrificer is two-footed, [and this serves] for the sake of firm standing.
They conclude with the *nidhana* on its verse.
The *ṛc* is indeed cattle, and the *rathaṃtara* is cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle.
Then follow the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*.
Either with the Uṣṇih and Kakubh meters, Indra struck Vṛtra with the thunderbolt;
he struck him down.
Indeed, the Uṣṇih and Kakubh are the thunderbolt.
With the thunderbolt itself, he who knows thus strikes down his hating enemy, evil, and rival.
In the *kakubh* [meter], he struck with the *uṣṇih* as it strove forward;
therefore, the middle syllables of the *kakubh* are the most numerous.
For while exerting himself, he gathered together its syllables;
therefore, the Uṣṇih has the most numerous syllables at the end. For the thunderbolt is heavy at the far end, yet lighter at the point of impact.
The Kakub said, "I am indeed loosened;
while I was striving, he has scrambled my syllables. Let them employ me first!
Then the Uṣṇih said, "Indeed, they used to call me first."
"So be it. They both performed the act accordingly. She chose a different preliminary practice; this was her prior declaration.
Therefore, they employ these two in this manner;
thus, they are called the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*.
These [verses] are used: "Flow on, most honey-sweet; these pressed juices toward Indra.
For this third pressing is indeed the dregs, the squeezed-out, the exhausted.
Therefore Indra went away in loathing;
for it was, as it were, stale.
The gods indeed purified it for him with the words, "Flow on! (RV IX 1.6).
With "O most intoxicating," they made it sweet.
"O Soma, for Indra, you are the most effective exhilaration that wins wisdom;
you are the great, heaven-dwelling exhilaration."

Thus they performed for him in due order, beginning with the word *madvat*. "These pressed [juices] toward Indra"—this very line is indeed one that approaches [the deity]. The verses dedicated to Pāvamāna are truly those belonging to Indra; they are full of vigor.
Therefore, these very *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses should be employed.
In them [is contained] the *sabha*, whose Brāhmaṇa has been stated;
then the *pauṣkala*, whose Brāhmaṇa has been stated.

Now, these [verses] occur: "O Soma, flow forth for the winning of booty"—these are *anuṣṭubh* verses with a "pipīlikā-madhyā" (ant-like middle) structure, containing the word "pari" (around), which is a form of the end.
For the *anuṣṭubh* is indeed the end among the meters.
This day is in the ānuṣṭubh metre.
Having hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, Indra, thinking "I have not struck him down," went to the furthest distance;
for the Anuṣṭubh is indeed the furthest.
He entered that very *parāvat*.
He drew out twelve syllables from it toward the east and twelve upward.
Then the *gāyatrī*, which consists of eight syllables in its middle, entered it.
He entered that very [gāyatrī].
That consists of twelve syllables for her. Brahmā is the gāyatrī.
Brahman alone entered into its midst.
He encompassed this very year on both sides.
Indeed, these verses are Indra-cups.
They rise up having entered into this very Indragraha;
therefore, one who is practicing sorcery or who has rivals should perform these.
For these verses are indeed the Indragraha.
Having thus entered the very vessel of Indra, he overcomes his hateful rival.
Indeed, he who, knowing this, praises with these verses, is consecrated in safety, sacrifices in safety, and rises up in safety.
They perform this as an *anuṣṭubh* in a cryptic manner (*parokṣam*).
For if they were to perform it as an *anuṣṭubh* in an explicit manner (*pratyakṣam*), the sacrificers would go to the furthest distance and would not find firm standing.
In that they perform the *anuṣṭubh* in a cryptic manner, it is for the sake of stability. Regarding those [verses], there is the *Śyāvāśva* hymn, whose Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
Its *nidhana* is "vāc."
Regarding this they say: "Those who bring the *yajñāyajñīya* back toward the midday pressing from the third pressing, they indeed depart from the third pressing.
In that the *nidhana* consists of the word *vāk*, by that very means they do not depart from the form of the *yajñāyajñīya*; by that [means].

They do not depart from the third pressing. Therefore, this *sāman* must not be omitted from this day. "Like the rays of the sun, they cause [the enemy] to flee"—these verses contain the word "sun" for the very purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*.
The stingy ones sleep away together;
the swift streams flow around the stretched-out thread. Without Indra, no station whatsoever is purified.
Thus, indeed, without Indra, no station whatsoever is purified.
“*The thought is joined; the honey is poured*” (RV 10.123.6). For today this world is indeed joined;
by this [verse], they procreate after this very world and establish cattle in this very world.
“The bull bellows; the milch-cows go toward him; the goddesses go to the appointed place of the god” (RV 10.123.7).
Soma has passed through the white fleece, the unshakable filter; he has clothed himself in it as in a washed garment.
(Ṛgveda 9.86.34) Thus there are verses containing the word *pari* (around), for this is the form of the end;
for this day is indeed the end.
JB 3.299 |v1 In those [verses], there is the *vājajit*.
|v2 Food, indeed, is *vāja*.
When indeed a cow, a horse, or a man becomes well-fed with food, then he becomes a *vājín* (possessor of vigor).
The gods and the Asuras contended for the eating of food.
Those gods desired, "May we win the eating of food from the Asuras."
They saw this *sāman*;
they praised with it:
"O conquerors of booty, [win] all riches!"—whatever wealth belonged to the Asuras, whatever cattle, and whatever food.
It existed; they appropriated it. That very thing is the source of the *vājajit*’s quality as a winner of the prize (*vājajittva*).
This is the *sāman* that secures the acquisition of food.
He secures for himself food and sustenance; he appropriates the wealth, the cattle, and the food of his hateful rival—whosoever knows this.
That [sāman] has the *daśākṣaranidhana*.
The first day is indeed established by means of a *nidhana* consisting of a single syllable, and the tenth day by a *nidhana* consisting of ten syllables.
Since there is a *nidhana* of ten syllables on the tenth day, by that very means the ten days are made complete.
Moreover, having thereby secured the food of the *virāj* consisting of ten syllables, they rise at the end.
By means of the twelve-day rite, the gods indeed ascended upwards to the heavenly world.
The Asuras and Rakṣases pursued them from behind; they [the gods] then made the meters their rear guard.
Those [verses] which were cut off settled upon the odd-numbered syllables;
therefore, they did not cause them to fall away.
Consequently, the odd-numbered *stomas* are more powerful.
For them, one should perform this *triṣṭubh*; they would both be victorious. This metre, however, is defeated;
thus, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, he establishes himself upon a metre that is already defeated.
They consist of thirty-three syllables.
There are indeed thirty-three deities in total.
Thus, they establish the sacrifice at its conclusion within all the deities.
These [verses] are *virāj* meters with long syllables; the *virāj* is indeed food, so it is for the attainment of the eating of food that they are *virāj* meters.
They belong to Agni;
thus the Udgātṛ makes both himself and the sacrificer the mouth, the preeminent one.
He who knows thus becomes the chief, the foremost, the eater of food, and the best among his own people.
JB 3.301 |v1 In these [verses], the Vāmadevya [Sāman] is performed.
|v2 Indeed, this Vāmadevya is the pacification of both the Stotra and the Śastra.
Whatever indeed is done in the sacrifice that is discordant or excessive, they rise from it having pacified that very thing by means of this [Sāman].
Truly, the Vāmadevya is the mind of the sacrifice.
Just as one might crush a large clod of earth with a hammer, even so do they quiet all the *stotra* and *śastra* chants with the Vāmadevya.
Indeed, the Vāmadevya is truly Prajāpati among the *stotras*.
Just as all branches of knowledge find their foundation in Prajāpati, even so do all hymns of praise find their foundation in the Vāmadevya.
The Vāmadevya is indeed the womb.
On the tenth day, they cause it to fall from the womb;
therefore, embryos in their tenth month fall from the womb for the sake of birth. The Vāmadevya is indeed the vital breaths.
Regarding this they say: "Those who carry out the sacrificial rite either fail to achieve their goal or do not fail to achieve it; they are as if deprived of their breath.
For who knows whether they actually carry it out or not?
In that regard, the fact that the Vāmadevya [Sāman] occurs here is for the sake of perfecting it through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Indeed, the Vāmadevya is the *sat* (the existent/real) among the hymns of praise; Agni is the *sat* among the deities; the Virāj is the *sat* among the meters; and the Trayastriṃśa is the *sat* among the Stomas.
It is indeed so: they arise while remaining present;
they truly exist.
Indeed, the performer of the twelve-day sacrifice pierces this four-footed, non-piercing throne of knowledge at the very end.
He ascends to the Vāmadevya Sāman, Agni as the deity, Virāj as the metre, and the Trayastrimśa Stoma;
he indeed ascends to these who knows thus.
Gaurīviti Śāktya indeed perceived this thirty-threefold hymn-form for the sake of securing both kinds of cattle, those that are domestic and those that are wild.
Then indeed he acquired both kinds of cattle.
Therefore, they do not omit the thirty-threefold hymn-form (stoma); thus the thirty-threefold hymn-form is performed at the end, for the sake of securing both kinds of cattle.
Verily, this man stands placed beyond;
indeed, there are ten fingers of a man for the attainment of the stalks.
Verily, this man stands placed beyond.
A person has ten fingers, ten toes, ten vital breaths, two supports, and the self as the thirty-third.
The wild animals of the forest move away from him.
Therefore, they resort to the deer as it is being released. For this [rite] is performed as one being released.
Indeed, these stomas of the twelve-day rite are the sons of Prajāpati who are each a single hero.
Regarding this, they say: "This day is twenty-fourfold.
Therefore, everything must be made twenty-fourfold, so that there may be no discord among these sons of Prajāpati, the Ekavīras.
And because these [verses] consist of thirty-three syllables, they do not miss the *trayastriṃśa* stoma;
however, more forms are omitted.
Indeed, the other forms are more numerous.
It should indeed consist of thirty-three [verses].
For all the deities are thirty-three;
thus they establish the sacrifice at its conclusion within all the deities.
Now, this indeed is the firm and well-established *stoma* belonging to all the deities, wherein there is the thirty-threefold (*trayastriṃśa*) one.
Therefore, the thirty-threefold *stoma* alone should be performed at the end.
But they do indeed entice one toward prosperity.
Taking nine *stotryā* verses from the *brahmasāman* itself, one should place them here.
The prosperities do not depart; they find firm support in both types of stomas—both those that are odd-numbered and those that are even-numbered.
Just as one standing on a crossroads might release [a load], even so at the end all the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns are released by means of the Vāmadevya.
Regarding this, they say: "Should one disperse [the fires] or not? They say: "One should not disperse them.
For those who come on this day enter into a contest.
Among them, he who is struck down is the one who falls away. Just as one would place a deficient [brick] back, so it is with that.
Indeed, for whoever places a deficient [brick], both of them fall away.
Moreover, they serve Prajāpati himself with this day.
Therefore, they do not speak out; for who indeed is fit to criticize the serving of one who is superior?
Indeed, he who criticizes the serving of one who is superior is afflicted by that very same distress with which he desired to serve him.
He leads [the horse] away.
Regarding this they say: "The Brahman priest alone should recite [the formulas].
For the Brahman is indeed the Brahman.
The Brahman priest alone recites that [response] at the sacrifice.
Now, some say that the Udgātṛ alone should recite it;
for the Udgātṛ is indeed Prajāpati.
Prajāpati himself then explained the sacrifice.
Now, some say that the sacrificer himself should explain it;
for the sacrificer is indeed the master of the sacrifice.
In that very sacrifice, he proclaims the sacrifice.
Moreover, one directs the serving of food according to one's desire, saying, "I have served," or "I have served.
Furthermore, they say that one should step forward toward the east and cry out, "Those people did this! Those people did that!"
That very thing is both separated (*vyukta*) and unseparated (*avyukta*).
Regarding this, they say: it is indeed separated.
For if it were not separated, they would remain silent; [in that case] they would surely be cut off from the sacrifice. Thus, there is no affliction for that which is worthy of sacrifice.
"Having approached, he should indeed speak without interruption.
To whatever extent he speaks, that he announces to the Hotṛ.
The Hotṛ thereby brings it to completion as an Anuṣṭubh, thinking: "This tenth day has been brought to its conclusion."
They converse about that which they chant here on the *anākṣara* verses and that which they exceed;
thus they bring this very thing to completion within Prajāpati, and he directs the serving around.
The *stomas* that end in pairs are indeed unfavorable to cattle, for they are smooth and even. Therefore,
when they settle upon the *trivṛt* *stoma*, it is for the sake of pairing and procreation.
From a union that is deficient or excessive, offspring and cattle are born.
He who knows this is propagated with offspring and cattle.
This earth was indeed the world, and the intermediate space was the sky.
He desired, "May I nourish the speckled form.
He saw this mantra: "This speckled cow has stepped forth.
Then indeed this earth nourished the speckled form.
Verily, O Deva, he who knows thus prospers with offspring and cattle, even as Pṛśni did.
Regarding this they say: "Those who sacrifice indeed ascend upwards to the heavenly world;
they are liable to fall forward [backwards]."
