Now, when they chant the *sarparājñī* verses, this earth is indeed the queen of serpents (*sarparājñī*); it is upon her that they thus find firm support.
For she is the queen of all that creeps.
Verily, no creeping creature harms him who knows this.

They chant on *gāyatrī* verses; the *gāyatrī* is indeed among the meters that which is not exhausted (*ayātayāman*). It is for the sake of non-exhaustion itself. They chant on three [verses]; these worlds are three; it is for the attainment of these worlds.
Now, there are indeed three vital breaths: the out-breath (prāṇa), the in-breath (apāna), and the diffused breath (vyāna).
It is by connecting these very breaths and establishing themselves therein that they attain the upward course.
The Gāyatra Sāman is used; for the Gāyatra is indeed never-wearied, and it serves for the sake of that state of being never-wearied.
Now, the Gāyatra is indeed the mind.
It is by means of the mind that they bring it to completion, by the mind they turn toward it, by the mind they utter the *hiṃ* call,
by the mind the *prastotṛ* begins the chant, by the mind he takes up the *ādi*, by the mind he sings the *udgītha*, and by the mind the *pratihartṛ* responds.
They reach the end by means of the mind, for the sake of completing what has not been completed.

For whatever of the sacrifice the gods did not complete with speech, that they completed with the mind. Therefore, when they chant with the mind, it is for the sake of completing what has not been completed.
The essence (rasa) of this day indeed flowed away.
They grasped it with the mind alone.
This, verily, is that essence.
Therefore, when they praise with the mind, it is for the sake of not overstepping the essence.
These verses are indeed the vessel for the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*).
Whatever one obtains through the Great Vow, that much one obtains while praising with these verses.
One day belonged to the mind, and another to speech.
That which was the day of the mind, the gods took hold of it and ascended upwards to the heavenly world.
Then that which was the day of speech became this very day.
By means of that, they became established in this world through offspring and cattle.
Therefore, when they praise with the mind, it is for the sake of illuminating that very day. The Hotṛ recites the Caturhotṛ formulas; the Caturhotṛs are indeed the Brahman.
Verily, he is worthy to attain the *brahman* through the *stotra*s and *śastra*s.
These, indeed, are the secret names of the gods, namely the *caturhotṛ* formulas;
it is these very names that he thereby causes to become manifest.
When these have become manifest, they cause him to attain manifestation.
He who knows thus attains manifestation. Therefore, if a Brahmin who is worthy of glory does not attain glory, he should go away into the forest.
Having untied the knots, he should explain the Caturhotṛ formulas to them, or having made a Brāhmaṇa his supervisor.
Indeed, these Caturhotṛ formulas are the secret names of the gods.
He causes those very [lights] to reach luminosity. Having reached luminosity, they cause him to reach luminosity. He who knows thus reaches luminosity.
The chant performed in silence he recites aloud.
Therefore, what one attains with the mind, that one expresses with speech.

Therefore, plants are born from their roots and ripen from their tips. Regarding this, they ask: "Should [the sacrifice] be performed when the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings have been completed, or when they have not been completed? They say: "When they have not been completed."
In these very western [days] they place embryos;
yet there is both female power and a state of inverted order (pāpavasyasa).
One should perform the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings at the very end for the sake of averting that state of inverted order.
Moreover, the strength of a woman is not like that [of a man].
Furthermore, they place embryos only in those [women] who are facing away.
And indeed, human beings are born both facing toward and facing away.
Therefore, one should praise only when the offerings have been completed.
They take hold of the Audumbarī post; for the Udumbara is strength and food, [and this is] for the attainment of strength and the eating of food.
They restrain their speech.
Speech, indeed, is the Brahman. Thus, they restrain that speech—the Brahman—within themselves as the sacrifice.

"Here is steadfastness, here is self-steadfastness; delight, the mind of delight"—with these [formulas] they restrain that very mind, that steadfastness, that thought, and that speech. If they were to release them after [the sun] has set, they would leave behind the day, which is the world of the enemy.

If they were to release [the fires] before the sun has set, they would leave the night—the world of their rival—remaining. Having gone toward the Āhavanīya fire when half the sun has set, they release them.
Thus, by means of both day and night, they exclude their hateful rival.
He who knows this excludes his hateful rival by means of both day and night.
Regarding this, they say: "It should be released only after [the sun] has set;
for as day and night revolve, they attain the year."

The year is the sacrifices. Having thus attained the sacrifice, they release it with the words: "Releasing the supporter for the mother, may the supporter, suckling the mother, maintain for us the increase of wealth, food, and strength—svāhā!"
Just as one would drive away a cow after yoking it to its stall, even so they yoke both the speech and the sacrificer together and drive them away.
For in whatever manner she speaks by means of this [speech], in that same manner she becomes impossible for them to escape.
Whatever desire they may wish for, let them meditate upon it;
that very desire will indeed be fulfilled for them.
They release their speech with the Subrahmaṇyā formula.
The Subrahmaṇyā is indeed Brahman;
the Subrahmaṇyā is speech.
Thus, by means of Brahman itself, they release speech.

Agni is the first day, Indra the second, Prajāpati the third, Bṛhaspati the fourth, the Maruts the fifth, the Viśve Devas the sixth, the Vasus the seventh, the Rudras the eighth, and the Ādityas [the ninth].
The ninth [is Prajāpati], and Prajāpati himself is the tenth day.
This very direction is the departure, and this is the return.
Therefore, yonder sun sets from here and rises from here.
He follows this very same [sequence] for both the departure and the ascent:
the *āśu* is the *trivṛt*, the *bhānta* is the *pañcadaśa*, the *vyoma* is the *saptadaśa*, the *dharuṇa* is the *ekaviṃśa*, the *ojas* is the *triṇava*,
the *pratiṣṭhā* is the *trayastriṃśa*, the *brahma* is the *caturviṃśa*, the *kṣatra* is the *catuścatvāriṃśa*, and the *vivarta* is the *viś*.
The Stoma is the forty-eightfold; Prajāpati himself is the tenth day.
Regarding that which is called "the swift Trivṛt": as a bird is swift, so is this Trivṛt Stoma.
Then, regarding "the fifteenfold [Stoma] shining in heaven," for that is indeed the Kṣatra (the ruling power).
The ruling power indeed shines forth.
Now, as for the statement "the seventeenfold is the void," it is Prajāpati who is that;
for Prajāpati is indeed the void.
Now, as for the fact that the twenty-onefold [stoma] is the Support (Dharuṇa), it is indeed that sun;
for upon this [sun], all this universe is supported.
And as for the fact that the twenty-sevenfold [stoma] is Might (Ojas), it is indeed the Maruts.
The Maruts are indeed force and vigor; the twenty-sevenfold [stoma] is force and vigor. Now, as for the fact that the thirty-threefold is the foundation, it is because that is the end.
Now, as for the statement that "the Brahman is the twenty-fourfold," it is indeed the Gāyatrī;
for the Gāyatrī is the Brahman. And as for the statement that "the Kṣatra is the forty-fourfold," it is the Triṣṭubh.
The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the *kṣatra*. Now, as for the statement that the *vivarta* is the *viś*’s *stoma* of forty-eight [verses], it is indeed the *jagatī*,
for the *jagatī* is the *viś*.
Indeed, this entire universe is the Anuṣṭubh.
This very [Anuṣṭubh] is the departure, and this is the emergence.
Therefore, from this very [place] they depart, and from this they emerge.
Agni indeed is the departure, and Āditya is the rising.
He who knows this goes forth, clearly perceiving this world, straightway.
The first three-day period has the Gāyatra at its head;
therefore, this Agni shines upright in this world.
The second three-day period has the *gāyatrī* at its middle;
therefore, Vāyu blows across this intermediate space.
The third three-day period has the *gāyatrī* at its end.

Therefore, this sun shines hitherward from the sky. These, indeed, are the divine arrows placed in position—unsharpened yet never resting—which stand dispelling all evil from these worlds: Agni on earth, Vāyu in the intermediate space, and Āditya in the sky.
These [verses], when one knows thus, go forth driving away all evil from him.
By means of these victories and separations, these worlds were won and separated according to their respective places.
Because, while being part of the same sacrificial performance, they yet become distinct, for that reason indeed the gods [are so called].
The ancestors and humans, dwelling in the same world, perceived one another;
by these victories and separations, they were conquered and separated according to their respective stations.
While Prajāpati was creating offspring, evil seized him from the mouth. He desired, "May I strike away this evil."
He beheld this first three-day period with the Gāyatra as its opening;
by means of it, he struck away evil from the front and bound it in the middle.
He beheld this second three-day period with the *gāyatra* at its center.
By means of it, he struck away evil from the middle.
He bound it at the feet.
He beheld this third three-day period, the Gāyatrī-uttama.
By means of it, he struck away evil from his feet;
he bound it to his feet.
He beheld this third three-day period, the highest of the Gāyatrī meters.
By means of it, he struck away evil.
He who knows thus strikes away evil.

By means of the three-day period ending with the *svara* (intonation), Prajāpati saved himself from death; by means of that ending with the *nidhana* (concluding formula), he saved his offspring; and by means of that ending with the *iḍā* (invocation), he saved his cattle.
Truly, there is only this much: the self, offspring, and cattle.
In that it was protected (*atrāyata*) while being existent (*sat*), that is the reason for the name *sattra*.
He who knows this is protected from all evil.
Indeed, with the *triya* [chant] ending in *svar*, Prajāpati created the gods; with the one ending in *nidhana*, the ancestors; and with the one ending in *iḍā*.
[He created] humans.
Because he created the gods with that which ends in a vowel (svarānta), therefore they are immortal;
for he created them by means of the immortal vital breath (prāṇa).

Then, because he created the ancestors with that which ends in the *nidhana*, they therefore have the *nidhana* as their conclusion. Then, because he created human beings with that which ends in the *iḍā*— and the *iḍā* is indeed cattle— therefore, men flock to whoever possesses cattle.
JB 3.312 |v1 Now, Keśin Dārbhya dwelt with Kabandha Ātharvaṇa.
|v2 At that time, the meters were indeed only contracted (samūḍha), not expanded (vyūḍha).

To him, Kabandha Ātharvaṇa taught this twelve-day sacrifice with its expanded meters to Keśin Dārbhya, saying: "Satisfy the *gāyatrī* three times, the *triṣṭubh* three times, and the *jagatī* three times. [He added:
"Others shall covet the life of your offspring, but your offspring shall not belong to them."
Therefore, indeed,
from that time onward, the meters have been arranged in this reversed order.
For this reason, even though they are not wealthy, people look toward the Pañcālas for their very livelihood.
Regarding this, there are these two verses:
“Why do the streams flow upward from the earth? Why do they flow crosswise along the intermediate space?
Why, when released, do they flow downward from the northern sky, following the rays of the sun?”
The Gāyatrī, clothed in the Trivṛt, pushed the Triṣṭubh out from the intermediate space;
she [pushed] the Jagatī out from its abode in heaven; therefore, the streams flow hitherward.
Speech, indeed, when it had created the sacrifice, became hungry and thirsty.
The gods desired to satisfy it with an oblation within the sacrifice;
they did not, however, satisfy it.
Desiring to satisfy her with Soma-libations and Havis-sacrifices performed in the forward direction,
they did not indeed satisfy her.
They then perceived this twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) with its expanded meters (vyūḍhacchandas).
They brought it;
they sacrificed with it. Then, having become the meters (*chandāṃsi*), they sought her out.

They, for the sake of each other's portion, were satisfied by the wandering about of the cows. Therefore, animals are satisfied by the wandering about of the cows for the sake of each other's portion.
She was satisfied.
He who thus knows this satisfaction of both speech and the meters is satisfied himself; his progeny is satisfied.
The gods, having yoked the divine dogs to the divine chariots, ascended these worlds.
The meters are indeed the horses of the gods, and the hymn-forms are the chariots of the gods.
They made the Gāyatrī the right yoke-horse, the Triṣṭubh the left yoke-horse, and the Jagatī the left side-horse.

By means of that, they ascended to this world. They said, "The path is indeed too long; let us turn back. They made the Jagatī the right yoke-horse, the Gāyatrī the left yoke-horse, and the Triṣṭubh...
The left side-horse.
With that they ascended this intermediate world.
They said, "The path of the gods is superior; let us indeed pile it around."
They made the Triṣṭubh the right yoke-horse, the Jagatī the left yoke-horse, and the Gāyatrī the left side-horse.
By means of that, they ascended to yonder world.
In this way, indeed, the gods, having yoked these divine horses to the divine chariots, ascended to these worlds. He who knows thus ascends to these worlds.

JB 3.315 |v1 Indeed, that which has a *sapad* [verse-division] is the metre that raises up the first day; the *vipad* [metre], the second; the *nānāpad* [metre], the third; the *anupad* [metre], the fourth; the *atipad* [metre], the fifth; and the *abhipad* [metre], the sixth.
The Gāyatrī indeed has feet; the Gāyatrī has three feet;
these worlds are three.
The *triṣṭubh* has stepped-out feet (*vipadā*), for its feet consist of eleven syllables. The *jagatī* has various feet (*nānāpadā*), for its feet consist of twelve syllables.
The *anuṣṭubh* has consecutive feet (*anupadā*).
For that [Gāyatrī] is indeed without a supplement by means of its syllables.
There are eight syllables in the feet of the Gāyatrī, and eight syllables in those of the Anuṣṭubh. The Paṅkti is the Atipadā, for it consists of five feet.
The verses are of exceeding desire;
for indeed, no one else possesses such syllables.
When Prajāpati created the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans], he first perceived the Bṛhat as the mind and uttered the Rathantara as speech.

Because he uttered the *rathantara* in response to speech, therefore the *rathantara* attained its first union. And because he saw the *bṛhat* first with his mind, therefore they are called the "Bṛhat and Rathantara."
Mind indeed comes first, then speech.
Mind is indeed the *bṛhat*, speech is the *rathantara*.
The *rathantara* is indeed the spiritual power (*brahman*), the *bṛhat* is the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
Then this mind (manas) held itself in contempt above speech; it was the ruling power (kṣatra) [in relation to] the sacred word (brahman).
Then this Rathantara [sāman] perceived: "He indeed holds me in contempt. It created the Vairūpa [sāman].
He moved around it from the front.
Having become two, they thought themselves superior. Then this Bṛhat knew: "They indeed think themselves superior to me."
He created that Vairāja.
With it, he surrounded [the sacrifice] from the front.
Having become two, they thought themselves superior; then this Rathantara perceived: "They indeed think themselves superior to me."
He created the Śākvara;
with it he drove away [the evil] from the front.
Having become three, they thought themselves superior.
"This Bṛhat-sāman here—know it! Surely he thinks too highly of me!
He created the Raivata [sāman].
With it, he went around from the front.
Having become three, they considered themselves noble.
They went to their limit.
They perceived: "The self (sva) is indeed common; one does not transcend the other."
Those were the six *pṛṣṭha* chants, and there were three meters (*chandas*).
These three meters could not encompass the six *pṛṣṭha* chants.
That Gāyatrī created the Anuṣṭubh;
it raised up the fourth day.
By means of it, the fourth day was fashioned. The *triṣṭubh* created the *paṅkti*;
she brought forth the fifth day.
By means of that, the fifth day was prepared.
She created the *jagatī* and the *aticchandas*.
She brought forth the sixth day.
By that, the sixth day was prepared.
Those were the six *pṛṣṭha* stotras and the six meters;
they were formed into pairs.
Offspring and cattle come to him in pairs who knows thus.
Indeed, the first day is extended by means of the Gāyatrī, the second by the Triṣṭubh, the third by the Jagatī, the fourth by the Anuṣṭubh, the fifth by the Paṅkti, and the sixth by the Atichandas.
Therefore, the *aticchandās* verses are recited on the sixth day.
Just as one would seek a firm footing in the deepest water by means of the highest [bank], even so did the gods seek a firm footing on the sixth day by means of the *aticchandās* meters.
Now, they indeed desire this for the sake of the pervasion of the sixth day itself, and for the sake of the continuity and non-interruption of the subsequent three-day period.
JB 3.318 |v1 In the beginning, this world was indeed the great waters.
|v2 In them, Prajāpati desired a firm foundation.
He saw this Vaiśvānara Prāyaṇīya Atirātra;
he established it. He spread out this very world upon that water.
Because it spread out (*apra-thayat*), therefore it is called the Earth (*pṛthivī*). Upon that [Earth], he established himself.
That, indeed, was like darkness.
For the night is subsequent to the day.
He beheld this threefold Agniṣṭoma;
he laid it down upon this very earth, even upon this fire.
By means of that light, he beheld these worlds.

He extended these eight Ukthya-stomas, consisting of eight parts, over the directions as cattle; the Vāmadevya-sāman over the intermediate space; the Āditya-stoma as the tenth day; and that world above as the Atirātra.
He pervaded this pervasion;
he became this entire universe. He who knows thus pervades this very pervasion and becomes this entire universe.
The six-day period consisting of the *pṛṣṭhya* [stomas] is indeed the seasons; the *chandomas* are the quarters; these two worlds are the two *atirātras*.

The six-day period consisting of the *pṛṣṭhya* [stomas] is indeed the half-months, the months, and the days and nights; the *chandomas* are the half-months, the months, and the days and nights; these two worlds are the two *atirātras*.
Now, those two Agniṣṭomas that occur in between are indeed Indra and Agni. Therefore,
because the first day has fewer stomas while being closer [to the central day], this Agni, though being closer, burns more mildly.

Now, because the last day, which is the highest *jyotis-stoma*, is furthest away, therefore that sun, being furthest away, burns with greater intensity. Indeed, all desires come to him who knows the twelve-day rite as attaining its own self in its entirety.
They attain [it].
The first *atirātra* is indeed a counterpart to the feet;
there are nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person.
It is threefold;
the introductory day is threefold;
by that it is perfected.
There are ten fingers on the hands and four [fingers] on the chest and arms.
That which is above the navel is fifteen [units].
The second day is the fifteenth.
By that, it is perfected.
There are ten fingers and toes, and seven vital breaths in the head;
that makes seventeen.
The seventeenth [stoma] is the third day; by it it is perfected.
There are ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, and the self is the twenty-first.
The twenty-first [stoma] is the fourth day.
Through that, it was perfected.
There are ten fingers, ten toes, and seven vital breaths in the head;
that makes twenty-seven.
The twenty-seventh [section]: the fifth day.
By that it was perfected.
There are ten fingers of the hand, ten toes of the foot, ten vital breaths, mind, speech, and the heart—that is it.
The thirty-third [day].
|v21 The sixth day is the thirty-third.
|v22 By that, it is perfected.
The vital breaths themselves are the seventh day, in the *gāyatrī* metre;
the eye itself is the eighth day, in the *triṣṭubh* metre; the ear itself is the ninth day, in the *jagatī* metre.
Speech itself is the tenth day, belonging to the *anuṣṭubh* metre.
Now, that which is above the two ears is the subsequent *atirātra*.
The former *atirātra* is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and the latter is the up-breath (*udāna*).
They call those two the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices by an indirect designation.

He stands firm in the out-breath and the in-breath; he does not falter from the out-breath and the in-breath; he attains a full lifespan. Thus indeed the entire twelve-day sacrifice attains its own self, and all desires attain him.
Whoever knows thus.
JB 3.320 |v1 This twelve-day rite is indeed the central day (*viṣuvat*) of the sacrificial session (*satra*).
|v2 He who knows the central day of this sacrificial session—verily, the central day is prosperity; as the central day, he becomes the most excellent among his own people.
It comes to pass: "The person (*puruṣa*), indeed, is the *viṣuvant* of this sacrificial session;
for the person is the *viṣuvant* of these worlds."
"These worlds indeed are this twelve-day rite; thinking, 'I am the Viṣuvat of this sacrificial session,' one should perform this twelve-day rite.
For him, in this very sacrificial session, the Viṣuvat is thereby attained."
This very [sacrifice] is established in the day alone.
It shines forth day after day as "the introductory day," "the second day," and "the third day.
Indeed, that sun is the day.
Verily, by this they prosper; they go to share the same world as him.
JB 3.321 |v1 Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning.
|v2 He desired: "May I become many; may I procreate; may I attain abundance."
He produced eighteen syllables. He divided them into two groups of nine each. He became the Trivṛt Stoma and the Gāyatrī metre.
This Trivṛt Stoma was complete, while the Gāyatrī had the Praṇava as its ninth syllable.
The Praṇava was her ninth syllable.
This Trivṛt Stoma said to that Gāyatrī, "Come, let us unite."
Being equal, the two were unable to unite.
He said to her: "Now, being equal, we shall not be able to unite.
Let that ninth syllable of yours be displaced."
"What will that become?
"That which exists will become so. "It shall be thus."
He blew upon it;
that very [breath] became the *praṇava*.
That *pratigara* is the *udgītha*, and that is the *āśrāvaṇa*.
Therefore, one utters the *praṇava* as "Om," one responds with "Om," one sings the *udgītha* as "Om," and one causes the *āśrāvaṇa* as "Om."
"This indeed exists, which was [previously] non-existent.

He said to her: "Now indeed, this is sufficient for us; let us procreate! Come, let us procreate! He said to her: "Be joined together; you shall procreate the meters, and I shall procreate the hymns (stomas)."
This very Trivṛt Stoma brought twenty-four stotriyas.
Then the Gāyatrī was born with twenty-four syllables.
He said to her, "Become as great as you are in extent."
That [goddess], being of eight syllables, made the syllables into three-syllable groups.
They became twenty-four;
there were twenty-four [syllables] in the former [set].
Thus, forty-eight offspring were born from her.
This Gāyatrī took four syllables;
she became the Uṣṇih.
The other took six.
He became the fifteenfold hymn-form;
he took four [of them].
It became the *anuṣṭubh* metre.
The other took six [verses];
it became the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) hymn-form (*stoma*).
He took four;
she became the Bṛhatī.
He took six.
It became the twenty-sevenfold hymn-form (*triṇava-stoma*).
She took four [syllables];
she became the *bṛhatī* [meter].
The other took six;
he became the twenty-sevenfold hymn-form (*triṇava-stoma*).
She took four.
That became the *paṅkti* [meter].
The other took six;
that became the *trayastrimśa* [stoma].
He reached the end of that;
he took up four [syllables];
she became the *triṣṭubh*.
He took four others;
she became the Jagatī.
They went to the end [of the earth]; he said to her, "We shall not procreate beyond this; come,"
"As many syllables as she was at first, so many syllables she remains.
Having become eight-syllabled,
therefore the husband leads his wife according to his desire.
Having arranged the fifteenfold and the twenty-onefold [stomas] on both sides, they stood together in the middle.
That very Prajāpati became this seventeenfold stoma, the eater of food.
To him, he offered the Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa as oblations from below, and the Ekaviṃśa, Triṇava, and Trayastriṃśa from above.
He said to her, "May you give birth to the meters; I shall produce the Stomas."
"I shall procreate.
This very Trivṛt-stoma procreated these Mṛga-stomas: the Catuṣṭoma, the Caturdaśa, the Ṣoḍaśa, the Aṣṭādaśa, the Navadaśa, the Pañcaviṃśa, and the Ṣaṭtriṃśa.

Then Gāyatrī extended toward these meters of wild beasts (*mṛgacchandas*): the one-footed, the two-footed, the syllable-row (*akṣarapaṅkti*), the wide-row (*viṣṭārapaṅkti*), the sovereign (*virāj*), the exceeding meter (*aticchandas*), and the immeasurable meter (*amitaṃ chandaḥ*).
She, indeed, is Prajāpati of both the *stomas* and the meters.

Then Caikatāneya questioned Śaunaka Kāpeya: "Since the *stomas* are generated by means of the six-over (*ṣaḍuttara*) and the meters by means of the four-over (*caturuttara*), then what is this *aṣaḍuttarī* *stoma*, which, being the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*), is excluded and placed in the middle?"

He said: "The *stomas* and the *chandases*, when they were not yet produced, were indeed this Prajāpati; standing in the middle, he remained engaged in bringing them forth as the seventeenfold [sacrifice].
He who knows this as the unexhausted (*ākṣita*)—he indeed becomes unexhausted everywhere.
"Prajāpati is indeed eyeless,
for all this is of Prajāpati. Those Caikitāneyas, however, were as if possessed of eyes.
These very meters were fashioned by means of the *stomas*.
By means of the *trivṛt* [stoma], the *gāyatrī* was formed; by the *pañcadaśa*, the *triṣṭubh*; by the *saptadaśa*, the *jagatī*;
by the *ekaviṃśa*, the *anuṣṭubh*; by the *triṇava*, the *paṅkti*; by the *trayastrimśa*, the *virāj*; and by the *pañcaviṃśa*, the *bṛhatī*.
From eighteen and nine [syllables] come the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters. Those which are nine *gāyatrīs*, those twenty-four are the *trivṛts*.
Then those which are fifteen *triṣṭubhs*, those forty-four are the *pañcadaśas*.
Now, those seventeen *jagatī*s [consist of] forty-eight syllables; these are the seventeen-fold stomas.

Now, those twenty-one *anuṣṭubh*s [consist of] thirty-two syllables; these are the twenty-one-fold stomas. Now, those twenty-seven *paṅkti*s [consist of] forty syllables; these are the twenty-seven-fold stomas.
Now, as for those thirty-three *virāj*s, those thirty are the [sets of] thirty-three.
Now, as for those twenty-five *bṛhatī*s, those thirty-six are the [sets of] twenty-five.
Now, as for those eighteen and nineteen *uṣṇih*s and *kakubh*s, those twenty-eight are the [sets of] eighteen and nineteen.
In the beginning, this was indeed one imperishable syllable, which was speech alone.
It desired: "May I become many, may I procreate, may I attain abundance, may I extend the sacrifice."
She offered oblations twelve times, saying "Svāhā! Svāhā! Svāhā!
She deposited thirty [syllables] each time;
thus she became thirty syllables by her very self.
Two syllables crept up behind her;
she became this very *anuṣṭubh*.
Therefore, when a woman is with child, two breasts seem to creep up behind her.
This very Virāj is she who thunders.
When he offered oblations twelve times, he thereby created these twelve months.
These very [oblations] became the twelve days of the Dvādaśāha sacrifice, and they themselves became the twenty-four half-months.
They became exactly seven hundred and twenty days and nights.
He created this year as a sacrifice;
for this year is indeed the sacrifice.
She did not know whether she had created the sacrifice or not;
she thought only, "Have I indeed created something?
Then Modas came toward her.
Then he perceived: "I have indeed created the sacrifice.
He thought: "Since I have created this sacrifice, come, let me extend it from out of my own self."
With eight syllables he extended the first day, with eleven the second, and with twelve the third.
Only the single syllable remained as a tri-syllable.
He distributed that very [syllable] over the subsequent three days.
Thus he performed this Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha.
He beheld this six-day *pṛṣṭhya* sacrifice and considered: "By what means, indeed, shall I extend this third three-day period?
He saw only himself, thinking: "That which is my self is indeed this [sacrifice].
Come, let me extend it from out of myself."
With eight syllables he extended the seventh day, with eleven the eighth, and with twelve the ninth.
Then that syllable which remained became this tenth day of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*).

This very speech, exhausted and drawn out from its source, bore the sacrifice; it was like a lioness, or a tigress, or a porpoise that has recently given birth. If they were now to seize it directly before their eyes, they would fall into misfortune for her sake.
If they were to go away from this, they would go away from everything.
Therefore, they perform that very *anuṣṭubh* in a hidden manner.
The Hotṛ does not recite the Anuṣṭubh verses; he recites only the Virāj verses.
Those gods said, "This one, this very one, has released the sacrifice; let us sacrifice with these."
They said to the Bṛhatī: "Carry this third day for us. [The Bṛhatī replied:
"That which is won by us is indeed not yet pervaded.
Now, the Bṛhatī truly becomes "existent" (sat) when it serves as the *pṛṣṭha* chant.
Having carried this third day, the Bṛhatī did not desire to carry it further.
They [the gods] won this world by means of the Rathantara, the intermediate space by means of the Bṛhatī, and yonder world by means of the Bṛhat.
By means of this triad of days, they conquered.

Just as they go with what has been won, they drive Sindhava horses, they carry an elephant, a chariot goes with the pole grasped, it goes with two *hulu* poles, or with two *vicchidvaha* poles— in the same way [they go] with a donkey-chariot.
Thus the gods passed over this second three-day period.
Those two, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, restored these forms: the Vairūpa, the Vairāja, the Mahānāmnīs, and the Revatīs.
Then the *bṛhatī* drew back toward the *virāj*, the *śakvarī* toward the *revatī*.
These [verses] then moved forward.
The gods perceived them, just as one might perceive a fish moving along a stream.
On the seventh day, they emerge together like fish leaping up from the water.
All these [melodies] are combined within the *Chandoma* days.
Thus, the *Bṛhat* occurs in the *Bṛhatī*, and the *Rathantara* occurs in the *Bṛhatī*.
Just as one might cross over a fierce and deep place by exerting oneself, even so did the gods cross over this third three-day period.
They arrived at this tenth day, which is the world of heaven;
for this tenth day is indeed the world of heaven.
That makes twenty-four.
Of these, the twenty that there are are the Virāj;
then, the four that remain are the very summit of the firmament (*bradhnasya viṣṭapa*).
In that [fire], the gods milk all desires.
He offers with the mantra: "Bestowing support upon the mother, the supporter suckling the mother—may he maintain for us the increase of wealth, food, and vigor;
svāhā! Thus he sacrifices.
Whatever desire he may desire, let him meditate upon it.
When this [oblation] has been offered, that very desire is fulfilled for one who knows thus.
Śāṭyāyani used to say: "How could it not be fulfilled for one who knows thus?"
It comes, having departed, as that which is swift, accompanied by food, adorned with gold, and radiant; this is the form of the first day,
of the *trivṛt* stoma, of the *gāyatrī* metre, and of the *rathantara* sāman.
[The hymn] beginning with *vṛṣavat*, *vṛtrahavad*, *rayimad*, and *viśvavad* is the form of the second day, of the fifteenfold *stoma*, of the *triṣṭubh* metre, and of the *bṛhat* sāman.
[The hymn] beginning with *udvat*, *trivat*, *digvad*, *gatavat*, and *purāṇavat* is the form of the third day, of the seventeenfold *stoma*.
For the Jagatī metre, for the Vairūpa Sāman; [for the king-like, for the people-filled, for the Virāj, for the sun-like— this is the form of the fourth day, of the twenty-one-fold Stoma,
of the Anuṣṭubh metre, of the Vairāja Sāman].
Variegated, accompanied by children, consisting of *paṅkti* meters, with syllables in excess, rich in cattle, rich in bulls, containing the *vajra*,
and accompanied by the beloved— this is the form of the fifth day, of the *triṇava* stoma, of the *paṅkti* meter, and of the *śākvara* sāman.

The *parivat*, the *prativat*, the seven-footed verse, the two-footed verse, that which lacks the *nārāśaṃsa* cup, the one containing the word "cow," the one containing the word "bull," and the one containing the word "thunderbolt" directed against the enemy—
these are the forms of the sixth day; [they belong] to the thirty-three-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), to the *aticchandas* metre, and to the *raivata* sāman.
Because this division of the six-day period, while being uniform, yet becomes manifold, therefore the year is of manifold form, and after it, offspring are born in manifold forms.
"O Agni! is the case-ending for the first day; "Agni" for the second; "by Agni" for the third; "Agni" for the fourth; "of Agni" for the fifth; and "O Agni" again for the sixth.
These two [words] join together at both ends.
In accordance with this, the year is infinite.
Its two ends are winter and spring.
In accordance with this, the two ends of a village meet; in accordance with this, the two ends of a necklace meet; in accordance with this, a serpent [unfolds] its coils.
Having brought it around, he lies down.
This is food.
That wheel of the gods, imperishable and ever-renewed, revolves both hitherward and thitherward.

He who knows this thus wins this very infinity, this imperishability, and this ever-newness. With the verse, "O Agni, come for the feast," they indeed call him; with the verse, "We choose Agni as our messenger," they indeed choose him.
"By Agni is Agni kindled"—with these words they truly kindle him.
"May Agni slay the Vṛtras"—by this they indeed conquer.
"The splendors of the one who moves among men like lightning"—with this they bestow splendor upon him.
He who indeed knows the division of the sixth day reaches a full lifespan. "O Jātavedas" is the division of the sixth day, and also "O Agni.
He who knows thus reaches a full lifespan.
The gods, indeed, sought prosperity during the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha.
They did not find it on the first day with the [verse] beginning "O Agni."
On the second day they did not find her with the words "Agni.
On the third day they did not find her with the words "By Agni.
On the fourth day they found her with the words "Agni" alone.
In the subsequent [sections], they spoke only of what has already occurred.
For although this division of the fires is common, it becomes manifold for those who have entered [into them].
Moreover, by means of these very fires, all the seasons become possessed of fire.

The *prasṛteḍā* is for the first day; the *ūrdhveḍa* for the second; the *pariṣṭubdheḍa* for the third; the *iḍābhir iḍa* for the fourth; the *adhyardheḍa* for the fifth; and the *ihakāreṇābhyasteḍa* for the sixth.
Now, Vāsyaska once asked the Naimiśīyas: "What do you perform with the first day?"
"Come," he said.
"What is the use of a second?
"We shall make a dwelling," they replied.
"What is the use of the third?
"We shall float around.
"What is the use of the fourth?"
"By means of the existent, we have placed the existent," he said.
"What [is accomplished] by the fifth? "It is for severing the cattle," he replied. "We have come."
"What is the use of the sixth?
they asked. "Let us come," they said, "and let us heal these cattle."
Regarding that [phrase] "when he goes forward" (*praiti*): it is indeed set in motion (*pra-sāryate*) when he goes forward;
thus, the *iḍā* is extended on the first day.

JB 3.333 |v1 Now, as for [the practice] "they perform the *avasaṃ*": they perform the *avasaṃ* either having indeed ceased [the previous action] or having indeed unyoked [the breaths]. |v2 For the *iḍā* indeed goes to its conclusion (*nidhana*) on the second day, having ceased.
Now, as for [the phrase] "or we shall float around," it is because on the third day one reaches the *iḍā*-finale after having, as it were, floated around.
And as for [the phrase] "we have placed being upon being," that is [placing] the *iḍās* by means of the *iḍās*, and cattle by means of cattle.
Thus, this is "being covered by being."
Now, as for why they say "aim" while cutting up the portions for the cattle: this *iḍā*, when prepared with one and a half portions, is indeed cut asunder.
The *iḍā* is cattle;
therefore, cattle consume their food in a state of being cut apart and modified.
Now, when they said, "Let us come," "Let us go," they established themselves right here. Moreover, this was a healing for those very cattle.
Since this *iḍā*—though being common to the sacrifice—is divided, yet becomes manifold, therefore cattle are of various forms.
Various forms are produced after them.
That which begins with a *ṛc* is the form of the first day;

that which is enclosed on all sides (*pariṣṭubdha*) is the form of the second day; that which is enclosed on both sides (*ubhayataḥ-pariṣṭubdha*) is the form of the third day; and that which is not pressed down (*anutunna*) is the form of the fourth day.
The fourth [syllable] is repeated; the fifth is repeated with the syllable *iha*; [the repetition] of the sixth is as follows:
"Because this division of tone, while being uniform, becomes diverse, therefore this wind blows according to the seasons—cold in winter, warm in summer."
"Indra" is the case-ending for the first day; "Indram" for the second; "indreṇa" for the third; "indra" for the fourth; "indrāt" for the fifth; and "indra" again for the sixth.
Since this case-ending for Indra, while being the same, yet becomes different [in form], therefore that sun follows the seasons.
The cold [wind] blows during the winter, and the hot [wind] during the summer.
JB 3.334 |v1 Thus indeed this was in the beginning.
|v2 It desired: "May I be many; may I procreate; may I attain abundance."
That mind reflected.
Having found a second companion, it called out to him.
Therefore, having found a second companion, one calls out to him.
Then it became heated along with this mind.
Indeed, the mind is heat;
being heated, it emitted speech.
To those two he said, "Praise! Praise! I am praised! In that he said, "I am praised," that is the reason for the name *stoma* (praise).
One who knows thus praises with this [hymn], thinking, "May my own kin consider me the best."
These two indeed became these two *stomas*, the backward-facing and the forward-facing.

They are inhalation and exhalation; they are day and night; they are the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight; they are these two worlds; they are Indra and Agni; they are Mitra and Varuṇa; they are the Aśvins; they are that divine couple; whatever exists here [is they].
They became a pair.
They two, indeed, were born within Prajāpati.
Then this mind leaped upon speech.
That golden embryo was placed there as the immortal.
This Agni, indeed, is death.
Whatever gold they cast into him becomes more excellent.
This very embryo was born.
When it was born, they cleansed it, just as a mother cleanses a newborn calf from its impurities.
Of that [embryo], when they first removed the outer membrane (*ulba*), it became black iron;
when they removed the second membrane, it became silver.
That third membrane which they tore away became the greenish-yellow [flesh]. Therefore, that part is most radiant;
for it was his internal organ, whereas that which was the afterbirth remained in the umbilical cord.
That became iron;
therefore it is most foul-smelling.
From that, seventeen syllables were produced.
He divided them into two parts: nine on one side and eight on the other.
That very [set] became the *trivṛt* stoma and the *gāyatrī* metre.
He reflected: "This stoma and this metre—these two indeed are sufficient to bring forth progeny."
"Come, let me say to these two, 'Procreate yourselves!
Having praised with the *trivṛt*, he said to the *gāyatrī*: "Be abundant; be as large as you are!
Being composed of eight syllables, she made [the others] consist of three syllables each.
They became twenty-four.
He took six syllables from this Gāyatrī of twenty-four syllables.
He became the fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*).
He took two others.
It became the seventeenfold hymn-form (*stoma*).
He took four others;
it became the twenty-onefold hymn-form.
With half of that, Gāyatrī went to the Viṣuvat;
she took six others,
and it became the Triṇava Stoma.
He took six others; it became the thirty-three-fold hymn-form (*trayastriṃśa-stoma*). He did not find anything beyond that.
He reflected: "I shall run back toward these very powers already praised; I shall combine them two by two on each day."
He combined the Trivṛt and the Pañcadaśa;
that became the twenty-fourfold [stoma], the seventh day, with the Gāyatrī as the metre among the metres.

Therefore, both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara are performed here; for both these stomas belong to the Bṛhat and the Rathantara. While the Rathantara is indeed [the norm] in terms of measure, the Bṛhat is nevertheless employed as the *pṛṣṭha* chant.

He established the seventeenfold and the twenty-sevenfold [stomas]. Thus, that very forty-fourfold became the eighth day, with the *triṣṭubh* as the metre among the metres. Therefore, the *rathantara* is performed here as the *pṛṣṭha* chant.
He settled upon the twenty-first and the thirty-third.
Then six syllables remained over.
Now, those forty-eight which were left over became the forty-eighth, the ninth day.
The Jagatī became the meter of the meters.
Therefore, the Bṛhat is used here as the *pṛṣṭha* chant;
for both of these are *bārhata* stomas. Indeed, the Rathantara would be appropriate here by measure, but then there is the Bṛhat.
The back is made.
He uttered the *abhihiṃkāra* over those six syllables;
from that, he fashioned the six [seasons].
They became twenty-two.
He breathed upon them again with the *abhihiṅ* sound;
from that, he fashioned six.
They became eighteen.
He breathed upon them again;
from that, he fashioned six.
They became twenty-four.
That very tenth day became the twenty-fourth, and the *anuṣṭubh* became [the preeminent] among the meters. Therefore, the *sāman* has three *hiṃ*-utterances.
Regarding this they say: "The *stomas* pass beyond the *trivṛt*, but not the *gāyatrī* among the meters.
One should not say, "The *stomas* do not pass beyond the *trivṛt*, nor the *gāyatrī* among the meters," for the *stomas* have a threefold beginning, a threefold middle, and a threefold conclusion.
Moreover, the Gāyatrī does not exceed all the meters.
Therefore, this twelfth day is the nourishment of both the Trivṛt stoma and the Gāyatrī meter.
Indeed, the Gāyatrī is the Brahman.
The *kṣatra* is the threefold [stoma]. That which is the thunderbolt (*vajra*) is the *kṣatra*. Thus, this twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) is both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*.
Regarding this, they say: "The Trivṛt is indeed Brahman; the Gāyatrī is Brahman; this twelve-day rite is Brahman;
this entire twelve-day rite is indeed Brahman"—thus it should be understood.
Of this, there are these two verses:
In the beginning, four [winds] carry [the breath] forward when harnessed; they become six in the highest heaven.
Having become two by twos, they fly forth with their wings; having gone, upon what do they rest?
In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this world. He desired: "May I become many; may I procreate; may I attain abundance.
He performed austerity.
He beheld this twelve-day sacrifice with its meters arranged in expanded form (*vyūḍhachandas*).
He took it up; he sacrificed with it.
He separated it. In that he separated it, he separated his very limbs.
Those which were his bodily parts became these mortal creatures.
Then the Self became composed of mind. His body was the mind, and the vital breaths entered into it.
He was, as it were, spread out.
He said to the gods, "I desire a body. They asked, "What kind of body do you desire?
He replied, "Sacrifice me with the twelve-day rite using the *samūḍha* meters."
"So be it.
They caused him to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite by means of the *samūḍha-chandas* (the condensed meters).
In that they condensed [the meters], they thereby condensed his very limbs.

He became Prajāpati, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of speech, consisting of the Ṛgveda, consisting of the Yajurveda, consisting of the Sāmaveda, consisting of the Brahman, consisting of gold, and immortal.
This indeed is lightning.
This very thing is the threefold Veda:
that which is the upward flash of lightning are the Sāmans; that which is the horizontal flash are the Ṛcs; and that which repeatedly thunders are the Yajus.
He who knows this thus becomes this very deity.
Indeed, when this deity is praised, it becomes the sacrifice.

If they should ask, "By which deity is the sacrifice consecrated?", one should say, "By lightning. For this deity indeed is the one by whom the sacrifice is consecrated. Therefore, even if one should sacrifice with the twelve-day rite arranged according to its meters (*vyūḍhachandas*), [it is by this deity].
One should sacrifice with both [types of] *samūḍha* meters; for one who knows thus, the *āveṣṭi* sacrifice is indeed accomplished by means of both.
JB 3.341 |v1 There is indeed one deity who is self-existent: Prajāpati alone. |v2 He desired: "May I become many; may I procreate."
In this world, by means of the threefold hymn-form (*trivṛt-stoma*), he created the gods, the Vasus. They rushed toward him, saying, "Sweet! Sweet! and they ate him.
He drank from it, just as a newborn calf would suckle its mother.
He reflected: "If I remain here, they will exhaust me; come now, let me ascend upwards.
Then he thought: "Come, let me mix myself with those who, thinking of me and seeing me..."
Thinking, "Let them rest here," he created fire.
Having deposited him in this world, he ascended upwards by means of the fifteenfold [stoma].
He went to where this wind is.
They indeed created those very Rudras.
These [beings] followed after them, they rushed toward them from all sides;
they resolved to devour him.
He thought, "Come now, let me ascend upwards.
Having established Vāyu as his representative in this world, he ascended upwards by means of the seventeenfold [stoma].
He went to where that moon is.
They indeed created those very Ādityas.
These [beings] followed after them; those [others] rushed toward them. They resolved to devour him.
He thought, "Come now, let me ascend upwards."
Having established the moon as his representative in this world, he ascended upwards by means of the twenty-first [stoma] and went to where that sun is.
They created those very Viśvedevas. They created that end; these [beings] came together toward it, and those [others] rushed against it.
They resolved to devour it.
He thought, "Come now, let me ascend upwards.
Having established the sun as his representative in this world, he ascended upwards by means of the *triṇava* [stoma].
He went to where that Varuṇa was.
He created those [beings].
They followed after him;
they resolved to devour him.
He thought, "Come now, let me ascend upwards."
Having established Varuṇa as his representative in this world, he ascended upwards by means of the thirty-threefold [stoma] and went to where that Death was.
That became Death.
It made its limbs its mouth.
Having approached that Death which had become all-facing, they remained looking on with indifference.
They were unassailable.
They did not devour him there.
He reflected: "I am indeed evil; I am that which is death."
"Come now, let us ascend upwards! He, having deposited Death in this world, ascended twenty-four finger-breadths upwards. He went to where that world named Rocana is.
That became food (*aśanāya*).
Frightened by that state of hunger, the beings did not follow after it;
they stood gazing at it, saying, "He shines! He shines! (asau rocate).
That is his luminosity.
He thought: "I am indeed evil, for I am hunger.
Come now, let me rise upward."
Having deposited death itself in this world, he ascended twenty-four finger-breadths upward.
He went to where that world named Rocana is;
there, it became hunger.
Fearing him as a being of hunger, they did not follow after him;
they remained gazing at him, saying, "He shines! He shines!
That is his quality of shining.
He reflected: "I am indeed evil, for I am hunger.
Come now, let me ascend upwards.
He deposited day and night [as his support].
These two became thirst and hunger.
Day was thirst, and night was hunger.
Just as two door-panels might be set together, even so were these two, day and night, set together.
For the sake of non-overcoming;
indeed, those two overcome only one who knows thus.
Having deposited day and night in this very world, he ascended upwards by means of the forty-fourth [syllable].
He went to where that world named Kāma is.
By uttering those various sounds, he created rivers between [the worlds] so that this evil might not follow after him;
he made them indeed yielders of all desires.
He thought: "Come now, let me rise upward."
He ascended forty-eight finger-breadths upward. He went to where that world named Suvar is.
There he took great delight, thinking, "Much of his own property exists there."
That was his womb.
He thought, "Come now, let me gather these worlds into one world. He gathered these worlds into one world.

That very thing became the tenth day of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). He said, "Indeed, this has not become pleasant (*aka*) for me. Because he said, "Indeed, this has not become pleasant for me," that is the etymology of *nāka*.
This very tenth day is indeed the vault of heaven (nāka), this is the world of bliss (svarga-loka), this is the summit of the radiant one (bradhna).
Just as one might look down after climbing a tree or a mountain, even so does one look down upon other worlds from this world.
He looked upon these creatures who were tormented by hunger.
They rushed toward him in two forms: blue and golden.
That which is the black color of the rain-cloud when it is about to rain is the blue.
Then, that which flashes within the waters is gold. It rained down upon them;
from that, cooked rice was born.
Having eaten that, he exhaled;
he became *udana*.
That is the essence of *udana* being called *udana*.
This, indeed, is named Udana; they call him "Odana" (the Rice) cryptically. A second, superior food was born.
Having attained that, they churned it;
that became the *mantha*. That is the reason for the name *mantha*.
These two alone are the forms of food and drink: that which one eats and that which one drinks.
That which one eats is the form of boiled rice; that which one drinks is the form of the stirred drink.
He who knows this finds both of these available in his house.
These two, rice and barley, are indeed the two breasts of Prajāpati;
by means of them, he sustains these creatures.
JB 3.347 |v1 That world is named Upodaka, in which this fire [resides]. |v2 Then there is Ṛtadhāman, in which the wind [resides].
Then there is Śiva, in whom is the moon; then Aparājita, in whom is the sun; then Adhidyu, in whom is Varuṇa.
Then there is Pradyu, in whom death [resides]. Then there is Rocana, in whom hunger [resides].
Beyond this, day and night do not follow; for from here onwards, they have entered together but once, just as it is beyond this point.
The form of lightning would be that of kindled logs of wood piled together; thus it is.
Now, these worlds of Prajāpati extend upwards from here.
Desire is the eighth, heaven is the ninth, and the firmament is the tenth day.
This indeed is the departure, and that is the emergence.
These worlds are these very twelve days of the twelve-day rite.
He who knows this thus—these worlds indeed become his.
The world named Upodaka is situated in food; humans are its guardians, Agni is its overlord; whatever is the form of the flame, that is its form; it is established in water.
The world named Ṛtadhāman is pervaded by birds; its guardians are the Gandharvas and Apsarases; Vāyu is the overlord; its form is white; it is established in the vital breath (prāṇa).
The world named Aparājita is pervaded by the lunar mansions (nakṣatras); the Moon is its guardian; the Sun is the overlord; it is that which has risen.

And the form of the sun and that form from which it sets are established in the mind. The world named Adhidyu is situated in the sacrifice; the Ādityas are its guardians, Varuṇa is the overlord; the blue form is that of Parjanya when about to rain—that black is blue—or that of a kārtasvara gem, [which appears so] in falsehood.
Established.

The world named Pradyu is situated in the Immortal; the Rudras are its guardians, Death is its overlord; its form is red, which serves as a covering for the cow or as a garment for the great ascent; it is established in the Immortal, that which does not perish therein.
The world named Rocana is established in austerity; the Vasus are its guardians, for they were indeed the first among the gods to go [to that realm].
Therefore, they are the most excellent. Sacrifice is the overlord. That which is the form of golden treasure—that is its form.
He is established in truth.
These indeed are the worlds, these are the guardians, these are the overlords.
For one who knows thus, these indeed become his worlds and these his overlords.
Prajāpati created the gods;
he created them together with prosperity and speech, and together with food and water.
Those gods, having attained food and prosperity, were as if engaged in a communal feast through their speech; for prosperity is indeed food, and he (Agni) felt anxious.
He reflected: “How might I gather this prosperity of theirs?”
Having become the mind (*manas*), it entered them.
It stripped away all their splendor (*śrī*)— just as one might strip out jujube fruits—
and with its own mind, it seized their speech (*vāc*).
Even today, this speech is held by the mind.
For whatever one desires with the mind, that one speaks with speech. He reflected: "By what means now shall I take up speech from these [senses]?"
He assumed a human form.
Through that human form, he took up speech for them.
Therefore, a human being speaks all forms of speech.
Having gathered these waters, he ascended upwards.
He went to where that world of food named Ṛṣabha is. Now, the bull is indeed food.
When he eats, he then exerts himself.
He reflected: "What form indeed should I assume, so that another shall not surpass me?
He became a speckled goat.
Therefore, we do not obtain the unborn speckled one.
Those waters which he carried away are these very waters that are above.
And that speech which he carried away is this very thundering above; and as for [the water] that was in the waters...
It flashed within;
he looked upon these creatures who were hungry.
While they were prattling in blind darkness,
he cut off one syllable from this speech and emitted it as "vāk" (speech).
Having flown down, it came to rest in the midst of these worlds.
That became this very mandala;
he followed after that.
He became breath.
He shone forth from them.
Yet he was hungry; he tasted a single drop of those waters and let it fall. "Is this enough for them? [he wondered].
"It shall come to be.
He became tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold; he became as vast as this earth is.
Having attained that state, he shook it apart.
It became *mantha*. That is the origin of the name *mantha*.
Having eaten it, he breathed out.
That became *udana*.
That is the reason for the name *udana*.
Thus, these two are the very forms of food: that which one drinks and that which one eats.
That which he drinks of the stirred drink is its form; that which he eats of the cooked rice is its form.

Indeed, both of these—what he drinks and what he eats—are obtained in the house of one who knows thus. Regarding this they say: "Three drops come," namely, a drop of water, a drop of clarified butter, and a drop of honey.
Then, that drop which enters this [earth] becomes a drop of ghee among the plants and a drop of honey among the trees.
Regarding this, Āmalaka Ākūpayeya, Ahīna Āśvatthi, and Keśin Dārbhya held a deliberation:
"Which drop do you consider to be the first to arrive? Which drop do you consider to be the first? Which drop do you consider to be the first?"
Keśin said, "I consider it a drop of ghee.
Then Ahīnā said, "I consider it a drop of honey. Then Āmalaka said, "I consider it a mere spray."
In that very [water], they indeed brought it to completion:
"All this is born from water alone;
that speech which he emitted is Agni."
Now, that vital breath which he followed was Indra;
and he who was the progenitor of creatures, [resides] within the bull, in the world of food, and within the waters.
That is indeed the moon;
and he is indeed Prajāpati.
This very radiance, fashioned both beyond and within, stands shining forth as Agni and Indra.
This is the case with respect to the self.
That which is speech is this very speech; this vital breath sits above it.
Now, he who is the progenitor of creatures, that bull, in the world of food, within the waters—he is this very Puruṣa.
These deities are the same here and there;
they go here, and they go there.
Those which are these are those; those which are those are these.
He who meditates upon them as being within himself becomes one whose divinity is non-decaying. For the selves of those very gods are contained within Prajāpati.
Now, the selves of these vital breaths are gathered together in this person. Taking hold of this person, they guard him.
Regarding him, there is this verse:
The world is a bull, a truly great Yakṣa; there was nothing before him, nor anything after him.
That god whom the vital breaths (prāṇas) surround as a person and keep watch over, he knows the world and the Great Person.
Thus it is said.
Indeed, the gods, who are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), having taken hold of this person, remain awake as that very god.
He who is here within the eye—that is indeed Vāmana.
Whoever worships him as "the Dwarf" (Vāmana), this deity leads him toward what is desirable (vāma) after desirable thing.
For this reason, the kinsmen of a king (rājanyabandhu) always desire a dwarf from someone for some purpose;
they know him to be near to the name of this deity.
This very one does not decay;
it is indeed equal to both the young and the old.
Having withdrawn the vital breaths and shaken off the body, it ascends upwards together with those vital breaths.
By this [knowledge], indeed, Death drives away the bodies.
For this very deity, the two feet are fixed within the heart just as two blades of grass might be stuck into a lump of clay.
When those two tear it away, then he dies.
Therefore, even those who are ignorant say, "It will surely tear it away from him.
He who knows this thus—this deity does not depart from him until old age; he reaches a full lifespan.
The gods, through toil, austerity, and wandering in the forest, overcame the Asuras and the Rakṣases.
When those Asuras perceived this, thinking, "They are surely being defeated," they assumed the forms of women, appearing as the first and last [of their kind].
Those clad in rags, whatever among forms is most auspicious—that [they took].
They approached the gods;
the gods set them down.
For indeed, no one has women who are not dear to them.
Whatever brilliance, sensory power, and vigor they had won through their exertion, they poured into those [women].
When the Asuras realized, "So much indeed is the brilliance, sensory power, and vigor that these [gods] have acquired," they seized it and fled away.
It was unpleasant for those gods;
they felt as if they were depleted.
They said, "How indeed might we regain this brilliance, sensory power, and vigor?"
They saw these *vyāhṛtis*.
Having approached it, they took up the *rathantara* with the single-syllable [formula].
Therefore, it is performed on the first day.
With the two-syllabled word *pramā*, they took up the Bṛhat;
therefore, it is performed on the second day.
With the three-syllabled word *pratimā*, they took up the Airūpa.
Therefore, that is performed on the third day.
With the four-syllable phrase *asrīvaga*, he took up the Vairāja;
therefore, that is performed on the fourth day.
With the five-syllable [phrase] *śirikamasī*, they took up the Śākvara;
therefore, it is performed on the fifth day.
With the six-syllable [phrase] *chardir indriyāvat*, they took up the Raivata.
Therefore, it is performed on the sixth day.
[The verse] "O you who know, bestow upon us a dwelling, strength, and a womb, as a shade for the people"—with these words, they take up the Vāmadevya;
therefore, it is performed in the middle of the sacrifice.
When the *yonis* had become displaced beyond [their proper place], they took up the *yajñāyajñīya* chant with the words, "Then, O gods, bestow wealth.
Therefore, that [chant] is performed at the latter part of the sacrifice.
JB 3.354 |v1 Now they also say: "The gods are indeed free from evil; |v2 they do not sleep."

They, moreover, were overcome by the abundance of their exhaustion. While they were thus sleeping and heedless, the Asuras took away their brilliance, sensory power, and strength, and cast them down into the waters.
Viṣṇu perceived that. As those gods were waking up, there was something unpleasant for them.
Viṣṇu said to them, "Let there be nothing unpleasant for you."
"I indeed saw that," he said.
He caused them to descend into the waters. They looked all around within the waters; it was as if a hump were raised from the back.
Having taken that very thing with these same *vyāhṛtis*, they gave it to Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu, maintaining that splendor, sensory power, and vigor, measured it out.
Therefore, Viṣṇu is short.
Therefore, they immolate a short-necked ox dedicated to Viṣṇu.
When he strode forth while supporting [the earth], that very place became the footprint of Viṣṇu (viṣṇupada).
Therefore, the sacrifice of the Kaikeyas, which pertains to the footprint of Viṣṇu, is most excellent.
For they found this very sacrifice within him.
He who knows this thus takes away the splendor, the sensory power, and the vigor of his hateful rival.
Prajāpati created these worlds and these quarters.
Having created them, he created both the gods and the asuras.
He found them together.
They deposited that Brahman in Prajāpati.
Prajāti did not grasp it.
He caused it to enter into the waters. Those gods conquered the Asuras.
Having conquered and returned, they said, "O Prajāpati, grant us that Brahman which you possess."
He said, "Indeed, I did not lift it up;
I cast it into the waters.
He caused them to descend into the waters after it.
They beheld it within the waters, just as a hump might be raised above the back.
They said, "Let us create from here.
Saying "Om," they [proceeded] with this syllable toward her.
They released the *rathantara* as the radiance of the eastern quarter;
after that, the roar of Agni was released.
Therefore, they churn the fires from the *rathantara* hymns.
With this very syllable "Om," they released the great light from this southern quarter.
After that, the roar of Parjanya was released.
Therefore, they cause the drums to resound during the Bṛhat-stotra;
consequently, Parjanya becomes rain-giving.
With this very syllable "Om," they emitted the Vairūpa-sāman from this western direction.
From that, the sound of the wind was emitted.
Therefore, during the chant of the Vairūpa, they shake [the vessels] with fans;
hence, a downward wind comes forth.
With this very syllable "Om," they emitted the Vairāja luster from this northern quarter.
Thereupon, the cry of birds was emitted after it;
therefore, just as birds utter their voices by repeatedly taking them up again, so too does one utter the Vairāja by repeatedly taking it up again.
Thus they praise.
With this very syllable "Om," they emitted the Śākvara luster from this upward direction.
That was emitted following the sound of the waters.
Therefore, during the Śākvara chant, they chant while placing water down [as a substrate].
By means of this very syllable *om*, they released the radiance of the Raivata [Sāman] from this quarter;
after that, the lowing of cattle was released.
Therefore, during the chant for Raivata, they make the sound of cattle; they cause the calves to low together with their mothers.
They said, "We know that from which these were created.
They perceived the Vāmadevya hymn within the waters itself.
He took that up.
From it, all speech was emitted, as were the individual *pṛṣṭha* chants. These *pṛṣṭha* chants, once emitted, scorched the quarters.
At that time, these [rays] indeed shone forth.
He shines for himself; they say of him who knows this, "He shines.
This deity meditated upon them.
That which was uttered here before was indeed this form of a person. She took the splendor of the *rathantara* by means of the *trivṛt* stoma and the *gāyatrī* metre;
she deposited that from here.

With the fifteenfold *stoma* and the *triṣṭubh* metre, he took the share of the *bṛhatī*. He deposited that here. With the seventeenfold *stoma* and the *jagatī* metre, he took the share of the *vairūpa*.
They took that from there.
With the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*) and the *anuṣṭubh* metre, they took the radiance (*bhās*) of Vairāja;
they took that from there.
With the twenty-sevenfold hymn-form (*stoma*) and the *paṅkti* metre, he took the share of the Śākvara Sāman;
that he deposited from here.
With the thirty-threefold hymn-form and the *aticchandas* metre, he took the share of the Raivata Sāman.
They took that from here.
Therefore, all beings are ultimately established within the waters.
As they were taking it up, the voices cried out, "Adita! Aditi! (The Undivided).
That is the reason for the Āditya’s being called Āditya.
O you who revile! That brilliance, sensory power, and vigor of yours—this impurity, the reviler releases upon himself, provided he knows thus.
All beings approached him, saying, "He is noble! He is noble!
That is why he is called Sorya.
This one is indeed named Sūrya. They call him "Sūrya" cryptically.
"You are our noble one, you are our supporter," thus do his own people and the wandering ascetics worship him who knows this.
When he took it up facing westward and made it resound (*svarayan*), that is why the *saura* [cup] is called *saurya*.
Indeed, that which consists in making it resound is the very essence of the *svara* (the tone).
Those gods said, "He has not indeed stolen it."
That day became [the day];
"What has been given to him has indeed come into being," he thought, and that very thing became the night.
This, indeed, is the birth of day and night.
He who thus knows this birth of day and night attains day and night; he does not pass beyond them. Indeed, everything else here is finite, but these two—day and night—are indeed infinite.
Those two indeed reach everything as this [universe] revolves;
just as one standing on the seat of a chariot would look out at the wings [of the vehicle], even so do these two, day and night, look out from their position in the world of the sun.
He said to his father Prajāpati, "Therefore, give this splendor, this sensory power, and this vigor of yours to me. "So be it," [the father replied].
He gave it to him.
Therefore, even while still living, a father hands over these [powers] to his son.

He took from the sky its sovereignty, from the stars their lordship, from the intermediate space his own self, from the wind his form, from men their command, from the cattle their sight, from the waters their vigor, and from the plants their sap.

The movement of the trees, the generative organ of birds, the flame of fire, the heart of the earth, the fragrance of gold, the thunder of speech, the assembly of the ancestors, and the light of the moon—
because he took these from those beings, that is the *ādityatva* (the nature of the Āditya) of the Āditya.
He who knows thus takes away the splendor of his hateful rival.
This very deity, when consecrated, has the black antelope skin as her hair and the beard.
Of her, those rays which are directed downward are the beard; those which are directed upward are the hair.
The black antelope skin is indeed day and night.
Because he made his dwelling in heaven, therefore he is consecrated (*dīkṣita*).
Verily, he who sacrifices makes his dwelling in heaven.
Whatever victory one wins through initiation and whatever prosperity one attains, he who knows this wins that victory and attains that prosperity.
The Dawn is his wife; the Moon is the Soma-drink. Therefore, one should undergo initiation together with one's wife.
This very deity takes away the splendor, the sensory power, the vigor, and the fame of one who undergoes initiation.
Therefore, one who is about to be initiated should worship the sun with the mantra: "O deity, you are the initiated;
as such, you take away the splendor, the sensory power, the vigor, and the fame of the one being initiated."
"Do not take away my brilliance, sensory power, vigor, and fame;
may I follow your consecration with skill.
For one who consecrates himself with this [formula], his deity does not take away his brilliance, sensory power, vigor, and fame.
This, then, is the support of the *uktha* itself.
Those rays of his which are directed hitherward— by them these worlds are supported, as well as whatever breath-possessing beings there are that are hitherward, together with their bodies.
Then, by those [rays] which are upward, those worlds of his that extend beyond this one are supported; and furthermore, whatever is unmanifest and bodiless—that is so.
Because this deity stands supporting both the gods and the asuras from within, therefore it is called *stambha* (the Supporter).
He would indeed become paralyzed;
moreover, if anyone were to examine him while he is paralyzed, one should say to him: "I deliver you to that deity who is paralysis."
"I shall cut away this affliction; you shall be led down [to safety].
He is indeed led down to that divine affliction. Those rays which are directed downward are these *avaśas*, possessed of food, belonging to Death.
Now, those that go upward are indeed the worlds of immortality.
Those rays which go downward are called *horayaḥ*, like a reed or a *vasuśiras*—or rather, an *arva*. And those that go upward are called *uparīyaṃsaḥ*.

Just as an elephant might take up [something] with its trunk and place it upon its back, even so this deity, having taken up the one who knows this with its broad rays, places him upon a wider space. This world belongs to him who is beyond this [world].
Neither non-being nor being existed then; there was not the atmosphere, nor the sky beyond it.
What was concealed? Where? In whose protection? Was there water, unfathomably deep?
Thus it was said.

When that [unmanifest] did not exist, and when nothing at all existed, the light of Truth (ṛta) surged forth, the light of Reality (satya) surged forth, and the light of austerity (tapas) surged forth.
In that regard, "Ṛta" is speech; "Satya" is breath; and "Tapa" is mind.
Of these, food alone was their light. They became one.
Having become one, it swelled with this food and this light.
It became like a honeycomb when a bee has poured [honey] into it, yet not quite so.
It thought: "Come now, let me create a lower vital breath."
Below that, he created the vital breath (*prāṇa*), just as there is space below a woman. From that, the waters were emitted with the sound "balabalabali. This was the great expanse of water.
Now, as for what they say here: "In the beginning, this was indeed the waters, a great ocean"—these are those very waters. Their waves were swelling, *phālphāśli*. That became a golden egg.
Its lower skull was green and its upper one was silver.
Having lain there for a hundred years of the gods, it burst open, or rather, [there emerged] a thousand splendors.
At that time, they were indeed called *dyumnā*. As great as this year is, so many were the images of the year.
By means of the *dyumnas*, they used to discern the year.
Now, previously, day and night were indeed joined together and undifferentiated.
They understood it as the year.
Then, previously, day and night were indeed joined together and undifferentiated.
These two were indeed distinguished by the Agnihotra itself.
Then it was split apart by this speech: "O ladle, O vessel, O two bowls, O two potsherds, move apart!
Toward what world shall we be born?"
With the sound "Phaṭ," the cosmic egg was split asunder.
Of that [egg], the lower shell became this earth;
then, the upper shell became that sky.
Then that which was between became this intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
The speech he uttered while being born became the threefold Veda. Whatever deity he uttered while being born at the beginning, that indeed became Brahman.
He thought: "I have indeed created this great foundation, these worlds.
But if I create anything further than this, it will surely know its own foundation. Come now, let me create."
He meditated upon himself with his mind. From that, two drops came into being: the two months of spring.
He said to them both, "Be created.
They asked, "In which direction shall we go?"
"‘This one’—thus [it was said]. Those two were created with the utterance ‘Om.
That itself was their food, that was their light, and that shone for them."
Then those two became the *rāṣṭra*.
Indeed, he who knows this becomes a *rāṣṭra*.
He then meditated upon himself once more by means of the mind alone.
In that [drop], two drops came into being: the two summer months.
He said to them, "Be created.
"To which direction shall we go? they asked.
"Into this [world]. They two created by means of this very speech, "Om.
Having fallen into this direction, they both established themselves.
From them, the great light was emitted. That itself became their food and their light; it shone for them.
Thereupon, they became the kingdom.
He who knows this indeed becomes the sovereign of a kingdom.
He then meditated upon himself once more by means of the mind alone. From that, two drops came into being: the two months of summer.
He said to them, "Be created.
"In which direction?
"In this one."
Those two were emitted with the very word "Om.
Having fallen in this direction, they became established.
Great light was emitted after them.
That very thing was their food, that was their light; by means of that, they heated themselves. Thereupon, the two of them became *rāṣṭra*.
Indeed, one who knows thus becomes *rāṣṭra*.
He meditated upon himself once more with his mind alone. From him there arose two drops, the two months of the rainy season.
He said to them, "Be reproduced."
"Which direction shall we go? "This one," he replied.
Then, with the very word "Om," those two were emitted.
Having fallen in that direction, those two came to rest. Vairūpa radiance was emitted after them; that indeed became their food, that their light, and by that they were warmed.
Then those two became the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*).
Indeed, he who knows thus becomes the kingdom.
He [the Self] again meditated upon himself by means of the mind alone.
In that [drop], two drops came into being: the two autumn months.
He said to them, "Be created.
"To which direction shall we go? they asked.
"Into this"—
saying "Om," those two were emitted by that very speech. Having fallen in that direction, they established themselves there.
From those two, the Vairāja splendor was emitted.
Their food was that very thing; that was their light, and by that they shone.
Thereupon, they became the kingdom.
He who knows this indeed becomes the sovereign of a kingdom.
He then mentally entered back into himself.
Within him, two drops came into being: the two winter months.
He said to them, "Be created.
They, saying "Om," were created by that very word.
Having fallen in this direction, they established themselves there.
From them, the Śākvara luster was emitted. That became their food, that became their light, and that shone for them.
Thereupon, they became the kingdom.
He who knows this indeed becomes the possessor of a kingdom.
He meditated upon himself once more with his mind alone. From that, two drops came into being: the two months of the cold season (śiśira).
He said to them, "Be created.
"In which direction?
"In this one."
Those two were emitted with the very word "Om.
Having fallen in this direction, they took their stand there.
Following them, the light of Raivata was emitted.
That very thing was their food, that was their light; by means of that, they heated themselves. Thereupon, those two became the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*).
Truly, one becomes a kingdom who knows thus.
Then he sought [the cattle] by means of two *jy* verses.
Therefore, in the winter season, cattle seek [their fodder] by means of two *jy* verses.
He reflected: "Since I have created these three, let me now create from this [fifth].
He meditated upon the Gāyatrī with the Trivṛt Stoma;
from that, he created the Vasus.
They went toward this quarter.
By means of the fifteenfold hymn-form (*stoma*), they attained the *triṣṭubh* meter.
From that, he created the Rudras.
They followed this direction.
He attained the Jagatī metre by means of the seventeenfold Stoma;
from that, he created the Ādityas.
They followed this direction;
by means of the twenty-first [stoma], he attained the Jagatī meter;
from that, he created the Ādityas.
They proceeded toward this quarter.
By means of the twenty-onefold hymn-form (*stoma*), they ascended to the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
From that, he created the All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*).
They went toward this direction.
By means of the Triṇava Stoma, they attained the Paṅkti;
from that, he created the Maruts.
They proceeded toward this direction.
By means of the thirty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*), they attained the *aticchandāḥ* metre. From that, he created the Sādhyas and the Āptyas.
They proceeded toward this direction.

JB 3.364 |v1 These deities, once created—the *stomas*, the *chandases*, the seasons, and the *grahas*—remained as it were separately, each with its own splendor shining forth; they did not stand in relation to one another’s superiority. |v2 They did not acknowledge each other's preeminence.
They said, "Indeed, we shall not stand for one another's superiority. Let us seek him who may rule over us.
They went to Prajāpati, their progenitor, and said, "Indeed, we shall not stand for one another's superiority."
"Let us remain;
release us from him who has power over us.
