Prajāpati said, "Indeed, this much was the brilliance, sensory power, and vigor that existed in him."
"I have created you.
"Then, indeed, do you perform penance for a year.
"Having performed penance for a year, do you come together to me, [saying]: 'What one has attained, what one [has attained], what one [has attained]!'"
They performed austerities for a year.
Having performed austerities for that year, they came together.
What one [of them] perceived, what the second, and what the third—those [perceptions] they poured into his womb through their fervor (*manyu*).
From that Indra was born.
Regarding this, the following verse is recited:
"When they say, 'He has come forth from the horse,' I consider him to have been born from vital power (*ojas*)."
"He has gone from wrath; he stood in the dwellings, from which Indra was born—Indra knows this.
Thus [it is said].
"He has gone from wrath" means that they poured him into his womb within wrath.
"He stood in the *harmya*s"—the *harmya*s are indeed the hearts;
for it is the heart that becomes angry.
"I consider him born of vigor."
JB 3.365 |v1 They asked Gaurvīta: "Did you indeed see Indra being born?
|v2 He replied as follows.
"Regarding what they say, 'From the horse he has gone forth,' I consider him to have been born from *ojas* (vital force).
He has gone forth from *manas* (mind) and has taken his stand in the dwellings; from whence he was born, Indra alone knows.
"I consider him born from *ojas*," he said. "So do I," he replied.
"Indra alone knows from whence he was born.
Having extracted his head, he looked out;
he saw that all this [world] of theirs had been seized.
He said, "Since all this of theirs has been won, for which world shall I be born? Give that indeed to me!"—
"These two, then, are yours."
"Give me the two months of spring," [he said].
"I shall give these to you," [she replied]. Thus, crying out "Food! Food!", she fell down before him toward the eastern direction; the *Rathantara* [Sāman] was her portion.
He took it up.
He placed it from here. One who knows thus bestows the vigor of two upon one.
He entered him once again.
He said to him, "Be born indeed.
He replied, "In that case, let him grant these two summer months to me."
"Let me give these to you," he said; and saying "Food! Food! he fell down and took from this southern quarter the great light.
He deposited that here.
He who knows thus bestows vigor upon the four;
he entered into him once again. He said to him, "Be born indeed!"
He said, "Indeed, give those to me; give me the two months of the rainy season.
"I shall give these to you," he replied; and thinking, "Food! Food!", he fell down and took from this western direction the *vairūpa* luster.
He deposited that here. He who knows thus obtains the vigor of six in one.
He entered into him once again.
He said to him, "Be born! He replied, "Will he indeed grant these to me? Will he grant me these two autumn months?
[The other said,] "I shall grant them to you. Thinking, "Food! Food!", he fell from that northern direction as the Vairāja light.
He took it up.
He placed it from here. He who knows thus bestows the vigor of the eight upon himself.
He entered that very [body] once again.
He said to him, "Be born!
He replied, "But surely he must grant me these two winter months; let him grant them to me."
"I shall give these two to you," he said; and saying "Food! Food! he fell down and took from the upward direction the Śākvara light.
He deposited that from here.
He who knows thus bestows the vigor of ten upon one.
He entered into him once again.
He said to him, "Be born indeed!"
He said, "Indeed, let him grant these two winter months to me; let him grant them to me.
"I shall grant these to you," he replied. Thinking, "Food, food! he fell [upon them] and took from this direction the splendor of Raivata. He deposited that here.
He who knows thus bestows the vigor of twelve upon one.
He reflected: "How indeed might I seize these seasons?"
He saw them lying on their backs.
With his head he grasped these two [fires] facing eastward; with his arms, these ones separately; and with his feet, those two facing westward.
The two upper ones are directed upward, and the two lower ones by the ribs.
Having grasped them thus, he swept them around below.
This very [fire] shines, overlaid upon this glory, throughout the seasons and the year.
He entered him again together with all of this.
He said to him: "Indeed, I was not able to lift you up at first alone;
you will certainly not be able to lift yourself up together with all of this. Be born [again]."
In that [place], the waters surged; he looked all around.
He said: "Surely let him give these to me; let him give me the waters, and then I shall be born.
To him, he gave six thousand of the waters.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"No other crosses over them; no one is able to pervade them.
In them, honey, milk, clarified butter, and curd flow from all sides—six thousand [streams] with their mother."
Thus it is said.
These indeed are the Ambayas; they are the very quarters of space.
It is these that flow for him by the thousands, and it is these that satisfy him.
He was born. When he was born, they approached him [saying]: "Splendor has been born; power has been born; vigor has been born; the *brahman* has been born; the *kṣatra* has been born;

the driver of the seven animals has been born; the sustainer of the seven directions has been born; as one born, he has been born; as a progenitor, he has been born; as a father of progenitors, he has been born."
"He was born," he said. "Indeed, Jānitrī caused even himself to be approached for procreation. He who knows this becomes one who causes [himself] to be approached for procreation.
When he was born, they placed this royal throne for him;
upon it, they consecrated him.

The Vasus [attain] sovereignty; the Rudras, over-sovereignty; the Ādityas, self-sovereignty; the Viśve Devas, imperial sovereignty; the Maruts, universal sovereignty; and the Sādhyas and Āptyas, the supreme office.
While he was thus situated, his father Prajāpati desired him.
He said to the Vasus, "Give this one to me.
They replied, "We shall not be able to do so; we cannot harm our father Prajāpati."
He spoke to the Rudras; they did not desire it. He spoke to the Ādityas; they likewise did not desire it.
Then he spoke to the Maruts: "What would come of that for us?"
"That midday pressing which is exclusively mine shall become common to you as well.
"So be it," [they replied].
They handed him over to him.
As he was saying, "This is mine, this is mine," they took away that splendor by which the sun shines there. Because he said, "This is mine (candram ma)," therefore it is called *candramas*.
Whenever he would take from it again and again, it would remain exactly as it was before.
Therefore, even today, this [sun] possesses light.
Just as it shines thus by day, so does it glow by night.
He knew: "This [world] is indeed inexhaustible.
He seized it.
He said to him: "Do not let me regret that [act] toward you!"
"No," he said, "I shall simply warm myself toward it.
Therefore, they see him on both days and nights;
indeed, they warm themselves toward him.
These two, indeed, are father and son: namely, the moon and the sun.
The moon is the father; the sun is the son.
The moon is the further (para); the sun is the nearer (apara).
These two have attained the state of preeminence among all the deities.
Just as these two have attained the state of preeminence among all the deities, even so does he who knows this attain the state of preeminence among his own people.
Thus with reference to the deities; now with reference to the self:
this very moon is [the heart], this sun is [the eye].
Therefore, one should worship it in this way with reference to the self.
That, indeed, is the Bhṛgucakṣus.
If he should hate someone, he should say of him, "Look at him with the Bhṛgucakṣus!
He certainly does not become fit to be enjoyed [by others].
When the *chandases* performed the sacrifice, the *bṛhatī* alone sang the *udgītha*.
Now, those two which are the subsequent *pragāthas* were the *prastotṛ* and the *pratihartṛ*.
The householder is Amitacchandas, Virāj is Brahman, Gāyatrī is Maitrāvaruṇa, Jagatī is Hotṛ, and Paṅkti is Adhvaryu.
That which is its fifth foot is Pratiprasthātṛ; Triṣṭubh is Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
The Uṣṇih and Kakubh meters are the Neṣṭṛ and Āptor; the Anuṣṭubh is the Acchāvāka; the Dvipadā is the Unnetṛ;
the Akṣarapaṅkti is the Grāvastut; the Ekapadā is the Subrahmaṇya; and the Aticchandas is the Āgnīdhra. This twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) is indeed the Gāyatrī, for it possesses all meters.
For by all these meters the twelve-day sacrifice is performed;
indeed, all these meters are employed in the twelve-day sacrifice.
Therefore, if one should desire an invitation (*upahava*) within these meters, one should then desire an invitation among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

When Yadu sacrificed, he sacrificed having become these very metres; when Yadu officiated as priest for another, he officiated having become these very metres. For him who knows this, there is indeed no affliction whatsoever.
Whoever speaks ill of him meets with misfortune.
Regarding this they say: "In what Stoma, in what metre, and in what deity is the Dvādaśāha finally established?"
He should say: "In the *trivṛt* stoma, in the *gāyatrī* metre, in the deity Agni, the twelve-day rite is ultimately established.
For it is indeed by means of the *trivṛt* stoma, the *gāyatrī* metre, and the deity Agni that they set out.
With these, they indeed rise up.
Regarding this, they say: "What is the one *stoma*, what is the one *chandas*, and which is the one deity that carries the twelve-day rite?
He should reply: "The *trivṛt* is the one *stoma*, the *gāyatrī* is the one *chandas*, and Speech (*vāk*) is the one deity that carries the twelve-day rite."
He should say: "The *trivṛt* stoma is one; the *gāyatrī* metre is one; the goddess Vāc is one; these carry the twelve-day rite."
For indeed, all the *stomas* are produced from the *trivṛt*, and all the meters (*chandas*) are produced from the *gāyatrī*.
Speech as a single deity carries the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). Regarding this, they ask: "What is its *stoma*, what is its meter, and what is its deity?"
He should say: "The twenty-onefold hymn-form, the *virāj* metre, Āditya as the deity, and the twelve-day rite.
For Āditya indeed is the twenty-onefold, Āditya is the *virāj*, and Āditya is the deity of the twelve-day rite.
Regarding this, they say: "That which is the *sāman* of the twelve-day rite is the *sāman* of all this."
"What is the *stobha* of the *sāman*, what is its *pada*, and what is its *akṣara*?
He should reply: "The sun indeed is the *stobha* of the *sāman*, the intermediate space is its *pada*, and speech is its *akṣara*.
Regarding this, they ask: "What is the *stobha* of the *stobha*, what is the *pada* of the *pada*, and what is the *akṣara* of the *akṣara*?"
He should say: "The eye alone is the stobha of the stobha; the mind alone is the pada of the pada; the vital breath alone is the syllable of the syllable."

Regarding this they say: "How do the *stomas* become a single *stoma*? How do the *chandas* become a single *chandas*? How do the days (*ahāni*) become a single day? How do the forms (*rūpāṇi*) become a single form?"
"How do the *pṛṣṭhas* become a single *yajus*; how do the *sāmans* become a single *sāman*; how do the Vedas become a single Veda; and how, having all become one, is this established in what?
He should reply: "By means of the *stoma*, the *stomas* become one; by means of the *chandas*, the *chandases* become one."

"Day" (*ahar*)—the days become one; "form" (*rūpa*)—the forms become one; "back-chant" (*pṛṣṭha*)—the back-chants become one; "deity" (*devatā*)—the deities become one; "Ṛc verse" (*ṛk*)—the Ṛc verses become one;
"Yajus formula" (*yajus*)—the Yajus formulas become one; "Sāman chant" (*sāman*)—the Sāman chants become one; "Veda" (*veda*)—the Vedas become one.

[They say: "The mind, having become one, is all this; it is established in the vital breath (prāṇa). Regarding that, they ask: "If the mind, having become one, is all this and is established in the vital breath, in what then is the vital breath established?"
"One should say, 'The person' (puruṣa).
For the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed established in the person."
He who knows that which is in the person—verily, for one who knows thus, the vital breath (prāṇa) is firmly established.
Therefore, indeed, one who knows thus should be heavy; he should not make all this light.
Moreover, he should know: "I am indeed all this; in me all this is established."
His world does not perish.
Regarding this, they say: "One should know him today for twelve days, or one should think, 'He indeed knows,' provided that he knows him as established in all directions."
There are indeed ten directions.
There are twelve days of the ten-day rite (*dvādaśāha*).
Of that [rite], these two worlds are the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*) and the concluding day (*udayanīya*): this world is the introductory day, and yonder world is the concluding day.
The concluding [offering]. Of that,
this eastern direction is the first day, this the second, this the third,
this the fourth, this the fifth, this the sixth, and this intermediate direction is the seventh day, this...
This is the eighth; this is the ninth; this is the tenth.
This very twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) is established in all directions; he becomes of the same world as all the gods.
Neither the gods nor he himself can prevail over him, were he not to follow after them.
He who knows this is indeed one of the gods. Prajāpati is the twelve-day sacrifice;
its worlds are the quarters.
This very twelve-day sacrifice is established in all the worlds.
He who knows this twelve-day sacrifice as established in all the worlds becomes established in all the worlds.
This very one who shines yonder is indeed the twelve-day sacrifice; he is Indra, he is Prajāpati, and he alone is all this.
Thus, when this [sacrifice] has been performed, the Brahman shines forth, having been established therein.
The ruling power and the kingdom, the phenomenal and the real— these are below; asceticism and splendor, the ancestral offering and the immortal— these are above.
Thus, whatever here is the *kṣatra*—whether it be Indra, or Varuṇa, or King Soma—that is that. And whatever is the kingdom, whatever are the divine subjects, the Maruts—that is that.
The Night is the *ṛta*.
Truth is that day;
austerity is lightning; and the brilliance is that thunderbolt which falls from the lightning.
Svadhā is rain;
that food is the immortal.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
The kṣatra, the kingdom, cosmic order (ṛta), truth (satya), and the lower forms of sacred power (brahman) are established therein.
Heat, splendor, self-power, and immortality—these abide in the upward-tending [rays]; in their midst, the supreme sacred power (brahman) shines forth.
Thus it is said.
And this very Brahman shines forth in the middle. Those who know it thus sit upright.
Just as a kṣatriya would be placed in a position of authority, even so is this Brahman placed for the sake of non-transgression.
[The text provided contains only punctuation marks.]
When the gods performed the sacrifice, Bṛhaspati alone was their Udgātṛ;
Gauḥ and Ayāsya were the Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ respectively.
Prajāpati himself was the householder;
Indra himself was the Brahman priest.
He (Indra) recited from the Brāhmaṇa.
Mitra and Varuṇa were the two Maitrāvaruṇas;
Agni was the Hotṛ.
He made the Āgnīdhra, the Aśvins the two Adhvaryus, the Maruts the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ, and the Viśve Devās [the other priests].
The Acchāvāka [is the priest], Arbuda is the Grāvastut.
Viṣṇu praised the sacrifice.
Soma is the Unnetṛ; it was Brahmā himself who called out the Subrahmaṇyā, or Gāyatreya.
This twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) is the sacrifice to all the deities.
Indeed, the twelve-day sacrifice is performed with all these deities;
for all these deities are brought into being within the twelve-day sacrifice.
Therefore, when one desires an invitation (*upahava*) from these deities, one should likewise desire an invitation from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
For when he sacrifices, he sacrifices having become these very deities; and when he causes [others] to sacrifice, he causes them to sacrifice having become these very deities.
For him who knows this, there is indeed no suffering whatsoever;
he who speaks ill of him meets with suffering.
Regarding this they say: "Since other sacrificial sessions (satra) are designated by nights, why then is the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha) designated by days?"
He should say: "All the gods, having approached Prajāpati their father, said, ‘How great indeed are you?
He replied, ‘I am twelve days.
Because he said, ‘I am twelve days,’ that is the reason for the twelve-day nature of the Dvādaśāha."
This, indeed, was Prajāpati Saṃvatsara.
He spoke of these very twelve months as "I am the twelve-day [rite].
Regarding this, they say: "What is the door? What are the ten? What is the day?"
He should say: "The sun indeed is the door; the sun is the ten; the day.

When he says, "The sun indeed is the door," it is because this [sun] alone is the door to the heavenly world. And when he says, "The sun is the ten," it is because this [sun] alone shines in these ten directions.
Now, as for [the statement] "The sun is the day," for he indeed is the day.
Regarding this, they say: "Should one perform the sacrifice with the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha) or not? One should say: "No."
He who causes one to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite attains the *stomas*, he attains the *chandases*, he attains the gods, he attains the worlds, and he attains his desires.
And he becomes free from evil through these worlds.
Moreover, both those who understand it and those who do not consider him one who performs what has already been done.
Therefore, one should certainly not cause [someone] to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite; yet they also say that one must indeed cause him to sacrifice.
The twelve-day sacrifice is indeed Prajāpati; the Udgātṛ is Prajāpati; the sacrificer is Prajāpati.
The deity of the Udgātṛ and the sacrificer are indeed the same.
These two attain the same prosperity, conquer the same world, and [attain union] with the same deity.
They both find firm support.
Furthermore, the sacrificer is indeed the sacrifice, and the Udgātṛ is the Brahman.
Having thus found support in the sacrifice itself, he wins the same world as the Brahman.
He becomes one who shares the same world as the sacrificer.
Regarding this, they say: "Since this single deity has become everything, even the twelve-day sacrifice, which deity is that?"
"One should say, 'The vital breath (prāṇa),' for the vital breath indeed became this entire universe."
As for [the syllable] *dvā*: this entire world indeed lives by means of that door (*dvāra*).
And as for [the syllable] *dā*: he indeed gives all this. And as for [the syllable] *śā*: he indeed touches all this as peace (*śam*).
Now, as for "dhā," this indeed carries all this [universe].
He who knows this thus— whether he performs what is good or whether he does not— nevertheless, only what is good is accounted as his doing.
Then he should know: "I do only what is good, not what is evil;
that world which is attained by one who does good—that shall be my world.
For him, that very world indeed becomes his.
Indeed, the world of everything else decays;
but the world of one who knows this does not decay.
This is that deity who leads [the sacrifice].
For this deity indeed caused all this to breathe;
because it caused [it] to breathe (*prāṇayat*), therefore it is called *prāṇa*. When one who knows thus departs from this world, this very deity carries him up and forth.
It leads him to that world from which there is nothing beyond.

Regarding this, they say: "He who knows this [sacrifice] as established in the sun should perform the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) himself, or he should cause another to perform the twelve-day sacrifice. For the twelve-day sacrifice is indeed the sun; its day and night are [the constituent parts].
The *prāyaṇīya* and the *udayanīya* [offerings].
The day itself is the *prāyaṇīya*, and the night is the *udayanīya*.
Those rays of his which extend eastward constitute the first day.
Those that go southward are the second; those that go westward are the third; those that go northward are the fourth;
those that go upward are the fifth; those that go downward are the sixth; that which shines is the seventh; and that which... [is the eighth].
That which shines is the eighth; that which is like copper is the ninth; the solar disc itself is the tenth day.
This very twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha) is established in the sun.
He who thus knows this twelve-day rite as established in the sun stands firm in the sun; he reaches a full lifespan, strikes away evil, and goes to the heavenly world—he who knows thus.
This is with reference to the deities.
Now, with reference to the self:
this very person who is in the eye is the twelve-day sacrifice.
Its eyelashes are indeed the opening and concluding days; those eyelashes which are directed inward are the opening day (*prāyaṇīya*).
Those which are the upward ones are the *udayanīya*;
its lower track is the first day.
The second [layer] is the *uttarā*; the third is the *samameṣa*; the fourth is the white; the fifth is the black; the sixth is the pupil.
The vital breaths of this very person are those subsequent days:
the breath itself is the seventh day, the eye the eighth, the ear the ninth, and speech itself is the tenth day.
As for why it is *dvāc*: indeed, these two persons are seen here.
And as for why it is *dā*: for he gives (*datte*) all this. And as for why it is *śā*: for he touches (*spṛśati*) all this as peace (*śam*).
Now, as for "dhā," he indeed bestows all this;
as for "śā," he indeed touches all this with peace;
and as for "hā," he indeed takes away all this.
This very one is the Uktha.
For he, as it were, raises up all this;
therefore, he alone is the Uktha.
This very [breath] is the Ukthya;
for it touches all this [world] with peace (*śam*). And as for the word "dhā," it is because it carries (*harati*) all this [world].
This very one is the Uktha;
for he, as it were, raises up all this world.
Therefore, he alone is the Uktha.
This very one is the *ṛc*. His name is indeed "ūrka. They call him "ṛc" cryptically.
Therefore, he alone is the *uktha*;
he alone is the *yajus*,
for he, as it were, causes all this to decay (*jarayati*).
Therefore, this alone is the Yajus; this alone is the Sāman;
for all this is indeed gathered together in this.
Therefore, this alone is the *sāman*.
This very thing is the *udgītha*;
for by the syllable "ut," all this is upheld.
Now, as for its being "gīti," it is because this [Prāṇa] swallows (girati) all this;
and as for the syllable "tha," that is indeed food for it.
Therefore, this alone is the Udgītha.
This very one is Brahman;
for he, as it were, causes all this to age. Therefore, he alone is the Yajus.
This very one is the *sāman*. For all this is gathered together (*sameta*) in him;
therefore, he alone is the *sāman*.
This very thing is the *udgītha*. Because it is "ut," by this all this is upheld;
and because it is "gīti," for this indeed swallows up all this.
Now, as for the syllable *tha*, that is indeed his food.
Therefore, this very [syllable] is the Udgītha;
it is this very [syllable] that is Brahman.
For he indeed sustains all this;
therefore, he alone is Brahman.
Indeed, his name is "the Sustainer" (bharma).
They call that "Brahman" in its hidden sense.
This deity indeed sustains him in this world and in the yonder world, who knows thus.
He who thus [knows] this twelve-day rite with respect to the deities, with respect to the sun, with respect to the person, and with respect to the self—
He knows it as established; he stands facing the sun. For him, all the Vedas, all the gods, and all the worlds milk their desires.
Having surpassed the gods, he wins residence in the same world as Brahman.
This very one is the *uktha*, this is the *ṛc*, this is the *yajus*, this is the *sāman*, this is the *udgītha*, this is the *brahman*; "this is indeed all this"—thus should he be meditated upon.
JB 3.380 |v1 This very thing was the intermediate space in the beginning; |v2 and even now it is indeed that same thing.
This is that canopy which pervades these worlds;
therefore it has two names.
It desired: "May I exist, may I be procreated, may I attain abundance."
He performed that austerity. While he was performing that austerity, it shone forth.
"Truly, this has shone forth," [he thought].
This became lightning;
this is the flame, this is the light. Having become lightning, it heated itself.
From that, the thunderbolt was born.
Therefore, when it lightens, then it thunders. Having become the thunderbolt, it heated itself.
Then rain was produced.
Therefore, when it thunders, then it rains. This [universe] was then the waters, a vast expanse of water.
Now, as for what they say here: "In the beginning, this was indeed the waters, a great ocean"—these are those very waters. Having become the waters, it heated itself;
from that, food was born.
Having become food, it heated itself. From that, the person consisting of food was born, the progenitor of creatures.
He, within those waters, uttered: "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ."
These very worlds came into being.
Then the quarters were created after them.
Now, because he uttered the words "karat janat vṛdhat," these very worlds came into being.
Then the seasons were created after him. He said, "Truly, these have come into being for me. They became the months.
Then the seasons were created after him. He said, "Truly, these have become mine. They became the months.
"Or in prosperities"—these became the half-months. "I have prospered; I have burned up"—that which was "I" became those days;
that which was "I have prospered" became those nights; and that which was "I have burned up" became the dawns.
The speech which he uttered while being born became the threefold deity.
Whatever deity this one uttered while being born at the beginning, that indeed became the Brahman. He reflected: "I have created this triple Veda; come now, let me create from it."
With the *trivṛt* stoma he bellowed toward the *gāyatrī*.
From that, he emitted the Vasus, having Agni as their head.
With the fifteenfold hymn-form (*stoma*), he roared toward the *triṣṭubh* meter;
from that, he created the Rudras, headed by Indra.
With the seventeenfold hymn-form, he roared toward the *jagatī* meter.
Then he created the Ādityas, headed by Varuṇa.
With the twenty-one-fold Stoma, he roared toward the Anuṣṭubh.
Then he created the Viśvedevas, headed by Viṣṇu.
With the twenty-sevenfold hymn-form (*stoma*), he bellowed toward the *paṅkti* meter.
From that, he created the Maruts, headed by Īśāna. With the thirty-threefold hymn-form, he bellowed toward the *aticchandas* meter.
Then he created the Sādhyas and the Āptyas, who have Savitṛ as their head;
with the twenty-five-fold hymn (stoma), he roared toward the Bṛhatī;
then he created the Gandharvas, who have Mitra as their head.
He cried out toward Virāj.
From that, he created the Apsarases with Tvaṣṭṛ at their head.
He cried out toward Kakubh.
Then he created the serpents with Aṅgiras at their head;
he cried out to the Uṣṇih;
then he created the Aṅgirases with Atharvan at their head.
He cried out to the *akṣarapaṅkti* meter;
from it, he created the Asuras with black faces.
He cried out to the *viṣṭārapaṅkti* meter.
Then he created the Pitṛs, headed by Yama;
he cried out for the sake of bipeds.
Then he created human beings, headed by Death.
He cried out to Ekapadā.
Then he created birds, which were indeed the very mouths of Death.
Amitacchandas cried out.
Then he created the animals, headed by Dhātṛ.
Having created all this, he ascended upwards;
he went to where they now perceive him above.
In this eastern direction, the Vasus, with Agni at their head, sought him;
they found him in that which is the form of the flame.
Those very ones worship that of his.
The Rudras, with Indra at their head, sought him in this southern direction;
they found it—that which is the form of Āditya.
Those very [beings] worship that of his.
The Ādityas, with Varuṇa at their head, sought him in this western direction;
they found it, which is the form of the moon.
Those very [beings] worship that of his.
The All-gods, with Viṣṇu at their head, sought him in this northern direction;
they found it—that which is the form of lightning.
Those very ones worship that [form] of his.
The Maruts, headed by Īśāna, sought him in this upward direction;
they found him in that which was his white form.
Those very [beings] worship him as such.
In that other world, the Sādhyas and Āptyas, with Savitṛ at their head, sought him out.
They found him: that which is his black form.
They venerated him as that very [entity].
The Gandharvas, with Mitra at their head, sought him in this very intermediate region;
they found it—that which is the form of honey.
Those very [beings] worship him as such.
The Aṅgirases, with Atharvan at their head, sought him;
they found him in that which is the form of clarified butter.
Those [gods] worshiped that very [essence] of his.
The Asuras, with blackened faces, sought after him;
they found that which was the form of *surā*.
They worship that very thing of his.
Therefore they have perished;
for they worship him in his most evil form.
The ancestors, headed by Yama, sought him in the world of the fathers.
They found that which was the form of the milk-rice;
that very thing they worship for him.

In the beginning, this very form of food was indeed rice cooked with milk. This [world] which humans now enjoy is a transformation of that. Birds sought after it, for they are truly the mouths of death.
They found them, saying, "The golden-winged bird.
That very thing they worship as his [the sun's] forms.
The animals sought him out, with Dhātṛ at their head.
They found it: "A black bull with golden horns and golden hooves.
They worship that very thing of his as such.
Indeed, they worship this very form of that deity as the Sātyayajña, namely, the one with golden horns.
"The black bull with golden hooves"—
he who knows this thus becomes a bull among his own people;
moreover, he is he who shines yonder.
He sought him in this upward direction;
he found him sitting there together with all these forms.
He bestowed all these forms upon him.
Thus, whatever beautiful form is born here, it is that very thing which he bestows that is born here.
When he uttered "Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ," these very three worlds came into being: Upodaka, Ṛtadhāman, and Aparājita.
Then, when he uttered "Karaḥ, Janaḥ, Vṛdhaḥ," these other worlds above the heavens came into being.
From of old, shining upon the firmament, even so the seventh world is the world of Brahman, in which this Truth shines.
This deity, having become Truth, entered into it.
That is indeed Being; the vital breaths are Truth, and all creatures are Truth.
By that truth of his, all this is held together. Whether he speaks the truth or not, what he utters becomes nothing but truth.
Furthermore, he should know: "I speak only the truth, not falsehood; the world of one who speaks the truth is my world."
Thus it is said.
That very world indeed becomes his.
Just as we here investigate, saying, "This is Brahman, this is Brahman," even so is this [investigation].
The deity questions this one who knows; yet even he does not know that. (v14) "The month has entered the deity"—only he who knows that truly knows it.
(v15) "That deity has entered this."
Indeed, for one who knows thus, there is nothing whatsoever that remains unknown, nor is there any deity whatsoever [that remains unknown].
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"He is beyond the further shore, further than the further, even beyond the third or the fourth."
"In the thousand-pillared, firm, and formidable pavilion where the God of gods resides.
Thus [it is said]. He who shines yonder is indeed that God of gods.
His is this thousand-pillared, firm, and formidable pavilion, which is the year, the seasons, and the months.
The half-months are the days and nights; they are the dawns.
He who knows this entire twelve-day rite as being thus fully realized within the self—for him all desires are fully realized.

In the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), indeed, all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, all the meters (*chandāṃsi*), all the pressings (*savanāni*), all the sacrificial animals (*paśavaḥ*), all the gods, all the worlds, and all desires are contained; they are distributed throughout the twelve-day rite, they find satisfaction in the twelve-day rite, and they are perfected in the twelve-day rite.
They are established at twelve days.
Regarding this, they say: "Since these are only ten days, why then is it called the *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day rite)?
He should reply: "Because these [ten] result in twelve *agniṣṭoma*s."
Regarding this they say: "Since the year consists of thirteen months and the year itself is the fourteenth, by what means do they obtain both the thirteenth month and the fourteenth year?"
"One should say, 'By means of two Atirātras.
By the introductory Atirātra they attain the thirteenth month, and by the concluding [Atirātra] the fourteenth, the year."
Regarding this they say: "Only he would truly know the twelve-day rite today, or he might think 'I know it,' who would know it as established in all the worlds.
The days of the twelve-day rite are indeed the months; they are the worlds, and they are the worlds of the gods.
The month of Phālguna is indeed the first day of the twelve-day rite; Caitra is the second, Vaiśākha the third, the full moon of Āṣāḍha the fourth, Śroṇā and Śraviṣṭhā the fifth,
Śatabhiṣaj the sixth, Proṣṭhapada the seventh, Āśvayuja the eighth, Kārtika the ninth, and Mārgaśīrṣa [the tenth].
The tenth is Taiṣa, the eleventh is Māgha, the twelfth is Phālguna; the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra is the thirteenth month, and the Udayanīya is the fourteenth, the year.
This very twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha) is established in all the worlds.
He who thus knows this twelve-day rite as established in all the worlds becomes established in all the worlds.
This twelve-day rite is indeed he who shines yonder; he is Indra, he is Prajāpati, he is indeed all this.
Thus it should be venerated:
"This very one is all this"—thus it should be venerated.
